title: Arms and Artefacts
text: Arms and Artefacts The objects of the Obligatory Quest: swords above fireplaces, hats required by forms, benches in eleven pieces, and one crate, stencilled on all six faces, which you should not have opened. The descriptions are mine. The column headed Provenance is Nix's, from her ledger, by her leave, and in her words, and she has asked me to say that where an object never passed through the back room she has entered it anyway, for completeness, and marked it so. Where she says the party of the second part she means the client, and the client has been identified, and it does not make any difference to the paperwork. For her, see Nix . - H.B. Arms Object What it is Provenance (N.) The Village Sword The sword over the fireplace in Bram Thistle's house, which came off the wall when he was chosen with a sound that can only be described as smug. It had waited, Thistlewick says, a century. There is a clean rectangle of wall where it used to be. Not located. Taken down, by the owner, off his own wall. Entered for completeness. * The Sword of Ultimate Ending * A sword in a window at Penultima, behind a rope, at 9,999,999 crowns. Not located. Not on any list. Some things are better in a window. The Star-Iron Sword One sword, out of the Sky Anvil , by Hob Grumnir. Takes the light like frost on a window. He has not said who it is for. One stone, sky. Traded, not located. Held overnight. Returned. Beatrice Hob Grumnir's hammer, which he did not make. Disqualified at the Assize of Hammers under clause one, and right about everything. Not located. Not entered. She would know. The Drawn Sword Out of a stone under Carn Drey, in an afternoon, with help. Roland Fairweather wears it. It has had one afternoon, and would like another. Drawn, not located. From a stone, by R. Fairweather, with help. Witnessed. Papers Object What it is Provenance (N.) The Prophecy The Forty-Eighth's copy of the Prophecy of Thistlewick, in triplicate. Clause twelve has been underlined by somebody worried. Issued, free, regrettably. From the Committee, by the hand of the Elder. A Character Reference Elder Wispel confirms that Bram Thistle is the Chosen One, is of good character, and grows a decent turnip. The last part is underlined. It is framed in the Guild at Nether Sopping. Written on request. Committee stationery. Not returned; framed. The Elder has been told. Form A-1 Mislaid for eleven years. Under the mat, six feet from the man looking for it. Located, under a mat, by the Forty-Eighth, not by me, and I would like that noted. The Guild Card Provisional, until the Stair; now not. The first the Guild has issued in forty years. Issued, Nether Sopping. Exchanged on Form Z for one without. A Receipt Proof of purchase for one Dark Lord, renewable, signed in a hand that has been at this a while. Bram has it. Given, at the top, to B. Thistle. Not my ledger. Entered, because it is the only receipt in this volume for anything that size. Certificate of Fitness Bram, certified fit to travel under clause eleven: scales, a good light, a clean surface and a witness. Does nothing. Enormously official. Issued by Sister Merribell. The scales were lent by the fish stall, and went back, smelling of haddock. Certificate of Completion For walking, talking, opening and hitting. The first the Guild of Guides has issued. It goes in the accessory slot. Issued, Firstfield. Kept in a cupboard, with a stick. A Key, Labelled On a Committee label: CLAUSE NINETEEN. NETHER SOPPING. AT SUCH DISTANCE AS IS MUTUALLY AGREEABLE. It opens Ambrose Fitch's cottage. Posted, through a door, the morning after. From the Committee. Not located; delivered, which is a different column. Footnote Hosea Bellwether has written you into the history. Small type, bottom of the page, but there. Issued by H. Bellwether. Small type. Entered in larger. Things for the road Object What it is Provenance (N.) A Hat Form A-1 requires a hat, and does not say which, so Mrs Barrow sells this one, for thirty. Bought. Mrs Barrow. Not related. A Stick It is dangerous to go alone. Old Hollis at Firstfield has given eleven thousand, two hundred and six. One came back. Given; returned; exchanged for a straighter one. The first is on a mantelpiece. A Bench (Flat-Packed) One bench, in eleven pieces, with a mallet and a diagram that is wrong. For the Forty-Fourth, who wanted somewhere to sit. Carried out to the Barrow, built, facing the sea. Not located: commissioned. Lamp Oil One gallon, for the Lighthouse of Saint Bother, sold by Mrs Barrow, who marks it up. Bought, at the mark-up. I would not have paid it. I was not asked. The Keeper's Lamp A small lamp off a large lighthouse. It is what the ones who come back walk home by. Given, at the light. Forty Bolts of Oilskin Forty. Mrs Barrow counted them twice, out loud, and made somebody count them again after her. Bought on account, Nether Sopping, for the Hoyle Works. Counted three times. The Lamp (Borrowed) Off the hook by the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost. Lent to the Forty-Eighth by Sir Dunstable, who had borrowed it. Back directly. Lent, by Sir D., who borrowed it. On loan. Not entered as returned. Not entered as anything else either. A Bag, Packed Spare Cotterill's. Packed two years before the Quest. Contents: yes. Not located. Packed, by its owner, at seven, and kept by the door. A Washer, Off Shim Shim Cotterill's second-best. Flat the whole time, which is why it is a good one. Worn on a bootlace. Given, by Shim, to Spare. A good washer. Not the bearing. Things given back Object What it is Provenance (N.) Previously Owned Goods Eleven things, labelled for their owners: a pie dish, a chair, a gate key, a pair of good boots, a cradle and six more, across three towns. Located, 1989 to 2000. RETURNED, eleven times, in the right column, with a ruler. Lorrimer's Tools Picks, a jemmy, a hood-pin and a list of things he meant to take. Left in a huff. Located. Returned, with a receipt, which he keeps. Gran's Coat Long, dark, well made and much mended. Eleven years in bond at Great Dunnage. It fits. First entry. No provenance for eleven years. Now: hers, by inheritance; bonded by N., aged fifteen; collected by N., on behalf of the party of the second part. The Feud Locket Two sisters, one portrait each, facing resolutely away. Thirty years of this. Given, at the end of a thirty-year correspondence, by both parties, facing away. The Forty-Fourth's Signet Grave goods, given rather than taken, which he was very particular about. Given. Not taken. He was particular, and so am I. The Table's Kit A candle-end, a coil of gut string, a splint and a very good sash, rolled up in canvas. It goes to the youngest. Not located. Not for locating. Ysolde's Kit Forty years of field medicine in one canvas roll. Lent for the road north. Lent. Returned. I have heard what she said about the state of it. The Governor A brass ball governor off Attempt Eighty-Four, which kept her from running away with herself. She never needed it. Given, not taken, two turns of a spanner, by the works. Number-Plate, 112 A brass oval off an airship, stamped HOYLE WORKS 112, out in the weather for a hundred years on a sea stack. Recovered, one turn of a spanner. On the bolts in the Long Field now. It fits. The crate Object What it is Provenance (N.) ITEM 1 A crate, heavier than it looks, stencilled ITEM 1 on all six faces. Entered in the stores book of the Hoyle Works in 1802, one off. Issued a hundred and ninety-nine times; returned a hundred and ninety-eight. Nobody in four generations has improved on its description, and I am not going to try. Not located. Carried, with permission, off a crag. Disposition: see the stores book, Upper Clanging, which is not open to the public. Not my ledger, and I would not want it in mine. I asked Nix whether there was anything in this volume she would have liked to locate and had not. She said the Sword of Ultimate Ending, for a moment, in 2000, and that the moment had passed. I asked her about the crate. She said that it was not on any list, and that it was not that sort of crate, and that she was not that sort of person. - H.B.

title: The Sky Anvil
text: The Sky Anvil For the smith, see Hob Grumnir . For the churchyard gate that taught him gates, see Thistlewick . For the sword, read on, and then stop where I stop. The Sky Anvil What it is A stone that fell out of the sky Fell 1749, into the top field, on a Tuesday Then A gatepost, for two hundred and fifty years Gates outlasted Eleven Shrine Built round the foot of it by pilgrims, 1750 Owner Elias Meech , farmer, of the top field Traded 2000, for a gate Made into Exactly one thing For He has not said The Sky Anvil is a round grey stone which fell out of the sky in 1749 into the top field of a farm in the snowy north, and was set up by the farmer as a gatepost, because it was there, and was a very good gatepost for two hundred and fifty years. Pilgrims built a shrine round the foot of it and come up every summer to look at it. In the year 2000 it was traded for a gate. It is now a sword. The gatepost The stone came down out of the sky into the Meeches' top field in 1749, on a Tuesday. Elias Meech's great-great-grandfather set it up for a gatepost, because it was there, and it was the best gatepost in the county. It outlasted eleven gates. Mr Meech never threw a gate out: all eleven were in the hedge-bottom along the top field, where each was put when it went, rusting quietly in order. In 1750 the pilgrims came. They call it the Sky Anvil, and they built a little stone shrine round the foot of it, so that the stone sat in the top of the shrine like an egg in an egg cup, and they came up every summer to look at it. Mr Meech did not mind. It kept the frost off. He would not sell it. It was not for sale. It was a very good gatepost. He would take a gate for it, mind; the last one had gone at Michaelmas, and he was between gates. Asked what he would hang a gate on, then, he said the shrine, which was a very good shrine. The trade In the year 2000 Hob Grumnir came up the road with the Forty-Eighth's company, and stopped at the shrine, and put his hand flat on the grey stone in the top of it, the way you would put it on a horse. He had lately become quite good at gates, having mended the churchyard gate at home, and he had in his pocket the spring that had been in his pocket since the churchyard. He had the eleven gates out of the hedge-bottom, one after another, and sorted them on the snow into what would do and what would not, and worked the afternoon through, cold, with what he carried in his pack, and made a gate out of eleven gates, true on its hangings. Then he fitted the spring to the latch. Mr Meech hung it on the shrine himself. It swung to, and the latch dropped, and stayed. Then Hob lifted the Sky Anvil out of the top of the shrine like an egg out of an egg cup, and put it under one arm. It is very heavy. He did not mention this. The sword Star-iron makes exactly one thing. Hob knew it would. He put it in the fire at his own forge in Thistlewick and said nothing for a long time, which for Hob is about a minute, and made a sword: plain, long in the blade, that takes the light like frost on a window. Hob cannot use a sword. Everybody in the smithy knew it, and nobody said so. Asked who it was for, he said nobody; it was a sword, and swords are for whoever. Then he listened to the hammer at his belt for a while, and said that she says a sword is no use on its own, and that it was not on its own. He wrapped it in sacking and put it in the Forty-Eighth's pack, and did not look at anybody, and went to see about the fire. He has not said who it is for. I have a theory, and I have been asked not to print it, by Hob, and by Beatrice, through Hob, and by two other people who have the same theory. I am not printing it. Afterwards The shrine has a gate on it now, and nothing in the top. The pilgrims still come up every summer, and open the gate and shut it all afternoon, because nobody had ever given them anything to open before. Mr Meech says that it is the best gate in the county, and leans on it. Nix 's ledger has the star-iron in it, because it went through the back room on its way to the forge, overnight, wrapped in a sack. The entry reads: One stone, sky. Traded, not located. From E. Meech, for a gate, fair. Held overnight for H. Grumnir. Returned. She showed me the word RETURNED, and pointed out that it is in the right column. - H.B. See also Hob Grumnir Arms and Artefacts The Worshipful Company of Smiths , who would want to know whose work, from the ore up

title: The Sword of Ultimate Ending
text: The Sword of Ultimate Ending For the shop, the town and Mr and Mrs Markup , see Penultima . For a sword you can actually have, see the catalogue , which has several. The Sword of Ultimate Ending What it is A sword, and a shield, in a window Where Ye Final Shoppe, Penultima Behind A velvet rope Price 9,999,999 crowns Priced 1969, by Gideon Markup Polished Every morning, after the tea Held, by a customer Never Sold Never Provenance See below. Briefly The Sword of Ultimate Ending is a sword, with a shield, mounted in the window of Ye Final Shoppe at Penultima , the last town before the Obligatory Tower , behind a velvet rope, with a card beside it. It has been in the window since 1969. Every Chosen One of living memory has seen it. None of them has held it. The card THE SWORD OF ULTIMATE ENDING. 9,999,999 CROWNS. Gideon Markup wrote the card in 1969, and has not changed it. He set the price, he has told me, at one crown more than a purse will hold, so that it should be beyond the reach of anybody who has ever walked up the road. I have since asked a banker in Nether Sopping how much a purse will hold, and he says that a purse will hold a great deal more than that, if it is a good purse, and the owner is careful. I have not told Mr Markup. He has not checked, in thirty-three years, and he is not going to, and I am not going to be the one. The sword I have looked at it through the glass. It is a sword. It is long and bright and very well kept, with a plain cross-guard and a grip wrapped in something dark, and the shield beside it is round and has nothing on it. It may be a very great sword. It may be an ordinary one, polished every morning for thirty-three years, which comes to much the same thing in a window. Nothing about it is engraved, that I could see, and nothing about it is said, by anybody, except the card. Of where it came from, Mr Markup will say only that it came with the shop. I asked Mrs Markup, who keeps the ledger. She said that he is in the window again, and that he is always in the window. Would sir like to hold it? Mr Markup asks everybody who comes in whether they would like to hold the Sword of Ultimate Ending. Everybody would. He then tells them, warmly, that sir cannot afford to hold it. He said it to the Forty-Eighth. He has said it to everyone who has ever come through that door, and he is not going to stop now. It is not unkind. I have watched him do it, on the occasion of my visit. He said it to me as well. I did not ask to hold it; I was asked. It is the most sincerely meant refusal I have had in the course of writing this volume, and I have written to the Collegium Arcanum . Afterwards The sword is still in the window. Penultima does a trade, since 2000, in people walking up the road to see Grimspite 's chair, and most of them stop at the Final Shoppe on the way, and look at the sword, and are asked whether they would like to hold it, and are told. Mr Markup says that it has never been better for business, and that he has had to have the rope re-velveted. He brings Mrs Markup her tea every morning, and then he does the window. In thirty-three years he has never once had to be asked. I asked Nix , for the provenance column of this volume, whether she had ever considered the Sword of Ultimate Ending. She said that she had looked at it, in 2000, for some time, and that it was not on any list, and that some things are better in a window. Then she said that the price was wrong, and that she had not told him either. - H.B. See also Penultima Arms and Artefacts A Glossary of Cliches , for the last shop before the end

title: Bramus agricola
text: Bramus agricola Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary. For the man it is named after, see Bram Thistle . For the field, see Thistlewick . The Forty-Eighth has read this entry, and asked me to say that he does not mind it, and went pink. - H.B. Bramus agricola (Halloway) What it is A small brown burrowing animal of turnip fields Described 2000, by W. Halloway Type locality The Thistle turnip field, Thistlewick, one row in Named for Bram Thistle , Chosen One #48 Diet Turnip Predators Everything Consequence None whatsoever Survival Statistically indefensible Distinguishing features None. Goes pink when it is looked at Bramus agricola (Halloway, 2000). A small brown burrowing animal of turnip fields. New to science in the year 2000, although not new to the field, which has always had them. What it is. A small brown animal, which lives in a burrow in the turnip rows, with a neat round entrance and a rim of turned earth. Nobody has ever described one. Nobody had ever looked. They are all over the field. I am not able, yet, to place it in a family; it is brown, and it is small, and it lives in turnips, and every one of those is true of several families. I have described what I saw, and named it, and the rest is for volume two. What it is called. Bramus agricola, after the Forty-Eighth, in whose field it was found. There are no synonyms. Nobody else ever named it, because nobody else ever noticed it, which is the first thing it has in common with its namesake and not the last. In Thistlewick it is called "one of them things", which is not a name. Where. Turnip fields about Thistlewick; the type locality is the Thistle field, one row in from the lane, where a labelled stick marks the burrow: BRAMUS AGRICOLA (HALLOWAY). DO NOT PLOUGH. IT WILL NOT HELP. Description. Small. Brown. Distinguishing features: none. Goes pink when it is looked at. Diet. Turnip. Predators. Everything. Behaviour. Of no consequence whatsoever, except in one attribute, which is that it survives things it has no business surviving. By luck. Repeatedly. I observed the type specimen for something under a minute. In that time it came out of its burrow, looked at nothing in particular, and walked directly into the path of a wheelbarrow. The barrow went over it. It came out of the other side of the barrow a little flatter, shook itself, and carried on. A crow dropped on it from a height, missed, hit the barrel, and left with a great deal of dignity. The animal did not notice either event. I have called this, in print, statistically indefensible, and I stand by it. Method. None was needed. It was not fought, because it did not know that it was in anything, and it was not measured, because it would not keep still, and it was not collected, because I did not have the heart, and because it would have got away, by luck. It was observed, and described, and named, and left in its burrow. I am aware that this departs from my own practice for a type specimen. The holotype is the one in the burrow. It is still there. Etymology. Bramus, for Bram Thistle of Thistlewick, Chosen One #48, a turnip farmer, who was chosen while he was asleep and therefore unable to object, and walked north, and walked into very nearly everything, and came home. Agricola, a farmer. I named it after him because the description fitted, and I told him so, and why, and watched him think about the Gloamwood and the Tower and everything since the vote, and how much of it he had walked away from, and why. He went pink. Then he said nothing at all for some time, and had to sit down on a turnip. I wrote that down under his name. He would have liked to discuss which name, and could not find a way to begin. I want it understood that it is not a joke. Nobody had ever described him accurately before. It is an accurate description. Remarks. The Prophecy does not read journals. It has, I am told, read this one; its own account of the Quest mentions the animal by name, and spells it correctly. The stick is still there, and the hole, and I am told by the Forty-Eighth that the animal is too, or one very like it, and that he ploughs round it. I asked him whether he had ever seen it hurt. He said no. I asked whether he thought that was luck. He said that he was not the person to ask. - H.B. See also Bram Thistle Wren Halloway The Turnip , its habitat The Bestiary

title: Bestiary
text: Bestiary Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer The creatures of the road, as reported by the people they were rude to. I have not met any of them myself and do not intend to. For the classification I commissioned Wren Halloway, who has met them, and who will tell you what they are whether you have asked or not. What follows is hers, every page of it, and I have not altered one word, because she would know. For her life, see Wren Halloway . - H.B. Preface This is a bestiary of the country between Nether Sopping and the Obligatory Tower, and from Upper Clanging to the bottom of the Stair under Hithermost, as it was in the year 2000, written up in the winter of 2001 and corrected in January 2002. Everybody else names monsters after how they died. I name them after what they are. It is the same job done properly. Every entry here is filed under what the animal is, and gives after it what people call it, and the people are generally adventurers, and the names are generally the circumstances. The Crow of Foreshadowing is a crow. The Thing at the Bottom is a badger. The Slain Wyvern is a goose. I have not been rude to anybody's name. I have only moved it from the heading to the line underneath, which is where a name for how something died belongs. Where Doctor Amias Rowbotham, FRS, has named an animal, his name is given as a synonym, and is not to be used. He named some three hundred species after himself, his subscribers, his wife and his dogs, and never had a type specimen for one of them. The eleven I have replaced are in The Fauna of the Valley . The other two hundred and eighty-nine are for volume two. Nobody may say, anywhere in this Bestiary, that anything in it is basically a dragon. Nothing in it is basically a dragon. I have drafted a clause. Method A cataloguer does not hunt animals. She documents them. A fight is a step in the methodology which I resent, because you cannot measure a wing that is actively in use, but it is sometimes the only step that will get an animal to hold still, and so where there was a fight each entry has a line, Method, saying what it was. I have done what I could at range. I take armour off things, because the armour is not the animal. I collect two of whatever an animal drops, because one is an anecdote. A type specimen is measured, not killed. Every type specimen in this Bestiary was let go afterwards. Every one of them minded being measured more than it would have minded being fought. I describe only what I have seen, or what has been described to me by a witness I would trust with a ruler. Where I have not seen a thing, I say so, and list it, and do not describe it. The plates are mine, not Miss Halloway's. They were drawn for me from the accounts of the adventurers who met these animals, which is to say as each one looked while somebody was hitting it, and one or two by people who had plainly never seen a crab. Miss Halloway agreed to them on two conditions: that every caption gives what the thing is called, and not what it is, that being where a name for how something died belongs; and that wherever a plate is wrong, the caption says so. Several captions say so. - H.B. The catalogue Filed under Also called Where Entry Badger, Meles meles The Thing at the Bottom The Bottomless Pit The Coast Bat The Tower Bat The Tower; the Pit The Road North Bramus agricola One of them things The Thistle turnip field Bramus agricola Carrion crow, Corvus corone The Crow of Foreshadowing Fields; the road The Road North Chest mimic The Chest (Definitely A Chest) The Gloamwood The Road North Crested grass snake, nine of The Thing in the Woods The Gloamwood, the deep clearing The Road North Goose, greylag, Anser anser The Wyvern; the Slain Wyvern Over a mantel, Nether Sopping The Goose Herring gull The Gull With Ambitions The coast; the Pit The Coast Hound The Barrow Hound; Budge The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth The Coast Oak The Grumblewood Treant The Gloamwood The Road North Shore crab The Territorial Crab The coast road; a well The Coast Shore crab, very large The Crab of Unusual Size The west beach, until 2000 The Coast Turnip, Brassica rapa The Militant Turnip The fields about Thistlewick The Road North Weasel The Draught The Stair The North, and Below Worm The Worm of Carn Drey Under Carn Drey The North, and Below Unscheduled Something Unscheduled The bottom of the Stair The North, and Below The eleven type specimens Rowbotham's names The valley The Fauna of the Valley Not animals Listed because they are fought, and people will look for them; not described as animals, because they are not. The marsh light (the Wisp of Mild Concern), masonry (the Load-Bearing Gargoyle), an urn (Lost Property), a suit of armour (Grave Goods, Animated), the Hoyle Works' attempts and steam (Loose Pressure; Attempt, Unnumbered; Ambulant Salvage; Attempt Eighty-Four), a chapel's damp, the small hours, a small temptation and a light going away, and the Stair's dark and echo. Each is on the page for where it is met. THE PROPHECY. A document. Not fauna. It fought, at the top of the Obligatory Tower, when clause twelve enforced itself. So does a great deal of paperwork. See The Prophecy of Thistlewick , in another hand. Persons The following appear in adventurers' accounts as monsters, and are persons. I do not catalogue persons, because a person is described by a biographer, not a cataloguer, and because they read it. A goblin, who had a list of grievances and read from it. A bandit in the fourth week of a six-week apprenticeship, and the bandit chief who runs it, Meredith Crooke , who has a syllabus. A skeleton, interning. The previous occupant of a barrow. A warden of a half-way landing. A man contracted to lose at Firstfield. A mother at Upper Clanging, who was right. Three entrants at the Bell, and the regulars at the back table. The Forty-Fourth. Grimspite. For all of them, see the People volume, or nobody; most would prefer nobody. Not seen Something in the sand, off the west beach at Nether Sopping. Something in the crack, in the north wall of the Bottomless Pit, which is asleep, and gravid, and I know what it is, and I am not saying. Somebody coming up, on the Stair, whom nobody could see. I do not catalogue what I could not see, and I do not guess who. Withdrawn One entry, on a subject living near Fairholme, was withdrawn at the request of the subject, over a hand of whist. A cataloguer honours a withdrawal. I will say only that the subject was very gracious about it, and that I lost the hand. I asked Miss Halloway how many entries there would be in volume two. She said about three hundred, and that two hundred and eighty-nine of them were somebody's dog. - H.B.

title: The Coast and Under It
text: The Coast and Under It Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary: the animals of the south coast about Nether Sopping, the Bottomless Pit and the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth. For the places, see Nether Sopping , The Bottomless Pit and The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth . The goose has an entry of its own: The Goose . - H.B. The south is better documented than the north, because Nether Sopping is full of people who came back and have told everybody what they met. It is not better described. The shore Shore crab The Territorial Crab, from an account. It is green. The adventurer had red. What it is. The common shore crab. Green, broad, sideways. Called. The Territorial Crab. Where. The shingle of the coast road and the west beach; one in the well in Nether Sopping, which looks up. Description. The beach is its beach. It has held its position, without documentation, since before the village. Remarks. Nether Sopping's rule two is that the crab on the west beach is nobody's fault and is not to be provoked. It is a good rule for any crab. Shore crab (very large) The Crab of Unusual Size, by the same adventurer, who had run out of red. What it is. A shore crab, the same species as the above. Very large. The size of a garden shed. Called. The Crab of Unusual Size. Everybody in Nether Sopping wishes it recorded that they said unusual, and not large. Where. The west beach, until 2000. Description. It is not unusual. It is large. Crabs go on growing for as long as they go on living, and this one had gone on living for longer than the town, and had not been interfered with. That is the whole of it. Method. Engaged on the Guild's bounty, which wanted a witness, and got one. Underneath it, in the shingle, were eleven years of other people's bad afternoons. Remarks. Four smaller crabs hold the beach now, between them, badly. They are the same species. They will be large in time, if nobody minds them. Herring gull The Gull With Ambitions, as an adventurer drew it. Miss Halloway asks me to say that it is a gull. What it is. The herring gull. Called. The Gull With Ambitions. Where. The coast road, the beach, and the mouth of the Bottomless Pit, which it has worked out. Description. Has worked out that adventurers carry food and that adventurers are, as a class, slow. Both observations are correct. Not described: something in the sand Something in the sand, drawn by somebody who was standing on it at the time. Not described. What it is. I do not know. I have not seen it. Nether Sopping does not swim off the west beach and has never written down why, and I have not swum off it either. I have measured the hole it leaves. The hole is a good size. I am not entering an animal on the strength of a hole, and I would ask everybody else not to. The Bottomless Pit The Pit is a hole in a hillside, four feet deep, with a turnstile. It is called bottomless as a courtesy. Badger The Thing at the Bottom. A badger. What it is. The badger, Meles meles. Very large. Called. The Thing At The Bottom. Where. The far end of the Pit, until 2000; then up a slope nobody knew was there. Description. The size of a hay cart. It had been eating two centuries of lost property, which cannot have helped. It was asleep on a mattress of everything Nether Sopping had ever failed to come back for, and it opened one eye and had a strong opinion. Method. The Forty-Eighth's company came and saw the badger, which is what the custodian had been asking the Guild to do for forty years. The Guild had told him that a badger was not a monster. The Guild was correct. It was a badger. It left, at speed, and took one boot with it, and had earned the boot. Urn Lost Property. Unclaimed. What it is. An urn. Not an animal. Called. Lost Property. Remarks. Two hundred years at the bottom of a pit will do this to anything, apparently, including an urn. I do not know why it moves. Neither, so far as I could tell, does it. Not described: something in the crack What it is. It is asleep in a crack in the north wall of the Pit, running back further than a lamp reaches. It is not small, and it has not noticed anybody. It is gravid. Remarks. I was asked, by the Forty-Eighth, whether that was bad. It is the single most normal thing in the cave. I know what it is, and I am not going to wake it to tell you. It is still asleep. It is still enormous. Everything about it is entirely normal, and it is entitled to be left alone, and I would ask visitors to the Pit to pay their two crowns, go down the four feet, and not shine a lamp into the crack. The Barrow Hound The Barrow Hound, on duty. What it is. A dog. A large one. Called. The Barrow Hound. Where. The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth, the passage, and an alcove off it with a dish, a collar and a name: BUDGE. Description. Buried with him, which nobody asked the hound about. Remarks. Something still uses the alcove. On a mossy pillar near it, at the height of a big dog's shoulder, the moss has been worn smooth by something leaning there, every day, very contentedly, for a very long time. I have not catalogued what. I have catalogued the moss. I am not a sentimental woman, and I left the dish where it was. Not animals Grave goods (animated). A full suit of armour, buried with a man who would have preferred the money. Not an animal. The previous occupant. Was in the mound first, and has views about the extension. A person, and long dead, and entitled to the views. Not catalogued. Grave goods (animated) The previous occupant, with views See also The Bestiary The Goose Nether Sopping The Bottomless Pit The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth The North, and Below

title: The Fauna of the Valley
text: The Fauna of the Valley Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary: the eleven type specimens of her monograph, The Fauna of the Valley, by What They Are , shelved at the Collegium Arcanum , abridged by her for this volume. I asked whether the abridgement lost anything. She said that it lost the footnotes, and that there had been exactly enough. - H.B. The Fauna of the Valley, by What They Are Author W. Halloway Published 2000, by the Collegium Arcanum Bound by Sub-Librarian Prewitt, by hand Type specimens Eleven. Measured, not killed Reviewers Professor Mott; Dr Furze; the Honorary Fellow Subscribers Bound in at the back Supersedes Rowbotham, in eleven places Page four hundred Goose Preface to the abridgement The previous authority on the animals of this valley is Doctor Amias Rowbotham, FRS, who in forty years named some three hundred species after himself, his subscribers, his wife and his dogs, and never had a type specimen for one of them. A type specimen is the individual animal that a name belongs to. Without one, a name is a name for whatever the namer was thinking of at dinner. That is the whole of my objection to Rowbotham, and I would like it understood that it is not personal. He named a beetle after one of his own students. The student is now Professor Mott, and reviewed this monograph, and has asked me to say that he is a person now, and not a beetle, and that you would be surprised what a difference it makes. A monograph of the Collegium requires a type specimen for every entry, three Fellows to review it, and a list of subscribers. I took eleven type specimens, one for each entry, in eleven fights that I objected to and conducted anyway. Every specimen was measured, not killed. Every one minded being measured a great deal more than it would have minded being fought. Every one was let go. Each entry gives the animal under what it is, and then Rowbotham's name for it, which is a synonym, and is not to be used. The eleven Common hedge egg Rowbotham's Breakfast. Not where it was drawn. What it is. An egg. It has legs. It lives in hedges. Synonym. Rowbotham's Breakfast. It is not a breakfast, whatever he says. Behaviour. It is not where you measured it. This is the whole of its defence and it is a good one: by the time a measurement is written down the egg is a foot to the left of it. I measured it eleven times and took the mean. Frilled wall lizard The frill, up. What it is. A lizard with a frill, which lives on walls. Synonym. Rowbotham's Magnificent. He said it was magnificent. It is a lizard. Behaviour. Does something sudden. The frill goes up, and then the observer's notebook goes up, and the observer has to start the page again. Hearth salamander Warm. What it is. A salamander which lives in hearths. It is warm. Synonym. Rowbotham's Comfort. It is not a comfort to anyone. Behaviour. Bites the note-taker. Not the person holding it; the person writing. I have the scar on my writing hand and I consider it a professional credential. Turnip gnome Of fixed opinions. What it is. A gnome that lives in turnips. Small, brown, bearded, and of fixed opinions. Not to be confused with * Bramus agricola *, which also lives in turnips, and has no opinions at all. Synonym. Mrs Rowbotham. He named it after his wife. She knew. Behaviour. Not where you measured it. Barn cait Somewhere else, a moment later. What it is. A cat. A large black cat of barns, with a white mark on the chest. Synonym. Biscuit, which was his dog. I have never forgiven him that. Behaviour. Bolts for cover, and is somewhere else. I measured it on the third attempt, in a hayloft, and it bit nobody, and looked at me the whole time. Striped warren hare Rowbotham's Tiger. It is a hare. What it is. A hare with stripes, which lives in warrens. Synonym. Rowbotham's Tiger. It has never once been a tiger. Behaviour. Bolts for cover. Very fast. Upright fox Upright. What it is. A fox that walks upright. Otherwise a fox, in every particular. Synonym. Pelham-Rudd's Fox. A subscriber paid to have it named. I have not removed Mr Pelham-Rudd from the record. I have moved him from the name to the history, where he belongs, and where he paid to be. Behaviour. Does something sudden. Many-eyed grazer Checking. What it is. A large grazing animal with a great many eyes, of the high pastures of the north. White, horned, placid. Synonym. Rowbotham's Ox. It is not, in any sense, an ox. Behaviour. Grazes. Is not where you measured it, which in an animal of that size takes some doing. It watched me measure it with all of its eyes at once, and I have never been so thoroughly checked. Draught sylph With the doors open. What it is. A small sylph which lives in draughts. Synonym. Lady Amberley. Named for a subscriber, who had a cold. Behaviour. Bolts for cover. It is very difficult to measure a draught. I shut the doors. Tall marsh wader Rowbotham's Self-Portrait. It does look like him. What it is. A tall wading bird of the marshes, long in the leg and the beak, solemn, grey, with a crest. Synonym. Rowbotham's Self-Portrait. It does look like him. Behaviour. Bites the note-taker. Pond kappa The dish, level. What it is. A kappa, in a lake. Green, with a dish of water in the top of its head, which it keeps level. Synonym. Captain. Captain was a spaniel. His other dog. Behaviour. Bites the note-taker. Reviews The rules require three Fellows. Two were Rowbotham's own students, who reviewed my first paper when I was twenty-three. Professor Mott said then that it lacked respect, and it did. He read the monograph for a long time, and stopped at the eleventh type specimen, and took his spectacles off, and said that Rowbotham named things after whoever was at dinner, and that he should like, before he died, to be a person. Accepted. Dr Furze said, at twenty-three, too many footnotes. There were exactly enough footnotes. He turned the pages without hurrying, and stopped at page four hundred, and read one word several times, and said that he had been in the Slain Wyvern the night they asked me to leave, and had always known. Accepted, with no corrections, which he had never written before. The third Fellow was the Honorary Fellow. It lives on a pond. Its review is a footprint on the title page, in the right place. I asked Miss Halloway whether she had enjoyed the eleven fights. She said no. I asked whether she would do it again. She said that volume two will need more than eleven. - H.B. See also The Bestiary The Goose , page four hundred Wren Halloway The Collegium Arcanum Fenmarch Hall , for the other kind of collection

title: The Goose
text: The Goose Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary. For the tavern, see The Slain Wyvern . For the man who made the wyvern, see Halloran Vance . I asked Miss Halloway whether this entry might be filed under W, as it is generally known. She said that it is filed under what it is. - H.B. The Goose What it is A greylag goose, Anser anser Sex Female Age Adult, at death Of A farm on the coast near Nether Sopping Called The Wyvern; the Slain Wyvern; ONE WYVERN (SLAIN) Additions Two bats' wings; wire; varnish; a jaw, opened Mounted 1940, over the fireplace Plaques Two Specimen status Not a type. Not required. It is a goose What it is. A greylag goose, Anser anser, adult, female, of a farm on the coast near Nether Sopping. The commonest grey goose of the region. It has a goose's bill, a goose's neck, a goose's feet and a goose's posture, which is the posture of a bird that has decided to be offended in advance. What it is called. The Wyvern. The Slain Wyvern. ONE WYVERN (SLAIN), on the board outside the tavern, with (GOOSE) scratched off underneath and painted on again. These are not synonyms. A synonym is another name for the same animal. These are the name of a different animal applied to this one, and the different animal does not occur on this coast and never has. I list them because readers will look for them. Where it is. Over the fireplace of the Slain Wyvern, Nether Sopping, wings out, jaws open, since 1940. Description. About the size of a large goose. Two bats' wings have been wired on at the shoulder, over the goose's own, which are folded underneath and visible from the left side of the bar if you stoop. The bill has been opened and set, and teeth added, carved, I think from bone, and very well; I would like to know whose. The whole is varnished, which has preserved it. The plumage under the varnish is in good condition. The feet are a goose's feet and nobody has done anything about them, because there is nothing you can do about a goose's feet. How it came to be there. In 1940 Halloran Vance, Chosen One #41, came back to Nether Sopping from the marshes with nothing, and the town was waiting on the quay for a monster. He went to a farm, and came back two days later with this. I have the account from Mrs Thrupp, who keeps the Wyvern, and from the second plaque, which says so, and I have no reason to doubt either. He did not smile about it once. The first plaque. Under the goose: SLAIN BY H. VANCE, CHOSEN ONE #41, IN THE MARSHES, AFTER A LONG STRUGGLE. I have been asked to comment on this plaque and I decline. It is not a description. It is a memorial, and a memorial is not wrong in the way a description is wrong. I did not understand that when I first said what the bird was, out loud, in Mrs Thrupp's house, and I was asked to leave, and I would like it on record that I was right about the goose and she was right to ask. The second plaque. Beside the first: A GREYLAG GOOSE, ANSER ANSER, OF A FARM ON THIS COAST. MADE INTO A WYVERN IN 1940, IN TWO DAYS, WITH WIRE, BY H. VANCE, CHOSEN ONE #41, BECAUSE THE VILLAGE WAS WAITING ON THE QUAY. It was engraved at Wick & Barrow's at a crown a letter, a hundred and twenty-eight crowns, which is why it is as short as it is; I had a great deal more to say. It does not correct the first plaque and it does not repeat it. Mrs Thrupp read it first, and twice, and said nothing, and put it up herself. Both are polished. I do not know by whom. Method. None. It was not fought, measured or collected. It is not a type specimen; it does not need to be one, because the species was described long before I was born, by people who looked at it. I examined it from the floor, at a distance of about six feet, for some time, on the evening I was asked to leave, and I have examined it every evening since from the seat under it, which is now mine. Remarks. It is the only animal in this Bestiary I have been thrown out of a building for. It is the only one with a bucket by the fire marked FOR THE GOOSE, filled every morning. It is the only one whose entry in my monograph, on page four hundred, was read aloud in the Slain Wyvern by somebody else, to applause, while I was in the room. I sat through it. I have asked that it not happen again, and it has happened twice. The farm it came from is still there. I have been to see the geese. They are greylags, and they are very rude, and they are exactly right. I sit at the next table. Miss Halloway has written, in the evenings, under the goose, for the best part of two years, and in all that time I have not once seen her look up at it. I asked her why not. She said that she knows what it is. - H.B. See also The Slain Wyvern Halloran Vance Wren Halloway The Bestiary

title: The North, and Below
text: The North, and Below Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary: what is met in the Long Field and on the crag, under Carn Drey , in a chapel at Weeping Bottom at night, and on the Stair under Hithermost . Very little of it is an animal, and Miss Halloway has said so, at the top, so that nobody can say she did not. - H.B. I was asked to write up everything a party is likely to fight between Upper Clanging and the bottom of the Stair. I have done so. Most of it is machinery, weather, the time of night, or architecture, and one of it is a weasel. I have been strict about what I describe and lenient about what I list, because people will look. The Long Field and the crag None of these is an animal. All of them are the Hoyle Works ', and I have referred them to Miss Hoyle , who has replied that they are attempts, and are documented, and that their documentation is not open to the public. Loose pressure. A hundred and forty years of stored steam, finding the way out all at once. It is not attacking anybody. It is just leaving. Stand aside. Attempt (unnumbered). Too early to have been given a number. It has been getting one foot off the ground since before anybody now alive was born. Ambulant salvage. Parts of nine different attempts, walking. Nobody assembled it, and nobody can prove that it was not assembled. I asked Miss Hoyle which. She said that it was under review. Attempt Eighty-Four . Came down in the Long Field in 1860 and repaired herself out of her neighbours, a piece at a time, for a hundred and forty years. Stopped in 2000. Miss Hoyle's, and in her bay, and the subject of a paragraph in the memorandum on the field , which I recommend. I note only that she is the one thing in this volume which nobody taught to do what she did, and which did it anyway, and that in an animal I should have called that behaviour. Loose pressure, leaving Attempt (unnumbered), one foot off the ground Ambulant salvage, under review Attempt Eighty-Four, in the field, out of her neighbours Under Carn Drey Worm The Worm of Carn Drey. Not basically anything. What it is. A worm. A very large, very old, legless serpent of the deep earth, coiled three times round a chamber under Carn Drey. Called. The Worm of Carn Drey. Never, in my hearing, basically a dragon, and if anybody calls it that in my hearing it will not be the Worm I am cross with. Where. Under Carn Drey, east of Great Dunnage , at the bottom of a long stair, beyond a stone with a sword in it. Description. Old. Very large. It had been waiting since before Roland Fairweather was born for a hero of nineteen. It is patient, and it had been looking forward to it. Method. Engaged, under a prophecy, by Roland Fairweather, aged thirty-four, with help. It was over in about the time it takes to say so. The prophecy was discharged. The Worm was not harmed in any way a worm minds, and went back to sleep. Remarks. It is the only animal in this volume that anybody has been back to visit for tea. Mr Fairweather goes down. I am told that it is very good about it. A chapel at Weeping Bottom, at night These are reported by the watch who kept Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore's vigil with him in the chapel across the yard from the Sisterhouse, in the year 2000, dusk to dawn. Sir Aldric did not move or speak, by the rules, and so is not a witness to any of them, though he took all of them. He has asked that they be recorded. None of them is an animal. The damp. It comes in under the chapel door every night. It always has. It is condensation, and it is Weeping Bottom's, and it is, in my professional opinion, the most dangerous thing in this section. The small hours. Cannot be fought, only got through. Gone at dawn. A period of time. A small temptation. Sits on the end of the altar rail. Very reasonable. Not described, at the request of everybody who was there. A light going away. Bobs off down the valley, saying THIS WAY. A marsh light, of the kind I have described under The Road North , with the one addition that it speaks, which I do not believe and which every member of the watch reports. Sir Aldric has followed every light in that valley but this one. The damp, under the door The small hours A small temptation. Not described; drawn, which nobody thought to forbid A light going away, THIS WAY The Stair The Stair goes down from the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost, and the parish has posted a Schedule of Hazards at the top, and I have catalogued it in its own order, because it is a good schedule and I could not improve on it. 1. The dark. Some of it. A condition. The reason the board on the Door says what it says. A lamp is the treatment. 2. The draught. It puts lamps out. It is a weasel; see below. 3. The echo. Do not answer it. Everybody does. An acoustic property of a long stair in rock; I have heard it described as having lovely manners, which I do not doubt. Not an animal. 4. Somebody coming up. Not catalogued. The Stair is one wide and the dark is total, and nobody who has met it has been able to see who it is. I do not catalogue what I could not see, and I do not guess who. 5. The warden of the half-way landing. A figure in black armour at the head of a flight, with a hook on its belt and nothing on the hook, which inspects whoever comes down. It is employed, and I do not catalogue staff. It is not half way. Nobody had told it. It has been told now, and is getting used to it. 6. Anything else: NOT ANTICIPATED. The dark (some of it) The echo, which has lovely manners Somebody coming up. Not seen; drawn anyway, by somebody who also did not see them The warden, half way, in the opinion of the warden Weasel The Draught, as the parish imagined it. It is a weasel. What it is. A weasel. Called. The Draught. Where. The upper flights of the Stair, in company with the dark. Description. A weasel. Very fast, very thin, very cold, and in the dark entirely without substance, so that the parish took it for the wind and posted it as a draught. It is not made of wind. It moves the air, which is not the same thing, and it puts out lamps because it goes past them very close, and it goes past everything very close. I am told by people who have been down that it has been described as a weasel made of wind. It is a weasel. The wind is incidental. Method. Relit the lamp. Something Unscheduled Something Unscheduled, delighted. What it is. Unscheduled. Called. Something Unscheduled . That is its own name, and it is the most accurate name in this Bestiary, and I have not been able to improve on it either. Where. The bottom of the Stair, below D. 212, in a chamber with lamps on every ledge, all lit. Description. Large. Purple. Delighted. It is not on the schedule, except as item six; it is not in the Prophecy ; and it asked. It had written itself a bounty card, a long time ago, because nobody would put it on anything. Method. It asks whether you have the afternoon. Nobody is obliged to fight it, and it says afterwards that that is what it liked best about it. Remarks. I have been down since, with the Forty-Eighth, on one of his free afternoons, and asked it what it is. It said that it would love to tell me, if I had the afternoon. I had the afternoon. I filled eleven pages. I am not going to print them, because at the end of the afternoon it asked whether I would, and then said, oh, oh no, was that too much, and that it was sorry, it did not get the practice. I said that it was not too much. I have kept the pages. It is in volume two, under U, with the footnotes. I have asked Mr Bellwether not to call it a Thing. He has not. See also The Bestiary The Long Field Carn Drey Weeping Bottom The Stair

title: The Road North
text: The Road North Contributed by W. Halloway, Cataloguer From Miss Halloway's Bestiary: the animals of the fields about Thistlewick, the road north, the Gloamwood and the Obligatory Tower. For the places, see Thistlewick , The Gloamwood and The Obligatory Tower . - H.B. Every Chosen One of Thistlewick has walked this road, and forty-seven of them have reported what they met on it, by how it died. None of the reports describes an animal. This is the first list of what is actually there. It is short, because most of what is on the road north is not an animal, and a good deal of it is a person. The fields Turnip The Militant Turnip, from an account. It is armed. That is the part I cannot account for. What it is. A turnip, Brassica rapa. Called. The Militant Turnip. Where. The fields about Thistlewick, in the open, generally in company with crows. Description. A turnip, in every particular but one, which is that it has had enough. I have examined one closely. Its anatomy is a turnip's. Its conduct is not. I cannot account for it, and I have tried, and I would ask readers not to send me theories. Method. Engaged at range. Two of whatever it dropped, which was turnip. Remarks. The Forty-Eighth takes these personally, and was not, I noticed, in the least surprised by them. Carrion crow The Crow of Foreshadowing, about to caw. Count them. What it is. The carrion crow, Corvus corone. Called. The Crow of Foreshadowing. Where. Fields, the road, and the edges of the Gloamwood. Description. A crow. Black throughout. Caws, it is said, exactly three times whenever anything important is about to happen. Remarks. Crows caw in threes. They also caw in twos, fours and elevens. The threes are remembered, because something important is generally about to happen to a party of adventurers, and the twos are not. I counted for a week. The crow is not foreshadowing anything. The adventurers are. The road and the wood Oak The Grumblewood Treant, objecting. What it is. A tree. An oak, I think, from the leaf; it would not hold still for the bark. Called. The Grumblewood Treant. Where. The Gloamwood, and the wooded stretches of the road. Description. Objects to being walked past. Method. We walked past it. It objected. It was then engaged, which is a step I resent in a tree more than in anything else in this volume, because a tree has nowhere to go. Marsh light The Wisp of Mild Concern. Mildly. What it is. A light. Not an animal. A small burning gas, which hovers, and is seen at dusk in damp places. Called. The Wisp of Mild Concern. Where. The Gloamwood, the road west and the hills. Description. Hovers nearby, looking worried. Attacks anyway. Remarks. I list it because it is in every adventurer's account of the road, and because it looks worried, and readers have asked me what about. It is not worried. It is a gas. The worry is the observer's, and I would not presume to say what about. Chest mimic The Chest (Definitely A Chest), open. What it is. An ambush predator, chest-shaped. Called. The Chest (Definitely A Chest). A mimic. Where. One, in the Gloamwood, on the path, alone, in perfect condition. It is splinters now. Description. A treasure chest, alone, in the middle of a wood, in perfect condition. Everybody knows. Nearly everybody opens it. It carried an Elixir as bait, which is either very clever or very sad, and I have decided it was clever, because I prefer it. Method. Opened. Then engaged. I would like it noted that I said so first. The Thing in the Woods The Thing in the Woods, as the adventurers saw it: one animal, with a great many heads. It is nine snakes. What it is. Nine crested grass snakes, courting. Called. The Thing in the Woods. The Thing. In Thistlewick, for two hundred years, a bear, several bears, and a bear-shaped hole in the idea of a wood. Where. The deep clearing of the Gloamwood, mostly in late spring, always at dusk. Description. The crested grass snake is common. It is about four feet long, banded, with a crest feather the colour of a boiled sweet, and it sheds its skin whole. It nests in the forks of trees; there is a nest on the first path, at head height, with a crest feather caught in the rim of it. The crest is not for fighting. It is a display structure, for attracting a mate. It works. That is why there are nine of them. In spring they gather to court, and nine is usual, and they knot together. From the path, at dusk, it looks like one large thing with a great many heads. The record. The Gloamwood Society has kept forty years of sightings in its newsletter, The Sighting. Every one of them has between one and nine heads. I read all forty years in an afternoon. Every sighting is accurate as to the heads and inaccurate as to the number of animals. One sighting, Miss Edith Pellow's of 1971, counts nine, and is the only accurate one in the forty years. I have told her so, in writing, and she has the letter. Method. The party that disturbed the knot in the year 2000 was four people with a sword, which is not a method, and I was not consulted. The knot dispersed, as a courting knot does when four people with a sword walk into it. There is nothing in the Gloamwood. There never was. There are snakes, which are not a Thing, and which are none of anybody's business in the spring. Remarks. Everything we killed that week was in the middle of courting. I do not say that to upset anybody. I say it because it goes in the monograph. The Tower The Obligatory Tower is, I am told, under contract, and so is most of what is in it. I have catalogued what I could. Bat The Tower Bat. What it is. A bat. Several species; the commonest in the Tower is a small brown bat of a kind found in any roof. Called. The Tower Bat. Where. The Tower, every floor; and the Bottomless Pit . Remarks. There are always bats. It is said to be in the contract. I have not seen the contract. I have seen the bats, and they would be there anyway. A tall stone building with a roof is a bat's idea of a good contract. Gargoyle The Load-Bearing Gargoyle, off its post, which raises the questions. What it is. Masonry. Not an animal. Called. The Load-Bearing Gargoyle. Where. The Tower, in the walls, until it is not. Remarks. It is structurally important, and it attacks anyway, which raises questions about the Tower. Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging asked one of those questions, in writing, and it went up the Tower with the Forty-Eighth, and I understand that it was not answered. I am not competent to answer it. I list the gargoyle so that the next person who asks what the Tower is made of has a place to start: in part, it is made of things that do not want to be in it. Persons The following are met on the road north and are reported in adventurers' accounts as monsters. They are persons. A goblin is a person: the one I met had a list of grievances and read from it, which is more than most people do. A bandit (trainee) is a person, in the fourth week of a six-week apprenticeship, with a syllabus. A skeleton (intern) is the remains of a person, employed, unpaid, for the experience, and I do not catalogue staff. I have not described any of them. See the index . A goblin, with grievances A bandit, in week four A skeleton, interning See also The Bestiary Bramus agricola , the only animal in the fields anybody had not noticed The Gloamwood , and the Society The Coast and Under It

title: A Glossary of Cliches
text: A Glossary of Cliches An adventuring convention is a thing that happens on every quest because it happened on the first one, and nobody has thought to stop it. The Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. This volume lists them, with where he walked into each, and who was still annoyed about it. The Prophecy's own account of the Quest keeps a tally of the conventions a Chosen One walks into on the way, and reads the total back to him at the end. I have not seen the number in the Forty-Eighth's account; I have seen the words, which are very nearly all of them , and the reason given, which is that he read the notice board, searched the barrels, opened things that were obviously not chests, and went south, which nobody does. By my own count there are a little over two hundred to be walked into between Thistlewick and the top, and more since. What follows is a selection, alphabetical, and each headword is marked as a convention the way I have marked them in my notes, with a dotted line, so that the reader can see where one has been walked into. - H.B. A The abridged edition. A work too long to read, made shorter for the reader's convenience. The Prophecy of Thistlewick (Abridged) is on Elder Wispel's desk in Prophecy Hall , and is exactly as long as the unabridged one, the abridging having been done by the Committee. The ambush. See The tutorial, and Norbert, who is contracted to lose. The amnesiac. A young person found on a beach with no memory, an excellent posture and something expensive on their head, whom everybody is very kind to and nobody will tell anything. Perpetua Small woke up on the beach at Nether Sopping six years before the Quest, in a tiara she has not noticed. The whole of the Slain Wyvern looks very hard at the ceiling. Still annoyed: nobody; that is rather the point. B Barrels. A barrel is searched. It is the law. The one at Firstfield says WELL DONE. YOU HAVE SEARCHED A BARREL. THERE WILL BE MANY MORE. There were. The Prophecy's account names this as one of the four reasons for its verdict. The beanstalk. Goes straight up into the canopy of the Gloamwood , and stops, as though it had thought better of it. A card at the bottom: GIANT NOT IN. PLEASE DO NOT CLIMB. THIS MEANS YOU, JACK. The bed that mends everything. In stories, heroes lie down on any bed they find and wake up feeling much better. At the Gilded Turnip it is twenty crowns, and Prudence would like you to know that it is still twenty crowns. At Restwell it actually works, which is the whole of that town. The blue potion. Is mana. Everybody knows that, and nobody knows how. The one in Nix's Emporium says so, with the small print OR IT IS BLUE WATER. ONE OF THOSE. The bounty board. A cork board of monsters with prices on, behind a rope eleven inches high. At the Adventurers' Guild , members only. The Crab of Unusual Size and M. Crooke , both discharged. C The cell. FOR CHOSEN ONES WHO HAVE BEEN CAPTURED. In the Obligatory Tower . In four thousand eight hundred years nobody has ever been captured. It seemed rude. The chest that is not a chest. Alone, in the middle of a wood, on a path, in perfect condition. Everybody knows. Nearly everybody opens it. Miss Halloway's entry is under chest mimic . Still annoyed: the mimic, which is splinters. The Chosen One. Selected by prophecy from among the humble, to go north. The Forty-Eighth was chosen by the Prophecy Committee while he was asleep, and was therefore unable to object, and pointed out several things when he woke up, none of which helped. Still annoyed: nobody he will name. The coffins. A dark tower ought to have coffins, for the look of it. Every coffin in the row in the Obligatory Tower says RESERVED. The convenient cupboard. Just before the end, a cupboard of exactly what the party needs. In the Tower there are ten hooks with brass labels, CHOSEN ONE, HEALER, SMITH and so on, and two added later in a cheaper brass, RIVAL and CATALOGUER, and a tenth for GUEST, with a note in pencil. Somebody has been keeping the list up to date for four thousand years, which is unnerving. The courier who finds you. The post reaches a hero anywhere, in any weather, in any cave. A man in a red coat and a flat cap with a satchel found the Forty-Eighth's company in a good many towns, on behalf of Spare Cotterill's correspondence, and once, at the edge of the lamplight, a long way down the Stair . Post? D The doomed rival. Dark, brooding, carries a black sword, and is fated to be overshadowed. Corvin Ash held the post. At the Sable Hart five other doomed rivals keep a league table and are very fair about seating. Still annoyed: the league table, which stops at fourth. The dungeon rumour. A child runs up to you to say that there is a DUNGEON! To the NORTH! You have heard. You will hear again. E The elder who gives the quest. Unrolls a scroll. It reaches the far wall. Says that it has worked forty-seven times, and, asked about the other times, that it has worked forty-seven times. See Elder Wispel . F The fetch quest. Somebody's sheep are lost and must be found. At Firstfield the sheep are pigs, and are not lost, and have been asked to lose themselves a bit. If you decline, you are told But thou must, and then told sorry, the Guild gave her that line. The fortune teller. NEVER WRONG. TWO CROWNS. Mother Selvidge , at the Fair , a long way from anywhere, the way fairs always are. I have not printed her reading, because it was not mine. The founder's stone. A stone, a date, a name and a reason, with a joke cut into it underneath by a later hand. Weeping Bottom's says the sea air is the finest cure for the chest, in the opinion of every physician consulted, and somebody has added, None of whom had been. H The haystack. Searched, out of habit, for a needle. NO NEEDLE. THIS IS MUCH POTTERING. The hermit. A man on a rock , looking at the middle distance with great authority, who says You seek wisdom, and then gives you his shopping list. He has been up there nineteen years and would like some cheese. The hoard. A dragon's, of gold, which a hero may take a coin from. It is dusted every morning with a feather. You could take a coin. Mrs Emberthwaite looks at you over her spectacles. You could not. K The key under the mat. The door of the most dangerous building in the world has a mat in front of it that says WELCOME, and under the mat there is a key labelled SPARE - DO NOT LOSE AGAIN. Nix would not use it: the bar was on the inside. The Adventurers' Guild's form was also under its mat. Still annoyed: Mr Pell, who is aware of the tower, and does not find the pattern amusing. L The last shop before the end. Priced accordingly. Penultima has two, and the actual last one is shut. In the window of the other is the Sword of Ultimate Ending , which sir cannot afford to hold. The library of forbidden books. In the Tower: Villainy for Beginners, read once, carefully, with a bookmark in chapter one, and The Monologue: A Handbook, whose chapter one is called Don't. In the Forbidden Archive at Olde Evermore : a book stamped FORBIDDEN in four languages, which is biscuit recipes. The lockers. The key is never in the lockers. A card in the first one says so. M The mysterious advisor. Kindly, old, and watched from week three, because in every story the kindly old advisor turns out to be the villain. Councillor Dree was watched for eleven weeks and then tied up, and was not the villain, and sits alone in the Slain Wyvern now, deliberately, with great composure. Still annoyed: Councillor Dree, very politely. N The notice board. Read in every village, because it is the law. Thistlewick's has LOST: ONE GOAT. ANSWERS TO COUNCILLOR, and WANTED: CHOSEN ONE. POSITION FILLED. The Prophecy's account names reading it as one of the four reasons for its verdict. O The old man who gives you something. It's dangerous to go alone. Take this. Old Hollis at Firstfield has given eleven thousand, two hundred and six sticks. Thistlewick's own old man gave the Forty-Eighth something else, which was: Everyone tells you it's an honour. Nobody tells you it's a rota. Come back, lad. His boy was the Forty-Seventh. P The pots. Looked in, or under, in case. In the Tower, a note: I WOULDN'T EITHER. - G. At Hithermost : STILL NO. At the Gilded Turnip, a pot labelled POT, and inside it a label, INSIDE OF POT. The princess in the tower. Waiting to be rescued. Princess Rosamund of Fairholme has been rescued a great many times, and has written a memoir, Rescued Again, now in its eleventh volume, in which every chapter is named for a rescuer, and every one of them is written about very kindly. The prophecy. Ancient, binding and vague. Ours was precise. See The Prophecy of Thistlewick , and Councillor Fenn, who said it was a subscription. R The real last boss. The villain falls, and then the thing behind the villain rises. At the top of the Tower, after Grimspite, the Prophecy unrolled itself to enforce clause twelve. It was the real last boss. It lost. See The Obligatory Quest . The retired hero. Has a sword over the fireplace, exactly like the one that was over yours, with dust on the upper edge, which takes a long time and a great deal of not looking. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth. Also the Forty-Sixth, on his log, who decided that the woods were enough. S The save point. A book, or a crystal, at which progress may be kept. The one at Hithermost is a Book, and is Sir Dunstable's name all the way down the page. Firstfield reminds the visitor that he may save at any time, which he always could. The secret passage. One volume of the minutes sticks out further than the rest. You pull it. Something goes clunk. The sword over the fireplace. Kept for exactly this occasion. It came off the wall of Bram Thistle's house with a sound that can only be described as smug. See Arms and Artefacts . T The ten-foot pole. Every adventurer needs one. It does not say what for. Nobody has ever said what for. Everybody buys one. Wick & Barrow's keep them round the back, because they would not fit on the shelf. The thing in the woods. Which everybody fears, and nobody has ever got close enough to describe. It was nine snakes, courting. See the Bestiary , which is very firm about it. The town sign. Names the town, so that you know where you are. Penultima's says THE LAST TOWN BEFORE THE END, and under it LAST CHANCE FOR POTIONS, and under that (WE MEAN IT). Hithermost's says that it is the last village before the mountain, and, added later, AND, FOR SOME, THE FIRST ONE AFTER IT. The tutorial. Explains walking to somebody who has just walked. Forty-seven Chosen Ones skipped it, by pressing the button really fast. The Forty-Eighth did not, because nobody had told him you could. See Firstfield Meadow and the Guild of Guides . V The village that has never heard of you. The watchman at Great Dunnage had never heard of the Forty-Eighth. He has since found him in the ledger, for me: BRAM (THISTLEWICK) - PROPHECY, SOME SORT. W The wardrobe. In stories, a way into another world. Halbert Quy's has coats in it, and behind the coats more coats, and then the back. If you want another world, the back door is through there. It is the garden. The wayshrine. A roof, a bench, and a box of supplies: FOR CHOSEN ONES. PLEASE REPLACE WHAT YOU TAKE. NOBODY EVER REPLACES WHAT THEY TAKE. In the book, forty-seven names, the last of them Feeling good about this one! The Forty-Eighth added his name and no comment. The well that is not a wishing well. Says so. Is wished at anyway. Nothing happens. The sign was right. The wrong dragon. A cave, something very large inside, breathing slowly, the way people breathe when they are reading. Come in, come in. Mind the books. Not in the Bestiary; it was not asked, and I am told it would rather be in the library. I asked the Forty-Eighth which of these had annoyed him most. He thought about it for some time, and said the barrels, and then said no, the barrels were fine, it was the pot that said INSIDE OF POT. I asked him why. He said that he had looked. - H.B.

title: History
text: History The history of the world, so far as anyone has written it down, is very largely the history of one document. Everything before the Prophecy of Thistlewick belongs to the elves, who will tell you about it if you ask and who have never been asked. Everything since belongs to the Prophecy, which has been asked a great deal and has answered, every time, in clauses. This volume holds the articles that are about time rather than about a person or a place. Article What it covers The Prophecy of Thistlewick The document itself: its signing, its clauses, and what it turned out to be. The Chosen Ones All forty-eight of them, so far as they are known, with what became of each. The Obligatory Quest The quest of the Forty-Eighth, from the bed to the throne room, and after. Two Reckonings Why the Tower is two thousand years old and four thousand eight hundred, and both are true. Timeline Every date I could pin, in order. Events Things that happened once, and that a town has been talking about since. The Quest of the Forty-Eighth is the largest of them and has its own article above; these are the others, in order. Article When What happened The Cold Winter 1919 Six weeks at Upper Clanging with the foundry banked down, and the Class of 'Nineteen. The Eleven Days 1960 A man walking north breaks the winter at Frostwick, and on the twelfth day the town puts it back. The Thrupp Feud 1970-2000 Two sisters, two inns, forty miles and thirty years of parcels. The Day of the Water 1989 Old Ashcombe goes under the lake, and is dry by teatime. The Incident at the Collegium 1989 A very small room, rather more fire than it had been told about, and a duck. The Flight of the Two Hundred 2000 The two hundredth airship of the Hoyle Works reaches the Tower, and lands adjacent.

title: The Chosen Ones
text: The Chosen Ones For the document that chose them, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the last of them, see Bram Thistle . The Chosen Ones of Thistlewick Number Forty-eight First In the first century of the Third Age Last Bram Thistle, Third Age 2000 Chosen by The Prophecy Committee, in session, with or without the candidate Equipment A sword (one). Companions, up to three. Potions, three, from the parish fund Success rate Forty-seven out of forty-seven, according to the Committee Commemorated The Wall of the Forty-Seven, Prophecy Hall; the Obelisk, the Obligatory Tower; the memorial, Nether Sopping Next There isn't a forty-nine The Chosen Ones are the forty-eight people whom the village of Thistlewick sent north, under the Prophecy , to put down the Dark Lord in the Obligatory Tower . It worked forty-seven times. Thistlewick will tell you so. Ask it what happened the other times, and it will tell you that it worked forty-seven times. "Everyone tells you it's an honour," the father of the Forty-Seventh told the Forty-Eighth, on the morning he left. "Nobody tells you it's a rota." How a Chosen One is chosen By the Prophecy Committee , in session, at a moment it finds convenient (see Two Reckonings). The candidate does not need to be present, and the last one was not: the minutes of the meeting at which Bram Thistle was chosen list, under apologies for absence, his name and one goat. He was asleep. The goat has not been found. The Chosen One is then summoned to Prophecy Hall , where Elder Wispel unrolls the Prophecy until it reaches the far wall and gives the charge: take companions, up to three; go north; kill the Dark Lord; come home. "In that order, ideally." The Chosen One receives a copy of the Prophecy in triplicate, five hundred crowns and three potions from the parish fund, and a sword. Every one of them did the sword. What happened next was, for forty-seven of them, the same. They went north. They climbed the Tower. They found the Dark Lord, Grimspite the Inevitable , reading, and he put his bookmark in and said, "So, you have come at last," which he meant the first time. They fought him, and they won, and before they reached the stairs clause twelve renewed him. They came home and Thistlewick said that it had worked. "Forty-seven of us," Halbert Quy told the Forty-Eighth. "We all did the sword. Not one of us ever asked the man why he doesn't stop." And forty-seven went before, and every one took up the sword, and not one asked him what it was for, and that is all the old record. From the notebooks of P. Quill, by permission Miss Quill has asked me to point out that "record" is stressed on the second syllable here, for the rhyme, and that this is allowed. I have pointed it out. What became of them They came home, and they were awkward. A Chosen One who has come back knows what is at the top of the Tower, and says so at meetings, and asks why the Committee is already drafting the next one. Somewhere about the Ninth, Thistlewick wrote clause nineteen, and from then on a returning hero received a pension, a cottage, and such distance from the village as was mutually agreeable, which was forty miles, to Nether Sopping . That is where they are, those of them who are anywhere. Most of them drink in the Slain Wyvern . Thistlewick does not write. The forty-eight The Committee keeps a souvenir book, The Forty-Seven, with a portrait, a date and a pressed flower on every page. The flowers are all turnip flowers. I have seen it, across a table, and was not permitted to copy the dates, which are Committee property. So I have printed below only what I could get from somebody who was there, and where nobody was, I have left the space. No. Set out Name What is known 1 The first century of the Age Not recorded Shown in the stained glass of Prophecy Hall, slaying the Dark Lord. The glazier has given the Dark Lord a very patient expression, like a man waiting for a bus he has been told is coming. 2-8 A century apart Not recorded The Committee found a hundred years convenient, at first. 9 About the year 900 Not recorded Came home, and was awkward. Clause nineteen was written somewhere about him. 10-38 Closer and closer together, always in a round year Not recorded The Committee began to find shorter periods convenient. Nobody in Thistlewick has remarked on it. 39 About 1930 Not recorded The cousin of a regular in the Gilded Turnip , who will tell you so. 40 Before 1940 Not recorded 41 1940 Halloran Vance Came back from the marshes with nothing and a whole town waiting on the quay for a monster. So he brought them one: two days, with wire, and a goose. It has been a wyvern over the mantel of the Slain Wyvern for sixty years. He was a good man, and he needed it to be a wyvern. 42 The 1940s or 1950s Not recorded He and his wife drink in the Slain Wyvern, and come every year for the anniversary. 43 The 1940s or 1950s Not recorded 44 1960 Ambrose Fitch Pensioned to Nether Sopping and ignored for forty years, watering a pot with a dead thing in it every morning. Died about 1999. Thistlewick cut THISTLEWICK REMEMBERS over the door of his mound; somebody has chalked under it that Thistlewick did not write once. He asked for a bench. He has one now. 45 1970 Halbert Quy Declined Grimspite's tea, because he thought it was a trick, and has thought about it ever since. Asked at the next meeting why there was always a next one. The cottage was ready by the Friday. He is next door to Fitch's. 46 1980 Godfrey Stopford , off the envelopes Got as far as the Gloamwood , said the woods were enough, and sat down on a log, where he still is. His party said: fair. Two of them, Nabb and Tolly , write to him every month, and he reads every letter, and that is his answer. 47 1990 Not given The Old Man's boy. Came off the ledge at Olde Evermore and landed on his feet, for five point nine, the best score since the First Age. He did not come home to Thistlewick. 48 2000 Bram Thistle A turnip farmer, chosen asleep. Asked the question. See The Obligatory Quest. Forty-seven, or forty-six. Grimspite says he said "so, you have come at last" forty-seven times and was renewed forty-seven times, and the Obelisk in his tower lists forty-seven RENEWED. The Forty-Sixth says he got as far as the woods. Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging , who counts for a living, counts forty-six that went up that road. I have all three numbers, and I have not been able to make them into one. I set them down here side by side, which is what an encyclopedia is for.
