Monuments The Wall of the Forty-Seven, in Prophecy Hall: forty-seven portraits. Forty-six of them are looking at the viewer. One of them is looking at the door. I have asked which, and why, and was told that it was a very old portrait. At the end of them there is now a forty-eighth frame, new and empty, with a card pinned in it: PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. The sitter is not at the coast. He is at home, two fields away, and has been for two years. Nobody has changed the card. A second card, the Quills ', is tucked into the corner to make room. The Obelisk, in the Obligatory Tower: forty-seven entries, each a date and a name and the word RENEWED. There is room for a forty-eighth. It will not be needed. The memorial at Nether Sopping: a hundred and eighty-one names. It lists everybody who went north with them - healers, hired swords, cousins, a cook, somebody listed only as "the lad who carried the rope" - and not only the Chosen Ones, which is the difference between Nether Sopping and Thistlewick in one stone. The end of the list When the Forty-Eighth had read the Prophecy through and it had stopped being binding, Grimspite signed him a receipt and sent him home with a message. "Grow your turnips. There isn't a forty-nine. Say that to them, when you get in. Say: there isn't a forty-nine." He said it. The Committee minuted it. It has not, so far as I can tell, been believed, but it has been true for two years, which is the longest anything has been true in Prophecy Hall. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Obligatory Quest Two Reckonings Nether Sopping

title: The Cold Winter
text: The Cold Winter This article is about the January of 1919 at Upper Clanging. For the people born that autumn, see Winnie Marsden . For the census, see Mrs Tunnicliffe . Not to be confused with the winter at Frostwick , which is kept on purpose; see The Eleven Days . The Cold Winter When January and February 1919 Where Upper Clanging How long Six weeks Cause Want of coke The foundry Banked down. The first and only time Work None Heat What was in the houses Recorded in The census, which is dates Commemorated A dinner, every year, on the second Saturday The Cold Winter is what Upper Clanging calls the January of 1919, when the foundry was banked down for six weeks for want of coke. There was no work. There was no heat in the whole town but what was in the houses. In the autumn two hundred and forty children were born, near enough all together, and the town has called them the Class of 'Nineteen ever since. They have a dinner. The six weeks The coke for the foundry came up the valley by cart, and in the second week of January 1919 the snow shut the valley road, a long way down, and kept it shut. The foundry had a week's coke in the yard. It was banked down on the tenth of January, to keep the fires in without burning anything, and it stayed banked down until the road was cleared and the carts got through, on the twenty-first of February. It has never been banked down before or since, and the town is proud of the record, and does not count the six weeks against it. There was no work. The foundry is the first thing in Upper Clanging, and everything else in the town is downstream of it, the Hoyle Works included, which in 1919 had nothing to put together. The register of the Parish Rooms reads AT THE WORKS on every line for eighty years, and for six weeks in 1919 there was nowhere for anybody to be at. There was no heat anywhere but in the houses: not in the foundry, not in the street, not in the Parish Rooms, which shut. Everybody stayed in. That is the whole of what is recorded about the six weeks, and I have looked. There is nobody now living in Upper Clanging who remembers them, and the people who did are in the churchyard, and they did not, I am told, discuss it. The census "Class of 'Nineteen. The Cold Winter lot. Foundry was banked down six weeks that January. No work. No heat in the whole town but what was in the houses. Two hundred and forty of them. All born the same autumn, near enough." That is Mrs Tunnicliffe , who has kept the census at the Parish Rooms since 1951, and it is the whole of the official account. The register for the autumn of 1919 runs to eleven pages, in the hand of the clerk before the clerk before her, which was a good hand, and got smaller as it went on. The town's average, before and since, is a page and a half. I put down here only what the census says, which is dates. The Class of 'Nineteen The two hundred and forty went to school together in 1923, at four, in two rooms. The teacher, Miss Agnes Thewlis, sat them in alphabetical order on the first morning and wrote the order down on a sheet of foolscap. That sheet is the seating plan. It has been used at every dinner since the first, in 1939, when the Class was twenty, and Winnie Marsden , who was born Winifred Platt on the fourth of October in the middle of them, has kept it in a biscuit tin since 1950. "There is a seating plan. There has been a seating plan since we were four. You cannot get in. I am not being unkind about it. You had to be born in it." The dinner is on the second Saturday in October, at the Safety Valve. Every place on the plan is laid, every year, and a place that is not filled has a card on the plate with the name on it, in Winnie's hand. A little over sixty came last October. The plan has two hundred and forty places and no column for anything else, and in the year 2000 a column was needed, because Winnie's granddaughter Bessie had married Cotter Cotterill , the eldest of nine, then ten, and the Cotterills would all want seats. There is a column now. It is in pencil. June Mrs Tunnicliffe was born Edna Hargreaves on the eleventh of June 1919, four months before the Class, and has been at school with all of them, at the end of the alphabet, and is not invited. "They have a dinner every year. I am not invited. I was born in June." She says it as a matter of record. In the winter just gone Winnie asked her whether she would help with the urns on the second Saturday, and she said that she would be delighted, and she will be at the urn, where, she says, she has always been invited everywhere. I was born in Nether Sopping , in March, in a year with nothing to be said about it, and I belong to no Class and have no dinner of any kind, and I find, having written this article, that I mind a little. - H.B. Since The foundry has kept six weeks' coke in the yard since the February of 1919, by standing order, and the standing order has never been needed. The Class of 'Nineteen is eighty-two this year. The plan is in the tin. The dinner is on the second Saturday in October, as ever. See also Winnie Marsden Mrs Tunnicliffe Upper Clanging The Eleven Days , the other winter Timeline

title: The Day of the Water
text: The Day of the Water This article is about the flooding of old Ashcombe in 1989. For the village as it is now, and the street under the lake, see Ashcombe . For the plan, see Hubert Weir . For the one who was away, see Corvin Ash . The Day of the Water Also called The Ashcombe Flood; the flood; a tremendous success When 1989, on a Tuesday Where Old Ashcombe, in the valley that is now Ashcombe Lake Cause The valley, which had always been wet; and the drain, which was not up to it Foreseen by Mr Weir, for thirty years Plan Drawn 1961. Carried in a coat for twenty-eight years Out by Dinner Dry by Tea On the Roll Two hundred and six, DRY. One, Away. (Written to.) Lost Not so much as a hen Decided, by teatime To build it again, only better The Day of the Water is what the plaque at Ashcombe calls the Tuesday in 1989 when the lake came up over the old village. Every soul in it walked up the hill with the kettles, by a plan that one man had carried in his coat for twenty-eight years, and was out by dinner and dry by tea, and by teatime had decided to build the whole thing again, only better. It did. Ashcombe regards the flood as the best thing that ever happened to it, and has a dinner about it every year. The valley Old Ashcombe stood in the bottom of a valley in the east, which had always been wet. It had a church, a school, an inn called the Anchor, a maypole and a street, and one drain, in the high street, under a stone carved DRAIN. The stone is the first exhibit in the Drainage Museum now, and the card beside it says, kindly, It was not up to it. The blackboard in the new school gives the history of the village in full: 1. IT WAS THERE. 2. IT WAS WET. 3. WE MOVED IT. Hubert Weir was born in 1936 three doors from the drain, and stood on the stone at six in a rainstorm and watched the water go round it, and knew. He went away and learned drainage and came back, and told the parish for thirty years that the valley would flood, and the parish said that it had always been wet. In 1961 he drew a plan of what to do on the day, and put it in his coat, and it was in his coat every day for twenty-eight years. The Tuesday It rained, in 1989, and went on raining, and on a Tuesday the water in the bottom of the valley stopped going anywhere and began to come up. Mr Weir took the plan out of his coat. "Oh, the flood. It was a Tuesday. We all went up the hill with the kettles, and by teatime we'd decided to build it again, only better." That is Mrs Ash , and it is the account of the day that everybody in Ashcombe gives, nearly word for word, because it is the true one. They went up the hill in the order on the plan, which was by streets, and took the kettles, which were not on the plan but which everybody took regardless, and the church bell, which came up on a cart, because nobody saw why it shouldn't. The schoolmistress brought the strongbox of reports up as far as the schoolroom door, decided that it was safer where it was, and left it there in oilcloth, and she was right. The water came up over the street and the Anchor and the school, and up the church to its eaves, and stopped there, and has stayed. The Roll The Roll was taken on the hill, in the rain, in the schoolmistress's hand: every name in the old village, a tick by each, and after every tick one word, DRY. There are two hundred and six ticks. Beside one name, in place of a tick, in the same careful hand: Away. (Written to.) That one was Corvin's. He was nineteen, and in a corner of the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping , being away, on purpose. Two hundred and six people stood on a hill and counted, and when they got to him they wrote down where he was, and then they wrote to him. "A tremendous success. Everybody out by dinner, everybody dry by tea, and not so much as a hen lost. We have the Roll." Teatime The decision was made on the hill, at about four, over tea, from the kettles. There was no meeting. Mr Weir says that somebody said it would be a shame to lose the name, and somebody else said that you could see your hand in front of your face up here, which you never could in the old kitchen, and that by the second cup everybody was agreed. They would build it again, only better, with the light, and with drains. They built it on the shore, eight miles from the old village by the road, which goes all the way round the lake, and a stone's throw by any other measure. Everything is new. The church is pale stone with a green roof and the old bell in the tower, and it rings at six for dinner. Mr Weir drained it: fourteen hundred yards of culvert, a fall of one in two hundred, and not one puddle in Ashcombe since the day they went in. Corvin took the name Ash, after the village, in its memory. His mother took it too, to save the postman. Remembered The plaque faces the lake, with the gilt still bright: HERE, ON THE DAY OF THE WATER, EVERY SOUL IN OLD ASHCOMBE CAME SAFE UP THE HILL, AND WAS DRY BY TEATIME. WE BUILT IT AGAIN, ONLY BETTER. MIND THE DRAINS. THEY ARE VERY GOOD. VISIT THE MUSEUM! (FREE.) The Drainage Museum has an empty plinth, beautifully polished: THE FLOOD (ON LOAN TO THE LAKE). In one front room a line is painted on the wall at knee height, with the date beside it, and a smiley face. There is a Flood Dinner every year in the church hall, in sluice week, with soup, a fish, a pudding and speeches, and the toast is TO THE WATER, WHICH WAS VERY GOOD ABOUT IT. The speaker has been, in order, the Curator, the Curator, Mrs Ash on knitting, the Curator and the Curator. In the year 2000 it was Corvin Ash, who gave the village its name back, and in 2001 it was the Curator, on culverts, for some time. The papers of the Flood Dinner Committee are kept in what was Corvin's bedroom; Hon. Sec., Mrs Ash. Once a year, in the same week, the lake is let down for the sluices, and the old street comes up for air. The bell, they say, can be heard ringing under the water on a still day. It cannot. It is up the road, calling somebody in for their dinner. They took it with them. I have been to the Flood Dinner, in 2001, as Mrs Ash's guest, and I have heard the toast drunk by most of the two hundred and six who are on the Roll as DRY, and by the one who is on it as Away, and was early. I have been to a good many commemorations in my time, and this is the only one I have ever been to at which nobody was sorry about anything, and I have thought about it since more than about any of the others. - H.B. title: The Eleven Days
text: The Eleven Days This article is about the thaw at Frostwick in 1960. For the inn named after it, see Frostwick . For the man who did it, see Perce Stagg . For the winter as it is now, under contract, see Pargeter . Not to be confused with the Cold Winter , which was somebody else's, and was six weeks. The Eleven Days Also called The Thaw; the Breaking of the Winter When Spring 1960, the year of the Forty-Fourth Where Frostwick Broken by Percival Stagg, of Fenny Stretton. Not chosen Before A winter that had got stuck Snow depth during The line is on the floor Takings during Nil. Noted, with concern Ended by A meeting, on the twelfth day Outcome The winter retained, on a sensible footing. A Festival. One ribbon The Eleven Days were the spring of 1960 at Frostwick , when a young man walking north broke the town's winter, and it thawed, for the first time in living memory, for eleven days. On the twelfth day the town held a meeting, and retained a practitioner to put the winter back on a sensible footing, and asked the young man to cut a ribbon. He has cut forty-two. The old winter Before 1960 Frostwick was under a winter that did not end. It was not a cold spell. It was a winter that had got stuck, and had been stuck since before anybody in the town could remember, and the town believed it to be a curse, and had built a living on it: carols, lanterns, the snow, and visitors who came a long way to stand in it. Ida Stagg , who was born there in 1937, says that until she was twenty-two she had never seen a gutter run. Everybody went north In the spring of 1960 the Forty-Fourth, Ambrose Fitch , set out from Thistlewick for the Tower , and the whole of the south went north with him, or after him, or a little before him, on the general understanding that something was going to happen and that it would be a shame to miss it. Farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat. One of them was Percival Stagg , twenty-six, a cabbage grower of Fenny Stretton, in his father's red coat. He got as far as Frostwick square in a drift up to his waist, and could not get further, and asked what was the matter, and was told that it was a curse. He said that it did not look like a curse to him; it looked like a winter that had not been told to stop. He asked who was in charge of it. Nobody was. So he went up to the top of the town, where the cold came down from, and saw to it. "I wasn't, you know. Chosen. Nobody chose me. Everybody went north, that year. Farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat. I got as far as here, and the winter was in the way, so I saw to it." What he did up there he has never said, and he says that he does not entirely know. It took most of a day and a great deal of shovelling, and at the end of it there was a noise like a door shutting a long way off, and the snow began to drip. He came down the hill at dusk. The town was standing in the square, with the snow running down the gutters, and somebody started to cheer. Ida says that she was not the first, but that she was the loudest, and that he looked at her because of the noise and went pink, and that she had decided by the time he got to the bottom of the hill. The eleven days It thawed for eleven days. Mrs Marchpane, at the inn that is named for them, will tell you about every one of them whether you ring the bell or not; the card on the bell reads RING FOR SERVICE, OR FOR THE STORY OF THE THAW, and in practice they are the same thing. The short version is on a brass plate by the fire, over a line painted along the skirting board: THE ELEVEN DAYS. SNOW DEPTH DURING: THIS HIGH. The line is on the floor. In those eleven days the gutters ran and the roofs showed, and the square turned out to be cobbled, which surprised a number of people who had lived on it all their lives. Three people planted peas. Nobody sang a carol, because there was nothing to sing it about, and nobody lit a lantern, because nobody could see the point of one, and nobody came a long way to stand in anything. By the eleventh evening the town had worked out what this meant, and on the twelfth morning it had a meeting. The twelfth day The founding minutes of the Working Group on the Winter are on the table in its rooms, and I copy them as I found them: MINUTES OF THE WORKING GROUP ON THE WINTER. Extraordinary meeting, the twelfth day. Item 1. That the winter has stopped. Noted. Item 2. Takings, carols and lanterns, since: nil. Noted, with concern. Item 3. That a practitioner be retained to put it back, on a sensible footing. For, 41. Against, 3, who had planted peas. Carried. Item 4. That Mr Stagg be asked to open the first Festival. Carried unanimously, with one abstention: Mr Stagg. Item 5. Any other business. The peas. Deferred. The minutes were taken by Wilhelmina Thorley, nineteen, who kept the books for her father, the town's accountant, who took the chair that morning and kept it until 1979, when she took it from him. She is Mrs Blagg now. The peas are still deferred. Mr Stagg was not consulted about putting the winter back. I asked him whether he minded. He said that a winter on a sensible footing is a very different thing from a winter that has got stuck, and that he had only ever had a quarrel with the second sort. I asked him what had stuck it in the first place. He said that nobody had ever asked, and that he expected it was the same as most things, and that somebody had simply never been told to stop. - H.B. The first Festival The practitioner was retained, the winter was put back, four inches overnight and not on market days, and in the spring of 1961 Frostwick held its first Winter Festival, on the twelfth, with a ribbon at noon. Mr Stagg cut it, and the town cheered, and he went pink. He married Ida the next day. The ribbon has been cut and tied so many times since that it is mostly knots, and lives in a gilt case at the Working Group's rooms: THE RIBBON. 40 FESTIVALS. 1 RIBBON. There are forty-two now. The winter is kept now by Miss Eudora Pargeter , who is not an ice witch, and who does refrigeration, and who does January in an afternoon. Her Schedule of Snowfalls provides, for Festival Day, a light dusting, commencing at the ribbon, to settle on Mr Stagg's hat. It does. Since The Eleven Days are the only spring Frostwick has had since anybody can remember, and it was eleven days long, and the town has never once wanted another. The winter is first in the register of assets, depreciating at four per cent a year, towards spring, eventually, which has been budgeted for. The inn is still the Eleven Days. Mr Stagg is sixty-eight, and still does the lanterns, and still does the face. Ida ties a plain blue ribbon to the crown on the post every year, under his, a little lower, with nothing written on it. See also Frostwick Perce Stagg and Ida Stagg Pargeter Wilhelmina Blagg The Chosen Ones , for the Forty-Fourth Two Reckonings , which Miss Pargeter found The Cold Winter

title: The Flight of the Two Hundred
text: The Flight of the Two Hundred This article is about the day. For the airship and the technical account, which is Miss Hoyle's, see The Hoyle Works . For the hundred and ninety-seven that came down, see The Long Field . For the engineer, see Ott Hoyle . The Flight of the Two Hundred When 2000, the last of the winter From The Hoyle Works, Upper Clanging To The Obligatory Tower Attempt The two hundredth, in two hundred years Fabric Forty bolts of oilskin, Wick & Barrow, Nether Sopping . Counted aloud Spar Ollerenshaw 's. One afternoon, two smiths Instruction Do not set her down on anything with a roof on it Landed On the grass, two squares from the Tower door The log REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW Best china Used The Flight of the Two Hundred was the day in the year 2000 when the two hundredth airship of the Hoyle Works at Upper Clanging went up, and stayed up, and came down where it was meant to, beside the Obligatory Tower, two squares from the door. It is the only one of the two hundred that did. The works had been trying since about 1800. The attempt log gives the cause as under review, and will not say anything else until the review has found something. Two hundred years The Hoyle Works was begun by Miss Hoyle's great-grandmother to stop the Dark Lord, and has built an airship to do it, on and off, for two hundred years, under four generations of Hoyles. A hundred and ninety-seven of them came home to the Long Field, and two did not; and the town has turned the ornaments in its front rooms round to face the works, which is what it thinks of the works. Isaac Sowerby , who did sixty years on the rivets, has seen a hundred and ninety-nine go up and the same number come down, never in a hurry about it, mind. "It is the coming down that wants the work. She will get to it." What she wanted The Two Hundred was finished, all but two things, when the Forty-Eighth walked into the drawing office in the year 2000. She wanted forty bolts of oilskin and a spar that would hold. The oilskin came from Mrs Barrow at Nether Sopping, who would not have forty, and was made to find forty, and Miss Hoyle counted all forty out loud in front of the Forty-Eighth, and did not hurry any of it, and said that nobody had ever brought her forty of anything. The spar came from Ollerenshaw's at the bottom of the hill, and was made in an afternoon, by two smiths, without a word, after which the two smiths went for a drink and the town lost its mind. It held. The tube plate for her boiler was made by four hands as well. She was handed over to the Forty-Eighth with one instruction: "Do not set her down on anything with a roof on it. You would be astonished how often that has been the finding." The day I have spoken to a good many people in Upper Clanging about the day she went up, and all of them were in the street, and none of them can agree what time it was. It was a working day, and nobody worked. The works' hooter was sounded once, which it is not supposed to be except for the shifts. She went up from the yard behind the drawing office, slowly, the way the others had gone up, and then she kept going, which the others had not, and the whole of the street cheered, except for Mr Sowerby, who was watching for the coming down. She was seen over the Long Field, and over the stack where the Hundred and Ninety-Ninth is still on her crag, and over the Gloamwood . Then she was not seen, from Upper Clanging, and the town went to the Safety Valve to wait. The landing She came down on the grass beside the Tower, ticking as she cooled, two squares from the door, on nothing with a roof on it. The company got off, and walked the two squares, because the Prophecy says in clause seven that the Chosen One shall come unto the Tower upon his own two feet, and somebody at the works had copied that clause onto the flyleaf of a ledger, in a hand a hundred and sixty years dead, with four generations' worth of notes under it in four inks, the last of them one word in pencil: quite. The log reads: 199. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Two hundred years, and the one thing at the works that Miss Hoyle will not write down is the reason it worked. She does not write down anything she has not checked. The night The Safety Valve's best china had stood on the dresser under a card, FOR WHEN SHE FLIES, for as long as anybody could remember, and had been dusted every week and never used. That night it was used, for the whole of the house. Miss Hoyle came down the hill, and drank one cup of tea out of it, standing up, and said that it would do, and went back up the hill. The china has been dusted since and put back, with a new card in front of the old one: FOR WHEN SHE FLIES AGAIN. When word came up the valley that she had come down, beside the Tower, in her own time, Mr Sowerby said that it was very well done, in the voice other men keep for a rivet, and went back to his bench. At the top of the Tower, Grimspite the Inevitable was asked two questions on Miss Hoyle's behalf, and gave it as his view, in passing, that she would never get one off the ground in sight of his Tower. Nobody has told him that she did, and nobody has told her that he said so, and I have been asked by everyone concerned to leave it there, and I am leaving it there, in a book which I am aware they both may read. - H.B. Since The Two Hundred was put to the use of the Forty-Eighth and his company, and has since flown to a number of places that nobody can walk to. The Hoyle Works laid the keel of the Two Hundred and First in 2001. She is to land on the Tower. Not adjacent. On. She is on the slip. She is behind. See also The Hoyle Works Ott Hoyle Isaac Sowerby Mr Kell , and the china The Long Field The Obligatory Tower The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause seven

title: The Incident at the Collegium
text: The Incident at the Collegium "A very gifted young woman, a very small room, and rather more fire than the room had been told about." For the young woman, see Zephyrine Vance . For the Dean, who is fine, see Dean Fenwold . For the duck, see the Duck's Pond . The Incident Also called The incident. Nobody at the Collegium has ever needed to say which When 1989, after dinner Where The Collegium Arcanum ; a very small room Present Miss Z. Vance; the Dean; a duck Fire An unsanctioned quantity (the enquiry, twice) Hurt Nobody. The Dean is fine. The duck is fine Eyebrows Grew back. Magnificently Point at issue Whose name was on Dr Hapgood's paper Expulsion Drafted, initialled, referred. Never filed Consequences Eleven years of study leave; one Honorary Fellow; four hundred and six items, referred The room Wrong The Incident took place at the Collegium Arcanum in 1989, when a student called Zephyrine Vance, the best of her year, produced what the subsequent enquiry called, twice, "an unsanctioned quantity of fire", in a very small room, in the vicinity of the Dean and a duck. Nobody was hurt. She left. The Dean has been fine ever since, professionally. The duck was elected a Fellow, and the Collegium did not manage to hold a quorate meeting for the next eleven years, and nobody noticed why until the year 2000. High Table The facts, so far as I can establish them, are these. At dinner at High Table in 1989, Miss Vance said aloud that a paper, On the Kindling of Damp Materials, by Dr Hapgood, a junior fellow, had gone out under the name of the Master, and the Master is a committee. She was told to let it go. She did not let it go. Some time later in the evening, in a smaller room, the discussion was continued with the Dean, and there was fire. "An incident. A very gifted young woman, a very small room, and rather more fire than the room had been told about. The eyebrows grew back. Magnificently, I'm told." Why there was a duck in the room is not in the enquiry's report, which says only that it was present, and that it gave evidence. I have asked three Fellows. Each of them said that it had always been there, and then looked as if they had never thought about it before, and did not want to start. The enquiry The enquiry sat for a week and found that the fire had been unsanctioned in quantity, and said so twice, and found nothing about the paper, because nobody had asked it to. Miss Vance's expulsion was drafted, initialled by the Dean, and referred to the Registrar, and the Registrar did not file it, and the Collegium did not notice, because a student who leaves is referred, and a referral is not a departure. She went to Thistlewick and became a hedge mage and drank at the Gilded Turnip like somebody waiting for a letter. In the spring before she went she had borrowed three books from the Library, at a penny a day. The Dean's portrait was painted that year. The painter was asked to be accurate about the eyebrows, and then, on reflection, to be a little less accurate. The duck The duck had survived the incident, and the Collegium, not knowing what else to do with a bird that had given evidence at a formal enquiry, elected it an Honorary Fellow, and gave it a chair at the end of High Table with a cushion on it, and it went home to its pond, four miles off, and did not come back. The Collegium has twelve Fellows who are entitled to sit in Congregation, and needs twelve for a quorum. Eleven of them come to things. The twelfth is a duck. Every meeting of Congregation from 1989 to 2000 was inquorate, by one, and everything that came before it was referred: four hundred and six items, including the Library roof, and every one of them with the word REFERRED against it in the minutes, in a hand that got more resigned as the years went on. Nobody worked out why. I have been through the minutes, and I can tell you exactly why, and I want to say in fairness that it took me two days, with the answer already in my hand. The year 2000 Three things were put right in 2000, each of them by Miss Vance, and none of them in the way the Collegium would have chosen. The letter. Her pigeonhole was full. The letter in it informed her that she was on study leave, and had been for eleven years, in good standing, and owed eleven years of library fines on three books. How that ended depends on whom you ask, and both ends are in her article. The duck. She read the notice of an inquorate meeting, eleven present, twelve required, and looked at it for some time, and then at the Lodge, and then at the road, and said, "We are going to fetch a duck." The duck saw her, and stopped paddling, and came out of the pond, both of them having been at the enquiry. It was walked four miles, into everything, and set on its cushion, which it fitted exactly. Congregation was quorate for the first time in eleven years. Dr Hapgood was elected to a Senior Fellowship, five for, five against, the chair abstaining, and the Honorary Fellow walking into the Dean's water jug and saying, once, quite clearly, quack. Items two to four hundred and six were carried by half past six. The duck named its proxy by walking into Miss Vance and staying there: PROXY - Z. VANCE. PERMANENTLY. She has not used it yet. The room. The Dean asked her to do it again, small, in Hall, with buckets, for his talk. She agreed, on terms. It went wrong in exactly the way it had gone wrong in 1989, for exactly the same reason, which is that the room was wrong. The Dean did not move. He had not moved in 1989 either. "She said the room was wrong, you know. At the time. I remember thinking she was very probably right." Dr Hapgood's paper has Dr Hapgood's name on it now. The talk Dean Fenwold has given an after-dinner talk on the incident, The Man Who Was Fine, forty-one times before the year 2000 and a good many since. They laugh in all the right places. The line about the room being wrong was in it all forty-one times, and it was never there on purpose until the forty-second. It is the end of the talk now. The Dean has had the Hall measured since, and the measurements are before the room committee, which will consider them. I asked whether the Collegium had considered measuring the very small room. He said that it had not, and that nobody had been in it since 1989, and that he was not sure, now that I mentioned it, that anybody knew where it was. - H.B. See also Zephyrine Vance Dean Fenwold The Collegium Arcanum The Duck's Pond Timeline

title: The Obligatory Quest
text: The Obligatory Quest This article is about the quest of the Forty-Eighth, in the year 2000. For the forty-seven before it, which went the same way as each other, see The Chosen Ones . For the man, see Bram Thistle . The Obligatory Quest The Forty-Eighth, after the event Date Third Age 2000, the last of the winter Chosen One Bram Thistle, No. 48 Companions Up to three at any one time (that is the clause); eleven in all, at one time or another Objective Go north. Kill the Dark Lord. Come home. In that order, ideally Outcome The Dark Lord retired. The Prophecy read in full, and no longer binding. The Chosen One home Cliches encountered Very nearly all of them Receipt Yes The Obligatory Quest of the year 2000 was the forty-eighth expedition sent north by the village of Thistlewick under the Prophecy , and the last. It set out like all the others, and went where all the others went, and differed from them in one respect, which is that when it arrived the Chosen One asked the Dark Lord a question and then stayed for the answer. I have told the whole of it in Volume Two, from first-hand accounts, at length. What follows is the short version. It is still not short. The choosing Bram Thistle was a turnip farmer, and was asleep when the Prophecy Committee chose him. The minutes give his name under apologies for absence, with one goat. He woke chosen, took down a sword he did not seem entirely comfortable holding, and went to Prophecy Hall , where Elder Wispel unrolled the Prophecy to the far wall and told him it had worked forty-seven times. He asked what had happened the other times. He was told that it had worked forty-seven times. He was given five hundred crowns and three potions from the parish fund, and the Prophecy, which was, regrettably, free. A neighbour in the lane, a farmer, asked who was doing the west field. Nobody had an answer to that either. The company The clause allows a Chosen One three companions, and Bram, over the course of the Quest, went through rather more than three, though never more than three at once. In the order in which people generally list them, which is not the order in which anybody joined, they were: Merribell , Thistlewick's healer; Hob Grumnir , its blacksmith; Zephyrine Vance , a hedge mage, with a history at the Collegium Arcanum ; Nix , in acquisitions; Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III , a knight errant who could not find the north gate; Piper Quill , a bard, who was writing it all down; Corvin Ash , a doomed rival, from a corner of the Slain Wyvern; Wren Halloway , a cataloguer, from another corner; Roland Fairweather , a guest star, from a table near the door, who had somewhere to be; and Spare Cotterill , the ninth of the Cotterills of Upper Clanging, aged nine, who joined after a discussion with his mother. Which three of them were with him at the top of the Tower is a matter on which I have taken evidence from all of them, and every one of them has told me, kindly and firmly, that it was them. I have not adjudicated. I have noted that Roland Fairweather is the only one who does not claim it, because he left at the door, as he always does. See his article for why. The road north The north gate of Thistlewick turns back a Chosen One who goes alone, and is where it has always been, whatever Sir Aldric tells you. Beyond it is the Gloamwood , where the Thing In The Woods, about which Thistlewick had argued for two hundred years - is it a bear? several bears? a bear-shaped hole in the idea of a wood? - stopped being in the woods. Thistlewick will never believe it. Bram has not told them anyway. In the Gloamwood, on a log, the party met the Forty-Sixth , who had got as far as the woods in 1980, decided the woods were enough, and sat down. He asked whether the Forty-Seventh had come back. He has a sack of letters beside him from two members of his old party, who write every month. The south, which nobody does Then the Forty-Eighth did the thing that no Chosen One before him had thought to do. He went south. Forty miles south is Nether Sopping , where clause nineteen sends the heroes who come back, and in Nether Sopping is the Slain Wyvern , where they drink, and in the Slain Wyvern is a table by the fire, and at the table, at the time, was I. I asked him to do what I could not: to go round the room and be told. Six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. He did. He found forty-seven of them in a tavern, and sat down, and listened, and in the course of it he found out that the wyvern over the mantel is a goose. My history was finished on the strength of it. He paid the fee later, as I shall come to. He did a good deal else in the south, and all of it is in Volume Two: he registered with the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , on the strength of a character reference, a hat and the mat, and both of its bounty cards came off the board while he was there; he got oil up to the Lighthouse of Saint Bother , which is lit again, and can be seen from the crossroads, which is the whole of what it is for; he went down into the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth , where Ambrose Fitch was waiting to fight him, because that is what is done, and stopped when asked, which is not, and asked for a bench; and Bram built him one, facing the sea; and he walked to the cottage of Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, who told him the only thing he had come home with that was worth the trip. Ask him why. The north North and west of the road is Upper Clanging , where the Hoyle Works had been trying for two hundred years to fly to the Tower. With the Forty-Eighth's help Miss Ott Hoyle 's two hundredth attempt reached it. The attempt log reads REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Clause seven requires a Chosen One to go on foot, and he did, from the grass beside the door, which was as far as the airship would set down. Attempt Eighty-Four , who had been repairing herself out of the wrecks either side of her since she came down in 1860, was stopped, and is being rebuilt. ITEM 1 came off its crag for the first time since 1802. Hob Grumnir met Bryd Ollerenshaw , and they went for a drink, and are still arguing about rivets. The Tower The door of the Obligatory Tower was barred. There is a key under the mat, labelled SPARE - DO NOT LOSE AGAIN, which is the most honest thing in the building. Nix did not need it. ("Bar's on the inside. Classic.") Inside is a plaque that says the building was established approximately four thousand eight hundred years ago, under the same management; an Obelisk with forty-seven RENEWED on it; and a cupboard of hooks with the companions' trades on brass labels, one of them reading GUEST and always empty. The party climbed it. At the top there is a throne, and there was a Dark Lord on it, and he was reading. The top "Forty-eight," said Grimspite the Inevitable . "Right on time. Sit down. No? Fine. Standing is traditional." He had said "so, you have come at last" forty-seven times, he told them, and meant it the first time. Then the Forty-Eighth asked him why he did not stop. "Ah. The clever one. They're rarer than you'd think." He could not stop, and he showed them why: the sentence carved forty-seven times into the wall behind them, THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN, which is clause twelve, and which is not a threat but a renewal notice. When Bram told him who had sent him with the question, he asked him to go back and tell Halbert that the tea was just tea, and to listen to all of it, because he would like, once, for somebody to have listened to the whole of it. Bram listened. Then they fought, because the Dark Lord does not stop until he is stopped, and at the end of it Grimspite went down on one knee and said: "...Thank you." The Prophecy came down from the ceiling to renew him, and found instead a party of the correct size, at the correct place, on the correct date, and appointed it. Grimspite told Bram not to kill it but to read it, out loud, all of it. He read it, and it came apart in the middle of a sentence, and Grimspite the Inevitable stood up and waited to be renewed and was not. "Four thousand eight hundred years," he said, "and it was an admin problem." He signed a receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable, in case anyone asked whose fault this was, and gave it to Bram, and sent him home. "Grow your turnips. There isn't a forty-nine." The account An account of the Quest was drawn up afterwards, and is kept on a lectern in Prophecy Hall, as amended. It lists everything, in order: who came back, how many cliches were walked into and turnips eaten, what was lit and built and flown and rebuilt, and which verses the Committee struck. Of my own work it says this: There is a song about it now. Hosea Bellwether wrote it from first-hand accounts and it is, therefore, complete. It is not remotely accurate. It is not a song. It is four hundred pages and a pamphlet, and none of it rhymes, and I would refer whoever drew up the account to Miss Quill, who writes the songs. The rest of the sentence I accept. That is what Volume Three is for. Miss Quill's ballad was finished on the road, in the Gilded Turnip , after an afternoon on which the whole party tried to find her a rhyme for turnip. There is none. She moved the turnip down a line, in nine seconds, and everybody who had spent the afternoon on it was furious. The last verse, as she fixed it: 'And so he came home to the fields, and hung his sword above the grate, and sat down with a turnip, which was worth the journey, and the wait.' P. Quill, the ballad, last verse Of the official account of the Forty-Eighth there are, depending on whom you ask, one or two, and I have been asked by everybody named Quill not to say which is the right one. I have not. The morning after The next morning there were still turnips. There was also a letter on the mat, in the Committee's envelope: clause nineteen, a quarter's pension, and the key to a cottage at Nether Sopping. We trust Friday will suit. At the top of the Tower, Grimspite was in his chair with a kettle, and the book at the bookmark. The Committee struck clause twelve from its records and wrote in its place SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Bram walked south. He told Halbert Quy what Grimspite had said, all of it, in order, including the part about the tea. It took most of an afternoon. Then he came into the Wyvern and told me, and that was the fee, and I filled the last page. Six months later, after a very long meeting, the Committee struck clause nineteen as well. Afterwards The Quest is over, but it did not quite stop, and some of what came after is as much a part of it as the throne room. Bram has been in and out of the cottage clause nineteen gave him, which was Ambrose Fitch 's. Roland Fairweather came back. Sir Dunstable lent Bram a lamp, and the party went down the Stair behind the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost , which I have written up under the Stair , and found something at the bottom of it that the Guild had a card for. In the spring, which he had asked about every morning, Spare Cotterill went home to Upper Clanging for the birth of the tenth Cotterill. And every year, on the day, Bram walks up to the top of the Tower, and the kettle is on. Bram reads this article every time he comes south, and every time he corrects something in it, and every time it is the same thing, which is that he did not do any of it on his own. I have let it stand. He has asked me to add that it was a very long walk. It was. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Timeline Bram Thistle Grimspite the Inevitable

title: The Prophecy of Thistlewick
text: The Prophecy of Thistlewick For the people it chose, see The Chosen Ones . For the last occasion on which it chose anybody, see The Obligatory Quest . The Prophecy of Thistlewick Kind A prophecy, according to the title. A contract, according to everything underneath it Signed Third Age 1, three times by everybody Length Unrolled in Prophecy Hall, it reaches the far wall Copies The Committee's own; one issued to each Chosen One, in triplicate; a fair copy in the Forbidden Archive at Olde Evermore Clauses known Two, four, seven, eleven, twelve, fourteen, nineteen, thirty-one Marginalia One horse Read in full Twice that I know of. The second time was fatal Status Not binding, since the year 2000. Still kept The Prophecy of Thistlewick is a document of very great length, kept by the Prophecy Committee in Prophecy Hall , which for very nearly two thousand years told the village of Thistlewick that every hundred years the Dark Lord would rise in the Obligatory Tower and that somebody had better go. It was right every time. That should have been the first clue. It was never a prophecy. It is an employment contract, with numbered clauses, and the post it filled was the Dark Lord's. That was not understood until the year 2000, and then only because a turnip farmer did the one thing nobody in Thistlewick had ever done with it, which was to read it. The signing The Prophecy was signed in the first year of the Third Age, and Thistlewick has always held that the Age began with it. The elves of Olde Evermore , who were there, say the Age began with a great many things and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have not been able to get either party to say more, and I record both. What is agreed is that the signing was ever so long. I have that from an eyewitness: Mirabel , the oracle of Olde Evermore, who attended as a child of about two thousand and was bored. Everybody had to sign it three times. So she drew a horse on it. The Forbidden Archive at Olde Evermore keeps a fair copy made at the signing by a copyist who copied everything, and I can confirm that "everything" includes the margins. The horse is in the margin beside clause twelve. It is a good horse. I have nothing further to say about it, and when I asked the copyist whether he had anything further to say about it, he went on copying. Nobody has told me where the original is, or who held the pen for the other side. What it says The Prophecy has never been printed entire, and I have not attempted it here; Volume Two is large enough. These are the clauses I have been able to establish, from the copy, from the people they were done to, and in one case from a leaflet. Clause two: a hundred years "A hundred years" is a defined term. It means "such period as the Committee shall find convenient." This is the most important sentence in the document, and for two thousand years nobody noticed it. It was found by Miss Pargeter of Frostwick , who keeps the winter there under a contract of her own and reads contracts the way other people read weather. She went all the way through the Forty-Eighth's copy, which nobody had ever done, and turned back to clause two. The consequences are in Two Reckonings, which is a separate article because it needed one. Clause four I do not know what clause four says. It appears on the back of the Committee's leaflet, So You've Been Chosen, which is one page long and says CONGRATULATIONS!, and then, in very much smaller print, CLAUSE FOUR APPLIES. I have asked every Chosen One I could reach what clause four was. All of them said that it applied. The companions clause Elder Wispel gives the charge to every Chosen One, and includes this: take companions, up to three. "That is the clause," he says, "not my preference." I have not been able to find its number. The Tower has a cupboard on its fourth floor with ten hooks in it, each with a small brass label: CHOSEN ONE, HEALER, SMITH, MAGE, SPECIALIST, KNIGHT, MUSICIAN, and two added later in a cheaper brass, RIVAL and CATALOGUER. The tenth reads GUEST, and is always empty. So the clause is at least well provided for. Clause seven: on foot The Chosen One goes on foot. Grimspite himself explained why, when he was asked: "Because a thing that flies over and drops something is not a story. It is a Tuesday." The town of Upper Clanging has spent two hundred years building ships that fly to the Tower, and kept the ones that did not in the Long Field . Grimspite was of the view that Miss Hoyle would never get one off the ground in sight of his tower, and that it had nothing whatever to do with her spars. Her two hundredth attempt landed beside the Tower that same year, with a Chosen One aboard. As far as I know nobody has mentioned this to him, and I do not intend to be the first, in an encyclopedia or out of one. Clause eleven: fit to travel A Chosen One is certified fit before departure. It had been done forty-seven times. The Forty-Eighth's certificate was blank, because the Committee chose him while he was asleep, and nobody had examined a man who was asleep. Merribell found the blank on a pad of works fitness forms in Upper Clanging and did it properly, on the road, with stamped scales borrowed from the fish stall at Nether Sopping, the light of a lit lighthouse, and a witness. He is certified fit to travel. He had, by then, travelled. Clause twelve: the renewal THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. For two thousand years Thistlewick read this as a warning. It is not a warning. As Councillor Fenn of the Committee told his colleagues for years, to no effect: "That's not a warning. That's a subscription." Grimspite put it more shortly, and he had more right to: "It isn't a threat. It's a renewal notice." Every time a Chosen One beat the Dark Lord, clause twelve renewed him, "before you reach the stairs". It renewed him forty-seven times. The sentence is carved forty-seven times into the wall behind his throne, and on the Obelisk in the Tower there is a list of forty-seven dates and names, each ending in the word RENEWED, with room left at the bottom for a forty-eighth. In the copy issued to the Forty-Eighth, clause twelve has been underlined by somebody worried. The Committee struck it in 2000, nem. con., and in its place wrote a note: SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Clause fourteen: the first meeting The first meeting shall not go well. I have this from Merrow Halgate , whose party of twenty - the best-equipped that ever went north - fought the Dark Lord at the bridge and lost, as the clause required, and as was written down in advance. He has made his peace with losing. He has not made his peace with the paperwork. Clause nineteen: the Resettlement Clause A returning Chosen One shall receive a pension, a cottage, and such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable. It was added later, somewhere about the Ninth, when Thistlewick found that a hero who comes home is awkward: he knows what is at the top of the Tower, and he asks at meetings why the Committee is already drafting the next one. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, asked exactly that - "if it works every hundred years, why is there always a next one?" - and the cottage was ready by the Friday. The mutually agreeable distance turned out to be forty miles, which is how I come to be writing this in Nether Sopping , among most of the people in it. "They're not cruel," Mr Quy told the Forty-Eighth. "They're embarrassed." It was applied to the Forty-Eighth the morning after he got home, by letter, on the mat: his pension, one quarter, in advance, with no mention of the next one, and the key to a cottage at Nether Sopping. We trust Friday will suit. Six months later, after a very long meeting, the Committee struck clause nineteen as well. Forty miles south, a man in a garden read the notice twice and then went indoors. The meeting was eleven hours. I have read the minutes. They are, for the most part, about the biscuits. Clause thirty-one: mechanism THE DARK LORD SHALL NOT BE CONCLUDED BY MECHANISM. This is why ITEM 1, which had stood unticked in the Hoyle Works ' stores book since 1802, did nothing whatever when it was finally set down in front of the throne, except make smoke and knock Grimspite's bookmark on to the floor. "Ordnance is not provided for," he said. "Nothing is provided for. That is what a renewal notice is." How it ended Clause twelve, enforcing itself. The Forty-Eighth beat Grimspite, as forty-seven had before him. Clause twelve unrolled - the Prophecy itself, the width of the room, moving like something with an opinion - to renew him, and then, instead of renewing him, it turned to the party. It had found a party of the correct size, at the correct place, on the correct date. THE CHOSEN ONE SHALL BE CHOSEN. A NEW DARK LORD SHALL BE APPOINTED. THE ROLE IS VACANT. CONGRATULATIONS. "Yes," said Grimspite. "That's how I got the job." It was Grimspite who told the Forty-Eighth what to do. Not to kill it: to read it, out loud, all of it, because a contract that has been read in full has never once survived the experience. He read it. It came apart in the middle of a sentence. It did not burn or explode. It simply stopped being binding, which for a contract is the same as dying. "Four thousand eight hundred years," said Grimspite, "and it was an admin problem." The Committee keeps it still, rolled, in Prophecy Hall, with two clauses struck. It is not binding on anybody. The Committee consults it anyway, at every meeting, out of habit, and minutes that it has been consulted. Why the role was vacant this time. Grimspite said clause twelve had renewed him forty-seven times before anybody reached the stairs. On the forty-eighth it declared the post vacant instead. Nobody has told me why, and I have three theories from three tables in the Wyvern , which I give without preference: that it was because he said thank you, which in forty-seven fights he had never said; that it was because the Forty-Eighth was still in the room, listening, which in forty-seven fights none of them had been; and that the clause had always said so and nobody had read that far down. Grimspite, asked by letter, replied that it was a very good question and that he had a kettle on. See also The Chosen Ones The Obligatory Quest Two Reckonings Timeline The Prophecy Committee

title: The Thrupp Feud
text: The Thrupp Feud "That's not a falling-out." For the elder party, see Dorcas Thrupp . For the younger, see Prudence Thrupp . For the locket, see Arms and Artefacts . The Thrupp Feud Parties Dorcas Thrupp, of the Slain Wyvern , the elder; Prudence Thrupp, of the Gilded Turnip , the younger Began 1970. One day Cause Not remembered, by either party Conducted by Parcel Front Forty miles long Words exchanged None, for thirty years Ended 2000, by a jar, a reply and a locket Casualties None. A great deal of string Since Four pages a month, each way The Thrupp Feud was a silence of thirty years between two sisters who keep inns forty miles apart, Dorcas Thrupp at Nether Sopping and Prudence Thrupp at Thistlewick , conducted entirely by parcel. Neither of them will call it a feud, and neither of them can remember what it was about. It was ended in the year 2000 by the Forty-Eighth, who carried a jar south and something heavier north and was not told what was in either. The stopping Dorcas and Prudence Thrupp were both born at the Gilded Turnip, in 1948 and 1951, and were both behind its bar by the age of ten, and were by every account the best of friends and a terror to their father's customers. In 1970 they stopped speaking. There was no quarrel that anybody saw. There was no door slammed. "Thirty years we've not spoken. That's not a falling-out. We just stopped one day and neither of us started again. So we send each other things instead." The next year the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping wanted a landlady, and Dorcas went south to take it, and Thistlewick did not mention it, Thistlewick having never mentioned that there was a town on the south coast at all. Prudence took the Turnip over from their father in 1976. They were forty miles apart, and stayed so, and kept the silence up on both ends, which, I have been told by a good many people who have tried, is harder than it sounds. Thirty years of parcels They did not write. They sent things: by carrier, by tinkers, by the occasional hero going south and the more occasional one coming back, by anybody who would take a parcel and not ask. Nobody in either inn knows what went, because nobody was ever told, and nobody asked twice. The carriers on the coast road say that a Thrupp parcel was always very well tied, and that you could tell which way it was going by the knots, and that it was always a little heavier than the last one going the other way. I asked both sisters what had begun it, separately, a year apart. Dorcas said that she would not say. Prudence said that she would not say either. I am now fairly sure, from the way that each of them said it, that neither can remember, and that each of them believes the other can, and would rather die than ask. - H.B. The jar In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth came through the Gilded Turnip on his way out of the village, properly out, roads and everything, and Prudence looked at him for slightly too long and gave him a jar. "There's a town on the south coast. Nether Sopping. Follow the road out of the gate and turn left at the sea. There's a woman there runs a tavern. Dorcas Thrupp. My sister. Give her this. Don't shake it. Don't ask what's in it. Tell her I said nothing. She'll know what I mean by it." It was warm on one side. Dorcas knew the hand on the label at once. She held it up to the light, went an interesting colour, and said, "Thirty years. THIRTY. And she sends me THIS." It went on the highest shelf behind the bar, where it can be seen from every table in the room, and it is there still, and sealed. The reply There was then a sound from the back room of the Wyvern like somebody doing carpentry to a hamper. What came out had been under construction for some time, against exactly this day, and it was heavier than the jar was. Considerably heavier. "Don't open it. Don't shake it. Don't let it near a fire. And tell her I send my love, because I do, and she knows I do, and that's her lot." It went north. Prudence weighed it in both hands, put it on the bar, and did not open it for long enough that the whole room noticed. Then she opened it. Whatever was in there was worse than what had gone south, and deliberately worse. "...The cow." She was laughing. The regulars of the Gilded Turnip say that they had not heard her laugh properly, from the bottom, in thirty years. The locket Then she went upstairs and came down with the locket: two little portraits on ivory, one of each sister, facing resolutely away from each other, made at the Michaelmas fair in 1962, when Dorcas was fourteen and Prudence eleven, and kept in a drawer since. "It's hers and mine and it's been in a drawer since we were girls and I'm sick of the sight of it. That was HER idea, that was. I'll write to her. Don't tell her that. I'll write to her at the weekend." Dorcas says that the facing away was Prudence's idea. Neither of them has looked for the man who painted it. The terms Prudence wrote at the weekend: four pages, two of them about the Forty-Eighth, and one of those complimentary. Dorcas wrote back. It was the first letter either of them had written to the other in thirty years, and they have written every month since. Prudence's go south by the carrier on the last Friday of the month and Dorcas's come north on the first Thursday, so that each has the other's letter for a week before she must answer it, which Prudence says is the right amount of time. They have not met. Each has written to say that the other must come to her: Dorcas because she is the elder, Prudence because Dorcas was the one who moved. Each has had a reply saying exactly the same thing the other way round. Dorcas says that they are getting somewhere. See also Dorcas Thrupp Prudence Thrupp The Slain Wyvern The Gilded Turnip The Obligatory Quest

title: Timeline
text: Timeline All years are years of the Third Age, counted the way the sun does. Where the Prophecy counts otherwise, see Two Reckonings . This is every date I have been able to pin, in order. A date I have from a headstone, a ledger or a plaque is given plainly. A date I have from somebody's memory is given as "about". Where I have nothing, I have left a gap, which in a timeline is more honest than it looks. Several of these dates have been corrected by post, from the top of the Obligatory Tower , in a very beautiful hand. I have accepted all of the corrections. I have not been told the date of the correspondent's birth, and I have not printed one. Before the Third Age When What The First Age Olde Evermore is where it is. Thalion begins judging every arrival off the ledge, out of six. The Second Age Mirabel is born, about two thousand one hundred and thirteen years before the Prophecy. Elder Lirien and Elder Faelan marry. Calder begins fishing for the one fish in the pond. Before the year 1 The Dark Lord's engagement is held at the castle on the cloud, the Former Premises , so that no hero could ever reach it. None ever does. What began the Third Age is not known to me. It was not the Prophecy. The first nineteen centuries Year What 1 The Prophecy of Thistlewick is signed, three times by everybody. A horse is drawn in the margin. The engagement moves to the Obligatory Tower, which has a door at the bottom, and the first hero to arrive gets the job. The caretaker of the Former Premises is retained. 100s-900s The first nine Chosen Ones, a real century apart. About 900 About the Ninth: Thistlewick finds a returning hero awkward, and writes clause nineteen. 900s-1930s The Tenth to the Fortieth, closer and closer together, always in a round year. 1400 The Collegium Arcanum is founded, by the Founder, in one afternoon. 1500 The First Dean's portrait is hung, pending the Hanging Committee. 1702 Weeping Bottom is founded by Mother Ursula Pym , for the sea air. Her Rule of Life is four lines long, and one of them is about socks. 1749 The Sky Anvil falls into Meech 's top field. His great-great-grandfather makes it a gatepost. 1750 Pilgrims build a shrine round the gatepost. 1788 Great Dunnage seals its Counting House, "when the key was lost". J. Pocklington, Clerk to the Corporation, leaves behind the Door one chair and a note: WE SPENT IT. 1794 Sump : wasps in the well. The Water Committee is wound up. Cursed 1794. 1795 Sump: a general sense that things used to be better. The parish drafts Standing Orders for the Lifting of the Curse, and does not use them. About 1800 Nether Sopping begins throwing things down the Pit . 1802 The Hoyle Works begins its stores book. ITEM 1 is written into it. Bond No. 40, one cabbage, very large, "for the show", goes into the Bonded Warehouse at Great Dunnage. 1804 The Hoyle Works takes its first apprentice. 1811 Dame Honoria Pemberton-Gore's portrait is painted. 1840 Rollo, a dog, is painted. 1841 The clock at Upper Clanging goes four minutes fast. 1860 Attempt Eighty-Four comes down in the Long Field . 1890 Mabel Thistle, Bram's great-grandmother, is born. She grows a turnip as big as a chair. The twentieth century Year What About 1900 Attempt 112 comes down on her rock. 1902 Elspeth Moore is born. She will win the Thistlewick turnip show forty-one years running. The forty-second was fixed. 1908 A crate of ship's biscuit is stencilled for the store at Saint Bother's. 1909 The shipping stops. The Lighthouse of Saint Bother is kept lit for the ones coming home. 1919 The Cold Winter at Upper Clanging: the foundry is banked down for six weeks in January and February, for want of coke. Edna Hargreaves, later Mrs Tunnicliffe , is born in June. In the autumn, the Class of 'Nineteen, two hundred and forty of them. Beatrice Grumnir is born. About 1930 The Thirty-Ninth sets out. Mr Ottershaw of Fenmarch Hall begins the animals. 1931 Mrs Pardew's gran makes her last jar of gooseberry jam at Sump, and labels it BETTER. 1940 *The Forty-First, Halloran Vance *, comes home from the marshes with nothing, and makes a wyvern out of a goose and wire in two days. Upper Clanging, which sets its watches by its clock, begins to be four minutes early for everything. 1940s-1950s The Forty-Second and the Forty-Third. 1941 Abel Thrush begins carrying the post between Little Gore , Fenmarch and Sump, every day, for fifty years. 1949 Corvin Ash 's grandfather makes the black sword and cuts its name into his doorstep at Ashcombe , with MIND THE STEP under it for visitors. 1959 Wick, of Wick & Barrow, outfitters, of Nether Sopping, goes north, in the spring. His peg is still on the wall. 1960 The Forty-Fourth, Ambrose Fitch . Beatrice Grumnir makes a sword at the Thistlewick forge and sells it to a man going south. Perce Stagg breaks Frostwick 's winter, and it thaws for eleven days . The Adventurers' Guild is founded, provisionally. The Gloamwood Society is founded, to prove the Thing In The Woods is not there. 1961 Frostwick's first Winter Festival, on the twelfth. Perce Stagg cuts the ribbon, and marries Ida Frome the next day. 1969 Gideon Markup prices the Sword of Ultimate Ending . 1970 *The Forty-Fifth, Halbert Quy *, declines the tea. Dorcas and Prudence Thrupp stop speaking, and the Thrupp Feud begins, by parcel. Tobias Frayne 's first revival of eleven. Sir Aldric , sixteen, is due to keep his vigil, and keeps it in the wrong chapel. Mr Tinder, the parish's last fire person, retires, and the Cinder Fen is not burnt again for thirty years. Mr Cobley begins fishing for Old Tom. 1971 Edith Pellow sees the Thing In The Woods, and counts nine heads. 1972 K and M marry, and carve it into the driftwood on the beach at Nether Sopping. STILL is cut under it later. 1974 Walt Ashbury begins at the Eight Hours, Restwell . 1977 Roland Fairweather , aged eleven, is page to Dame Florence Ickworth against the Wyrm of Ickworth. 1978 Roland Fairweather is told that his prophecy is nearly ready. 1979 Mabel Thistle dies. 1980 The Forty-Sixth sits down in the Gloamwood . 1981 The Hermit goes up the hill to find out whether he has any wisdom, and stays. 1986 Sir Hamo Tench comes to Weeping Bottom for the sea air. 1987 Bryd Ollerenshaw wins BEST IN HALL at the Smiths' Hall in Great Dunnage. Hob Grumnir does not enter, having a cold. The Committee begins meaning to water the plant in Prophecy Hall . 1989 A year of beginnings and endings. Corvin Ash, nineteen, sits down in the corner of the Slain Wyvern , and Ashcombe floods in his absence, on the Day of the Water . Nix , fifteen, puts her gran's coat into bond until it fits, and starts the ledger. Attempt 199 is lost in sight of the Tower. Zephyrine Vance 's incident at the Collegium , with the Dean, a duck and an unsanctioned quantity of fire. Beatrice Grumnir dies. 1990 The Forty-Seventh, the Old Man's boy, comes off the ledge at Olde Evermore and lands on his feet. 1991 Sir Aldric goes out errant, with an invitation to deliver to Little Gore. Abel Thrush dies, in the spring. 1992 Sir Aldric talks to the Wrong Dragon about Horace until dark. 1993 Maud Penhallow , nine, becomes Roland Fairweather's understudy. 1994 Elspeth Moore dies. Perpetua Small wakes on the beach at Nether Sopping, with no memory and a headache. Sir Aldric reaches Thistlewick and cannot find the north gate. That winter his horse walks into a yard at Great Dunnage on her own, saddled. 1996 Mr Pilbeam rescues Princess Rosamund from the eagle. Merribell leaves the Sisterhouse at Weeping Bottom, because it has begun holding symposia. 1997 Much Pottering twins with Upper Clanging. Effie Gotobed and Spare Cotterill , both six, become pen pals. About 1999 Ambrose Fitch dies, in his cottage at Nether Sopping. The masons come within a fortnight. The year 2000 When What The last of the winter *The Forty-Eighth, Bram Thistle *, is chosen in his sleep. The Obligatory Quest, from the bed to the throne room. The Prophecy is read in full and stops being binding. Grimspite retires. The same winter On the way, and because of it: the Two Hundred flies , and lands adjacent. A jar goes south and a reply comes north, and the Thrupp sisters write to each other. A duck is walked four miles, and the Collegium Arcanum is quorate for the first time since the incident . Corvin Ash speaks at the Flood Dinner. The next morning There are still turnips. The letter on the mat: clause nineteen, a quarter's pension, a key. We trust Friday will suit. Clause twelve is struck, and SEE BRAM written in its place. Spring Washer , the tenth Cotterill, is born at Upper Clanging at six in the morning, on the hooter. Clevis Cotterill 's book pays twenty to one. That year Bram walks to Nether Sopping and tells Halbert Quy everything Grimspite said, including the part about the tea. My history is completed, and the last page filled. Autumn Clause nineteen is struck, after a meeting of eleven hours. Winter The forty-eighth frame on the Wall of the Forty-Seven still reads PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. Since When What 2001 Merribell addresses the Healers' Table , for eleven minutes, on water. It is the shortest address in the Table's history, and is minuted as the most useful. 2001 The Gloamwood Society's annual walk, three hundred and twelve strong. Nothing is found. The Society minutes it with satisfaction. 2001 Ott Hoyle lays the keel of the Two Hundred and First. 2001 Corvin Ash is asked back to the Flood Dinner at Ashcombe, and goes, and is early. 9 June 2001 Sir Aldric finds the north gate of Thistlewick, unaided. He has not found it since. 2001 Hob Grumnir and Bryd Ollerenshaw judge the Smiths' Hall prize together, and disagree for nine hours. Harvest 2001 Bram's first full crop since the Quest, and the best in the parish. The Committee asks whether it was prophesied. It was not. 21 March 2002 The first day of spring, which Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter. I sign this volume. See also Two Reckonings The Chosen Ones The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Obligatory Quest

title: Two Reckonings
text: Two Reckonings For every date in order, see Timeline . For the clause responsible, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick, clause two . The two reckonings The calendar Kept by The elves, and everybody who is not the Prophecy Counts The way the sun does The year Third Age 2002, at the time of writing The Tower About two thousand years old The contract Kept by The Prophecy, and everybody who works for it Counts Whatever the Committee finds convenient A century Lately, about ten years The Tower Approximately four thousand eight hundred years old There are two reckonings of time in the world, and the history of the Obligatory Quest is written in both of them at once, usually in the same sentence. The calendar is the elves' Third Age, in which this is the year 2002. The contract is the Prophecy's, in which a hundred years is whatever the Committee says it is. By the one, the Obligatory Tower is about two thousand years old. By the other it is four thousand eight hundred. Both are correct, and it took a woman in Frostwick with her gloves on to find out why. The calendar The years in this book, and in most books, are years of the Third Age, which is the elves' count. Olde Evermore counts in Ages, and has been where it is since the First; Mirabel has been making her prophecy about biscuits since the Second. The Hoyle Works ' stores book was begun in 1802, Weeping Bottom was founded in 1702, the Collegium Arcanum in 1400, and the Forty-Eighth set out in 2000. Those are all the same kind of year, a year of the sun, and they add up. Thistlewick signed the Prophecy in the first year of the Third Age, and has said ever since that the Age began with it. It did not. What did begin it, I do not know, and Elder Faelan would only tell me that the Age began with a great many things and the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have not been able to find out what the others were. I suspect that nobody has ever asked, and I suspect that is the reason. The contract The Prophecy counts in years of its own. Its clause two defines a hundred years as such period as the Committee shall find convenient, and every figure that comes from the Prophecy's side of things - from the Tower, from the Dark Lord , from the people who are paid to look after him - is a figure of that kind. These are some of them: What Says Means The Dark Lord rises Every hundred years Whenever the Committee found it convenient. Latterly, every ten The plaque in the Tower Est. approx. 4,800 years ago, UNDER THE SAME MANAGEMENT Forty-eight Committee centuries, give or take the first few Grimspite's tenure Four thousand eight hundred years, this job The same The Contingency Cache, fourth floor RESTOCKED EVERY CENTURY Every Chosen One. Nobody has ever opened it. It is six feet from the stairs The wayshrine's visitors' book The last entry, "Feeling good about this one!", is dated a hundred years ago The Forty-Seventh's, 1990 The Former Premises Two thousand years of Dark Lords, and nineteen thousand two hundred quarterly reports Contract years again: four a year, for four thousand eight hundred The calendar and the contract ran together at first, while the Committee still found a hundred years convenient, for the first nine Chosen Ones or so. Then it began finding shorter periods convenient, and then shorter still, and always in a round year. By the end the Forty-First went in 1940 and the last five went ten years apart, which is how the Forty-Fifth, a man who set out three centuries before the Forty-Eighth, is in his seventies and potting things on his kitchen table forty miles from here. Who notices It depends, very largely, on how far you live from the Committee. I have made something of a study of it, from a table in the Slain Wyvern , which is forty miles away and is where the people who noticed were sent. In Thistlewick nobody notices. The village holds both reckonings at once, comfortably, like a man with a pie in each hand. The Old Man's boy was the Forty-Seventh. A regular in the Gilded Turnip will tell you his cousin was the Thirty-Ninth. They went a hundred years apart. Nobody in the village is over a hundred. I have put all of this to nobody in Thistlewick, because I like it there and should like to go back. In Nether Sopping , everybody noticed, which is why they are in Nether Sopping. Halbert Quy asked at a meeting why, if it worked every hundred years, there was always a next one, and the cottage was ready by the Friday. Down here we talk in plain years, sixty and forty and thirty, and we do not make a point of it. We do not have to. * Upper Clanging believes the text.* The Hoyle Works read "every hundred years" two hundred years ago and made an engineering programme of it, and has not counted since, because the document had done the counting for it. Noticing grows with distance, I find, but it is not guaranteed by it, and engineers who take a document literally are their own case. In Frostwick, far to the north, there is one person who reads contracts, Miss Pargeter , who keeps the winter there under a contract of her own - nine years, renewed on time. She read the Prophecy through, all the way, and found clause two, and read it out. She does not do the arithmetic for you, and does not see why she should. The elves simply tell you. Elder Faelan told the Forty-Eighth that the Forty-Seventh came off the ledge ten years ago, a lovely boy, and that the Committee will have told him it was a hundred. "It counts the way the Prophecy does. We count the way the sun does." And the Prophecy's own people do not notice either, because to them there is nothing to notice. The Tower is four thousand eight hundred years old. They have the paperwork. I wrote to Grimspite, after the Quest, to ask whether he had ever thought it strange that his Tower should be four thousand eight hundred years old in a world where the oldest dated thing in the Collegium is six hundred. He wrote back, in a very beautiful hand, that the Tower was four thousand eight hundred years old, that he had been there for all of it and would know, and that he had the paperwork, if I should like to see it. He has also corrected three of my dates in Volume Two, all of them correctly. I asked him, in the same letter, how old he was. He replied that he had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, and that how old he had been when he took it was his own affair, and that he hoped I was keeping well. Reading the two together The rule I have used in this book is the one the world uses without meaning to. A date is a calendar year unless it comes from the Prophecy, the Tower or the Former Premises, and "N years ago" means two thousand less N, counted from the Quest. A span the Prophecy gives is in contract years, and should not be added to anything. Where the two disagree I have printed both. Where they agree, which is mostly in the first nine centuries, I have been grateful. See also Timeline The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Frostwick Olde Evermore

title: The Thistle-pedia
text: The Thistle-pedia Being Volume Three of A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , arranged alphabetically so that people will stop coming to my table to ask me things. The compiler, at work, at his table in the Wyvern, with the book. The hand at the temple is thought. The ink on it is also thought, after a fashion. My name is Hosea Bellwether , and I am the historian of the Obligatory Quest. I am not the only historian of the Obligatory Quest - the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick keeps minutes, and the minutes are very thorough about biscuits - but I am the only one who has ever gone and asked the people it happened to. I do my asking from a table of my own by the fire in the Slain Wyvern , in Nether Sopping , where the book lives. It needs a table of its own. You will understand why when you try to lift it. This is the third volume. Volume One was a pamphlet, and there is still a copy upstairs in the Wyvern for any guest who finds themselves short of something to read and long on time. Volume Two is downstairs and is the size of a door; it has been mistaken for one, twice, by people coming in out of the rain. This volume is the same history again, cut up into articles and put in order, with pictures, so that you may look up a turnip farmer, a goose or a clause of a contract without having to read the four hundred pages in between. The compiler I should say at the outset that I have never been on a quest. That is the qualification. Everybody else in the Slain Wyvern has been on one, and not one of them would tell a historian about it - they told me about the weather, and their knees, and what Thistlewick charges for a pint. So for a long while my great work was complete , in the sense that it had a beginning and an end and a great many chapters in the middle, and it was not accurate , in the sense that nobody in it had been consulted. Then, in the year 2000, a young man from Thistlewick came in out of the wet with a sword he did not seem entirely comfortable holding, and stood about. I wrote him down at once. Chapter Three Hundred and Twelve: The Forty-Eighth arrives, and stands about. It remains, I think, the most accurate sentence in the history, and he read it over my shoulder and did not dispute it. His name was Bram Thistle . He was the forty-eighth Chosen One of the Prophecy of Thistlewick , a turnip farmer by trade, and the Prophecy Committee had chosen him while he was asleep.
