I asked him to do the one thing I could not: to go round the room and be told . Six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. He did. Nobody does. They get two and go and look at a dungeon. He got six, and came back, and I paid him handsomely for a man with ink on both hands, and I wrote him into the history in small type at the bottom of page four hundred and one. The footnote says that he listened. Nobody else has one. Then I told him to go north, and that I would leave the last page blank until I heard how it went, and that coming back to tell me was the fee. He came back. He paid. This book is what he paid for. That was two years ago, near enough, and in the two years since I have gone round again and asked everybody what became of them afterwards, which is a question nobody in the Slain Wyvern had ever been asked either. Their answers are at the end of their articles. The world, briefly It is a small world and a long one, and most of it is weather. * Thistlewick * is a village in the middle of it which believes, sincerely and on paper, that it is the middle of it. Every hundred years - or every hundred years as the Committee reckons them, which is a separate subject and has its own article - the Dark Lord rises in the Obligatory Tower to the north, and Thistlewick sends a Chosen One to put him down. It has worked forty-seven times. Thistlewick is extremely proud of this, and has never once asked why there is always a next time. * Nether Sopping *, where I am writing this, is a wet fishing town on the south coast, forty miles from Thistlewick and the better part of a world away. It is where Thistlewick's Chosen Ones go when they come back, under clause nineteen , which gives a returning hero a pension, a cottage and "such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable". The distance turns out to be forty miles, and the agreement turns out to be Thistlewick's. As a consequence every adventurer in the world who has finished adventuring has pooled down here, in one tavern, with their old companions, their old grudges and a stuffed wyvern over the mantel which is a goose. The north belongs to Upper Clanging , a town of engineers who have been trying for two hundred years to build a ship that flies to the Tower, and to the Long Field , where they keep the ones that did not. Further north still there is snow, and Frostwick , and a chapter house that has filed everything. The west has Great Dunnage , a city of guilds, and in the south-west the elves of Olde Evermore , who have been here longer than the calendar and are very nice about it. The east has a magical college and a village that was flooded in somebody's absence, and the south-east a great house whose portraits watch you. And above all of it, on a cloud, there is a castle that nobody has ever reached, with a caretaker in it, who has been waiting. There are, besides, a great many standing stones, wells, signposts, hermits, chests and old men who know things. I have tried to give each of them their due. Some of them have asked me not to. What happened What happened, to put it as shortly as I am able - and I am not, by temperament, able - is that the Forty-Eighth went north, as forty-seven had before him, and climbed the Tower, and met the Dark Lord, and found that the Dark Lord did not want to be there either. Grimspite the Inevitable had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, by the Prophecy's own count, under a contract that renewed itself every time a hero beat him. He had been beaten forty-seven times, and every time it had counted as a renewal. The Prophecy, you see, was never a prophecy. It was an employment contract, and it had a clause twelve, and when the Forty-Eighth beat him the contract itself unrolled to enforce it. The Forty-Eighth beat that as well. You may read about it under The Obligatory Quest , and about clause twelve under The Prophecy of Thistlewick . Thistlewick struck clause twelve from its records afterwards and wrote in its place a note reading SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Six months later, after a very long meeting, it struck clause nineteen as well. He did not go alone. He went with friends - a healer, a smith, a hedge mage, a shopkeeper, a knight, a bard, a brooding man, a naturalist, a guest star and, in the end, a boy from a boiler - though never with all of them at once, and which three of them climbed the last stair with him depends on whom you ask, and everybody I asked says it was them. I have given all of them articles. I have not adjudicated. A historian who adjudicates between a blacksmith and a knight about who was standing nearest the Dark Lord does not remain a historian for long. He becomes a footnote, in somebody else's book, in small type. How to use this book The volumes are these: Volume What is in it History The Prophecy and its clauses; the forty-eight Chosen Ones; the Quest of the Forty-Eighth; the two calendars and why they disagree; a timeline. People The Forty-Eighth and his companions; the Dark Lord; and the people of the towns, villages and holes in the ground. Places Every settlement, ruin, tower and tavern I have been able to visit, write to or hear about. Institutions The Prophecy Committee, the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , the Hoyle Works , the Collegium Arcanum and other bodies with minutes. Bestiary The creatures of the road, with notes on which of them are what they say they are. Arms and Artefacts Swords, hats, benches and one crate, stencilled on all six faces. A Glossary of Cliches The well-worn conventions of the adventuring life, as the Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. Words in a different colour lead to other articles. Words in red lead to articles I have promised and not yet written; I am told this is normal in an encyclopedia and I find it a great comfort. The box at the top of the page will search the whole work, which is more than I can do with Volume Two. A word on accuracy Everything in this book is complete. Not all of it is accurate. Where my sources agree, I have said so. Where they disagree I have given both sides, or all eleven, and said which I believe and why, and you may believe the other. Where they cannot both be true - Merrow Halgate 's account of the bridge and Councillor Dree's account of the chair, for instance, cannot both be true on a Tuesday - I have printed both, because that is what complete means. Where nobody knows, I have said that nobody knows, and then, being human, I have usually guessed, and marked the guess as mine. I have been asked by the Prophecy Committee to make clear that this work is not authorised by the Prophecy Committee. It is not. I have also been asked by the elves of Olde Evermore to make clear that the Third Age did not begin with the Prophecy. I asked them what it did begin with, and Elder Faelan said that it began with a great many things, and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have left it there. So, I think, should you. Acknowledgements To the regulars of the Slain Wyvern, who told me nothing for years and then told the Forty-Eighth everything in a fortnight. To Dorcas Thrupp , for the table. To the goose. To Piper Quill , who was also writing it all down, and whose version has more rhymes in it and fewer footnotes, and whom I consider a colleague and, in the matter of scansion, a rival. And to Bram Thistle, Chosen One Number Forty-Eight, who came back and told me how it went - all of it, in order, including the part about the tea - and so paid the fee. H. B. The Slain Wyvern, Nether Sopping The twenty-first of March, Third Age 2002, which Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter is spring

title: Institutions
text: Institutions An institution is a group of people who have agreed to keep minutes. The world has a great many of them, and the minutes are where most of my evidence comes from, which is to say that my evidence is very thorough about biscuits. I have grouped them as they group themselves, which is by what they would most like to be asked about. Every one of them was written to for this volume, and every one replied, and two of the replies were in one word. Of the Prophecy Institution Seat What it does The Prophecy Committee Prophecy Hall, Thistlewick Chooses, sends, minutes The Quills Thistlewick Writes it down, in metre The Turnip Thistlewick, on three sides Grows. Filed here at the parish's request Of the road Institution Seat What it does The Guild of Guides Firstfield Meadow Explains everything, once The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Nether Sopping Registers adventurers, pending a review The Order of the Errant Coldbarrow Keeps a pin for every knight Of healing Institution Seat What it does The Order of Whatever Works Weeping Bottom Water; sitting down; socks The Healers' Table The Slain Wyvern, the back room Item one, round the table Of learning, and of work Institution Seat What it does The Collegium Arcanum The east, since about 1400 Refers it The Hoyle Works Upper Clanging Builds airships, behind schedule. By O. Hoyle The Worshipful Company of Smiths Great Dunnage Judges against the Schedule Smaller bodies Some institutions have no article, because everything there is to say about them is said where they sit, or because they asked. The Fete Sub-Committee, which strikes verses: under Prophecy Hall . The Gloamwood Society, which walks the wood and finds nothing, with satisfaction: under The Gloamwood . The Class of 'Nineteen, which dines: under Upper Clanging . The council of Fairholme, which defers: under Fairholme . The Working Group at Frostwick, which has a ribbon: under Frostwick . The Sable Hart's league table, which is not an institution, and would be very hurt to be told so: under The Sable Hart . The hedge mages' association, which meets in a lay-by and has no name: under Zephyrine Vance . The Order of What Ought To Work, which was, for a while: under The Order of Whatever Works .

title: The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional)
text: The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) For the town, see Nether Sopping . For the monument that only members may enter, see The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth . Not to be confused with the Guild of Guides , which explains things, nor with the Worshipful Company of Smiths , which judges them. The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Seat The front, Nether Sopping Founded 1960, provisionally Pending A review. Scheduled Registrar Mr Pell Crest A sword, a scroll, and a small question mark Requirements A reference, a hat, and Form A-1 Form A-1 Under the mat, 1989-2000 Filing By surname of the least important member Members, not provisional One The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) registers adventurers in the district of Nether Sopping , posts their bounties, and keeps their monuments. It was founded in 1960, provisionally, pending a review. The review is scheduled. It has been scheduled for forty-two years. The Charter On a stone tablet by the door: THE ADVENTURERS' GUILD (PROVISIONAL). Founded forty years ago, provisionally, pending a review. The review is scheduled. The review has been scheduled for forty years. The tablet says forty, and it is 2002. Mr Pell says that the tablet will be recut when the review sits, and that it would be a waste of a mason to do it twice. The crest over the door is a sword, a scroll and a small question mark. The question mark is the provisional part. The sign it hangs from is held on with six bolts; the last sign had one bolt, and was taken by somebody who needed a sword more than the Guild did. Registration "You cannot be an adventurer in this district unregistered. You can DO the adventuring. You just can't be one." * Mr Pell *, the Registrar, keeps the Guild, and has kept it for forty years. There are three requirements, and he will recite them to you whether you have asked or not. One: a character reference from a recognised authority, which means somebody with a chain. Two: a hat. The form requires a hat. It does not say why, and it does not say which; Mrs Barrow across the way sells one for thirty crowns, and no, they are not related. Three: Form A-1. Form A-1 was mislaid in 1989. For eleven years nobody registered, because nobody could, and Mr Pell looked for it every day, everywhere in the hall. It was under the doormat, which says WELCOME, six feet from his desk. The Forty-Eighth found it. "Do not say it. I am aware of the tower. I am aware that the key was under the mat. I do not find the pattern amusing." In forty years nobody had brought him all three at once. The Forty-Eighth's reference was written by Elder Wispel of Thistlewick , with the good pen. It confirms that Bram Thistle is the Chosen One, is of good character, and grows a decent turnip, and the last part is underlined. The Elder asked the Guild, through Bram, for a reciprocal arrangement, by which he meant that he would like them to know that Thistlewick's Committee exists. The Guild kept the reference. It is framed, on the wall, beside the Charter. I am not sure that is what the Elder meant, but he was delighted. The filing Every party that ever went north is in the Guild's filing, on its shelves, filed by the surname of the party's least important member, because that was the rule when the rule was made, and nobody has been able to unmake it. Finding a party is therefore a matter of deciding who in it mattered least, which has caused, Mr Pell says, a certain amount of feeling. Where the Forty-Eighth's company is filed I was not told, and I did not ask, because everybody I asked about the Tower said it was them, and I could not face asking them which of them was least. Cobb Lorrimer , a thief, is registered under T. The board The bounty board is in the hall, behind a small rope. A card on the rope says MEMBERS ONLY. The rope is eleven inches high, and could be stepped over by a determined duck. In 2000 there were two cards on it: The Crab of Unusual Size, which held the west beach and would not be reasoned with, and had been there longer than the town. Nine hundred crowns, on production of a witness. * M. Crooke, Bandit Chief *, who had a camp in the western hills and ran a six-week banditry apprenticeship with a syllabus. Twelve hundred crowns and the Guild's quiet relief. Both are discharged, in Mr Pell's hand. The fish stall added two bowls of chowder to the first, because it was extremely pleased about the beach. Monuments The Guild keeps the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth as a Scheduled Monument of the district, entry restricted to registered adventurers. The stone is not locked. There is simply a sign, and you are simply not registered, and that is enough. It is the Guild's only monument, and it has done more good there than anywhere: a registered party went in, and the Forty-Fourth stopped, and asked for a bench. The southern roster Mr Pell also holds Form C-12(S), by which a Chosen One may strike off any companion picked up south of the wall. It is the southern half of the Prophecy Committee 's Form C-12 and nothing to do with registration. "A-1 registers you. C-12(S) unregisters them. Entirely separate instruments, and I will not hear otherwise." Nobody had suggested otherwise. He had the answer ready, which means somebody once did, and that he has been waiting. Form Z In a drawer of Mr Pell's desk which most people never notice there was a single sheet, yellow at the edges: Form Z, Matters Not Anticipated. He kept it for forty years. In case. In forty years he never once used it, because every matter had been anticipated, by somebody, on something. After the ending the Forty-Eighth put a bounty card on his desk that had no authority, no number and a drawing of an octopus on the back, for Something Unscheduled , at the bottom of the Stair under Hithermost , which the party had fought and beaten. There was no form for it. Mr Pell said so twice, the second time more slowly. Then he opened the drawer. His hand, I am told, was not quite steady. He stamped the card DISCHARGED, and then held out his hand for the Guild Card (Provisional), and gave back one without. "A discharged bounty is a completed engagement. A member with a completed engagement is not provisional. The first in forty years. I shall mention it to the review. When it sits." He did not smile, quite. It was a near thing. Afterwards The review has not sat. Mr Pell has mentioned the Forty-Eighth to it, by letter, and the letter is in the filing, under the review, pending. The Guild is still provisional. One of its members is not. Mr Pell has had a second Form Z printed, at his own expense, and it is in the drawer, in case. He says that he does not expect to need it, and that he did not expect to need the first. The board has been empty since 2000, except for a card that says NO VACANCIES, which Mr Pell put up because a board with nothing on it looked, he said, as if the Guild had stopped expecting things. Mrs Barrow still sells the hat. See also Nether Sopping The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth Something Unscheduled The Prophecy Committee , for Form C-12 Cobb Lorrimer , under T

title: The Collegium Arcanum
text: The Collegium Arcanum For the Dean, see Dean Fenwold . For its most famous former student, who was on study leave for eleven years without knowing it, see Zephyrine Vance . For its most famous monograph, see Wren Halloway . For the duck, read on. The Collegium Arcanum Known as The Collegium; the old place Seat The east, near the coast, at the end of a dirt road Founded About 1400, in one afternoon, by one wizard Governed by Congregation; everything since the afternoon has been done by committee Motto REFERATUR ( Let it be referred ) The Master Out. Thought to be a committee Real power The Porter's Lodge Grace Six to seven. Referred for shortening Library roof Referred Honorary Fellows One. A duck The Collegium Arcanum is the oldest school of magic in the land, a college of cream-coloured stone, all towers and purple spires, on open grass near the east coast. It has given six hundred years of the finest magical education there is. Nobody there has ever been rude to anybody, and nothing there has ever been refused. Everything is referred. The arms Over the window of the Porter's Lodge are the arms of the Collegium, carved and gilded, and on a ribbon under them is the motto: REFERATUR. Let it be referred. Six hundred years of the finest magical education in the land, and that is the part they put over the door. I have come to think it is the most honest motto I know. Thistlewick 's is Not us, unless it has to be, which is a hope. The Collegium's is a description. The Founder In the middle of the lawn stands the Founder, in stone, in a pointed hat, holding up his staff. The plinth says that he founded the Collegium in one afternoon, by himself. Underneath, in smaller letters, it says that everything since has been done by committee, and that a committee is considering the plinth. You cannot read the plinth from the path. You have to stand on the grass, and the grass is reserved to Fellows, and the public is asked to keep to the path, which goes round. Everybody who has ever read the plinth has heard, from the gateway behind them, somebody clear his throat. The Forty-Eighth did it twice. The Lodge The real power in the Collegium is the Porter's Lodge, and the Lodge knows it. Mr Gedge, the Head Porter, is a large man in a dark suit with a ginger beard, and he stands in the gateway. He does not own it. He has the air of somebody who could, and has decided not to bother. A visitor needs a pass, which is issued by the Lodge, on the recommendation of a Fellow, and countersigned by the Lodge. Nobody knows any Fellows. "They don't come out." So Mr Gedge recommends you himself, and countersigns it, and issues it, three times on one card in the same hand, and the whole thing takes about four seconds. He put it to the Forty-Eighth like this: "The Master needs a meeting. The Dean needs a form. I need a pencil." Then: "Hall's on the left, Library's on the right. Keep off the grass." By the Lodge window is a board of names, with a brass slide by each that says IN or OUT. THE MASTER: OUT. The slide has rusted there. THE DEAN: OUT, and under it in the Porter's pencil, In Hall. Out to callers. THE SUB-LIBRARIAN: IN. THE HEAD PORTER: IN. The two who are in are the two who run it. Congregation Congregation is the governing body, and it meets to receive the minutes of the last meeting, which received the minutes of the one before. Its notices are posted in the court. I copied one: Item 2. That the matter of the Library roof be referred to the Committee for the Library Roof. Item 3. That the Committee for the Library Roof be referred back to Congregation, with thanks. Dr Hapgood, Junior Fellow of twenty-two years, goes round the lawn quickly with a great many papers. The Bursar refers them to Estates, Estates refers them to the Junior Fellow, and the Junior Fellow takes them back to the Bursar. In the year 2000 what he was carrying was a request for somebody to carry things. It had been going round since March. "Once more round! Nearly there. Never there." Dr Hapgood's paper On the Kindling of Damp Materials, which once went out under a more senior name, now has his own name on it, with a note by the Dean. That is one matter the Collegium did not refer. It was settled for it, by a former student, on terms. The Library The Library is where money goes to die. Its Appeal, for the roof, raised 1,412 crowns in the year 2000, and spent 1,412 crowns on the Appeal. The Library thanks you for your interest. On the floor under the notice is a bucket. Sub-Librarian Prewitt sits at a desk with nothing on it but an hourglass and a very large ledger, in a navy jacket and a tie, and she is immovable, courteous and correct. A book may be borrowed on a reader's ticket, which is issued on a letter from a Fellow. Mr Gedge's card will not do. "Mr Gedge is not a Fellow. Mr Gedge is a great deal more than a Fellow, and the Library cannot accept his letters on that account." It is never a no. Nothing at the Collegium is ever a no. It is not from this desk. She can refer you to the Committee for Readers, which meets in the Library, so that its members must all hold readers' tickets. A young man at the reading table asked for a book at Michaelmas. It has been referred to the shelf it is on, which he is told is a very long way off. The Register of Outstanding Fines lies on a pile of lesser registers. It is the size of a gravestone, with a brass clasp, locked, and Mr Gedge lifts it for her on Mondays. Most of what is in it is in one account. Miss Prewitt could not say whose. It was the largest number she had ever written down, and she wrote it down again every morning with the day's interest, and it was never once wrong. I asked her, by letter, whether that number is in the Register still. She replied that the Register is confidential, and very heavy, and that Mr Gedge still lifts it on Mondays, and that she hoped I was keeping well. Readers who want more should consult Miss Vance's article , which prints both of the documents I have, and decides between neither. On the shelf of the Collegium's monographs, in order of publication, are On the Habits of the Lesser Wyvern, The Lesser Wyvern, Revisited and The Lesser Wyvern: A Reply To My Critics. For some years there was a gap about an inch wide. Wren Halloway found it, in the year 2000, and looked at it for some time, and said "There's room." It is filled now, by * The Fauna of the Valley , by What They Are*, by W. Halloway, reviewed by three Fellows, one of them the duck. The Bestiary in this encyclopedia is hers. The Hall Dinner in Hall is at seven. Grace is at six. It is a long grace, and it has been referred to a committee for shortening since before anybody now an undergraduate came up. * Dean Fenwold *, in the Collegium's white and purple, stands under his own portrait, which was painted after the incident; the painter was asked to be accurate about the eyebrows, and then, on reflection, a little less accurate. Beside it is the First Dean's portrait, with a card tucked into the frame to say that it is hung pending the approval of the Hanging Committee. It has been pending for five hundred years. The Dean's talk, The Man Who Was Fine, is given in Hall, Thursday week, with light refreshments, and questions afterwards if nice. Tickets from the Lodge. Fellows The Fellows do not come out, and I have not met one, with one exception. At the end of High Table, a little apart from the others, is a chair with a cushion on it, and a card: RESERVED. HONORARY FELLOW. There is a dent in the cushion, and in the dent a feather. Nobody would dream of moving it. The Honorary Fellow is a duck. It was present, in 1989, at the incident in a very small room, and it gave evidence at the enquiry, and the Collegium, not knowing what else to do with a bird that had given evidence at a formal enquiry, elected it. It has sat in Congregation since, and has views on the endowment. It lives on a pond four miles off , with a Fellow's medal round its neck. In the year 2000 Congregation found itself short of a quorum by one duck, and the duck had to be walked, and the Forty-Eighth's company walked it, and it walked into everything. Its vote has since been held by proxy, permanently, by Miss Vance, who has not used it. The Collegium has been quorate ever since. It is the only body I know of that a duck has made more efficient. Former students The Collegium does not keep a list of its former students, because a student who leaves is referred, and a referral is not a departure. Miss Vance left in 1989 under papers that were drafted and initialled and never filed, and was therefore on study leave, unpaid and in good standing, for eleven years. A good many people in the Collegium's history may be on study leave still. The hedge mages who meet in a lay-by on the west road are, between them, better than the Collegium at exactly four things, because one of them learned from a book with four pages missing; none of them was a student here, and they would like that known. Afterwards Nothing at the Collegium has happened since 2000, which is what the Collegium is for. The Library roof is with the Committee for the Library Roof, or with Congregation, depending on the week. The bucket has been emptied. The Dean has had the Hall measured, and the committee for rooms will consider it. Grace is still an hour. Dr Hapgood's request for somebody to carry things came round to me, by post, in the autumn of 2001, as a historian with an interest; I have referred it back, with thanks. I wrote to the Master to ask whether he would read this article before it went to press. Mr Gedge wrote back, in pencil, that the Master was out. See also Dean Fenwold Zephyrine Vance Wren Halloway The Duck's Pond The Prophecy Committee , for comparison The Incident at the Collegium

title: The Guild of Guides
text: The Guild of Guides For the meadow it keeps, and everybody in it, see Firstfield Meadow . Not to be confused with the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , which registers adventurers and does not explain anything to them. The Guild of Guides Chapters Firstfield, at least Explains Everything, once Does not cover Lore Grades Tutorial Sprite, Third Class; Boss Warning Sprite, First Class; others Contractors One bandit per tutorial Procurement Sheep, ordered Received Pigs Restocks At nine Certificates issued One The Guild of Guides is the body that explains things to heroes at the start of their journeys: walking, talking, that a chest is for opening, and that the thing with a handle in the wall is a door. Its Firstfield Chapter has kept Firstfield Meadow , at the foot of the rainbow, for every Chosen One of Thistlewick . Forty-seven of them pressed the button really fast. It has one graduate. The rules The Guild has two rules that everybody in the meadow knows by heart, because they have been told. Once. A guide explains everything once. "Once! The Guild is very firm on once!" It does not say what happens the second time, because there is not supposed to be one, and Fizz , who has explained doors three thousand times, on several occasions to somebody already holding one open, has never yet had to find out. No lore. The Guild does not cover lore. The Dark Lord's weakness, the location of the Sacred Key and what happens if you pull the lever are all lore. A guide asked about any of them says LORE, and is required to. I wrote to the Guild, for this article, to ask what else counted. The Guild wrote back to say that that was lore. There is a third rule, which is not written anywhere and which every guide keeps: a guide appears directly in front of your face whenever you try to read a sign, to tell you that it is a sign. Grades A guide starts as a Tutorial Sprite, Third Class, and works upward. The grade every sprite wants is Boss Warning Sprite, First Class, who waits outside the last door and shouts IT'S WEAK TO FIRE. Fizz, of the Firstfield Chapter, practises at the sheep, which are pigs and are not weak to fire, and would ask you not to check. The grades in between are, I was told, lore. Contractors The Guild contracts one bandit per tutorial, to ambush the hero at the top of the meadow and lose. The post at Firstfield has been held for nineteen years by * Norbert Pelling *, who in the year 2000 had lost three thousand, one hundred and five times, and had never won, which is the job. The contract provides for a lie down afterwards. He announces every swing a turn in advance, for the education of the young. The Guild also contracts the stick. Old Hollis , by the tent, gives every hero one, and his wife Nell cuts them. In forty-one years they had given eleven thousand, two hundred and six, and not one had ever come back, until 2000. Procurement The Guild holds that a meadow has to have a fetch quest. It ordered sheep for one. It was sent pigs. The form says sheep, so they are sheep, and the farmer whose sheep they are has been told to lose them a bit. The chest in the flowers, with a Potion in it and a note asking you to close it, is restocked by the Guild at nine every morning. It is signed The Guild of Guides, and it is the only chest in the world that has ever been expecting you. The certificate At the top of the meadow is a sign: TUTORIALS COMPLETED IN THIS MEADOW: ONE. The one is painted over a nought. The Forty-Eighth was presented, by the power vested in Fizz by the Guild of Guides, Firstfield Chapter, with a Certificate of Completion, the first the Guild has ever issued. It goes in the accessory slot, next to the stick. Nobody knows why. He keeps it in the cupboard at home, with the stick. Afterwards Fizz has applied for Boss Warning Sprite, First Class, with the Forty-Eighth as her reference, and the application is with the Guild. I asked whether he had been consulted, and was told that that was lore. I asked the Guild for the number of its chapters, its seat, its founding date and the name of its chair, and the answer to all four was the same. It is the only institution in this volume about which I know less after writing to it than before, and I have written to the Collegium Arcanum . The sign at the top of the meadow still says ONE. Nobody else has come. There will be nobody else from Thistlewick, now, and Fizz knows it, and practises anyway, at the sheep, in case. See also Firstfield Meadow A Glossary of Cliches , for the tutorial The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional)

title: The Healers' Table
text: The Healers' Table For the room, see The Slain Wyvern . For its chair, see Ysolde Marrow . For its youngest member, see Merribell . The note at the foot of this article is Sister Merribell's, printed with her leave and at her insistence. The Healers' Table Sits Once a year Where Behind the red curtain, the back room of the Slain Wyvern On the door THE TABLE. MEDICS ONLY Members Every party medic within forty miles Chair Mrs Ysolde Marrow Item one The worst thing you ever had to improvise with The Table's Kit Goes to the youngest Shortest address Eleven minutes, 2001. On water Historians admitted No The Healers' Table is the annual meeting of every surviving party medic within forty miles of Nether Sopping , at a long table in a cellar room behind a door behind the red curtain by the fire in the Slain Wyvern . It has one item of business, and has had it for as long as anybody at it can remember, which is a long time, because the people at it are old, and good at keeping people alive. Item one The Table is sitting when its chair says so. Item one is the worst thing you've ever had to improvise with, round the table, in turn. There is no item two. I have not been in the room, and am not on the list, and the door says so, and somebody inside says so too. But the door was not quite shut in the year 2000, and I was at my table in the bar, and the members have since told me which of their answers I may print, and they are these. Mother Grizel, eighty-three, seven parties: a femur, set with a church candlestick, in the church, during the service. The vicar carried on. The candlestick is on her mantelpiece. Dr Hobday, seventy-two: a barbarian, stitched with a lute string. The bard wanted it back. He got it back, eventually. Do not ask the bard about the lute; he will play it. Nan Gilly, ninety: a wizard's leg, splinted with his own staff. He walks with it now. He has never said thank you, and sends a card. He is ninety-two, and still cross. Mr Spence: a tourniquet, out of a paladin's sash. The paladin minded about the sash. Mrs Marrow, in the chair: a duke's son, four hit points, nine weeks. Everybody has heard it. Everybody nods anyway, because it is a very good one. The four of them look up at once when the door opens, the way people do who have spent their lives listening for somebody falling. The youngest Until 2000 the youngest at the Table was Mr Spence. Then Mrs Marrow saw a Sister in the bar with a flask, and asked whether she was a medic, and said that if so she was on the list, and in, and not to dawdle. Merribell of Thistlewick was the youngest at the Table by thirty-eight years. Mr Spence says he was the youngest until about four minutes before that, and that it was lovely. When it came round to her she had nothing. Water, and sitting down, and socks; it always works. "I've never lost anybody. I know what that means. It isn't a virtue. It's an average." Nobody said that she would. Nobody said that she would not. Nobody laughed, and nobody patted her hand. The four of them looked at Mrs Marrow, which is what the chair is for. "Then write it down. All of it. Every cup of water and every pair of socks. Now, tonight. While you still think it's boring. Because one day it won't be, and you'll want to know what you did. And the day it doesn't, you come down here, and you tell us. That's what the Table is for, love." The Table's Kit Then Mother Grizel put a candle-end on the table, and Dr Hobday a coil of gut string, and Nan Gilly a splint, and Mr Spence, after some thought, a very good sash, and they were rolled up in canvas, and that is the Table's Kit, and it goes to the youngest. It always has. It had been a while. Merribell took out her book, the one with every ailment in Thistlewick in it, and turned to a clean page, and started writing down that day. The Table's Kit is not to be confused with Mrs Marrow's own kit, forty years of field medicine in a canvas roll, which she lent the Forty-Eighth for the road north, and which came back, and about the state of which she was very rude, as promised. 2001 The Table sat again the next year, as it always does, and Merribell had something to tell it, as the Prophecy 's own account said she would. She spoke for eleven minutes, which is the shortest address in the Table's history, and the Table minuted it as the most useful. The subject was water. The minutes are the Table's and not mine, and I have not seen them. But Sister Merribell has given me a note, which she says is the same thing, shorter, and which she would like printed where adventurers will find it. Here it is, entire. Contributed by Sister Merribell, of the Order of Whatever Works, Thistlewick, February 2002 Common complaints of adventurers, and their treatment. Dehydration. The commonest condition on any road north, and the cause of most of the others. Signs: headache, tiredness, being cross, saying you are fine. Treatment: a glass of water. Then another one. Exhaustion. Signs: walking into things. Treatment: sit down. Not on a mound with a curse on it. On a bench, facing the sea, or a chair. Wet feet. Left alone, this becomes a real condition with a real name, and I am not going to tell you the name, because you will like it. Treatment: dry socks. Two pairs, and a spare. Minor wounds, most of which adventurers call major. Clean it. Bandage it. Stop showing it to people. Revival. A person who has fallen over and is not breathing needs a medic, at once. A person who has fallen over and is breathing, and is lying there because it is pleasant to be knelt beside, needs to be asked to tea, by the parish, on purpose, through the door. Fitness to travel. I have certified one Chosen One fit, under clause eleven. His knee jerked. His pulse was good. He had not had water since Tuesday. He has had water since. Then see how you feel. I have set Sister Merribell's note in the box that this volume keeps for disputed matters, which is not what the box is for, and she has asked me why. It is because every one of the medics at the Table, on reading it, disputed a different line, at length, and then agreed with the last one. Mrs Marrow says that item five is the best thing anybody has said at the Table in forty years, and that she will not have it repeated in front of her. - H.B. Afterwards Mrs Marrow chaired in 2001, and will chair this year, and has told me that she is not going to retire. Nan Gilly's wizard sent a card. Nobody at the Table has died since 2000, and Merribell says that is not a virtue, it is an average, and that she is keeping an eye on it. See also Ysolde Marrow Merribell The Slain Wyvern The Order of Whatever Works Tobias Frayne , for item five

title: The Hoyle Works
text: The Hoyle Works Contributed by O. Hoyle, of the Hoyle Works, Upper Clanging I sent Miss Hoyle a list of questions about the works, having learned my lesson over the Long Field. She sent back the list, with every question answered in one word, and this memorandum attached, which answers them properly, and which I print whole. For the town, see Upper Clanging . For the field where the works keeps its attempts, see The Long Field . For Miss Hoyle, see Ott Hoyle . - H.B. The Hoyle Works Where The top of the street, Upper Clanging Sign None. It is where the noise is Plate DANGER. HOT. LOUD. EARLY Founded About 1800. Thinking, 1802 Chief engineer O. Hoyle , the fourth Apprentices Forty since 1804 Attempts Two hundred Reached the Tower One. Landed adjacent Cause Under review On the slip The Two Hundred and First. Behind THE HOYLE WORKS. MEMORANDUM. TO: Mr H. Bellwether, Nether Sopping. FROM: O. Hoyle. RE: Your questions, "The Hoyle Works", nineteen of them. DATE: 18 March 2002. Your questions are returned, answered. One word was enough for each of them and I have given you one word, and since you will want more I have written it out below. Where you asked the same thing twice I have answered it once. That is how a works runs. What the works is. The Hoyle Works builds airships to reach the Obligatory Tower. That is what it was started for and it is what it is for. It does other jobs, for the town and the valley and anybody who pays, because the town needs the work and a shed needs a roof. But the jobs are jobs. The airships are the work. Who started it. My great-grandmother, about 1800, to stop the Dark Lord . The parish register has the earliest entry I can find: AT THE WORKS (THINKING), 1802. Somebody has pencilled HOYLE beside it and rubbed it out, because the register does not take marginal notes. I did not do that. I would like that recorded, since you are recording things. 3.1. My grandmother kept it on because the town needed the work. My mother kept it on out of spite. I am not criticising her. Spite is a perfectly good reason. It built most of this shed. 3.2. I keep it on because I like it. You asked whether that was the reason. It is the reason. Two hundred years, and we have got to "I like it", and I think that is fine. The premises. The shed, the drawing office, the stores, the slip, and the yard. The plate beside the door says DANGER. HOT. LOUD. EARLY. All four are true and the plate is checked monthly. 4.1. There is a line on the floor of the shed. It is not decorative. Everything past it is hot, sharp, or under pressure, and three of them are all three. Visitors stand on the NO side. So does my apprentice. She always has. 4.2. There is a tank marked COAL OIL, and under it, chalked, NO WIZARDS WITHIN TEN YARDS. The chalk is not mine and I have not removed it. Miss Vance has asked me to. The answer was no. She asked why, and I told her it was a coal oil tank. She said that was fair. 4.3. The hooter sounds at six. It sounds at six on Sunday as well. The parish has asked about this, and the parish has considered it. The records. The works keeps four. Visitors read one of them and should read the others. 5.1. The attempt log. One line for each attempt: the number, where it was lost, and the cause. Everybody reads the log. The log is only where it stopped. 5.2. The drawings. Every attempt, drawn, before and after. Nobody reads the drawings. The drawings are where the work is. 5.3. The drawing office day book. What was done each day and by whom. It has one underlining in it in my hand. You know which. I am not going to discuss it. 5.4. The stores book. A ledger, ruled in columns, kept since 1802. Everything ever issued from the stores has a line through it when it comes back. It has been kept honestly for two hundred years and it is the only document in this works that has never once been under review. 5.4.1. You asked about ITEM 1. ITEM 1 is a line in the stores book, entered 1802, one off. The description column says ITEM 1. Four generations of this works have not improved on that description and I am not going to try. What became of it is in the stores book. The stores book is not open to the public. That is not a secret. It is a stores book. The attempts. Two hundred. One hundred and ninety-seven came home to the Long Field, and the Long Field has its own memorandum, which you have, and which you printed with my corrections, for which thank you. Eighty-Four is one of the hundred and ninety-seven and is in her bay now. Two did not come home, 112 and 199, and I have accounted for both of them to you separately and will not do it twice. The two hundredth is not in the field and is not going to be. 6.1. The last four entries in the log: 197. LOST OVER THE LONG FIELD. CAUSE: ENVELOPE, SEAM. LOST OVER THE LONG FIELD. CAUSE: ENVELOPE, THE OTHER SEAM. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. 6.2. Entry 199 was made in 1989. Entry 200 was made in 2000 in a fresh hand at the bottom of a page that had already said UNDER REVIEW once. You have asked me what the review has found. It has not found anything yet. That is what UNDER REVIEW means. When the review finds something, the log will say so, and not before. I do not write down anything I have not checked. The Two Hundred. She wanted forty bolts of oilskin and a spar that would hold. The oilskin came from Mrs Barrow , Nether Sopping , who would not have forty and was made to find forty. The spar came from Ollerenshaw 's, bottom of the hill, and it held, and it was made in an afternoon, by two smiths, which I had been saying for some years that it wanted. The tube plate for her boiler was made by four hands as well. I mention this because you asked who else worked on her, and the answer is most of the town, and two smiths in particular, and a lad from Thistlewick who carried things. 7.1. She was handed over with one instruction: do not set her down on anything with a roof on it. You would be astonished how often that has been the finding. She was not set down on anything with a roof on it. She landed on the grass beside the Tower, two squares from the door. The party walked the two squares. The staff. If you read the parish register at OCCUPATION you will find that it says AT THE WORKS on every line for eighty years. That is the staff. I am not going to give you a list. You would put them in alphabetical order, and half of them would be under C. 8.1. My apprentice is the works' fortieth since 1804. She has asked me nine times whether we are going to manage it, and been told nine times that it is not a question with an answer. It is a question with a schedule. She has stopped asking since 2000. I asked her why. She said that we had managed it. I told her that we had landed adjacent. She said that was managing it. We are not agreed. It is on the schedule. The town. You asked what the town thinks of the works. The town has turned the ornaments in its front rooms round to face the works. That is what the town thinks. You also asked what Great Dunnage thinks, and I have been told that Great Dunnage would like it known that this is only one works. That is correct. It is one works. It has built two hundred airships. I do not know how many Great Dunnage has built, and I am not going to write and ask. The Two Hundred and First. Her keel was laid in 2001. She is to land on the Tower. Not adjacent. On. You asked what she was for, and I have told you, and I would ask you not to put it in, and I expect you will. She is on the slip. She is behind. 10.1. Since you will ask what she is behind: schedule. Everything in this works is behind schedule. That is what a schedule is for. A works that is ahead of its schedule has written the wrong schedule. Visitors. The works does not give tours. People come up anyway, since 2000, to look at the slip. They are shown the line on the floor, and asked to stand behind it, and they do. Mr Kell at the Safety Valve sells them a cup of tea after. I am told it is very good for trade. That is all your questions. You asked one more, at the bottom, in pencil, which was whether the works will stop now that there is no Dark Lord to stop. I have answered it in one word on your list, and I will give you the same word here, since it will not take long. No. O. HOYLE. CHIEF ENGINEER. I had not, in fact, asked about the Dark Lord in pencil. It was in ink. Miss Hoyle has corrected me on this point as well. - H.B. See also Ott Hoyle Upper Clanging The Long Field Bryd Ollerenshaw , for the spar The Obligatory Tower , beside which The Flight of the Two Hundred

title: The Order of Whatever Works
text: The Order of Whatever Works For the mother house, and the afternoon it was settled, see Weeping Bottom . For the Sister in Thistlewick, see Merribell . For the annual meeting of every medic within forty miles, which is not a religious order but would like to be thought as serious, see The Healers' Table . The Order of Whatever Works Founded 1702, by Mother Ursula Pym Mother house The Sisterhouse, Weeping Bottom Prioress Aveline Stope Founding document A pamphlet. Four pages, stitched, damp at the corners Rule of Life Four lines, one about socks Doctrine None, and does not want one Symbol None; there was a meeting about it, and somebody made tea Habit White Soup Leek, for everything The Order of Whatever Works is an order of healing Sisters, founded in 1702 by Mother Ursula Pym at Weeping Bottom , for the sea air. It holds that theology is a distraction from the actual problem, which is usually that you have not had any water today. It has a pamphlet instead of a doctrine and soup instead of a symbol, and it has never been beaten on points. The Rule of Life The whole of the Order's rule is on the first page of Mother Ursula's pamphlet, and it is four lines long: I. Drink a glass of water. II. Sit down. III. Dry socks: two pairs, and a spare. IV. Then see how you feel. Mother Ursula Pym, 1702, the Rule of Life That is not verse, and Piper Quill has told me so. I have set it as verse because it is the only thing in this volume that everybody I asked could recite, and because the parish of Sump has adopted it as a by-law, and walked it, in order, down the street and back, and is the better for it. Socks were the line nobody in Sump had ever had. The Order's Sisters keep it. Asked what they believe, they will tell you to sit down. Asked when you last drank water, you will find you are being asked, not telling. The mother house Mother Ursula chose the valley for its air, the sea air being the finest cure for the chest in the opinion of every physician consulted, none of whom had been. It drizzles there, and has since about 1702, and the Order has not moved, because the founder is on the stone at the gate and it seemed rude. The Sisterhouse, its ward, its physic garden of ferns, and its shore, where patients breathe in through the nose twice a day on the Founder's orders, are described under Weeping Bottom . There is one dry thing in any window of the Order, and it is a pair of socks, held up by Mother Ursula in the chapel glass like a relic. What Ought To Work For some years before 2000 the Order was two. The Sisterhouse had begun holding symposia, and a party of the Sisters under * Sister Bewick * had found that it had a doctrine, and had been examined on it, and had passed, and dyed the trim of its habits black, and called itself the Order of What Ought To Work, east door. There was one door. The ward was divided down the middle by a line, and the patients crossed it in the night, because they said there was soup on the other side. The Prioress, * Aveline Stope *, held symposia on the question. An order that holds one is thinking, she said; an order that holds eleven has stopped. The minutes of ten of them ended Resolved, that the matter be referred to the next symposium. It was settled in the year 2000, without the eleventh. Merribell, who had left the mother house at twenty-two because it had begun holding symposia, came back for an afternoon and proposed that the door be opened, and twenty patients seen by each half, and whoever was through first was right. Whatever Works won, nineteen to one, on points, with Sir Hamo Tench of the Errant keeping the score from the bed on the line. The one was Sister Bewick's, and it was a real case of the Weeping Bottom ague, the first anybody had seen in nine years, and at stage eleven of her Correct Treatment the patient sat up and felt better, and Merribell said that was a point to the east, fair's fair. Then Sister Bewick asked to be examined on the Order's doctrine, since that is how a doctrine is settled, and the Prioress took the pamphlet out of a drawer, and Sister Bewick read it twice, and passed. She said that it was very short, and that she could find nothing wrong with it, and that that was very annoying. She wrote in her notebook Intervention. Supported. The eleventh minute reads: Not held. A queue instead. Whatever Works, on points. Soup. Whether that makes one Order again, or two that agree, nobody at Weeping Bottom would tell me; the Prioress said it was a question for a symposium, and that there will not be one. There has been soup on both sides of the line ever since. Sister Bewick's eleven volumes of notes are in the Sisterhouse library, where volume eleven is still very thin, and is consulted, I am told, more than the other ten together. Outside the valley The Order keeps chapels where it has Sisters, and lends them. Its chapel at Weeping Bottom, across the yard, has been lent for a knight's vigil, and it was the right chapel. Its chapel at Thistlewick , the Chapel of Whatever Works, has a teapot over the door on a bracket, because the Order never chose a symbol: it held a meeting about one, and somebody made tea, and that was the meeting. On cold mornings it steams. In Thistlewick the Order is Merribell , who is the only member of it for eleven miles. She keeps the most complete medical record in the county, every ailment of every soul in the parish, dated, in a good hand, and she has never lost a patient. On the coast road, Tobias Frayne , who had been revived eleven times in thirty years by kind people going that way, was told by the Order's Sister that there was nothing wrong with him, that that was the trouble, and that nobody would raise him a twelfth time. That is the Rule of Life applied to a whole cottage, and it worked. Afterwards The Sisterhouse holds no symposia now. The chairs in the chapel, which stood in two rows facing one another for the eleventh, have been put back in rows facing the same way. The patients sit down. Merribell has been back twice to see the Prioress, and they talk. I asked the Prioress, by letter, whether the Order would now consider a symbol, there being only one of it again. She wrote back that the matter had been raised, and that somebody had made tea. See also Weeping Bottom Merribell Sump , for the by-law The Healers' Table The Order of the Errant , for Sir Hamo

title: The Order of the Errant
text: The Order of the Errant For the Chapter House and its great map, see Coldbarrow . For the knight with nine pins, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . For the knight with one, see Sir Dunstable . The Order of the Errant Chapter House Coldbarrow , in the snow of the far north Clerk Mordaunt Knights In the field Reporting Quarterly. IN THE FIELD The system One knight, one pin Ranks Knight Errant; Knight Commander of the Chapter; Knight Errant, At Large (one) Admission A vigil, under the knight's own shield Armour Issue pattern. Sizes run small Motto Too small to read from the floor The Order of the Errant is the order of knights who ride out, and keep riding, and write home. It keeps a Chapter House at Coldbarrow , in the far north, with a great map of the island in it and a pin in the map for every knight in the field, and a clerk who reads the map the way other people read a will. One knight, one pin. That is the system. Admission A knight of the Errant is made by a vigil: dusk to dawn, in a chapel, under a shield that the Order hangs there for him beforehand, with a sponsor standing by and friends keeping the watch. It is a short ceremony and an old one, and it goes wrong in exactly one way, which is that the knight has to find the chapel. Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III was due to keep his at sixteen, at Weeping Bottom, under a shield showing a knight in a field, looking back over his shoulder. He kept it in the wrong chapel eleven times, two of them the Order's own Chapter House at Coldbarrow, which says CHAPTER HOUSE on the door and which he thought was being modest, and one of them a barn with a weathercock. The shield hung over the right chapel's door for thirty years, and the Sisters who own the chapel took it for a pun about vigilance. In the year 2000 he kept the vigil in the right chapel, with Sir Hamo Tench standing sponsor. Something came in under the door at midnight; his article tells the rest. The pins Every knight in the field has a white-headed pin in the great map at Coldbarrow, where they were last reported. A knight reports every quarter, IN THE FIELD, and is written back to, and the pin is moved, in ink. Not pencil. Pencil, Mordaunt says, is how they got there. The pins I know of, in March 2002: * Dame Winifred Cope *, at Little Gore , who writes every quarter NOTHING TO REPORT, and is written back to, VERY GOOD. Her pin has never once needed reviewing. Sir Hamo Tench, in a bed exactly on the line in the ward at Weeping Bottom , where he came for the sea air sixteen years before 2000 with a cough. He writes IN THE FIELD, and it is true; it is a field of a sort. * Sir Dunstable *, at the Chapel of Continuance at Hithermost . Mordaunt says that it is the one pin in the map he has never had to move. I put that down here without comment, because it is evidence of something, and the Order has not said what, and his own article does not decide. * Sir Aldric *, who has no pin in the map. See below. The review Until 2000 there were nine red pins in the map for one knight, six of them correct on different dates, and three of them correct in the same week, which is not possible, and was true. The Order kept nine files on him, each certain that it was the real one. A committee was formed to review the pins. It sat on Thursdays, and it was Mordaunt, appointed four times, and quorate. It could not fault the pins, and so had to fault the knight, and he agreed that that was fair. It offered him Knight Commander of the Chapter, with a desk at Coldbarrow, and a pin that did not move, if he would stay in one place. It was the one thing he could not do, and the one thing he had always wanted to be asked, and he declined, beautifully, and asked for that to be minuted, in ink. The committee then resolved that the pin should go with the knight, and created a rank that Thursday: Knight Errant, At Large. Wherever the knight is, the map is correct. Sir Aldric carries his pin. The rest of the story, and the full minute, are under Coldbarrow . Squires The Order permits a knight a squire, whose duties are the knight's armour, the knight's horse and, in the one case I know of, the knight's whereabouts. Sir Aldric's squire is his nephew, Pemberton-Gore the Fourth, who finds the gates. Every week since the review the Fourth has sent Mordaunt a note of where his uncle is, and the date, and the time, in ink, and Mordaunt keeps them in a tenth volume, which is the only one of the ten that agrees with itself. The Chapter House The Order's motto is on a scroll in the stained glass at Coldbarrow, over a kneeling knight, and is too small to read from the floor and, one suspects, too long to fit. I have asked for it by letter. Mordaunt wrote back that the motto was in the window. There are two suits of armour in the hall. One says CEREMONIAL. DO NOT GO ON A QUEST IN. The other says ISSUE PATTERN, KNIGHTS ERRANT, ONE, and under it, in pencil, SIZES RUN SMALL. The pencil is the only pencil in Coldbarrow, and Mordaunt has left it, because it is true. Afterwards There are no red pins in the great map now. In the margin there is a small card: PEMBERTON-GORE. AT LARGE. PIN CARRIED. The Order's daybook still says PINS REVIEWED, PINS REVIEWED, PINS REVIEWED (WITH TEA), and the tea is new. Sir Aldric found Thistlewick 's north gate unaided, once, on the ninth of June 2001, at about eleven in the morning. I sent the date to Mordaunt, with the names of my three witnesses. He wrote back to say that he had it already, from the Fourth, and that it agreed. See also Coldbarrow Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Sir Dunstable Weeping Bottom , for the chapel and Sir Hamo Little Gore , for Dame Winifred

title: The Prophecy Committee
text: The Prophecy Committee For the building it sits in, see Prophecy Hall . For the document it keeps, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the people it has chosen, see The Chosen Ones . The Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick Seat Prophecy Hall , Thistlewick Chair Elder Wispel , for a good while Sits Always Sub-committees The Fete; others, in the minutes Chooses The Chosen One, at a convenient moment Defines "A hundred years" (clause two) Forms C-12; S-7; others; C-12(S) is not theirs Funded by The fete Largest expense Scroll Biscuits Minuted The Prophecy Committee is the body that keeps the Prophecy of Thistlewick , chooses each Chosen One, sends him north, and minutes it. It has done so forty-eight times. It has worked forty-seven times. Since the year 2000 it has been the custodian of a document that is not binding on anybody, and it has not missed a meeting. What it is for The Committee was constituted to discharge Thistlewick's side of the Prophecy, which it reads, and has always read, as an obligation on the village to send somebody. The clauses that touch it are these. Clause two makes "a hundred years" mean such period as the Committee shall find convenient, and so the Committee decides when the century is up; it has lately found ten years convenient, and it prefers years that end in nought. Clause eleven requires a Chosen One to be certified fit before he leaves. Clause four applies; it says so on the back of the leaflet. And clause nineteen, which the Committee added itself, somewhere about the Ninth, concerns a cottage at the coast. None of the Committee has ever remarked on the arithmetic of clause two, in my hearing or in the minutes, and I have read the minutes. I am a Nether Sopping man, and I counted. I put the sum in Volume Two and in Two Reckonings , and the Committee has read both, and filed them, and nobody in Thistlewick has mentioned it to me since. I have stopped expecting them to. It is not that they disagree. It is that, in Thistlewick, it does not come up. Who sits on it The Elder chairs. Elder Wispel has done so for a good while; asked how long, he says a good while, and means it. He gives each Chosen One the Prophecy by unrolling it until it reaches the far wall, and the gold from the parish fund, and the potions from the parish fund. "The prophecy is, regrettably, free." The Clerk sits at the end of the table, by the door, with Form C-12, and the weariness of a man who has answered every question before you ask it. He has no name in the minutes; he is the Clerk. The councillors sit down the side. One has, for as long as anybody remembers, been asking whether the Dark Lord shall be slain or shall be defeated, because slain is a commitment. Another, Councillor Fenn , held for twenty years that clause twelve was the problem. "That's not a warning. That's a subscription." He was right, and the minutes of the week of the ending say that he wished it minuted that he had been saying so. He carries the key to the struck material on his belt. The Fete Sub-Committee reports to the Committee on everything that is to be read aloud at the fete, which is where the Prophecy Fund's income comes from, and strikes what cannot be. Its most famous minute is the one on the wall of the Hall, carried four to one; the one against was Mrs Wispel. How it chooses In session, at a convenient moment. The candidate need not be present. The Forty-Eighth was not; he was asleep, two fields away, and the minutes of the meeting at which he was chosen give his name under apologies for absence, with one goat. I do not know why there is a goat, and I have asked, and the Clerk said that the minutes were the minutes. Nobody has ever been chosen who said no, because nobody has ever been asked. This is also why the Forty-Eighth's certificate of fitness, under clause eleven, was blank when he set out: nobody had examined a man who was asleep. It was filled in, eventually, on the road, by Merribell , in front of a witness, with a halibut. Its paperwork The Committee's forms are numerous and I have not seen all of them. The ones that every Chosen One meets are: The leaflet, So You've Been Chosen. One page. CONGRATULATIONS! and then, smaller, CLAUSE FOUR APPLIES. Form C-12, Roster Amendments, held by the Clerk, by which a Chosen One may strike a companion off and send them home to think about it. Thistlewick personnel only. A companion struck off keeps the kit and the experience; it was tried the other way once, and there is a form about why not. Anybody picked up south of the wall is on Form C-12(S), which is held in Nether Sopping by Mr Pell of the Adventurers' Guild . "Not my circus." Form S-7, Application to Consult Struck Material (Verse), countersigned as to the wording, which admits the bearer through the door behind the red curtain to the box. It has been used once that I know of, by Piper Quill , who signed for it in metre. The certificate of fitness to travel, under clause eleven. The rest are on the shelves of the Hall, which are nearly all minutes, and include The Meeting To Decide When To Hold The Meeting, which is in at least four volumes, and What To Do If The Chosen One Is Not In, which recommends leaving a note. What it keeps The Committee keeps everything. It keeps the Prophecy, rolled. It keeps the Wall of the Forty-Seven, and since 2000 a forty-eighth frame. It keeps a box of two hundred years of struck verses, one to a slip, dated and initialled, behind a door behind a curtain, under lock, so that nobody may read them; and it keeps them in the best box it owns. It keeps a potted plant, which it has meant to water since 1987, because it is in the minutes. It keeps the accounts of the Prophecy Fund: income, the fete; expenditure, swords, forty-seven, and scroll, a great deal. It keeps its own minutes most carefully of all, because the minutes are how the Committee knows that it has met. The year 2000 The Committee's minute book lies open, in the Hall, at the week the Forty-Eighth came home, and anybody may read it: ITEM 3. Clause twelve. Struck, nem. con. In its place, a note: SEE BRAM. ITEM 4. Clause nineteen. Applies. Letter sent, cottage aired. Friday suggested. ITEM 5. Councillor Fenn wished it minuted that he had been saying so. Minuted. I wish to be fair to the Committee here, because it is easy not to be. Item three was carried without a vote against. It was the end of the thing it existed to do, and it struck it, and wrote in its place the name of a turnip farmer, which is as near to an apology as a committee can get. Item four was the Committee being a committee. Six months later, after a meeting of eleven hours which Elder Wispel chaired throughout, it struck clause nineteen as well. I have the minutes of that meeting. They are mostly about the biscuits. They are also, on the last page, about clause nineteen, and it is struck, and the cottage at the coast is Bram 's to use when he comes south. Since the ending there has been a lectern by the door, and on it a ledger, The Obligatory Quest, as amended, which is kept up to date, and ends The account ends there, for the present. It is the only document the Committee has ever kept that admits it is not finished. Afterwards The Committee still meets. It has nothing to choose, nobody to send, and no clause twelve, and it meets anyway, as it always has, and consults the Prophecy at every meeting, out of habit, and minutes that it has been consulted. Twice since 2000 it has minuted that it might need to see Bram, as the note says; neither time did it, and neither time has it said what about. It offered him a seat. He declined, because it meets in planting time. The minutes record his apologies for absence, without a goat. The forty-eighth frame on the Wall still says PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. I have written to the Committee three times to say where the sitter is. My letters are filed under no change. I asked the Clerk, for this article, what the Committee is for now. He looked at me with the weariness of a man who had answered the question before, and said that it was for meeting. I have thought about it a good deal since, and I do not think he was being unkind, or wrong. Thistlewick has a great many things in it that are for nothing in particular now, a sword above a fireplace among them, and the village is fond of all of them. - H.B. See also Prophecy Hall The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Elder Wispel Councillor Fenn The Quills , who write the account

title: The Quills
text: The Quills For the senior chronicler, see Ambrosine Quill . For the junior one, see Piper Quill , and her own page, From the Notebooks of P. Quill . For the body they write for, see The Prophecy Committee . The Quills of Thistlewick Office Chroniclers to the Committee For Four generations Accounts written Forty-eight, by some reckoning Wear Crimson House style Never let the truth spoil the metre Wolves Customary Approved by The Committee, unread Senior Ambrosine Junior, and first to write down what happened Piper The Quills are the family of Thistlewick that writes the official account of each Chosen One for the Prophecy Committee , in metre, and has done so for four generations. They are very good at it. Until the year 2000 none of them had ever written down what actually happened, and none of them had needed to, because the shape is known. The office When the Committee chooses, a Quill begins. The account is begun the morning the Committee votes, and is approved on the Tuesday, and is very often finished before the Chosen One is, because a Chosen One has a beginning and an end, and in between he walks, and the walking can be written ahead. The Committee approves every account. It does not read them. The Quills have known this for a long time, and have gone on writing them well, which I think is the most professional thing in Thistlewick. The Quills also write the text under the portraits on the Wall of the Forty-Seven, every one of them, and their cards are tucked into the frames. The Prophecy's own preamble quotes one of them, Piper's grandmother, who wrote numbers forty to forty-three. I have noticed, being a Nether Sopping man, that four generations is a short time in which to write forty-seven accounts that are a hundred years apart. Nobody in the family has remarked on this, and I have not raised it with them, because the answer is in clause two, and in Two Reckonings , and because it is not the Quills' fault what the Committee finds convenient. The house style The house style is one line long: never let the truth spoil the metre. It is not cynical. It is a craftsman's rule, and it is kept by craftsmen. It produces accounts that scan, which is more than most history does; I have read Volume Two again, and I know. Its conventions are easily learned, and every account keeps them. The Chosen One is an orphan of humble birth, because nobody goes north with a mother; it does not scan. One of his companions dies, in about canto nine, of nothing in particular, because it scans. He slays the Dark Lord at the top of the Tower in a thunderstorm, in a rhyme on tower that was never going to be anything but hour. And there is a wolf. Piper's grandmother had a wolf in forty-one, forty-two and forty-three, and it was the same wolf. A good wolf. The rebellion Piper Quill's whole professional rebellion has been to let the truth spoil the metre. She narrates things as they happen, in the third person, at volume, whether or not it is convenient, and writes them down, and some of them scan. She walked north with the Forty-Eighth to do it, which no Quill had done before, the shape being known. On the way she read every verse in the Committee's box of struck material, on Form S-7, and printed none; finished the ballad; and came second at the Bell in Great Dunnage , by one point, to a man who does birdcalls. She is, as her family has noticed, the first Quill ever to win a prize for writing down what actually happened, and it was for coming second, and she says that is about right. The account of the Forty-Eighth The official account of the Forty-Eighth is The Lay of the Forty-Eighth , by A. Quill, in twelve cantos, with a very good middle. What it says now is a matter on which the Quills disagree with one another, very civilly, and have asked me not to settle. The card in the forty-eighth frame on the Wall gives the account, and who wrote it, and a stamp; I have seen the card, and I say only that there are, depending on whom you ask, one official account of the Forty-Eighth or two, and that both are the authorised version. The articles on Ambrosine Quill and Piper Quill give both, and so does the Committee's own Clerk, who has been heard to say either APPROVED or AMENDED, depending on the day, and looking pleased about it either way. What is not in dispute is that, for the first time in four generations, somebody told a Quill that her account was very good, and meant it, and that she has not forgotten it. Afterwards There is no Forty-Ninth to write. The Quills are Chroniclers to the Committee still, and the Committee still meets, and the Quills still attend, and take the minutes in metre when the Clerk is not looking. Ambrosine reads her own account again most mornings, she says, for the middle. Piper is writing everything else down, and her notebooks are in double figures. The two of them nod to one another now, across a room, as one professional to another. I asked each of them, separately, which of them was the better writer. Ambrosine said Piper. Piper said Ambrosine. Then they both said that I was not, and that it was not close, and I have decided to take that as a family resemblance. See also Ambrosine Quill Piper Quill From the Notebooks of P. Quill Prophecy Hall , for the Wall and the box The Prophecy Committee

title: The Turnip
text: The Turnip This article is about the turnip, as an institution of Thistlewick. For the turnip as a creature of the road, which has had enough, see the Bestiary . For the one on the plinth, see The Gilded Turnip . For the small brown thing that lives in them, see Bramus agricola . For a rhyme, there isn't one. The Turnip Also called Brassica rapa (W. Halloway); a turnip; in Thistlewick, generally, "it" Seat Thistlewick , on three sides Founded Before the minutes What it does Grows. Is eaten. Is painted, on occasion Heraldry Rampant, on a field of slightly different turnips Price Two crowns, at the market stall. "Fresh! Mostly!" Restores A measurable amount. I have the measurement. It is not large Vintages The '87, very good. The '91, not spoken of Furniture One chair Militant On the road, occasionally. Not in Thistlewick, which would like that understood Rhymes None. Parsnip is a different vegetable Swords found in None. They have checked. All of them The turnip is a root vegetable, and is grown, eaten, painted, sat on, sung about, pressed between the pages of souvenir books, carved into the shape of a sword for an occasion, kept back for a supper that is a hundred years late, and taken very seriously indeed in Thistlewick , which grows nothing else, and has never seen the need. It is the produce of the village, the charge on its crest, the name of its inn, the subject of its only song and the profession of its most famous son. Thistlewick asked that it be filed in this volume under Institutions. I have done so. I would like it understood that I did not argue, and that this was not because I agreed. A note on the filing I define an institution, in the introduction to this volume, as a group of people who have agreed to keep minutes. The turnip keeps no minutes. When I put this to the parish of Thistlewick, by letter, I received in reply a letter of four pages from the clerk to the Prophecy Committee , setting out that the turnip had been in the village longer than the Committee had, that it had sent forty-eight Chosen Ones north on its strength, that it was on the crest and over the door of the inn, and that if those were not the marks of an institution then the clerk would be glad to know what were. The fourth page was about biscuits, and I think was from another letter. Wren Halloway , who keeps the Bestiary in this volume and who does not care for any of this, wrote to say that the turnip is a plant, Brassica rapa, and that she has already given it an entry, under its militant form, and that if it went anywhere else it should go in the Bestiary, and that nobody should send her theories. I have not sent her a theory. I have sent her this article, which is not a theory, but is long, and she has written back one word, which was fine, and was underlined, which I have chosen to read as approval. A vegetable, then, filed under the institutions, between a college that has been referring things since about 1400 and a works that has been building airships for two hundred years behind schedule. I have looked at it there for some time, in proof, and I think it holds its own. - H.B. What a turnip is I had better say at the start what a turnip is, because I am a Nether Sopping man and we do not grow them, and so I have had to find out, and it has taken me the best part of two years, and I am still not certain I have it all. A turnip is a root. It is round, or roundish, white at the bottom and purple at the top, where it has seen the sun, and it has leaves, which Thistlewick does not eat, except in a hard winter, and does not talk about afterwards. It grows in the ground. It is planted in the spring and pulled in the autumn, and between the two it does nothing at all that anybody can see, which I am told is the whole art of it, and which I am told also by the farmers of Thistlewick is a great deal harder than it looks, and I believe them, because they say it with the face of people who have tried to explain it before. I asked a farmer of Thistlewick what made a good turnip, and he thought about it for a long time, leaning on a gate, and then said, "Being a turnip." I asked another, and she said, "Not being a parsnip," and looked at me as if I might be one. I asked Bram Thistle , who is the authority, and he said that a good turnip was one that came up where you put it, and was a turnip when it did, and that you would be surprised how often that was all anybody needed, and that he did not only mean turnips. I have thought about that a good deal since. I think it is the best definition in this volume, and I have looked. The Bestiary gives the turnip one line of description, which is that it is "a turnip, in every particular but one". Thistlewick gives it no description at all. Asked to describe one, a Thistlewick person will hold one up. The fields The turnip fields of Thistlewick go round the village on three sides. The fourth side is the pond, which has no fish in it, and would, I suspect, have been turnips also if anybody had been able to work out how to drain it. The village fingerpost on the square reads: NORTH: The Obligatory Tower. 200 leagues. SOUTH: The turnip fields. 40 paces. EAST: The pond. There are no fish in it. WEST: Also the turnip fields. It is the most accurate signpost I have ever read, and I have read a great many, some of them in Firstfield , which explain themselves at length. It does not mention that the fields to the south and the fields to the west are the same fields, going round the corner, because to a Thistlewick person this does not need mentioning. To a visitor it is the first thing you notice, and then the only thing. Several of the rows are worth seeing, and I give them in order, walking down from the lane. The Thistle row. Bram Thistle's own row, planted the spring of the year 2000, a few weeks before he was Chosen. It came up beautifully, he says, "which felt a little pointed, at the time". It has a neat hole in it with a label on a stick, which is the type locality of a species of science, and is under Bramus agricola . The species eats turnip. Its namesake does too. Neither of them has been asked to comment on this and I am not going to be the one. The flag. In the next row but one is a turnip with a tiny flag stuck in it, very old, reading KEPT BACK FOR THE CHOSEN ONE'S SUPPER. Nobody knows which Chosen One. The flag is older than anybody's grandmother's grandmother, and they plant a fresh turnip under it every spring, just in case, and pull the old one out in the autumn and eat it, which I think is the most sensible thing Thistlewick does, and it has, I am told, been very good for the turnips. I asked whether the Forty-Eighth had been given the turnip, when he came home, it being presumably his. I was told that he had not asked. I asked him whether he wanted it, and he said it was the Chosen One's, and he was not sure he was, now, particularly, and that whoever was going to have it should have it fresh. It is still there.
