There is still a new one every spring. The sign. The row after that has a small and tired sign: PLEASE DO NOT PULL THE TURNIPS UP TO SEE IF ONE OF THEM IS A SWORD IN A STONE. NONE OF THEM IS. WE HAVE CHECKED. ALL OF THEM. It is the only sign in Thistlewick in the past tense, and the farmer whose row it is says that it went up after the twenty-third Chosen One, or thereabouts, and has been needed by every one since, and by a great many people who were not Chosen at all, but had hopes. It is a very tired sign. I believe every word on it. The string. The last row before the lane is so straight that somebody must have used string. Somebody did. The string is still there. It is the Farmer's best string, and he would like it back after the harvest, and he has said this every year that I have been visiting, and the string is still there, and I have begun to suspect that he would not like it back after all, and only likes to say so. The scarecrow wears Bram's old coat, with a note pinned to it: CHOSEN ONE (RESERVE). It has not been called on. It stands among the turnips facing north, and I do not think it is my place to say what it is thinking. The crest Over the door of Prophecy Hall is the arms of Thistlewick: a turnip rampant, on a field of slightly different turnips. The motto beneath is in Old Thistlewick, NON NOBIS, NISI FORTE: not us, unless it has to be. A turnip rampant is a turnip standing on its hind leg, with its fore-leaves raised, which no turnip in nature has ever done, and the herald who drew it, whoever that was, had clearly never seen one rampant either, and got round the difficulty by drawing a turnip and leaning it slightly. It has been repainted so often that it is now mostly paint, and with every coat it has become a little more rampant, so that by now it is leaning very nearly at the angle of a man going up a hill into the wind. In another hundred years, I estimate, it will be lying down. The field of slightly different turnips has given me more trouble than anything else in this article. I have asked three people in Thistlewick what the difference is, and have been told: that the turnips of the field are ordinary turnips, and the turnip rampant is the turnip of Thistlewick, which is not ordinary, and that I should be able to see this; that the turnips of the field are last year's; that there is no difference, and there never was, and the word "slightly" was put in by the Committee to make a motion pass. I have looked very hard at the crest for some time and I cannot see a difference either. I am inclined to the third account, which is the most like the Committee. I am also inclined to the first, because the woman who gave it to me had not the slightest doubt about it, and I have seldom been looked at with such pity. The motto is the best thing about the arms, and Thistlewick does not seem to know it. Not us, unless it has to be. It is a very modest motto for a village that sends a hero north every hundred years. I put this to a member of the Committee, who said that the motto was about the turnips. At table Breakfast In Thistlewick breakfast is turnip. It is turnip at the Gilded Turnip, where Prudence Thrupp 's bed is twenty crowns and includes breakfast and breakfast is turnip, and she has never been asked to change this and would not, and it is turnip in the houses, and it was turnip on the morning the Forty-Eighth was Chosen, when his mother did it for him as a steak, for the occasion, and cut his into the shape of a sword. He has told me that it was the most supportive thing anybody did for him all day, and that he did not eat it at the time, and ate it later, as a sort of rehearsal. I have stayed a night at the Gilded Turnip, and breakfast was turnip. It was a very good turnip. I would like that on the record, in case it is thought that a Nether Sopping man came to Thistlewick and was rude about the breakfast. The four kinds The Thistles' pantry has jars and preserves and four kinds of turnip, and I asked Mrs Thistle what they were, and she told me, ticking them off on her fingers: turnip; turnip, mashed; turnip, for visitors; the other one. I asked what the other one was. She said it was for when the first three would not do. I asked when that had been. She said, "Not yet." I have thought since that this is the turnip equivalent of the sword above the grate, and I said so, and she said that the sword had been a good deal more trouble. The turnip for visitors is the same as the first kind, on a better plate. The cellar The Gilded Turnip keeps turnip on its shelves in sacks and boxes, labelled by year like wine, and it has opinions about the years. The '87 is said to be very good, and is not for sale, and is brought down for weddings and shown to the couple and taken back up. The '91 is not spoken of. I tried. I asked Prudence, who looked at me; and the Regular, who looked at his drink; and a farmer, who looked at the '91 on the shelf, and then at me, and then said that it had been a wet year, and that was all he would say, and he would thank me not to bring it up in front of the sacks. I have tasted the '87. It tasted of turnip. I said so, and was told that this was the point, and that the '91 had not, and that this was the point also. - H.B. Cordial, and further afield Prudence makes a cordial of elderflower and turnip, which is better than it sounds, and would more or less have to be. The Field Tonic that is sold to adventurers in the south, which restores a whole company at once, also tastes of turnip, and nobody in the trade has been able to tell me why, and I have stopped asking, because the last man I asked said that most things did if you were from Thistlewick, and looked at me as though I might have been. The market stall on the square at Thistlewick sells turnips, for two crowns, under a card that reads FRESH! MOSTLY! A turnip eaten in the field restores the eater by an amount which the Adventurers' Guild has measured and which I will not print, because it is very small, and the turnip is not to blame for that, and would be hurt. The Guild's own description of the article reads in full: A turnip. Bram grew it and would prefer you did not throw it away. I asked the Guild who had written that, and they said it had come with the turnip. The chair The most famous turnip in the history of Thistlewick is not the one on the plinth. It is the one in the Thistles' front room. Bram's great-grandmother, Mabel Thistle, 1890 to 1979, grew a turnip as big as a chair, and sat on it, and then it was the chair. Her headstone in the churchyard says so, in capitals: SHE GREW A TURNIP AS BIG AS A CHAIR, AND SAT ON IT, AND THEN IT WAS THE CHAIR. It is the only headstone I know of that records an item of furniture, and the family speaks of it in the tone other families keep for a war. The chair is still in the family. Mrs Thistle uses it for the good visitors. I have sat on it. I would like to say two things about it, as its first historian. The first is that it is very comfortable. It has been upholstered at some point, in green, and the upholstery has worn through at the arms, and underneath, where it has worn, it is turnip. The second is that it ought not to be there. A turnip of the 1910s or thereabouts, which is my guess at the year, and Mrs Thistle's too, has no business being anything at all in 2002, let alone a chair. I put this to Mrs Thistle as delicately as I could, which was not very. She said that it had been well brought up. I have no better explanation and I am not looking for one. I have sat in a great many chairs in the course of this history, some of them thrones, and one of them a duck's, and the Thistles' turnip is the one I would go back for. The show Thistlewick has held a turnip show at the end of every harvest for longer than the Committee has minutes, in the yard behind Prophecy Hall, on trestles. There are classes for the heaviest, the roundest, the most even in colour and the most like a turnip, and a class for children which is for the turnip that looks most like somebody on the Committee, and is always the best-attended, and has caused two resignations. The show is remembered for one woman. Elspeth Moore, 1902 to 1994, won it forty-one years running. Her stone in the churchyard says so, and under that, in smaller and much angrier capitals: THE FORTY-SECOND WAS FIXED. I have tried to find out who won the forty-second. Nobody will tell me, which in Thistlewick is unusual, because everybody in Thistlewick will tell you everything, at length, at the gate. The minutes of the Committee for that year record that the show was held and was a credit to the parish, and the rest of the minute is about the biscuits. I asked whether it had been fixed, and was told that Elspeth had always said so, and that it was not for anybody now to say she was wrong, and that she had been very good with a turnip, and that this was more important. I agree. There is a rosette on her stone every autumn that says SECOND. I had thought this was a joke against her, and was ready to be cross about it in print, and asked. It is put there every year, the morning after the show, by whoever has won it, and it is the first thing they do. It has been every winner since 1994, and none of them has ever discussed it with any of the others. I have stood in front of it, in the autumn, with my hat off, and I would do so again. Bram Thistle's crop of 2001, his first since the Quest, was the best in the parish, and the Committee asked whether it had been prophesied, and it had not. He did not enter it in the show. He says it was harvest, and he was busy. I think he did not want to have to put a rosette on Elspeth's stone, not because he minded doing it, but because he would have had to stand there in front of the whole village while he did. - H.B. The turnip and the Prophecy I come now to the part of this article that I expect to be read most closely, by the Committee, with a pencil. The Prophecy of Thistlewick does not mention the turnip in any of its clauses. I have read them all, more times than anybody who is not a clerk ought to, and it is not there. And yet every Chosen One that Thistlewick has ever sent has gone north from among the turnips, and the village has never seen this as a coincidence, and has treated the turnip throughout as something between a mascot and a guarantor. The flowers. The Committee keeps a souvenir book, The Forty-Seven: A Souvenir, with a portrait, a date and a pressed flower on every page. The flowers are all turnip flowers. A turnip flower is small and yellow and nobody has ever looked at one on purpose, and there are forty-seven of them, pressed, each between two pages and each a little browner than the last, and I have seen the book, across a table, and was not allowed to touch it, and I think it is the most moving thing in Prophecy Hall, and I do not think the Committee knows that. The reference. When the Forty-Eighth went south to the Adventurers' Guild at Nether Sopping, which would not register him without a character reference, Elder Wispel wrote him one, with the good pen. It confirms that Bram Thistle is the Chosen One, is of good character, and grows a decent turnip. The last part is underlined. I asked the Elder why, and he said that the first two parts were the Committee's opinion, and the third was a matter of record. The portrait. Over the fireplace in the Thistles' house hangs a painting of the family: six generations of Thistles, all holding turnips. Not one of them is holding a sword. Bram has told me that he looked at it on the morning he was Chosen and thought that he was going to be the odd one out. He is not, as it turned out. He came home and put the sword back, and he has a turnip. The road. He took turnips with him. His mother's pantry gave him some on the morning he left, because they were his, and he ate them on the road, and the account of the Quest that is kept in Prophecy Hall, as amended, records the number, as it records everything else: who came back, how many of the well-worn conventions of adventuring were walked into, and how many turnips were eaten. I have the figure. He has asked me not to print it, on the grounds that it is nobody's business, and I agree, and I will only say that it is a real number, and that it is the right one. Mother Selvidge , who reads fortunes in a striped booth at the back of a fair in the far south, read his, and told him that he would go a long way, and meet a great many people, and that at the end of it somebody would be very surprised to see him; "and you'll eat a turnip," she said. "That one's free." He did. On the way home. I have checked. The top. At the top of the Obligatory Tower , when it was all over, Grimspite the Inevitable signed him a receipt, and sent him home with a message: "Go home, forty-eight. Grow your turnips. There isn't a forty-nine. Say that to them, when you get in." I have considered this sentence at length. It is the only instruction about the turnip ever given by a Dark Lord, so far as the record goes, and it was obeyed. The next morning there were still turnips. That is the first line of the history of Thistlewick after the Prophecy, and it is also, I think, the whole of it. The Committee has asked me to add that the turnip is not a party to the Prophecy, was never a party to the Prophecy, and is not in any way responsible for clause twelve. I add it. Nobody had suggested otherwise. - H.B. The turnip in the arts Music Thistlewick has one song, and it is Turnips in the Morning. It is played on the piano in the Gilded Turnip, which has a sign on the lid saying PLEASE DO NOT PLAY THE PIANO, and under that, smaller, THIS MEANS YOU, BRAM, and he played it anyway, with one finger, on the morning he left, it being the one tune he knew, and the whole inn went quiet and then went back to being loud, a little faster than before. The tin tankard that hangs on a bracket over the inn door creaks when the wind blows, in exactly the rhythm of Turnips in the Morning, and has taught it to three generations of the village. I do not know whether the tankard learned it from the village or the village from the tankard. Nobody in Thistlewick finds this an interesting question. It was thought for a long time to be a bad tune. It is not. It was played, in the year 2000, properly, by Piper Quill , who is a professional, on the same piano, and it turned out that it had been a good tune all along, and had been waiting for somebody to use more than one finger. The village has not got over this. Some of them, I am told, are rather annoyed. The words, which I was sung at the Turnip by four regulars at once, I will not give here, because there are eleven verses, and the first ten are about turnips, and the eleventh is about turnips also, but in the morning. Verse There is no rhyme in the language for turnip. This is well known now, and it is well known because the whole of the Forty-Eighth's company sat down one afternoon in the year 2000 in front of the gilded turnip on its plinth and tried to find one for Piper Quill, who had needed one since the night she joined, for the last verse of her ballad, and had said she would get one on the road, and had not. The afternoon is in her notebook, which is printed in this volume , and I will not give all of it, because everybody I asked says that they were there, and that their suggestion was the best, and some of them were not there, and I am not going to adjudicate between a blacksmith and a knight about a rhyme. I give the ones I have been able to confirm, in the order of the notebook, which is the order of how bad they were: Burnip. From the blacksmith, who said that it was a word now, and that he had made worse out of less. Nothing ending in -nip. From the naturalist, pre-emptively, on the grounds that a nip is a bite, or a pinch, or catmint, genus Nepeta, and is inadmissible. Navet, which is turnip in the old tongue of Sir Aldric 's house, and rhymes very beautifully with nothing, in that tongue either. Turnip. Located, on behalf of a client, by Nix , written on a folded slip, with the provenance on the back. The client had not said it had to be a different word. Sherbet. A slant rhyme, defended by the hedge mage on the grounds that the Collegium would accept it, which I am told is not, in itself, a defence. Something anatomical. From the field medic, who began at the scalp and went down, aloud, in order, and the Gilded Turnip went quiet somewhere around the pelvis, and she went right down to the feet, and there was nothing. Parsnip. From the Forty-Eighth, who pointed out that it was very nearly there. It is a different vegetable. The answer, in the end, was that there is no rhyme for turnip and there does not need to be, and Piper Quill moved the turnip down a line and ended the other line on grate, which has several, and it took nine seconds, and everybody who had spent the afternoon on it was furious: 'And so he came home to the fields, and hung his sword above the grate, and sat down with a turnip, which was worth the journey, and the wait.' P. Quill, the ballad, last verse It is the last verse. The turnip is in the middle of a line, where nothing has to rhyme with it, and I have come to think that that is where a turnip is happiest. Her mother's Lay of the Forty-Eighth, which the Committee approved on a Tuesday, is in twelve cantos, and there is no turnip in any of them. The Forty-Eighth read all twelve again, looking for one. I have read them too. It is very good. There is not a turnip in it anywhere, and I think it is the worse for it, and I have said so to Mrs Quill , who said that a Lay is not the place for a vegetable, and I said that it depended on the hero. The turnip abroad Outside Thistlewick the turnip is not well understood, and the turnip farmer less so, and the Forty-Eighth found, on the road, that saying what he did for a living had a curious effect on people with clipboards. I set some of them down. At the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant , at Coldbarrow , he was asked whether he was a knight, and said that he grew turnips, and the clerk said that in that case he was not on the map, and seemed very relieved. At the Smiths' Hall in Great Dunnage he was asked whether he was a smith, and said that he was a turnip farmer, and was told that in that case he might look, and was not to touch. At the edge of the Cinder Fen he was asked by the Drainage Commissioner whether he was a fire person, and said that he was a turnip person, and she explained that the Fen wanted burning, nine hundred acres of it, and did not seem to feel that his answer had made any difference. In Fairholme , where the kingdom has been divided among everybody who ever rescued its princess, one of the shareholders told him that she had got a turnip field and the north bridge, and that the bridge was the troll's, and they took turns. I have been to see the field. It is not as good as Thistlewick's. She knows. At Nether Sopping , in the outfitters, there is a crate marked RETURNS, full of compasses, and every one of them is pointing at the Gilded Turnip in Thistlewick. Mrs Barrow says it is a known fault. I do not dispute it. I have only to say that I have held one of those compasses in my hand, in Nether Sopping, forty miles away, and turned round with it, slowly, and it stayed pointing at Thistlewick the whole time, and at the turnip, and I put it down rather quickly. A guess, and marked as one. Thistlewick has believed for as long as it has had a fingerpost that it is the middle of the world. I do not believe this. I am a Nether Sopping man. But I have seen the compasses, and I am not, after that, as certain as I was. - H.B. And at Number Forty-Five's cottage, in Nether Sopping, there is not one turnip. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, who came home from the Tower in 1970 having been offered a cup of tea at the top and said no, grows roses, and has crates of seed labelled in a careful hand, SEEDS, MORE SEEDS, SEEDS (ROSES), and SEEDS (NOT TURNIPS), and has had no turnip in the house for thirty years, as a policy. He told me in 2001 that the policy had outlived its purpose, and that he was keeping it up out of loyalty, and I asked him to whom, and he said that he was not entirely sure, and that it was a nice policy, and that the roses liked it. The creatures of the turnip The turnip is host to at least three kinds of creature, by the Bestiary's count, and the Bestiary would like it known that it does not count the Committee. The Militant Turnip. In the fields about Thistlewick, on the road, in company with crows, there are turnips that have had enough. Wren Halloway has examined one closely. Its anatomy is a turnip's and its conduct is not. The Bestiary has it, and the Forty-Eighth, who takes these personally, has told me that he was not in the least surprised by them, and that if I had grown them for twenty years I would not be either. Thistlewick does not acknowledge the Militant Turnip at all. Asked about it, the village will say that those are not Thistlewick turnips, and that they must have come from somewhere else, and look south, at Nether Sopping, where we do not grow turnips, which I have pointed out, and which they say proves it. The turnip gnome. A gnome that lives in turnips, small, brown, bearded and of fixed opinions; the Bestiary gives his name as Mrs Rowbotham, after the wife of the man who named him. She knew. Bramus agricola (Halloway, 2000). A small brown burrowing animal of turnip fields, which eats turnip, survives things it has no business surviving, and is of no consequence whatsoever. It was named in the year 2000 after the Forty-Eighth, at a burrow in his own row, by the naturalist of his company, who had him sit down on a turnip while she explained it. Its article is the most affectionate thing in the Bestiary, and I do not think its author would like me to say so, and I have said so. The gilded one The most looked-at turnip in the world is a single turnip on a plinth in an alcove of the Gilded Turnip , painted gold, under a small plaque that reads THE GILDED TURNIP. It is not a metaphor. It is just a turnip somebody painted. It gives the inn its name, and the inn gives the turnip its reputation, and neither will say which came first. I asked how long it had been there. I was told that it had been there since before Prudence's father, and that it had been repainted every so often, and that nobody had ever looked at whether it was the same turnip under the paint, and that nobody was going to, and that it did not matter, and that I was not to touch it. Piper Quill called it "the problem", and she meant the rhyme. I have come round to thinking that she was right in a larger way than she meant. It is a turnip that somebody painted gold, because they wanted something in the room to be grand, and it is still very obviously a turnip, and everybody in the room knows it, and everybody in the room loves it. If you wanted a picture of Thistlewick you could do a great deal worse. The Committee has, and has it on the wall in Prophecy Hall, forty-seven times. Since Since the year 2000 the turnip has gone on very much as before, which Thistlewick regards as the victory. The Forty-Eighth farms the Thistle ground with his mother, as he did before he was Chosen, and his crop of 2001 was the best in the parish. He declined a seat on the Prophecy Committee, which was offered, because it meets in planting time. He keeps The Turnip Grower's Almanac for 1997 by his bed, and he tells me that it is still right about everything but the weather, and was never right about that. There is a turnip in a pot on the sill of the Thistles' front window, beside his mother's geraniums, which he is growing as an experiment. It has not done anything you would call an experiment. He has told me what the experiment is, and I have promised not to say, and I will say only that it is about whether a turnip minds where it is, and that so far it does not seem to. On the sill of Prophecy Hall's other window the village school has made a row of little clay figures, one for each Chosen One, and the forty-eighth is mostly turnip, and has since been given a sword, which it is holding by the wrong end. The children are very pleased with it. So, I think, is he. The fields go round three sides of the village. The flag is in its row. The sign has not needed amending. The rosette is on Elspeth's stone. And every morning since the morning after, there have still been turnips, and Thistlewick has got up, and looked, and been satisfied, and gone out to them. I have written a good many articles in this volume on things that tried to end the world, and things that tried to save it, and one long article on the contract that made both of them necessary. This is the only one I have written on something that was never in any danger at all, and I find, having finished it, that it is the one I most wanted to write. I do not understand turnips. I have tried, for two years, and I have not got anywhere. But I think I understand now why a village would send forty-eight of its own north to keep them, and why the forty-eighth would come home and grow them, and why the Dark Lord, of all people, would tell him to. - H.B. See also Thistlewick The Gilded Turnip , and the turnip Bram Thistle , by trade Mrs Thistle , and the chair Prudence Thrupp , and breakfast From the Notebooks of P. Quill , a rhyme for turnip The Bestiary , the Militant Turnip Bramus agricola The Prophecy Committee , which is not responsible

title: The Worshipful Company of Smiths
text: The Worshipful Company of Smiths For the town and the hall, see Great Dunnage . For the hammer that was right about everything, see Hob Grumnir . For BEST IN HALL, 1987, see Bryd Ollerenshaw . The Worshipful Company of Smiths of Great Dunnage Hall The Smiths' Hall, Great Dunnage Prime Warden Stannard Junior Warden Crabbe, who reads the Schedule out Appraiser Miss Fettle, who asks after the tang Motto BY HAMMER AND HAND (and, in chalk, BY SCHEDULE) Shield STRIKE WHILE IT IS HOT. AND THEN LET IT COOL. WE ARE NOT ANIMALS The Assize of Hammers Every three years, in the spring The Schedule Forty-one clauses. Very good Last prize piece A hinge The Worshipful Company of Smiths of Great Dunnage is the body that judges the work of smiths, and has done so for longer than anybody in Great Dunnage will admit to not knowing. Every smith in the land may submit one piece to its Assize. Very few manage to submit one. It is a very good Schedule. The Assize of Hammers Every three years, in the spring, the Company holds the Assize of Hammers in its hall, and every smith in the land may submit one piece, to be judged by the Wardens against the Schedule. The prize is the Company's mark. The prize piece of the last Assize stands on the Company's own anvil in the hall, with a card beside it: Clauses one to forty-one, satisfied. The Company's mark, awarded. It is a hinge. It is a very good hinge. The Hall also gives a prize of its own, BEST IN HALL, which is not the Assize and is not judged against the Schedule, but by judges, who are smiths, and argue. Bryd Ollerenshaw of Upper Clanging won it in 1987, the year Hob Grumnir did not enter, having a cold. The Schedule The Schedule of What Constitutes a Piece, being the rules of the Assize of Hammers, is on the wall of the hall. It has forty-one clauses. Warden Crabbe reads it out at the Assize as well, all forty-one, and it takes most of the day. People ask why they don't just pin it up. They do. He reads it out as well. It is a very good Schedule. I give the clauses I have: A piece shall be the entrant's own work, from the ore up. A piece shall be the entrant's own property. A hinge is a piece. Half a hinge is not a piece. A pair of hinges is two pieces, unless submitted as a door. A pair of tongs is one piece. A tong is not a piece. Nobody has ever tried. The decision of the Wardens is final, and so is the Schedule. Clauses four to thirty-nine I have not seen in writing, and Warden Crabbe has offered to read them to me, in full, in Great Dunnage, on any day I like, and has said that it would be no trouble. I am going in the spring. The officers Prime Warden Stannard is a tall woman in black, with iron-grey hair pinned up and gold at her collar, who stands at the Company's table as if it might try something. She asks whether you are a smith. If you are not, you may look. Do not touch. Warden Crabbe, the Junior Warden, keeps the Schedule, aloud, and the cards on the hall's exhibits, in writing, among them the one on a suit of armour entered for the prize by a smith who wishes to remain anonymous. Miss Fettle, Appraiser to the Company, is a young woman in round spectacles who looks at swords the way other people look at sunsets. She will ask after the tang. Everybody looks at the blade. Nobody ever asks after the tang. It is the most important part of the whole sword, and it is hidden, and she always asks. She does not charge for tangs. She also does curses, elective, on Form C-1, in triplicate, and they are mostly paperwork; the economy one lasts until you next sleep in a proper bed. Beatrice In the year 2000 Hob Grumnir of Thistlewick came to the Assize. He had never entered. He had never owned anything he made, because clause two is about property and Hob gives everything away, and when he went round eleven people to ask for one thing back, every one of them said no, with a better reason than his. So he laid his hammer on the Company's table instead. Beatrice was disqualified under clause one, not being his own work, and passed clauses two to forty-one, and the Wardens' notes are pinned up beside the hinge: BEATRICE. A hammer. From H. Grumnir, Thistlewick. Clause one: not satisfied. Two to forty-one: satisfied. DISQUALIFIED. Remarks: in the Wardens' opinion, right about everything. It is the only entry in the Company's history to be disqualified with a remark. Hob said that she would be unbearable. He has not entered again, because he had what he came for. Afterwards In 2001 the Hall asked Hob Grumnir and Bryd Ollerenshaw to sit together as judges of BEST IN HALL, which was either a compliment or a joke, and the Prime Warden will not say which. They disagreed for nine hours. The prize was awarded. Neither of them will say to whom, and the Company has not published it, and Warden Crabbe, when I asked, read me clause forty-one. The next Assize is in the spring of 2003. The Schedule has not been amended. It is a very good Schedule. See also Great Dunnage Hob Grumnir Bryd Ollerenshaw The Hoyle Works , which Great Dunnage would like you to know is only one works

title: Ambrose Fitch
text: Ambrose Fitch For his mound, see the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth . For his cottage, see Nether Sopping . For the woman who kept him alive, see Ysolde Marrow . Ambrose Fitch Not in the circle Known as The Forty-Fourth Born 14 May 1934, Thistlewick Died About 1999 Sex Male Chosen 1960 Kept alive by Ysolde Marrow, nine years, on and off Pensioned to Nether Sopping , by clause nineteen Written to by Thistlewick Never Watered A pot with a dead thing in it, every morning, forty years Buried In a barrow, by masons, within the fortnight Asked for A bench Got One Ambrose Fitch was the Forty-Fourth Chosen One of Thistlewick , who went north in 1960, came home, was given a cottage at Nether Sopping by clause nineteen, and was ignored for forty years. Then he died, and within a fortnight there were masons out in the eastern hills building him a barrow, with a curse on it. He did not want a barrow. He wanted a bench. He is the only person in this encyclopedia who was set in a mound to be fought, and fought because it was expected, and stopped when he was asked. The forty years He went north as they all did, with a sword and a medic, and the medic was Ysolde Marrow , who kept him alive for nine years on and off and has never been entirely sure how. He did the sword. He came home. Clause nineteen sent him forty miles south to a cottage on the front, with a window that looks out at the sea and at the end of the north road where it comes over the hill, and a pension, and nothing else. Thistlewick did not write. He had a chair, turned to face the window, and on the sill a pot with a dead thing in it, which he watered every morning for forty years. It was dead when he bought it. Ysolde asked him why, and he said it was the principle. Halbert Quy , who lived next door from 1970, says that nothing ever grew. "Nothing grew then, either." Ysolde says that he used to say there was a whole trade in it: you keep someone alive, and then they go and live, and you don't get to see much of it. She says he was right about most things. The mound The way this went, and they both knew it. He died about the year 1999. Thistlewick, which had not once written, sent masons. In the eastern hills above the north road they raised a long barrow, at some expense, with a stone door, a curse, and THISTLEWICK REMEMBERS cut over the entrance, and inside it, in a chamber chalked with a circle, they set the Forty-Fourth in armour, with a sword, in the exact centre, the way the dead hero in the mound is set, so that he could fight the living one. It is on the sign outside. It is in the chalk. It is in the shape of the room. So that is what he did. When the Forty-Eighth came, with a Guild Card, Ambrose Fitch said that he would shake his hand but there was a way this went and they both knew it, and they did what's done, and it took four minutes. "Forty years I've been waiting to have that fight and it took four minutes." Then he sat down on the floor of his own burial chamber, which the shape of the room does not allow for, and explained why he had done it, if he did not want to. "Because it's what's done. Weren't you listening? That's the whole trouble with the lot of us. It's what's done, so we do it." He gave the Forty-Eighth the sword and the ring, given rather than taken, which he was extremely particular about, because they had never been his: they were what a hero is supposed to be buried with. He was asked whether there was anything he wanted. "A bench. Top of the mound. Facing the sea. You can see the north road from up there. People walk that road tired and there's nowhere for them to sit down for four miles. Forty years of standing in a circle and that's what I want. A bench. Anyone's bench. Not mine. Anyone's." And a message: if they saw Ysolde, and they would, tell her he said she was right about the four hit points. The bench It was built. How, and by whom, and with what timber, is in the article on the Barrow , and I will not tell it twice. The burial chamber is empty now. The circle on the floor has gone unswept for the first time in forty years, and there is nobody standing in it. If you want him, he is on the top of the mound, on a bench, facing the sea, and I have been out and sat at the other end of it, and he did not mind. I have been asked whether a man who has died can sit on a bench. I am a historian, not a theologian, and I can only report that the bench is sat on, and that the view from it is of the sea and the north road, and that the people who walk that road tired now have somewhere to sit down. He asked for nothing for himself, and was very firm about it, and I have decided that what he is doing on top of the mound is none of my business, which is a rule I have also had to apply to Sir Dunstable . Afterwards The bench is on the mound, and he is on the bench. When I went out, there was a cup on the end of it, not mine; I do not know whose. Merrow Halgate thinks that Ambrose may have known about the older bench on the Middle Distance, which has no plaque and faces the sea, and wanted one nearer the road. The cottage on the front was the Committee's to give again, and the Committee gave it, with the key, to the Forty-Eighth, and trusted that Friday would suit. Bram does not live in it. He uses it when he comes south. The chair is still turned to the window, and Bram has never moved it, and has never sat in it. He waters the pot. It goes on being dead, but it has been watered. Mrs Pimm, who has the other key, still airs the place on Tuesdays. Thistlewick has not written. I have checked. But the Committee's minute book for the autumn of 2000 records that clause nineteen, the clause that sent him south, was struck, after a very long meeting, and I have chosen to read that as a letter, late. See also The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth Ysolde Marrow Halbert Quy , next door The Chosen Ones Merrow Halgate

title: Ambrosine Quill
text: Ambrosine Quill For her niece, see Piper Quill . For the family, see the Quills . Ambrosine Quill At the Committee's table Known as A. Quill, Chronicler to the Committee Born 2 December 1950, Thistlewick , in the room over the Quills' front door, which has the good light Sex Female Of Thistlewick , and the Quills Wears The Quills' crimson House style Never let the truth spoil the metre Work The Lay of the Forty-Eighth , twelve cantos, APPROVED Begun The morning they voted Finished Before he got back Wolves Always Niece Piper , who has a face Ambrosine Quill is the senior chronicler of the Quills , the family that has written the official account of every Chosen One of Thistlewick for four generations, and the aunt of Piper Quill . She is an extremely good writer. She wrote the official account of the Forty-Eighth, and finished it before he had finished, because the shape is known. The house style The Quills write in metre, and the house style is one line long: never let the truth spoil the metre. Ambrosine Quill has kept to it all her working life, as her own mother did before her, who wrote numbers forty to forty-three and had a wolf in forty-one, forty-two and forty-three - the same wolf. A good wolf. The Committee approves every account. It does not read them. Ambrosine Quill has known this for a long time, and has gone on writing them well anyway, which I think is a kind of courage, and she would think it a very odd thing to call it. The Lay of the Forty-Eighth THE LAY OF THE FORTY-EIGHTH. Being the Authorised Account of the Chosen One, Bram Thistle. By A. Quill, Chronicler to the Committee. APPROVED. She started it the morning the Committee voted, and the Committee approved it on the Tuesday, and when the Forty-Eighth came into Prophecy Hall with Piper she had it squared off on the table in front of her, twelve cantos, and a pen she was no longer using. "He hasn't finished yet," Piper said. "The shape has, dear." It is very good. I have read it. It is properly metred, and it begins with an orphan boy of humble birth, which Bram is not - he has a mother, who was making a pie when he last saw her - because nobody goes north with a mother; it doesn't scan. There is a wolf. Merribell dies in canto nine, of nothing in particular, because it scans; Merribell, reading it, said that she would have had a glass of water and sat down. He slays the Dark Lord at the top of a tower in a thunderstorm, in a rhyme on tower that was never going to be anything but hour, and comes home. Bram read all twelve cantos twice, looking for a turnip, and did not find one. And it has a very good middle. Everybody has a beginning and an end, she says, and in between they walk; nobody does the middle. She did the middle. Piper, who had come to fight, read canto six and said nothing for a moment, and then said, "It is a very good middle." What came of it What came of it is the subject of a disagreement among the Quills which I have been asked, by all of them, not to settle. I give both accounts, as I give both reckonings, and I do not say which is which. In one, the Forty-Eighth told her it was very good, which it was, and she took her spectacles off and held them, and did not put them back on for some while, because in four generations nobody had said so before. The account stands, as she wrote it, with a single footnote at the foot of canto twelve, in small type: None of this happened. It is very good. - P.Q. She read the footnote twice and initialled it, as to the wording. In the other, the two of them sat down and put what happened into metre, and it took the afternoon. She gave up the orphan for a mother in a kitchen, and Merribell for a glass of water, and fought for the wolf for an hour, and lost it to a goat which had sent its apologies to the meeting at which Bram was chosen, and which is in the minutes. "A goat is a sort of wolf. If you squint." She said the middle was worse, and Piper said the middle was true, and she said that it scanned, just, and signed it A. QUILL and handed Piper the pen, and it is the first account in four generations with two Quills on it. The Clerk stamped it AMENDED, which he had not had cause to do before, and looked pleased. Both of these are, I am assured, the authorised version. Afterwards She is still Chronicler to the Committee. Asked about the account, she says either that it is a very good middle and she reads it again most mornings, and the footnote; or that it has a goat in it now, and the goat is in the minutes, so she cannot object. I have heard her say each of these, on different days, and have decided that this is a matter for the Quills. What is not in dispute is that she and her niece nod to one another now, across a room, as one professional to another, which is new. Ambrosine Quill has asked to read this encyclopedia before it is bound, and has read the article on her niece, and returned it with one remark in the margin, which was that it does not scan. I have taken that as approval. See also Piper Quill From the Notebooks of P. Quill The Quills Prophecy Hall Elder Wispel

title: Aveline Stope
text: Aveline Stope "The Prioress." For the Order, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the valley and the ward, see Weeping Bottom . For the founder, whose pamphlet was in her drawer, see Mother Ursula Pym . Prioress Aveline Stope In the chair Known as The Prioress; Mother Aveline, to the patients, which she discourages Born Aveline Stope, 25 March 1944, at Brede Saltings, two valleys east, where it is dry Sex Female Professed The Order of Whatever Works, 1964 Prioress Since 1983 Symposia chaired Ten. Very well Eleventh Whether Anything Works. Not held. A queue instead Score Whatever Works, nineteen to one, on points Laughed at Merribell 's proposal Once In her drawer The founder's pamphlet, damp at the corners Aveline Stope is the Prioress of the Sisterhouse of the Order of Whatever Works at Weeping Bottom , the Order's mother house. For some years before 2000 she held symposia. An order that holds one symposium, she says, is thinking; an order that holds eleven has stopped. She said it the way a physician names a symptom she has seen before, in other people. The eleventh was never held. The chair She was born in 1944 at Brede Saltings, two valleys east of Weeping Bottom, where it is dry, which she has never let the Sisters forget, and came into the Order at twenty, in the drizzle, and took to it. She was a good nurse, and a better administrator, and was made Prioress in 1983, at thirty-nine, the youngest the Order had had. She found, as Prioress, that the Order had no doctrine, and that this worried the bishops, and the physicians, and some of her own Sisters, and so in 1990 she held a symposium on the question, in the chapel, with the chairs in two rows facing each other, and she chaired it very well. It was referred to the next symposium. She held ten. "I stayed for the symposia. Eleven of them. I chair them very well. The eleventh is at three. Whether Anything Works. It will be referred to the twelfth." The line By the year 2000 a party of the Sisters under Sister Bewick had found a doctrine, and called themselves What Ought To Work, and dyed the trim of their habits black, and the ward was divided down the middle by a line, with the Prioress's half on the west and Sister Bewick's on the east. The patients crossed it in the night, because there was soup. Merribell, who had left the mother house in 1996, at twenty-two, because it had begun holding symposia, came back on the day of the eleventh. "Sister. We'll talk. It's today, now, and I know it is. You left at twenty-two. You said we'd started holding symposia, and you'd come to look after people." Merribell's proposal was: don't hold the symposium; open the door; twenty patients to each half, and whoever is through first is right. The Prioress laughed at it, once, which the Sisters say they had not heard her do since about 1990. Then she agreed. Whatever Works was through its twenty while What Ought To Work was on patient one. Nineteen to one, on points. The eleventh minute, in her hand, reads: Not held. A queue instead. Whatever Works, on points. Soup. I asked her whether she minded that her last symposium was never held. She said that it was the only one that had ever reached a conclusion, and that she was very proud of it, and that she had chaired it from the soup pot. - H.B. The pamphlet When Sister Bewick asked to be examined on the Order's doctrine, since that is how a doctrine is settled, the Prioress took Mother Ursula's own pamphlet out of a drawer, where it had been since the first symposium. Four pages, stitched, damp at the corners, with the Rule of Life on the first page. I asked her why she had put it away in 1990. She said that she had put it away because she was going to hold a symposium, and you cannot hold a symposium about a thing that is four lines long and lying on the table, and that she should have noticed that at the time, and that she had, and had held the symposium anyway, and that that was the whole of the trouble. Afterwards She is fifty-eight. The Sisterhouse holds no symposia. The chairs in the chapel have been put back in rows facing the altar. Merribell has been back twice since, to see her, and they talk. The pamphlet is back in its drawer, but the drawer is left open now, so that anybody who wants the doctrine can see it, and the Prioress says that in two years nobody has asked to, and that everybody has had some soup. See also The Order of Whatever Works Sister Bewick Merribell Mother Ursula Pym

title: Bessie Cotterill
text: Bessie Cotterill "Bessie Marsden. Cotterill, now." For the family she married, see The Cotterills . For the family she was born in, see Winnie Marsden , her gran, who would like a word about the seating. Bessie Cotterill Her gran's face, forty years earlier Known as Bessie; Young Mrs Cotterill, which she does not answer to, because it makes her look round for the other one Born Elizabeth Marsden, 5 May 1977, Upper Clanging Sex Female Married Cotter Cotterill , the eldest, 18 September 1999 Has her dinner At her mother-in-law's. There is always more than they need Has the house to herself Second Saturday Cradle Her gran's. It went years ago. It came back. Nobody has said anything Child Summer 2000, on time. Unnamed, here, by request Second-best at being on time In the family Bessie Cotterill , born Bessie Marsden, is the wife of Cotter Cotterill, the eldest of the Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and the granddaughter of Winnie Marsden of the Class of 'Nineteen. She has her grandmother's face, forty years on, which everybody in the town remarks on, and which Winnie says is the face's own business. She married into a family of ten and has her dinner with them every day, because there is always more than they need. The Marsdens She was born in 1977, in the house behind the Safety Valve, the only child of Winnie's only son, a pattern-maker at the foundry, and was brought up in the town on the clear understanding that the Marsdens were the Class of 'Nineteen's own family and that there was a seat at the dinner with her name on it one day, near the top, as soon as somebody died, which Winnie said briskly and nobody was to take to heart. She was christened Elizabeth, which nobody has ever used, except the vicar once, and he apologised. The match She and Cotter Cotterill had known each other all their lives, in the sense that in Upper Clanging you cannot not know a Cotterill, there being too many of them, and she had walked past him at the chapel door every Sunday for twenty years. She says that he asked her out on the first Saturday he walked home from Great Dunnage , in 1994, eleven miles, and that he was too tired to say anything else, and that she said yes to stop him falling over. He says he asked on the second Saturday, and that on the first he had been too tired to ask. Mrs Cotterill says it was the third, and that she knows, because he came in and ate two dinners. They married in September 1999, at the chapel, on a Saturday, so that he could walk home for it. Winnie Marsden spent the reception drawing the Cotterills into the Class of 'Nineteen's seating plan, and found that there was no column for nine of them, ten in the spring, and that the plan had been settled when she was four, and she went home early and sat up with it, and nobody has been told what she said to it. Her dinner She lives with Cotter in a cottage two doors up from the Cotterills', and has her dinner at the house at the end of the street every day, because Mrs Cotterill does more potatoes and there is always more than they need. "Mrs Cotterill says I am to ask her anything at all," she told the Forty-Eighth, of the baby that was coming in the summer. "My gran says a lady does not discuss it." She has the house to herself one evening a month, on the second Saturday, when her gran has her dinner. She would like it known that she has never once told her gran how much she looks forward to it, and that she has done the arithmetic, and that if the Class of 'Nineteen had settled on a weekly dinner when they were four she would never have married at all. The cradle There was a cradle by her range in the year 2000. Nobody had mentioned it, and everybody had looked at it. It was her gran's. It had gone years ago, out of Winnie's back room, in 1989, and nobody in the family had said anything, because the Marsdens do not say things. In the year 2000 it came back. It was on the doorstep one morning, polished, with a label tied to it in a clear hand, and it is entered in a ledger in Nether Sopping in a column headed RETURNED, ruled with a ruler. "Gran's cradle?" she said, when she was asked about it. "It went years ago." And then: "Nobody has said anything." Nobody has. Winnie came round the next day and looked at the cradle for some time and said that it wanted a new rocker, and went home. Bessie says that was the most she has ever said about anything. Afterwards The baby came in the summer of 2000, as she had said it would, on time. Mrs Cotterill says it is the second Cotterill ever to be on time, after Washer , and that it is a very good start. The baby is not named in this encyclopedia, at Winnie's request, until the seating plan is settled. The seating plan has a high chair in it now, in pencil, which Winnie drew in herself. It is the first thing on that plan that has ever been in pencil, and Bessie says it is the first time she has ever known her gran to leave anything open to revision. She still has her dinner at the end of the street. She still has the house to herself on the second Saturday, though now it is the house, and Cotter, and the baby, and she says that is a better house. See also Cotter Cotterill Winnie Marsden The Cotterills Nix , about whom nobody has said anything either

title: Bram Thistle
text: Bram Thistle For the expedition, see The Obligatory Quest . For the forty-seven before him, see The Chosen Ones . For the small brown thing in the turnip field named after him, see Bramus agricola . Bram Thistle Sat for, under protest Known as The Forty-Eighth; Chosen One No. 48; Bram Born 3 October 1979, Thistlewick , in the room under the sword, in the middle of the turnip harvest, which was brought in on time Sex Male Of Thistlewick , two fields from Prophecy Hall Trade Turnips Chosen Third Age 2000, in his sleep, by the Prophecy Committee , nobody objecting Equipment One hoe. One sword, off the wall Good at Everything, slightly Bad at Nothing, impressively Luck Statistically indefensible (see Bramus agricola ) Holds A receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable Status At home. SEE BRAM Bram Thistle is a turnip farmer of Thistlewick , and was the forty-eighth and last of the Chosen Ones . He was asleep when he was chosen, and so did not object, which the Prophecy Committee took as consent. He went north, as forty-seven had, and beat the Dark Lord , as forty-seven had, and then did the one thing none of them had done, which was to ask the Dark Lord a question and stay for the whole of the answer. He would like it known that he did none of it on his own. I have known him for two years and that is the only correction he has ever made to anything I have written about him, and he makes it every time. Early life The Thistles have farmed the same ground outside Thistlewick for as long as anybody has written anything down, which in Thistlewick is not long. His great-grandmother, Mabel Thistle, grew a turnip as big as a chair, and the family still speaks of it in the tone other families keep for a war. He lives with his mother, who keeps the house, irons his good shirt on a Tuesday, and on the morning of the Quest told him there were eleven people outside and one of them had a scroll. I record, because one version of events in circulation says otherwise, that his mother is alive, well, and has read that version. She asked me to put in that she makes a good pie. She does. There was a sword on the wall above the grate. It had been there, his mother said, a hundred years, waiting for exactly this, "and frankly it has been unbearable about it." I have tried to date the sword and cannot. A hundred years is what Thistlewick says about anything that has been anywhere for a while, and in Thistlewick that is not a measurement (see Two Reckonings ). It is back on the wall now, and is, I am told, quieter. The choosing The minutes of the meeting give his name under apologies for absence, with one goat. He was not consulted, because he was asleep, and he was not woken, because the Committee did not think it would make a difference, and it did not. Elder Wispel gave him the charge in Prophecy Hall , the parish gave him five hundred crowns and three potions, and a neighbour in the lane asked him who was going to do the west field. His own account of that morning, which I have had from him several times, is that he did not know what else to do, so he went. I have put this to forty-seven people who did the same and they all recognised it at once. The Quest The whole of it is under The Obligatory Quest, and the longer version is Volume Two. What distinguishes him from the forty-seven is not what he did - they all went north and did the sword - but the things he did that were not on the way: He went south. Nobody does. He came into the Slain Wyvern , sat down with a room full of people the Committee would rather he had not met, and listened to six of them to the end. I paid him for it, and he found out the wyvern is a goose. He asked. Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, told him what to ask at the top, and he asked it. He listened to the answer. All of it. Grimspite had been waiting four thousand eight hundred contract years for somebody to. He read the document. Out loud, in full, in the middle of a fight, because somebody he had just beaten told him to. It is the only recorded case of a Chosen One reading the Prophecy , and it was fatal to the Prophecy. He also, on the way, helped fly a ship, light a lighthouse, build a bench, stop a wreck, examine a goose, register with a Guild, name a beetle (it is not a beetle; I have been corrected), find a rhyme that does not exist, and walk into, by the account's own count, very nearly every cliche there is. He was certified fit to travel at about the point at which he had finished travelling. The account in Prophecy Hall also records how many turnips he ate on the road. I have the figure. He has asked me not to print it, on the grounds that it is nobody's business, and I agree. The question of companions The clause allowed him three at a time and he had eleven, in one combination or another, and so whatever you have heard about who was at the top of the Tower with him, somebody else has heard something different, and both of you heard it from the person concerned. Bram's own answer, when I asked him, was "all of them", which is not possible under the clause, and which he says is true anyway. The articles on each of them are listed below, and each says what they told me. Character He is not clever, and does not claim to be, and is the only person I have met who has had the whole Prophecy explained to him and understood it. He is polite to everybody, including the people who were about to kill him. He has a quantity of confidence that has never once been audited, and has never needed to be. He is, it must be said, very lucky; Miss Halloway has described his luck in print as "statistically indefensible", and he took it as a compliment, after some thought, because it was accurate. He does not like being written about. He comes south anyway, about once a month, to correct me. Afterwards The next morning there were still turnips. There was also a letter on the mat: clause nineteen, one quarter's pension, and the key to Ambrose Fitch 's old cottage at Nether Sopping , with the Committee's trust that Friday would suit. Friday did not suit. He stayed at home and farmed, and six months later the Committee struck clause nineteen, after a meeting of eleven hours. He kept the key. He uses the cottage when he comes south, which is about monthly, and every time he is in it he waters the pot on the sill, which has had something dead in it since Mr Fitch's day. Nothing has grown. I check. The Committee struck clause twelve as well, and wrote in its place SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to see him yet. The Committee has twice minuted that it might. It has also offered him a seat, which he declined, because it meets in planting time. His harvest of 2001 was the best in the parish. The Committee asked whether it had been prophesied. It had not. Once a year, on the day, he walks up to the top of the Obligatory Tower . The kettle is on. In Prophecy Hall, at the end of the Wall of the Forty-Seven, the forty-eighth frame is still empty, and the card in it still says PORTRAIT TO FOLLOW. SITTER AT THE COAST. He is not at the coast. He is two fields away. Nobody has changed the card, and he has asked me not to tell them. See also The Obligatory Quest The Chosen Ones Grimspite the Inevitable Thistlewick The Turnip , though he asked that the count not be printed

title: Brother Quillon
text: Brother Quillon For the chapel, see Hithermost . For the knight he does not look at, see Sir Dunstable . Brother Quillon Not reacting Known as Brother Quillon; the Keeper of the Record Born 16 August 1932. He does not say where, and the Book does not, and it is the only thing in the chapel that is not written down Sex Male Of The Chapel of Continuance, Hithermost Keeps The Book, which glows Services Continuous Vows One prohibition Which is Saying that he remembers Smile Serene; eyes shut; forty years in the making Tea Ten past four, on the lectern Says under his breath A number in the low two hundreds Brother Quillon keeps the Record in the Chapel of Continuance at Hithermost , beside the only door into the mountain. Travellers going in write their names in the Book, in case of misfortune; in case of misfortune they come back in through the chapel porch and write them again, and he welcomes them, every time, as if for the first time. His Order forbids exactly one thing, which is saying that he remembers. He has therefore developed the most expressive silence in the Church. The Record "Welcome, traveller. Brother Quillon. I keep the Record." The Record is the Book, which lies open on the lectern and glows, softly and evenly, with nothing to account for it. Those going into the mountain write their names in it. Asked what happens in case of misfortune: "They come back in through the porch, and write their names again." Asked whether he remembers them: "The Order forbids it, traveller. It is the only thing the Order forbids." Then he smiles, serenely, with his eyes shut. It is a very expressive smile. It has had forty years. A traveller who signs a second time is welcomed, and asked whether he will write his name in the Book, and Brother Quillon looks down at the page, where the name already is, and says: "...Again? Of course. Of course you will." I have been a historian for most of my life and I think that is the best thing anybody in this encyclopedia says about the keeping of records. It is the whole of my trade, said by somebody whose trade forbids him to say it. The silence He does not remember. His vows say so, and he keeps them. When a party comes back in through the porch and its name is in the Book already, he looks up, and down again, and says nothing, with enormous tact. His theology is simple: every soul deserves a second chance. He does not add anything to that, aloud. He does not look at Sir Dunstable while he says it. He does not look at him very clearly indeed. And under his breath he says something that sounds like a number in the low two hundreds, which I have tried, on three separate visits, to hear exactly, and have not, and I have come to think that he has had forty years' practice at being not quite heard, as well. The tea Every afternoon at ten past four he pours a cup of tea and sets it on the lectern. At a quarter past four Sir Dunstable comes in by the porch and finds it, and is delighted. "Oh, how kind. Every time! The fellow's a mind-reader." Brother Quillon says nothing. The kettle is the village's, and is at the chapel so often that the tea room's card says TEAS. HOT FOOD. KETTLE PERMITTING. He has never been heard to say whom the tea is for. He has never been seen to drink it himself. It is still warm at a quarter past four. It is always still warm. Whether that is the tea, he will not say; and whether he has any view at all on the question that the village argues about, I asked him, and he smiled, with his eyes shut, for some time, and that was the answer, and I could not tell you which way. Afterwards Nothing has changed at the Chapel of Continuance, which is what it is for. The Forty-Eighth's party went down the Stair after the Quest, with the lamp, and came back in through the porch at least once. Brother Quillon does not remember it. The Order forbids it. The Book has their names in it, more than once, and he welcomed them each time. He has asked me to say that the chapel is open to everybody, whether or not they are going into the mountain, and that the services are continuous, and that there is tea. He asked me to say nothing else about him, and I have said a great deal, and he has read it, and returned it, and said, "Of course." See also Sir Dunstable Hithermost The Stair

title: Bryd Ollerenshaw
text: Bryd Ollerenshaw For the forge, see Upper Clanging . For the other smith, see Hob Grumnir . Bryd Ollerenshaw Waiting for a spar to get ready Known as Ollerenshaw Born 22 June 1959, Upper Clanging , over the forge Sex Male Of Upper Clanging , at the foot of the street Trade Smith. If it is iron and it has to hold The forge His, his father's, and his father's mother's Sign BRYD - SMITH. THE BEST IN THE NORTH. (SAYS WHO) Best in Hall 1987 (Grumnir not entered; a cold) Says Aye; we shall see Apprenticed with Hob Grumnir Bryd Ollerenshaw keeps Ollerenshaw's, the forge at the foot of the street in Upper Clanging , which was his father's and his father's mother's before that. If it is iron and it has to hold, it goes to him. He was apprenticed alongside Hob Grumnir , and they have been rivals for twenty years, and are both enormous, and between them they have said perhaps forty words in that time, most of them aye . The forge Miss Hoyle of the works sends him a drawing every spring, and every spring it is a spar. "One of these springs I will get it right." He means the drawing, not the spar; his spars are right. He says we shall see of every job he takes, and Miss Hoyle knows what he means by it, and so does everybody else in the town, and none of them has ever explained it to me. There is a certificate on his wall, BEST SMITH IN THE NORTH, awarded by B. Ollerenshaw to B. Ollerenshaw, in real gold leaf. There is also a real one, from the Smiths' Hall at Great Dunnage , BEST IN HALL, 1987, which is the year Hob did not enter, having a cold. Hob says he would have won. Bryd says aye. Neither of them has suggested settling it, and I have come to think that neither of them would want it settled. His apprentice is Grommet Cotterill , who is put upon, and who is small enough to go inside a boiler, which in a smith's apprentice in Upper Clanging is a qualification. The spar When the Forty-Eighth brought Miss Hoyle's drawing down the hill in the year 2000, the spar was not ready. "It will not get ready by being asked." It wanted two smiths, he said. It had always wanted two. Asked whether there was anybody else who could do it, he said, "There was. He went south twenty year ago come spring. Grumnir. You will not know him." He said the name the way a man reads a dimension off a drawing he has known by heart for a very long time. Hob was in the company. What followed was this. Each of them said the other's surname. Neither said anything else. Each of them looked at the other's anvil and found something wrong with it. Then Hob took his coat off, and they made the spar in an afternoon, without a word, and stood and looked at it for a while. "That will hold." "Aye." "There is a house at the bottom of the hill that does a pale." "Aye." A child of the town, asked about it, said that this is what they do every time. Bryd says it was a good spar, and a good afternoon, an' all. He asked the Forty-Eighth to tell Miss Hoyle that he said we shall see. She knew what he meant by it. The tube plate Later the same year Hob came back up the hill, about a tube plate for the Two Hundred 's boiler, which wanted four hands, one heat, and somebody small enough to go inside it afterwards. Everybody in the forge looked at Grommet. Hob took his coat off, which is not a sentence, but is the nearest either of them comes. Grommet went in after, and came out black to the eyebrows, and looked at the two of them, and said what he had to say about it to the Forty-Eighth, not to them. Afterwards In 2001 he and Hob sat as joint judges of the Smiths' Hall prize at Great Dunnage, and disagreed for nine hours. The prize was awarded. Neither of them will say to whom. They are still arguing about rivets. He has a cabinet in the forge of three drawers: RIVETS; OTHER RIVETS; RIVETS (GRUMNIR'S - DO NOT USE). I asked him whether the third drawer was ever opened. He said, aye. The sign over the forge still has its third line, SAYS WHO, in Hob's paint. Bryd has repainted the first two lines since, and not the third. Half the town has money on which of them will admit the other is the better smith. Nobody has collected. Miss Hoyle sent him a drawing this spring. It is a spar. See also Hob Grumnir Upper Clanging Ott Hoyle The Cotterills The Worshipful Company of Smiths

title: Clem Blagg
text: Clem Blagg "I do the lanterns. I'm seven." For the town, see Frostwick . For Nan, see Wilhelmina Blagg , who has asked that this article be short. It is not short. Clem Blagg "Item three. The winter. CARRIED." Known as Clem Born 3 January 1993, Frostwick , in the snow, which was on schedule Sex Male Does The lanterns Has read Everything Knows off by heart All the minutes Nan says Mrs Stagg has never once been cold. Not in forty winters Theory It's his lanterns. He does ever such good lanterns Since 2001 Co-opted to the Festival committee, without a vote, to take the minutes Clem Blagg does the lanterns at Frostwick , and has read everything, and knows all the minutes of the Working Group on the Winter off by heart, and was seven in the year 2000. He is a reliable reporter of every fact, and has a theory about Mrs Stagg, and the Working Group finds the ceiling very interesting whenever he gives it. Everything Clem was born in 1993, in Frostwick, in the snow, which was on schedule, and learned to read at four off the Working Group's minutes, which Nan kept on the kitchen table. By five he had read every minute of every meeting since the extraordinary one on the twelfth day, in 1960, and by six could recite them. His favourite is item three of the founding minutes: "I know all the minutes off by heart. Item three. The winter. CARRIED." He says that it is the best item because it has a vote in it, For, 41. Against, 3, who had planted peas, and because it is the one that made the town what it is, and because he likes the word CARRIED, which is said very firmly. The lanterns "Are you here for the lanterns? I do the lanterns. I'm seven." There are two hundred and twelve lanterns for the Festival, and they are on the asset register, item three, and Mr Stagg has done them every year since 1961, and since 1999 Clem has helped. He lights them, one at a time, with a taper, on the evening of the twelfth, going round the square in a fixed order which Mr Stagg devised and which he has improved, by eleven seconds, and written down. The theory To the Forty-Eighth, unprompted: "Nan says Mrs Stagg's never once been cold. Not in forty winters. Not once. And that's Mr Stagg, that is. I think it's his lanterns. He does ever such good lanterns." The committee found the ceiling very interesting. Mrs Blagg found it most interesting of all. I have asked Clem since whether the theory still stands. He said that it had been revised, on new evidence: Mrs Stagg had said it was the fire, every morning, before she is up, for forty years, without once being asked. Clem said that this fitted the facts better than the lanterns, and that he had changed the theory accordingly, because that is what you do with a theory, and that Nan had asked him to stop having theories in the kitchen, and that he had minuted the request. - H.B. Afterwards Clem is nine. Since 2001 he has been co-opted to the Festival committee, without a vote, to take the minutes, which he takes off by heart and writes up afterwards, in full, including everything said in an undertone. The minutes are, Mrs Blagg says, the most accurate the Working Group has ever had. The Working Group has, since his appointment, held more of its business in the corridor. He has noticed. It is in the minutes. See also Wilhelmina Blagg , Nan Perce Stagg , of the lanterns Ida Stagg , never once cold Frostwick

title: Clevis Cotterill
text: Clevis Cotterill For the family, on whom the book was run, see The Cotterills . For the name that came in, see Washer Cotterill . Do not encourage Clevis; see Ferrule Cotterill . Clevis Cotterill Do you want to put money on the name? Known as Clevis; "the bookie", by the works; "that child", by the Parish Rooms Born 1 February 1987, Upper Clanging Sex Male Named for A clevis, which is a U-shaped shackle with a pin through it. Grommet has not ruled on it Ran A book on the tenth one's name, 1999-2000 Opening prices Gib evens; Cleat two to one; Washer twenty to one Winner Washer, at twenty to one Paid out Most of Upper Clanging Book Closed Odds of Clevis running another Not quoted Clevis Cotterill is the seventh of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and in 1999 and 2000 ran a book on the name of the tenth, which was the most popular wager in the history of the town, and which he lost, comprehensively, because Mr Cotterill had said not Washer , and he had priced Washer at twenty to one on the strength of it, and had not reckoned with Spare . The book Clevis has run a book on something since the age of seven: on which of the family would be first down to breakfast, on whether the rain would stop by the dinner hour, on how many times Mrs Cotterill would get up while she was meant to be sitting down. The stakes are farthings, and buttons, and on one occasion Shim 's bearing, which Shim would not put up, and which he has been trying to get onto the board ever since. He keeps the book in a penny notebook with a pencil in the spine and keeps it honestly, which everybody in the town agrees about, and which is, he says, the whole of the trade. When the tenth was on the way, he opened a book on the name. The Forty-Eighth was offered a price at the door. "Do you want to put money on the name? Gib is evens. Cleat is two to one. Washer is twenty to one, because Da has said not Washer." The reasoning was sound. Mrs Cotterill had always said that she had Washer in reserve, and Mr Cotterill had said, very firmly, not Washer, and in that house, in twenty-four years, a thing Mr Cotterill had said very firmly had generally been listened to, at least for a while. A week later, he reported, "Gib has shortened. I would get in now." Twenty to one Half the works put a farthing on Washer, because Da had said not Washer, and the works has known Mr Cotterill a long time, and has a feeling about the things he says very firmly. He took all of it, and laid it off against nobody, because there was nobody to lay it off against, and was, by the time it was spring, holding a very great deal of the town's money against a single name. Spare got to it first. "He said call it Washer," said Mrs Cotterill, "and I was tired." "Washer came in at twenty to one. Half the works had a farthing on it because Da said not Washer. I have had to pay out most of Upper Clanging. The book is closed. Mam says there is not going to be another one." He paid every farthing. It took three days, and a loan from Gudgeon at no interest, and the sale of the notebook's spare pencil, and Tappet 's sweepstake winnings on the dragon, which Tappet lent without being asked, and which he says is the only time in the family's history that anybody has lent a bookmaker money without first asking what the odds were. I asked Clevis whether there was any lesson in it. He thought about it for some time, and then said that the lesson was that you should never price a name on what Da says, because Da says things, and that you should price it on who is going to be in the room when Mam is tired. And then, after a moment: that it had been Spare, and you could not have priced Spare. Nobody could. That was the whole trouble with Spare, and the whole point. - H.B. Afterwards Clevis is fifteen. The book is closed, and has stayed closed, on the subject of names, Mam having said that there is not going to be another one. The whole street now has money on what Washer's first word will be, and he has been begged, by the works, by the Safety Valve and by the vicar, to make a book on it. He will not. "The family," he says, "has been through enough." That is the official position. I have it from Shim that the true position is that he has worked out that Spare will be in the room for it, and has declined to be beaten twice by the same brother. He has begun a second notebook, on the airship, the Two Hundred and First, and when it will fly, and is offering six to four on the spring of 2003, and is not taking any bets at all from Miss Hoyle , who has asked, because Miss Hoyle has the schedule. See also The Cotterills Washer Cotterill , twenty to one Ferrule Cotterill , who is not to be encouraged either, but in a different way Spare Cotterill , who could not be priced

title: Cobb Lorrimer
text: Cobb Lorrimer For the professional on the other side of the contest, see Nix . Cobb Lorrimer Under protest Known as Lorrimer Born 1 April 1956. He has the certificate, and would like it noted that the date is a coincidence Sex Male Trade Thief Registered With the Adventurers' Guild , under T Wears A teal hood, about it Does not Fight. He is a professional Second post Dark Lord, afternoons (WHO LOSES) Signed for Yes. He read it after Tools Located Cobb Lorrimer is a thief of Nether Sopping , registered with the Guild under T, who steals things and says so, and wears a hood about it, and has never in his life been ashamed of anything except one signature. He plays the Dark Lord for the children on the front, in the afternoons, and loses. The contest He leant on the Guild's wall in the year 2000 with his arms folded, the way a man leans who would like to be asked what he does, and when Nix came by he told her. He found her whole vocabulary an insult. "LOCATES. AHEAD OF SCHEDULE. THE CLIENT. It's stealing with a waistcoat on. It's a job you've failed to apply for." She said that nothing in her shop was stolen, and that she could tell him how she had got every piece of it. He said, prove it, and produced a list, in a child's hand, from the two children on the front who were playing Chosen One with no kit: ONE ROPE. ONE HELMIT. ONE SWORD. ONE DARK LORD (WHO LOSES). First back with the lot. A client, a list and an afternoon. No fighting. He was back before dinner with a rope off the ferry, a helmet out of the outfitters' window, and the very good sword off the knees of a man who was having a day off, and who came up the street after it in his socks. Sops and Tibb sat on a barrel each, as judges. "Where'd you get them?" "I STOLE them. I'm a thief. It's the whole point of me." Tibb said that his mother said they were not to have stolen things, and said it twice. Nix laid out a coil of rope, a pot and an oar, each with a receipt on top: lent until sundown, and signed for. The ferry, the outfitters and the man in his socks took their things back off Mr Lorrimer, one at a time, politely, and he watched them go. "You can't win a THIEVING contest on PAPERWORK." She said it had not been a thieving contest. It had been a list. The fourth item There was one more thing on the list, and nobody in Nether Sopping would be it, and you cannot steal a Dark Lord. Nix took out a form and a pen and offered him the post: Dark Lord, afternoons. Villainous. A proper criminal position. He would be good at it. "...Villainous?" He signed. He read what he had signed, (WHO LOSES), a moment too late, and the children were already running at him with an oar and a pot on. He lost magnificently, three times before sundown, and stormed off up the street in a huff, and left his tools on the barrel, which meant they were located. Nix wrote him a receipt. Afterwards He has come back every afternoon since, under protest. "Don't. I signed it. I read it after. It's afternoons." He is getting very good at losing. The children say that he has a speech now, before the end, and that it is very long and very frightening and has a bit at the end where he says he will return, and then he does, the next afternoon, which they consider the best part. He has asked Nix for a receipt for his tools at every meeting since, and she has given him one at every meeting, and he has kept them all, and he would like it known that he has not used a single one of them, because it would be admitting something. He is still registered under T. Registrar Pell has asked him whether he would like an entry under D as well, and he said no, and then asked what the form was called. See also Nix Nether Sopping Grimspite the Inevitable , who held the other post, mornings and afternoons, for some while

title: Corvin Ash
text: Corvin Ash For the village he is from, see Ashcombe . For the one under the lake, see Old Ashcombe . They are both Ashcombe.
