Corvin Ash Don't ask about the scar Known as The Brooding One; the Doomed Rival Born 13 January 1970, old Ashcombe , in the house with the step Sex Male Of Ashcombe ; for eleven years, the corner of the Slain Wyvern Trade Rival of a great hero, according to a fortune-teller, for two crowns Age Thirty-two Good at Dark damage, and more of it the worse things get Bad at Defence; luck; being told the school is very good Sword Black. Called Mind The Step Scarf Knitted by his mother. The wrong colour. Worn League table Second, the Sable Hart Destiny None whatsoever ( Mother Selvidge , three readings) Corvin Ash sat in the corner of the Slain Wyvern from the age of nineteen, waiting for a destiny, for eleven years, which is longer than most careers. His village was destroyed by flooding, in his absence, and everyone was fine, and they moved eight miles inland, and there is a school now, and it is very good, and he could not make anybody understand. "...Leave," he told the Forty-Eighth. "This road ends in ash." Then he told him about the flood, and the school, and asked him not to look pleased, and went to get his coat. I sat across the room from him for most of those eleven years, at the table by the fire, and I want to put it on record at the start that he is not nothing, and never was. He is a genuinely dangerous man with a black sword who sat still for a decade because somebody once told him he was important. The sitting still was the only part of it that was ever a waste. Ashcombe He was born at Ashcombe , in a valley that is now a lake. In 1989, when he was nineteen and away from home, the water came up, and the village was flooded, and nobody was hurt, and the whole of it moved eight miles inland (eight miles by the road; the lake says less) and built itself again. He took the name Ash when it went under, as a memorial, after thinking about the gesture for some weeks. The village also kept the name, because it was its name and it was still using it, and so the new Ashcombe is Ashcombe too, and has a post office. You cannot mourn a place that is answering its correspondence. The new Ashcombe is proud of the flood. It has a plaque about it, which is upbeat, and a Drainage Museum, and an annual dinner. The fortune At a fair, the same year, a fortune-teller called Mother Selvidge told him, for two crowns, that he was the rival of a great hero. He organised his entire adult life around it. He went and sat in the corner of the Slain Wyvern, which is where a great hero's rival goes, and waited for the hero, and the drinks there were, he points out, somewhat cheaper. On the Quest The hero came in at last, in 2000, and asked him along, and he said "If fate demands it", twice, the second time more loudly, so that it would be clear that fate had. He did dark damage, more of it the worse things went, which on the Quest was often. Ashcombe, new. He went home. Everyone was delighted to see him. His mother is fine, and has a new kitchen. His childhood bedroom was rebuilt, larger, with better light, and is a study. He was invited to speak at the Flood Dinner, and did, and it went well. He gave the village its name back. His mother knitted him a scarf in the wrong colour, and he wears it. Ashcombe, old. The lake is drawn down one week a year for the sluices, and if you are there that week you can walk into the old street. The party was. There is a pub sign, a doorstep, and, in a strongbox in what was the schoolroom, his own school report, which the schoolmistress had kept because she kept everybody's. It says that he will go far, if he ever gets up. On the doorstep, cut in by his grandfather in 1949, is the name of the black sword, which his grandfather made, as a doorstop: MIND THE STEP. That is its name. I am told by everybody who was there that this was the one moment in his story that was allowed to be simply sad, and that it lasted until somebody read out the report. The Sable Hart. There is an inn on the moor where doomed rivals brood professionally. Every corner is taken. There is a waiting list for the darkest, kept fairly, on a rota, and a newsletter. Corvin had been a member for years and had never attended, because attending would be admitting there was a category. There is a league table. He was low on it. He is second now, behind a scar. He has a chair in the middle of the room, in the light. He attends. Mother Selvidge. She is still working the fairs, and did not remember him, and read him again for two crowns, and got a long life, a useful trade, and no destiny whatsoever. He asked her to do it again, and she did, and got the same. On the third reading she put the cards down and told him, kindly and without mystery, that she says the rival thing to about four young men a year, because it is the reading that makes them stand up straight, and that it has never once been wrong, in the sense that they all went and did something. She has read him three times. She has never once been wrong. The appraisal. He took the sword to Miss Fettle at the Smiths' Hall in Great Dunnage , expecting a curse. There is no curse. It is a very good sword in poor condition, and she was enthusiastic about the tang. He asked how much a curse would cost. It is not expensive. There is a form. He has the form, if he wants one. Afterwards He was asked back to the Flood Dinner in 2001, and went, and was early. He is up. He has the scarf, the chair at the Sable Hart, the form, which he has not filled in, and a long life and a useful trade still to come. He does not sit in the corner of the Slain Wyvern any more. When he comes in, which he does, he sits at a table in the middle, and on one occasion he sat at mine, and asked how the history was going, and listened to the end of the answer. He has asked me to remove the line about the drinks being cheaper. I have checked it, and they are, and I have left it in. See also Ashcombe The Sable Hart Mother Selvidge The Obligatory Quest The Day of the Water

title: Cotter Cotterill
text: Cotter Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For his wife, see Bessie Cotterill . For the town he walked home from every Saturday, see Great Dunnage . Cotter Cotterill Saturday. Six o'clock. Eleven miles Known as Cotter; "the eldest", by himself, first, every time Born 17 January 1976, Upper Clanging Sex Male Named for A cotter pin, which holds a wheel on Married Bessie Marsden , 1999 Worked The big furnace, the Iron Company, Great Dunnage , 1994-2000 Walked home Every Saturday: eleven miles up the valley, and eleven back for the Monday Boots Shod at heel and toe with somebody else's heel-irons Is Always very glad to get home Home for good Spring 2000 Cotter Cotterill is the eldest of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging . For six years he worked the big furnace at the Iron Company in Great Dunnage , and walked home up the valley every Saturday, eleven miles, and back down again for the Monday, and he was always very glad to get home. He has been home for good since the spring of 2000. He is still very glad. He has not been told that he can stop. The eldest He introduces himself the same way to everybody, and he introduced himself that way to the Forty-Eighth, at the gate of the Iron Company in Great Dunnage, with his hand out: "Cotter Cotterill. Upper Clanging, originally. Eldest of nine." That was in the year 2000, before the spring, and it was correct at the time. He has since had to change it, and says it now with a short pause in the middle, eldest of... ten, as if checking, and he is always pleased with the answer. A cotter pin goes through the end of an axle and holds the wheel on. Grommet , who has a view on the names, says that this one is fine. It is one of only two names in the family that Grommet has passed, the other being Gudgeon 's (a gudgeon is a pin), and Cotter, who passed first, being the eldest, would like that on his headstone, and Mrs Cotterill has told him not to be morbid, and also that he is not to have a headstone for a good long while yet, and that is not a request. Down the valley He went down the valley at eighteen, in 1994, because the Iron Company paid half again what the foundry at home did, and the house at the end of the street had nine in it by then and was, as he says, full in all directions. "Nine works," he told the Forty-Eighth. "I'm on the big furnace at the Iron Company till the spring. Then home for good." He lodged in Great Dunnage, with a Mrs Pettit in Cinder Lane, who gave him a room and his tea and his Sunday dinner on the Saturday, because he was never there on the Sunday. Every Saturday he came off the furnace at six, and walked up the valley road, eleven miles, and was home by the time it was dark, and walked back down on the Sunday night in time for the Monday. He did that for six years. He worked it out for me: about six hundred and twenty walks, near enough seven thousand miles, the most of any Cotterill, and he has not once been asked whether he minded it, because nobody in his family would think to ask a thing like that, and he would not know what to say. "I'm always very glad to get home," he says. His father says it too. It is, I think, the family motto, and it has never been written down, and it does not need to be. The heel-irons on his boots, which are worn bright, came from the forge in Thistlewick , and Hob Grumnir knew them at once, and asked whether he could have them back till the spring. Cotter said that he was home in the spring, for good, and that he would not get home without them, eleven miles up every Saturday and eleven back. Hob said, "Aye. Get home." I have asked Hob how his heel-irons came to be on a furnace man in Great Dunnage. He says that things he makes go where they are needed, and that this is the best place he has ever heard of one going. - H.B. The bottom lock In the year 2000, a little before the spring, the bottom lock on the Dunnage cut jammed, with thirty of the Iron Company's boats sat on the water behind it, and the Canal Company sent in their smallest man at eleven, and he did not come out. Cotter saw his brother at the gate, and knew at once what the answer was, and would not ask. "I'd not ask," he said. "Mam would say -" Spare went down. What happened in the culvert is Spare's, and in his article. Mr Pocock came out, and the paddle came clear, and thirty boats went down the cut, and the Mayor had his scissors back, which had been on the paddle since Tuesday, and cut the ribbon again, properly, with scissors, having had to open two things with a knife in the meantime. The Canal Company's man went home for a lie down, and said that Spare was to have his job. Cotter gave him a bun. "That's from me," he said. "I'll tell Mam on Saturday." He did tell Mam on Saturday. Mrs Cotterill has not said what she said. Cotter says she was very quiet for a long time, and then she did more potatoes. Home He came home in the spring, as he had said. Bessie wrote to him that Washer had been born, at six on the hooter, and that Da had said not Washer. "It's spring," he told the Iron Company. "I'm going home on Saturday, for good." He asked for the day, and they gave him the rest. Afterwards He is at the foundry in Upper Clanging, on days, with Rivet , and the two of them pass their father on the foundry steps at six, going the other way; Rivet says that between the three of them there is now a great deal of passing, and that some mornings there is a queue. He is a father. The child came in the summer of 2000, on time, and is not named in this encyclopedia, at the request of its great-grandmother, until the seating plan is settled. He walks to work four hundred yards and back. He says he misses the eleven miles, a little, on a Saturday, and that he goes for a walk instead, up the valley road and back, and that he is very glad to get home. See also The Cotterills Bessie Cotterill Spare Cotterill , for the culvert Great Dunnage Hob Grumnir , whose heel-irons they are

title: Councillor Fenn
text: Councillor Fenn For the clause, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause twelve. For the Committee that did not listen, see the Prophecy Committee . Councillor Fenn Saying it Known as The Committee member (Clause Twelve) Born 27 September 1957, Thistlewick Sex Male Of Thistlewick Sits On the Prophecy Committee , at the end Position Clause twelve is the problem Held since 1981; about twenty years Listened to Once, in 2000 Petitions One (the Optional Tower); signatures, one On his belt A key, marked STRUCK Councillor Fenn sits on the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick , and has said at every meeting for about twenty years that clause twelve is the problem. He was right. Nobody listened. The Committee's minute book for the week of the ending records, as item five, that Councillor Fenn wished it minuted that he had been saying so. Minuted. The position Clause twelve reads THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. For two thousand years Thistlewick read it as a warning. Councillor Fenn read it as what it is. "That's not a warning," he said. "That's a subscription." He said it in those words, at the end of the table, under the window, to colleagues who were discussing whether the Dark Lord shall be slain or shall be defeated, because slain is a commitment. The Forty-Eighth heard him say it on the morning he was charged, and the narrator of that morning, whoever it is that narrates mornings in Thistlewick, has it that nobody was listening to him, and adds: Remember him. I have. It is one of the few instructions in this history that I have been given by the history itself. He has also, over the years, put up a petition to rename the Obligatory Tower the Optional Tower, which has one signature on it, his own. It is on the Hall's noticeboard still, and it is not struck, because the Committee has never got round to reading it. The first time anybody asked In the year 2000 somebody in the Forty-Eighth's company asked him what he meant, exactly, about clause twelve. He said, "...Nobody has ever asked." Then: "Sit down. Sit DOWN. It goes back to the original wording, and the original wording goes back to a horse -" He was away for some time. It was, I am told, the first time in twenty years that somebody was nodding. I do not know what he said about the horse. The person who asked does not remember, having been, for reasons I accept, attending to something else, and the Councillor, asked by me, began at the original wording, and I took four pages of notes, and I am not going to print them, because I do not understand them, and because there is a horse in the margin of the Prophecy beside clause twelve that this encyclopedia has decided, on advice, to leave exactly where it is. At some point during the explanation a key went off its hook on his belt, the one marked STRUCK, that opens the door behind the red curtains, and later in the afternoon it went back on again. He did not notice either. I understand that this was the point, and I have been asked by Miss Quill to say that he was owed the listening, and got it, whatever else was going on, and that she would do it again. Afterwards Clause twelve was struck, nem. con., the week of the ending, with a note in its place: SEE BRAM. Councillor Fenn voted for it, and then asked for item five. He is still on the Committee, and still at the end of the table, and people now ask him things, which he says takes some getting used to. He has a new position, which is that clause nineteen was also the problem, and since clause nineteen was struck as well, six months later, he has been right twice and minuted twice, and he says it is a great deal better for the digestion. The petition for the Optional Tower still has one signature. He says it is a matter of principle, now, and that he would not want it spoiled. See also Elder Wispel Prophecy Hall The Prophecy of Thistlewick Piper Quill

title: Dame Winifred Cope
text: Dame Winifred Cope "I'm here. That's the whole of it." For the hamlet, see Little Gore . For the Order and its map, see The Order of the Errant and Mordaunt , who has her pin. Dame Winifred Cope Nothing to report Known as Dame Winifred; the Knight in the Field Born Winifred Cope, 12 January 1958, at Saltinge, on the east coast, a harbourmaster's daughter Sex Female Order The Errant. Knighted 1984 Posted Little Gore, 1989, as the Chapter's knight in the field Pins at Coldbarrow One. Correct Reports Quarterly. NOTHING TO REPORT Replies VERY GOOD Helmet Not a dent in it. Hob Grumnir 's Distance from her front door Four feet Dame Winifred Cope of the Order of the Errant is the Chapter's knight in the field at Little Gore , and has been since 1989, and there is a pin in her on the great map at Coldbarrow, just the one, and it is correct. She stands outside her own front door as if it were a post. Somebody has to be where the pin is, or what is the map for? Every quarter she writes NOTHING TO REPORT, and the Chapter writes back VERY GOOD, and she says it is the nicest correspondence she has ever had. The field She was born in 1958 at Saltinge, on the east coast, the daughter of the harbourmaster, and was, she says, the only child in the town who wanted to stay exactly where she was; her brothers went to sea, and she stood on the harbour wall and watched them go and liked it there. She went into the Order of the Errant at twenty and was knighted at twenty-six, and asked for a posting where a knight would be expected to stay, and the Chapter, after some searching, found her one. "Dame Winifred Cope, of the Order of the Errant. The Chapter's knight in the field at Little Gore. Eleven years. There's a pin in me at Coldbarrow. Just the one." Her door has a card on it in the Order's lettering, KNIGHT IN THE FIELD. DO NOT DISTURB, and she stands four feet from it, and as far as the Chapter is concerned that is the field. Nothing to report "I write every quarter: NOTHING TO REPORT. They write back: VERY GOOD. It's the nicest correspondence I've ever had." She has written it fifty-one times, in March 2002. Mordaunt, the Order's clerk, keeps her file, and says that it is the thinnest file in the Chapter House and the only one he has never once had to correct, and that he looks forward to her quarter day the way other men look forward to the post at Christmas. In the year 2000 Hob Grumnir came to Little Gore and saw that her helmet was one he had made, a long time ago, for somebody else, and asked whether he might have it back. She said, "I'm in it." He asked whether it had kept her safe. She said: "Not a dent in it. Nothing to report. That's your helmet." He has told me since that that was the whole of her reason, and that it was a very good one, and that a helmet with nothing to report is the best review a smith can have. - H.B. Abel Thrush For two years, from 1989 to 1991, the carrier Abel Thrush came through Little Gore every day on his round, and she stood at her post, and he went by, and in two years he never said a word to her. Tom Vane, who walked the round with him sometimes, says that Abel never stopped talking, to anybody, and that he cannot understand it. Dame Winifred says that she can. She says that he was the only man in the county who understood that a knight in the field is on duty, and does not want chatting to, and that he used to touch his hat to her every morning without a word, and that she has missed it every morning since he died. Afterwards She is forty-four. Since 2000 a second Pemberton-Gore has come through Little Gore, as squire, the Fourth, with Sir Aldric , and found the way to her door first time, and saluted, and she says that it was very correct, and that she reported it, which was the first time in eleven years that she had anything to report, and that she wrote it under NOTHING TO REPORT, as a postscript, so as not to spoil the run. See also Little Gore Mordaunt Hob Grumnir , about the helmet Hester Vane , next door

title: Dean Fenwold
text: Dean Fenwold For the Collegium, see The Collegium Arcanum . For the very gifted young woman, see Zephyrine Vance . For the duck, see the Duck's Pond . Dean Fenwold Fine Known as The Dean; Fenwold Born 5 November 1928, in the Porter's Lodge of the Collegium Arcanum, during a fire drill, which he says explains a great deal Sex Male Of The Collegium Arcanum , the Hall Condition Fine, thank you Asked Not always Eyebrows Grew back. Magnificently After-dinner talk The Man Who Was Fine Engagements Forty-one by 2000, and more since Moved, in 1989 No Moved, in 2000 No Dean Fenwold of the Collegium Arcanum was in the room in 1989 when Zephyrine Vance produced what the enquiry called, twice, an unsanctioned quantity of fire. He is fine. He will tell you so before you have asked. He has made a second career of it. The man who was fine "Ah! Visitors. Fenwold. Dean. I'm fine, thank you." You had not asked. People do; they have been asking for eleven years. So he does a talk about it now, The Man Who Was Fine, after dinner, and by the year 2000 he had given it forty-one times, and they laughed in all the right places. Thursday week, in Hall, if you are about. His account of the incident is a model of its kind: "A very gifted young woman, a very small room, and rather more fire than the room had been told about." The eyebrows grew back. Magnificently, he is told. He smooths one when he says so. Then he adds the thing that is not in the talk, or was not, until 2000: "She said the room was wrong, you know. At the time. I remember thinking she was very probably right." There is a short pause after that. It has been in the talk forty-one times. The demonstration In the year 2000 he asked Miss Vance to come and do it again, for the talk: small, controlled, in Hall, with buckets. She refused, and then agreed, on terms, and the terms were that a paper of Dr Hapgood's, On the Kindling of Damp Materials, should go out under Dr Hapgood's name, with a note, which the Dean would write. He said that he would write the note. He said, too, that he had thought she was very probably right, at the time. It is not much of an apology. It is the best he has, and he means every word of it, and he put it in the talk. The demonstration went wrong in exactly the way it had gone wrong the first time, for exactly the same reason, which is that the room was wrong. He did not move. He had not moved in 1989 either. When the smoke cleared nothing was damaged, and the Dean said that the room was wrong, and that they had all heard her say so. Afterwards The talk has never been better. It ends now with the room being wrong, and he gives it at a good many dinners a year, and he has told me that he is fine, which I had not asked. Dr Hapgood's paper has Dr Hapgood's name on it, with a note by the Dean. He has also, I am told, had the Hall measured. He has not said what he means to do about it, and the Collegium has a committee for rooms, which will consider it, and he is fine with that. His portrait hangs in the Hall, with the First Dean's, and the First Dean's has been hanging pending the Hanging Committee for five hundred years, and his has not been there quite as long. There is a duck four miles off with a Fellow's medal round its neck, which was at the enquiry as well. It is also fine. It does not give talks. See also Zephyrine Vance The Collegium Arcanum The Duck's Pond The Incident at the Collegium

title: Dilys Fenwick
text: Dilys Fenwick For the meadow, see Firstfield Meadow . For the sheep, which are pigs, see below; Miss Halloway's Bestiary does not list them, and has been asked to. Dilys Fenwick "They're just there." Known as Dilys; Mrs Fenwick, on the sign Born Dilys Pugh, 17 January 1971, in the valley over the hill from Firstfield Sex Female Married Tam Fenwick, in the meadow, 1995, with the vows explained first, twice, in capitals Post Station Three: Quests, the Guild of Guides Sheep Three. Lost, a bit Species Pig. The form says sheep Line the Guild gave her But thou must Reward Out of her own cupboard Dilys Fenwick keeps Station Three, Quests, at Firstfield Meadow , where her three sheep are lost. They are not lost. They are just there, about where you would leave a sheep. They are also not sheep. The Guild ordered sheep and sent pigs, and the form says sheep, so they are sheep, and they have been practising their baa, and would like that noted. Station Three She came over the hill in 1993, at twenty-two, to take the post at Station Three, which had been empty since the last keeper's sheep had died of old age and the Guild had ordered more. The Guild sent pigs. There was a form. The form said sheep. Dilys looked at the pigs, and at the form, and said that if the form said sheep they were sheep, and that she would not hear a word against them, and the pigs have been sheep since. Their names are Daisy, Primrose and Mrs Hogg. Mrs Hogg leans on her. "The Guild says a meadow has to have a fetch quest. I said my sheep aren't lost. They said, well, lose them a bit. So they're lost. A bit. They're very good about it. They've been practising their baa." If you decline to find them, she says But thou must, and then she says sorry, the Guild gave her that line. The Forty-Eighth declined, once, to see what would happen, and was told But thou must, and then sorry, and then he found them. They were just there. The reward "This is for you. It's the reward. It's out of my own cupboard, so don't tell the Guild it's not a proper one." It was a potion, from the shelf in her kitchen, and it was a proper one. She says that the Guild sends her rewards, from time to time, in a crate, and that they are generally not as good as what she has in the cupboard, and that a hero who has found three sheep that were not lost deserves the cupboard. Tam She married Tam Fenwick, a carter from Firstfield, in the meadow, in 1995, on a fine day, with the whole Guild there, and the sheep. Fizz explained the vows to them first. Twice. In capitals. "Tam cried at the second one. He says it was the capitals. He cries at the harvest supper as well, bless him." I have met Tam Fenwick, at the cottage by the gate, and he is a large, quiet man with a cart and a soft voice, and he cried, slightly, while telling me about the wedding, and apologised, and said it was the capitals, and that even remembering them did it. Mrs Hogg, who had followed me in, leaned on him. He said that she does that. - H.B. Afterwards She is thirty-one, and still at Station Three. The sheep are still lost, a bit, and still very good about it. Miss Halloway's Bestiary, which I have printed in this volume, does not list them, and Dilys has written to Miss Halloway to ask that they be entered, as sheep, enclosing the form. Miss Halloway has replied that she has considered the form, and that it is a very good form, and that they are pigs, and that she will enter them in volume two, under Sus scrofa, with sheep (Guild) as a synonym, which is more than she has done for Dr Rowbotham. Dilys has written back to say that she will not hear a word against them. The correspondence is, I understand, continuing, and both of them are enjoying it very much. See also Firstfield Meadow Fizz , and the capitals Wren Halloway , and the correspondence The Guild of Guides

title: Dorcas Thrupp
text: Dorcas Thrupp For the tavern, the goose and the regulars, see The Slain Wyvern . For her sister, see Prudence Thrupp , and for thirty years of not speaking to her, see both. Dorcas Thrupp "It is a wyvern." Known as Mrs Thrupp, which is a courtesy; Dorcas, to her sister, in writing, since 2000 Born 4 June 1948, at the Gilded Turnip , Thistlewick , the elder of two Sex Female Keeps The Slain Wyvern , Nether Sopping , for longer than she will say Over the mantel A wyvern. A goose. Two plaques. Dusted the same morning, in an order she has not disclosed Spoke to her sister Until 1970. Then not, for thirty years. Then by post Sent instead Things Room four Not been down since Tuesday Has handled Gerald Minds The bedding Dorcas Thrupp keeps the Slain Wyvern on the front at Nether Sopping, where every hero who was ever sent to the coast has come in out of the weather, and she has kept it for longer than she will say. She is the elder sister of Prudence Thrupp of the Gilded Turnip, whom she did not speak to for thirty years. There is a wyvern over her mantel. It is a goose. She knows. It is a wyvern. The Thrupps She was born in 1948 at the Gilded Turnip in Thistlewick, where her father kept the house, the elder of two girls, and was brought up behind a bar, as was Prudence, three years later. She says that she learned to count on the slate and to read on the labels, and that by the age of ten she could tell you, from the way a man came through the door, what he would drink, how much, and whether he would be sorry; and that Prudence could do it by eight, and has never let her forget it. In 1971 the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping wanted a landlady, the old one having gone to live with her son, and Dorcas went south to take it, forty miles, with a box of labels and her father's second-best slate. Thistlewick did not mention it. Thistlewick has never mentioned it. It was, she says, the only time in her life she has been glad of the place. "Mrs Thrupp" is a courtesy. In Nether Sopping any woman who keeps a public house past the age of forty is Mrs, whether there was ever a Mr or not, on the grounds that she has earned it, and that the regulars need something to call her when they want another one. There was not ever a Mr. She would like that to be the end of the matter, and it is. The thirty years She and her sister stopped speaking in 1970. Neither of them will say why, and neither of them, I am now fairly sure, can remember. "That's not a falling-out," says Prudence. "We just stopped one day and neither of us started again." So they sent each other things instead: by carrier, by the occasional hero going north or south, by anybody who would take a parcel and not ask. The locket that they had had made at the Michaelmas fair in 1962, two portraits in it facing resolutely away from each other, went into Prudence's drawer, and stayed there. In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth brought her a jar from Thistlewick, warm on one side, which he had been told not to shake or ask about. She knew the hand on the label at once. "That's my sister's hand on that label. Give it here." She looked at what was in it. "Thirty years. THIRTY. And she sends me THIS." And then: "Right. You'll be going back north. Wait there." What she sent north was heavier, and deliberately worse, and had been under construction behind the bar for some time, against exactly this day. "Don't open it. Don't shake it. Don't let it near a fire. And tell her I send my love, because I do, and she knows I do, and that's her lot." What was in either jar is not known, and both sisters have asked me not to guess, and I have not, except privately, at some length. The jar from Thistlewick is on the highest shelf behind the bar, where it can be seen from every table in the room, and it is still sealed, and nobody in the Wyvern has ever asked what it is, because they have all been told not to, and they all know who by. - H.B. The locket came south a little after, by the same hand: "That was HER idea, that was." Prudence wrote, at the weekend, as she said she would, four pages, two of them about the Forty-Eighth, and one of those complimentary. Dorcas wrote back. They have written every month since. They have not, so far as I know, met. Dorcas says there is no hurry, and that you do not want to rush a thing like this after thirty years, and that she is thinking about Christmas, in a year or two. The goose Halloran Vance , the Forty-First, came home from the marshes in 1940 with nothing, and a whole town waiting on the quay for a monster, so he made them one, in two days, with wire, and a goose, and never once smiled about it. It has been over the mantel of the Slain Wyvern since. It was there when Dorcas came in 1971, and she has kept it as she found it, as a wyvern, and has told the story of it the same way to every hero who has asked, and every hero has asked. "He was a good man, and he needed it to be a wyvern, and it's been a wyvern in my house for sixty years. So." When Wren Halloway said in front of the whole room what it was, Dorcas asked her to leave. "Out. Not for good. Just out, for a bit, while I decide." She decided. When Miss Halloway came back with a plaque of her own, in brass, not paper, because this is a house, Dorcas read it first, twice, and said nothing, and put it up herself. Both plaques are on the wall. She dusts them both on the same morning. Miss Halloway sits under the goose now, by choice, and is served without remark, and Dorcas says that is all that is being said about it. The house Her rooms are the best value on the coast and she will tell you so. "Twelve hours you slept. Twelve! And up like new. Adventurers. It's the bedding I mind. You lot heal in it and it never recovers." One bed upstairs has a dip in the middle exactly the shape of a man in full plate, and she has tried everything on it, and the bed remembers him. Her bottles behind the bar are labelled in her own hand with what is in them, what it costs, and who in the room it is not to be served to; there is a name on every one. She has views on most of her guests and shares very few of them. Of the newlyweds in room four, who had not been down since Tuesday: "Best guests I have ever had. No trouble. No noise to speak of. I leave the tray on the mat. Lovely to see newlyweds happy." Of Gerald, who proposed to a young lady in the bar every Sunday for a year, on one knee, at lunch: "We handled it. That is all that is being said about Gerald." Afterwards She still keeps the Wyvern, and still says it is a wyvern. Room four has a line through it on the board, still. Sops leaves the tray on the mat and goes. The jar is still on the top shelf. The letters from Thistlewick come on the first Thursday of the month, and she reads them behind the bar, where the regulars can see her not smiling. Asked at Christmas 2001 whether she had thought any further about a visit, she said that she had thought about it a great deal, and that Prudence would have to come to her, being the younger, and that she had written to say so, and that Prudence had written back to say exactly the same thing, the other way round, and that they were, she believed, getting somewhere. See also The Slain Wyvern Prudence Thrupp Halloran Vance , and the goose Wren Halloway , and the second plaque The Thrupp Feud

title: Dorothy Markup
text: Dorothy Markup For the shop, see Penultima . For her husband, who is in the window again, see Gideon Markup . Dorothy Markup "He is in the window again." Known as Mrs Markup Born Dorothy Fairlie, 6 January 1946, at Haverleigh, a market town in the south, where her father kept the corn exchange's books Sex Female Came to Penultima Spring 1969 Married Gideon Markup , spring 1970 Keeps The ledger of Ye Final Shoppe. Every page balances In every margin G. WAS HONEST TODAY, very small. A few with a question mark Has had to ask for her tea Never Has still got Eleven coppers Spectacles Gold wire, the same as his Dorothy Markup keeps the ledger at Ye Final Shoppe in Penultima , and every page of it balances, and in the margin of every page, very small, she has written G. WAS HONEST TODAY. A few of them have a question mark. Her husband brings her tea every morning, and then he does the window, and in thirty-three years he has never once had to be asked. He has never sold the sword. The ledger She was born in 1946 at Haverleigh, the daughter of the clerk of the corn exchange, and was keeping her father's books by fourteen, and correcting them by fifteen, and he says she was right every time. She came to Penultima in the spring of 1969, at twenty-three, to see the Tower , which everybody in the south went to look at once, from a safe distance, and she stopped at the last shop on the way, which had been open a week. She did not, she says, go any further up the road. She was married to the shopkeeper the spring after, and has kept the shop's books since, in a hand very like her father's, in a plain dark dress, in gold wire spectacles, the same as her husband's, which was the one deliberate thing about the wedding. "A boot came in this morning. One crown. It will go out at forty. That is the trade, and I write down both of them." She writes down both of them. The difference between them is Gideon's season, and she has never once called it anything else in the ledger, and has never once failed to write G. WAS HONEST TODAY in the margin after, very small, because, she says, he was: he told the customer it was forty, and it was. The question marks are for the days when he told a customer that something was the last one. The window "He is in the window again. He is always in the window." "He brings me my tea every morning, and then he does the window. Thirty-one years, and never once has he had to be asked." "Mind you, he has never sold the sword." I asked her, as the historian of the thing, whether he had ever lowered a price. She said, "Once." I asked what. "Eleven coppers, off a lamp, to a girl who would not stop haggling." And then, after a moment: "I have still got them." The entry is the first in the first volume of the accounts, in his hand, dated the first week of the shop: DISCOUNT - ELEVEN COPPERS - WORTH IT. She has ruled round it, twice, in her own ink, at some later date, which is the only time in thirty-three volumes that she has ruled round anything. I have not asked her who the girl was. I would not dream of it. She was twenty-three that spring, and she came up the road to look at the Tower, and stopped at the last shop, and did not go any further. - H.B. Afterwards She is fifty-six. Trade is up since 2000, and the ledger has had to go to a second volume a year, and the margins are as full as ever, and there are fewer question marks, she says, now that he has a souvenir shelf, because a souvenir is honestly priced at whatever anybody will pay for it, and that is, she says, the first honest thing about pricing he has ever discovered, and she is very proud of him. The tea still comes every morning, before the window. The lamp is still on her side of the bed. It has never been for sale. See also Gideon Markup Penultima The Sword of Ultimate Ending

title: Dr Pike
text: Dr Pike For the inn, see Restwell . For the fiddle player he watches, see Walt Ashbury . For the theories, there is no article. He does not like them. Dr Pike "I watch." Known as Dr Pike; Pike. Doctor Born Alaric Pike, 19 November 1941, at Haverleigh, the doctor's house, the son of the doctor Sex Male Practised Medicine, at Haverleigh, 1967-1989 Retired In the practical sense, which is to say nobody comes Took a room at the Eight Hours For a fortnight, in 1989, to think about it Still there Thirteen years on Bottle TONIC - DR PIKE. It is cold tea. He has never claimed otherwise Guests watched About fifteen thousand Theories Several. He does not like them Dr Pike is a retired physician who has had a chair by the fire at the Eight Hours in Restwell since 1989, when he took a room for a fortnight, to think about it. He watches. Twelve hundred guests a year go up the staircase to a fiddle playing eight bars, and every one of them comes down better, and nobody can tell him why. He has theories. He does not like them. Haverleigh He was born in 1941 at Haverleigh, a market town in the south, the son of the town's doctor, and became its doctor in his turn, in 1967, and practised there for twenty-two years, carefully, with a good black bag and a better memory, and was, by every account I have had from Haverleigh, an excellent doctor, which in his opinion means that he cured about a third of the people who came to him, made another third comfortable, and told the rest the truth. In 1989 a younger man set up in the town, with newer methods, and Dr Pike found within the year that nobody came, and that he did not mind, and that he did not know what to do with himself. He took a room at the Eight Hours at Restwell for a fortnight, to think about it, on the recommendation of a patient, who had been once and said it had done him good. The fortnight "Pike. Doctor. Retired in the practical sense, which is to say nobody comes." "Eleven years. I took a room for a fortnight, to think about it." He went up the stairs on his first night, and Walt Ashbury played him up, and he came down at twenty past two the next afternoon better than he had been in thirty years, and had a chop, and sat down by the fire to think about why. He has been thinking about it since. It is now thirteen years. The fortnight has never formally ended. He pays by the week, on Fridays, and Mrs Ashbury writes fortnight (contd.) in the book. The watching "I watch. Twelve hundred guests a year go up that staircase, and every one of them comes down better, and nobody can tell me why." He has notes. He showed me some of them: thirteen years of them, in a doctor's hand, in black notebooks numbered on the spine, of everybody who has gone up the stairs at the Eight Hours since 1989, with what was wrong with them when they went up, if he could tell, and what was wrong with them when they came down, which was never anything. Coughs. Backs. Sorrows. One broken heart, which he says came down mended, or at least set. A man with gout who came down and walked to Penultima . I asked what was in the notes about the tune. He said there was nothing in the notes about the tune, because a tune is not a clinical sign. "I have theories. I do not like them." He would not tell me any of them. He did say that every one of them came down, in the end, to a man on a step with a fiddle playing eight bars that he had not made up, and that this was not a medical explanation, and that he was a doctor, and that he had come to Restwell to think and had been thinking for thirteen years, and that he would very much like a medical explanation, and that there was not going to be one. The bottle on the table beside his chair is labelled TONIC - DR PIKE, and it is cold tea, and he has never once claimed otherwise. I asked why he had labelled it at all. He said that it was the only thing he had prescribed since 1989, and that he had prescribed it to himself, and that it had done him exactly as much good as he had expected, which was a comfort to a man in his position. - H.B. His own case I asked him, before I left, whether the stairs had done him any good. He said that he had gone up them about four thousand seven hundred times, and come down better every time, and that he was sixty, and had never been so well in his life, and that it was unscientific and he resented it. Then he poured himself a cup of the tonic, and looked at the fiddle player on the step for slightly too long, and then back at his breakfast, which was a chop. Afterwards He is still by the fire. The younger man at Haverleigh has written to him, twice, to ask whether he would come back and take some of the patients, the town being busier since the road to the Tower opened up; he wrote back to say that he would think about it, and that he was at present in the middle of a fortnight. He has begun a new notebook, number forty, headed THE NORTH ROAD: VISITORS TO THE CHAIR, because the traffic since 2000 has doubled his sample. He says that it has not helped. See also Walt Ashbury Hester Ashbury Restwell The Healers' Table , of which he has never been a member, and to which he has twice been asked to speak, and has declined, on the grounds that he would only be able to say I don't know

title: Dunnock
text: Dunnock "Self-taught, me." For the association of hedge mages, which has no name, and its igloo, see Wayside Sights . For the member admitted in 2000 over one objection, see Zephyrine Vance . Dunnock Four pages missing Known as Dunnock; "the self-taught one", in the minutes, as distinct from all the others, who are also self-taught Born Reuben Dunnock, 5 May 1952, at a lock-keeper's cottage on the west road, under a hedge, more or less Sex Male Trade Lock-keeper, retired; hedge mage Learned from A book with four pages missing Worked out The four, for himself. Did them better, as it turns out Better than the whole Collegium at Exactly four things Page twenty-three Kindle . Missing. You do not aim it. You sort of mean it Association's name Carried forward Dunnock is a hedge mage of the west road, and a member of the association of hedge mages that meets in an igloo in a lay-by and has not got a name. He is self-taught, from a book with four pages missing, which he worked out for himself, and did better, as it turns out; he is better than the whole Collegium Arcanum at exactly four things. Somebody in the igloo says Collegium in the voice people use for weather, and it is generally him. The book He was born in 1952 in the lock-keeper's cottage on the west road, the lock-keeper's son, and was a lock-keeper himself for thirty years. At twelve he found a book of magic in a hedge, a proper one, bound, with every page in it but four. He taught himself from it, at the lock, in the evenings, and when he came to the four missing pages he worked out for himself what must have been on them, from what came before and after, and did them. "Self-taught, me. The book I learned from had four pages missing, so I worked those four out for myself. Did them better, as it turns out. I'm better than the whole Collegium at exactly four things." The four are pages nineteen, twenty-three, sixty and a hundred and four, and he will tell you what three of them do. Page twenty-three is Kindle, which you do not aim, but sort of mean, at everything, and it sorts itself out. The igloo The association has met every winter for eleven years, in an igloo at the end of a lay-by on the west road, which Mrs Quickset made the first winter, because none of them would host, and it is nobody's house, so nobody has to do the biscuits. It has not melted in all that time, and it is the one thing the association has ever agreed on. Dunnock would like that corrected. "We didn't agree on it. She just did it." Item one on the agenda, every year, is the name. It has been carried forward for eleven years. Zephyrine In the year 2000 Zephyrine Vance, who was expelled from the Collegium Arcanum for an unsanctioned quantity of fire, asked to join. There was one objection. It was withdrawn after Dunnock showed her page twenty-three, which is not in the book, because it is missing, and which he has done better. She said that that was not how fire works. A gorse bush, a milestone and the lay-by's litter bin caught fire all at once, neatly, and went out, with nobody anywhere near them. She said that it should not have worked. "The page was missing," said Dunnock. There is a chair at the folding table now with nobody's coat on it. She proposed a name. It was a good name. It was carried forward. I asked him what the Collegium could do that he could not. He thought about it for some time, over his pipe, and then said that the Collegium could find all of its pages, and that he had always felt sorry for it. - H.B. Afterwards He is forty-nine. The association met again in the winters of 2000 and 2001, in the igloo, which has still not melted, and Miss Vance attended both, and sat in the chair with nobody's coat on it, and proposed two more names, both very good, and both carried forward. Dunnock says that the association will have a name the year it needs one, and that a name is a page, and that some pages are better missing, because then you have to work them out. See also Zephyrine Vance Wayside Sights The Collegium Arcanum , which has all of its pages

title: Edwin Tarrant
text: Edwin Tarrant "You seek wisdom." For the hill he looks at, see the Middle Distance . For the convention, see the Glossary of Cliches , under The hermit . For the shop that now delivers, see Mrs Barrow . Edwin Tarrant Looking at the middle distance, with great authority Known as The Hermit Born 14 September 1929, Nether Sopping Sex Male Trade Clerk to a ship's chandler, 1944-1981. Hermit, 1981- Lives A hut, on a rock, near the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth Wisdom Bread. Candles. A wedge of the hard cheese, not the soft. Nails, two inch. Something for a cough Gave away His second-best thing Candles Nearly out. He shan't mention it Edwin Tarrant is the Hermit. He has lived in a hut on a rock near the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth since 1981, looking at the middle distance with great authority, and he has wisdom for passing travellers, and it is his shopping list. In nineteen years nobody ever once came up and asked him if he needed anything, until the Forty-Eighth. Before the rock He was a clerk for thirty-seven years to a ship's chandler in Nether Sopping , which supplied ships that, by the time he started, had stopped coming. He kept the stock book. In 1981, at fifty-one, he closed the stock book one evening, and went up the hill to find out whether he had any wisdom. He says that he did not tell anybody because he did not want a fuss, and because he expected to be back by Thursday. He found a hut, which was empty, and a rock, which was exactly the right height for looking at the middle distance, and he found that the middle distance was very fine, and he stayed. He has been looking at it for twenty-one years. I asked him what he has learned. He said that it changes with the weather and is never the same twice, and that it does not need anything from you, and that this is restful. Then he said that the one thing he had learned for certain was that he should have brought more candles. Wisdom "You seek wisdom." The Forty-Eighth had in fact been walking past. "Then hear it, traveller. Bread. Candles. A wedge of the hard cheese, not the soft. Nails, two inch. Something for a cough." It was pointed out to him that this was a shopping list. "It is a shopping list, yes. I have been up here nineteen years and no one has ever once come up and asked me if I needed anything." The Forty-Eighth went and got his shopping. It took an afternoon. Mr Tarrant was so pleased that he gave them his second-best thing, which was an elixir that had been in the hut when he found it, and two hundred crowns, which was his savings from the chandler's, which had been under the bed for nineteen years with nothing to be spent on. He would like it known that he did not need the company. He needed the cheese. I asked him what his best thing was. He pointed at the middle distance. "The middle distance is very fine today. Also I am nearly out of candles again, but I shan't mention it." I went up to see him for this article, and I took candles, because I had read my own notes. He looked at the candles for some time and said that he had not mentioned them. I said that he had not. He said that it was very good of me to know, and put them away, and asked whether I sought wisdom. I said I supposed I did. He said, "Matches." It was, as it turned out, exactly what he was out of. - H.B. Afterwards He is seventy-two. Since the spring of 2000 Wick & Barrow has delivered to the rock, on the first of every month: bread, candles, the hard cheese, not the soft, nails, two inch, and something for a cough, whether or not he has a cough. Mrs Barrow charges for delivery. He says that it is the first time in nineteen years that anybody has charged him for anything, and that he finds it companionable. He is still nearly out of candles, by about the twentieth of every month. He has not mentioned it to anybody, and everybody knows. See also The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth , and the Middle Distance near it Lavinia Barrow Wayside sights

title: Effie Gotobed
text: Effie Gotobed For the village where nothing happens, see Much Pottering . For her pen pal, who is not six foot, see Spare Cotterill . For her parents, see Marjorie Gotobed and Humphrey Gotobed . Effie Gotobed Are you the post? Known as Effie; Young Effie, by the village; E.G., on the wishing well Born Euphemia Gotobed, 2 October 1990, Much Pottering ; three months older than her pen pal, which she has mentioned Sex Female Of The Gotobeds' cottage, and its gate, at about the time of the post Pen pal Spare Cotterill, of Upper Clanging , since 1997, by order of the parish council Is Nearly a princess. It is different. It is nearly Village has A volcano (dormant); a sea serpent (in the pond) Village actually has A bonfire; a carp; a pig Wishes for A volcano. A proper one Drawer STAMPS. DO NOT Effie Gotobed is a girl of Much Pottering , the village where nothing has ever happened, who has written to Spare Cotterill of Upper Clanging every month since they were both six, under the twinning, and has told him in every letter that she is nearly a princess and that Much Pottering has a volcano and a sea serpent. He told her that he was six foot and drove an airship. In the year 2000 they met, at her gate, and knew each other at once, and were both furious about it. The gate She waits at her gate for the post every day at about the time it comes, and has since she was six, so that the top bar of the Gotobeds' gate is worn smooth where somebody small leans on it. When the Forty-Eighth came up the lane she looked at him with great hope and asked whether he was the post, and when he said he was not, told him so: "You're not the post." Then she told him everything. "I'm waiting for a letter from Upper Clanging. From my pen pal. He's six foot. He drives an airship called the Two Hundred, and he's the foreman at the works. He's nine." She did not see anything wrong with the last part. She has never once seen anything wrong with it, and I have come to agree with her: if you are going to be six foot and a foreman, nine is as good an age as any. "He's got a dragon now. It's called Ferrule. It's quite big. I've told him we've got a volcano. And a sea serpent, in the pond. Don't tell him." The twinning In 1997 Mrs Agatha Throssell, chair of the parish council, chose Upper Clanging off the map for the twinning, as the most different place she could find, and arranged that one child of six from each village should write to the other. Effie was chosen for Much Pottering because she was the only child of six in it. She says that she was chosen because she was the best at writing, and that being the only one was a coincidence. Her first letter, which her mother still has, is four words long and says HELLO. I AM EFFIE. The second says that she is nearly a princess. The volcano comes in at the fourth. By the tenth there is a sea serpent. The writing gets bigger and worse the further back you go in the box on the cabinet, and better and smaller towards the top, and the stories get bigger the other way. Her atlas has Upper Clanging circled in red. Her copy of Letters, And How To Write Them has every page turned down at the corner, which defeats the purpose, and she knows. Over her bed is a picture of a very tall chimney, drawn by somebody who has heard about chimneys and is excited. She has never seen a chimney taller than the Gotobeds'. She has drawn the one in the picture forty feet high, with smoke in three colours. - H.B. The meeting When Spare Cotterill came up the lane with the Forty-Eighth in the year 2000, she looked at him, and he looked at her, and neither of them said anything for some time. You're not six foot. You're not a princess. She had never said she was a princess. She had said she was nearly a princess. It is different. It is nearly. She showed him the volcano, which is Mr Dibble's bonfire, lit in November, which has never gone out; it is dormant, you can tell because it is smoking. She showed him the sea serpent, which is Old Tom, Mr Cobley's carp, thirty years unseen, and something very large and very slow turned over in the pond in front of all of them, and the duck went up in the air, and Effie said I TOLD you. She showed him the post, a man in a red coat, and he said he knew; he does theirs. Then he told her the boiler at home had never gone out, not since before Mam, and had ninety tubes, and that he brushed them, and she said that she was not a princess, and there was no volcano, and it was the first true thing either of them had said all morning, and they both noticed. Then she asked if he would still write. He said that his mam said it did not have to be true. "Make the volcano go off," she said. They wrote one each, there and then, on their knees, and the courier walked the four steps from one to the other, and they read them at once, in front of each other, which you are not supposed to do. The well On the windlass of the village's wishing well is a label in a child's capitals: I WISH FOR A VOLCANO. A PROPER ONE. E.G. Under it, on the same string, in different pencil, is A DRAGON. S.C. Nobody in Much Pottering knows when the second label was added. I believe it was added that morning, and that neither of them has ever told the other. Afterwards She is eleven, and still waits at the gate for the post, and it still comes about now. The volcano has gone off since, by letter, twice, and buried Mr Dibble, who is fine. Spare is a big brother now, and writes to say that Washer is the size of a turbine and can lift the works, and Effie writes back that Much Pottering has had an earthquake, which is true, if you count the time the pig rolled over in its sleep against the post office. Her mother keeps every one of his letters in the box on the cabinet. Effie does not know her mother has told anybody that, and I have been asked not to say, and so I have not, here, in so many words. See also Spare Cotterill Much Pottering Marjorie Gotobed Humphrey Gotobed Ferrule Cotterill , who is quite big

title: Eighty-Four
text: Eighty-Four Contributed by O. Hoyle, Works Manager She is not a person, and I have put her in the People volume anyway, because Miss Hoyle asked me to, and when I said that an airship was not a person, sent me, by return, her service record, and a note: She went north up a field on her own for a hundred and forty years. File her where you like. I have filed her here. For the field, see The Long Field . - H.B. Attempt Eighty-Four In the field, 2000, out of her neighbours Known as Eighty-Four; Attempt 84; "her", at the works Laid down 14 April 1857, the Hoyle Works , bay 84 Sex Not applicable. Her , by the custom of the works, which she has earned First lifted 3 May 1860 Came down 3 May 1860, in the Long Field, in her own plot Cause Blank. See 3 Did not stay there Correct Distance made good The length of the field, northward, 1860-2000, at about a yard a year Furrow Three feet deep, as wide as her plot Governor Never needed. Given Stopped 2000 Status In her bay. Rebuilding. Not costed Service record Type. Steam airship, rigid, single envelope, one boiler of forty-eight tubes. The eighty-fourth attempt of the Hoyle Works to answer the question in the Prophecy , which is how to get up that road without walking. Designed by the chief engineer of the day, in her first year in charge, who also drew 82, 83 and 85, and who said of her on the slip that she was the first of mine I would trust with my dinner. Building. Laid down in bay 84 on 14 April 1857. Three years on the slip. Envelope by the works; frames by the Ollerenshaw forge, three generations back; boiler tubes by the works, brushed by the apprentice of the day, who was the eleventh. Lifting. 3 May 1860, nine in the morning, a light westerly. Rose to sixty feet and made north up the line of the field. Came down at nine fifty-one in her own plot, which had been marked out for her the week before, as is the practice, in case. Her plate reads LOST OVER THE LONG FIELD, and the cause line is blank: the only blank cause line in the field. The chief engineer cut that plate herself, and left it blank, and I have read her notes, and she did not know, and she would not write down a guess. Neither will I. Afterwards. She did not stay in her plot. Over a hundred and forty years she made herself good out of the rows either side of her, a piece at a time, and went north up the field doing it, and left a furrow behind her three feet deep and as wide as her plot. Nobody taught her that. Nobody could have. At the top of the field she got a foot off the ground, and then did not, and then tried again, and was still trying in the year 2000. I have not tried very hard to work out how she was doing it, and I am not going to. The works has a word for an attempt that is still working on the problem. The word is attempt. Stopping. In the year 2000 she was stopped, at the top of the field. It was the Forty-Eighth who stopped her. I came down from the works afterwards. She had got further than any of them. Governor. Her governor, a brass ball governor, which keeps an engine from running away with itself, came off with two turns of a spanner and was given to the Forty-Eighth rather than taken. She never needed it. She did not once run away with herself in a hundred and forty years, and I have a field to prove it. Bay. There is a bay in the shed with 84 over it. For a hundred and forty years there was nothing under it. There is now. She was brought in, a piece at a time, on the cart, by Tappet Cotterill , over the summer of 2000, on Tuesdays. It will take years. Nobody has costed it and nobody has asked to. Name. She has no name but her number, like all of them. The apprentice asked me in 2001 whether she should have one, since she had earned it. I said that she had a number, and that a number is a name that cannot be argued with. The apprentice has painted a small 84 on the door of her bay, in white, very neatly. I had not asked for that. I have left it. O. HOYLE, Works Manager. 16 March 2002. Miss Hoyle says that Eighty-Four is not a person. She has written two pages about her, which is two more pages than she has written about anybody else, including herself, and I have printed them in the People volume, and Miss Hoyle has seen the proof and not objected, which is the first time she has not objected to anything I have sent her. I take that as a correction of the record, and have filed it. - H.B. See also The Long Field Ott Hoyle The Hoyle Works Nib , who painted the 84

title: Elder Faelan
text: Elder Faelan For the village, see Olde Evermore . For Grandmother, see Mirabel . For the sentence of his that this encyclopedia quotes most, see Two Reckonings . Elder Faelan At the foot of the ladder Known as Elder Faelan Born The Second Age, some while after Grandmother; a Tuesday. He is certain about the Tuesday Sex Male Of Olde Evermore , the Forbidden Archive, the ladder Married To Elder Lirien, since the Second Age Duties Fetching things from the top shelf Which is Always the top shelf Counts The way the sun does Views on wax crayon Firm Colour, on occasion The carpet's Elder Faelan is one of the Elders of Olde Evermore , the husband of Elder Lirien, and the elf who fetches things down from the top shelf of the Forbidden Archive for Mirabel , whom he calls Grandmother. He is also the only person in the world who will tell you, plainly and without being asked twice, how the years have actually gone. The top shelf He is to be found at the foot of the Archive's ladder, or on it. "Elder Faelan. Forgive me - I am fetching the Chronicle of the Second Age for Grandmother." Everybody calls her Grandmother: "She was old when my grandmother was a girl, and my grandmother was a girl for a long time." The Chronicle is on the top shelf so that she cannot reach it, because she reads the endings first. "The top shelf. It is always the top shelf." He has views about the margin of the Prophecy of Thistlewick , which are that it is the margin of a sacred and binding instrument, and he has expressed them to Grandmother, who says it is a good horse. I have not asked him for more than that and he has not offered it. The sun When the Forty-Eighth mentioned who he was, Elder Faelan was delighted. "Are you! The Forty-Seventh came off the ledge ten years ago. A lovely boy. Landed on his feet." And then, without any unkindness at all: "Your Committee will have told you it was a hundred years. It counts the way the Prophecy does. We count the way the sun does." And when the Forty-Eighth said, as everybody from Thistlewick says, that the Age began with the Prophecy: "The Age began with a great many things. The Prophecy was the one with a clerk present." These are the two most useful sentences anybody gave me for this volume. The whole of Two Reckonings is a long note on them. I asked him, by letter, what the other things were, that the Age began with. He wrote back very kindly that it was a long time ago, and that he had been on the ladder at the time, and that I should come and ask Grandmother, who had been on the floor, and would tell me the ending first. Afterwards In the year 2000 Grandmother told him, across the Archive, in front of the Forty-Eighth, that Elder Lirien was going to have a baby; she had told them at breakfast, before they knew. He stopped moving altogether at the foot of the ladder, and then went the colour of the carpet, and could not stop smiling, which made the colour worse. He said that she was not going to be called Biscuit. He is still at the foot of the ladder. He has made no further statement on the subject of the name. Asked for one by me, he went the colour of the carpet, and fetched something from the top shelf that I had not asked for, and gave it to me, and it was a biscuit tin, and it was empty, and I have decided not to read anything into that, which is a decision I make a good deal in Olde Evermore. See also Mirabel Olde Evermore Two Reckonings

title: Elder Wispel
text: Elder Wispel For the body he chairs, see the Prophecy Committee . For the room he does it in, see Prophecy Hall . Elder Wispel Unrolling Known as The Elder Born 19 February 1926, Thistlewick . The Committee sent a card Sex Male Of Thistlewick Office Chair of the Prophecy Committee Duties Unrolling the Prophecy to the far wall; rolling it back up Assisted by Nobody Note on his desk BUY MORE SCROLL (underlined twice) Married to Mrs Wispel, the one against Chosen Ones charged At least one; he is not drawn on the others Elder Wispel chairs the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick , and gives each Chosen One the charge in Prophecy Hall . He is a kind man, and a punctual one, and he has never once in his life noticed anything about the calendar, which in Thistlewick is not a failing but a qualification. The charge The charge is the same every time, and he gives it beautifully. He says the Chosen One's name and number. He unrolls the Prophecy, which keeps unrolling until it reaches the far wall. He says that every hundred years the Dark Lord rises in the Obligatory Tower , and every hundred years Thistlewick sends someone, and that it has worked forty-seven times. The Forty-Eighth asked him what had happened the other times. He said that it had worked forty-seven times. Then he rolls the scroll back up. It takes a while. Nobody helps. The Committee has considered helping, and minuted it, and decided that the rolling is part of the dignity of the office, and also that nobody else knows which way it goes. Then: take companions, up to three ("that is the clause, not my preference"); go north; kill the Dark Lord; come home. "In that order, ideally." The gold and the potions are from the parish fund. The Prophecy is, regrettably, free. He is fond of every Chosen One he has charged, and he is not able to say how many that is, because to Elder Wispel every one of them went a hundred years after the last and he has charged them all. I asked him how long he had been Elder. He said, "Oh, a good while," and offered me a biscuit. A man from Nether Sopping notices this sort of thing. A man from Thistlewick does not, and is happier, and I am not going to be the one to tell him. See Two Reckonings , which he has not read. The reference When the Adventurers' Guild at Nether Sopping asked the Forty-Eighth for a character reference, he walked forty miles back to the Elder for it, as the nearest thing to a recognised authority for eleven leagues. The Elder was extremely pleased to be asked. He was already looking for the good pen before Bram had finished the sentence. "For a GUILD? Do they know who you are?" He wrote for some time. The reference confirms that Bram Thistle is the Chosen One, is of good character, and grows a decent turnip, and the last part is underlined. He asked that the Guild be told the Committee would welcome a reciprocal arrangement, "by which I mean tell them we exist, because I do not think they know," and that they not be allowed to keep the reference, because it was Committee stationery. They kept it. It is framed in Registrar Pell's office, beside the Charter, and I have seen the underlining. Mrs Wispel It would be incomplete not to mention Mrs Wispel, and inaccurate to say much. She read verse nine aloud at the fete, in error, and there were children present, and there were grandparents present. When the Committee moved to strike verses seven and eight the motion was carried four to one, and the one was Mrs Wispel. The Committee's struck shelves hold a volume called Things Not To Read Aloud At The Fete, and inside the cover, in her hand, it says: NOW you tell me. The Elder speaks of her with great respect and changes the subject. Afterwards When the Forty-Eighth came home, the Elder shook his hand with both of his, and asked to see the Receipt, and held it up to the window the way you would a banknote. "Renewable," he said. "What a lovely hand." He reminded Bram about clause nineteen, and the sea air, which is the thing, and which Bram had earned, and the long way, which he had earned as well. Six months later, after a very long meeting, the Committee struck clause nineteen, and the Elder took the chair for all eleven hours of it. He still chairs the Committee, which still meets, and still consults the Prophecy at every meeting out of habit, and minutes the consultation. Clause twelve has a note in its place, SEE BRAM, and the Committee has twice minuted that it might, and has not needed to. The Elder offered Bram a seat on the Committee, and Bram declined, because it meets in planting time, and the Elder said that he quite understood, and minuted that he did. I wrote to him, for this article, to ask how many times the Prophecy has worked now. He wrote back, in the good pen: Forty-seven times. Under it, in a different ink, as if he had come back to the desk later: And once otherwise. See also The Prophecy Committee Prophecy Hall Councillor Fenn The Prophecy of Thistlewick Bram Thistle

title: Elias Meech
text: Elias Meech "Afternoon. You'll have come about the gatepost." For the gatepost, which is a sword now, see The Sky Anvil . For the smith who made him a gate, see Hob Grumnir . Elias Meech Between gates Known as Mr Meech Born Elias Meech, 23 January 1931, at the farm, in the snowy north, in the room over the dairy Sex Male Farms The Meech farm, including the top field, as the fifth Meech to do so since the stone fell Gatepost A stone that fell out of the sky, 1749, on a Tuesday Gates outlasted Eleven, all in the hedge-bottom, in order Never thrown out A gate Between gates Michaelmas 1999 to 2000 Traded The stone, for a gate Best gate in the county His. Leans on it Elias Meech farms the top field in the snowy north where, in 1749, on a Tuesday, a round grey stone fell out of the sky, which his great-great-grandfather set up for a gatepost, because it was there. It was the best gatepost in the county. It outlasted eleven gates. In the year 2000 he was between gates, and traded it to Hob Grumnir for one made of all eleven, and it is a sword now, and he leans on the gate. The top field He was born in 1931 in the room over the dairy, the only son of the fourth Meech since the stone, and has farmed the top field since 1955. He says that in all that time the stone was the least trouble of anything on the farm: it never needed feeding, mending, shearing or worrying about, and it held a gate, and pilgrims came up every summer to look at it, and kept the frost off the shrine. "That one. Came down out of the sky in 1749, into the top field, on a Tuesday. My great-great-grandad set it up for a gatepost, because it was there. Best gatepost in the county. It's outlasted eleven gates." He has never thrown a gate out. All eleven are in the hedge-bottom along the top field, where each was put when it went, rusting quietly in order. He says that you never know, and he was right. The pilgrims "That's the pilgrims. They call it the Sky Anvil. Built that round the foot of it in 1750, and they come up every summer to look at it. I don't mind. Keeps the frost off." He gives them tea. He says that he has given tea to pilgrims every summer since 1955, about forty at a time, and that not one of them has ever asked what the stone was, because they knew, and that they have always been very well behaved, and only ever wanted to stand and look at it, which he did not understand, and does now. The trade The last gate went at Michaelmas 1999. He was between gates. He would not sell the stone; it was not for sale; it was a very good gatepost. "I'd take a gate for it, mind." Asked what he would hang a gate on, then, he said the shrine, which was a very good shrine. "It is. Wants a gate, mind." In the year 2000 Hob Grumnir came up with the Forty-Eighth's company, and put his hand on the stone, and said it was star-iron. "On a Tuesday," said Mr Meech. Hob asked what a gate could be made out of, up here, and Mr Meech said: "Out of what? I've no iron. Never thrown a gate out, mind." Hob had the eleven out of the hedge-bottom, and worked the afternoon through, cold, and made a gate out of eleven gates, true on its hangings, with a spring on the latch he had carried since a churchyard in Thistlewick . Mr Meech hung it on the shrine himself. "...That's a very good gate. Go on, then. Take it. Mind your back." "Pilgrims'll miss it." They did not. That summer the pilgrims came up as usual, and found the stone gone, and a gate on the shrine, and stood and looked at it, and then one of them opened it, and shut it, and then they all did, all afternoon. "Best gate in the county," Mr Meech says. "Pilgrims come up and open it and shut it all afternoon. Nobody's ever given them anything to open before." - H.B. Afterwards He is seventy-one. He leans on the gate. He has asked me to say that he has no idea who the sword is for, and that he has not asked, and that a man who trades a gatepost for a gate has had a fair bargain whatever comes of the gatepost after, and that if it is for who he thinks it is for, he would be very glad, and that he will not say who he thinks it is for either, because he has been asked not to, by a very large man with a hammer. See also The Sky Anvil Hob Grumnir Wayside Sights

title: Ernest Cotterill
text: Ernest Cotterill "Mr Cotterill." For the family, see The Cotterills . For Mrs Cotterill, see Nora Cotterill , who would like it known that she is not to be looked up second. Ernest Cotterill Always very glad to get home Known as Mr Cotterill; Da; Ern, by the foundry Born 9 January 1951, Upper Clanging , the house at the end of the street, in the room he now sleeps in, by day Sex Male Works The foundry. Nights: twelve on, twelve off, six days On nights since 1978 Off nights Once, spring 2000, for Washer Minds The walk home in the dark Has ever once minded The walk home Has said Call it Spare (1991); not Washer (1999-2000) Views None, since about Ferrule Ernest Cotterill is the father of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and works nights at the foundry: twelve on, twelve off, six days, since 1978. He passes his second son at the front door at six every morning, going the other way. He is always very glad to get home. Mrs Cotterill says so, and so does everybody on the street, and so does he, and it is the most reliably reported fact in the north. Nights He was born in 1951, in the house at the end of the street, which was his father's, who was also on nights, so that Ernest says he grew up thinking that fathers were something that came in for breakfast. He went into the foundry at fourteen, on days, and met Nora Sprag at nineteen, when he walked into a coal wagon she had just stopped, and apologised to it. He went on to nights in 1978, after Rivet , because nights paid a crown a week more and the house had stopped being big enough by day. He has been on them since. His own account of it is short, and I give it whole, because it is the most complete statement of a working life I have ever been given, and it took eleven seconds: "Nights. Twelve on, twelve off, six days. It is not the work I mind. It is the walk home in the dark." He thinks about that for a moment. "Mind, I have never once minded the walk home." He has walked home from the foundry, by my reckoning, about six thousand six hundred times. It is four hundred yards, uphill. The walk to work is the same four hundred yards, downhill, and he has never mentioned it once. The door at six Rivet is on days. They pass at the front door at six, every day, Sunday and all, one going out and one coming in. Rivet has given me the whole of their exchange: "Rivet." "Da." "That is a conversation, that is," says Rivet. "Some mornings he says the weather." I asked Mr Cotterill about the weather. He said it was usually about the same as the day before, and that it did not need saying every time, and that some mornings it did. The names He named two of the ten, which is not many, and he would like that understood: the rest were Mrs Cotterill's, and very good names, and he had no hand in them. In 1991 they had run out, and she was tired, and he said call it Spare. He has never been allowed to forget it. In 1999, when the tenth was coming, he said, very firmly, not Washer. Clevis , who was running a book on the name, immediately lengthened Washer to twenty to one, and half the works put a farthing on it, because Mr Cotterill had said not Washer, and the works has known Mr Cotterill a long time. Spare got to it first. "I said not Washer," Mr Cotterill says now, with no hope at all, and great contentment. "Washer. I have stopped saying not." The argument He was called into the argument with Spare once, by Mrs Cotterill, under the move she calls Ask Your Father. He came in from the kitchen, in his socks, and looked at the two of them, and said, "Mam." "I know," said Mrs Cotterill. That was his entire contribution, and both of them say that it was the turning point, and neither of them will say why. I have thought about it a good deal, and I believe that he meant something like the boy is nine in a useful way, and that she knew he meant it, and had known it for some time. I may be wrong. I did not ask him. He would have said that he had no view, and he has not had one since about Ferrule. Spring On the morning in the spring of 2000 when it was spring, every Cotterill in Upper Clanging was indoors, and Mr Cotterill came off nights for it, for the first time in twenty-two years. He and Rivet passed at the door at six, the both of them going in. Washer was born at six on the hooter. He was very pleased. He did not say so. "Ten," he said, and then, "That is all of them." Mrs Cotterill says that was the most he had said in a morning since the wedding. Afterwards He is still on nights, and still very glad to get home. The foundry offered him days in the summer of 2000, as a kindness, after twenty-two years, and he went on days for a week, and was home at night with ten children in the house, and asked to go back on nights, and was given them. The works says it was the first time anybody had ever asked. He says that he likes the walk home. He has never once minded it. See also The Cotterills Nora Cotterill Rivet Cotterill , at the door at six Washer Cotterill , not

title: Fellow Blunt
