text: Fellow Blunt "Not ready." For the prophecy he kept, see Roland Fairweather . For the stone, see Carn Drey . For his yard and who is in it, see Maud Penhallow . Fellow Blunt Quarterly Known as Fellow Blunt; "(FELLOW BLUNT, QUARTERLY.)", on a plate Born 2 October 1937, Great Dunnage . His first name is not in the minutes, and he has not given it to me Sex Male Fellow of Mr Fairweather's review, one of four under the Convenor, 1978-2000 His department The stone Not his department The stairs. It's minuted Checked the stone Quarterly, from the gate, eighty-eight times Report Not ready, eighty-eight times Keeps A yard at Great Dunnage: sword, horse, lineage, the lot Fellow Blunt was the member of Roland Fairweather 's review responsible for the stone. For twenty-two years he went out to Carn Drey once a quarter, looked at the stone from the gate, came back, and reported at the next meeting, under item three, that it was not ready. He never once went down the stairs to it. The stairs were not his department. Readiness The review sat in the snug of the Bell at Great Dunnage , under a Convenor, with three Fellows: Fellow Grice, who reported the sorcerer's apologies; Fellow Amory, who took the minutes; and Fellow Blunt, who reported on the stone and the sword. At the hundred and forty-first meeting, which the Forty-Eighth's party attended, item three went like this, and I am told it had always gone like this: The Convenor: Item three. Readiness. The stone? Fellow Blunt: Not ready. The Convenor: The sword? Fellow Blunt: In the stone. He said nothing else at that meeting. Before it, while they waited for the asset, he said, "The stone is not ready. I check the stone." I am told by people who were at the table that he did not say it unkindly, or as a man who doubted it. He said it as somebody saying where he lives. The gate There is an iron gate across the mouth of the cave in Carn Drey's south face, and on it is a plate: THE WORM. NOT READY. (FELLOW BLUNT, QUARTERLY.) That is his. He put it up in 1978, when the review began, and he came out to it every quarter, by his own account in all weathers, and stood at the gate, and looked down the stairs into the dark at a stone he could not see from there, and went home and said that it was not ready. The gate was not locked. Nobody ever tried it. In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth suggested to Roland Fairweather that somebody might go down the stairs and look, and there was a very long pause, and then he said, "...Today?" The stone was ready. It had, as far as anybody can tell, been ready for some time. The sword came out of it in Roland's hand, and the Worm under the hill was ended that afternoon. Under NOT READY on Fellow Blunt's plate somebody has since written, in pencil: READY. DONE. (R.F.) I wrote to Fellow Blunt to ask whether, in twenty-two years, he had ever been tempted to go down. He wrote back by return, two lines: The stairs are not my department. It is minuted. Then, underneath, in a different ink, as if added the next morning: It was, I find, ready. I have not been able to improve on either line. - H.B. The yard He also keeps a yard at Great Dunnage, where the review had its understudy taught: sword, horse, lineage, the lot. In case. Maud Penhallow went into it in 1993, at nine, and was told that the prophecy was nearly ready, which was his report and the review's, and was true, as far as the gate went. Everything Miss Penhallow knows about a sword she learned in his yard. She says he was a very good teacher, and very patient, and that he never once told her she was ready either, about anything, which she has decided was a matter of department. Afterwards He is sixty-four. The review met once more after the Worm, to minute the prophecy discharged. It took four minutes. Under item three Fellow Blunt reported, for the first time, that the stone was ready. Fellow Amory underlined it. The review has not met since, and Fellow Blunt has nothing left to check, but he still goes out to Carn Drey once a quarter, in all weathers, and stands at the gate and reads the pencil, and comes home. Miss Penhallow is still in the yard. He has not asked her to leave. He has started asking her opinion. See also Roland Fairweather Maud Penhallow Carn Drey Great Dunnage

title: Ferrety Bother
text: Ferrety Bother "It's a family name." For the light, the tower and everything in it, see The Lighthouse of Saint Bother . For the oil, see Mrs Barrow , who charged for it. Ferrety Bother At the bottom of the stairs Known as Mr Bother; the keeper Born 3 February 1938, in the lighthouse, on the ground floor, under the tapestry of the storm Sex Male Keeper of The Lighthouse of Saint Bother , since 1970. The fourth generation Great-grandmother The saint. She'd have hated the fuss Stairs climbed Eleven thousand times, by 2000 Jumpers A great many, all identical, all with a lighthouse on Has walked to the crossroads Once Ferrety Bother keeps the light at the point east of Nether Sopping , as his father did, and his grandmother, and his great-grandmother before her, who is the saint. No ship has passed the point since 1909. The light is not for the ships. It is for the ones coming back down the north road at night, who can see it from the crossroads, and walk home by it. The family "Ferrety Bother. It's a family name. The saint was my great-grandmother and she'd have hated the fuss." Her book, on the top floor, is signed S. Bother. Her first name is not in it, or anywhere in the lighthouse, and the family says she would have hated the fuss of a first name too. The tapestries of her on the ground floor were made by her son's wife, Ferrety's grandmother, who also found something on the rocks one winter, which is in a pickling jar in the store and has never been named. The deckchair tapestry, with SHE'D HAVE HATED THE FUSS embroidered underneath, is Ferrety's, done in the winter of 1971, his first as keeper, when he had a great many evenings. He was born in the tower, in February, in a gale. His father, who was keeping the light that night, came down the stairs between trimming the wick and trimming it again, and went back up. There are no other Bothers. He has never married. He says that there was never anybody who wanted to live up eleven floors of stairs, and when I pointed out that it is six, he said that it is six going up. Out of oil The Guild paid a stipend for the light until the shipping stopped, and then stopped paying it. The family went on buying oil out of their own pockets for ninety-one years, until the spring before the Quest, when the oil ran out and so did the pocket. Mrs Barrow at Wick & Barrow had oil, and also had a price. "One gallon. That's all it takes. Mrs Barrow, across from the Guild. Tell her it's for the light. She'll still charge you. Tell her anyway." The Forty-Eighth was told this by a man sitting at the bottom of a dark lighthouse in the dark, which is a thing you notice about a lighthouse immediately. He was told that a lighthouse with no ships was not a lamp on a rock, because it had not been for the ships for four generations. He went to Mrs Barrow, who charged him, and brought the gallon back, and Mr Bother said, "You'll be wanting to go up, then," and did not get up. He had been up those stairs eleven thousand times. He wanted somebody else to do it once. When they came down he pressed a keeper's lamp on them without a word, which, from him, is a speech. The crossroads "You can see it from the crossroads. I checked. I walked out to the crossroads at midnight to check, and I stood there, and I looked back." It is the only time in his life he has walked to the crossroads. He went the night the light was relit, after the company had gone, and locked the door behind him, which he had never done, and walked out along the road in the dark as far as the crossroads, and turned round. He says that it was lit. He says that he stood there for some time. He did not say anything else about it, and I have put it in this article in his words and not added any. He has made one ship in a bottle a year since 1970, each with a tiny lighthouse in it, lit, for the shelf, because his father did and his grandmother did. I asked him what he would put in the bottle for 2000. He said a lighthouse, lit, the same as every year. Then he took it down to show me, and there is a very small figure in it, at the foot of the tower, with a gallon can. He said that it was in proportion. - H.B. Afterwards He is sixty-four. The lamp needed oil again in the spring of 2001, and somebody got it, now that somebody has, and it has not gone out since. He has not walked to the crossroads again. He says that he does not need to, and that he might, one night, if somebody was coming home. He still uses one plate, and washes it, and dusts the other twenty-nine on Sundays, and he still trims the wick square every week, regardless. See also The Lighthouse of Saint Bother Lavinia Barrow The Chosen Ones , who walked home by the light

title: Ferrule Cotterill
text: Ferrule Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills , who are not to sit down. For the dragon of the same name, there is no article, because there was no dragon; see Spare Cotterill , and Effie Gotobed , who was told about it. Ferrule Cotterill In charge from six Known as Ferrule Born 6 February 1984, Upper Clanging Sex Female Named for A ferrule, which is a collar. It fastens nothing. It only stops a split. ( Grommet ) In charge From six, when Da goes to work Policy Nobody gets to sit down Exceptions Mam, spring 2000, one week, by order Times Mam got up anyway Four. Counted Has a dragon named after Yes, in a letter. It is quite big Do not Encourage Clevis Ferrule Cotterill is the fifth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and is in charge from six, when Da goes to work, and then nobody gets to sit down. Ferrule introduced the whole position to the Forty-Eighth in three sentences, in the voice of a foreman reading a notice: "I am Ferrule. I am sixteen. I am in charge from six." From six The arrangement began in 1996, when Ferrule was twelve, on an evening when Mr Cotterill had gone down to the foundry and Mrs Cotterill had gone up to the Parish Rooms about a christening, and Cotter was in Great Dunnage , and Rivet was asleep, and Gudgeon was at the Rooms with Mam, and Tappet was out with the cart, and so the oldest Cotterill awake in the house was Ferrule. When Mrs Cotterill came home at nine the floor had been swept, the younger ones were in bed in order of size, the kettle was on, and Clevis had been made to give back three farthings. Mrs Cotterill looked round the kitchen for some time and then said, "Right, then," and that was the appointment. It has not been revoked. She has been in charge from six every evening since, for six years, and the house runs, in the evenings, the way a works runs: to time, and standing up. "Da goes to work. Then I am in charge and nobody gets to sit down." I asked what would happen if somebody did sit down. She looked at me for a moment as if I had asked what would happen if the river ran uphill, and then said that nobody did. Mam The difficulty of the position is Mrs Cotterill, who is not in charge after six, and who does not accept it. In the winter of 2000, before Washer , she was not to lift anything, by Ferrule's order, and lifted things the moment Ferrule's back was turned. "She lifts things the moment I turn round." Ferrule had taken to walking backwards round the kitchen, to keep her in view, which she said was very unsettling and a sign of a disordered household, and lifted a coal scuttle to make the point. The family had given all the small clothes away, thinking there would be no more, and Mrs Cotterill had to go round the town and ask for them back. Ferrule went with her, carrying the basket, so that she would not. After Washer, it was worse. "Mam is to stay sat down for a week," Ferrule announced, at six, to the whole family and the midwife. A week later Ferrule reported the outcome to the Forty-Eighth: "She has been up four times. I have counted." And then, with the air of somebody making a very great concession to circumstances: "Nobody gets to sit down. Except Mam. Mam has to." Mrs Cotterill disputes the figure. She says she was up eleven times, and that Ferrule only saw four, and that it is not her fault if some people turn round slowly. Ferrule says that the other seven were not counted because they were reported, by Shim , after the fact, and that a reported rising is not an observed rising. I have printed both figures. Clevis offered me odds. - H.B. Clevis "Do not encourage Clevis." It is the one standing instruction Ferrule gives every visitor to the house, and the only one she gives twice. She and Clevis are three years apart, and share a landing, and Clevis runs a book on everything that happens in the family, and Ferrule is in charge of everything that happens in the family, and so the two of them are, in a sense, in the same line of work from opposite ends. Clevis has never once taken a bet against her. He says it is not a sporting proposition. The dragon In the year 2000, writing to his pen pal at Much Pottering , Spare told her that he had a dragon now, and that it was called Ferrule, and that it was quite big. Effie Gotobed told the Forty-Eighth this at her gate, with great satisfaction, and asked him not to tell Spare she had told. Ferrule heard about it in the summer, from Shim, who hears about everything, and was quiet for some time, and then said that it was a very sensible name for a dragon, because somebody would have to be in charge of it, and went back to sweeping. Afterwards Ferrule is eighteen, and still in charge from six. With Cotter married and the eldest four at work, the evening household is now Clevis, Shim, Spare, Washer and Mrs Cotterill, and Ferrule says that is not fewer, it is younger, which is more. She has been offered a place at the Parish Rooms, by Gudgeon, and at the works, by Tappet, and at the Safety Valve, by Mr Kell , who said that he had never seen anybody keep a room standing up like it. She has declined all three, on the grounds that the position at home is not vacant, and nobody else could fill it, and Washer is beginning to walk. See also The Cotterills Nora Cotterill , who lifts things Clevis Cotterill , who is not to be encouraged Grommet Cotterill , on the name

title: Fizz
text: Fizz HEY! LISTEN! For the meadow, see Firstfield Meadow . For the body that employs her, see The Guild of Guides . For lore, see nobody. That is lore. Fizz Every. Journey. Begins. HERE. Known as Fizz; Tutorial Sprite, Third Class Born Issued 1 March 1981, by the Guild of Guides, Firstfield Chapter, out of a dandelion clock, on the stroke of nine. The Guild says the date is lore. Fizz says it was a Sunday, and that she remembers, and that she was doing so well Sex Female Size Small Volume Audible from the road Explains Everything, once. ONCE Doors explained About three thousand, several to somebody already holding one open Does not cover Lore Ambition Boss Warning Sprite, First Class Graduates One Fizz is the guide at Firstfield Meadow , at the foot of the rainbow: a Tutorial Sprite, Third Class, of the Guild of Guides , small, bright and audible from the road. She has explained walking, talking, chests, signs and doors to every Chosen One of living memory, or tried to; forty-seven of them pressed the button really fast. The Forty-Eighth did not. He is her only graduate, and she painted the number on the sign herself. Issue She was issued by the Guild's Firstfield Chapter in the spring of 1981, out of a dandelion clock, at nine in the morning, which is when the Guild restocks. The Guild will not confirm the date or the clock, because both are lore. Fizz will confirm both, at length, and will add that she knew how to explain doors before she knew how to fly, and that the first thing she ever said was HEY, and the second was LISTEN, and that the Guild was very pleased, and that she was doing so well. She has been at the meadow ever since: twenty-one years, every day, waiting at the bottom of it for somebody to walk in off the rainbow, so that she could tell them that every journey begins here. Most of the time nobody came. The Chosen Ones came once a generation, or once a decade lately, and pressed the button. Between them she practised on the pigs, which are sheep. Once The Guild is very firm on once. A guide explains everything once. Fizz is very firm on it as well, and explained it to the Forty-Eighth, once, and then again, in capitals, and then a third time in case he had not heard the capitals, and then told him that she knew he had heard, she knew. She is firm, too, on signs: a sign is a sign, and signs are for reading, and you press the button to read it, and she knows you already did, she knows. She appears in front of your face whenever you try to read one, to tell you that it is a sign. It is not in the Guild's rules. It is in every guide's heart. When the Forty-Eighth said that his journey had begun some time before, in a turnip field, and that since then he had walked out of a village and down a road, she said: Every. Journey. Begins. HERE. and then explained walking to him, because he had just done it, and told him he was doing so well. He has told me since that she was right, in a way, and that he did not know it at the time; that a journey had certainly begun in the turnip field, but that it had been somebody else's, the Committee's, and that the meadow was the first place anybody had asked him to do anything, and then told him he had done it well. Lore Asked what the Dark Lord 's weakness was, where the Sacred Key was, or what the lever does, she says LORE, three times. She was right about the lever, which does not exist, and which there always is. I have asked her other things, for this article: how old she is, what a sprite eats, whether she sleeps, and what the Guild pays. All of them were lore. I asked what was not lore. She said that doors were not lore, and explained one to me, and I was holding it open. Boss Warning Sprite, First Class Her ambition is to be a Boss Warning Sprite, First Class, and wait outside the last door, and shout IT'S WEAK TO FIRE. She practises on the sheep, which are pigs, and are not weak to fire, and she asks you not to check. Since the Quest she has applied for the post, and has put the Forty-Eighth down as a reference. When I wrote to the Guild to ask whether he had been consulted, the Guild wrote back to say that that was lore. I asked the Forty-Eighth whether he would give her a reference. He said that he already had: that the Guild had written to him, in 2001, asking whether the sprite had been helpful, and that he had written back yes, and that he had been asked to say what about, and had written doors . I have since learned that the Guild has no grade between Third Class and First, or that if it does, it is lore. Either way, I hope she gets it. I hope the last door she waits outside is a long way off, and that whatever is behind it is very weak to fire. - H.B. Afterwards She is still at the meadow, still Third Class, pending. The graduation sign at the top still reads TUTORIALS COMPLETED IN THIS MEADOW: ONE, the one painted over a nought, very carefully, by somebody with small hands and no experience of paint. The paint has run a little at the bottom of the one. She has not touched it up. She says that it is how you can tell it is real. See also Firstfield Meadow The Guild of Guides Old Hollis , Dilys Fenwick and Norbert Pelling , of the meadow Bram Thistle , her graduate

title: From the Notebooks of P. Quill
text: From the Notebooks of P. Quill Contributed by P. Quill, chronicler, of Thistlewick and the Slain Wyvern Miss Quill's notebooks are in double figures, and I asked whether I might print some of them. She chose what follows, and the order, and the headings, and wrote the notes in between, in the third person, which is her house style and not a mistake of mine. I have not corrected anything, and I have been told that if I do she will put me in a verse. For her life, see Piper Quill . - H.B. Piper Quill is a chronicler, of the family that has written the Committee's accounts for four generations, and the first of it to write down what actually happened. She would like that understood before anybody reads any further. What follows is true. Some of it scans. The first notebook Piper Quill joined the Forty-Eighth in the Gilded Turnip , mid-verse. She had been writing the verse for a month, walking past the inn every day, which is named after the problem. She stood on nothing. She said it at volume: 'And lo, the Chosen One drew near, smelling faintly of turnip, and the tavern fell silent -' P. Quill, the Gilded Turnip, the first line of the first notebook The tavern had not fallen silent. Piper Quill wrote that down as well. The same notebook, the same evening, has two more beginnings, and she prints them because a chronicler who prints only her endings is a Quill of the old kind: 'And she went WITH him, and it was...' 'And the Chosen One turned to his chronicler, and said unto her -' P. Quill, the Gilded Turnip; both unfinished, and both true He did not say anything unto her. He was looking for his hat. A rhyme for turnip There is no rhyme for turnip. The whole company sat down in the Gilded Turnip one afternoon and offered her one each, and every one is in the notebook, with who offered it, and every one is wrong, and Piper Quill would like that recorded, at volume. The draft, as it stood: 'And so he came home to the fields, and sat down with a single turnip, and hung his sword above the grate, and -' P. Quill, the ballad, last verse, as drafted And as it stands, nine seconds later: 'And so he came home to the fields, and hung his sword above the grate, and sat down with a turnip, which was worth the journey, and the wait.' P. Quill, the ballad, last verse It was always going to be the last verse. She just had the lines the wrong way round. Everybody who spent the afternoon on it was furious. Piper Quill has asked for the nine seconds on her headstone. Not the verse. The nine seconds. From the road Most of a notebook is not verse. Most of a notebook is weather, and who was cross, and how far. But some of the road went into metre whether she wanted it to or not, and here are the parts that did. During an examination for fitness to travel, conducted in front of a witness, with a halibut: 'And lo, the medic smote his knee, and the Chosen One kicked a halibut, and -' P. Quill; the Committee will strike it, and she knew, and wrote it down anyway At the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth , on the bench, afterwards: 'He did not want a mound, or fame, or masons, or a curse, or chalk; he wanted, by the road they came, somewhere to sit down from the walk.' P. Quill, on the bench, facing the sea At Upper Clanging , from the ninth Cotterill, who asked the company every morning on waking whether it was spring yet: 'He asked each morning, "Is it spring?" and every morning it was not, until one morning everything was spring, and Washer, on the dot.' P. Quill; Spare Cotterill has asked for a copy, and says it is untrue, which from him is a compliment The Contest at the Sign of the Bell Piper Quill entered Ballad (Not Sad), at Great Dunnage , before three judges, one of whom cannot hear and one of whom gives everything a two. The damage was heckling. She finished. She scored eighteen. Mr Tweddle , who does birdcalls, scored nineteen, and the thrush got a three from Miss Quayle, and the birdcalls were, in fairness, extraordinary. Piper Quill has framed the certificate. It is the first prize a Quill has ever won for writing down what actually happened, and it is for coming second, and she says that is about right. What she sang is not printed here. You had to be in the room. The struck verses The Committee strikes any verse it cannot have read aloud at the fete, and keeps them in a box behind a red curtain, and Piper Quill has read every one of them, and prints none, because they are the Committee's, and some of them are very good, and the Committee does not know which. Verse forty-one is about a cat. It scans. Piper Quill has been asked about verse seven by everyone she has ever met, including the compiler of this volume, at every meeting. Piper Quill's answer, which she has given every time, and which is complete, is that it is very good. The elegy Abel Thrush, Carrier, nine lines, is on the fingerpost at Little Gore , under a little roof somebody made for it, and is printed whole in the compiler's article on her , by her leave. She would only add that Mrs Vane asked whether it might have a bit more of a tune, and that Piper Quill laughed, out loud, at her own work, for the first time, and said: next time. There has not been a next time yet. There will be. She is working on the tune. The tea Written at the Slain Wyvern , the evening the Forty-Eighth came in from the cottage of the Forty-Fifth and told the compiler the end, and the compiler filled his last page, and Piper Quill was at the next table, and wrote this, and did not show either of them: 'Forty-seven did the sword. The one who asked him why, and stayed to hear the whole of it, when it was done, went home. The kettle's on, all year.' P. Quill, the Slain Wyvern For the historian Piper Quill and the compiler of this volume meet at the Slain Wyvern about once a month, to disagree. He says her songs are accurate and do not scan. She says his history is complete and not accurate. They are both right, and the evenings are long, and she has written him a verse, and he has asked that it be printed at the foot of this page so that he can be seen not to mind: 'Hosea Bellwether, who writes it down, has never climbed a tower, or hill, or anything above the town, and has bought boots. And sits there still.' P. Quill, for H. Bellwether, March 2002 I do not mind. It is accurate. The boots are by the door. - H.B. See also Piper Quill Ambrosine Quill The Quills The Obligatory Quest Hosea Bellwether

title: Gideon Markup
text: Gideon Markup "Welcome! What are you buying?" For the shop, see Penultima . For the sword in the window, see The Sword of Ultimate Ending . For the ledger, see Dorothy Markup , who keeps it, and him. Gideon Markup Everything has always been priced Known as Mr Markup; Gideon, to Mrs Markup, when he is in the window again Born 30 September 1944, Penultima , over the shop, which was then a saddler's Sex Male Keeps Ye Final Shoppe, since 1969 Married Dorothy , 1970 Prices Seasonal. It is a very reliable season Buys at One crown Sells at Forty Warranty None. Asking about it is free Discounts given One. Eleven coppers, off a lamp Would sir like to hold it? Sir cannot afford to hold it Gideon Markup keeps Ye Final Shoppe at Penultima , the last town before the Obligatory Tower , where everything is priced and everything has always been priced. In the window, behind a velvet rope, is the Sword of Ultimate Ending, at nine million, nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine crowns, which he priced in 1969, and which he asks every customer whether they would like to hold, and then tells them, warmly, that they cannot afford to. He brings his wife her tea every morning, and then he does the window. The last shop before the end He was born in 1944 above a saddler's in Penultima, the son of the saddler, and grew up watching heroes go up the road to the Tower and noticing that every one of them stopped at the last shop on the way, which was his father's, and bought a bridle they did not need, because it was the last chance. In 1969, when his father retired, he turned the saddler's into Ye Final Shoppe, and painted the sign himself, and on the first morning he put the sword in the window, and wrote the card. The sword, he says, came with the shop. He will not say more than that, and Mrs Markup, asked, says that he is in the window again. My own enquiries, at the saddlers' guild, establish that his father never sold a sword in his life, and that nobody in Penultima remembers one in the shop before 1969, and that I should leave it at that, and I have. Seasonal "Welcome! What are you buying?" "Of course, of course. Take your time. Everything is priced. Everything has always been priced." Asked about the prices, which are high, he says seasonal. "Thirty-one years in this trade and it has been seasonal every one of them. It is a very reliable season." The shop buys at a crown and sells at forty, and Mrs Markup writes down both, and the difference is, he says, the season. He believes it. He has a crate of things bought at a crown each, among them half a potion, and he is waiting for somebody who needs exactly half a potion, and he is sure they are on their way. He sells forty potions each labelled LAST POTION, and two jars each labelled UMBRELLAS - THE LAST ONE, and he does not see a difficulty, because each one is the last one, for somebody. The sword "Ah. The Sword of Ultimate Ending. Would sir like to hold it?" "Sir cannot afford to hold it." He has said it to every customer for thirty-three years, including the Forty-Eighth, and including me, who did not ask. He set the price at one crown more than a purse will hold, so that it should be out of the reach of anybody who ever walked up the road. A banker in Nether Sopping has told me that a good purse holds a great deal more than that. I have not told Mr Markup. Neither, I understand, has Nix , who looked at the sword once, in the year 2000, for some time, and said afterwards that the price was wrong, and that some things are better in a window. The discount He has given one discount in thirty-three years. It was on the first day the shop was open, in 1969: eleven coppers, off a lamp, to a girl who would not stop haggling. It is the first entry in the first volume of the Markup accounts, in his hand: DISCOUNT - ELEVEN COPPERS - WORTH IT. Mrs Markup, who keeps the ledger, has ruled round that entry twice, and has still got the coppers. She came to Penultima in the spring of 1969, at twenty-three, and was married to him the spring after. I have not asked her whether she was the girl. I have noticed that there is a lamp on her side of the bed which is the oldest thing in the house after the sword, and that it has never been for sale. - H.B. Afterwards Penultima has done a trade since 2000 in people walking up the road to see Grimspite 's chair, and most of them stop at the Final Shoppe, and look at the sword, and are asked whether they would like to hold it, and are told. Mr Markup says it has never been better for business, and that he has had to have the rope re-velveted. The sign over the town has had a fourth line added, LAST CHANCE FOR A SOUVENIR, and he has added a shelf of souvenirs, priced seasonally. He is fifty-seven. He has never once been asked to bring the tea, and he has never once been asked to do the window, and he does both, every morning, in that order. See also Dorothy Markup Penultima The Sword of Ultimate Ending A Glossary of Cliches , for the last shop before the end

title: Godfrey Stopford
text: Godfrey Stopford For the forty-seven, see The Chosen Ones . For the wood, see The Gloamwood . For the log, there is no article. It is a log. Godfrey Stopford Sitting down Known as The Forty-Sixth; Number Forty-Six; G. Stopford, Esq., The Log Born 14 March 1956, Thistlewick Sex Male Chosen 1980, Chosen One number forty-six Got as far as The Gloamwood , the first path, about half way Decided That the woods were enough Party Five, who said: fair Armour Very good, and oiled Correspondence Two letters a month, received; none sent; all answered Songs about him None. One four-bar rest Age Forty-six, as of last week, which he finds very satisfying Godfrey Stopford is the Forty-Sixth Chosen One of the Prophecy of Thistlewick , who set out in 1980, got as far as the Gloamwood, and decided that the woods were enough. He is still there, on a log, half way along the first path, in very good armour, sitting down. "Nobody writes songs about that. But I'm here, and I'm forty-six, and I'm sitting down." He is the only Chosen One who neither went up the road nor came home, and the only one, so far as I know, who is entirely content about it. The name My last volume did not give his name, and nor did the Committee's souvenir book, The Forty-Seven, which I am told has a portrait on his page, and a date, and a pressed turnip flower, and the word FORTY-SIX in very small letters, as if the Committee were not sure it ought to count him. It counts him. Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging does not. I did not get the name from him. He does not write. I got it from Tolly , of his old party, who addresses the envelopes, in the narrow hand. Every one of them, every month for twenty-two years, is addressed the same way: G. STOPFORD, ESQ. THE LOG. THE GLOAMWOOD. BY HAND. and carries two stamps, because it is a long way, and he is worth two stamps. The G is for Godfrey. Tolly told me that, and then told me not to make anything of it, and I have not. It is a perfectly good name. It is his mother's father's. Before the woods He was born in Thistlewick on the fourteenth of March 1956, the only son of a thatcher, and was a quiet boy who liked to sit on walls. He was chosen in the spring of 1980, at twenty-four, in the usual way, which is to say that the Committee met and he was not at the meeting. His armour was made for him at the village forge by Beatrice Grumnir, who made a good many things in her time for people going north, and who said of this suit that it was the best she had done, and that it was a pity about the wearer, who had told her when he was measured that he did not expect to need it. He did not need it. It has never been struck. It is the best-kept suit of armour in the country, and I have been to the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant , where they oil theirs on Fridays. Halbert Quy , who knew him slightly, says that young Stopford came to see him in Nether Sopping the week before he set out, and asked him one question, which was whether it was a long way. Mr Quy said that it was. Young Stopford said, "Right," and thanked him, and went home. Mr Quy says that he has thought since that it was the most sensible question any Chosen One ever asked him, and that it was the only one he answered correctly. - H.B. The woods The party was five, and set out on a Tuesday. Half way along the first path in the Gloamwood there was a log across the way, and Godfrey Stopford stopped at it. Nabb , who was there, has told the story many times at the Slain Wyvern , and it does not get any longer: "He stopped. Just - stopped, on the path, and said the woods were enough. And we looked at each other, and we said: fair." Everyone wants there to be more. There isn't more. They were tired, and he said the woods were enough, and he was right, and they went home. He sat down. That was twenty-two years ago this spring, and he has not got up since, except for the necessary, and the post. There is a cushion on the log now, with a card on it, RESERVED - NUMBER FORTY-SIX. Nobody knows who put the card there. He says it was there when he sat down, and that it would have been rude not to. The letters Nabb and Tolly write every month, both of them, one round hand and one narrow. The letters go out from Nether Sopping on Thursdays and come to him by hand, and he reads every one, twice, and puts it in the sack beside the log, which is now a great many letters going back a great many years. He has never once written back. "I read them," he says. "Reading them's the answer. They know that. Nabb doesn't, but Tolly does, and Tolly does the stamps." Tolly, for her part, says that Nabb thinks Tolly does not know the letters are unanswered, and has thought so for eleven years. Nabb, for her part, would like it known that she has never once been worried about it, and has only asked the man who collects the post whether he reads them in order to be sure of the postage. I have printed all three. They are all true. There is nobody in this encyclopedia who is better at being a friend than those three, and two of them have not seen the third since 1980. Thistlewick The Gloamwood is under a mile from the north gate of Thistlewick. Nobody from the village has been to see him. When I asked why, I was told, at the Gilded Turnip , that the Forty-Sixth had set out, and that you do not go and look at somebody who has set out, any more than you would read the last page of a book first. I asked whether they knew he was sitting on a log less than a mile away, and was told that he had set out. It is why he did not know, when the Forty-Eighth came through, that the Forty-Seventh had come after him. "Did he? Good for him," he said, and then, "Did he come back?" Nobody answered. He has not asked again. He says it is not the sort of thing you ask twice. The Lay At Olde Evermore , Aelwen sings the Lay of the Chosen, which has a verse for every Chosen One who has come off the ledge, and is three days long, and nobody has heard the end. The Forty-Sixth never came at all, and so his verse is a rest, four bars long, and she says it is the best bit. I told him so. He was quiet for a while. Then he asked me to tell her that it was very kind, and that four bars was about right, and that if she ever needed it to be longer she was not to go to any trouble. Afterwards He is still on the log. The Forty-Eighth stopped on the way north, and talked to him, and the company went on to the Tower and did what forty-seven before them had not, and when the news came south the letters that month were longer than usual, and he read them three times. Nabb and Tolly write still, every month. The armour is still oiled. He became forty-six on the fourteenth of March this year, and says that it is the first time in his life that the number and the man have agreed, and that he intends to enjoy it, and that he will think about forty-seven when it comes, sitting down. See also The Gloamwood The Chosen Ones The Slain Wyvern , where Nabb and Tolly drink Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth Olde Evermore , for the rest

title: Grimspite the Inevitable
text: Grimspite the Inevitable For the contract, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the building, see The Obligatory Tower . For the forty-eight people who came up the stairs, see The Chosen Ones . Grimspite the Inevitable At the bookmark Known as The Dark Lord; Grimspite the Inevitable; latterly, Grimspite Born Not stated. Asked by letter, he declined (see Two Reckonings ) Sex Male Of The top of the Obligatory Tower Post Dark Lord, under the Prophecy of Thistlewick, renewable Held Four thousand eight hundred years, by the contract Renewed Forty-seven times Appointed The same way the post was nearly filled in 2000 Age His own affair Hand Very beautiful Status Retired, 2000. Receipt issued Kettle On Grimspite the Inevitable was for four thousand eight hundred years, by the Prophecy's own count, the Dark Lord of the Obligatory Tower , against whom the village of Thistlewick sent forty-eight Chosen Ones. He did not want the job. It was an employment contract, and he could not get out of it, and every time a Chosen One beat him it renewed him before they reached the stairs. The forty-eighth asked him why he did not stop, and listened to the answer, and read the contract, and Grimspite has been retired since. He reads. He was reading when every one of the forty-eight came up the stairs, and he put the bookmark in every time. He is very tired and very polite, and he writes to me. The post The post of Dark Lord was held, before the Prophecy, at the castle on the cloud that its caretaker now calls the Former Premises , which no hero could ever reach. Grimspite has never been there. "I've read the file. The drains were a disgrace, and the east wing faced the wrong way." He holds, or held, the post at the Tower, under clause twelve of the Prophecy. Every hundred years, by the Committee's reckoning of a hundred years, a Chosen One came up the stairs, and he said, "So, you have come at last." He said it forty-seven times. "And I meant it the first time." They fought him and they won, and clause twelve renewed him. It is carved forty-seven times into the wall behind his throne: THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. "It isn't a threat. It's a renewal notice." How he came to hold it in the first place he told the Forty-Eighth in four words, at the moment when the Prophecy had just declared the post vacant and congratulated the party on it. "That's how I got the job." I have not been able to find out any more than that, and I have tried, and I have been told by letter that he hopes I am keeping well. The forty-seven All forty-seven did the sword. Not one of them asked. Clause fourteen says the first meeting shall not go well, and it never did: Merrow Halgate 's party of twenty fought him at the bridge and lost, as was written down in advance, and he tells me that halfway through, Grimspite stopped, and apologised, and then carried on. Nobody ever believes him about that part. I do. One of them, Halbert Quy , the Forty-Fifth, was offered a cup of tea, and declined it, because he thought it was a trick, and has thought about it ever since. Grimspite has wondered too. None of them died, at the top. "Forty-seven of them, and they all won. Do you know how that looks, to the forty-eighth?" He has four skeletons up there, in plaster, for the look of the thing. One of them has an extra foot, because there was a foot over and it seemed a shame. The forty-eighth "Forty-eight," he said. "Right on time. Sit down. No? Fine. Standing is traditional." The Forty-Eighth asked him why he did not stop. He said: "Ah. The clever one. They're rarer than you'd think. I can't." He showed them the wall. He asked who had told Bram to ask, and when he heard it was Halbert he asked him to go back and tell Halbert that the tea had just been tea, and to listen to all of it, because he would like, once, for somebody to have listened to the whole of it. Bram did. He answered the other questions he was brought. Clause seven requires a Chosen One to go on foot, "because a thing that flies over and drops something is not a story. It is a Tuesday." He was of the view that Miss Hoyle of Upper Clanging would never get one off the ground in sight of his tower. Asked, on her behalf, what the Tower is made of, he said that nobody had ever asked him that, that he did not know, and that he had leaned on that wall every day for four thousand years and never once wondered. "Tell her the work was good." When ITEM 1 was set down in front of his throne, it smoked, and knocked the bookmark on to the floor, and did nothing else, because of clause thirty-one. He looked at it for some time. "That is the first new thing in four thousand eight hundred years, and I would like a moment with it. Whoever made that has never once been told that it was any good." Then they fought, because that is the part they were for, and at the end of it he went down on one knee and said, "...Thank you." The rest is under The Obligatory Quest. It was his idea to read the thing. "Four thousand eight hundred years, and it was an admin problem." He signed the Forty-Eighth a receipt for one Dark Lord, renewable, and sent him home with a message: "There isn't a forty-nine." The top of the Tower At work, which he does not enjoy, and is very good at. The room at the top is furnished in the traditional manner, and he will tell you about every piece of it, which nobody did before the ending because nobody stayed. The tablet over the door was a present from the Prophecy, in the year one, and was the only joke it ever made. The two statues are of an aunt, who sat for both and would not stop talking, and did not like either of them, "and you don't throw away an aunt". One mirror is late, because of the altitude. The other shows where you would rather be, and he has put his name down for a bungalow. There are two seeing-orbs, which are very old and very heavy and show only each other. Afterwards He is retired. He stays in the Tower, in his chair, with a kettle and the book at the bookmark. He is still on the same book. The forty-eighth carving will not be needed. He receives visitors and has about one a month, most of them people who would like to see the chair. Bram comes up once a year, on the day, and the kettle is on. Halbert Quy, who said no to the tea thirty years ago, has been told all of it, the tea included, and has not been back up for a cup; the kettle is always on now, and he knows it. Mr Quy sends his regards up the hill. He writes to me, in a very beautiful hand, about my dates. He has corrected three of them in Volume Two, all of them correctly. I asked him how old he is. He said he had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, and that how old he had been when he took it was his own affair. I have sent him this article for his corrections. He returned it with none, and a note: that it was very fair, that the east wing still faced the wrong way, and that if I should ever be passing there was a kettle. I have not yet been passing. I am a historian, and I do not climb things. But I have begun to think about it. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Chosen Ones Bram Thistle Halbert Quy The Obligatory Tower

title: Grommet Cotterill
text: Grommet Cotterill For the family, whose names are wrong, see The Cotterills . For his master, see Bryd Ollerenshaw . For the other one, see Hob Grumnir . Grommet Cotterill Has got the makings Known as Grommet; "the lad", in the forge; "the apprentice", in his own account, with some weight on the "the" Born 19 January 1985, Upper Clanging Sex Male Named for A grommet, which is a ring that keeps a rope from chafing. It is not a fastener either, and he knows Apprenticed To Bryd Ollerenshaw, at the forge, autumn 1999 Has got The makings. Said slowly (1999-2000); said a little faster (2002) Has been inside A boiler tube plate, with a candle and a drift. All forty-one holes true Corrects the family Every day They do this Every time Grommet Cotterill is the sixth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and is apprenticed to Bryd Ollerenshaw at the forge, where he is put upon. Mr Ollerenshaw says he has got the makings, and says it slowly. He is the only Cotterill who has studied what the family are named after, and he has found that most of the names are wrong, and he has told them so every day since, and none of them has changed their name, and he does not expect them to, and he is going to keep saying it. The names He went into the forge at fourteen, in the autumn of 1999, and in his first month Mr Ollerenshaw taught him the names of things. He came home that evening and stood in the kitchen and told the family what he had learned. "Shim is not a fastener. A shim is a packing piece." "Ferrule is a collar. It fastens nothing. It only stops a split." "A gudgeon is a pin. That one is fine." He has said it every day since, and they have taken it, he says, very badly, by which he means that they have taken no notice of it at all. Mrs Cotterill says that the names are not wrong; they are what she called them. Shim says that she does not mind being a packing piece, because a packing piece is what you put in to make a thing fit, and that is a good thing to be. Ferrule says nothing, and makes him stand up. He has not been asked about his own name, and so I asked him. He said that a grommet is the ring that goes round a hole in a sail, so that the rope does not chafe it, and that it is not a fastener either, and that he had known that since his first week, and had decided not to bring it up. "Somebody has to be right in this family," he said. "It doesn't have to be me." The forge Mr Ollerenshaw's forge at Upper Clanging has a sign over it that says BRYD - SMITH. THE BEST IN THE NORTH. (SAYS WHO), and the third line is in Hob Grumnir's paint, and Grommet was told on his first day not to mention it, and has not. Grommet's duties are those of an apprentice everywhere: he blows, he fetches, he sweeps, he quenches, and he is sent inside things, because he is small enough to go inside a boiler, and has. "Mr Ollerenshaw says I have got the makings," he told the Forty-Eighth. "He says it slowly." I asked Mr Ollerenshaw how slowly. He said, "Aye," after a while, and I took that to be the answer. The tube plate In the year 2000 a drawing came down the hill from the Hoyle Works on the morning spike, and it was not a spar. It was a tube plate, for the refit. Mr Ollerenshaw and Hob Grumnir looked at it, and then at each other, and neither of them finished a sentence. It wanted four hands, one heat, and somebody small enough to go inside it afterwards. Everybody in the forge looked at Grommet. "I knew it," said Grommet. It was done in one heat, because it could only be done in one, and in the whole of it the four hands were never once in each other's way. Then Grommet went in, feet first, with a candle and a drift, and sighted the holes from the inside. "They're true. All of them. Can I come out." Mr Ollerenshaw said, "When it's -" and Hob said, "Let the lad out," and he came out black to the eyebrows, and looked at the two of them, and said it to the company, not to them: "They do this every time." Miss Hoyle tried every one of the forty-one holes with a gauge pin, and nodded at every one, and asked who had gone in. She was told. "Good lad," she said. In the Hoyle Works that is not framed, because "that will do" is framed, and there is only so much wall; but Grommet has it written down, on the inside of his cap. "I've been inside a tube plate," he says now, to anybody. "Mr Ollerenshaw says I did it right." And then, because he is a fair-minded boy: "He said it quick, an' all." Rivet , who shares a bed with him, would like it known that he sleeps with his elbows. Grommet would like it known that Rivet has never once said so to his face, and that a man who has things to say about elbows should say them in the bed, where the elbows are. - H.B. Afterwards He is seventeen, and two years and more at the forge. Mr Ollerenshaw still says he has got the makings, and says it a little faster, and on one occasion in 2001, Grommet says, he said it before he had finished looking at the work, which Grommet regards as the high point of his career so far. He still tells the family every day that the names are wrong. Washer , two today, has not said a word yet, but looks at him, when he starts, with what Grommet calls an expression. The whole street has money on what the first word will be. Grommet says that if it is wrong he will consider the matter closed. See also The Cotterills Bryd Ollerenshaw Hob Grumnir Ott Hoyle , who said "good lad" Rivet Cotterill , about the elbows

title: Gudgeon Cotterill
text: Gudgeon Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills , whose ages in this encyclopedia are hers. For the form, see Spare Cotterill . For the Parish Rooms, see Upper Clanging . Gudgeon Cotterill Two t's and two l's Known as Gudgeon; Miss Cotterill, at the counter, where it is official Born 12 January 1980, Upper Clanging ; entered in the register in somebody else's hand, which she has looked at, and would have done better Sex Female Named for A gudgeon, which is a pin. Grommet says that one is fine Works The Parish Rooms: the register, the census, and the forms Hand The best Mrs Tunnicliffe has had, out of eleven Has written Cotterill A hundred and twelve times, by the year 2000. More since. One column ruled extra Knows where Form P-9 is, without looking Everybody gets It wrong Gudgeon Cotterill is the third of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and clerks at the Parish Rooms, where she copies the register in the best hand Mrs Tunnicliffe has had in eleven clerks. She has written Cotterill more times than anybody alive, and spelt it right every time, which she says is more than can be said for anybody else. She knew which drawer Form P-9 was in without looking, although nobody had ever asked for one, and she read it to the Forty-Eighth one section at a time, and wished him good luck, and meant it, roughly. The register She went to the Parish Rooms at fifteen, in 1995, to help Mrs Tunnicliffe with the census, and stayed, because she was good at it and because it was the only room in Upper Clanging with nobody else in it from her family. She copies the register: the births, the marriages and the deaths, in ink, in a braid and spectacles, in a hand that Mrs Tunnicliffe says is the best she has ever had. Mrs Tunnicliffe has had eleven. "Cotterill," she told the Forty-Eighth, "hundred and twelve times." Then she gave him the family's ages, out of the register, all at once, which is a thing she does for visitors whether they ask or not: "It is all in here. Cotter is twenty-four. Rivet is twenty-two. I am twenty. Tappet eighteen, Ferrule sixteen, Grommet fifteen, Clevis thirteen, Shim eleven, Spare nine. And Bessie is a Cotterill now, which is another one to write." And then, after a pause: "You have gone quiet. Everybody goes quiet just there." They do. I did. It is a great many Cotterills to have read out to you in one breath, and she knows it, and she has, I think, a quiet relish for it, the way a man who keeps bees enjoys telling you how many. She would like it recorded, and I record it: two t's and two l's. Everybody gets it wrong. I got it wrong in my notes, and she corrected them, in ink, in the best hand Mrs Tunnicliffe has had. I have kept the page. - H.B. Form P-9 When Spare applied to go with the Forty-Eighth, it was Gudgeon who told him there was a form for it, P-9, Application by a Minor to Accompany a Chosen One (Parish of Upper Clanging), and that nobody had ever asked for one, and that it wanted a parent or guardian, signed, in ink. "And Mam signs it, or nobody does." Then she said, "Good luck," which is the first time I have heard anybody wish a person good luck in the voice you use for you will need it. She read it out section by section. Section one. The applicant has been heard in full. "You have not heard him in full. He has more. He always has more." Section two. The applicant's family has been met. All of it. "It is a long section. Mam has the list. So do I." Section three. Means of travel. "He is nine. He is not walking to a tower through the Gloamwood." And then, looking at nobody in particular, and particularly at the Forty-Eighth: "If somebody had a way of getting there that was not walking, it would be different." It was the most helpful thing anybody said to him in the north, and she said it as if she were reading out the minutes. I have asked her whether she meant it to help. She said that she reads out what is on the form. The column On the morning of Washer , in the spring of 2000, she entered the tenth Cotterill in the register before anybody else in the town knew there was one, in ink, at a quarter to seven. "Washer Cotterill. Entered in the register this morning, in ink. Two t's and two l's. Everybody gets it wrong." Then: "Ten. The column was full. I have had to rule another one." I have seen the page. The new column is ruled with a ruler, and is the straightest line in the parish register of Upper Clanging, which goes back to 1748, and has had a good many clerks. Afterwards She is still at the Parish Rooms, and is now the clerk, Mrs Tunnicliffe having become, in 2001, the clerk's assistant, at her own request, so that she could do the urns. She has entered Bessie 's baby, in a column of its own. She has begun, in the evenings, a fair copy of the whole of the register from its first page, which is 1748, because the early hands were bad, she says, and somebody ought to, and she is up to 1790. She says that there were a great many Cotterills then as well, and that they could not spell it either. See also The Cotterills Spare Cotterill , section one Mrs Tunnicliffe , who has had eleven Upper Clanging

title: Halbert Quy
text: Halbert Quy For the cottage, see Nether Sopping . For the man he did not have tea with, see Grimspite the Inevitable . Halbert Quy Potting something Known as Number Forty-Five; the Forty-Fifth Born 7 February 1929, Thistlewick Sex Male Chosen 1970 Of Thistlewick , and then, by the Friday, Nether Sopping Age In his seventies Grows Roses. No turnips, as a policy Declined A cup of tea Asked Why there is always a next one Thought about it Thirty years Distance from Thistlewick Forty miles. He has walked it Halbert Quy was the Forty-Fifth Chosen One of Thistlewick , who went north in 1970, did the sword, was offered a cup of tea at the top of the Tower and said no, and came home and asked one question at a meeting, and has lived in Nether Sopping ever since. He is the reason the Quest of the Forty-Eighth ended the way it did, and he would like that left out. I have not left it out. The tea He went up as they all went up, with the sword, and at the top a tall, tired, very well-read man offered him a cup of tea, and he said no, because he thought it was a trick. It was not a trick. He has thought about that tea, by his own account, every day for thirty years. The question He came home, and the Committee was already drafting the next one, and at the next meeting he asked: if it works every hundred years, why is there always a next one? The cottage was ready by the Friday. That is clause nineteen, the Resettlement Clause: a pension, a cottage, and "such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable". "Turned out to be forty miles," he says. "They're not cruel. They're embarrassed. A hero who came back asks questions." He has had thirty years to measure the distance and makes it forty miles, which is a great deal further than the signpost says, and I believe him over the signpost. He can tell a Thistlewick man from the way he stands. His cottage is one of the two at the north end of the town. There are roses, and there is not one turnip, as a matter of policy. The Committee's framed commendation is face down on the shelf, dusted round rather than moved. The sword over his fire is exactly like the one over every Chosen One's fire, and has dust on its upper edge, which takes a long time and a great deal of not looking. Next door was Ambrose Fitch 's, the Forty-Fourth's, and they were neighbours for thirty years. What he told the Forty-Eighth In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth walked in, and Mr Quy told him to sit down, because he was blocking the light, and said Thistlewick, from the standing. Then, at the kitchen table, turning a pot a quarter turn at a time, he told him what Grimspite was like - "Polite. Tired. Very well read." - and then put down the trowel and told him the only thing he had come home with that was worth the trip. "Nobody asks him why. Forty-seven of us. Forty-seven. We all did the sword. Not one of us ever asked the man why he doesn't stop." "Ask him. That's all. Ask him why. And then listen to the whole answer, because it's long, and because I didn't." The Forty-Eighth asked. What the answer was is in The Obligatory Quest and the article on the Prophecy, and it was long, and he listened to all of it. At the top of the Tower, Grimspite stopped, and asked who had told him to ask, and was told, the Forty-Fifth, a man in a garden forty miles south, and said, "Halbert," and asked to have a message taken back: that the tea was just tea. It is the most consequential conversation in this encyclopedia and it happened over a seed tray. I asked Mr Quy whether he had known, when he told the boy to ask, what would come of it. He said that he had known what came of not asking, and that he had had thirty years to get tired of it. Then he said I was blocking the light. Afterwards Bram walked south again, after the ending, and sat at the kitchen table, and told him what Grimspite had said, all of it, in order, including the part about the tea. It took most of an afternoon. What was said at the end of it is between the two of them, and in Nether Sopping that is a complete answer, and I have not asked twice. He still grows roses. He still has no turnips, and says the policy has outlived its purpose and he is keeping it out of loyalty. He has not been back up the Tower, though the kettle at the top is always on now, and he knows it. He sends his regards up the hill, by Bram, once a year, on the day, and Grimspite sends his back. When Bram comes south, about once a month, and stops next door at Fitch's, Mr Quy tells him he is blocking the light, though he is outside, and on the other side of a hedge. See also The Chosen Ones Ambrose Fitch , next door Grimspite the Inevitable Bram Thistle Nether Sopping

title: Halloran Vance
text: Halloran Vance For the goose, see the Slain Wyvern , and Miss Halloway's entry , which is the last word on the subject. Halloran Vance Known as The Forty-First Born 30 April 1914, Thistlewick Died 2 November 1968, Nether Sopping , at the window over the quay Sex Male Chosen 1940 Went North, by way of the marshes Came back with Nothing Waiting on the quay A whole village Gave them A monster. Two days, with wire, and a goose Smiled about it Never once On a plaque Twice Halloran Vance was the Forty-First Chosen One of Thistlewick , who went north in 1940 and came back from the marshes with nothing, to a whole village waiting on the quay at Nether Sopping for a monster. So he brought them one. It took him two days, with wire, and a goose, and he never once smiled about it, and it has been a wyvern over the fireplace of the Slain Wyvern for sixty years. There is no portrait of him in this volume. There is one on the Wall of the Forty-Seven in Prophecy Hall , with a line of Quill verse under it, and I have not reproduced the verse, because it mentions a wyvern. The goose What happened in the marshes he never said. That he came home with nothing, to a quay full of people who had been promised a monster, is the whole of what is known, and Dorcas Thrupp , who keeps the Wyvern and who had the story from those who were there, tells it the same way every time: "He was a good man, and he needed it to be a wyvern, and it's been a wyvern in my house for sixty years. So." For sixty years the whole of Nether Sopping agreed that it was a wyvern, which in a town of people who were pensioned for noticing things is a remarkable act of kindness, kept up daily. In the year 2000 Wren Halloway looked at it, and said what it was, Anser anser, greylag, adult female, with two bats' wings wired on and the whole thing varnished, and was asked to leave, not for good, while Dorcas decided. She was entirely right, and she was asked to leave, and both of those were true at once. The plaques There are two plaques now, one either side of the fire. The first is the wyvern's, as it has been for sixty years. The second, which Miss Halloway paid for at a crown a letter, a hundred and twenty-eight crowns, reads: A GREYLAG GOOSE, ANSER ANSER, OF A FARM ON THIS COAST. MADE INTO A WYVERN IN 1940, IN TWO DAYS, WITH WIRE, BY H. VANCE, CHOSEN ONE #41, BECAUSE THE VILLAGE WAS WAITING ON THE QUAY. It does not correct the first plaque, and does not repeat it, and it is, I think, the only memorial anywhere to the Forty-First that has his reason on it. It is the kindest thing in the room. Both plaques are true. Nobody in the room looks at either of them while you are looking at them, which is its own kind of answer. Afterwards Both plaques are still up, and neither mentions the other. Miss Halloway is welcome in the Wyvern now, and sits under the goose, by choice, and Mrs Thrupp dusts both plaques on the same morning, in the same order, and has never said which she does first. On the anniversary of the quay, which nobody marks and everybody knows, somebody puts a half on the mantel under the bird, and it is gone by closing. See also The Slain Wyvern Wren Halloway The Goose The Chosen Ones

title: Hester Ashbury
text: Hester Ashbury "Ten crowns a night, love. Breakfast included." For the inn, see Restwell . For the man on the stairs, see Walt Ashbury . Hester Ashbury "Whenever you come down." Known as Mrs Ashbury Born Hester Quine, 3 March 1949, at Restwell, the baker's Sex Female Married Walt Ashbury , 1973 Keeps The Eight Hours, Restwell , since 1977 A room Ten crowns. Breakfast included Breakfast Whenever you come down Argued about that For a year Breakfast, in practice A chop Resurrection Extra Wants the room back by Noon. It is generally twenty past two Hester Ashbury keeps the Eight Hours at Restwell , where a room is ten crowns, breakfast included, and breakfast is whenever you come down. She argued about that for a year. Now she just cooks. Every guest in her house sleeps the night through to the eight bars her husband plays them up with, and comes down better, and very late, and is given a chop, because in Restwell breakfast is generally after lunch. The baker's daughter She was born Hester Quine in 1949 at the baker's in Restwell, two doors down from the Eight Hours, and was up at four every morning of her girlhood to help with the bread, which she says gave her strong views about mornings that she has never been able to put into practice since. She married Walt Ashbury, the innkeeper's son, in 1973, a year before he sat down on the step, and took the house over with him when his father retired, in 1977. Breakfast The Eight Hours served breakfast from seven until nine, when she came to it, because every inn does. Nobody came down for it. The guests, who had been played up the night before, slept until eleven, or one, or three, and came down better than they had been in years, and asked for breakfast, and were told that it was over. She argued about it for a year: with Walt, with the guests, with the clock, and principally with herself, because she had been brought up at a baker's, and breakfast was at seven, and that was what breakfast was. In 1978, on a Tuesday, a guest came down at twenty past two and asked for breakfast, and she opened her mouth to tell him that it was over, and found that she was too tired of saying it to say it, and gave him a chop. She has given every guest since a chop. "Whenever you come down. I argued about that for a year. Now I just cook." Resurrection "Resurrection's extra. And I'll want the room back by noon." That is what she says when guests ask her about the eight bars, and how they work, and whether it is true that a man came in with one foot in the grave and went out dancing. It is a joke, and it is meant as one, and she has never in her life charged anybody for anything but the room, and the room is ten crowns. I asked her whether anybody had ever come in very ill. She said that people came in all sorts of ways, and that they all went up the stairs the same way, and came down the same way, and that she did not ask, and that it was not a hospital, and that Dr Pike would tell me otherwise and that I was to take no notice. She wants the room back by noon. It is generally twenty past two when anybody comes down. She has never once, in twenty-five years, asked anybody to hurry. I asked her why she says noon at all. She said that you have to say something, and that noon was what her father-in-law said, and that it was a comfort to the guests to be told a time they could then miss. - H.B. Walt She has listened to the eight bars from the kitchen twelve hundred times a year for twenty-eight years, and has never once asked him to stop. "He is very good at it." I asked her whether she minded hearing the same eight bars every night. She said that she did not hear them any more, as such; that they were like the sea, if you lived by the sea. Then she said that she heard them every time, and that she always stopped what she was doing until they were over, and that it took eleven seconds, and that she had worked out once that it came to about sixty hours of her life spent standing still in the kitchen listening, and that it was the best sixty hours she had. Afterwards She is fifty-three. The Eight Hours is busier than it has ever been, since 2000, with people going up to see Grimspite 's chair, and she has taken on a girl from the baker's to help with the chops. The register at the foot of the stairs has a column for remarks, and the remarks have all said much the same thing for twenty-eight years; she has had a second column added, at the guests' request, headed HOW LONG, so that they can write down how long they slept, and nobody has ever written down a number. They write eight hours. See also Walt Ashbury Restwell Dr Pike

title: Hester Vane
text: Hester Vane "You're a long way from anywhere. Well - you're four miles from Fenmarch, which round here is the same thing." For the hamlet, see Little Gore . For the wedding invitation that arrived nine years late, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Hester Vane Plainly delighted to see anybody Known as Mrs Vane; Hester Plumb, on the banns Born Hester Plumb, 7 June 1967, Little Gore , in the end house Sex Female Married Thomas Vane, gardener, at Fenmarch , summer 1991, in the rain Furthest she has been Fenmarch. Four miles Children Bess, Alfie and Nell, on the green. They will marry you if you stand still Wedding guests All eleven of Little Gore Invited None, at the time. All, since 2000. The invitation was on its first errand On the mantelpiece The invitation, propped against the clock. FOLLOWED. (P-G.) Hester Vane of Little Gore is plainly delighted to see anybody, because nobody comes. She has been to Fenmarch, and that is the furthest; she was married there, in the summer of 1991, and the whole of Little Gore walked over for it, all eleven of them, in their best, in the rain, and nobody minded at all, and nobody had been invited. The invitation came in the year 2000, by hand, by a knight, on his first errand. It is on the mantelpiece. Little Gore She was born Hester Plumb in 1967, in the end house of the hamlet's single street, and grew up in it, and has lived in it since, and has been, in thirty-four years, to Fenmarch Hall and back a great many times and to nowhere else at all, and does not see any reason to. Little Gore is eleven people, a green, a fingerpost and a log with daisies on it, and she says that it has everything you could want, and that if it wants anything else, it is four miles to Fenmarch. The wedding She married Tom Vane, the under-gardener at Fenmarch, in the summer of 1991, at Fenmarch, because Little Gore has no church. The banns were read three times, and are still pinned up on the board on the green, HESTER PLUMB AND THOMAS VANE, THIRD TIME OF ASKING, and under them, INVITATIONS TO FOLLOW. They did not follow. The invitations were with Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Second, at Fenmarch, who gave them, the morning before, to his son, the Third, to carry to Little Gore as his first errand, and the Third went out errant that morning and did not find the way, and went on not finding it for nine years. Little Gore did not know any of this. It walked over anyway, in the rain, because nobody had told it not to. "The whole of Little Gore walked over for it. All eleven of us, in our best, and it rained the whole way, and nobody minded at all." The letter In the year 2000 a man in armour came up the street to her door and took off his helmet, which nobody had ever seen him do, and held out a letter in both hands. SIR ALDRIC PEMBERTON-GORE THE SECOND REQUESTS THE PLEASURE OF THE PARISH OF LITTLE GORE AT THE WEDDING OF HESTER PLUMB AND THOMAS VANE, AT FENMARCH. She opened it on the doorstep with the children round her. "...It's my wedding." He said that it was, and that he did apologise, it was his first errand. "Oh, but we all came anyway! All eleven of us. In the rain. Nobody had told us not to. And now we're invited. Properly. It's going on the mantelpiece. Bess, fetch the good pin." He stopped for tea. He said that he might not find his way out afterwards. She said that then he would stop for supper. It is on the mantelpiece now, propped against the clock, where you can see it from the road, and under INVITATIONS TO FOLLOW on the banns, in a fresh hand, very neat, is FOLLOWED. (P-G.) Mrs Vane has written to me, to say that I should be very welcome at Little Gore, and that it was only four miles from Fenmarch, and to mind the children, who would marry me if I stood still. She enclosed a drawing by Nell, of the wedding, with all the hats much bigger, and a man in armour at the back, holding a letter, very late. I have it framed. - H.B. Tom "Tom's in the gardens at Fenmarch. He walks it every day - four miles there and four back - and he says it's the best part." Tom Vane has been at Fenmarch since he was fourteen, and head gardener since 1998, and since 1991 he has also carried the Fenmarch half of the old post round, from Little Gore to the Hall, which Abel Thrush carried for fifty years until he died that spring. Tom never stops talking, on the road, to anybody he meets, and to the hedges when there is nobody. Mrs Vane says that is why it is the best part. Afterwards She is thirty-four. The children still play weddings on the green, and Bess is still the bride, or Mum, which is the same thing, and Alfie still stands there and looks pleased, and Nell is still everybody else. Since 2000 there has been a new part in the game, played by whoever is smallest: a knight, at the back, very late, holding a letter. It is the most sought-after part. They take turns. See also Little Gore Dame Winifred Cope , next door, in the field Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Fenmarch Hall , four miles

title: Hob Grumnir
text: Hob Grumnir For the hammer, see below; she does not have an article, and has said she would not want one. Hob Grumnir Listening to Beatrice Known as Grumnir the Smith Born 12 August 1960, Thistlewick , next door to the forge, which he was in by the afternoon Sex Male Of The forge, Thistlewick Trade Blacksmith, third of that forge Trained by His aunt, Beatrice Grumnir, from the age of nine Hammers Several. Two named. One talks back Good at Taking a hit; giving one, very large, once Bad at Speed, magic, being subtle Pricing "Take it" Invoicing A shelf Rival Bryd Ollerenshaw, of Upper Clanging Hob Grumnir is the blacksmith of Thistlewick , third of that forge, and an enormous man who talks to his hammers. Two of the hammers have names. One of them, he insists, talks back. She is called Beatrice , and she joined the Forty-Eighth's company on the same morning he did, because, as he explained, "Beatrice comes. I come with Beatrice. That's the arrangement and it's not up for discussion, mainly because she'd win." The forge Hob learned the trade from his aunt, Beatrice Grumnir, who was born in 1919, kept the Thistlewick forge for most of the century, and died in 1989. By every account in the village she was right about everything and never once said anything anybody wanted to hear. Her headstone is in the churchyard. It now has a good gate in front of it. He has made a very great many things and owns almost none of them, because when somebody needs a thing he makes it and says "take it", and the record of what is owed is a shelf. Half the village has something of his. When he asked for a few things back, for a competition, every one of them was glad to see him and none of them would give it up, and each of them had a better reason than the last, and he said that was fair. Beatrice Beatrice is a hammer. I want to be precise about this, because I am a historian. She is a forging hammer of the ordinary kind, well used and well kept, and she is right about everything. She told him the Forty-Seventh had come in for a sword, and got a good one, and it had not helped. She told him a sword is no good on its own, and that somebody has to swing it who knows what breaks. When the company was full she said that was a shame; "Beatrice says a lot of things." She said nothing for a fortnight once, which Hob said was not sulking, because hammers do not sulk; it was her being professional about it. I asked in the village about Beatrice, and everybody I asked told me the same thing, which is that Beatrice was always right. Nobody in Thistlewick has ever said anything more than that, and nor shall I. On the Quest The Assize of Hammers. The Worshipful Company of Smiths at Great Dunnage judges work every three years, and Hob had never entered, having nothing he owned to enter. In 2000 he entered Beatrice, who is not his work. She was disqualified under clause one. The Wardens' notes, which I have seen, say that she is right about everything. He was entirely satisfied. The gate. Beatrice went quiet, and he admitted at last that the last thing she had told him to do, eleven years before, was make a marker, and that he had never been able to get the words right. He made three markers, each one magnificent, and rejected all three ("It's right. It's not her."), and then made the churchyard a gate with a good latch, because the old one stuck and she would have hated the fuss. Beatrice began talking again on the walk home, and said the latch wants a spring. * The Sky Anvil .* A thing fell out of the sky into Elias Meech 's top field in 1749 and has been a gatepost since. Mr Meech would not sell it, it being a very good gatepost, but he would swap it for a gate, and Hob had lately become good at gates. The star-iron made exactly one sword. Hob has not said who it is for. The anvil. His own anvil was stolen, once, by two apprentice bandits on Meredith Crooke 's six-week syllabus. They got it eleven feet, in the dark. He was angry for nine seconds and then impressed. Their apology is framed in the smithy, next to nothing he made. The sword at the door. Roland Fairweather 's sword, which Roland left at the tower door, has a maker's mark on it. Hob looked at it for some time. "That's my aunt's. She made this here. On this. Forty years back, near enough. Sold it to a man going south." And then: "She did good work." Beatrice, on that occasion, said nothing at all. He later put a Thistlewick haft on it, so that it would swing for a Thistlewick hand. "Still hers. Handle's mine." Bryd Ollerenshaw Bryd Ollerenshaw , of Ollerenshaw's at Upper Clanging, was apprenticed alongside him, and they have been rivals ever since. He won Best in Hall at the Smiths' Hall in 1987, the year he did not enter, having a cold. They met again in 2000, and went for a drink, and are still arguing about rivets. Later the same year they made the tube plate for the Two Hundred 's refit at Ollerenshaw's, in one heat, by four hands, which neither of them has mentioned since. Miss Hoyle says it will do. One of the Cotterill children says they do this every time. I record that they are rivals. Both of them have read this sentence and both of them asked me to leave it exactly as it is. Afterwards He is at the forge. The churchyard gate swings well, and the latch has a spring now. He still has not said who the star-iron sword is for. I have a theory, and I am not allowed to print it. In 2001 he and Bryd Ollerenshaw sat as joint judges of the Smiths' Hall prize at Great Dunnage, and disagreed for nine hours. The prize was awarded. Neither of them will say to whom. I read this article to him at the forge. He listened to all of it and said it was fair. Then he said that Beatrice says I have spelled Ollerenshaw right and the rest of it is soft. I have let it stand. See also Bryd Ollerenshaw The Worshipful Company of Smiths Roland Fairweather The Sky Anvil

title: Hosea Bellwether
text: Hosea Bellwether This article is about the compiler of this volume, and was written by him, against his judgement, on the advice of everybody else. For his work, see the front page . Hosea Bellwether With ink hands Known as The historian at the table by the fire Born 9 November 1965, Nether Sopping , in the room over the Slain Wyvern's bar.
