I have checked this, against the register, which was the first thing I ever checked Sex Male Of Nether Sopping , the Slain Wyvern , the table by the fire Trade Historian Work A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , three volumes Complete Going well Accurate The problem Quests undertaken None Things climbed None Footnotes awarded One Hosea Bellwether is a historian of Nether Sopping , and the compiler of A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , of which this is the third volume. Complete is going well. Accurate is the problem. He has never been on a quest, and has written about little else. I did not want to write this article. An encyclopedia that leaves its compiler out is, I was told by everyone I asked, inaccurate, and they were right, and I have done it, in the third person where I could bear to and the first where I could not. Nether Sopping He is a Nether Sopping man, which is to say that he counts in plain years, sixty and forty and thirty, and that he lives forty miles from Thistlewick , among the people Thistlewick sent there. Clause nineteen of the Prophecy sends a returning Chosen One to a cottage at a mutually agreeable distance, and the distance has been Nether Sopping for most of a century, and Nether Sopping is consequently the only place in the world where everybody in the bar has been to the top of the Obligatory Tower except the historian. I have sat at the table by the fire in the Slain Wyvern for most of my working life, under the goose, as it now is, with ink on my hands, listening. I have had a great many stories. I have had very few of them to the end. Volume Two Volume Two, the history proper, was compiled at that table, from first-hand accounts. Everybody in the room had been on one, and not one of them would tell a historian. They told the Forty-Eighth. He was going north; he was in it. So I asked him to do the thing I could not, and go round the room and be told: six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end, and then come back. I paid, handsomely, for a man with ink hands. Nobody does it. They get two and go and look at a dungeon. He did all six. They came from Ysolde Marrow , Hulda Bole , Nabb , Merrow Halgate , Councillor Dree, and the young lady with the tiara , who is going to work it out any day now, and it will be marvellous. With those, the history was complete. It is not accurate, because Merrow's bridge and Dree's chair cannot both be true on a Tuesday, but it is complete. It runs to four hundred pages and a pamphlet. At the bottom of page four hundred and one, in small type, there is a footnote that says the Forty-Eighth listened. Nobody else has one of those. I left the last page blank, until I heard how it went, and told him that hearing it was the fee. He came back, after the Tower and after Halbert Quy , and told me, and I filled it. The account in Prophecy Hall says that I wrote a song. I did not. I have dealt with this elsewhere, and calmly. Volume Three This is Volume Three. It is the encyclopedia: every person, place, institution, creature, artefact and cliche of the Quest, in order, with the cross-references the history could not hold. It is signed on the twenty-first of March, Third Age 2002, which is two years after the Quest and the first day of spring, as Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter. I have not written all of it. Where somebody knew a thing better than I did, I asked them to write it, and printed what they sent me whole, with my notes in the margin: the Bestiary is Miss Halloway's, the technical articles are Miss Hoyle 's, the songs are Miss Quill's, and there are letters from the top of the Tower which have been the greatest pleasure of the work. Method I believe what I am told, and then I write down who told me. Where two accounts disagree I print both. Where the Committee's account and the calendar disagree I print both, and say which is which (see Two Reckonings ). Where a matter is none of my business I have tried to say so, and to leave it there, and I have not always managed the second part. Where I do not know a thing I have said so, which in a history is more honest than it looks and in an encyclopedia is rarer than it should be. Afterwards The last page of Volume Two is filled. Volume Three is this. Bram Thistle comes south about once a month, to correct me, and is always right, and always about the same thing. Miss Quill and I meet at the Wyvern to disagree. Spare Cotterill writes. Grimspite writes. I have had a kind letter from Miss Pargeter of Frostwick , pointing out a clause. I am told that I am in Miss Quill's notebooks, at some length, in the third person. I have asked to see the verses and been told that I may when they are finished, and that she has been finishing them since the Quest, and that they will scan. It has been suggested to me, more than once and by a dark lord, that a historian of the Obligatory Quest ought one day to climb the Obligatory Tower. I have said that I do not climb things. I have also, this winter, bought a pair of boots. See also The front page The Obligatory Quest The Slain Wyvern Piper Quill

title: Hubert Weir
text: Hubert Weir For the village and its museum, see Ashcombe . For the longest culvert, see below. It is called Hubert. Hubert Weir Curator Known as Mr Weir; the Curator Born Hubert Weir, 8 August 1936, in old Ashcombe, on the high street, three doors from the only drain Sex Male Trade Drainage engineer, retired; Curator, the Ashcombe Drainage Museum, since 1990 Built Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, at a fall of one in two hundred Puddles in Ashcombe since None The flood A tremendous success Longest culvert Hubert Flood Dinner speaker Most years. Has kindly offered. Again Hubert Weir is the Curator of the Ashcombe Drainage Museum, which is free, and so is the enthusiasm. He stands in the middle of it with his hands behind his back, in a coat with gold frogging, the way a man stands in a room he is proud of, and he has every right to: he drained the new Ashcombe, fourteen hundred yards of culvert at a fall of one in two hundred, and there has not been one puddle in it since the day they went in. The only drain He was born in 1936 in old Ashcombe, in the valley, three doors from the only drain the village had, which had a stone over it carved DRAIN, and which was, he says, not up to it, and he knew that it was not up to it from the age of six, when he stood on the stone in a rainstorm and watched the water go round it. He went away to learn drainage, and came back, and spent thirty years telling the parish that the valley would flood, and the parish said that it had always been wet, and the blackboard in the school still has the history of the village on it: 1. IT WAS THERE. 2. IT WAS WET. 3. WE MOVED IT. The flood It flooded in 1989. Mr Weir had the village out by dinner and dry by tea, by a plan he had drawn in 1961 and kept in his coat for twenty-eight years, and not so much as a hen was lost. They have the Roll. He says it was a tremendous success, and it was, and he says it the way other men talk about a battle they won. The village moved up the hill, and he drained it. Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, every one named in copperplate on the great plan in the museum. The longest is called Hubert. Grown men have stood in front of that plan and gone quite quiet. The first exhibit is the stone from over the old drain, carved DRAIN, and the card beside it, in his hand, says kindly: It was not up to it. I asked him whether he bore it any ill will. He said, none whatever; that it had done its best, in impossible circumstances, for two hundred years, and that he had put it first in the museum because everything after it is only what it would have done if it could. - H.B. The Flood Dinner Every year there is a Flood Dinner at the church hall, with soup, a fish, a pudding and speeches, and the toast is TO THE WATER, WHICH WAS VERY GOOD ABOUT IT. The menus are pinned up in the museum, and at the foot of each is the speaker: the Curator; the Curator; Mrs Ash , on knitting; the Curator; the Curator. The notice for the year 2000 read SPEAKER: TO BE CONFIRMED, and under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Again. It was confirmed: C. ASH. And under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Next year. He did not mind in the least, he says; it was a very good speech, and the boy brought the name back, and that is worth more than culverts, which he does not say lightly. Afterwards He is sixty-five. He spoke at the Flood Dinner of 2001, on culverts, for some time. The empty plinth in the museum still reads THE FLOOD (ON LOAN TO THE LAKE), and he says that the loan is indefinite and that the lake is a very good custodian. He has drawn a new plan, which is in his coat, for what to do if the lake should ever want to come back up the hill, and he says that it will not, but that he has been wrong about water exactly once in his life, in 1936, when he thought the stone was keeping up. See also Ashcombe Mrs Ash Corvin Ash , confirmed The Day of the Water

title: Hulda Bole
text: Hulda Bole "It wasn't FOR. It was a list. I was the legs." For the room she told it in, see The Slain Wyvern . For her first job and her last, which were the same parcel, see Nix . Hulda Bole Totting something up, and not liking it Known as Mrs Bole; the Fetcher Born 19 April 1967, Nether Sopping Sex Female Trade Fetching, 1989-2000 Jobs Four hundred and six, in a ledger nine pages long Bear pelts Twelve. Then twelve of a different sort. Then the first sort after all Boots Her good ones, back since 2000 Advice Ask what the thirteenth is for Hulda Bole was, for eleven years, the person you sent for things. She fetched four hundred and six things, for whoever asked, from wherever they were, and wrote each one down. She told her story to the Forty-Eighth in the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping , where she sits with the ledger and a stub of pencil, totting something up and not liking it. It was one of the six tales I paid for, and it is the one I think about most. The list "Twelve bear pelts. That was the job. Fine. Went and got twelve bear pelts. Comes back. He says: ah, no. A DIFFERENT sort of bear." The ledger is nine pages long, and every line is a thing somebody wanted fetched. It has three columns in the section about the pelts: BEAR, BEAR (DIFFERENT SORT) and BEAR (THE FIRST SORT AFTER ALL). The third column has a great many crossings-out in it, and one very firm full stop. She did not tell me who the client was. I do not think she knows his name. She says that most of them did not leave one, and that it did not matter, because it was never about who. Asked whether she ever found out what any of it was for: "For? It wasn't FOR. That's the bit nobody tells you. It was a list. I was the legs." She has nothing against the people who asked. She says that most of them were perfectly pleasant and paid on time. It is only that nobody, in eleven years, ever told her what the thing was for, and after the first few hundred she stopped asking. Her advice to anybody starting out: "If anyone asks you to fetch twelve of anything, ask what the thirteenth is for." The last job Her last job was also her first. In 1989 a client of fifteen gave her a parcel in brown paper and string, to be delivered when the client was twenty-six, to the address given. She wrote it into the ledger as JOB 1. She carried it, between the other four hundred and five, for eleven years, and in the year 2000 she took it to the address given, and the client had moved, with no note. She wrote MOVED on the docket in capitals and put the parcel under the bench, and that was the end of fetching. Later that year the client came into the Wyvern, which was Nix , with Hulda Bole's good boots, which had been left outside to air in 1989 and taken, by Nix, to be aired. They were the fourth line on the first page of Nix's ledger. "My good boots?" said Mrs Bole. "I've done four hundred and six jobs in the other pair." Nix said that she knew; she had written them down. They looked at each other's ledgers. Give or take the handwriting, it was the same book. Then Mrs Bole got the parcel out from under the bench and handed it over, and said: "Here, then. You're the legs now." Neither of them knew, at the time, that it was addressed to Nix. Mrs Bole had always assumed the client was a he. She still says he. Nix has not corrected her, and nor have I. When I was getting this article up I asked Mrs Bole whether she would fetch me the Wyvern's copy of the tide tables from the bar, which was eleven feet away. She looked at me for some time and asked what it was for. I said it was for the article. She said, "That's better," and went and got it, and wrote it in the ledger, on a new page, as job four hundred and seven, PURPOSE: GIVEN. - H.B. Afterwards She is thirty-four. She does not fetch any more, except for people who say what it is for, which in two years has been four people. Mr Bole, who fishes, says that he was never once asked to fetch anything in eleven years, being on a boat, and that he has started to feel left out. She wears the good boots every day. She keeps looking at them. On Sundays she walks, in them, along the front and back, with nothing in her hands, and nothing on a list. See also Nix The Slain Wyvern Hosea Bellwether , who paid for the tale

title: Humphrey Gotobed
text: Humphrey Gotobed "H. Gotobed - Adventurer (Retired)." For his wife, whom he rescued by mistake, see Marjorie Gotobed . For his daughter, see Effie Gotobed . For the village where nothing has needed slaying since, see Much Pottering . Humphrey Gotobed Known as Mr Gotobed; H. Gotobed, Adventurer (Retired), on the brass plate Born 7 November 1944, at Brinkworth Halt, a railway cottage "on the way to everywhere" Sex Male Trade Adventurer, 1962-1983. Retired Roads taken Every one on the map, out to every edge, and then quite straight back to Much Pottering Last quest To rescue a lady. Knocked on the wrong door Lady rescued The wrong one, who did not need it; married her Swords Two, crossed, oiled every Sunday Slain since Nothing. He puts this down to the swords Current duties Spiders, out of the window Map annotation FOUND IT Humphrey Gotobed is a retired adventurer of Much Pottering , where nothing has ever happened, and where he has lived since 1983, when he came down the lane on a quest to rescue a lady and knocked on the wrong door. It was Marjorie Thorne's. He has been rescuing her ever since, mostly from spiders. He was out on both of the occasions that I called, and I have written this article from his things, which say a great deal, and from his wife, who says the rest. The road He was born in 1944 in a railway cottage at Brinkworth Halt, which is a junction on the old lines where trains stopped on the way to everywhere and nobody ever got off, and he says that he grew up watching people go past to places and decided at an early age that he would like to go to all of them. He went at eighteen, in 1962, with a sword and a pair of very good boots and a map of the world, and he set out to go down every road on it. The map is on the wall of the Gotobeds' bedroom, over the drawers. It has a dotted red line on it, which is every road Mr Gotobed ever took, and it goes to every edge of the map, and then it comes back, quite straight, to Much Pottering. Much Pottering is circled twice, and beside it, in the same red ink, is written: FOUND IT. The red line goes, I noticed, nowhere near Thistlewick , or the Obligatory Tower , or the Gloamwood . I asked Mrs Gotobed about that. She said that he had always said that there was a Chosen One for that sort of thing, and that it was rude to take another man's quest. I think this is the most considerate thing I have ever heard of an adventurer doing, and I have heard of a great many adventurers. - H.B. The career He was an adventurer for twenty-one years, of the kind that does not get into books: he found lost sheep and lost rings and one lost bishop, he cleared a great many cellars of rats and two of something worse, he walked a great many people to places they were frightened to walk to on their own, and he was paid, he says, generally in dinners. He killed nothing larger than a boar, which he regrets, because it was a very old boar and he thinks now it only wanted to be left alone, and he has had a soft spot for pigs ever since, which in Much Pottering, where the pig has right of way, is just as well. The wrong door In the spring of 1983 he took his last quest, to rescue a lady from a tower on the far side of the county, and on the way, in the rain, he knocked on the wrong door. Marjorie Thorne opened it. He told her that he had come to rescue her. She told him that she did not need rescuing, and that he had better come in, because it was raining. The lady in the tower, it turned out, had got herself out on the Tuesday, by the stairs, which nobody had thought to try. She sent on the reward anyway, to the adventurer who had been engaged, who was him. It is on the dresser in the Gotobeds' bedroom, on its stand, where it can be seen from the bed: a necklace, one green stone on a gold chain. Under the stand is a card in his hand, and it is the best thing in the house: THE REWARD, FOR WHOEVER RESCUED THE LADY. SHE GOT HERSELF OUT, AND SENT IT ON TO ME. SHE WROTE: GIVE IT TO THE ONE YOU DID RESCUE. I DID. Retired He hung up his swords in 1984, on the bedroom wall, crossed, with a brass plate under them, H. GOTOBED - ADVENTURER (RETIRED), and he oils them every Sunday and puts them back exactly crossed. Nothing in Much Pottering has needed slaying since. He puts this down to the swords. Mrs Gotobed puts it down to Much Pottering. Both of them are right, and both of them know, and neither will say so. Under the kitchen clock is a card in his hand: NOTHING HAPPENS AT ANY OF THESE TIMES. He put it up on the morning after the wedding, and he says it is the only promise he has ever made that he has been able to keep to the minute. The daughter He taught Effie to read off the map. He is, his wife says, the reason Effie thinks there might be a volcano somewhere, because he has seen one, on the edge of the map, in 1971, and has told her so, and Effie thinks that if there was one there, there might as well be one here. He has never once told her there is not. He says that it is not an adventurer's business to tell anybody what is not at the end of a road. Afterwards He is fifty-seven. He was out when I called, the first time rescuing Mrs Throssell's cat from the oak (it was the branch, which is marked, and then the trunk), and the second time walking Mr Cobley round the pond, in case Old Tom should turn over again, which he has not. I left my questions with Mrs Gotobed. They came back by Effie, in the post, a fortnight later, answered in red ink, on a map. See also Marjorie Gotobed Effie Gotobed Much Pottering A Glossary of Cliches , for the retired hero, with a sword over the fireplace

title: Ida Stagg
text: Ida Stagg "You've met Perce. Everybody meets Perce." For him, see Perce Stagg . For the town, see Frostwick . Ida Stagg "Mind it? I love it." Known as Ida; Mrs Stagg Born Ida Frome, 9 December 1937, Frostwick , in the winter, which was the only season there was Sex Female Married Perce Stagg , 1961, the day after the first Festival Festivals Forty-two. Loved every one Cold Never once, in forty winters, by Clem 's account Ribbons for the great many things since None Don't tell him He'll only go pink again Ida Stagg is the wife of Perce Stagg, the man who broke the winter at Frostwick , and she loves the Festival, and she will tell you so, and then she will tell you that he did one great thing forty years ago, and a great many things since, and that none of those ever got a ribbon. Then she will ask you not to tell him she said so, because he'll only go pink again. Frostwick She was born in 1937 in Frostwick, under the old winter, and grew up in it, and says that until she was twenty-two she had never seen a gutter run. She was in the square on the evening in the spring of 1960 when a young man in a red coat came down the hill at dusk and the snow began to drip, and she says that she was not the first to cheer, but she was the loudest, and that he looked at her, because of the noise, and went pink, and that she had decided by the time he got to the bottom of the hill. They were married the next spring, the day after the first Festival, at which he had cut the ribbon, and on which, she says, he had been so pink all day that she was worried he would go pink at the altar and not stop, and he did, and it has never really stopped since, and she has never minded. The great many things since "Mind it? I love it. Forty years of it. He cuts the ribbon, the whole town cheers, and he goes pink." "He did one great thing forty years ago. And a great many things since. None of THOSE ever got a ribbon." I asked her for the great many things, for this article, and she gave me a list, on condition that it did not go any further than the encyclopedia. It is long. It includes the lanterns, every year, two hundred and twelve; the roof of the Working Group's room, twice; Mrs Blagg 's mother's garden wall; the year the well froze and he carried water up the hill for six weeks; the dog; and every morning, the fire, before I am up, for forty years, without once being asked. I have not printed the rest. She has asked me to say that it goes on. Clem Blagg, at seven, told the Forty-Eighth that Nan says Mrs Stagg has never once been cold, not in forty winters, and that it must be Mr Stagg's lanterns, because he does ever such good lanterns. The committee found the ceiling very interesting. I put Clem's observation to Mrs Stagg. She said that it was the fire, every morning, before she was up, and that the boy was quite right, and that I was to say so, and that Mrs Blagg was to stop looking at the ceiling. - H.B. Afterwards She is sixty-four. She has seen forty-two Festivals, and loved them all, and has started a ribbon of her own, which she ties to the crown every year, under his, a little lower, plain blue, with nothing written on it. I asked her what it was for. She said it was for the great many things since, and that nobody had to know, and that he did not, and that I was not to tell him, because he'll only go pink again. See also Perce Stagg Frostwick Clem Blagg The Eleven Days

title: People
text: People A great many people have been on the Obligatory Quest, and a great many more have stood beside the road while it went past. title: Isaac Sowerby
text: Isaac Sowerby "Rivets. You cannot beat a rivet." For the works, see Ott Hoyle . For the field where the attempts came down, see The Long Field . For his snap tin, see Nix . Isaac Sowerby On the other bench Known as Old Sowerby Born 12 October 1925, Upper Clanging Sex Male The works Apprentice, 1939; on the rivets, 1939-1999. One of the six apprentices who stayed Started on The rivets Finished on The rivets Attempts seen go up A hundred and ninety-nine, by his count Bench FOR SOWERBY. SIXTY YEARS ON THE RIVETS. He sits on the other one Snap tin Returned, 2000, with the sandwich in it Isaac Sowerby , Old Sowerby to the whole of Upper Clanging , gave the Hoyle Works sixty years, and started on the rivets, and finished on the rivets. He is the town's memory. He is entirely cheerful about what he remembers, which is a great many airships going up and the same number coming down, and he sits on a bench in the street, in a knit cap, and will tell you about it. Sixty years "Sixty years I gave that works. Started on the rivets. Finished on the rivets." He went into the works at fourteen, in the autumn of 1939, as an apprentice, with a number. The works has numbered its apprentices since 1804, and Miss Hoyle's present apprentice, Nib , is the fortieth. Of the thirty-nine before her, thirty-three left, and six stayed, and one of them is Sowerby. He was put on the rivets in his first week, because somebody had to be, and he found that he liked it, and asked to stay on them, and he did, until the autumn of 1999. He says that he was offered other work, several times, and that he always asked what was wrong with the rivets, and nobody could tell him. "I have seen a hundred and ninety-nine of them go up. I have seen the same number come down. Never in a hurry about it, mind. They come down like a man sitting." I am bound to say, as a man who counts in plain years, that the first of the hundred and ninety-nine went up a long time before he was born. I raised this with him. He said that he had seen the drawings. Then he said that he had riveted forty of them himself and could tell you where every rivet went, and that a man who has done that has seen the others too, near enough, and I found I did not want to argue. "It is the coming down that wants the work. She will get to it." She is Miss Hoyle. He says it the way other men say the sun will come up. The benches There are two benches in the street outside the works. One has a brass plate, FOR SOWERBY. SIXTY YEARS ON THE RIVETS, which the works put up when he retired. He sits on the other one. He says that his is for visitors. If you sit on his, he will nod at you, and you will feel welcome, which is, I think, the idea. The snap tin In 1989 his snap tin went south in a carrier's crate nobody claimed, and he did not see it again for eleven years. In the year 2000 Nix brought it back to him, as a return and not a location, with the sandwich still in it. He opened it, and regarded the sandwich with respect, and said: "Dripping. She always did me dripping." He did not say anything else about who she was, and I did not ask. He held out a rivet, for Nix's trouble. Nix said that she could not, because it went in the book as returned and not as sold. He said, "It's a rivet. You cannot beat a rivet." I am told that she took it in the end, and that it is not in the book at all. In the Long Field, among the things in the grass, there is a single rivet with a ring of small white stones round it, so that nobody treads on it. The stones are Mr Sowerby's. Miss Hoyle's memorandum says that he will not be told to move them and nobody has tried. I asked him which attempt the rivet was off. He said that it was off one of them, and that it did not matter which, and that it was a good rivet, and he had put it in. - H.B. Afterwards He is seventy-six. In the year 2000 he saw the two hundredth go up, and he was, I am told, the only man in Upper Clanging who did not cheer. He was watching for the coming down. When she came down, beside the Tower , in her own time, he said that it was very well done, in the voice other men keep for a rivet, and went back to his bench. He still sits on the other one. The two hundred and first's keel was laid in 2001, and he has been down to look at the rivets, and has said that they will do. See also Ott Hoyle Nib , the fortieth Nix Upper Clanging The Long Field The Flight of the Two Hundred

title: Jack Furrow
text: Jack Furrow "Good evening. We are peasants." Not to be confused with Jill Furrow , to whom he is no relation, and whom he met on the road. Yesterday. For the table they share, see The Slain Wyvern . Jack Furrow In a peasant crown Known as A very ordinary traveller. "Jack Furrow, farm", on Dorcas 's board Born On a farm. Beans, mostly Sex Male Trade Peasant Wears A peasant crown, very common where he comes from, which is a farm Luggage One crate, PEASANT LUGGAGE, gold corners, velvet cushion Dinner Beans, untouched. Roast pheasant, to the bone Acquainted with Jill Furrow No Ring New, gold, and not to be read into Jack Furrow is a peasant, of a small farm, beans mostly, who has been in Nether Sopping since the autumn of 1999, at a corner table of the Slain Wyvern , with Jill Furrow, whom he does not know. He wears a crown. It is a peasant crown. The town let him get away with this for four months before the Quest, and was starting to enjoy it, and has gone on enjoying it for two years since. A very ordinary traveller "Good evening. We are peasants." You may remark, as the Forty-Eighth did not quite, that he is wearing a crown. "Peasant crowns. Very common where we come from. Which is a farm." Miss Furrow, at his side, adds that it is a small farm, beans mostly. If you speak to him again, he will tell you: "Beans. As discussed." Their table has two plates. One is beans, untouched. The other was roast pheasant with all the trimmings, and has been eaten down to the bone. There is a bottle of wine with a royal crest on it and a label stuck over the crest in a hurry, FARM WINE. Their luggage is a crate stencilled PEASANT LUGGAGE, with gold corners and a little velvet cushion on top, for sitting on, and he sits on it. Room four On the board by the bar in the Wyvern, room four has a line drawn through it. Dorcas Thrupp says that room four has not been down since Tuesday, that they are the best guests she has ever had, no trouble and no noise to speak of, and that she leaves the tray on the mat, and that it is lovely to see newlyweds happy. Put to Mr Furrow, this produced: "We are peasants, and we are unacquainted." Miss Furrow said that they had met on the road. Mr Furrow said, "Yesterday." Miss Furrow said, "Yesterday." They were holding hands, and had been the entire time, and under the peasant crowns both of them were wearing a new gold wedding ring, and both of them kept looking at it. He says that they have been discussing beans. The whole of Nether Sopping has asked me not to find out who they are. I have found that this is the easiest piece of research I have ever not done. I had a drink with Mr Furrow, at his invitation, and he told me a great deal about beans, all of it wrong, with tremendous authority, and paid for both drinks out of a purse that I will not describe, and asked me, as I left, very kindly, whether I had enough to manage on. I said I had. He looked relieved, and a little disappointed, as if he would have liked to help. - H.B. Afterwards He is still in Nether Sopping, and so is Miss Furrow, whom he does not know. They met on the road yesterday, which they have said every day for two years and four months, and it has not yet stopped being true to look at them. In the spring of 2001 they kept, by Dorcas's count, an anniversary of some kind, and had anniversary beans, and did not eat them. Room four still has a line through it. The tray is still left on the mat. See also Jill Furrow , no relation Dorcas Thrupp The Slain Wyvern

title: Jill Furrow
text: Jill Furrow "Do not curtsey. Nobody does." Not to be confused with Jack Furrow , to whom she is no relation, and whom she met on the road. Yesterday. For room four, see Dorcas Thrupp , who is delighted. Jill Furrow Beans people Known as Also a very ordinary traveller. "Jill Furrow, a different farm, no relation", on Dorcas's board Born On a different farm. Also beans Sex Female Trade Peasant Curtseys received None, by request Acquainted with Jack Furrow No. Do not read anything into the hand Ring Or the ring Jill Furrow is also a very ordinary traveller, and a peasant, from a small farm, beans mostly, and is staying at the Slain Wyvern in Nether Sopping , at the same table as Jack Furrow, whom she met on the road yesterday and does not know. She would like it understood that she is beans people, and that nobody curtseys. Beans people "Do not curtsey. Nobody does. We are beans people." The Forty-Eighth had not curtseyed. Miss Furrow considered this, and said: "Well. Don't start." It is the most regal thing I have ever heard said by anybody, and I have met a king. If you speak to her again she says, "Beans." She gave her name to Dorcas Thrupp the evening they arrived, after Mr Furrow had given his, and Dorcas wrote it on the board by the bar, in her small neat hand, against room four: Jill Furrow, a different farm, no relation. Miss Furrow watched her write it, and asked her to underline no relation, and Dorcas did. The hand, and the ring After the board by the bar with room four on it: "We are unacquainted. Do not read anything into the hand. Or the ring." The Forty-Eighth had not read anything into the ring. "Well. Don't start." Mr Furrow said that they had met on the road, yesterday. Miss Furrow said, "Yesterday." Asked again, she said, "Beans. Anniversary beans." I have asked her what the anniversary was of. She said, of the beans. I asked how long they had been in Nether Sopping. She said, since yesterday. Then she looked at Mr Furrow, who was looking at his ring, and she looked at hers, and I went and sat somewhere else for a bit. I have been asked by the town not to find out who she is, and I have not, and I want it on record that I have not even looked at the crest under the FARM WINE label, though it is on the table in front of me every time I go in, and would take a moment. Some research is better left undone, and some is better left to Nether Sopping, which has been enjoying this for two years and has no intention of stopping. - H.B. Afterwards She is still at the Wyvern, and has still not been curtseyed to, by anybody, and has twice had to stop a fisherman beginning to. Room four still has a line through it; the tray is still left on the mat. The Furrows, who are no relation, came down to the bar in the spring of 2001 for anniversary beans, which nobody ate, and a pheasant, which they did. Dorcas has kept room four for them for another year, and has not rubbed out the underlining. See also Jack Furrow , no relation Dorcas Thrupp The Slain Wyvern

title: King Aldous
text: King Aldous "Are you here about the rescue?" For the kingdom, what is left of it, see Fairholme . For his daughter, see Princess Rosamund , who is up the hill. It is Thursday. King Aldous of Fairholme "Oh dear." Known as King Aldous; His Majesty; Aldous the Generous, by the shareholders; "the Pater", by Rosamund, in her memoir, eleven volumes Born 3 January 1932, at the palace, Fairholme , when it was a good deal bigger Sex Male Reigned Since 1961 Married Queen Isobel, 1975; widowed 1983 Children One. Taken eleven times, twelve if you count the eagle Reward posted Her hand, or half the kingdom. Eleven times Taken The half. Every time. Very sensible Holds One two-thousand-and-forty-eighth of Fairholme Doors Fourteen kicked in; the fifteenth drawn; the hinges original King Aldous is the King of Fairholme , a small kingdom in the east whose princess has been kidnapped eleven times, twelve if you count the eagle, which the Palace does not. Every time, he has posted the traditional reward, her hand or half the kingdom, and every rescuer has taken the half. Very sensible. Nobody's fault. But there is only so much kingdom, and he is down, by Osric's arithmetic, to a two-thousand-and-forty-eighth, and it is mostly a ditch. The kingdom He was born in 1932, in the palace, when Fairholme ran from the hills to the marshes and had two rivers, a forest, nine villages and a very good cheese. He came to the throne in 1961, on his father's death, and was by every account a careful and well-liked young king, who kept the roads mended and the cheese up to standard, and was mentioned in two neighbouring chronicles as a sound man, which in that part of the world is the highest thing that can be said of a monarch. He married Isobel of the Marches in 1975, late, and very happily, and their daughter Rosamund was born in 1978. The Queen died in 1983, of a fever, and the King did not marry again. He says that one is enough, if it is the right one, and he says it about the Queen, and about Rosamund, and on one occasion, absent-mindedly, about the cheese. The reward Rosamund was first kidnapped in 1986, at eight, by a sorcerer, from her tower room. The King did what his father had told him a king must do, and what the old books say, and what everybody expected: he posted the traditional reward. Her hand, or half the kingdom. "Every time she's taken, I post the traditional reward. Her hand, or half the kingdom. They all take the half. Every one. Very sensible. Nobody's fault. But there's only so much kingdom." He has posted it eleven times. Every rescuer has taken the half, and he has never once been offended by it, because he says it would have been very awkward for everybody otherwise, and that Rosamund has views. The kingdom is now governed by a council of its shareholders, who are the rescuers, round three tables pushed end to end, and its chief business is drainage. The King sits in the middle. He has one vote. He has used it, in my hearing, to second a motion to lengthen the table, and he did it with great dignity. "If you do rescue her, take the half. Everybody does. We've a form." His portrait on the wall of the chamber shows him in his coronation year, holding the kingdom, on a map, in both hands. The map has been cut into eleven pieces since. Nobody has told the portrait. I asked the King whether he would like it brought up to date. He said that he would not, that it was a very good likeness of a young man who had not yet been asked to do any arithmetic, and that he was fond of him. - H.B. Mr Pilbeam His one sorrow is Mr Pilbeam , who was only passing, and rescued the Princess from an eagle in 1996, and has been sitting at the foot of the council table ever since, waiting for the council to decide whether the eagle counts. The Palace does not count the eagle. The King would like it to. He has said so, in council, eight times, and each time the matter has been deferred, and he has seconded the deferral, because it is not for the King to overrule his shareholders, and because Mr Pilbeam is, he says, such a comfort to have about the place, and he does not know what he would do on a Tuesday without him. When the Forty-Eighth told him that he was only passing, the King looked at him with great kindness, and said, "Oh dear. That's how Mr Pilbeam started." The hinges Hob Grumnir made the hinges on the door of the Princess's tower, a long time ago, and in the year 2000 asked whether he might have them back. "Your hinges? Oh dear. They're the only part that's held. We're on the fourteenth door. Every rescuer kicks it in, and the door goes, and the hinges are fine. Take the hinges and there's only so much door." Hob agreed that there was, and left them. Afterwards He is seventy. There have been no kidnappings since 1999, Rosamund having taken to walking up the hill on Thursdays of her own accord, which the Heroes' Guild has complained about, in writing. The fifteenth door is drawn on the council table, and the hinges are not on the drawing, because they will not be needed. The eagle is still deferred. He says that he has given away half of everything he had eleven times over, and that he has never once been poorer for it, because every half went to somebody who brought his daughter home, and that a man who has been given his daughter back eleven times is the richest king in the east, and is down to a ditch, and is perfectly content. Then he asks whether you are here about the drainage. See also Princess Rosamund Mr Pilbeam Fairholme Sir Dunstable , one share, back directly

title: Lavinia Barrow
text: Lavinia Barrow "Mrs Barrow." For the shop, its stock and its four things nobody needs, see Nether Sopping . For the Registrar, to whom she is not related, see Lionel Pell . Lavinia Barrow Everything an adventurer needs Known as Mrs Barrow Born Lavinia Barrow, 2 December 1936, Nether Sopping Sex Female Keeps Wick & Barrow, Outfitters, on the front In the trade Thirty-nine years in 2000, by her count; forty-two, by the sign's Sells Everything an adventurer needs, and four things nobody does The hat Thirty crowns. Form A-1 requires it Bench, flat-packed Four hundred. Nobody had ever bought it. Somebody bought it Wrote "on account" Once, in 2000, for forty bolts of oilskin Wick's peg Empty. Dusted Lavinia Barrow keeps Wick & Barrow, Outfitters, on the front at Nether Sopping : everything an adventurer needs, and four things nobody does. She sells the hat that the Guild's Form A-1 requires, and is not related to the Registrar. At the end of the row of pegs on her wall is one with nothing on it, which she dusts, which is Wick's. Wick went north, the same as they all do, forty-one years ago this spring. Wick and Barrow She was born in 1936 in Nether Sopping, above a chandler's, and went into the outfitting trade in 1958, at twenty-two, in partnership with Wick, who had the shop and the stock and the sign, and who needed, he said, somebody who could add. The sign went up that spring: WICK & BARROW, OUTFITTERS. Two names. In the spring of 1959 Wick went north. Everybody went north, that year and the next; it was a year ahead of the Chosen One, and not everybody went together. Wick has not come back, and nobody has heard where he got to. She counts her years in the trade from 1961, not 1958, and I asked her once why. She said that 1961 was when she stopped expecting Wick back on the Monday and started doing the books properly, and that before that she had only been minding the shop. She would not say what Wick was to her, beyond the sign, and I did not press it, and I have been told by three people in Nether Sopping three different things, and I am not printing any of them. "The sign says Wick and Barrow. That's two names, and one of them's still walking about, and the other one went north, and both belong on a sign." Wick's peg is the last on the row. Nothing has hung on it in forty-three years. It is dusted every morning, before the shop opens, after the counter and before the window, which is to say second. - H.B. The trade "Everything an adventurer needs, and four things nobody does." Which four, she will not say; she says that you would only buy them. She sells the hat for thirty, because the Guild's form requires a hat and does not say which, and she is not related to the Registrar, whatever anybody says, and nobody has ever said it to her face, because she sells the hat. She sells lamp oil, and DRAGON REPELLENT, which is lamp oil, and says so in the small print. She sells chalk for marking the walls of dungeons, finding your way out not included. She sells ten-foot poles. Everybody buys one. Nobody has ever said what for. She says that she has not asked, because it is not her business what a customer does with ten feet, and that it is the best-selling line in the shop. She also engraves. In the year 2000 Wren Halloway came in to have a brass plaque cut for the goose at the Slain Wyvern , and asked the price. "Letters, love, not words. Let's see." It came to a hundred and twenty-eight letters, and a great deal of money, and was paid, and was cut, and Mrs Barrow said, "That's yours, done. Mind the edges, and mind whose wall it goes on," which is advice she gives with every plaque, and which on this occasion was very much to the point. On account In the year 2000 the Hoyle Works at Upper Clanging , by the Forty-Eighth's hand, ordered forty bolts of oilskin from her for an airship. She counted them out loud, twice, and made somebody count them again after her. "Forty." And then, when the party said forty again: "I heard you the first time. I was enjoying it." They were bought on account. "Thirty-nine years in this trade, and I have never once had cause to write 'on account'." "North? Well. Something's going the right way up that road for once." The account was settled, in full, by Miss Hoyle , by post, inside the month, with a note that said Received with thanks. It flew. Mrs Barrow has it framed, beside the till, under the price of the hat. Afterwards She is sixty-five, and the shop is as it was, except that the bench in eleven pieces that leaned against the wall for years under its card, NOBODY HAS EVER BOUGHT THIS, has gone, to the top of a barrow in the hills, facing the sea, and she has not ordered another, because she says that it would not be the same bench, and that she does not stock things to make a point. She has taken down the card. She has kept it. It is on Wick's peg. See also Nether Sopping Lionel Pell , not related The Hoyle Works , on account The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth , where the bench went

title: Lettice Moon
text: Lettice Moon "Moon. Ballad (Sad). Fourteen verses. Nobody survives." For the Contest, see Mrs Harbottle . For the man on the serpent, see Septimus Dray . For the ballad in which nobody dies, see Piper Quill . Lettice Moon Between verses Known as Miss Moon Born 30 November 1975, Great Dunnage Sex Female Trade Seamstress, in Cordwainers' Row Category Ballad (Sad) The Contest at the Sign of the Bell Fourth, 2000, of four: 16 Verses Fourteen Survivors None, in 2000. One, briefly, since Lettice Moon of Great Dunnage is a seamstress, and the author and only performer of a ballad, Sad, in fourteen verses, in which everybody dies, including the narrator, who comes back for the chorus. She entered it in the Contest at the Sign of the Bell in the year 2000, and several of the back table were visibly moved, and said so, loudly. The ballad It has no title. She says that a title would give away the ending, and that the ending is the point. It begins with a shepherd and a miller's daughter and a wedding fixed for the spring, and I have been asked not to say what happens after the second verse, but I can say that by the eleventh there is nobody left in the parish, and that the twelfth is about the dog. In the thirteenth the narrator dies, of grief, mid-line. In the fourteenth the narrator comes back for the chorus, because, as she explains, somebody has to sing it. She wrote the first verse at fourteen, at her sewing, and has added to it ever since, a verse every year or so, as things occurred to her. She sings at her work. Her employer, Mrs Aske, of Cordwainers' Row, has asked her to keep it to the chorus during fittings, because of the effect on the customers, and she does, mostly. The Contest Ballad, Sad, fourth verse. "Moon. Ballad (Sad). Fourteen verses. Nobody survives." She went second, after Mr Dray. Nine from Mr Ambler, two from Miss Quayle, five from Mrs Harbottle, who said afterwards that she had marked the craft and not the body count. Sixteen. When Piper Quill took the stage with a Ballad (Not Sad), which nobody had ever entered, Miss Moon was part of the floor, with Mr Dray and the back table, and contributed, as is the custom of the Bell, a very sad verse of her own from the side, to bring the room's spirits down to where she felt they ought to be. Somewhere in the fourth verse she sat down, to a smattering, and heard the rest. It was a ballad about a farm boy who walked north, and nobody died in it, and it was all true. She told me that she sat through the whole of it waiting for somebody to die, and that nobody did, and that she found she did not mind. The next time the Forty-Eighth's company saw her, she said: "I've changed the ending. Somebody survives verse three. Briefly." Afterwards She is twenty-six. The ballad is now fifteen verses, because the survivor of verse three needed a verse of his own to die in. She is working on a sixteenth, in which he might not. She has not decided. She has written to Miss Quill, care of the Wyvern , to ask how it is done, and Miss Quill has written back, in the third person, four pages, and Miss Moon says that she has read them several times and is not sure she agrees with any of it, and is trying it anyway. She placed second in the Contest of 2001. Mrs Harbottle gave her a six. It was for the new verse. She sang me the whole ballad, fifteen verses, in the back room of the shop, between two fittings, so that I would get the article right. I have got it as right as I can without telling you what happens to the dog. I will say that I had not expected to mind about the dog. - H.B. See also Septimus Dray Mr Tweddle , who won Mrs Harbottle Piper Quill Great Dunnage

title: Lionel Pell
text: Lionel Pell "Registrar Pell." For the Guild he keeps, its forms and its review, see The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) . This article is about the man, which he regards as irregular, there being no form for it. Lionel Pell "There is no form for this." Known as Registrar Pell; Mr Pell; "the Registrar", in Nether Sopping, as if there were only one, which there is Born 11 April 1940, Nether Sopping , and registered the same day, by his father, who was the clerk Sex Male Registrar Of the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , since its founding in 1960, provisionally Requirements A reference; a hat; Form A-1 Form A-1 Mislaid, 1989. Under the mat, six feet away, 1989-2000 Form Z Kept forty years, in case. Used once Related to Mrs Barrow No Finds the pattern Not amusing Lionel Pell is the Registrar of the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) at Nether Sopping, and has been since it was founded, provisionally, in 1960. For eleven years he could register nobody, because Form A-1 had been mislaid, and he looked for it every day, everywhere in the hall, and it was under the doormat, six feet from his desk. He is aware of the tower. He is aware that the key was under the mat. He does not find the pattern amusing. A registered man He was born in 1940 in Nether Sopping and registered the same afternoon, by his father, who was the parish clerk and who did it, his son says, in a good hand and before tea, and who believed that a thing which had not been written down had not, in any sense that mattered, happened. Lionel Pell has believed the same all his life. He believes it more firmly, he says, than some men believe in a god, and with better evidence, because he has the forms. He was a clerk in the harbour office from fifteen until 1960, when the Guild was founded on the front, provisionally, pending a review, and wanted a Registrar who knew one end of a form from the other. He took the post at twenty. He has never taken another. The three requirements He recites them to everybody who comes in, whether or not they have asked, because a requirement not recited is a requirement nobody can be held to. "Form A-1. Three requirements. One: a character reference from a recognised authority. Two: a hat. Three: Form A-1." "The form requires a hat. It does not say why. It does not say which. Mrs Barrow across the way sells one for thirty, and no, we are not related." They are not related. I have looked into it, at his request, because he wished it to be in an encyclopedia where it could be pointed to. The Pells of Nether Sopping and the Barrows of Wick & Barrow have no ancestor in common back to 1712, which is as far as the Nether Sopping register goes. He says that people assume it because of the hat. He says that he did not write the form. The mat Form A-1 was mislaid in 1989. For eleven years nobody registered, because nobody could, and Mr Pell looked for it every day. "If you find it, you may fill it in. That is the whole of the process." In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth lifted the mat by the door, which says WELCOME, and found it. Mr Pell looked at it for a long time. "Form A-1: found. Astonishing." And then, before anybody could speak: "...Do not say it. I am aware of the tower. I am aware that the key was under the mat. I do not find the pattern amusing." Nobody said it. Everybody has been not saying it since. Form Z In a drawer of his desk which most people never notice he kept, for forty years, a single sheet, yellow at the edges: Form Z, Matters Not Anticipated. In case. "Never once used. In forty years every matter has been anticipated. By somebody. On something." After the ending, the Forty-Eighth put a bounty card on his desk that had no authority, no number and a drawing of an octopus on the back, for something that had been met at the bottom of the Stair under Hithermost . "There is no form for this," said Mr Pell. And then he said it again, more slowly, and opened the drawer. He discharged it on Form Z, and stamped it, and the Forty-Eighth was no longer provisional: the first member of the Guild in forty years who was not. "I shall mention it to the review," said Mr Pell. "When it sits." I asked him how it had felt, after forty years, to use Form Z at last. He said that it had felt like filing. I asked whether it had felt like anything else. He was quiet for a while, and then he said that he had had a second one printed, at his own expense, and that it was in the drawer, and that it was a very great comfort to him to know that it was there, and that I was not to read anything into that, and I have not, in print. - H.B. Afterwards He is sixty-one, and the review has not sat. He has mentioned the Forty-Eighth to it, by letter, and the letter is in the filing, under the review, pending. The board in the hall has had a single card on it since 2000, NO VACANCIES, because a board with nothing on it looked, he said, as if the Guild had stopped expecting things. He has had the mat taken up, and the floor under it inspected, and nothing was found, and he has had the mat put back, because a hall should have a mat, and he has written on the back of it, in a good hand, before tea: NOTHING UNDER HERE. CHECKED. See also The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Lavinia Barrow , not related Nether Sopping

title: Marjorie Gotobed
text: Marjorie Gotobed "Mrs Gotobed." For her daughter, see Effie Gotobed . For her husband, who came to the wrong door, see Humphrey Gotobed . For the village, see Much Pottering . Marjorie Gotobed "I've never had the heart" Known as Mrs Gotobed; Marjorie, to the parish council, at which she takes the minutes when Mrs Throssell has a cold Born Marjorie Thorne, 23 April 1955, Much Pottering , in the cottage she lives in Sex Female Married Humphrey Gotobed, adventurer, 1984, who had knocked on the wrong door Was being rescued No Has been rescued since Continually, mostly from spiders Tea cosies Two: one for an ordinary afternoon, and one to go on top of the first, for a really quiet one Keeps Every letter from Upper Clanging , in a box on the cabinet, tied by the year Has told nobody That she keeps them. Except you Marjorie Gotobed is the mother of Effie Gotobed and the wife of a retired adventurer, and keeps the Gotobeds' cottage in Much Pottering , where the kitchen is also the parlour and nothing happens at any of the times on the clock. Her daughter's pen pal has told her daughter that he drives an airship. Mrs Gotobed has never had the heart. The cottage She was born Marjorie Thorne in 1955, in the cottage she lives in now, which was her mother's, and her mother's mother's, and has never in its history had anything happen in it, which in Much Pottering is a family distinction. She grew up in it, and was a quiet girl, and read a great many books about ladies in towers, and liked the bits in the middle best, before the rescue, when nothing much was going on and the lady was sewing. The wrong door In the spring of 1983 a man in very good boots came down the lane on a quest to rescue a lady, and knocked on the wrong door. It was hers. She opened it, and he told her, with a sword in one hand and a map in the other, that he had come to rescue her. She told him that she did not need rescuing, and that he had better come in, because it was raining. He came in. He has been rescuing her ever since, mostly from spiders, which he puts out of the window. Her account of it is on a card tucked behind one of his swords on the bedroom wall, in her hand, and I give it whole, because I could not improve on it: HE CAME THROUGH ON A QUEST TO RESCUE A LADY. HE KNOCKED ON THE WRONG DOOR. IT WAS MINE. HE HAS BEEN RESCUING ME EVER SINCE, MOSTLY FROM SPIDERS, WHICH HE PUTS OUT OF THE WINDOW. They were married in 1984, at the church, in the morning, and the parish council minuted it as Nothing arising, which Mrs Throssell said was the highest compliment the parish could pay a wedding. The heart Effie writes to Spare Cotterill of Upper Clanging every month, and he writes back, and his letters are on the cabinet in a box, tied up by the year in string. Mrs Gotobed told the Forty-Eighth so in the kitchen, in a lowered voice, though Effie was at the gate: "Waiting for the post. Her pen pal writes from Upper Clanging. They've been at it since they were six. He says he drives an airship. I've never had the heart." And then, when he came back: "She keeps every one of his, on the cabinet. Don't tell her I said." She has never had the heart to tell her daughter that a boy of nine does not drive an airship. She has never had the heart, either, to tell her daughter that there is no volcano, or that Old Tom is a carp, or that nearly a princess is not a thing. I asked her whether that was wise. She said that the books she read as a girl were all about ladies being rescued, and that the bit she had liked best was the middle, before anybody came, when the lady was getting on with things and nobody had told her yet how it was going to turn out. She said she would like Effie to have as much of the middle as possible. On the best-plate shelf of her dish cabinet, kept with the best ones, is a plate with a crayon volcano on it. On the painting of a mountain by the fireplace somebody has added, in crayon, on the glass, a good deal of smoke coming out of the top. On a potted plant in the window is a little flag, VOLCANO (DORMANT). Mrs Gotobed has not removed any of them. She says that you do not clean a volcano off a mountain in Much Pottering; it is the most exciting thing that has ever happened in the house. - H.B. The tea cosies She keeps two. One is for an ordinary afternoon. The other goes on top of the first, for a really quiet one. I asked her how often she used the second. She said, most days. I asked her whether she had ever needed a third. She said that she had knitted one, once, in 1997, for the afternoon the parish council discussed the twinning, and that it had been put away since, because there was no point having a cosy for an afternoon that quiet if you were never going to have another one. Afterwards After the meeting at the gate in the year 2000, she found out that the airship was real, and was driven by somebody else, and that the boy was nine and the size of nine, and had come all the way from Upper Clanging, with a Chosen One, to see her daughter, and had brushed ninety boiler tubes since he was six. She sat down. She put the second cosy on. She says that she has never been so relieved in her life to find out that something was true, and that she has kept the letters since with a better conscience. She still has not had the heart to tell Effie that there is no volcano. She says that it seems a bit late now, because, by letter, it has gone off twice. See also Effie Gotobed Humphrey Gotobed Much Pottering Spare Cotterill , who does not drive an airship

title: Maud Penhallow
text: Maud Penhallow For the guest star she understudies, see Roland Fairweather . For the door, see The Obligatory Tower . This article is vague, at her request, about one afternoon, and silent, at mine, about one question. Maud Penhallow Studying how he stands Known as Miss Penhallow; the understudy Born 11 January 1984, Great Dunnage Sex Female Of Fellow Blunt's yard, Great Dunnage Age Eighteen In the yard since Nine Studied Sword, horse, lineage, and how he stands Understudy to Roland Fairweather In case The prophecy was ready and he was unavailable Asked One question Answered Not yet Maud Penhallow has been Roland Fairweather 's understudy since she was nine, in Fellow Blunt 's yard at Great Dunnage , learning his sword, his horse, his lineage and the way he stands, in case. She is the only person who ever went to see the end of one of his engagements, and the only person who ever told him how one ends. The yard She went into the yard in 1993, at nine, and was told that the prophecy was nearly ready. It had been nearly ready since Roland was twelve. She learned all of it: sword, horse, lineage, the lot. In case. She learned how he stands; she says that he stands differently when he is thinking, and that you can tell. She had never met him. When she did, in the year 2000, at the Bell, she said "Fairweather," and Roland's face did something very careful. She told him who she was. She asked him whether it was nearly ready, which had been her question since she was nine, and there was a pause of the kind that has eleven minutes in it. She asked to be told about the meetings, since she was not on the agenda. He told her. Then she asked him to look at her guard, and he did, for an hour, in the yard behind the Bell, and said almost nothing, which is how a good teacher looks at a guard. The question Then she asked him something else, which nobody in twenty-two years of meetings had asked, and Roland opened his mouth, and closed it. I have the question. I am not going to print it. It is hers, and she asked it of him, and he has not answered it, and I am not going to have it answered in an encyclopedia by somebody who was not there. I will say only that it was a good question, and short, and that the grown-ups had had twenty-two years to think of it and had not. The door She said that somebody ought to see the end of one. Eleven doors, he had said; he had left at the door of every one. What she did about it is the afternoon about which this article is vague, and I give both accounts, because I have both, and the people who gave them to me were all there. In one, she came north, and when Roland left the Forty-Eighth's company forty paces short of the Obligatory Tower, as he always does, she was there, beside the door, with a practice sword, and raised it to him, the way you are taught to at nine. "When you come out, I'll go and tell him how it ends." When the Forty-Eighth came out, she went, the whole way south, and told Roland all of it, in order. In the other, the Forty-Eighth had already been to the door by the time she asked where this one ended, and Roland said that he had left at the door; he always does. So she asked how it ended, and the Forty-Eighth told her, at the Bell, and it took the rest of the pie, and Roland listened to all of it with his chin on his hand and did not say a word. Then Maud said that she would go and see one for herself. Not the end. The bit after. In both, Roland laughed, properly, out loud, which nobody at the Bell had heard him do. In both, it was the first time anybody had told him the end of one. Afterwards She is eighteen. She is in the yard at Great Dunnage still, between, she says, which is a word she has borrowed from Roland and is using better than he does. She still practises his guard, and has improved it, and he has looked at it, and said almost nothing, and she knows what that means. Roland's prophecy was discharged under Carn Drey , with help, in 2000, and nobody needs an understudy for a thing that is done; she stayed in the yard anyway, and Fellow Blunt has not asked her to leave, and has, I am told, started asking her opinion. Roland has finished two further things since 2000, and keeps a list, and she has a copy of the list, and is on it, and will not tell me under what. The question has not been answered. She says she is in no hurry. She says the bit after is very quiet, and she likes it. See also Roland Fairweather The Obligatory Tower Great Dunnage Carn Drey

title: Mayor Gristwood
text: Mayor Gristwood "...AND WHEREAS the Corporation of Great Dunnage, being in Council assembled, and mindful -" For the town, see Great Dunnage . For the Door, which is open informally, see Nix , who took nine seconds. Mayor Gristwood In the hat Known as The Mayor; His Worship; Gristwood Born Josiah Gristwood, 4 March 1949, Great Dunnage , over the Chain Works, the son of the foreman Sex Male Mayor Since 1995, re-elected annually, unopposed, on account of the preamble Hat The most you have ever seen Preamble Forty minutes. Down to thirty-eight. Thirty-seven and a half Licensed persons None. There is a form Scissors Lost Tuesday. Found on a paddle. Ribbon cut again First Mayor to sit in The Counting House chair The money Not the Corporation's. The memorandum says they have enough Josiah Gristwood is the Mayor of Great Dunnage , a town of nine works, in the most hat you have ever seen. For five years he practised the preamble for the formal Opening of the Counting House, which was sealed in 1788 when the key was lost, and which is to be opened by a licensed person, when there is one, and there has never been one. The preamble takes forty minutes. He got it down to thirty-seven and a half. In the year 2000 the Door was opened informally while he was still on mindful . The preamble He was born in 1949 over the Chain Works, the foreman's son, and went into the Corporation's offices at sixteen, and rose, by being reliable, to Town Clerk's deputy, alderman, and in 1995 Mayor, the forty-first since Alderman Josiah Dunnage, who sold nails, and after whom he was named, by a mother with ambitions. On the evening of his election he was handed the preamble to the Opening of the Counting House, in the Corporation's book, as every Mayor has been since 1788, and told that it would be his duty to read it, in full, at the Opening. "Gristwood. Mayor. Forgive me. I'm practising the preamble, for the Opening. The Counting House! Sealed in 1788, when the key was lost. We've run the town on a memorandum." "It is to be opened formally, by a licensed person, with the preamble read in full. When there is a licensed person. The licence is a form. Nobody has ever filled it in. But the preamble is ready. It takes forty minutes. I'm down to thirty-eight." He was the first Mayor in two hundred years to practise it. The others had read it once, in their first week, and put the book back. He says that he could not see the point of being Mayor if you were not ready, and that he did not know when the licensed person would come, and that it would be a very poor show to be found at the Opening forty minutes long. Mindful In the year 2000 he asked the Forty-Eighth's company whether any of them was, by any chance, a licensed person, and was told no, and began the preamble anyway, while it was there. AND WHEREAS the Corporation of Great Dunnage, being in Council assembled, and mindful - Nix put an ear to the lock and did something small with two fingers, and it took nine seconds, and the Door stood open while he was still on mindful. That was not the Opening. The Counting House is opened informally; the Opening proper will follow on completion of Form L. Behind the Door there was one room, one chair, and on the chair a note: WE SPENT IT. J. POCKLINGTON, CLERK TO THE CORPORATION. 1788. He sat down on the chair, as the first Mayor to do so, and read the preamble to it, in full, twice. The money stacked under the note came to one thousand seven hundred and eighty-eight crowns, which nobody can explain, and the Mayor said that it was not the Corporation's, because the memorandum says they have enough. He has put it in the Bonded Warehouse, under Mr Tibbs , as Bond No. 1788, money, a little, provenance none whatever , and the Corporation pays the rent on it. He says that it is the first sound financial decision the Corporation has made since 1788, and that it is a very good chair. - H.B. The scissors The same week, the Mayor lost his ceremonial scissors, on the Tuesday, and had to open two things with a knife, which he felt very keenly. They turned up on the paddle of the bottom lock on the Dunnage cut, in the culvert, where a boy from Upper Clanging found them, along with the paddle, and thirty of the Iron Company's boats went down the cut, and the Mayor cut the ribbon again, properly, with scissors. Afterwards He is fifty-three, and still Mayor, and still in the hat. He has been composing a shorter preamble. It is, as of this spring, eleven minutes, and he is very proud of it, and says that it loses nothing of substance, and that the Corporation in Council assembled and mindful is all still there, only quicker. Form L is still blank. He keeps a copy in the hat, in case the licensed person should turn up while he is out. See also Great Dunnage Nix , nine seconds Mr Tibbs , who holds Bond No. 1788 Cotter Cotterill , about the scissors

title: Meredith Crooke
text: Meredith Crooke "Meredith Crooke. Principal." For the bounty on her, see The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) . For the anvil, see Hob Grumnir . For her cohort, Miss Halloway declines, on the grounds that they are persons; see the Bestiary 's introduction. Meredith Crooke "Did you all see the footwork?" Known as Crooke; M. Crooke, Bandit Chief, on the Guild's board; "Miss", to the cohort Born 14 September 1963 Sex Female Principal Of a six-week banditry apprenticeship, with a syllabus Camp The western hills: eight tents, a cook fire, and a board with a timetable on it Bounty 1,200 crowns and the Guild's quiet relief. Discharged, 2000 Pass rate Ninety per cent, 2000. "More than his Guild can say for anything" Week one Reading Meredith Crooke runs a six-week apprenticeship in banditry from a camp in the western hills, with a syllabus, a marking rubric, a timetable on a board and an unusually loyal cohort. The Adventurers' Guild put a bounty on her. When the Forty-Eighth came to collect it she was pleased to see him, and asked him not to hold back, because her cohort were in week four and needed to see one of these go badly for the tutor. "It's the only lesson that ever sticks." The syllabus The board at the camp gives the last three weeks: WEEK 4: INTIMIDATION (PRACTICAL) WEEK 5: DEMANDS - STRUCTURE AND DELIVERY WEEK 6: ASSESSMENT AND CERTIFICATE I have asked for the first three and been told that they are available to enrolled students. I know from the court of record, which is the anvil, that week one is reading, and that week four, module seven, is the acquisition of a heavy object. Her own way with a demand, I am told by people who were on the receiving end of one, is to make it with the syllabus open, so that you can follow along. The bounty In the western hills, with the trainees watching. The Guild's card read: BOUNTY: M. CROOKE, BANDIT CHIEF. Camp in the western hills. Runs a six-week banditry apprenticeship with a syllabus. Reward: 1200 crowns and the Guild's quiet relief. The Forty-Eighth's party went up into the hills in the year 2000 and found the camp, and her, and four trainee bandits in a semicircle behind her, taking notes. She fought with two of them at her side, as a demonstration. She lost, as a demonstration. When it was over she said, "Good! Did you all see the footwork?" and the cohort had, to a bandit, written down the footwork. She handed over the takings herself, and told the party to go and claim their bounty, and to tell Registrar Pell that her pass rate that year was ninety per cent, which was more than his Guild could say for anything. Mr Pell was told. He did not reply. The card on the Guild's board has DISCHARGED across it now, and somebody has pinned her syllabus up beside it, as a curiosity. To anybody who went back to the camp afterwards she said, "Week five. Come back Thursday, and let them see it done to you properly." Nobody did. Module seven Later that year two of her apprentices, Ivy Scrope and Hodge, stole Hob Grumnir's anvil out of the smithy at Thistlewick , in the dark, for module seven. It weighs three hundredweight. They got it eleven feet. In the morning it was face down on the grass outside the smithy door, with a head at either end of it, and when Mr Grumnir had lifted it off them a woman came down the lane with a clipboard. She looked at the anvil, and at the door, and at the eleven feet between them, and wrote something down. "Fail. Both of you." Hodge said that it was three hundredweight. "It says so on the side," said Miss Crooke. "Reading was week one." Miss Scrope asked if she might write to Mr Grumnir first, and wrote an apology on the back of her syllabus in a very good hand, and Miss Crooke said, "Week one. It's all week one," and took them both off up the lane, one ear each. If the party had beaten her in the hills, she knew them at once: "You. The footwork." The apology is framed in the smithy now. Mr Grumnir says it is the best-written thing in Thistlewick, which Elder Wispel has taken personally. I have seen it. He is right. - H.B. Afterwards She is thirty-eight. The course still runs, six weeks at a time, in the western hills, with the same board. She sends Registrar Pell her pass rate every year, on a card, unasked, and he files it, unanswered. It has not been below eighty-five. Module seven has been revised: the heavy object is now a coal scuttle, and the student is required to read the side of it first and write down what it says. Miss Scrope resat module seven in the autumn of 2000, and passed, and took her certificate in week six, and has since taken a post as clerk to the course. She writes the syllabus out fair. Hodge resat it twice, and is in the next cohort, and Miss Crooke says he will get there, because he does not give up, which she says is the whole of week four. See also Hob Grumnir Lionel Pell The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional)

title: Merribell
text: Merribell For her order, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the meeting she spoke at, see The Healers' Table . Sister Merribell She would like to know when you last drank water Known as Sister Merribell; the Sister of Whatever Works Born 4 February 1974, Thistlewick , in the chapel house; she was given a glass of water at once Sex Female Of Thistlewick , at the chapel Trade Village healer; field medic Order The Order of Whatever Works, the only member for eleven miles Trained The Sisterhouse at Weeping Bottom , until it began holding symposia Age Twenty-eight Good at Healing, reviving, Light Bad at Hitting things Carries The basin Patients lost None Merribell is the healer of Thistlewick , a Sister of the Order of Whatever Works , and the first person to join the Forty-Eighth, on the grounds that he had not had a glass of water since Tuesday. Her order holds that theology is a distraction from the actual problem, which is usually that you have not had any water today. She has never lost a patient. "Sit down. When did you last drink water?" is how she meets everybody, and it was how she met Bram . He gave an answer. "That wasn't the question," she said. "Water. When." The Order The Order of Whatever Works has a founding document, which is a pamphlet, and a Rule of Life four lines long, one of them about socks. It does not have a doctrine and does not want one. Merribell trained at the mother house at Weeping Bottom , a wet valley chosen by a founder who believed the damp was good for the chest, and left at twenty-two, in 1996, because the Sisterhouse had begun holding symposia. She keeps the most complete medical record in the county: every ailment of every soul in Thistlewick, dated, in a good hand. The Prophecy Committee has never once asked to see it, preferring the Prophecy. Manner She is a professional, and professionals have a vocabulary. She says the anatomical words the way other people say "elbow", plainly and at the volume needed to be heard over a fight, and the party learned early to look at the ceiling. "Where does it hurt? Be specific. 'Down there' is four separate systems and I will guess wrong." When Bram said ankle, she said, "Oh, thank goodness." She carries a basin. She brought it unasked. "Nobody has ever won an argument with me about hydration and I am not starting a losing streak on a Thursday." On the Quest Of all the things done on the road, three were hers, and the Prophecy's own account records each of them. Fit to travel. Clause eleven of the Prophecy requires a Chosen One to be certified fit before departure. It had been done forty-seven times. The Forty-Eighth's form was blank, because he had been asleep. She found the form on a pad at Upper Clanging and did it properly: stamped scales from the fish stall at Nether Sopping , the light of the lighthouse at Saint Bother 's, lit, a clean surface, and a witness, from among the company. It is, the account says, the first properly documented attempt in four thousand years. I have interviewed several of the witnesses and they all looked at the ceiling. The Sisterhouse. The mother house had split between the Order of Whatever Works and the Order of What Ought To Work, which wins every argument and loses patients, and the two agreed to settle it the way this world settles things, with a ward and a queue. Merribell asked the patients whether they had eaten. Whatever Works won on points, nineteen to one, in an afternoon. Sister Bewick , of the other order, has since been examined on Whatever Works' doctrine, and passed. It is four lines long. The curse of Sump. The village of Sump had been cursed since 1794, with headaches, poor sleep and a general sense that things used to be better. She diagnosed it in nine seconds. There were wasps in the well and nobody had had any water for two hundred years. The curse was lifted by the Water Committee, one member, with a glass of water, and the minutes record an item three. She also called on Tobias Frayne , who had been revived by passing adventurers eleven times, and declined to make it twelve. "There is nothing wrong with you, Mr Frayne. That's the trouble." She prescribed having the parish to tea, through the door, on purpose. He has not died since. The Healers' Table Every surviving party medic within forty miles meets once a year in the back room of the Slain Wyvern , under the chair of Mrs Ysolde Marrow , to compare the worst thing they ever had to improvise. Merribell was invited in the year of the Quest, the youngest at the Table by thirty-eight years, and asked to speak, and had nothing. "I've never lost anybody," she told them. "I know what that means. It isn't a virtue. It's an average." The room did not console her and did not laugh. Mrs Marrow told her to write it down, all of it, now, while she still thinks it is boring. She said, "Yes, Mrs Marrow." I was in the bar, and the door was not quite shut, and I have written down only what she has since said I may. Merribell has read this article and has one correction, which is that I should drink more water. I have noted it. Afterwards She spoke at the Healers' Table in 2001, as the account said she would. She spoke for eleven minutes, which is the shortest address in the Table's history, and the Table minuted it as the most useful. The subject was water. She is still Thistlewick's healer, still the only member of her order for eleven miles, and still has not lost anybody. She is writing it down. See also The Order of Whatever Works Weeping Bottom Ysolde Marrow The Obligatory Quest

title: Merrow Halgate
text: Merrow Halgate For the clause that decided his fight before he got up that morning, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick , clause fourteen. Merrow Halgate Drinking carefully Known as Merrow of the Bridge Born 8 March 1951, Nether Sopping Sex Male Of Nether Sopping , the Slain Wyvern Party Twenty. The best-equipped that ever went north Fought The Dark Lord, at the bridge Result Lost, as written down in advance At peace with The losing Not at peace with The paperwork Believed about the apology Rarely Merrow Halgate is a big man in old armour who drinks carefully in the Slain Wyvern , and was one of a party of twenty, the best-equipped party that ever went north, which fought the Dark Lord at the bridge and lost. They were meant to lose. It was written down. The bridge "Twenty of us. Best-equipped party that ever went north. We fought him at the bridge and we lost. And here's the thing. We were MEANT to lose. It was written down. In advance. Clause fourteen: the first meeting shall not go well." He puts the cup down very precisely at this point, every time, and I have watched him do it a dozen times, and the cup has never once made a sound.
