"Twenty of us, and a document decided how it went before we got up that morning. I've made my peace with losing. I have not made my peace with the paperwork." Which Chosen One the twenty went north with he does not say, and I have not pressed him, because it is one of the tales of the Wyvern, and one of the rules of the Wyvern is that a tale is told the way its teller tells it. It was a first meeting. The first meeting shall not go well, and it did not. The apology Ask him what Grimspite was like, and he will tell you that halfway through, the Dark Lord stopped, and apologised, and then carried on. "I think about that more than the losing." Nobody ever believes him about that part. He says so himself. I do. I believed him before the Forty-Eighth came back, and I believe him a good deal more since, having had three letters from the Dark Lord about my dates, each of them apologising for the trouble. It would be very like him. Afterwards He still drinks carefully. He has been told, by the Forty-Eighth and by me, what was said at the top of the Tower in the year 2000, and about the contract, and the clauses, and the forty-eight hundred years; and he listened to all of it, and was quiet, and then said that it was a comfort, in a way, to know that the paperwork had been bothering the other fellow as well. He has his own theory about the old bench on the Middle Distance, which is older than anybody's memory and faces the sea: that it was put there by somebody who had walked that road tired and done something about it, and had not wanted a plaque. He thinks Ambrose Fitch may have known about it, and wanted one nearer the road. He went out to Ambrose's bench, when it was built, and sat on it, and came back, and said that it was a good bench. People believe him about that. See also The Prophecy of Thistlewick Grimspite the Inevitable The Slain Wyvern Ambrose Fitch

title: Mirabel
text: Mirabel For the village and the Archive, see Olde Evermore . For the Elder who fetches things down from the top shelf, see Elder Faelan . Mirabel of Olde Evermore Not tired Known as The Last Oracle of Olde Evermore; Grandmother Of Olde Evermore , the Forbidden Archive, on a stepstool Born The Second Age, about two thousand one hundred years before the Third. She remembers the day, and what she had for breakfast Sex Female Age Four thousand one hundred and fourteen Looks Eight and a quarter; she would like that mentioned Foresaw The fall of empires; all forty-eight risings; a biscuit Speaks The Old Tongue, flawless and terrible Translated by Elder Lirien Bedtime Half past seven. Not a minute after Present at The signing of the Prophecy of Thistlewick Mirabel is the Last Oracle of Olde Evermore , the hidden village of the elves, which every party finds eventually by falling off the same ledge. She is four thousand one hundred and fourteen years old, and looks about eight, and a quarter. She has foreseen the fall of empires, and has to be in bed by half past seven. The Oracle She stands on a stepstool in the middle of the Forbidden Archive, with long silver hair and a silver circlet, and the look of somebody who has seen all of this before, because she has. When she prophesies she lifts her hands, and every candle in the Archive leans towards her, and she speaks in the Old Tongue, and it is flawless, and it is terrible, and Elder Lirien translates: "When the moon devours the sun, and the last bell falls silent, the one who was not chosen shall..." "...is that a biscuit?" It always is. It was in the Forty-Eighth's pocket, and he had forgotten it was there, and she had not. The prophecy does not get finished, and nobody minds. She has been doing that one since the Second Age, and it is always a biscuit, and I have come to think that the only thing in the world more reliable than the Prophecy of Thistlewick is Mirabel's appetite, which has the advantage of being honest about it. The Elders, every one of them visibly older than she looks and some thousands of years younger than she is, call her Grandmother, and are sent to fetch things from the top shelf, which is where the Chronicle of the Second Age is kept, so that she cannot reach it, because she reads the endings first. Elder Lirien translates for her when she prophesies, and when she asks for pudding, and the pudding is more urgent. The signing She was at the signing of the Prophecy of Thistlewick, in the first year of the Third Age, a child of about two thousand, and she is the only eyewitness I have been able to find. "It was ever so long. Everybody had to sign it three times." So she drew a horse on it. Elder Faelan has views about this, which are that it was in the margin of a sacred and binding instrument, Grandmother. She says that it is a good horse. It is. I have seen the Archive's fair copy, and the copyist copied everything, and it is there, very small, in wax crayon. I asked her nothing further about it, and she offered nothing further, and I record that we were both entirely satisfied with the arrangement. The secret She told the Forty-Eighth a secret, a real one, not a prophecy: that Elder Lirien was going to have a baby. Across the Archive, Elder Lirien dropped a scroll, and at the foot of the ladder Elder Faelan stopped moving altogether. She had foreseen it, and told them at breakfast, before they knew. "I've known since the ninth of March." It is a girl, and she is going to be called Biscuit. Elder Faelan said that she is not going to be called Biscuit. "She is, though." Bedtime The Archive clock is tall and beautifully kept and says a quarter past seven, and the pendulum is tied to the side of the case with a hair ribbon, in a very neat bow. "It's nearly half past seven. I'm not tired. I have seen the fall of empires. I can see the clock. It says a quarter past." Elder Lirien says that she has to be in bed by half past seven. They tried eight, once. She foresaw the fall of an empire in the middle of supper, out of sheer tiredness. It was only a small empire. Still. Her bed is in the corner of the Archive, turned down, with a stone hot-water bottle already in it, and on the pillow there is a note in the Old Tongue, flawless and terrible, which Elder Lirien translates without looking up: Not tired. Afterwards She is four thousand one hundred and fourteen now, and says that she is eight and a half, and the Elders have agreed to mention the half. The clock still says a quarter past seven. The ribbon has been changed, once, for a blue one. I wrote, for this article, to ask whether there was anything she would like to foresee for the readers of Volume Three. The reply came in the Old Tongue, in a large round hand, and Elder Lirien's translation was pinned to it. It began, When the moon devours the sun, and stopped, and under it, in Elder Lirien's hand: She has asked whether you have any biscuits. I have told her that you are a long way off. She says you are not as far off as you think. I am keeping a tin by the door. Elowen's tea cosy, with the two little sleeves and the B on the front, is finished. I have not been told what it is being used for, and when I asked, both Elders went the colour of the carpet, and Mirabel said that it was a secret, a real one, and that she was not allowed to tell this one, because she had told the last one. See also Olde Evermore Elder Faelan The Prophecy of Thistlewick Two Reckonings

title: Mordaunt
text: Mordaunt "Mordaunt, clerk. Are you a knight?" For the Chapter House and the great map, see Coldbarrow . For the Order, see The Order of the Errant . For the knight with nine pins, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Mordaunt In ink. Not pencil Known as Mordaunt; the Clerk; "the committee", on Thursdays Born Ambrose Mordaunt, 17 February 1936, at Coldbarrow, in the gatehouse, the son of the porter Sex Male Clerk Of the Order of the Errant, Coldbarrow, since 1968 System One knight, one pin Files on Sir Aldric Nine, then ten Committees appointed to Four, all the same one. Quorate Writes in Ink. Pencil is how we got here Rank created Knight Errant, At Large; one Thursday, 2000 The map Correct Mordaunt is the clerk of the Order of the Errant at its Chapter House at Coldbarrow , in the snow of the far north, where he keeps the great map of the island with a pin in it for every knight in the field, and reads it the way other people read a will. One knight, one pin. That is the system. For nine years one knight had nine pins, and three of them were the same week, and in the year 2000 Mordaunt solved it, on a Thursday, by creating a rank. The gatehouse He was born in 1936 in the gatehouse of the Chapter House, the son of the Order's porter, and grew up under the great map, which he says was the first thing he ever learned to read, before letters, by the pins: red for knights errant, blue for knights at home, black for knights who would not be coming home, with a little card. He was made under-clerk at eighteen, in 1954, and clerk in 1968. He has never been a knight, and has never wanted to be one. He says that somebody has to know where they all are, and that a knight never does. "Chapter House of the Order of the Errant. Mordaunt, clerk. Are you a knight? Then you are not on the map. Good. One knight, one pin. That is the system." Nine pins Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third went out errant in 1991. By the year 2000 the great map had nine red pins in it for him. "Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore. The Third. Nine pins. Six of them are correct, on different dates. Three of them are the same week." "Frostwick, sir. And Fenmarch. And a lay-by in the west." People said that the Order had lost his file. "The Order has not lost his file. The Order has nine of them." They are on the bottom shelf, nine fat volumes, each labelled PEMBERTON-GORE, and each certain that it is the real one. Mordaunt's ledger lay open at P, and every entry on the page had been crossed out and written in again somewhere else. "If you should see Sir Aldric, note the place, the date and the time. In ink. Not pencil. Pencil is how we got here." The committee A committee was formed to review the map, the pins and the week. It sat on Thursdays, at a table with two chairs and two stools, and the committee was Mordaunt, appointed to it four times, and therefore quorate. In the year 2000 Sir Aldric came to Coldbarrow, and Mordaunt said that it was Thursday, and the committee would see him now, and sat in each chair and on each stool in turn, and then stood behind all of them, and gave the committee's findings. "Finding one: nine pins. Finding two: all nine are correct. Finding three: three of them are the same week. The committee has been unable to fault the pins. It has therefore had to fault the knight." The committee recommended that Sir Aldric remain in one place for the duration of the review, and offered him, on that condition, Knight Commander of the Chapter: a desk, here, and a pin that does not move. It was, Sir Aldric said, the finest thing he had been offered in nine years, and he thanked the committee, and said no. A knight who stays put is a post. But Mordaunt had asked, and nobody asks a man to stay, and he would like that put in the minutes. In ink. Mordaunt wrote for some time, and crossed nothing out. "Then the committee has a data problem, sir. The knight cannot stay with the pin. Resolved: that the pin go with the knight. Knight Errant, At Large. A rank of the Order, created this Thursday. And wherever the knight is, sir, the map is correct. That is the system now." I have seen the card on the committee's table: REVIEW OF PINS (PEMBERTON-GORE): CONCLUDED. SIR A. INFORMED. OFFERED THE CHAPTER. DECLINED. And under it, smaller, in ink: Beautifully. (Minuted at his request.) It is the only adverb in the minutes of the Order of the Errant since 1890. I asked Mordaunt why he had allowed it. He said that it was accurate. - H.B. Afterwards He is sixty-six. There are no red pins on the great map now, and in the margin a small card in his hand: PEMBERTON-GORE. AT LARGE. PIN CARRIED. Every week since 2000 he has had a note from Sir Aldric's squire, the Fourth, giving his uncle's place, the date and the time, in ink, and he keeps them in a tenth volume, and it is the only one of the ten that agrees with itself. He says that he has never been so well informed about a knight's whereabouts in fifty years at the desk, and that he has never once known where Sir Aldric was going to be next, and that he has come to regard that as the correct state of affairs for a knight errant, and that the system has never worked better. See also Coldbarrow Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III The Order of the Errant The Fourth , who writes in ink

title: Mother Selvidge
text: Mother Selvidge "Cross my palm, dear. Two crowns." For the Fair, see Wayside Sights . For the young man she told he was the rival of a great hero, see Corvin Ash . Mother Selvidge Never wrong Known as Mother Selvidge; "dear", to everybody else Born Ruth Selvidge, 31 October 1922, in a wagon on the road between two fairs, which she says was the first reading she ever gave, and it was correct Sex Female Booth MOTHER SELVIDGE. NEVER WRONG. TWO CROWNS The cards Do not do credit Wrong Not once, dear. Ask anybody she has read Rival of a great hero About four young men a year Because It is the reading that makes them stand up straight Same again? It'll be the same again, dear. Keep your money Mother Selvidge reads the cards in a little striped booth at the back of a fair in the sand of the far south, a long way from anywhere, the way fairs always are, for two crowns, and has never once been wrong. Ask anybody she has read. She tells about four young men a year that they are the rival of a great hero. They all go and do something. The road She was born in 1922 in a wagon on the road between two fairs, the seventh child of a fairground family, and says that she was reading the cards before she could read, and that she was reading people before she could read the cards, and that the cards are only there so that people have something to look at while she reads them. She took the booth over from her aunt in 1946, and has had it since, and the sign has never changed, because she has never once had to change it. The reading To the Forty-Eighth, in the year 2000: "You're going to go a long way, and meet a great many people, and at the end of it somebody is going to be very surprised to see you. And you'll eat a turnip. That one's free." He went a long way, and met a great many people, and at the end of it somebody was very surprised to see him, and he ate a turnip, on the way home. I have checked. She was right about all four. She says that she generally is, and that the turnip was a gift, because a Chosen One from Thistlewick who does not eat a turnip on the way home has not been read properly. The rival In 1989, at a fair, she told a young man of nineteen, sat in a heap, that he was the rival of a great hero, for two crowns. He went and sat in a corner of the Slain Wyvern for eleven years, waiting for the hero. In the year 2000 he came back and asked her again. She did not remember him. She read him again, and got a long life, a useful trade, something with his hands, and no destiny whatsoever. He asked her to do it again. "Same again? It'll be the same again, dear. Keep your money." Then she put the cards down and told him, kindly and without mystery: "Shall I tell you a thing, dear? The rival of a great hero. I say that to about four young men a year. Lads like you, at nineteen, sat in a heap. It's the reading that makes them stand up straight. And it has never once been wrong. They all went and did something." He said that he had sat in a corner for eleven years. She said: "And then you got up. Look at you. You're stood in a fair a long way from anywhere with your friends." I asked her how many young men she had told they were the rival of a great hero. She said about four a year for fifty-six years, which comes to two hundred and twenty-four, and that she knew where about two hundred of them were, because they write, and that every one of them had gone and done something, and that one of them was a Mr Rook, who keeps a league table in the west and is fourth on it by his own choice, and that she was very proud of him too. - H.B. Afterwards She is seventy-nine. She is still in the booth, at the back of the fair, and the sign still says NEVER WRONG, and she still is. Since 2000 a great many more people have come to the fair, because the road to the Tower is busy, and she has read a great many of them, and told them that they will go a long way and meet a great many people, and she says that this is true of everybody walking to see a chair, and that it is the easiest money she has ever made, and that she has not put the price up, because the cards do not do credit, and nor do they do profiteering. See also Corvin Ash Wayside Sights The Turnip ; that one was free The Rivals of the Sable Hart , several of whom she has read

title: Mother Ursula Pym
text: Mother Ursula Pym For the Order she founded, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the valley, and the weather in it, see Weeping Bottom . For the socks, read on. Mother Ursula Pym "Better, thank you" Known as Mother Ursula; the Founder; "her in the window" Born 2 February 1659, at Sallow Cross, a market town as far from the sea as it is possible to get without leaving the island Died 11 November 1744, at Weeping Bottom , aged eighty-five, sitting down Sex Female Founded The Sisterhouse of the Order of Whatever Works, 1702 Chose the site For the air On the advice of Every physician consulted Who had been None Wrote One pamphlet, four pages, stitched; the first page is the whole Rule Relics One pair of socks, dry, in glass Last words "Better, thank you" Mother Ursula Pym (1659-1744) was the founder of the Order of Whatever Works and of its mother house at Weeping Bottom , which she chose in 1702, for the sea air, on the advice of every physician she consulted, none of whom had been. She wrote the Order's Rule of Life, which is four lines long, and she wrote it, by her own account, in the time it takes a kettle to boil, and then spent forty-two years being asked whether that was all, and saying yes. Sallow Cross She was born Ursula Pym in 1659 at Sallow Cross, a dry little market town in the exact middle of the island, the daughter of a chandler who sold candles, rope and remedies, and could not have told you which of the three did the most good. As a girl she kept the remedies shelf. By fourteen she had noticed that customers who were given a glass of water and a chair while they waited for their remedy very often went home without it, and she told her father so, and he told her to stop doing it, because it was bad for trade. She had a chest, all her life: not a bad one, but a chest. The physicians of Sallow Cross, of whom there were four, each prescribed something different for it, and each was very confident, and she took all four remedies in turn and kept a little book of how she felt afterwards. The book survives, at Weeping Bottom. Every entry ends the same way: Then I had a glass of water and sat down, and felt better. I do not think it was the remedy. I have seen the little book. It is the earliest clinical trial I know of on this island, and its findings have never been overturned. The Sisterhouse keeps it beside Sister Bewick 's eleven volumes, and I am told that it is very nearly as long as volume eleven. - H.B. For the air In 1701, at forty-two, she resolved to found a house of healing, and asked every physician she could find where it ought to be. They were unanimous. The sea air, they said, was the finest cure for the chest in the world. None of them had been to the sea. Neither had she. She bought a map, and found the nearest piece of coast with a valley in it, so that the house would be sheltered, and went. The valley was the hollow between the rock and the sea, which is where the fog comes in off the water and settles, and stays. It was drizzling when she arrived, in the spring of 1702. It has been drizzling since. She stood at the top of the valley path, I am told, with her bag, and looked down into it for a long time, and then she said, "Well, it is certainly air," and went down. She did not move the house. She was asked to, a great many times, by the Sisters, by the patients, and once by a bishop, who had come to see her about something else and caught a cold. She said that she had been sent there by every physician consulted, and that she would not like to contradict them all at once, and that in any case the patients were getting better, which was the point. They were. Nobody could say why. She said that she could, and handed them a glass of water. The founder's stone at the gate is her wording, and the line under it, None of whom had been, is not. Nobody knows who added it. It is in a newer hand, and the Sisters say it was a patient, and the patients say it was a Sister, and I have a feeling, from the shape of the letters, that it was cut after 1744 by somebody who had known her and thought she would have laughed. She would have. She laughed, the house records say, "frequently, and at length, generally at physicians". The Rule of Life I. Drink a glass of water. II. Sit down. III. Dry socks: two pairs, and a spare. IV. Then see how you feel. Mother Ursula Pym, 1702 She wrote it in her first week in the valley, on the first page of a pamphlet of four, stitched, because that was the size of paper she had. The other three pages are blank, and were left blank on purpose, so that anybody who thought the Rule needed adding to would have to look at three empty pages first and see how they felt. Nobody has added anything in three hundred years. It was nearly done, once, by the symposia, and the symposia have been discontinued. The third line has been more discussed than the other three together. It is generally agreed now that it was written in the valley, in the first week, in the drizzle, by somebody who had arrived with one pair. The window The chapel glass at Weeping Bottom shows her holding up a pair of socks like a holy relic. They are dry. It is the only dry thing in any window in the Order. The glazier, a man from the coast called Ezra Mapp, put it in in 1746, two years after her death, and the Sisters paid him in soup, which he said was the best bargain he had ever made, and he had been paid in money. They are said to be her own socks, the spare pair, which she kept dry in a tin box under her bed for forty-two years against an emergency, and never needed, because she always had the other two. The tin is in the Sisterhouse. It is empty. The Prioress says that the socks are in the window, in a manner of speaking, and that it would be a very poor kind of order that went looking for them. Her death She died in the Sisterhouse on the eleventh of November 1744, at the age of eighty-five, having drunk a glass of water and sat down. The Sister who was with her, Sister Agnes Lark, asked her how she felt, and she said, "Better, thank you," which were her last words, and which the Order regards as the finest thing anybody has ever said on the subject, and puts on its cards. She is buried at the top of the valley path, where she first stood and looked down into it, which is the only place in Weeping Bottom that the fog does not reach. On a clear day, which there have been, you can see the sea from it, and the valley full of cloud below, like a bowl of soup. Afterwards The Order is one again, or two that agree; the Prioress says it is a question for a symposium, and that there will not be one. The pamphlet is back in its drawer. The Rule of Life is a by-law of the parish of Sump , and the parish walked it in the year 2000, down the street and back, and saw how it felt, and felt better. Mother Ursula's name is on the stone at the gate and in the chapel glass, and in Sump's Standing Orders, and on the card in every Sister's pocket, and on a plaque at Sallow Cross, put up in 1902 by the chandler's great-great-great-grandson, which reads: SHE WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE WATER. HE WAS WRONG ABOUT THE TRADE. See also The Order of Whatever Works Weeping Bottom Sump , which has her by law Merribell , the Order's only Sister for eleven miles of Thistlewick Prioress Aveline Stope

title: Mr Gammage
text: Mr Gammage For the village and its curse, now lifted, see Sump . For the Rule of Life under which he finally got to sleep, see Mother Ursula Pym . Obadiah Gammage Not asleep Known as Mr Gammage; the Eldest, of Sump, for the purposes of the Standing Orders Born Obadiah Gammage, 2 February 1926, Sump Sex Male Trying to get off since Tuesday Eyes Shut. Not asleep The riddle What is wet, and in the middle of the village, and we have not had any since 1794? Took the parish Six generations, that one Asleep, properly Once, in 2000, sitting up, against the wall, under a by-law Obadiah Gammage of Sump sat against a wall with his eyes shut and was not asleep, and had been trying to get off since Tuesday, which in Sump was a condition of the curse. In the year 2000, as the eldest, he spoke the parish's riddle, and the curse was lifted, and the parish adopted Mother Ursula Pym's Rule of Life as a by-law and walked it down the street and back, and at the end of it Mr Gammage was asleep, sitting up against the wall, properly, for the first time since Tuesday. Sump Sump was cursed in 1794, when the wasps got into the well and the Water Committee was wound up, and in 1795 the parish drafted Standing Orders for the Lifting of the Curse, six clauses, and filed them, and never used them, because a curse that has been properly drafted against is, the parish felt, more or less under control. Things used to be better. Nobody in Sump could say when, exactly, but there was a general sense of it. Mr Gammage was born into it, in 1926, and grew up, and worked as a hurdle-maker for fifty years, and married, and was widowed, and through all of it never once, he says, had a proper night's sleep, or a proper afternoon's, or got off at all, really, after the first ten minutes. It was the curse. Everybody in Sump knew it was the curse. It was the only thing in Sump everybody agreed on. The riddle In the year 2000 the parish, with a Chosen One present and Merribell of the Order of Whatever Works in attendance, followed the Standing Orders of 1795 in order. Clause five required the eldest to speak the riddle. Mr Gammage was the eldest. He opened one eye. "What's wet, and in the middle of the village, and we've not had any since 1794?" He shut it again. It had, he said, taken them six generations, that one. Then the curse was called by its true name, and Merribell let a coil of rope and a tin cup down the well, which she had in her bag, of course, and it came up full, clear and cold, and only very slightly wasp-flavoured. I asked him, afterwards, why the parish had taken six generations over a riddle whose answer was the well. He said that the riddle had been easy; it was the asking that had been hard; you could not ask a thing like that if you had not slept since Tuesday, and nobody in Sump had slept since Tuesday since 1794. Then he shut his eyes. I waited. He was asleep. - H.B. Abel Thrush Sump was the far end of Abel Thrush's road, and Mr Gammage told Piper Quill , for her elegy, that for forty years, every Tuesday, a bottle of Fenmarch water was left on their well, by Abel, and nobody drank it, because it was not Sump water, and Sump did not take charity. She put that in the elegy: He brought the water nobody would drink. Mr Gammage says that it is the best line in it, and that he drinks Fenmarch water now, out of respect, every Tuesday, and that it is very good water, and that they were fools. Afterwards He is seventy-six. He sleeps. He sleeps after lunch, and after tea, and in church, and once, in 2001, during the parish council's motion to put up a plaque about the lifting of the curse, which was carried without him. He says that he is catching up, and that he has two hundred and six years to catch up on, on behalf of the parish, and that he is doing his best. The plaque reads: SUMP. CURSED 1794. NOT, 2000. QUIET PLEASE. MR GAMMAGE IS ASLEEP. See also Sump Merribell , with the rope and the cup Piper Quill , for the elegy Mother Ursula Pym

title: Mr Kell
text: Mr Kell For the inn, its plates and its list, see Upper Clanging . For the one part of a boiler whose entire job is to give up before anything else does, see any boiler. Hector Kell "We are very proud of it." Known as Mr Kell Born Hector Kell, 28 August 1968, Upper Clanging , over the bar Sex Male Keeps The Safety Valve, since 1993, his mother's before him Beds Thirty crowns. You will be dry House rule IN THE EVENT OF PRESSURE, GO TO BED Things Not To Happen Again Sixty-three, framed. Sixty-four, pending Number sixty-three One very long word. Not said aloud Best china FOR WHEN SHE FLIES. Used once Has known somebody sleep through the six o'clock hooter Once Hector Kell keeps the Safety Valve, the inn at Upper Clanging , named for the one part of a boiler whose entire job is to give up before anything else does. They are very proud of it. A plate under the sign reads IN THE EVENT OF PRESSURE, GO TO BED, and a plate on the foot of every bed reads IN CASE OF EMERGENCY, LIE DOWN. Beds are thirty crowns. You will be dry, and up here that is worth thirty. The Valve He was born over the bar in 1968, and took the house over from his mother, Mrs Ada Kell, in 1993, when she retired to the chair by the fire, which she gave up in 1997 to Winnie Marsden , after a discussion. The inn has been the Kells' since 1841, when his great-great-grandfather, a boilerman, was blown clean through the foundry roof by an engine without one, and landed in the street unhurt, and went straight into the business of putting people up for the night, on the grounds that he had had enough excitement. "The Safety Valve. Named for the one part of a boiler whose entire job is to give up before anything else does. We are very proud of it." He is very proud of it. He says it in a voice of such quiet satisfaction that you come to see, by the second half, that it is a whole philosophy, and that in a town of engines the one thing nobody has ever taught a man is when to stop, and that the Kells have been teaching it for a hundred and sixty years, at thirty crowns a night. The list On the wall is a framed list in a very good hand, Things That Are Not To Happen Again, numbered to sixty-three. It was begun by his great-great-grandfather and every Kell since has added to it. I give the items Mr Kell will discuss: 7. THE GEESE. 19. NOT LIKE THAT. 31. HOT. 44. MR PADGETT'S HAT (AND MR PADGETT). 58. ANY OF IT. 61. OLLERENSHAW. He would not discuss sixty-one, beyond saying that it was before his time, that it was entered by his mother, and that it concerned a night in 1987 when Mr Ollerenshaw came in from the Smiths' Hall at Great Dunnage with a prize. He would not discuss sixty-three at all, and nobody in the room will say it aloud. There is a commentary on the list, much longer, which is not allowed out of the inn. There is a pencil mark on the wall under sixty-three, where sixty-four would go. I asked about it. Mr Kell said that it had been put there in the year 2000, the night the Forty-Eighth's company stayed, by his own hand, at about two in the morning, and that by breakfast he had decided that it was not, after all, a thing that must not happen again, and had not inked it, and had left the pencil, because he had not decided whether it should happen again either. He would not tell me what it was. I believe it concerned Mr Ollerenshaw and Mr Grumnir. - H.B. The hooter The works hooter goes at six every morning, and nobody in Upper Clanging has ever slept through it, because it is the works hooter, and they are a works town, and it gets them up the way the sun gets up other towns. In the year 2000, the morning after they arrived, the Forty-Eighth came down at a quarter to nine. "You slept through the six o'clock hooter. Nobody does that." He said it, I am told, with something like awe. He has said since that he has kept the inn for nine years and had a great many people sleep in it, and that every one of them got up at six, cursing, and that the Forty-Eighth is the only guest he has ever had who slept as if the bed were for sleeping in, and that he has been thinking about it since, and that he has been thinking that perhaps it is. Afterwards He is thirty-three. On the dresser is the best china, under a card, FOR WHEN SHE FLIES, which was dusted every week for as long as anybody can remember, and never used. It has now been used once, on the night the Two Hundred flew, for the whole of the Safety Valve, and Miss Hoyle , who came down, and drank one cup of tea out of it, standing up, and said that it would do, and went back up the hill. The china has been dusted since and put back, with a new card in front of the old one: FOR WHEN SHE FLIES AGAIN. See also Upper Clanging Winnie Marsden , by the fire Rivet Cotterill , half an hour Bryd Ollerenshaw , sixty-one The Flight of the Two Hundred

title: Mr Ottershaw
text: Mr Ottershaw "Ottershaw. Ninety in March. I did the animals." For the house and the gallery, see Fenmarch Hall . For the naturalist who found the joins, once shown, see Wren Halloway . Jonas Ottershaw Composer Known as Mr Ottershaw; Mr J. Ottershaw, on the write-up Born Jonas Ottershaw, 14 March 1910, at Fenmarch, in the gamekeeper's lodge Sex Male Ninety In March, 2000 Did The animals. 1930 to the present Preserved them? Anybody can preserve. A cook can preserve. He COMPOSED them Cases Eighty. Seventy-nine composed, each of two animals Joins found None, in seventy years. Then all of them, once shown Case forty Not examined Write-up Over his bench. Finest underlined twice Jonas Ottershaw has done the animals at Fenmarch Hall for seventy years, three generations of the Pemberton-Gores, and the family will tell you that every one of them is rare, and the family are right: there is one of each. He did not preserve them. Anybody can preserve. A cook can preserve. He COMPOSED them, and in seventy years nobody found a join, because not one of them ever looked. The lodge He was born in 1910 in the gamekeeper's lodge at Fenmarch, the gamekeeper's son, and learned the knife at nine, on a crow, which he says was a very good crow and that he was sorry about it. In 1930, at twenty, Sir Aldric the First asked him to set up a bear for the long gallery, and there was no bear, there being no bears in the county, and he said so, and was told that the family would like a bear, and that he was a clever lad. He had a black bear's front half, from a dealer, and a very large marsh crab, and he went into the stillroom for a fortnight. The Marsh Bear came out. It is bear to the waist and crab below. The family looked at it for some time and said that it was the rarest thing they had ever seen, and that he must go on. He went on. Seventy years. "Seventy years. Three generations. The family'll tell you every one of them's rare. The family are right. There's one of each." The join "Look at the shoulder. Now tell me where it stops." You look. You look for a long time, at feathers and then at scales, and you find nowhere at all where the one becomes the other. "Seventy years, and nobody's found a join. Not one of them ever looked." In the year 2000 the family engaged Miss Wren Halloway, a naturalist, a proper one, with the jars, to look at them properly, and to tell the household what they were. When she told Mr Ottershaw that she had been engaged to authenticate them, he put down the needle, took off his lenses and put them on again to see her better, and said that in seventy years nobody had ever ASKED. Then he took her down the gallery at a pace you would not expect of a man of ninety, and showed her every join. The Phoenix is a salamander and the top of something that fell in Cook's fire. The Horse is crab and unicorn, and the plate is blank because nobody liked to ask what it was. She found each join only when he had put his finger on it, and wrote it down, and her hand was not quite steady. The joins are the finest work I have seen. I have looked for joins all my life. I could not find these without being shown, and then I could not stop looking at them. Case forty: not examined. W. Halloway. He has a copy over his bench, with finest underlined twice. He went past case forty, Miss Halloway tells me, the way you go past a door you don't open. I have not asked him about it. I asked him only whether he would like anything added to this article, and he wrote back, in a very fine hand, that there were eighty-three now. - H.B. Afterwards He was ninety-two this month. He is still at his bench at the far end of the gallery, in green lenses, with a needle and a great deal of thread, and there are eighty-three cases now, and he says that he is working on the eighty-fourth, and that it is going to be his best, and that it is going to be of three animals, which he has never attempted, and that he will not say which three, and that Miss Halloway will be told, and will be asked to find the joins, and will not be shown first, this time, because he would like to see her try. See also Fenmarch Hall Wren Halloway The Fourth , who said COMPOSED was better than real

title: Mr Pilbeam
text: Mr Pilbeam "I was only passing." For the council at whose foot he sits, see Fairholme . For the eagle, there is no article, pending a decision. Everard Pilbeam Passing Known as Mr Pilbeam; "Mr Pilbeam (passing)", in the minutes Born Everard Pilbeam, 26 September 1970, at Coddington, a long way from Fairholme Sex Male Trade Traveller in buttons, 1990-1996 Was Only passing There was An eagle Rescued Princess Rosamund , from it, 1996 Share Pending. Twelve, if the eagle counts. The potted plant is holding it Deferred Eight times, as of 2002 May he go? Deferred Everard Pilbeam was only passing. There was an eagle. That was in 1996. He rescued Princess Rosamund of Fairholme from it, and the council of Fairholme has not decided whether the eagle counts, and he cannot go until it does. He sits at the foot of the council table, and looks at the door the way a man looks at a door he has been looking at for six years. Buttons He was born in 1970 at Coddington, which is a long way from Fairholme in every direction, and became a traveller in buttons at twenty, for a firm of button-makers, with a case of samples on cards, horn and bone and brass and mother-of-pearl, which he carried from town to town on foot. He was, he says, a very good traveller in buttons: he could tell a draper's taste at a glance, and he never once oversold, and he was liked. He has the case still, under his chair at the council table. He has not opened it since 1996. The eagle In the spring of 1996 he was walking through Fairholme on the road east, only passing, when an eagle came down out of the sky on the palace and went up again with the Princess in its talons, by the shoulders of her cloak, which was, he learned afterwards, the one she now keeps labelled EAGLE. It went up the hill, struggling, because she had the bag. He ran after it. He says he does not know why. He says he had never run after anything in his life except a coach. The eagle came down on the ridge to rest, being out of breath, and he came up behind it and hit it with the case of samples, which is very heavy, and it let go and went off over the hill in a temper, and the Princess sat up, and thanked him, and asked him to carry the bag, and he walked her home. "I was only passing. There was an eagle. That was four years ago. They haven't decided if the eagle counts. I can't go till they decide if the eagle counts." The question The Palace does not count the eagle. An eagle is not a kidnapper; it is weather, or an animal, or an act of God, the council's lawyers are divided. If it does not count, he is not a rescuer, and has no share, and may go. If it counts, he holds share twelve, a two-thousand-and-forty-eighth of the kingdom, and must stay to be minuted. Until the council decides, he is neither, and may not go, because a man who might be a shareholder cannot leave the kingdom without notice, under the articles, and he cannot give notice of a share he may not hold. The minutes have deferred it eight times. Item five, at every meeting: The eagle. Whether Mr Pilbeam, who rescued Her Highness from the eagle, therefore holds a share. Deferred. Mr Pilbeam asks whether he may go. Deferred. The share is being held for him in the meantime by a potted plant by the wall, with a flag in it, SHARE TWELVE. I have had the minutes of every meeting since 2000 from Mr Pilbeam, who writes, in a very neat hand, and encloses a button with each letter, as a matter of habit, which he apologises for. I have nineteen buttons. They are very good buttons. The King has asked me to say that Mr Pilbeam is a great comfort to have about the place, and Princess Rosamund has asked me to say that the eagle counts, and that she has a cloak to prove it. Mr Pilbeam has asked me to say nothing either way, in case it prejudices item five. - H.B. Afterwards He is thirty-one. He still sits at the foot of the table. He has, since 2000, been made clerk to the council, unpaid, because he was there, and because he writes such a neat hand, and he takes the minutes now, and has had to minute his own deferral four times, and says that it does not get easier. On the last occasion he wrote Mr Pilbeam asks whether he may go, and then sat for a moment, and then, very small, in the margin, He does not, on reflection, particularly mind. The council has not noticed. I have. See also Princess Rosamund King Aldous Fairholme

title: Mr Tibbs
text: Mr Tibbs "Tibbs. Wharfinger. Goods in bond. Nothing out without the ticket, and the duty, and me." For the Bonded Warehouse and its bonds, see Great Dunnage . For Bond No. 1, see Nix , as much as she will allow. Barnabas Tibbs Nothing out without the ticket Known as Mr Tibbs; the wharfinger Born Barnabas Tibbs, 30 January 1934, Great Dunnage , on the quay Sex Male Wharfinger The Bonded Warehouse, since 1962 Rule Nothing out without the ticket, and the duty, and him Bond No. 1 One coat. Eleven years. Rent by post, never late, no name Asked whose Never. Not his place Wrote in the margin 'I shall return for it when I am somebody' Bond No. 40 A cabbage, 1802. Not checked Misses The rent, a little, every quarter day Barnabas Tibbs is the wharfinger of the Bonded Warehouse on the quay at Great Dunnage , in half-rimmed spectacles, and nothing comes out without the ticket, and the duty, and him. For eleven years he kept a locked wardrobe as Bond No. 1, ONE COAT, and the rent came by post every quarter, never late, no name, and he never asked whose it was, because it was not his place. It was in bond. It was safe. That is all a thing wants. The quay He was born in 1934 in a house on the quay, the son of a lighterman, and has lived within sight of the warehouse doors his whole life. He went into the warehouse as a boy, in 1948, and became wharfinger in 1962, and says that in forty years he has never once let a thing out without the ticket, and the duty, and himself, and that this has made him unpopular with merchants, the Corporation, the Iron Company, and on one occasion a duke, and that he sleeps very well. The bonds are numbered, and are a history of the town in themselves, and he knows every one by heart. No. 2, one statue of the First Mayor, actual size, duty on the hat. No. 7, ten thousand buttons, all different, declared as one button, repeated. No. 11, fog, one barrel, from Nether Sopping , duty paid in advance by Nether Sopping, to be rid of it. No. 31, rain, one barrel, returned by Upper Clanging as second-hand. No. 40, one cabbage, very large, for the show. The show was in 1802. Nobody has been brave enough to check on the cabbage, and he includes himself. Bond No. 1 "A coat. Bond number one. Eleven years. Rent comes by post every quarter, never late. No name. Just the money, and 'Bond No. 1'. Never asked, sir. Not my place. It's in bond. It's safe. That's all a thing wants." In 1989 a girl of fifteen came into the warehouse with a coat that was too big for her, and stood on a crate, and made a speech, and paid the first quarter's rent, and went out, and did not come back. Mr Tibbs wrote in the margin of the Bond Book what she had said: I shall return for it when I am somebody. He says that it was a good speech, and that he has had a great many speeches made to him in the warehouse, mostly by merchants about duty, and that it was the only one he ever wrote down. In the year 2000 she came back, by the long way round, with the Forty-Eighth's company. He knew her at once. "Ah. The party of the second part. Eleven years. You stood on that crate, there, and made a speech. 'I shall return for it when I am somebody.' I wrote it in the margin. It was a good speech. And then the rent came by post every quarter for eleven years, never late, no name." He opened the wardrobe. It fitted. "No duty owing. Rent paid to date. Always was." He asked her, then, whose it was. It is the only time in forty years he has asked anybody that, and he says that it was not his place, and that he could not help it, and that he has never regretted it. What she told him is in the Bond Book's first entry, which has a name now, and in her article, as much as she will allow, and not here. - H.B. Afterwards He is sixty-eight. The rent has stopped coming. He says that he misses it, a little, every quarter day, and that he goes down to the post on quarter days anyway, out of habit, and comes back without anything, and that it is the only thing in forty years he has ever missed that was not in bond. Since 2000 he has also held Bond No. 1788, for the Mayor, money, a little, provenance none whatever, and the Corporation pays the rent on it, by post, every quarter, and he says that it is not the same. See also Nix , the party of the second part Great Dunnage Mayor Gristwood

title: Mr Tweddle
text: Mr Tweddle "Tweddle. Birdcalls. I've been practising since Easter." For the Contest he won, see Mrs Harbottle , who chaired it. For the entrant he beat by one point, see Piper Quill , who took it very well. Wilfred Tweddle The thrush goes down very well Known as Mr Tweddle; Birdsong (Open) Born Wilfred Tweddle, 1 April 1939, Great Dunnage , at the Wire Works Sex Male Trade Wire-drawer, the Wire Works, 1953-1999. Retired Repertoire A nightingale; a curlew; a thrush that's lost its keys Practising since Easter The Contest at the Sign of the Bell First, 2000, by one point From Miss Quayle A three. The room gasped The keys Found, all round the room Wilfred Tweddle of Great Dunnage does birdcalls: a nightingale, a curlew, and a thrush that has lost its keys, which goes down very well. In the year 2000 he entered the Contest at the Sign of the Bell, Birdsong (Open), and the thrush went looking for its keys all round the room and found them, and drew a three from Miss Quayle, at which the room gasped, and he won, by one point, over Piper Quill. The Wire Works He was born in 1939 at the Wire Works, where his father drew wire, and drew wire there himself for forty-six years, from fourteen. The Wire Works is the loudest of the nine, and he says that he started doing birds to have something in his head that was not the drawing-bench, and that by the time he was twenty he could do any bird in the valley, and that the only one he could not do was a thrush, because a thrush never sings the same thing twice, and he could not settle on one. He retired in 1999 and started practising for the Contest, which he had meant to enter every year for forty years and never had, because there was always the bench. "Tweddle. Birdcalls. I've been practising since Easter. I do a nightingale, a curlew, and a thrush that's lost its keys. The thrush goes down very well." The thrush The thrush that has lost its keys was, he says, an accident. He was practising the thrush in his kitchen at Easter, and could not settle on what it was singing, and it went up and down, looking for something, and his wife said, from the scullery, It sounds as if it's lost its keys, and he said that it had, and went on, and the thrush looked under things, and in pockets, and behind the clock, and found them, and he has done it that way since. At the Contest he did the nightingale, which got sevens, and the curlew, which got sevens, and then the thrush, which went all round the room looking for its keys, and under the judges' table, and in Mr Ambler's hat, and found them, at the end, in the last place you would look, and Miss Quayle, who gives everything a two, gave it a three. The room gasped. I asked Miss Quill whether she minded coming second to a thrush. She said that it was a very good thrush, and that she had been beaten by better songs and worse birds, and that she had written him a verse, which is in her notebooks, and that it rhymes keys with please , which is not her best, but was what the thrush would have wanted. - H.B. Afterwards He is sixty-two. The cup is on his mantelpiece, beside his wife's clock. He has been asked to judge, and declined, and asked to enter again, and declined, on the grounds that the thrush has found its keys now, and that he would have to lose them again, and that it would not be the same. He still does the thrush in the kitchen, for his wife, on Sundays, and it still loses its keys every time, and finds them, and she still says, from the scullery, They're behind the clock, and they always are. See also Mrs Harbottle Piper Quill Great Dunnage

title: Mrs Ash
text: Mrs Ash "Mind the step. It's new. It's all new." For her boy, see Corvin Ash , who is very deep. For the village that is fine, see Ashcombe . Mrs Ash Knitting something long Known as Mrs Ash; Hon. Sec., the Flood Dinner Committee Born Margaret, 20 November 1947, in old Ashcombe, under what is now the lake. Her maiden name went under with it, and she has asked me to leave it there Sex Female Surname Ash, since about 1990, to save the postman Son Corvin, born 1970 Wrote to him Wednesdays and Saturdays, for eleven years, at the Slain Wyvern He wrote back Once, to the Ruins of Ashcombe. The Ruins wrote back Kitchen New. You can see every potato Scarf Most of the way down the aisle. Yellow. The wrong colour for everything he owns Mrs Ash of Ashcombe has a kitchen so new the paint still smells of it, with a big window over the lake under which the old village is, and she knits something long and does not stop. She is the mother of Corvin Ash, who sat in one corner of the Slain Wyvern for eleven years as the rival of a great hero, and to whom she wrote twice a week for all eleven of them. He is very deep, her boy. She thought he would like it if the Ruins wrote back. He did. The old village She was born in 1947 in the old Ashcombe, in the valley, in a house on the high street with a kitchen so dark you could not see your potatoes, and married there, and had her boy there, in 1970, and measured him on the kitchen wall, in pencil, every birthday that was a round number or felt like one. In 1989, when he was nineteen, he went off to sit in the corner of the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping , and Ashcombe flooded, in his absence, and was a tremendous success: everybody out by dinner, everybody dry by tea, and not so much as a hen lost. They have the Roll. The village was moved up the hill. The new houses have yellow roofs. She has a new kitchen. "Mind the step. It's new. It's all new. Isn't it lovely? The old kitchen was DARK; you couldn't see your potatoes. I can see every potato I own." The name Her boy wrote to say that he had taken the name Ash, after the village, in its memory. She thought, well, that's nice, and took it as well, to save the postman, and now they are all Ashes, and the post comes lovely. I asked her what the old name had been. She said that it was under the lake with the old kitchen, and that she had not been very fond of either, and that she was not going to dredge it up, and laughed, and went on knitting. The letters She wrote to him at the Slain Wyvern every Wednesday and Saturday for eleven years, about the village, the drains, the Flood Dinner, and his room, and he wrote back once, to the Ruins of Ashcombe, to the old address, under the water. The Ruins wrote back. She has never said who wrote it, and she has never needed to. His room upstairs is bigger now, and has the light, and is a study at the minute, where the papers of the Flood Dinner Committee are kept. Up the wall by the window are pencil marks with ages: C., 6; C., 9; C., 12; C., 16; C., 19. The old ones went under with the old wall. These were put back from memory, and every one of them is a little taller than a boy would have been, and the last is exactly the top of his head. She drew where he would be. I have stood in that room. The marks are on the wall beside the window, and I measured the last one against my own notes on him, and it is exactly right, to the inch, and she had not seen him for eleven years when she drew it. I asked her how she had known. She said that she had been knitting for him the whole time, and you get to know the length. - H.B. The scarf In the year 2000 her boy came home, and spoke at the Flood Dinner, and brought the name back, and the toast was to the water, which was very good about it. In the front row Mrs Ash cast off the last stitch, and stood, and held up a scarf that went most of the way down the aisle, bright yellow, the yellow of the new roofs, which is the wrong colour for everything Corvin owns. If she had done it in black, nobody would ever see him in it. He wears it everywhere. Afterwards She is fifty-four, and Hon. Sec. of the Flood Dinner Committee, and has already started the next one, which is not a scarf, and which she will not describe, except to say that it is long, and that it is for somebody who is coming up the road to see the chair, and that she does not know who yet, and that she is knitting it to the length anyway, because you get to know. See also Corvin Ash Hubert Weir , who has kindly offered Ashcombe The Day of the Water

title: Mrs Emberthwaite
text: Mrs Emberthwaite "Come in, come in, mind the gold, it gets everywhere." For the kingdom at the foot of her hill, see Fairholme . She is not in the Bestiary , at her own request, over a hand of whist. Mrs Emberthwaite Reading spectacles, on a chain Known as Mrs Emberthwaite; "dear", to herself, when she has lost a trick, which is rare Born Hatched 9 May 1930, in the hills above Fairholme, on a sunny ledge, the only egg of the clutch, which her mother said was plenty Sex Female Age Seventy-two this year, by Rosamund 's reckoning Married Mr Emberthwaite, 1951. He did the roaring, mostly Widowed 1984 Retired She has had a letter Hoard Dusted every morning, with a feather Whist Thursdays. All welcome. Has not lost to Rosamund yet Cheats Rosamund says so. The deck is fine. It is you Sponge Lovely Mrs Emberthwaite is a dragon, very large and very red, who lives in a cave on the hill above Fairholme , wears reading spectacles on a chain, and plays whist on Thursdays with Princess Rosamund, who walks up with a cake tin. She is retired. She has had a letter. The stone tablet by her door says PLEASE WIPE YOUR FEET. NO RESCUES, and under it, in chalk, WHIST THURSDAYS. ALL WELCOME. The hill She was hatched in 1930 on a sunny ledge in the hills above Fairholme, an only egg, and grew up in the cave she lives in now, which was her mother's. She says that she was always more of an indoor dragon: that she liked a book, and a fire, and a hand of cards, and that she never once saw the point of flying anywhere you could not be home from by tea. She married in 1951. Mr Emberthwaite was from the far side of the marshes, and was a great deal of dragon, and did the roaring, mostly, on her behalf, at knights, and was very good at it, and she says that he was the gentlest creature she ever knew, and that the roaring was a kind of courtesy, so that nobody coming up the hill should be disappointed. "That's Mr Emberthwaite's. He did the roaring, mostly. I was always more of an indoor dragon." His chair is drawn up to the card table, much sat in, once, with his pipe on the seat. He died in 1984. She has not moved the chair. There is a tapestry in the cave of two dragons asleep in the sun on a hillside, hung where the light catches it in the afternoon. I asked whether it was anybody. She said it was a very good likeness, and dealt. The letter When he died the knights went on coming up the hill, to slay the dragon, because that is what knights do. She kept a pot of umbrellas by the door for the ones who came in the rain, so that they at least went home dry, and gave them tea, and they went home. They wrote to her afterwards, and she has the letters in a bound volume: every one begins FOUL BEAST and ends YOURS FAITHFULLY. In 1990 she wrote to the Heroes' Guild to say that she was retired. The Guild wrote back to confirm it. She has had a letter. "You're not a hero, are you, dear? Only I'm retired. I've had a letter." Rosamund In 1999 two men from beyond the marshes carried Princess Rosamund up the hill in the rain, having been told that dragons keep princesses, and left her at the door, and ran. Mrs Emberthwaite opened it. (That evening, after a rubber, the Princess walked down again with a tin of cake, and Mr and Mrs Budge, who were mucking out, walked her the rest of the way, and took the half, and are the eleventh shareholders; see Fairholme .) "The first time they brought her up here, she had a bag packed and a card about her diet. I made up the spare room. I'd not had company in years." "Now she walks up on Thursdays, on her own two feet, with a cake tin. The heroes are furious." The spare room is at the end of a short passage: a bed with clean sheets, a washstand, a rag rug, and curtains hung over no window at all, because a room ought to have curtains. The card on the pillow reads ROSAMUND - THURSDAYS. AIRED WEDNESDAYS. NO EELS IN THE HOUSE. TEA AT FOUR, NOT STEWED. Rosamund has never stayed. There is a hot-water bottle in the bed every Thursday all the same, and it is warm. Whist "Passing! Lovely. Do you play whist?" She will win, by a margin that makes you check the deck. The deck is fine. "Don't feel bad, dear. Rosamund hasn't beaten me yet either." The stakes are a copper a hand, from a heap with a flag in it, and Rosamund is, by the score pad, ruthless, and is winning by a mile on coppers and has never once won a rubber, which Rosamund says is mathematically impossible and Mrs Emberthwaite says is whist. Her book of card games for two has TWO crossed out, and AND ON THURSDAYS, THREE written in. The third is whoever comes up the hill. I played, on a Thursday in the autumn of 2001, by invitation, with the Princess as my partner. We lost every rubber. I checked the deck. It was fine. I said so. Mrs Emberthwaite said, "It's you, dear," quite kindly, and put the kettle on, and the cup she gave me had a small scorch mark on the rim, from her cold of 1974, and I have never been happier to lose at anything. Miss Halloway, who has played her too, asked me to say that Mrs Emberthwaite is not in the Bestiary at Mrs Emberthwaite's own request, which Miss Halloway thinks is very proper, and that Miss Halloway lost that hand as well. - H.B. Afterwards She is seventy-two, by Rosamund's reckoning, which she says is very flattering and quite wrong, and will not correct. The Thursdays go on. The heroes are still furious, and still come up the hill, now and then, in the rain, and are given an umbrella and tea, and are asked whether they play whist, and most of them stay for a rubber, and lose, and go home and write FOUL BEAST at the top of a very long and complimentary letter. The cuckoo in the clock is a very small dragon that comes out on the hour and sneezes. It did that for Mr Emberthwaite too. She says it is a family trait. See also Princess Rosamund Fairholme Wren Halloway , who lost the hand A Glossary of Cliches , for the dragon who is not what you were told

title: Mrs Harbottle
text: Mrs Harbottle "We are practising." For the Bell and its Contest, see Great Dunnage . For the entrant who came second by one point, see Piper Quill . For the thrush that came first, see Mr Tweddle . Mrs Harbottle Your entrance was a five Known as Mrs Harbottle; the Chair Born Clementine Harbottle, née Joy, 17 August 1971, at the Bell, Great Dunnage , during a Contest, which her mother marked Sex Female Chairs The panel for the Contest at the Sign of the Bell, since 1996 The panel Herself; Mr Ambler, who gives everything a nine; Miss Quayle, who gives everything a two. It averages out Practises on Everything The fire A six The door A four. It creaks in the wrong key Your entrance A five. Your second entrance, a five Gave herself A seven, on her wedding day. She has asked me to say it was a strong seven Mrs Harbottle , in gold lace, chairs the panel for the Contest at the Sign of the Bell in Great Dunnage , and the panel practises on everything between contests, because the Contest is always tonight and has simply not had the entries. The fire was a six. The door was a four, because it creaks in the wrong key. Your entrance was a five. Your second entrance, a five. The panel She was born at the Bell in 1971, during a Contest, which her mother, who chaired the panel before her, marked. It got an eight. She was brought up at the judges' table, and was scoring the soup by six, and was co-opted to the panel at eighteen, and has chaired it since her mother retired in 1996. She married Mr Harbottle, a brass-founder, in 1994, and the panel gave the service a seven, and the cake a nine, and Mr Harbottle a six, which she says he took extremely well, and which she has since revised upwards, by private ballot, several times. "Harbottle. I chair the panel for the Contest at the Sign of the Bell. We are practising. Everything. The fire was a six. The door was a four; it creaks in the wrong key." "Mr Ambler gives everything a nine. Mr Ambler cannot hear. We have never had the heart. It averages out. Miss Quayle gives everything a two." The Contest The Contest at the Sign of the Bell is always tonight. In the year 2000 it had four entries, for the first time in some years: Mr Septimus Dray , on the serpent, for eleven minutes; Miss Lettice Moon , Ballad (Sad), in which everybody dies, including the narrator, who comes back for the chorus; Mr Tweddle, Birdsong (Open); and Piper Quill, Ballad (Not Sad), which nobody had ever entered. Mr Tweddle's thrush that had lost its keys drew a three from Miss Quayle, which had never happened, and the room gasped. Miss Quill came second, by one point, to the thrush. Mrs Harbottle announced the result standing, in gold lace, and says that it was the best Contest in the history of the Bell, and that she gave it, privately, a nine, which she has never given anything, and that she has told nobody but me. She gave this article, in draft, a six. She said that it was well constructed, and accurate, and that its second paragraph creaked in the wrong key. I have not been able to find where. She says that I would not, and that that is why she is on the panel and I am not. - H.B. Afterwards She is thirty. The Bell has had more entries since 2000 than in the twenty years before it, because people walking up to see Grimspite 's chair stop on the way, and because Piper Quill wrote about the Contest. Mr Ambler still gives everything a nine. Miss Quayle has given two threes since, and the room gasped both times. The fire is still a six. The door has been oiled, and is now a five, and Mrs Harbottle says that she preferred it before, because a four was at least something. See also Mr Tweddle Piper Quill Great Dunnage

title: Mrs Thistle
text: Mrs Thistle "You've been Chosen." For her son, see Bram Thistle . For the village, see Thistlewick . For the pie, there is no article. It was a good pie, that. Mrs Thistle "I know, love." Known as Mrs Thistle; Mother, to her son; "Bram's mum", to the whole of the Forty-Eighth's company, who were all fed Born Annie Brook, 6 June 1957, at the mill below Thistlewick Sex Female Married Will Thistle, turnip farmer, 1977 Son Bram, born 1979 Is Alive, well, and has read the version that says otherwise Makes A good pie. She asked me to put that in Pie dish Went in 1989. Came back in 2000. She never missed it Sword over the grate Unbearable about it, for a hundred years Good shirt Ironed Tuesday Mrs Thistle is the mother of Bram Thistle, the Forty-Eighth Chosen One, and was the one who woke him on the morning he was chosen, and told him, and sent him to see the Elder, and told him to take the sword off the wall, which had been up there a hundred years waiting for exactly this, and frankly had been unbearable about it. She is alive, and well, and has read the version of events in circulation that says otherwise. She makes a good pie. The mill She was born Annie Brook in 1957 at the mill below Thistlewick, and married Will Thistle, who farmed the Thistle ground, in 1977, and their son was born two springs later, in the house, in the room under the sword. Of Mr Thistle she would say only that he was a good man with turnips, and that he is not in the house, and that that is enough to say about him in an encyclopedia, and that the rest is hers. I asked in the village, where everybody had an answer and no two of them were the same, and I have respected hers rather than theirs. She has farmed the ground with her son since, and kept the house, and the chair that was a turnip, which she uses for the good visitors. I have sat on it. The morning "Bram. There are eleven people outside and one of them has a scroll." "You've been Chosen." "I know, love. Go and see the Elder. Then take the sword off the wall. It's been up there a hundred years waiting for exactly this, and frankly it has been unbearable about it." I asked her how she had known what to say. She said that every mother in Thistlewick knows what to say, because every mother in Thistlewick has a sword over the grate and has been told what it is for, and has looked at it every day, and has hoped that it would go on hanging there, and has had the words ready anyway. She said that she had had them ready since he was born, and that she had hoped never to need them, and that when she did, they came out in the right order, and that she was very proud of that, and then she went and made a pie. She asked me, when I first wrote to her, to correct one version in circulation which has it that the Forty-Eighth's mother was dead, as heroes' mothers generally are. She is not. She has read it. She asked me to put in that she makes a good pie. She does. I have had three slices of it, over two visits, and I would like to put that in as well. - H.B. The pie dish In 1989 her pie dish went from the kitchen windowsill, where it had been put to cool. She did not miss it, she says, because she had another, and it was a long time before she noticed. In the year 2000 it came back. It was handed to her, washed, with a label, by a young woman who said that she had taken it, at fifteen, and had kept it eleven years, and had never sold it. "That's not mine. ...So it is. I never missed it." And then, after a while: "Was the pie any good?" She was told that it had been. "It was a good pie, that," she said, and put the kettle on. The letter The morning after the ending, there was a letter on the mat from the Committee, which she did not open. "Morning, love. There's a letter come. It's on the mat. It's from the Committee. I haven't opened it. I've looked at it." It was clause nineteen, and a pension, and the key to a cottage by the sea at Nether Sopping . "A cottage! By the sea!" And then, being his mother: "You'll want your good shirt. I ironed it Tuesday." Afterwards She is forty-four. Her son is home, and farming, and has the cottage at Nether Sopping for when he comes south, which is about monthly. She has been down to see it once. She says that it is a very nice cottage, and that the sea is very large, and that she was glad to get home. The sword is not over the grate now. There is a clean rectangle of wall where it used to be, and she has not painted over it, and she says that she is not going to, and that it is the best thing that has ever been on that wall. See also Bram Thistle The Turnip , all four kinds Thistlewick Nix , and the pie dish

title: Mrs Tunnicliffe
text: Mrs Tunnicliffe "Parish Rooms. Births, deaths, and whatever else nobody else will take on." For the town, see Upper Clanging . For her clerk, who is now her clerk, see Gudgeon Cotterill . Mrs Tunnicliffe "What there is, is behind me." Known as Mrs Tunnicliffe; "the Rooms", by the town, as in "ask the Rooms" Born Edna Hargreaves, 11 June 1919, Upper Clanging Sex Female Class of 'Nineteen No. Born in June Married Walter Tunnicliffe, verger, 1942; widowed 1988 Keeps The register, the census, the counter, the tea, the urn, the hymn board, and everything else (see above) Urns Three: a funeral, a wedding, the fete Clerks Eleven. The best hand was the eleventh Since 2001 The clerk's assistant, at her own request, for the urns Mrs Tunnicliffe has kept the Parish Rooms at Upper Clanging since 1951: births, deaths, and whatever else nobody else will take on. She has the register, the census and the counter, and also the tea, the urn and the hymn board, and the rota says so, and under it, EVERYTHING ELSE - SEE ABOVE. She was born in the same year as the Class of 'Nineteen, in June, and is not invited to the dinner, and has kept the dates of every one of them for fifty years. June She was born Edna Hargreaves on the eleventh of June 1919, which is to say four months before the Cold Winter 's children, and she has never been allowed to forget it, and has never once complained of it. "Class of 'Nineteen. The Cold Winter lot. Foundry was banked down six weeks that January. No work. No heat in the whole town but what was in the houses. Two hundred and forty of them. All born the same autumn, near enough." "They have a dinner every year. I am not invited. I was born in June." She says it as a matter of record, which it is. She has the record. I asked her whether she minded. She said that she had been at school with every one of them, in the same two rooms, and had sat at the end of the alphabet, being an H among the Class's A to Zs, at a desk of her own by the stove, and that she had been the only one of them warm all that first winter, and that she had always thought that was fair. The Rooms She went to the Parish Rooms as the clerk's girl in 1934, at fifteen, and became the clerk in 1951. She married Walter Tunnicliffe, the verger, in 1942, and he did the hymn board until he died, in 1988, and then she did it. The three urns are hers: one for a funeral, one for a wedding and one for the fete, the three sizes of parish emergency, and every one of them is on a Saturday. "Parish Rooms. Births, deaths, and whatever else nobody else will take on. I have the register, the census, and the counter." Asked what else there was, she said: "What there is, is behind me." It was. It was everything. The register lies open at OCCUPATION, and every line for eighty years reads AT THE WORKS, in one hand or another, and in fifty years of the hand being hers she has never once written anything else, because nobody in Upper Clanging has ever been anything else, except the verger, who was AT THE WORKS (VERGER), which she says was a stretch, and which the vicar let go. - H.B. Ten clerks, and an eleventh She has had, she says, eleven clerks in the Rooms since 1951. Ten of them went to the works, which is where everybody goes. The eleventh was Gudgeon Cotterill, in 1995, at fifteen, to help with the census, and Mrs Tunnicliffe says that she knew on the first afternoon, from the way the girl ruled a line, that this was the best hand she had ever had, and has said so since to anybody who would listen, including Gudgeon, who says that she has heard it, and that it does not get any less nice. In 2001, at eighty-one, Mrs Tunnicliffe went to the parish council and asked to be made the clerk's assistant, so that Gudgeon could be the clerk, and so that she herself could do the urns, which she said was all she had ever really wanted to do, and the only part of the job nobody had ever let her do properly, because there was always the register. The council agreed. Gudgeon is the clerk. Mrs Tunnicliffe does the urns. Afterwards She is eighty-two. She is at the Rooms every morning at eight, before Gudgeon, to fill the urns, and she says that she has made, since 2001, the best tea of her life, and that it was the register all along that was spoiling it. She has still not been invited to the dinner. Winnie Marsden has, this winter, asked her whether she would like to come and help with the urns on the second Saturday. Mrs Tunnicliffe said that she would be delighted. There is no seat for her on the plan. She says that she would not want one. She will be at the urn, and at the urn, she says, she has always been invited everywhere. See also Gudgeon Cotterill Winnie Marsden Upper Clanging The Cold Winter

title: Nabb
text: Nabb For the man on the log, see Godfrey Stopford , the Forty-Sixth. For the other half of the correspondence, see Tolly , who does the stamps. Nabb "There isn't more." Known as Nabb, of the Forty-Sixth Born 14 October 1960, Nether Sopping Sex Female Party The Forty-Sixth's, 1980; cook Got as far as The Gloamwood , the first path, about half way Said Fair Writes Every month, in the round hand Has had back Nothing, which is the answer Thinks Tolly does not know That the letters are unanswered Tolly knows Yes Nabb was the cook in the Forty-Sixth's party, in 1980, and was there when he stopped on the path in the Gloamwood and said that the woods were enough, and looked at the others, and said: fair. She has written to him every month since, in the round hand, and drinks at the Slain Wyvern with Tolly, who writes in the narrow one, and gave the Forty-Eighth the shortest of the six tales in my history, which is also the only one with nothing missing from it. The whole story "He stopped. Just - stopped, on the path, and said the woods were enough. And we looked at each other, and we said: fair." "That's the whole story. Everyone wants there to be more. There isn't more. We were tired, and he said the woods were enough, and he was right, and we went home." I have heard her tell it eleven times, to eleven people, and it has never been a word longer, and it has never been a word shorter. In a tavern full of men who have improved their stories every year for forty years, this is a kind of genius, and I do not think anybody in the Wyvern but me has noticed it. She has not noticed it either. The cooking Nabb was taken on by the Forty-Sixth's party as the cook, in the spring of 1980, having cooked at the harbour eating house since leaving school and wanting, she says, to see whether food tasted any different further north. She never found out. The party got as far as the Gloamwood, and stopped, and came home, and she went back to the eating house on the Monday and has been there since. The Wyvern says that the eating house does the best fish on the coast, and that it is because she has had a great deal of time to think about it. The letters "We write. Every month, the both of us. He's never once written back. He reads them, though. The man who collects the post says so." "Post goes out Thursdays. Tolly does the stamps. It's something to do." That is the whole of what she says about the letters, and it is meant to sound like nothing. According to Tolly, Nabb has thought for eleven years that Tolly does not know the letters go unanswered, and Tolly has never let on. According to the Forty-Sixth, Nabb does not know that reading them is the answer, and Tolly does. I have the three accounts. I am not going to try to reconcile them, because they do not need reconciling; they are three people being kind to each other at forty miles' distance and twenty-two years, and the post goes out on Thursdays. I asked Nabb what goes into a letter every month for twenty-two years to a man who does not write back. She said, the weather, and what was on at the eating house, and who had come into the Wyvern, and how the fish were. I said that seemed a great deal to tell somebody who never answered. She looked at me for some time and then said that it was not a great deal at all, if you thought about it, and that I should think about it, and went to get the drinks. - H.B. Afterwards Nabb still writes every month, and so does Tolly, and she still does the stamps. The month the news came south that the Forty-Eighth had done what forty-seven had not, Nabb's letter ran to four sides, which is three more than usual, and Tolly says it was mostly about the fish, and that it was the best letter Nabb had ever written. See also Godfrey Stopford Tolly The Slain Wyvern The Gloamwood

title: Nib
text: Nib "I am the apprentice. There has been an apprentice here since eighteen oh four." For the works, see The Hoyle Works , in Miss Hoyle's memorandum. For Miss Hoyle, who wants the small can, see Ott Hoyle . Nib The fortieth Known as Nib; the Fortieth; "the apprentice", by Miss Hoyle, in every memorandum Born 22 January 1986, Upper Clanging , on Furnace Row Sex Female Apprenticed The Hoyle Works, 1998. The fortieth since 1804 The numbering Is not a joke. Nib has decided to believe so Cans One. There has only ever been the big can Has asked whether they will manage it Nine times. It is not a question with an answer Stands On the NO side of the line Sweepstake Had Thursday; lost Nib is the fortieth apprentice of the Hoyle Works at Upper Clanging, which has had an apprentice since 1804, numbered. Miss Hoyle says the numbering is not a joke, and Nib has decided to believe her. Nib has asked Miss Hoyle nine times whether they are going to manage it, and has been told nine times that it is not a question with an answer: it is a question with a schedule. In the year 2000 they managed it. The fortieth Nib was born on Furnace Row in 1986 and she went to the works at twelve, in 1998, which is the age at which the Hoyle Works has always taken its apprentice, because the apprentice has to fit in the places the works has. The works has a list of every apprentice since 1804, on a board in the drawing office, and her name is at the bottom, number forty, with a space under it. "I am the apprentice. There has been an apprentice here since eighteen oh four. We are numbered. I am the fortieth. Miss Hoyle says the numbering is not a joke, and I have decided to believe her." There is a line painted on the floor of the shed. On one side of it is written YES and on the other NO, and the works stands on whichever side it believes about the current attempt. Miss Hoyle stands on neither; she stands on the line, with a drawing. Nib always stands on the NO side. I asked her why. She said that somebody has to, so that when it flies there is somebody to be surprised, and that a works with nobody surprised in it is a works that has stopped trying hard enough. The can "She will want the small can. She always wants the small can." Every day for two years Miss Hoyle asked for the small can, and every day Nib brought her the big one, and she took it without comment. In the year 2000 it was established, by Nix , who was looking for things that had gone missing, that there is only one can, and that there has only ever been the big can. "She wants the small can every day," said Nib. "I give her the big can every day. I thought it was part of the numbering. I have decided to believe so."
