The sweep At the dinner hour the shift is Miss Hoyle, and Nib, and Tappet Cotterill , which at the Hoyle Works is all of it, and in the year 2000 Mrs Cotterill came up at the dinner hour to read out her son's letters from the road. The works ran a sweep, all month, on what the last letter would say. Nib had Thursday. Tappet had there is no dragon. There was no dragon. Nib paid, and she was not happy about it. A note on the apprentice Contributed by O. Hoyle, Works Manager Mr Bellwether has asked me for a line on the apprentice, and has asked me, before writing his own, whether she is she. She is. That is correct procedure: ask, then write it down. He tells me he went two volumes without asking anybody anything of the kind, which is not correct procedure, and which he has since put right, in this volume, throughout. I have checked a sample. It will do. She asked me nine times whether we were going to manage it. I told her nine times that it was not a question with an answer. On the tenth occasion she did not ask. She was on the gantry when it went, and she was on the NO side of the line, as instructed by herself, and she said, "Oh," and that was the correct response, and I have entered it. The can. I did know. I have always known. The small can was lost in 1981 by the thirty-seventh. I ask for it every day so that the apprentice will bring me the big one, which is the one I want, without either of us having to discuss the matter. It works. She worked it out in 2000, and has gone on bringing me the big one, and I have gone on asking for the small one. That is not a joke either. She has the makings. Ollerenshaw says that of his. I say it of mine, faster. O. HOYLE, Works Manager. 16 March 2002. Afterwards Nib is sixteen, and still the fortieth, and she is at the works for the keel of the Two Hundred and First, and stands, as before, on the NO side. There is still a space under her name on the board, and she says that it will be a long time before anybody needs it, because she has not finished being apprenticed, and does not intend to finish for some years, because there is a great deal of works. See also Ott Hoyle The Hoyle Works Tappet Cotterill , who had there is no dragon Eighty-Four , in her bay

title: Nix
text: Nix For the shop, see Nix's Emporium . For the provenance of particular items, see the notes in Arms and Artefacts , which are hers. Nix She did not take it Known as Nix; Acquisitions Born 23 January 1974, Thistlewick , in the room behind the general store. Nobody has the paperwork, and she says that is how she likes it Sex Female Of The back room of the general store, Thistlewick Trade Locating things, ahead of schedule On behalf of The party of the second part Ledger kept since 1989, at fifteen Age Twenty-eight. The parcel said not to open it until twenty-six Good at Speed, not being hit, several small hits, finding things in other people's pockets Bad at Taking a hit Opened The Obligatory Tower , without the key; the Counting House at Great Dunnage, without the form Coat Fits Nix runs the back room of the general store in Thistlewick . She does not steal things. She locates them, ahead of schedule, on behalf of a client who has not yet been identified. "Everyone asks eventually," she told the Forty-Eighth, before he had asked. "I like to get ahead of it. Same as everything else." She is not a thief, and the distinction is not a joke to her, and I have come round to her view of it. Every single thing in the back room was got somehow, and she can tell you how, from the ledger, by date, and the telling is always in order and is sometimes magnificent. The ledger At fifteen, in 1989, Nix worked out that "I wanted it" was not a sentence that got you anywhere in a village where everybody knows your mother, and opened a ledger instead. Every item in, every item out, every provenance, dated, in a hand that improves visibly from page to page. All of it was done on behalf of a client described in the front of the book as the party of the second part. I have been allowed to read the ledger, at the counter, with her watching. It is the most honest document in the county. The Committee's minutes are longer and the Prophecy is older, and neither of them can account for a single teaspoon. On the Quest She joined because the Tower was "a tower nobody's been inside for a hundred years, full of things nobody's counted". She had her coat on before he finished the sentence. Her terms were that three is a good number: "Small, quiet, splits four ways." The tower door. The door of the Obligatory Tower was barred. There is a key under the mat. She did not use it. "Bar's on the inside. Classic." Returned. In the front of the ledger, where the hand is worst, were eleven things she had never sold on: the longest loans she had. Bram 's mother's pie dish, the Old Man's chair, the gate key, Hulda Bole 's good boots, a cradle for Bessie Marsden at Upper Clanging , and six more, across three towns. "Everything's a loan, eventually. That's what the RETURNED column is for." The column had been ruled, very neatly, down eleven years of pages, and there was nothing in it. She returned all eleven in an afternoon that was not one afternoon. None of the owners had known the things were gone, every one of them was pleased to have them back, and two of them tried to pay. The ledger has a RETURNED column now, with eleven lines in it, and a double line under the last, blotted. The client. On the clean page after it, the first new entry was a parcel, brown paper, which Mrs Bole had been carrying for somebody since 1989, marked NOT TO BE OPENED UNTIL I AM TWENTY-SIX. The hand on it was Nix's own, at fifteen. Inside was a letter from the party of the second part, signed N., aged fifteen. The client, it said, wanted one thing, which was the first entry in the book, the only line in eleven years with no provenance, which was in bond at Great Dunnage , and which she had been avoiding. "Stop it." It was her gran's coat. It had gone down to her ankles. She would not wear it until it fitted, and would not sell it, so at fifteen she put it into the Bonded Warehouse, stood on a crate, and made a speech to the wharfinger, Mr Tibbs : I shall return for it when I am somebody. He wrote it in the margin. The rent came by post every quarter for eleven years, never late, no name, and she never went back, because he would have remembered the speech. He had. He unlocked the wardrobe. She put it on, and it fits. The first line of the ledger has a provenance now. Professional courtesy. Cobb Lorrimer steals things, says so, and wears a hood about it, and finds her whole vocabulary an insult. He challenged her to a contest: a list, an afternoon, and a client. She won on paperwork, having got everything on the list with permission. He has since taken a position in Nether Sopping , afternoons, signed for, in which he plays the Dark Lord for the children, and loses. The Counting House. Great Dunnage sealed its counting house in 1788, when the key was lost, and the Corporation wanted it opened by a licensed person, on Form L. She opened it in nine seconds while the Mayor was still reading the preamble. It held one chair and a note: WE SPENT IT. Form L remains blank. Half an encounter. She has a way of moving through a wood at night that halves the number of things that notice you. In 2000 the Works Band at Upper Clanging needed Mr Enoch Bagshawe, and his bassoon, brought through the Gloamwood by night without a single fight. He was brought through without one, or half of one. The Works Band has a bassoon. Afterwards The back room is open. The ledger is into its second volume, which began on the page after the coat, and its first entries are already in a better hand than the last of the old one. The party of the second part has been identified, and the book is still kept on her behalf. I asked Nix whether that made any difference. She said it made the paperwork simpler, and that she had always liked to be ahead of things, and that she had now been beaten to it once, by a girl of fifteen, and did not intend it to happen again. I have checked my pockets after every interview. Nothing has ever been missing. On one occasion there was something extra, a pencil, rather better than mine, with a note on it in a good hand: located. on behalf of the party of the second part. See also Nix's Emporium The Bonded Warehouse Cobb Lorrimer The Obligatory Quest

title: Nora Cotterill
text: Nora Cotterill "Mrs Cotterill." For the family, see The Cotterills . For the argument, see Spare Cotterill , who lost it a great many times and won it once, and would like the second number printed larger. Nora Cotterill "No, love." Known as Mrs Cotterill; Mam; "your mother", by the whole of Upper Clanging, to the whole of Upper Clanging Born Nora Sprag, 30 August 1954, at Haggit's Bank, a pit hamlet half way down the valley road, a pit family Sex Female Married Ernest Cotterill , 1975, at the chapel, on a Saturday, between shifts Children Ten. Not going to be another one Names Chose them. Has them off by heart. Was tired for two of them Has had him out of A boiler, nine times; a flue; a culvert; a drain we do not discuss Fighting style You Are Nine; Ask Your Father; That Is Not The Point; I Have Said No Record Undefeated, until she stopped at a quarter Potatoes More Nora Cotterill is the mother of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , all of whom she named, after the parts that hold an engine together, until she ran out. She is the only person in the north who ever won an argument with Spare, and she won it a great many times, in the front room, under rules she made up as she went along, and then one day, at a quarter, she stopped. She will ask you whether you have eaten. Your answer does not come into it. Haggit's Bank She was born Nora Sprag in 1954, at Haggit's Bank, a row of pit cottages half way down the valley road to Great Dunnage , where the coal for the foundries came out, the youngest of six in a family of colliers. A sprag is the wedge you knock under a wagon to stop it running away down the incline. Her father used to say that she was well named. Her brothers used to say so too, but more bitterly, because she was the one who told on them. She came up the valley at nineteen, to be a pit-head lass at the foundry's coal yard, and met Ernest Cotterill on her second day, when he walked into a coal wagon she had just sprag'd, and apologised to it. She says that she knew then. He says that he did not know anything for some time, owing to the wagon. The names They were married in 1975, and Cotter came in January twelve-month. She had decided by then that all the children would be named for the things that hold an engine together, because, she says, that is what a family is for, and because Mr Cotterill was at the works so much that she wanted him to feel at home when he came in. The plan went well for eight. She has the eight off by heart, and will say them for you in one breath, as she said them to the Forty-Eighth: "Cotter, Rivet, Gudgeon, Tappet, Ferrule, Grommet, Clevis, Shim. And Spare. We had run out. He said call it Spare, and I was tired." She would like it recorded that she had not run out. She had * Washer * in reserve. Mr Cotterill said not Washer. That is a different thing from running out, and she was tired, and the subject is closed, or was, until the spring of 2000, when Spare got to it first. "He said call it Washer, and I was tired." She has been tired, by her own count, twice in twenty-seven years, and both times somebody got named. Grommet , who is apprenticed at the forge, has pointed out to her every day since 2000 that the names are wrong: a shim is a packing piece, and a ferrule fastens nothing. She would like it printed that the names are not wrong. They are what she called them. I have printed it. - H.B. Out of a boiler Spare has been going into the works' boiler since he was six. His mother does not mind the boiler. She minds the coming out, which is where she is. "I have had him out of a boiler. Nine times. And out of a flue, and a culvert, and a drain we do not discuss. Every time, he came out. Every time, I was there." That was the whole of her case against the Tower , and it was a good case, and I have never heard it bettered by any lawyer. "You are going to a tower that eats the people who go to it. I would not be there." The argument In the front room. She was right. The argument was fought in the front room, many times, with Spare on his own, and the rest of the family arranged on the stairs to watch. Her moves have been written down by Clevis , who kept a book on the outcome, and who describes them as: You Are Nine, which hurt; Ask Your Father, which sent Mr Cotterill in, who said "Mam," and was told "I know"; That Is Not The Point, which does nothing whatsoever, and is not meant to; and I Have Said No, which is the one that ends it. She was immune to his tantrum. She is the only person in the world who is. She has had nine years' practice and eight children's before that. She won every time, until the day she did not. She stopped at a quarter. What she said then is in Spare's article, and I will only give the terms, which she set out like a contract, and which Miss Pargeter of Frostwick , when I read them to her, said were the best-drafted she had heard in the north: Jumper on. You do not go in first. You write. It does not have to be long, and it does not have to be true. And to the Forty-Eighth: "And you. Bring him back." He was brought back. "You did not," she said to Spare, when he told her that he had gone in first, which he had not, quite. "Tea is at six. Wash your hands." The letters He wrote. He wrote from every town the company went through, four lines each, every one untrue, and she read them out to the shift at the Hoyle Works at the dinner hour, with her reading glasses on, slowly, with the punctuation in. The last one said that the dragon was coming home with them for its tea, and that she was please to do more potatoes, because it had never had a potato. There was no dragon. "I know, love," she said. "I did more potatoes anyway." She has kept every letter, tied up in string. There is no dragon in any of them that came true, and she says that is not the point, and she would know, because that is one of her moves. Afterwards Washer was born in the spring of 2000, on time, the only one of them that ever was. Ferrule made her stay sat down for a week, and she got up four times, and was counted. She is still at the house at the end of the street, and still does more potatoes, and still asks whether you have eaten. I had eaten. It made no difference. I have never had a better dinner, and I was asked three times whether I wanted any more, and the third time it was not a question. She says there is not going to be another one. Mr Cotterill says that is all of them. They say it together, most evenings, as if one of them might forget. See also The Cotterills Ernest Cotterill Spare Cotterill Washer Cotterill , who was on time

title: Norbert Pelling
text: Norbert Pelling STAND AND DELIVER! For the meadow, see Firstfield Meadow . For his employers, see The Guild of Guides . Not to be confused with any rival of Corvin Ash 's; he is booked up through the spring. Norbert Pelling "Lovely stuff." Known as Norbert; the Ambush; "the best loser in the county", by his wife, nicely Born 12 May 1961, at Pelling's Farm, two fields east of Firstfield Sex Male Married Maud Pelling, née Crisp, 1983 Post Station Four: Combat. The ambush, contracted to lose, since 1981 Losses Three thousand, one hundred and five, by 2000 Wins None, which is the job First loss Framed, by Maud Lunch Packed, with a note: LOSE WELL, LOVE Contract Provides for a lie down after. Best part of the job On till Four Norbert Pelling is the tutorial ambush at Firstfield Meadow , contracted by the Guild of Guides to stand in the gap in the fence at the top of the meadow, say STAND AND DELIVER, ask for your best attack, if you would be so kind, and lose. He has done it since 1981. By the year 2000 he had lost three thousand, one hundred and five times, and had never won, which is the job, and he is extremely good at it. The gap in the fence Bandit (Tutorial), to lose. He was born in 1961, two fields over, on his father's farm, and worked it until 1981, when the Guild advertised a contractor's post at Firstfield, Bandit (Tutorial), to lose, and Maud Crisp, who was not yet his wife, read it out to him over the fence and said that he would be perfect, and meant it nicely. He applied. He was the only applicant. The Guild says that is lore. Maud says it is because nobody else in the county could lose with any conviction. The sign at the gap reads AMBUSH IN PROGRESS. PLEASE QUEUE. THE AMBUSH IS CONTRACTED TO LOSE. THE AMBUSH WOULD LIKE YOU TO KNOW HE TRIES. He tries. He puts down his sandwich. He wipes his hands on his trousers. Then: "STAND AND DELIVER! ...your best attack, if you'd be so kind. I'm the tutorial ambush. Norbert. Pleased to meet you." He announces every swing a turn in advance, for the education of the young. When hit, he goes down, quite convincingly: "Oh! Ooh. You've got me. Down I go. Lovely. Lovely stuff." Then he has a lie down, for twenty minutes, which is in the contract, and which he says is the best part of the job. "Mind the sandwich." The other way Twice in nineteen years, a hero has lost to him. He was mortified both times. "Oh. Oh dear. No, that's not how it goes. Tell you what, we'll call that one a practice. Nobody saw. I won't put it on the form." He did not put it on the form. His record remains unblemished, at no wins, and the two heroes concerned are, he says, both doing very well now, and he would not dream of naming them, and one of them sends a card at Christmas. He has also been run from. "Very sensible. Most heroes never think of running. Come back when you're ready. I'm on till four." Maud "The wife. She packs my lunch. There's a note in it every day. She says I'm the best loser in the county. She means it nicely. I asked." The note says LOSE WELL, LOVE. It has said that every day for nineteen years, on a slip of paper in the sandwich tin, and he has kept every one, in a biscuit box, and there are about five thousand of them, and she says that she has never once had to think what to write, which is the secret of a good marriage. She has the first loss framed, which is to say that she had a man come from the town in 1981 and paint Norbert lying down in the meadow in the gap in the fence, very peacefully, and it is over their fireplace, and visitors take it for a memorial and offer condolences, and Maud says thank you, he's at work. This is Maud Pelling, of Firstfield, Norbert's wife since 1983, and not Maud Penhallow of Great Dunnage , who is somebody else's understudy, and who has an article of her own. Both of them have been in the year 2000 at the edge of somebody else's fight, waiting for their moment, and both of them, I think, would like each other very much. They have not met. - H.B. Corvin Corvin Ash, who was in the habit of asking anybody he met in a gap whether they were his rival, asked Norbert. Norbert said, apologetically, "Oh, sorry, no. I'm booked up through the spring." Corvin Ash said that he quite understood. They shook hands. Norbert says that it was the most courteous exchange he has had at the gap in nineteen years, and that he would have been very happy to be Mr Ash's rival in the autumn, and that Mr Ash has not been back to ask, which he quite understands. Afterwards He is forty, and still at the gap, and has lost about three thousand, three hundred and forty times, and still announces his swings. The Forty-Eighth's loss he has described to me as textbook. "Lovely fight. Textbook. I have a lie down after." He says that nobody will ever beat the Forty-Eighth's record at Firstfield, because the Forty-Eighth is the only one who graduated, and that it was a privilege to lose to him, and that he would do it again tomorrow, at any time before four. See also Firstfield Meadow Fizz Corvin Ash , who asked Maud Penhallow , who is a different Maud

title: Old Hollis
text: Old Hollis "It's dangerous to go alone! Take this." For the meadow, see Firstfield Meadow . For the stick, see Arms and Artefacts . For his wife, read on; she cuts them. Amos Hollis "Ah. There you are." Known as Old Hollis, since his first day, at thirty-four, because the Guild's post was advertised as Old Man (Items) Born Amos Hollis, 8 August 1925, at Firstfield, in the cottage behind the tent Sex Male Married Nell Hollis, née Coombe, 1951 Post Station One: Items, the Guild of Guides , since 1959 Line It's dangerous to go alone! Take this. Adjusted for party size Sticks given Eleven thousand, two hundred and six, by 2000 Sticks come back One Mantelpiece Hollis; and, since 2000, a stick Amos Hollis , known as Old Hollis , stands by the tent at Station One of Firstfield Meadow and gives every hero a stick. He has said It's dangerous to go alone! Take this eleven thousand, two hundred and six times in forty-one years, adjusting it for the size of the party, and not one stick had ever come back, until the Forty-Eighth brought his back, and Old Hollis shouted for his wife across the meadow at the top of his voice. Old He was born in 1925 in the cottage behind the tent, which was his father's, who kept sheep in the meadow before the Guild took it over, real sheep, which the Guild has never been able to get since. He was a hedger for twenty years. In 1959 the Guild of Guides advertised a post at Firstfield, Old Man (Items), and he applied, at thirty-four, and was told that he was very young for it, and that he would grow into it. He has been Old Hollis since his first morning, and says that it took him about ten years to grow into it, and that he has since grown out the other side. The stick Every hero who comes into the meadow is met by Old Hollis with a stick, and the words, which he says are the Guild's, not his: It's dangerous to go alone! Take this. For a party, he adjusts. "It's dangerous to go- ...there's a few of you, isn't there." The Forty-Eighth's party was a three, and then, when he came back up the meadow, a four, and he was given the line twice, adjusted twice, without complaint. "Forty-one years I've stood here. Eleven thousand, two hundred and six sticks. And not one has come back." They go into cupboards. "Every hero's mother has a cupboard, and in it is a stick. I've seen them. Hundreds." I asked him how he had seen them. He said that heroes' mothers write to him, now and then, to thank him, and to ask what the stick is for, and that he writes back to say that it is for going alone, and that they always write back to say that their son did not go alone in the end, and that they have put the stick in the cupboard, in case. Nell "My Nell cuts them. Every evening, by the fire, forty-one years. She picks out the straight ones. She says a hero deserves a straight stick." Nell Hollis, born Nell Coombe in 1929 at the mill at the bottom of the meadow, married him in 1951, and has cut every stick he has ever given away, about two hundred and seventy a year, from the hazel along the hedge he used to lay. She sorts them by the fire into straight and not straight, and the not-straight ones go on the fire. She is small, and round, and has never once been in the meadow during working hours, because she says it is his meadow and her fire. I asked him whether she was, as I had heard, very particular. "She is. It's why I married her. Well. That and the sticks." One came back In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth, at the end of his tutorial, walked back down the meadow and held the stick out to him. Old Hollis looked at it. He looked at it for a long time. "You're... you're bringing it BACK?" "NELL! NELL! ONE'S COME BACK!" She came out of the tent, where she had never been during working hours, at a run, which I am told nobody at Firstfield had ever seen, and inspected it, and went back in, and came out with a straighter one. "She says you're to have this one. It's straighter." And then: "She's putting yours on the mantelpiece." I have been to the cottage, and seen the mantelpiece, by invitation, for tea. On it, until the year 2000, there was a photograph of Hollis on his first day, aged thirty-four, already called Old, and nothing else, because Nell does not hold with ornaments. Now there is the photograph, and the stick. She dusts the stick twice a day. "First thing on that mantelpiece in forty-one years that isn't me," said Hollis, and Nell said that was not quite true, because there had been a clock once, in 1966, but that it had not lasted, and that the stick would. - H.B. Afterwards He is seventy-six, and still at Station One, and still Old, and still adjusts the line for parties. He has given eleven thousand, seven hundred and forty sticks, to my last count, and two have now come back, the second from a hero who heard the story and walked back down the meadow on purpose, which Hollis says does not count, and which Nell has put on the mantelpiece anyway, at the other end, a little lower. See also Firstfield Meadow Fizz The Guild of Guides Bram Thistle , who brought one back

title: Ott Hoyle
text: Ott Hoyle This article is about the engineer. For the works, its airships and its two hundred years, see The Hoyle Works ; for the field, see The Long Field . Both are Miss Hoyle's own. This one is mine, and she has not been shown it, because she would put a line through it. Ott Hoyle Not looking up Known as Miss Hoyle; Ottoline, on the works deeds and nowhere else Born 18 July 1964, Upper Clanging , in the house behind the works, between the drawing office and the hooter, on a Tuesday, which was a casting day Sex Female Of Upper Clanging Office Chief engineer, the Hoyle Works Generation The fourth Carries A slide rule Attempts Two hundred, and one on the slip Landed Adjacent Embarrassment No capacity for it whatsoever Offence None intended. Some given Ott Hoyle is the chief engineer of the Hoyle Works at Upper Clanging , the fourth of her family to try to fly to the Obligatory Tower , and the first to manage it. She is deadpan, precise and kind, in that order, and she has never been embarrassed by anything in her life, which in a works where every second word is a technical term is a professional qualification. Four generations The Hoyle Works has been at it for two hundred years. "Great-grandmother started it to stop the Dark Lord. Grandmother kept it on because the town needed the work. Mother kept it on out of spite." She does not criticise her mother for this. "Spite is a perfectly good reason. It built most of this shed." And she? "I keep it on because I like it. I would rather be honest with you. Two hundred years, and we have got to 'I like it', and I think that is fine." When the Forty-Eighth walked into the drawing office in the year 2000 she was at the bench with a slide rule and her goggles pushed up into her hair, and she did not look up. "Two hundred years I have been at this. Four generations of us." Then she looked up. "And they have sent a lad." And then, so that there should be no misunderstanding: "No offence intended. Some given, I will grant you. But none intended." Her opinions I give a selection, all of them hers, all said in the drawing office in the course of ordinary work, and all of them, I am assured by people who know about engines, exactly correct. "The line on the floor is not decorative. Everything past it is hot, sharp, or under pressure. Three of them are all three." "Everybody reads the log. Nobody reads the drawings. The drawings are where the work is. The log is only where it stopped." "The union is weeping again. It is a union. It weeps. If it ever stops I shall be worried." "A curse is a load. It has a magnitude and it has a direction, and somebody has been extremely careless about writing down either." "Forty-six of them have gone up that road. They keep sending heroes. Nobody has ever once sent a surveyor." "Most of what goes wrong with an engine is somebody being in a hurry with it on the first morning." Her apprentice, Nib , is the works' fortieth since 1804, and has asked her nine times whether they are going to manage it, and has been told nine times that it is not a question with an answer: it is a question with a schedule. Nib stands on the NO side of the line on the floor. She always stands on the NO side. Merribell once asked her, politely, how the work was going, and was told about the drain cock and the gland on the big end, and that the engine primes if you heat her too fast, and that otherwise she is sound. Merribell nodded along, being a field medic, to whom this was a Tuesday. Bram found something to look at. The Two Hundred The Two Hundred wanted forty bolts of oilskin, and a spar that would hold. Mrs Barrow of Nether Sopping would not have forty, and was made to find forty, and Miss Hoyle counted all forty, out loud, in front of the Forty-Eighth, and did not hurry any of it, and said that nobody had ever brought her forty of anything. The spar came from Ollerenshaw's, at the bottom of the hill, and Bryd Ollerenshaw said we shall see, as he always does, and it held. She handed the airship over with one instruction - do not set her down on anything with a roof on it; you would be astonished how often that has been the finding - and asked the Forty-Eighth where he would take her first, and was told, and said that she was told that was traditional. She did ask. She had two questions for the top of the Tower, and sent them up with him. The first was clause seven, which somebody had copied onto the flyleaf of a ledger older than the building it is kept in, in a hand a hundred and sixty years dead, AND THE CHOSEN ONE SHALL COME UNTO THE TOWER UPON HIS OWN TWO FEET, with four generations' worth of notes under it in four inks, the last of them one word in pencil, recent: quite. The second was what the Tower is made of. The Two Hundred landed on the grass two squares from the Tower door. The party walked the two squares. The attempt log reads REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Two hundred years, and the only thing in that building Miss Hoyle will not write down is the reason it worked. The full technical account of all two hundred, and of the field, and of the stores book and its ITEM 1, is Miss Hoyle's, and she wrote it, and it is under her name, and if you have come here for tolerances you have come to the wrong article. I will say only that she does not write down anything she has not checked, and that she would like it known that what became of ITEM 1 is in the stores book, and that the stores book is not open to the public. Afterwards Grimspite answered both her questions. Clause seven, he said, requires a Chosen One to go on foot, because a thing that flies over and drops something is not a story; it is a Tuesday. He was of the view that she would never get one off the ground in sight of his Tower, and nobody has corrected him, and nobody is going to; I have been asked by everyone concerned not to, and I am not. As to the Tower, he said that nobody had ever asked, and he did not know, and he had leaned on that wall every day for four thousand years and never once wondered. "Tell her the work was good." Bram told her. She said that she had not asked whether it was good, she had asked what it was made of, and that it was a very poor answer to a perfectly clear question. Then she wrote it in the drawing office day book, in full, and underlined good, which nobody at the works has ever seen her underline before. The attempt log still says UNDER REVIEW. In 2001 she laid the keel of the Two Hundred and First, which is to land on the Tower, roof and all, and she has had a letter from nobody about it, because she has not told anybody it is for that, except me, and I have just told you. It is on the slip. It is, she says, behind. That appears to be the whole of the answer. See also The Hoyle Works The Long Field Upper Clanging Bryd Ollerenshaw The Obligatory Tower The Flight of the Two Hundred

title: Pargeter
text: Pargeter For the town whose winter she keeps, see Frostwick . For the clause she found, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick and Two Reckonings . Eudora Pargeter Gloves on, indoors Known as Pargeter; Miss Pargeter Born 6 December 1965, Frostwick , in a hard frost, which was on schedule Sex Female Of Frostwick , the Cold Room on the square Trade Retained practitioner. Refrigeration Not An ice witch Clients Larders, dairies, the fishmonger's, and the winter Contract Nine years, renewed on time Would sign it again Tomorrow Would sign the Prophecy Never Tolerance Plus or minus one flake Eudora Pargeter is the retained practitioner who keeps the winter at Frostwick , under a contract of nine years, renewed on time. She is not an ice witch, and would like that established before you ask. She is also the only person in the world, so far as I have been able to discover, who has read the Prophecy of Thistlewick all the way through, and the only one who found clause two, and read it out, and did not do the arithmetic for anybody. The practice "Refrigeration. Larders, dairies, the fishmonger's. The winter is one client. A good one." She keeps it the way you keep a larder, only bigger, and with the door open. She does January in an afternoon and is home by four. She works in pale blue, with sensible spectacles, and keeps her gloves on indoors as a matter of course, which is the only thing about her that anybody in Frostwick has ever called theatrical, and she says it is a matter of hygiene. Her own larder, in the Cold Room, is a shelf of frosted jars in neat rows, labelled JANUARY, and which week. Her box files read CONTRACT; CONTRACT (AMENDMENTS); CONTRACT (AMENDMENTS TO THE AMENDMENTS); and a slim one, COMPLIMENTS. The contract is on her desk, and Appendix C is the Schedule of Snowfalls, which I have read, with her permission, and which I think is the best-drafted document in this encyclopedia. Ordinary snow: four inches, overnight, not on market days. Blizzard: at the committee's request, in writing, on one week's notice, and not during carols. Festival Day: a light dusting, commencing at the ribbon, to settle on Mr Stagg 's hat. Tolerance: plus or minus one flake. Asked whether she minds keeping a town under a curse, she says that it isn't a curse, it's a contract. "I'd sign it again tomorrow." Clause two In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth showed her the Prophecy, because he had been told she read contracts, and she read it all the way through, at her desk, which nobody had ever done; not the Committee, not the Quills , not the forty-seven, and not me, until afterwards, and then only because she had. She had three remarks. "No break clause. No notice period. And clause twelve renews itself." "I'd never sign a thing like that. Somebody's underlined it, I see. Somebody's worried." And then she turned back to the beginning, to clause two, which every reader since the signing had read straight past, and read it aloud: "'A hundred years' is a defined term. 'Such period as the Committee shall find convenient.'" That is the whole of what she said about it. Then she mentioned that there would be a light dusting on Tuesday, for the look of the thing; it was in the schedule. She did not explain how forty-seven Chosen Ones could have gone "a hundred years" apart and the Forty-Fifth be alive in Nether Sopping and potting things. She did not do the arithmetic for him. She has never done anybody's arithmetic for them, and she sees no reason to start with a document she would not have signed. I have since done the arithmetic, at some length; it is Two Reckonings . I sent her a copy. She returned it with a note to say that the arithmetic was correct, and that she had not asked for it. Afterwards She is still in the Cold Room, and the contract is still renewed on time, and the winter is still kept to the flake. Frostwick has forty-two ribbons now. She says that the winter is in very good order, and that it is a client she would recommend. She has written to me, kindly, to point out a clause. Not one of the Prophecy's: one of mine. In Volume Two, she says, I wrote "a hundred years" eleven times without saying, once, in whose years, and she would draw my attention to the definitions, which in any document come first for a reason. She was right. Volume Three says, every time. She has not said whether she has read Volume Three, and I have not asked, because I would like to go on thinking that she might have, and that she found nothing to point out, and I would rather not know. See also Frostwick Two Reckonings The Prophecy of Thistlewick Hosea Bellwether The Eleven Days

title: Pemberton-Gore IV
text: Pemberton-Gore IV "Pemberton-Gore. The Fourth. Welcome to Fenmarch! Mind the moat. It's everywhere." For the house, see Fenmarch Hall . For his uncle, whose squire he is, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Aldric Pemberton-Gore IV Pointing confidently at the gate Known as The Fourth; young Aldric, by Mrs Puddifoot, when he has muddy boots Born Aldric Pemberton-Gore, 9 February 1981, at Fenmarch Hall , the son of Sir Aldric the Third's younger brother Sex Male Found the gate First time, at ten. First of the family who ever has Scratched FOUND IT, on the inside of the left-hand gatepost, at ten Portrait 1999. The only one in the gallery facing out Squire To Sir Aldric, Knight Errant, At Large, since 2000 Duties Gates. All of them Writes to Coldbarrow Weekly. His uncle's place, date and time. In ink Loves Everything. Ask anybody Aldric Pemberton-Gore , the Fourth, is the nephew of Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third, and the only member of the family in four generations who has ever found the gate at Fenmarch Hall first time, which he did at ten, and scratched FOUND IT on the gatepost to prove it. His portrait is the only one in the gallery facing out. Since the year 2000 he has been his uncle's squire, and finds the gates. The gate He was born at Fenmarch in 1981, the only son of the Third's younger brother, and grew up in a house where every portrait is of somebody's back and nobody can find the gate. His grandfather, Sir Aldric the Second, came over the wall until he was eighty, and said that it was quicker. It was not. He simply could not find the gate. The house is easy enough to find. It is the gate that the family has trouble with. At ten, in 1991, coming home from Little Gore on his own, the Fourth walked up to the wall and along it and found the gate first time, and stood in it, and could not believe it, and took out his penknife and scratched FOUND IT on the inside of the left-hand post, at the height of a boy of ten, where it still is. He says that it was the best day of his life until 2000. "Did you? So did I! I found the gate first time, when I was ten. First of the family who ever has. Grandfather came over the wall. Until he was eighty." The uncle His uncle went out errant in 1991, the same year, and never came back, and the family considered it the best story they had. The Fourth grew up on it. "He went out errant nine years ago and never came back. It's the best story we've got. Imagine being that busy. I'm going out myself, one day. Somebody ought to tell him how proud we all are." In the year 2000 Sir Aldric came back to Fenmarch, briefly, with the Forty-Eighth's company, and the Fourth was across the yard before anybody could say who it was. "UNCLE. Pemberton-Gore. The Fourth. I was ten when you went! And Mordaunt says you're AT LARGE. That's a RANK. They made it up for you. On a Thursday. Nine pins! Three in one week! Nobody's ever been three places in one week." "I want to squire for you. I can find gates. I found ours first time. I could find you all of them." And then, gently, to an uncle who had spent nine years going the long way round: "Grandfather said we always go the long way round. And the long way round is still a way. And nobody else in the family ever went OUT, uncle. They all came over the wall. You went OUT." When Miss Halloway told the household that none of the eighty animals in the gallery had ever lived, every one of them being two animals composed by Mr Ottershaw , it was the Fourth who said COMPOSED, by Mr Ottershaw; nobody else in the county has a COMPOSER; that's better than real; anybody can have real. I have thought about that a good deal since. I think he is the only person in this encyclopedia who has never once been disappointed by the truth about anything, and I do not believe it is because he is easily pleased. I believe it is because he is looking for what is good in it, and finding it first time, like the gate. - H.B. Squire He is his uncle's squire now, and finds the gates. Every week, by arrangement, he writes to Mordaunt at Coldbarrow, giving his uncle's place, the date and the time, in ink, and Mordaunt keeps the notes in a tenth volume of the Pemberton-Gore file, and it is the only one of the ten that agrees with itself. Afterwards He is twenty-one. He has been through more gates in two years, his uncle says, than the whole family managed in four generations, and has scratched FOUND IT on none of them, because, he says, it would be showing off, and because it is only special the first time. He has found the north gate of Thistlewick , which his uncle never could, three times. His uncle has found it once, on the ninth of June 2001, unaided, and the Fourth was there, a little way behind, and did not say a word, and I have the date from three witnesses, and one of them is him. See also Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Fenmarch Hall Mordaunt , who gets the notes Mr Ottershaw , the composer

title: Perce Stagg
text: Perce Stagg "Forty years ago this spring." For the town, the Festival and the ribbon, see Frostwick . For the woman who keeps the winter now, under contract, see Pargeter . For his wife, see Ida Stagg , who has views. Percival Stagg "I'll do the face. You'll see." Known as Perce; Mr Stagg; the Man Who Broke the Winter Born Percival Stagg, 1 March 1934, at Fenny Stretton, a long way south, on a smallholding Sex Male Went north Spring 1960, the year of the Forty-Fourth , with everybody Chosen No. Nobody chose him Got as far as Frostwick . The winter was in the way So He saw to it Married Ida, 1961 Festival The twelfth. Ribbon at noon. He does the face Lanterns Ever such good ones Has mentioned that he was not chosen Never. Nobody asked Percival Stagg , Perce, is the man who broke the winter at Frostwick , forty years ago this spring, as it was in the year 2000. He was not a Chosen One. Nobody chose him. Everybody went north that year, farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat, and he got as far as Frostwick, and the winter was in the way, so he saw to it. Frostwick has held a Festival in his honour every year since, and he cuts the ribbon at noon, and the whole town cheers, and he goes pink. Everybody went north He was born in 1934 on a smallholding at Fenny Stretton, far in the south, and grew cabbages until he was twenty-six. In the spring of 1960 the Forty-Fourth set out from Thistlewick , and the whole of the south went north with him, or after him, or a little before him, on the general understanding that something was going to happen and it would be a shame to miss it. Farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat. Perce put on his red coat, which was his father's, and went. "I wasn't, you know. Chosen. Nobody chose me. Everybody went north, that year. Farmers, tinkers, a man with a goat. I got as far as here, and the winter was in the way, so I saw to it." The winter Frostwick had been under a winter that did not end since before anybody could remember: not a cold spell, but a winter that had got stuck, and that the town believed to be a curse. Perce got as far as the square in a snowdrift to his waist, and could not get further, and asked what was the matter, and was told it was a curse. He said that it did not look like a curse to him, it looked like a winter that had not been told to stop, and he asked who was in charge of it, and nobody was, and so he went up to the top of the town, where the cold came down from, and saw to it. What he did, he has never said. He says he does not entirely know, and that it took most of a day and a great deal of shovelling, and that at the end of it there was a noise like a door shutting a long way off, and the snow began to drip. He came down the hill at dusk, and the town was standing in the square, and the snow was running down the gutters, and somebody started to cheer. He went pink. He has gone pink at that moment every year since. The Working Group's founding minutes, which I print in the article on the town, begin Item 1. That the winter has stopped. Noted. and proceed, by item three, to retaining a practitioner to put it back, on a sensible footing, because the town had lived on carols and lanterns and found it had no takings without them. Mr Stagg was not consulted about putting it back. He was asked, in item four, to open the first Festival, and abstained. He has opened every one since. He has never once said that he minded the winter coming back. I asked him. He said that a winter on a sensible footing is a very different thing from a winter that has got stuck, and that he had only ever had a quarrel with the second sort. - H.B. The Festival "Hello! You've come for the Festival? It's not till the twelfth. Everybody comes early." The Festival is on the twelfth. The ribbon is at noon. Perce stands beside the ribbon post as though it might need him, in the red coat with the white fur collar, and cuts the ribbon with the town's scissors, and the town cheers, and he does the face. The face is pink. Under Miss Pargeter's Schedule of Snowfalls there is, at the ribbon, a light dusting, to settle on Mr Stagg's hat. It does. He has never mentioned that he was not chosen. "Nobody's ever asked. They were all so pleased. And it's a lovely Festival." The iron crown on top of the ribbon post was made by Hob Grumnir , and in the year 2000 Hob asked whether he might have it back, for the spring. "The spring? The Festival's on the twelfth. Everybody ties a ribbon to that crown. You can't tie a ribbon to a bare post, you know. It slides down." Hob said that it did, aye. Afterwards He is sixty-eight, and has cut forty-two ribbons. He still does the lanterns for the Festival, two hundred and twelve of them, with Clem Blagg , who is learning, and whom he describes as having the makings of a very good lanterner, if not yet the patience. Frostwick has forty-two ribbons on the crown now, one for every Festival, and he says that he knows every one of them, and which year, and that the first is the one at the bottom, faded nearly white, and that it is his favourite, because it is the one he tied himself, before he knew there would be any others. See also Ida Stagg Frostwick Pargeter , who keeps it now Clem Blagg , of the lanterns The Eleven Days

title: Perpetua Small
text: Perpetua Small "Perpetua Small. I think." For the room that is being very kind to her, see The Slain Wyvern . For the convention, see the Glossary of Cliches , under The amnesiac , which I have asked the Wyvern not to leave lying about. Perpetua Small Excellent posture Known as Perpetua Small, which she thinks is her name Born Not known to her. The Wyvern has asked me to leave it at that, and I have Sex Female Found On the beach at Nether Sopping , 1994, with no memory and a headache Can Ride, fence, speak four languages, fold a napkin into a crown Wears A tiara, which she has not noticed Post One bottle of very good wine a month, with a crest, addressed TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN Theory Dairy. Possibly cheesemaking Perpetua Small woke up on the beach at Nether Sopping in 1994 with no memory, a headache, an excellent posture and an expensive tiara she does not appear to have noticed she is wearing. She has lived at the Slain Wyvern since. Everybody there has been very kind to her. Nobody will tell her anything. It has been eight years, and they want to see her get there on her own. A note on this article This article has been written so that it can be left on the bar. The Wyvern asked me to do that, by a show of hands, and Dorcas Thrupp read it before it went to the printer, and took one sentence out, and gave it back. I have not put the sentence back. If you know the thing that this article does not say, the Wyvern would be grateful if you looked very hard at the ceiling. What she knows "Perpetua Small. I think. I woke up on the beach six years ago with no memory and a headache. Everyone here has been very kind. Nobody will tell me anything, but they've been very kind." She can ride. She can fence. She speaks four languages and does not know why. She folds every napkin she is given into a little crown, without looking, and has no idea why, and is extremely good at it. And when she walks into a room, people stand up. "They stand up! For me!" When she told the Forty-Eighth this, the entire tavern behind her was looking very hard at the ceiling, and I am told that he considered telling her, and that the room, as one, silently begged him not to, and that he did not. I think it is to his great credit. It would have been very easy. Every month a bottle of very good wine arrives at the Wyvern from a palace somewhere, addressed TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN, and is put beside her plate, and she drinks one glass of it, on Sundays, and says that it is very good, and that somebody must have a lot of wine. Her theory "It'll come back to me. Probably something dull. Dairy, I expect." She has given this a great deal of thought, and has refined it. "Cheesemaking. It would explain the four languages." She means that a cheesemaker has to trade abroad. I asked how it would explain the fencing. She said that I had clearly never tried to cut a really old cheddar. Gerald There was a Gerald. I have been told by Dorcas Thrupp that he proposed to Miss Small every Sunday for a year, in the Wyvern, on one knee, at lunch, and that the Wyvern handled it, and that that is all that is being said about Gerald. I have found that it is. When I gave Miss Small the draft of this article to read, she read it all the way through at the bar, slowly, and then she said that it was very fair, and that she liked the bit about the cheddar, and that she couldn't help feeling there was something in it she was missing. The whole room looked at the ceiling. She said, "There! You're all doing it again," and laughed, and folded the proof into a crown. I have it on my desk. It is a very good crown. - H.B. Afterwards She is still at the Wyvern, and has not got there yet. In the summer of 2001 she remembered a word, out of nowhere, over breakfast, which was precedence, and she has decided that it is a kind of cheese. The bottle still comes every month. The room still stands up. She says it is a lovely town for manners. See also The Slain Wyvern Dorcas Thrupp Hosea Bellwether , who paid for her tale

title: Piper Quill
text: Piper Quill For her family's work, see The Quills . For her songs, see From the Notebooks of P. Quill . Piper Quill Mid-verse Known as Piper Quill, Chronicler Born 10 January 1976, Thistlewick , in the Quills' house. Her aunt wrote a verse for it, which does not mention her Sex Female Of Thistlewick , usually on a table Trade Bard; chronicler, unofficial Family The Quills, official chroniclers for four generations House style Never let the truth spoil the metre Her style Writes down what actually happened Age Twenty-six Good at Making everybody else better; making everybody else worse Bad at Raw numbers Prizes Second, the Contest at the Sign of the Bell, 2000 Rhymes for turnip None Piper Quill is a bard who narrates events as they happen, in the third person, at volume, whether or not this is convenient. She is a Quill, of the family that has written the official chronicles of Thistlewick for four generations, and she is the first of them to write down what actually happened, which is why at twenty-four she was standing on a table in the Gilded Turnip instead of being paid. She went north with the Forty-Eighth and wrote all of it down. "Piper Quill. Chronicler. I do the songs. You do the sword bit. It's a good system." She is my colleague, and my rival, and she has read this article, and she says it scans in places, which from a Quill is high praise and I am going to keep it. The Quills The text under all forty-seven portraits on the Wall of the Forty-Seven in Prophecy Hall was written by somebody in her family. Her grandmother did numbers forty to forty-three, and is quoted in the Prophecy 's own preamble. The house style is one line long: never let the truth spoil the metre. Piper's entire professional rebellion has been to let it. Her aunt, Ambrosine Quill , is the senior chronicler now, and is an extremely good writer. I have reason to know. On the Quest She joined in the Gilded Turnip, mid-verse: 'And lo, the Chosen One drew near, smelling faintly of turnip, and the tavern fell silent -' and immediately needed a rhyme for turnip, and said she would get one on the road. She always does. She did not, because there isn't one, and that, as it turned out, was the point. A rhyme for turnip. In the Gilded Turnip, which is named after the problem, the whole company sat down one afternoon and offered her rhymes. Hob offered burnip, without embarrassment. Zephyrine offered a slant rhyme with sherbet, which the Collegium would accept. Wren ruled everything ending in -nip inadmissible, pre-emptively, on the grounds that it is a genus. Sir Aldric offered the word for turnip in the old tongue of his house, which rhymes beautifully with nothing, in his tongue or anybody's. Corvin 's scanned perfectly, and was about drowning. Merribell went looking for something anatomical, right down to the feet, and found nothing. Nix located one, ahead of schedule, on behalf of a client, and it was turnip. Bram offered a parsnip, and was told it is a different vegetable. There is no rhyme for turnip, and any competent poet would have changed the other line in the first week, which she then did, in nine seconds, moving the turnip into the middle of a line where nothing has to rhyme with it. "It was always going to be the last verse. I just had the lines the wrong way round." Everybody who had spent the afternoon on it was furious. She has asked for the nine seconds on her headstone. The verse is quoted under The Obligatory Quest. The Contest at the Sign of the Bell. A bardic competition at Great Dunnage , with categories nobody can defend and a panel of three judges, one of whom cannot hear. She lost, by one point, to a man who does birdcalls. The birdcalls are, in fairness, extraordinary; his thrush in particular. She has framed the certificate. It is the first prize a Quill has ever won for writing down what actually happened. The official account. Ambrosine had already written the official account of the Forty-Eighth before he left, because the shape is known. It is properly metred, it has a good middle, Bram is an orphan in it, Merribell dies, and there is a bit with a wolf. Piper and the Forty-Eighth went to see it. What came of that is the subject of a disagreement among the Quills that I have been asked, by all of them, not to settle, and I am not going to. There is, depending on whom you ask, one official account or two, and if there is one it has a footnote by P. Quill, and if there are two the second has a goat in it, and the goat is in the minutes. The struck verses. The Committee strikes any verse it cannot have read aloud at the fete. Of course it keeps them, in a box, in Prophecy Hall. With the party's help Piper got into the box, and has read every verse in it, and printed none. The number of them is in the account, and is larger than the Committee would like. One of them, verse forty-one, is about a cat, and she showed it to the Forty-Eighth, and only that one; I have it from him that it scans. Verse seven was struck before the Quest began, and she has never told anybody what is in it. She has not told me. The elegy On the road at Little Gore there was a card nailed to the back of the fingerpost: WANTED: AN ELEGY. For Abel Thrush, carrier, who walked the road between Little Gore, Fenmarch and Sump every day for fifty years, from 1941 until he died, in the spring of 1991, and never had one. Something with a bit of a tune. She had never met him. She asked eleven people, and every one of them described a different man, and she wrote it out of the contradictions rather than choosing between them. She did not stand on anything. She did not read it out. She pinned it to the post, under the Fenmarch arm, and stepped back. It is still there, under a little roof that somebody has made for it, and people stop and read it on their way past, and with her leave I print it whole. ABEL THRUSH, CARRIER. LITTLE GORE - FENMARCH - SUMP. He never spoke a word. He never stopped. He came in at the gate. He climbed the wall. He read no letter, and he knew them all. He carried a cow, and wept over a bird. He brought the water nobody would drink, and stopped for tea, and was at eight each day where somebody looked up to see him wave. Eleven people knew him. All are true. The road is four miles long. He walks it still. P. Quill, the fingerpost at Little Gore Mrs Vane , of Little Gore, read it twice, and said that it was him, all of him, and that every one of them was in it. Then she said they had wondered whether it might have a bit more of a tune. Piper laughed, out loud, about her own work, which nobody had heard her do before. "Next time." Afterwards She is still writing it down. The ballad is finished. The elegy is on the post. The notebooks are, I am told, into double figures, and I am also told I am in them, at some length, in the third person, and not always in the metre I would have chosen. We are colleagues. We are rivals. She says my history is complete and not accurate, and I say her songs are accurate and do not scan, and we are both right, and we meet at the Slain Wyvern about once a month to compare notes and disagree about all of them. Some of her work is printed in this volume by her permission; see From the Notebooks of P. Quill . I have asked her what is in verse seven every time we have met. She has said, every time, that it is very good. I believe her. See also Ambrosine Quill From the Notebooks of P. Quill Little Gore The Turnip , and the rhymes for it The Obligatory Quest

title: Princess Rosamund
text: Princess Rosamund "Oh, are you the rescue? Lovely." For the kingdom, see Fairholme . For Thursdays, see Mrs Emberthwaite , who cheats at whist. Princess Rosamund of Fairholme The tiara for kidnappings Known as Princess Rosamund; Her Highness; "the bag by the window", by the Heroes' Guild Born 14 February 1978, at the palace, Fairholme ; the only child of King Aldous and Queen Isobel Sex Female Kidnapped Eleven times, 1986-1999. Twelve, if you count the eagle (1996). The Palace does not Rescued Eleven times, by eleven shareholders Bag By the window, packed. It is always the bag by the window Cloaks Eleven, labelled 1ST to 11TH, and one marked EAGLE Tiaras Two: FOR BALLS, and FOR KIDNAPPINGS Diet No eels. No mushrooms. Nothing in aspic Thursdays Up the hill, on foot, with a cake tin Memoir Rescued Again , eleven volumes Princess Rosamund of Fairholme has been kidnapped eleven times, and rescued eleven times, and has a bag packed by the window at all times, eleven sensible travelling cloaks, a tiara for kidnappings, and a card on her table for whoever it is this time. On Thursdays she walks up the hill to Mrs Emberthwaite's, on her own two feet, with a cake tin, to play whist, and the Heroes' Guild has written to complain. Already She was born in 1978, the only child of the King and Queen. Her portrait in the chamber shows her at six, in a ball gown, holding a small packed bag. She says that she does not remember why; that her mother had the painter in, and that she had packed it herself that morning, for a picnic, and would not put it down. Everybody who looks at the portrait now says already, and she says that she knows, and that she has found it very difficult to explain to people that it was only a picnic, and has stopped trying. Her mother died when she was five. She was brought up by her father and a series of governesses, and by the time of the first kidnapping, at eight, she had read every book in the palace library about princesses in towers, and had formed, she says, a very low opinion of the arrangements. The kidnappings The first, in 1986, was a sorcerer. She was carried off from her room in the tower, in her nightdress, in the rain, with nothing, and was three days in a cold tower in the hills before Osric came for her, and took the half, and sat down at the council table, where he has been doing the arithmetic since, and she says that she spent all three days making a list. The list became the bag. The bag has been by the window ever since. "It's the bag by the window, if anybody asks. It is always the bag by the window." In the bag: a book, a cardigan, sandwiches in greaseproof paper, made that morning, and a second round labelled OTHERS, for the kidnappers, who she says are generally very hungry and very badly organised. On the table beside it is the card: FOR WHOEVER IT IS THIS TIME. No eels. No mushrooms. Nothing in aspic. Tea at four, and not stewed. I will not be carried unless there are stairs. I would like to be home by Thursday. Thank you so much for having me. Under her pillow is a rope ladder. She has never used it, because she thinks it would be unfair on the rescuers, who have generally come a long way. She has been taken, in thirteen years, by five sorcerers (everybody had a sorcerer), a wyrm, two lots of bandits who were sorry about it, a rival kingdom by mistake, a witch who wanted company, and two men from beyond the marshes who left her on a dragon's doorstep; and once, by an eagle, which does not count. Each kidnapping has its cloak, labelled. Each rescuer has a chapter in her memoir, Rescued Again, eleven volumes, written about very kindly. The eagle has a cloak and no chapter, pending the council's decision. I asked her whether she was ever frightened. She said, the first time. She said that after that she had the bag, and the card, and that she found that most people who kidnap a princess have not thought it through, and are very relieved to be given a sandwich and told what to do, and that the frightening part, really, is the stairs. "Mind the seventh stair, it's a trap. The eighth is also a trap. The ninth is fine." She put the seventh in herself, at fourteen, for practice. - H.B. Thursdays The eleventh kidnapping, in 1999, was the one up the hill. Two men from beyond the marshes, who had been told there was a dragon on the hill and that dragons keep princesses, carried her up to the cave in the rain and left her at the door, and ran. Mrs Emberthwaite opened the door. She had not had anybody to talk to since Mr Emberthwaite. She made up the spare room. That evening, after a rubber of whist, which was a Thursday, the Princess came down the hill on her own, with a tin of cake, and Mr and Mrs Budge, who were only mucking out, walked her the rest of the way home, and were given the half, and did not know what to do with it, and put most of it back into the orchard. "I go up the hill on Thursdays. Mrs Emberthwaite does a lovely sponge, and she cheats at whist." "She said she hadn't had anybody to talk to since Mr Emberthwaite. So now I walk. It's quicker." She has never stayed the night. The spare room is aired on Wednesdays anyway, and there is a hot-water bottle in the bed, and the card on the pillow says ROSAMUND - THURSDAYS. She walks home after the whist. She has not yet beaten Mrs Emberthwaite at it, and says she will, and that it will be the twelfth thing she has escaped from. Afterwards She is twenty-four. There have been no kidnappings since 1999, because it is very difficult to kidnap a princess who is up a hill playing cards with a dragon, and the Heroes' Guild has written to the Palace to complain that she is unreasonably unavailable. She has replied, kindly, in writing, with a sandwich. The bag is still by the window. The twelfth volume of Rescued Again is in hand, and is about Thursdays, and has no rescuer in it at all, and she says it is the best of them. See also King Aldous Mrs Emberthwaite Mr Pilbeam , and the eagle Fairholme

title: Prosper Hollowell
text: Prosper Hollowell Submitted by P. Hollowell, Caretaker, for the file For the hall, the tour and the lift, see The Former Premises , which Mr Hollowell has written up himself. I asked him for a short account of his own life for this volume, and he sent me the following, in the form of a statement of service, which is the only form he says he has ever needed. I print it as it came, with the courier. - H.B. Prosper Hollowell Retained Known as P. Hollowell; Mr Hollowell; the Caretaker Born Not on file. The file was opened after I was retained, and I have never thought it my place to go back and enter myself Sex Male Retained Year one of the engagement, on its removal to the Tower : four thousand eight hundred years ago, in the engagement's years Post Caretaker, the Former Premises, the sky Quarterly reports Nineteen thousand two hundred, all filed Underlinings One. ITEM TWO: VISITORS. Yes! Released from retention Spring, 2000. No further action required Now Staying on, pending instructions. Unpaid. Content Lift Running. Beautifully Statement of service Name. Prosper Hollowell. Caretaker. Retained. Date of birth. I have been asked this by Mr Bellwether, and I have looked, and it is not on file. The file was opened when I was retained, and I was already here, and I have never thought it my place to go back and enter myself in a record I keep for somebody else. I am told that a great many people in this volume have had their dates filled in. I should not like to cause any trouble over mine. Please put pending. Previous employment. Before the removal I was under-steward of the Premises, in the engagement's old years, in charge of the cushions on the visitors' sofa. There were never any visitors. I plumped them every morning. I was told by the steward that this was the most important post in the building, because if a visitor ever did come, the first thing they would do was sit down. I have never forgotten it. Retention. When the engagement was moved into the Tower, with a door at the bottom, ground floor, very sensible, the steward retired, and I was retained to keep the Premises ready, in case they were re-let. I have kept them ready. Four thousand eight hundred years. Everything is in perfect working order. Duties. The hall. The throne, polished, with its dust sheet folded on the seat, ready to go back over it. The four suits of armour, one of which faces the door, and which I polish more than the others, and I could not tell you why. The sofa. The deeds. The potted plant, which is watered by the rain, from underneath. The visitors' book, which does not leave the lectern. The lift. The lift. Commissioned following a complaint, upheld. Courtyard to battlements. It goes up, smoothly and in perfect silence, and comes back down, smoothly and in perfect silence. It works beautifully. It always has. I have mentioned it in every report, and I should like to mention it here, as it is the best thing in the building, and I have had very little opportunity to say so to anybody who was not reading a report. Reports. Quarterly. Nineteen thousand two hundred. Each was acknowledged with the same form letter, THANK YOU FOR YOUR REPORT, WHICH HAS BEEN FILED, and I have found that very steadying. Under ITEM TWO: VISITORS every one of them says NONE, except one. Visitors. In the year 2000, one party, by air, from below, in an airship from Upper Clanging which I should very much like to see. They took a slip up the Tower for the current incumbent, and brought it back signed: Never been. Heard marvellous things about the lift. I pasted it in, square. That quarter's report says Yes!, underlined twice. It is my only underlining. I do not regret it. Release. In the spring of that year I received a NOTICE OF TERMINATION: The Engagement is concluded. The Premises are released from retention. No further action is required. I filed it under N, and under T, and under C, in case. That took me until about half past nine. Present position. I am staying on, pending instructions, unpaid. The Premises are in perfect working order and somebody ought to keep them so. I have written a quarterly report to say so, and had the reply, which is that it has been filed. I find I do not mind in the least. Remarks. I should like to thank the Forty-Eighth's party for coming, and for the slip, and the courier for bringing the post, which he has done throughout, on his rounds, without being asked whose. I should also like to say to any reader who is passing by air that the tour starts in the hall, and also ends there, and that the cushions are plumped every morning, in case. P. HOLLOWELL, Caretaker. The Former Premises, the sky. First quarter, 2002. I have done what he asked, and entered his date of birth as pending . He is, by the engagement's reckoning, a great deal older than anybody else in this volume, and he is, by the look of him in his portrait, about sixty-five, and a very kind sixty-five, and I do not think the two numbers need to be reconciled, any more than the Tower's. The courier brought his statement with a second sheet, which was not for the file: a drawing, in pencil, of what he imagines the airship at Upper Clanging to look like. It has a lift. - H.B. See also The Former Premises Grimspite the Inevitable , who heard marvellous things about the lift Two Reckonings , on the engagement's years

title: Prudence Thrupp
text: Prudence Thrupp For the inn, its turnip and its regulars, see The Gilded Turnip . For her sister, forty miles south, see Dorcas Thrupp , who is the elder, and will mention it. Prudence Thrupp "Don't shake it. Don't ask what's in it." Known as Prudence; Mrs Thrupp, by Nether Sopping , which has never met her and assumes Born 19 October 1951, at the Gilded Turnip, Thistlewick , upstairs, during last orders Sex Female Keeps The Gilded Turnip , since 1976, her father's before her Bed Twenty crowns. Includes breakfast. Breakfast is turnip Has not spoken to her sister 1970-2000 Has written to her sister Every month since, at the weekend Called her sister The cow, once, with great affection Could read a customer by The age of eight. Dorcas took till ten Prudence Thrupp keeps the Gilded Turnip , the inn on the square at Thistlewick, where three of the Forty-Eighth's companions were found, one of them on a table. She is the younger sister of Dorcas Thrupp of the Slain Wyvern at Nether Sopping, and the two of them did not speak for thirty years and sent each other things instead, which she says was not a falling-out. In the year 2000 she gave the Forty-Eighth a jar to take south. It was warm on one side. The Turnip She was born upstairs at the Turnip in 1951, during last orders, which her father said was the most consideration any child of his had ever shown the trade, and was behind the bar by eight, reading customers. She took the house over in 1976, when her father retired to the chair by the fire, from which he went on running it until 1991, by remark. Her bed is twenty crowns, and includes breakfast, and breakfast is turnip. She has never been asked to change this and would not. The turnip on its plinth in the middle of the room, painted gold, with a small plaque to say that it is not a metaphor, was her father's idea, and she has kept it gilded, every spring, in the same paint, and she says that it is the only thing in Thistlewick that has never once been chosen for anything. The jar When the Forty-Eighth came through the Turnip on his way out of the village, properly out, roads and everything, she gave him a jar. "There's a town on the south coast. Nether Sopping. Follow the road out of the gate and turn left at the sea. There's a woman there runs a tavern. Dorcas Thrupp. My sister. Give her this. Don't shake it. Don't ask what's in it." "Thirty years we've not spoken. That's not a falling-out. We just stopped one day and neither of us started again. So we send each other things instead." "Thirty years. Tell her I said nothing. She'll know what I mean by it." He brought the reply north, and she opened it in front of him, and looked at it for some time, and said, "...The cow," and laughed, which the regulars of the Turnip say they had not heard her do, properly, from the bottom, in thirty years. Then she went upstairs and came down with the locket, which had been in her drawer since they were girls: two portraits, one of each, facing resolutely away. "It's hers and mine and it's been in a drawer since we were girls and I'm sick of the sight of it. That was HER idea, that was. I'll write to her. Don't tell her that. I'll write to her at the weekend." The locket was made at the Michaelmas fair in 1962, when Dorcas was fourteen and Prudence eleven, by a man who did little portraits on ivory while you waited. Dorcas says that the facing away was Prudence's idea. Prudence says it was Dorcas's. The man who made it, if he could be found, would be able to settle it, and neither of them has looked for him, which I take to mean that both of them know. - H.B. Thistlewick She has never once remarked on anything that Thistlewick does not remark on, which is how she has kept a public house there for twenty-six years; she knows, for example, that the Regular's cousin was the Thirty-Ninth, and she has served the Regular every night for as long as she has kept the house, and she has never done any arithmetic about it, and would thank you not to do any in her bar. Nobody in Thistlewick mentioned to the Forty-Eighth that she had a sister. She would like it known that this is because nobody asked. Afterwards She wrote to her sister at the weekend, as she had said she would: four pages, two of them about the Forty-Eighth, and one of those complimentary. She has written every month since. The letters go south by the carrier on the last Friday of the month, and Dorcas's come north on the first Thursday, so that each of them has the other's letter for a week before she has to answer it, which Prudence says is the right amount of time, and that she does not know how they managed before. They have not met. Prudence says that Dorcas will have to come to her, being the elder, and having moved. She has written to say so. She has had a reply. See also The Gilded Turnip Dorcas Thrupp Thistlewick Arms and Artefacts , for the locket The Thrupp Feud

title: Rivet Cotterill
text: Rivet Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the man he passes at the door, see Ernest Cotterill . For the half an hour, see Upper Clanging , the Safety Valve. Rivet Cotterill Days Known as Rivet Born 3 February 1978, Upper Clanging Sex Male Named for A rivet, which holds two plates together, permanently, and is never asked whether it would like to Works The foundry. Days, while Da does nights Conversations with his father One a day, at six, two words long. Some mornings the weather Half an hour At the Safety Valve, every evening. Then bed Has shared a bed with Somebody, every night of his life. One of them is Grommet Nights spent in a room by himself One. See below Rivet Cotterill is the second of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging . He works days at the foundry while his father works nights, so that they pass at the front door at six every morning, one going out and one coming in, and that is their conversation, and he is entirely satisfied with it. He has shared a bed his whole life. He was twenty-two, in the year 2000, and had never once been in a room by himself. Days He went into the foundry at fourteen, in 1992, on days, because Da was on nights and Mrs Cotterill said that one of them on each was the only way the house would ever have a man awake in it at all times, which she felt it needed, for the lifting. He is on the moulding floor, where the sand is, and is good at it, and says so, once, and then does not mention it again for a year. He gave me his whole day in four sentences, which is two more than he gives most people: "Days. Da does nights. We pass at the door at six. Rivet. Da." "That is a conversation, that is. Some mornings he says the weather." I have stood at the door at six, by arrangement, and watched it. Mr Cotterill came up the street and Rivet came out of the house, and they met on the step, and Mr Cotterill said "Rivet," and Rivet said "Da," and they went past each other, and Mr Cotterill went in, and Rivet went down the hill. Then Mr Cotterill put his head out of the door again and said, "Close," and went back in, and Rivet called "Aye" up the street without looking round. Rivet told me afterwards that this was a very full morning, and that I had been lucky, and that it was the weather. The bed The house at the end of the street has three bedrooms and, until 1999, eleven people. Rivet has shared a bed, he says, his whole life, and one of the people in it is Grommet, and Grommet sleeps with his elbows. "I am twenty-two and I have never once been in a room by myself." He did not say it as a complaint. He said it as a fact, the way you might say you had never been to the sea, with a little wonder in it. When Cotter married and moved out, in 1999, there was a vacancy in Rivet's bed, and it was filled within the hour by Clevis , who had been waiting for it, and had a book on who would get it, and had backed himself. Half an hour Every evening after his shift he goes into the Safety Valve, where Mr Kell keeps a stool at the end of the bar that is understood to be his, and has a half, for half an hour, by the town clock, which has been four minutes fast since 1841, so that he is always home four minutes early, and is the only Cotterill who ever is. "Half an hour. Then bed. Then it is Tuesday." It is not always Tuesday. He says it is generally Tuesday, near enough, and that he has found it a great help to think so. Spring On the morning of Washer , Mr Cotterill came off nights for it, for the first time in twenty-two years, and he and Rivet passed at the door at six, the both of them going in. "Half an hour," Rivet said. "Then bed. Then it is the spring." I asked him whether they had said anything at the door, that morning. He said that his father had said, "Rivet," and he had said, "Da," and then they had both stood there, because neither of them was going anywhere, and it had been very strange, and they had gone in. Afterwards He is still on days, and still passes his father at six; Cotter is on days now as well, and passes with him, so that the conversation has become Rivet. Cotter. Da, which he says is a lot to take in at that hour. He is twenty-four. In the summer of 2001 the whole of the family went to Bessie 's to see the baby, on a Sunday, and Rivet came home early, from the foundry's cricket, and found the house empty, and his bed empty, and the whole of the room his own, for the first time in his life. He lay down in it. He says that it was very quiet, and very wide, and that he lay there for some time and looked at the ceiling. Then he went downstairs and sat in the kitchen with the door open until Grommet came home, and then he went up to bed. See also The Cotterills Ernest Cotterill Grommet Cotterill , and his elbows Upper Clanging

title: Roland Fairweather
text: Roland Fairweather For the door he left at, see The Obligatory Tower . For his understudy, see Maud Penhallow . Roland Fairweather Very sorry.
