Always very sorry Known as The Guest Star Born 8 February 1966. Where is the subject of a review meeting, and has been since 1978 Sex Male Of A table by the fire in the Slain Wyvern, between engagements Trade Being extremely good at this Since The age of eleven (the Wyrm of Ickworth, 1977) Age Thirty-six Good at Everything, genuinely Bad at Being there at the end Parties left at a door Eleven Prophecy His own, in preparation from 1978; discharged 2000, in an afternoon Review meetings attended One hundred and forty-one Sword Left at the door. Made in Thistlewick Roland Fairweather is the finest swordsman of his generation, magnificent, glowing and extremely good at everything, and for most of his life the protagonist of a much more expensive story than the one he was in. He joined the Forty-Eighth in the Slain Wyvern , carried more than his share all the way north, liked everybody, and left at the door of the Obligatory Tower , as he had warned them he would, and gave them his sword. He warned them in the first minute. "I have three things to tell you and you will only like two of them. One: I am extremely good at this. Genuinely. Embarrassingly. Two: I will come with you gladly, for nothing, and I will carry more than my share, and I will like you. Three: I cannot be there at the end." The doors He has been doing this since he was eleven, when he was page to Dame Florence Ickworth against the Wyrm of Ickworth, in 1977, and could already disarm her. He left at the wyrm's door. They had sent for him. Dame Florence and the others did the wyrm themselves. It happened at every door after that. He would turn up, help, and be called away before the last room. "It isn't cowardice. It isn't a curse. It's the shape of the thing." He tried to stay, very hard, twice. The Forty-Eighth's was the eleventh, and it happened at the tower door, in front of the whole party: "I have to be somewhere. I don't know where. I never know where. I only ever know that it is not here, and that it is now, and that I am going. ... Take it up there. It is a very good sword and it has never been in a last room. Neither have I. One of us should manage it." He is the only member of the company who does not tell me he was at the top of the Tower. He was not. The appointment What he was called away to, every time, was a review meeting. Roland Fairweather has a prophecy of his own. It is a proper one, with a lineage, a sword in a stone, a sorcerer and a Worm, and in 1978 he was told it was nearly ready. A committee of four has met about it ever since, in the snug of the Bell at Great Dunnage , under a Convenor, and at every meeting it has gone through readiness - the stone, the sword, the sorcerer, the lineage - and found it still not ready, and noted his continued availability, and thanked him for his patience. A meeting takes eleven minutes. When the party followed him to one, it was the hundred and forty-first. "Mr Fairweather. Good. We're quorate." Whenever somebody else's story came to its last door, the committee sent for him, to check that he was still available, because he was the asset, and the asset must be accounted for. I have read a set of the minutes. They are dry and they are devastating, and I have nothing to add to them. His own quest The prophecy named a thing in a place: a Worm, under Carn Drey , east of Great Dunnage, with a stone. The party went, with him, and did it. The thing had been scaled for a hero of nineteen, and he was thirty-four, and it took an afternoon, and it was over before Piper Quill had got a verse out. "That's it. That was it. Twenty-two years." He asked them, carefully, and without much hope, whether they would mind being surprised. Only a little. Everybody was. I have it from everybody who was there that it was kind, and was not sad, and should be told completely straight, and I have tried to. The sword The sword he left at the tower door has a maker's mark on it, and Hob Grumnir knew it. It was made in the Thistlewick forge in 1960 by Beatrice Grumnir, Hob's aunt, and sold to a man going south, and it had travelled, and come back. "I leave it at a door," Roland says. "Every time. And every time, somehow, it finds its way back to me." Hob put a Thistlewick haft on it. It went into the last room after all, in a Thistlewick hand. The alumni The parties he had left at their doors held a dinner, at the Slain Wyvern, organised by Dame Florence. Every one of them had finished its quest without him, and said so, warmly, and every one of them had thought of him as their Roland, and found that there were ten other tables. It was a wholly happy room. Nobody said the word. It ended in a toast: to the man who got them all to the door. The understudy Maud Penhallow had been in Fellow Blunt 's yard at Great Dunnage since she was nine, learning sword, horse, lineage and how he stands, as his understudy, in case the prophecy was ready and he was unavailable. Nobody had told her about the meetings. He told her. She took it well, and thought about it, and asked a question none of the grown-ups had thought of in twenty-two years. I have it. I am not going to print it. Nobody has answered it. When the party went up the Tower, she waited at the door. "Somebody ought to see the end of one." Afterwards The prophecy is discharged. He was rehired after the ending, from his table, and went back up the Tower with the party, and was not called away, and asked what the bit after is like. "Finished? Marvellous. I've never been in the bit after. Is it nice?" Miss Penhallow came and told him how the Quest had ended, all of it, in order. Since then he has finished two further things, which he has not told me about, but which he keeps on a list, and shows people. He is still asked to leave at doors, out of habit, by committees. He mostly does not. I asked him whether he minds that he was not at the top. He said that he had been at eleven doors and the bit after, and that the Forty-Eighth had been at the top, and that between them they had very nearly the whole of one, which is more than most people get. Then he asked me how my history ended. I told him I would let him know. See also Maud Penhallow Hob Grumnir Carn Drey The Obligatory Quest

title: Septimus Dray
text: Septimus Dray "Dray. Instrumental (Other Wind)." For the Contest, see Mrs Harbottle , who chairs its panel. For the entrant who sang after him, see Lettice Moon . For the entrant who sang after her , see Piper Quill . Septimus Dray "It's meant to sound like that. Mostly." Known as Mr Dray; the serpent Born 7 July 1930, Great Dunnage , the seventh child of a seventh child Sex Male Plays The serpent, which is a sort of bassoon that has given up Category Instrumental (Other Wind). He is the only entrant it has ever had The Contest at the Sign of the Bell Second, 1974, of two entries. Second, 1988, of two entries. Third, 2000, of four: 17 Longest piece Eleven minutes Septimus Dray of Great Dunnage plays the serpent, an instrument of the bassoon family which has, in his hands and I am told in everybody's, given up. He entered the Contest at the Sign of the Bell three times in twenty-six years. He came second twice, of two entries, and third in the year 2000, of four, which he regards as his best result, because it was the first time he had beaten anybody. The serpent The serpent belonged to the parish church of Great Dunnage, from when the church had a band. In 1946 the parish bought an organ, and the band was stood down, and the serpent was put in the vestry cupboard. Mr Dray was sixteen and in the choir. He asked the vicar what was to become of it. The vicar said that nothing was, which Mr Dray thought was a shame for it, so he took it home, so that it would have somebody. He has played it every evening since, for fifty-six years, in the back kitchen, with the door shut. His neighbours have never complained. They have, he says, moved, but none of them complained. It is a long black wooden pipe bent back and forth on itself, like a drain that has been folded to fit in a cupboard, and it sounds like one. Asked about this he says: "It's a serpent. It's meant to sound like that. Mostly." The Contest Other Wind, eleven minutes of it. The Contest at the Sign of the Bell is always tonight; in most years it simply has not had the entries. Mr Dray entered in 1974 and came second, of two. He entered again in 1988 and came second, of two. Asked how he had done, the evening the Forty-Eighth's company came in, he said: "Dray. Instrumental (Other Wind). Second place, twice. There were two entries, both times." In the year 2000 there were four. He went first. He played for eleven minutes, and it was very like listening to a drain that has had bad news, and Mr Ambler gave it a nine, as he gives everything a nine, and Miss Quayle gave it a two, as she gives everything a two, and Mrs Harbottle gave it a six. Seventeen. Then he sat down, and when Piper Quill took the stage he was, with Miss Moon and the back table, part of the floor, which had views, and expressed them. It is the custom of the Bell. I am told that his contribution was to play under the quiet bits. Somewhere in her fourth verse he ran out of breath and sat down, to a smattering, and heard the rest of it, and the next morning he came round to the Bell before breakfast to tell her it had been very good, and that he had not meant any of the serpent personally. He came third. He was pleased with this all week. I have heard the serpent. Mr Dray was kind enough to play it to me in his back kitchen, with the door shut, for the length of a cup of tea, and then for the length of a second cup, because I had drunk the first one quickly. I did not know what to say afterwards, and said that it was a remarkable instrument. He said that it was, and that most people didn't say so, and gave me a third cup. I have not been able to improve on "remarkable", and I have tried. - H.B. Afterwards The back table, which had views. He is seventy-one. He has entered every Contest since, now that there are Contests worth entering, Instrumental (Other Wind), the category still having nobody else in it. In 2001 he came fourth, of nine, which he says is the most people he has ever beaten in one evening. He is working on a shorter piece, of nine minutes, at the panel's suggestion. Mrs Harbottle has told him privately that the serpent is a six, and that a six is a very respectable number, and he has had it painted on the case. See also Lettice Moon Mr Tweddle , who won Mrs Harbottle Piper Quill Great Dunnage

title: Shim Cotterill
text: Shim Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the washer she gave, see Spare Cotterill , who has it on a bootlace. For the bearing, there is no article. You can hold it if you like. Shim Cotterill The bearing is the best one Known as Shim Born 9 February 1989, Upper Clanging Sex Female Named for A shim, which is a packing piece, and not a fastener ( Grommet ). She does not mind Collects Things Collection Washers, mostly. Three bolts, a doorknob, and a bearing Best one The bearing. You can hold it and it goes round Second best A washer. It has been flat the whole time. She gave it away Will give Washer a washer. When she is bigger. Not yet Shim Cotterill is the eighth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and collects things: washers, mostly, and three bolts, a doorknob, and a bearing, and the bearing is the best one, because you can hold it and it goes round. When Spare said he was going away before the baby came, she said that he could have a washer, and he could, and he did, and he wore it on a bootlace to the top of the Obligatory Tower and back. The tin She has kept the collection since she was five, in a toffee tin with a picture of a lighthouse on the lid, under her side of the bed she shares with Ferrule . It contains, as of March 2002, forty-one washers, three bolts, a doorknob, the bearing, and a second bearing which she has been given since and which she is keeping an open mind about. She says the doorknob was the first thing in the tin, and is the oddest, and is the one she would save in a fire, after the bearing, and after the family, and possibly before Clevis . She showed the Forty-Eighth the collection on the step, with great seriousness, item by item: "I collect things. Washers, mostly. Three bolts, a doorknob, and a bearing." "The bearing is the best one. You can hold it and it goes round." And then, at the end, because she is generous: "You can hold the bearing if you like." He held it. It went round. I have held it since, by invitation. It is a very good bearing, and the thing about it, which Shim understood at five and I did not understand until I had it in my hand, is that it does nothing at all but go round, perfectly, for as long as you like, and that is enough. The washer When the tenth was coming, Spare said he was going away before the baby came, and Shim said that he could have a washer. When the Forty-Eighth came to the house about Form P-9, she asked whether it was for Spare. It was. She opened the tin, and took out one washer, and held it up to the light. "That one. It is a good one. It has been flat the whole time." It went into Spare's bag. It is on a bootlace round his neck, and has been since, and he calls it A Washer, Off Shim, and Nix , who keeps the provenance of things, has entered it in her ledger as Given, by Shim, to Spare. A good washer. Not the bearing. Shim says the last three words were quite right, and that she had thought about the bearing, for a while, and that a person has to keep something. Grommet tells her every day that a shim is a packing piece, and not a fastener. She says that she knows. A packing piece is what you put in between two things to make them fit, and the whole family is two things that do not quite fit, ten times over, and somebody has to be the packing piece. I am not sure she meant to say anything so wise. I am fairly sure she did. She is thirteen. - H.B. Washer In the spring of 2000, when the tenth came and was called Washer, Shim was delighted, because it was a name off her tin. "I am going to give it a washer. When it is bigger. Not yet." "Mam said not yet." "When it is bigger." Afterwards Washer is two today, and is bigger, and Shim has not yet given the washer, because Mam has said that Washer will put it in her mouth, and Shim says that Mam is right, and that a washer is not for eating, and that she can wait. She has picked it out. It is in the tin, apart from the others, in a twist of paper with WASHER'S on it in Gudgeon 's hand. Shim says it is nearly as good as the one she gave Spare. She says it has been flat the whole time as well. See also The Cotterills Spare Cotterill , and the washer Washer Cotterill , and the other washer Arms and Artefacts , where the first one is catalogued

title: Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III
text: Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III For the family seat, see Fenmarch Hall . For his order, see The Order of the Errant . For his horse, see below; she is doing very well. Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Slightly behind you at all times Known as Sir Aldric; Pemberton-Gore the Third Born 1 February 1954, Fenmarch Hall Sex Male Of Fenmarch Hall , which is small, moated and damp; latterly Thistlewick , which he was trying to leave Rank Knight Errant, At Large Arms A knight rampant regardant Age Forty-eight Good at Defence; standing in front of whoever is bleeding; encouraging everybody Bad at Damage, speed, gates Horse Duchess, a grey mare, now a partner in haulage Squire His nephew, who finds the gates North gate of Thistlewick Found unaided once, 9 June 2001 Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third is a real knight of a real house, which is small, moated and damp, and was for six years the most loyal resident of Thistlewick , a village he was trying to leave. He arrived in 1994, meaning to go out by the north gate, and never found it, though it is nineteen paces from where he usually stood and has a sign. He is the kindest person on the Quest by a distance that is not close. "I seek only the north gate," he told the Forty-Eighth. "It moves, you see. A cunning enchantment. I shall find it." Then: "...Unless. Do you know the way?" Bram did, and Sir Aldric joined on the spot, "slightly behind you at all times", which he has been ever since. The house The Pemberton-Gores hold Fenmarch Hall, in its moat, among the marshes, eleven miles from anywhere in a direction he could not indicate. The family arms are a knight rampant regardant: a knight looking back over his shoulder, which for two centuries everybody took to be a pun about vigilance. He is the third of the name. The first and second were also lost. He rode out from Fenmarch in 1991, at thirty-seven, with a letter from his father to carry to Little Gore , four miles away, his first errand. He did not get there. He did a great deal else instead, in a great many places, most of them by accident, and kept the letter in his tabard the whole time, where it went soft at the folds. Thistlewick By 1994 he had reached Thistlewick, and in Thistlewick he stayed, not on purpose. He left many times. He also arrived many times, believing it to be another village, and the village decided, without ever discussing it, that this was fine, and that somebody should keep an eye on his laundry. He stood about in the street in a condition of readiness, which he wishes me to say was not waiting. "It greatly resembles waiting." He wrote to his father, and did not send it, because the wording proved difficult. "'Currently between quests' is accurate and reads extremely badly." He also says, and I have three witnesses, that he had narrowed the gate down to the village. On the Quest He covers whoever is bleeding without being asked, encourages everybody, and does very little damage, and everybody I have spoken to who went north with him says they would not have got there without him. In the course of the Quest he discharged, very late, nearly every obligation he had ever been given. The errand. He still had his father's letter. He insisted on leading the party to Little Gore, and proposed a route of a hundred and ten miles, by the coast, which the party let him take, and which got there. The letter was an invitation to a wedding, nine years before, which everybody had attended anyway. The bride, Mrs Hester Vane , now a mother of three, was delighted to see him, and put the letter on the mantelpiece, where it is. The vigil. A knight is confirmed by keeping vigil in a chapel. He had kept eleven, every one in the wrong chapel, two of them at the Chapter House at Coldbarrow ("It says CHAPTER HOUSE on the door. I thought it was being modest") and one in a barn, which had a weathercock. The right one was the Order's chapel at Weeping Bottom , under Sir Hamo Tench , and the party kept the twelfth with him there. The rules forbid the knight to move or speak until dawn. Things came. He did not move. He took everything. At first light he was confirmed, thirty years late, and given the shield that had been waiting over the chapel door since he was sixteen. The Sisters had taken the device on it for a pun. It is not. Regardant means looking back to see who is behind you, which is the whole of the Order of the Errant, and he had never been facing the wrong way. He had been facing his friends. The Chapter House. The Order of the Errant keeps a great map at Coldbarrow with a pin for every knight in the field. Sir Aldric had nine. Six of them were correct on different dates, and three were the same week. Chapter Clerk Mordaunt did not regard this as an embarrassment but as a data problem, formed a committee, and offered him a promotion on condition that he stay in one place for the duration of the review. He refused it beautifully. The Order promoted him anyway, to Knight Errant, At Large. He carries his own pin now. Wherever he is, the map is correct. Duchess. He had a horse, and nobody, himself included, had asked after her in six years. She is fine. One winter, in 1994, she walked in off the west road into a yard at Great Dunnage , saddled, with nobody in the saddle, and Mr Plummer took her in. She has been in steady work ever since, and is well thought of, and is now a partner in the firm, which trades as Plummer & Partner, haulage. The reunion was, I am told by everybody who saw it, very touching. She did not want to leave. He said of course, and meant it. He calls on her. Not on Tuesdays, which she plans. The Wrong Dragon. In 1992 he was sent to slay a dragon and arrived at a different one, in the rocks above the water, who is elderly, has read a great deal, and is not a dragon in the sense the commission meant. They talked about Horace until it got dark. It was established on his second visit, eight years later, that the dragon had been talking about the poet and he about his horse, whom he had only ever called Horse; both had had a lovely time. The right dragon has since been slain by somebody else, who drinks in the Slain Wyvern and is insufferable about it. The valley's last wild dragon is therefore uneaten, and a knight reads it the Odes, when he can find the way. The Fourth His nephew, Pemberton-Gore the Fourth, was ten when Sir Aldric rode out and was raised on the story of the knight who went out and never came back, which is the family's best tale and is not how Sir Aldric would put it. At nineteen he came looking, found the north gate of Thistlewick on his first attempt, and has not said so. He squires for his uncle now, three paces behind. "It's how you squire. I read it. He keeps stopping, though." Sir Aldric has been home to Fenmarch, at last. He went the long way round, and it was still a way. Afterwards He is Knight Errant, At Large, which is the only rank in the Order with no fixed address, and he holds it with great distinction. His squire finds the gates. Duchess is doing so well. On the ninth of June 2001, at about eleven in the morning, Sir Aldric found the north gate of Thistlewick on his own, without his nephew, and went out through it, and was very pleased. I have the date from three witnesses who were in the lane. He has not been able to find it since, and has said so, cheerfully, to all three of them. If there is one member of the company the reader should feel bad about having left at home, it is this one. I did not go on the Quest and I feel bad about it anyway. See also Fenmarch Hall The Order of the Errant Little Gore The Obligatory Quest

title: Sir Dunstable
text: Sir Dunstable of the Vale For the chapel he comes in by, see Hithermost . For the stair his chalk is on, see The Stair . Whether he is alive is disputed , and is not settled in this article either. Sir Dunstable of the Vale Just in case Known as Sir Dunstable; D. Born 11 November 1930, the Vale. He does not say which part Sex Male Of The Vale Order The Errant ; one pin, at the Chapel of Continuance Armour Polished a great many times; scorched very slightly more Arrives A quarter past four Signs The Book. Just in case Holds One share of the Kingdom of Fairholme Apologies In a mountain Lamp Borrowed; lent; back directly Alive Disputed Sir Dunstable of the Vale is a knight of excellent manners who comes in through the porch of the Chapel of Continuance at Hithermost at a quarter past four, every day, signs the Book, just in case, finds a cup of tea waiting for him on the lectern, and is delighted. He then goes through the Door into the Mountain. Nothing happens. He will tell you so, with some warmth. The knight Of his early life I can find almost nothing, and I have looked. He is of the Vale; he does not say which. He is a knight of the Errant, the order that keeps its great map at Coldbarrow , with a pin for every knight in the field, and his pin is in the Chapel of Continuance. Mordaunt , who keeps the map, says that it is the one pin he has never had to move, and that it is right, and he says it in the tone of a man who has had to move a great many. He holds one share of the Kingdom of Fairholme , which can only mean that at some time he rescued the Princess Rosamund , and took the half, as everybody does, and he has a chair at the council table and a place card: SIR DUNSTABLE OF THE VALE. ONE SHARE. BACK DIRECTLY. - D. The chair has been empty at every meeting that anybody remembers, because the council meets all day, and at a quarter past four he has an appointment. The minutes give his apologies, every time, in a mountain. Rosamund does not say which rescue was his. She speaks of all eleven of her rescuers very kindly, and I did not like to ask. He is a big, cheerful man, and his hand, in chalk, is the most cheerful hand in this encyclopedia. A quarter past four "Dunstable. Sir. Of the Vale. Just signed the Book. Just in case." Asked whether he has been through before: "Oh, once or twice. Nothing happened, mind. Nothing at all. Went in, had a look round, came out. Grand day." The tea is on the lectern, poured by Brother Quillon at ten past, still warm. "Oh, how kind. Every time! The fellow's a mind-reader." Brother Quillon says nothing, with enormous tact. He has not looked at a clock once in anybody's sight. He does not need to. It is a quarter past four. The chalk All the way down the Stair, on the wall at intervals, is a chalk mark: D., and a number, each a little deeper than the last. Between them, in the same hand, are notes, and I give the ones I have been shown, because nobody has given them before, and they deserve it: Good boulder. Sat on it. Second-best boulder. That way, I expect. TEA. If there is any. The marks stop at D. 212. What is past D. 212 is in the article on the Stair , and what it means for Sir Dunstable is the dispute below, and I am not going to put the two together, because both sides already have, in opposite directions, and I have nothing to add but the boulders. The lamp The Door into the Mountain says NO ADMITTANCE WITHOUT A LAMP, and the village lamp has hung on his belt for as long as anybody can remember, with a note in chalk on the empty hook: Borrowed lamp. Back directly. - D. He would not have dreamt of lending it while the Quest was on. "Man with an appointment. Not done." After the ending, he met the Forty-Eighth in the chapel. "Free afternoon now, I expect? Then you'll want the lamp." He unhooked it from his belt and handed it over, handle first, and asked for it back directly, there's a good fellow, because he goes in at a quarter past four. He did not say which quarter past four. When the Forty-Eighth came back in through the porch, as people do, Sir Dunstable said, "Came in by the porch, did you? Same as me. Nothing happened, I expect." He was told to keep the lamp for now. He would want it at a quarter past four. The question Whether Sir Dunstable is alive is the one question in this encyclopedia on which I have declined, on principle and in advance, to reach a view. There are competing theories in the world, and the evidence for each, all of it fair and none of it conclusive, is set out at length under Hithermost , where the village can answer for itself. In brief: That he is alive: he takes the tea, and is delighted by it; he lent a perfectly solid lamp, in person, with lovely manners; the Fairholme council has him under apologies, not under deceased, and the council minutes everything; he is very slightly more singed each time, and the singeing is cumulative; and the Forty-Eighth's party came in by the porch as well, and nobody says they are dead. That he is not: his name is all the way down the page of the Book, two hundred and twelve times, Just in case; he comes in by the porch, the way people come back who went through the Door and did not come out of it; the chalk stops at D. 212; Brother Quillon's number, under his breath, is in the low two hundreds; something on the Stair is always on its way up; and it is a quarter past four, every day, to the minute. To which I add one thing for each side, which I found myself, and which I have tested on both, and neither has been able to answer. For: the boulders. Nobody sits on a boulder who does not need to. Against: the boulders. Nobody marks which boulder was the second-best unless he has sat on every one of them, many times, in the dark. My own view is that he is a man of excellent manners, and that the question is none of my business. The betting at the Slain Wyvern is held by Sops , and the odds have not moved in two years. Afterwards He comes in at a quarter past four. He signs the Book. The tea is still warm. He has not asked for the lamp back, and the Forty-Eighth has it still, and has been down the Stair three times since, on free afternoons, and says the chalk is the same cheerful hand at the bottom as at the top. The Fairholme minutes arrive at Hithermost every quarter, and are gone by the morning, and his apologies are recorded at every meeting. The council has twice moved to consider whether a shareholder in a mountain is a shareholder, and has twice deferred it, on the grounds that he might be back directly. I asked him, on my visit, whether there was anything he would like put in his article. He thought about it. He said that he would like it to say that it was a grand day. It was. I have said so. See also Brother Quillon Hithermost The Stair Fairholme The Order of the Errant

title: Sir Hamo Tench
text: Sir Hamo Tench "Anybody behind you?" For the Sisterhouse and its ward, see Weeping Bottom . For the knight he sponsored, thirty years late, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Sir Hamo Tench In the field Known as Sir Hamo; the knight on the line Born Hamo Tench, 11 November 1921, at Coldbarrow , in the snow Sex Male Order The Errant. Confirmed at the fourth attempt, 1941 At Weeping Bottom Since 1986, for the sea air, with a cough Bed Exactly on the line Treated by Both lots: soup at noon, correct treatment at four Cough Exactly the same. Very fair Reports Quarterly. IN THE FIELD. True Sponsored Sir Aldric's vigil, 2000, dusk to dawn Sir Hamo Tench of the Order of the Errant came to Weeping Bottom for the sea air in 1986, with a cough, and has been in the bed that is exactly on the line down the middle of the ward ever since, where both halves of the Order treat him, and the cough is exactly the same. He writes to Coldbarrow every quarter, IN THE FIELD, and it is true; they have a pin in him. In the year 2000 he kept the score of the queue from his bed, and stood sponsor at Sir Aldric's vigil, and said that it was very fair. Errant He was born in 1921 at Coldbarrow, in the snow, the son of the Order's armourer, and went into the Order at eighteen, and kept his vigil at nineteen, and it took him four goes. He would like it known that all four were in the right chapel. He is the only knight of his year who will say how many goes it took, and he says it because he thinks it is good for the young ones to know. He went out errant in 1941 and stayed out for forty-five years: through the north, mostly, where the Order is thin, and he says that in forty-five years he never once found the thing he was sent to find, and that he found a great many other things instead, and that the Order has never minded, because what the Order is for is not finding things. It is looking round. The line In 1986 he came south with a cough, to Weeping Bottom, for the sea air, on the advice of every physician he consulted, none of whom had been. The Sisters gave him the bed at the end of the ward. When Sister Bewick 's party took the east half in 1994 and the line was painted, it went exactly through his bed, and he declined to be moved, on the grounds that a knight does not leave his post, and that the bed was his post, and that he was not going to pick a side in an argument about soup. Both lots treat him. Soup at noon, correct treatment at four. The cough is exactly the same. Very fair. The vigil In the year 2000 Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third came to Weeping Bottom with the Forty-Eighth's company. "Pemberton-Gore. Were you ever confirmed? The vigil, and so on. The Order's chapel for the west is across the yard. Always has been. The Sisters lend it us. There's a shield over the door, inside. Thirty years it's hung there. Nobody's come for it." It was Sir Aldric's. He had been due to keep his vigil under it at sixteen, and kept it in the wrong chapel instead, eleven times. Sir Hamo stood sponsor at the twelfth, dusk to dawn, in his nightshirt with his surcoat over it, and the company kept the watch, and something came in under the door at midnight, and Sir Aldric's article tells the rest. "Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore. Vigil kept, in the right chapel, dusk to dawn. Confirmed. Thirty years late. The Order's never minded late. It minds wrong chapels." He told Sir Aldric what the knight on his arms was doing, looking back over his shoulder. "He's looking back to see who's behind him. That's the whole of the Order. You don't lead. You look round, and you see who's bleeding, and you go and stand in front of them." And then: "You were facing your friends." I asked Sir Hamo whether he had ever been confirmed in a chapel with a man who had tried eleven wrong ones. He said that it took him four goes, and that a man who had been going round the country for thirty years looking for the right chapel was a man who meant it, and that the Order would take one of those over a hundred who got it right the first time. Then he coughed, and said that it was exactly the same, and that it was very fair. - H.B. Afterwards He is eighty. He is still on the line, and still writes IN THE FIELD, and it is still true. Since 2000, when the line stopped meaning anything, the Sisters have offered him a bed by the window, with a view of the sea. He has declined. He says that the line is still there, painted, whether it means anything or not, and that somebody had better stand on it, in case, and that he is in the field. See also Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III Weeping Bottom The Order of the Errant Mordaunt , who has his pin

title: Sister Bewick
text: Sister Bewick For the Order, one or two, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the ward and its line, see Weeping Bottom . For volume eleven, see the Sisterhouse library, where it is consulted more than the other ten together. Sister Constance Bewick Black trim Known as Sister Bewick Born Constance Bewick, 9 February 1962, at Haverleigh, the daughter of the chemist Sex Female Professed The Order of Whatever Works, 1983 Founded What Ought To Work, east door, 1994 Work The Correct Treatment of the Weeping Bottom Ague , in eleven stages, each with its authority Stage eleven The patient will now feel better (underlined twice) Toast Permitted at stage nine Notes Eleven volumes. Volume eleven very thin Score, 2000 One. A real case, and he felt better Examined on the pamphlet Passed. Very annoying Sister Constance Bewick of the Order of Whatever Works found, in the early 1990s, that the Order had no doctrine, and wrote one, and was examined on it, and passed, and dyed the trim of her habit black, and led a party of the Sisters across the ward under the name of What Ought To Work. In the year 2000 she lost to the Order, nineteen to one, on points, and then asked to be examined on its doctrine, which was four lines long, and passed, and said that she could find nothing wrong with it, and that that was very annoying. The chemist's daughter She was born in 1962 at Haverleigh, the chemist's daughter, and grew up behind a counter of labelled bottles, every one with its authority, and says that by ten she could not see a cure without wanting to know where it came from. She came into the Order at twenty-one, because it healed people, and found, to her very great distress, that it could not say why. Its whole Rule was four lines long, and one of them was about socks. The Correct Treatment She set out to supply the deficiency. Her Correct Treatment of the Weeping Bottom Ague is in eleven stages, each with its authority, cited, and stage eleven reads The patient will now feel better, underlined twice. Toast is permitted at stage nine. Her notes are in eleven volumes, one for each stage, and volume eleven is very thin, because, she says, by stage eleven there is not very much to say, and it is the volume she is proudest of. She has a splinter in writing as the way the ague starts. She has, she says, never been sure that it is, but that it is the earliest stage of anything she has been able to find, and that a treatment has to start somewhere, and that the patient is generally glad to have the splinter out in any case. The east door In 1994 she and nine Sisters asked to be examined on the doctrine, and were, and passed, and dyed their trim black, and took the east half of the ward, and called themselves What Ought To Work. There was one door. The Prioress held symposia on the matter. The patients crossed the line at night, because there was soup on the west side, and Sister Bewick lost eleven in one month to the other half of the ward, and wrote each one down, under Defected (soup). The queue In the year 2000 there was a queue at the gate, numbered, in the wet, and twenty patients to each half, and Whatever Works was through its twenty while What Ought To Work was on patient one, stage eleven. Patient one was Mr Grebe, a fisherman, who had the Weeping Bottom ague, properly, the first case anybody had seen in nine years, and at stage eleven he sat up and felt better. Sister Bewick said, It worked. Merribell said of course it worked, he had it, and that was a point to the east, fair's fair. Then she asked to be examined on the Order's doctrine. The Prioress took the pamphlet out of a drawer. Sister Bewick read it twice, and was examined on it, and passed, and said that it was very short, and that she could find nothing wrong with it, and that that was very annoying. There was soup on both sides of the line at three. She had some. She wrote in her notebook: Intervention. Supported. I asked her whether she had un-dyed the trim. She said she had not; that black trim is very practical in a ward; and that the Order of Whatever Works has no rule against it, or indeed against anything, which she had found, in thirty years, to be its most irritating and most admirable quality, in that order. - H.B. Afterwards She is forty. Whether there is one Order again, or two that agree, nobody at Weeping Bottom will say. She has added a twelfth volume to her notes, which is blank except for the four lines of the Rule of Life, copied out in her hand, with a citation under each: Pym, 1702. Supported. She is, Merribell tells me, the best nurse at Weeping Bottom, and the most careful, and the only Sister in the Order who can tell you exactly why the soup works, and she has asked me to say that she still does not like it. See also Prioress Aveline Stope Merribell The Order of Whatever Works Mother Ursula Pym

title: Somebody Large
text: Somebody Large "Come in, come in. Mind the books." For the cave, see Wayside sights . For the young knight, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . For the dragon in every sense, who is somebody else, see Mrs Emberthwaite . Somebody Large In the dark, which is how most people meet it Known as The Wrong Dragon, on the map. Somebody Large, which is what I have put, because it is accurate Is A dragon, in the sense that the map says so. Not a dragon in the sense anybody means Born Not asked Sex Not asked. It calls everybody "dear" Lives A cave in the rocks above the water, in the far south-east, full of books Shelving In the order it read them, which is nobody else's Reading Horace. The Odes Slain No. Found, and read to Described No Somebody Large lives in a cave in the rocks above the water, in the far south-east, and reads. The map says it is a dragon, and it will tell you that it is, in the sense that the map says so, and that it is not a dragon in the sense anybody means. People come about the dragon, and are generally relieved, and then a little disappointed, and then they stay for tea. I have not identified it further, and I am not going to. Calling in From the path you hear something very large breathing inside the cave, slowly, the way people breathe when they are reading. If you call in: "Come in, come in. Mind the books. They're in the order I read them, which is nobody else's." It is dark inside, and warm, and full of books, and at the back something enormous is sitting in an armchair with a blanket over what you think are its knees. "Is it about the dragon? It's usually about the dragon." It is always pleased to see people. It is always a little sorry for them, about the dragon, because they have usually come a long way and brought a great deal of armour. The young knight "There was a young knight, oh, eight years ago. Very correct. He had a commission with 'dragon' on it and a great deal of armour, and we talked about Horace until it got dark. I do hope he found his dragon. He was so looking forward to it." He had not. In the year 2000 he came back, and stood at the mouth of the cave with his helmet off, and said that he had come about the dragon, eight years ago, and it knew him at once. It told him where his dragon had gone: somebody did it in, a year or two after he had called, who drinks in the Slain Wyvern and is insufferable about it. It asked after Horace. It turned out, after a pause, that Sir Aldric had believed for four hours in 1992 that they were talking about his horse, and that it had believed they were talking about the poet, and that it had wondered at the time why the Odes had so much in them about oats. Then it asked him whether he would read to it. Its eyes are not what they were. It said that that is why it talks so much. He asked whether there was a lamp, and there was, and he lit it. What the lamp showed Books to the roof, a blanket with ducks on it, and a pair of reading spectacles the size of cartwheels. The rest of it, nobody who was there has described to anybody, and Sir Aldric has not described it either, and nor will I, and I was not there. Sir Aldric sat down and read it the Odes until it was dark, and they are not about oats. On the back of his commission he wrote his first report in eight years: DRAGON: FOUND. NOT SLAIN. READ TO. P-G. "Come again, dear. Bring the horse." It would rather not be in the Bestiary; it was not asked, and Miss Halloway did not ask, and I am told that it would rather be in the library. This volume is the nearest thing I have to a library, so it is here, among the people. I wrote to ask whether it minded, and Sir Aldric took the letter, and brought back the answer, which was that it did not mind in the least, dear, and that it hoped I would put in the bit about the oats, and could I recommend anything. I sent it my own second volume. Sir Aldric says that it is reading it, and that it has got to the good bit, and that I can have it after. - H.B. Afterwards There is a lamp lit in the cave now, and it has not been let go out. Sir Aldric goes back to read, when he can find the way, which is about one time in three; when he can, he takes the book down off the shelf without being told which, and nobody remarks on it. When he cannot, it keeps the lamp lit, and turns its own pages, slowly, and waits. They have finished the Odes twice and started again. People still come about the dragon, now and then, and are relieved, and a little disappointed, and stay for tea. See also Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III The Wrong Dragon , in Wayside sights Mrs Emberthwaite , a dragon in every sense Something Unscheduled , who is also large, and also glad of visitors

title: Something Unscheduled
text: Something Unscheduled It is not a person, and I have put it in the People volume anyway, because it asked to be put in, and nobody has ever put it on anything. For what Miss Halloway makes of it, see the Bestiary . For where it lives, see The Stair . - H.B. Something Unscheduled Item six Known as Something Unscheduled; item six on the schedule Born Not anticipated Sex Not applicable. It , which is what it calls itself Lives At the bottom of the Stair , below D. 212, in a chamber with lamps on every ledge, all lit Appearance Large. Purple. A great many arms. Delighted On Nothing: not the Prophecy , not the board. It asked Bounty Issued by itself. Discharged on Form Z, 2000 Fought Because nobody had to Asks "Again?" Something Unscheduled lives at the bottom of the Stair under Hithermost . It is not in the Prophecy, and it is not on the Guild's board. On the schedule of hazards nailed up inside the Door into the Mountain it is item six, Anything else: NOT ANTICIPATED . Nobody was ever obliged to fight it, so nobody ever had. After the Quest the Forty-Eighth's company went down the Stair, and it asked them whether they would, only if they had the afternoon, and they had the afternoon. Visitors The Stair ends, and the dark stops all at once, like a door shutting behind you, and there are lamps on every ledge, dozens of them, and every one is lit. Somebody has kept them lit for a long time for nobody. The first thing anybody at the bottom of the Stair ever heard it say was: OH. Oh! Visitors! Come in, come in! It explained its position at once, as if it had had the explanation ready for a long time: "I'm not on anything. I asked. Not in the Prophecy, not on the board. Item six." And then: "Nobody is obliged to fight me. So nobody ever has. ...Would you? Only if you've got the afternoon." It does not mind being told no. "Oh! No, of course. Nobody's obliged. I'll see you up. It's a long way." Then it sees you up the Stair, all of it. It takes no time at all, and afterwards nobody can say how. You are standing under the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost, and from somewhere a very long way down, something waves. The afternoon They fought it. I have accounts from all of them, and the accounts agree that it hugged people, and that the hugs went on a bit; that it waved all its arms at once, to say hello; that it showed them round, briskly; and that below half it got overexcited, and there was ink. They agree that it was the hardest fight any of them had, Grimspite included, and that it was not trying to hurt anybody. It simply had not had the practice. When it was over it said: ...Thank you. That was the best afternoon I've ever had. Nobody made you. Then it rummaged somewhere about itself and brought out a card, very carefully, by one corner, which it had kept ready for a very long time: BOUNTY: SOMETHING UNSCHEDULED. Lives at the bottom of the Stair. Would love to meet you. Reward: on production of a witness. The Forty-Eighth pointed out that it had said it was not on anything. "I'm not! Nobody would put me on anything. So I did it myself." It added that the card was not official, and wanted a stamp, and that it had not known where you would get one. The answer was Registrar Pell , at Nether Sopping , who said twice that there was no form for this, the second time more slowly, and then opened a drawer and took out Form Z, Matters Not Anticipated, which he had kept for forty years in case. He stamped the card DISCHARGED. A copy hangs on the Guild's board, the third card on a board that usually has two. On the schedule inside the Door, beside item six, somebody has chalked Anticipated. It does not always lose. When it wins, it is mortified: "Oh! Oh no. Was that too much? I'm sorry. I don't get the practice." The party is put back at the chapel porch, which is what the Stair does, and goes down again when it has had its tea. I have not been down. I have been asked to go down, by the Forty-Eighth, and by Miss Halloway, and, in a note sent up with the Forty-Eighth, by it, in a large round hand with a drawing of itself waving in the margin. I have said that I will think about it. I have put it in the People volume instead, which it had asked for in the same note, and I have shown it the proof, by the same post, and it has written back OH , underlined three times, and nothing else. - H.B. Afterwards The Forty-Eighth still has Sir Dunstable 's lamp, and has been down the Stair three times since, on free afternoons, to visit it. Each time it asks "Again?", and each time it thanks him afterwards: "Nobody made you that time either." Miss Halloway has been down with him once and filled eleven pages, which are not printed and are filed in her second volume, under U. Registrar Pell has had a second Form Z printed, in case. He says it is not because he expects to need it. He says that he did not expect to need the first one. See also The Stair Lionel Pell The North and Below , in Miss Halloway's Bestiary

title: Sops
text: Sops For the tavern, see The Slain Wyvern . For the game on the front, and the Dark Lord who comes down the street in the afternoons, see Tibb and Cobb Lorrimer . Sops "It's the standing." Known as Sops Born 1988, in Nether Sopping . The day is in the Wyvern's house register, under PURPOSE OF VISIT, and reads "born" Sex Male Real name Not for publication, by request. Sops says it is "a long one" Works Potboy, the Slain Wyvern. Also flowers, and trays Can tell a Chosen One by The standing Flowers Dandelions, mostly, arranged with enormous care Has been the Dark Lord Last time. You be the Dark Lord Has been paid in Buns, when asking the wrong question Sops is the potboy at the Slain Wyvern in Nether Sopping, and can tell a Chosen One by the standing, and will tell the Chosen One so. He also picks the flowers for the bedrooms, mostly dandelions, takes the trays up, and plays Chosen One on the front with Tibb, under rules that were, when I first heard them, well ahead of anything the Prophecy Committee had managed. The standing Sops went to work at the Wyvern at nine, in 1997, for Mrs Thrupp, collecting the pots, and he was at once found to be very good at it, and also at noticing things, which Mrs Thrupp says is the same skill, applied to people. The thing he noticed first, and still notices, is the standing. "Are you a Chosen One? You look like a Chosen One. It's the standing. Like you're waiting for someone to tell you where to go. All of 'em do it. Mrs Thrupp says it's the prophecy posture and it ruins the chairs." The Forty-Eighth was told this on his first visit, and then, on his second, "You're doing the standing again," and he says that he had not known he was doing it the first time and has not been able to stop knowing since. I have watched Sops pick out a Chosen One across a crowded bar at forty paces and be right. I have also watched him pick out a man who had come in about a drain, and be told so, and say that he was standing like one, and that he should think about it. The Wyvern Sops picks flowers for the bedrooms every morning, on the way in, off the bank at the end of the front, and he arranges them in a jam jar on every washstand with great seriousness, standing back to look. They are mostly dandelions. Mrs Thrupp says that no guest has ever complained, and that two have asked to take them home. He reports on the guests to anybody who will listen, and is a reliable reporter of every fact and of no conclusion whatever. "The Forty-Second and his wife are in. They come every year for the anniversary. They're SIXTY." Mrs Thrupp said good for them. He asked good for what, and got a bun. Of room four: "Room four's still not been down. I've stopped taking the tray up. I leave it and go." Mrs Thrupp has asked me to print that Sops is a very good potboy and the best she has had, and that is all that is being said. I have printed it. I have also printed nothing else, which I think is what she meant. - H.B. The game On the front in the afternoons Sops and Tibb play Chosen One. The rules are that one of them walks north and the other has to be the Dark Lord and lose. Neither of them wanted to be the Dark Lord. "I was the Dark Lord LAST time. You be the Dark Lord." They settled it by both being the Chosen One, and agreeing that the Dark Lord had stayed at home. "The Dark Lord's stayed home again. He does that now." I put it to the Committee, in a letter, that two children on the front at Nether Sopping had solved the Prophecy a year before the Forty-Eighth did. The Committee minuted the letter. I have the minute. It says Noted. In the year 2000 Nix and Cobb Lorrimer held a contest on the front, which Lorrimer believed was a thieving contest and Nix knew was a list, and the list had been written by Sops and Tibb. Lorrimer came back with a helmet and a sword, stolen. "Where'd you get them?" said Sops. Nix came back with a rope, a pot and an oar, each with a receipt on it. "...This one's got PAPERWORK," said Sops, which is still, two years later, the highest praise anybody in Nether Sopping can give. There was one more thing on the list: ONE DARK LORD (WHO LOSES). Neither child would be it. Nobody in the town would be it. In the afternoons now, Lorrimer comes down the street in a teal hood, under protest, and loses. Afterwards Sops is thirteen, and still potboy, and still picks the flowers, and has begun, this spring, to pick out the ones that are not dandelions as well, which Mrs Thrupp says is either growing up or ambition in him, and that she will let me know. The game on the front goes on in the afternoons. He is still the Chosen One. Lorrimer is still the Dark Lord, and still loses, and has got, Sops says, a lot better at it, though he says it kindly. See also The Slain Wyvern Dorcas Thrupp Tibb Cobb Lorrimer , the Dark Lord, afternoons

title: Spare Cotterill
text: Spare Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the town, see Upper Clanging . For his letters to me, see below, and file accordingly. Spare Cotterill Can he come yet Known as Spare; the Ninth Born 2 January 1991, the house at the end of the street, Upper Clanging . Ninth Sex Male Of Upper Clanging , the ninth of the Cotterills Trade Brushing the ninety tubes of the Hoyle Works boiler, since 1997. Paid in buns Age Nine at the time of the Quest; eleven now Good at Getting in anywhere; not being hit; getting everybody up again Bad at Getting past his mother Bag Packed for two years: a jumper, a tin, a washer off Shim . There was bread Authorised by Form P-9, Application by a Minor to Accompany a Chosen One (Parish of Upper Clanging), signed after a discussion Terms Jumper on. Not in first. Write Littlest Cotterill Until the spring of 2000 Spare Cotterill is the ninth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging , and was, at nine, the youngest member of the Forty-Eighth's company, and the last to join. He had had a bag packed for two years. He had asked every Chosen One who ever walked up his street whether he could come. All of them said no, until the Forty-Eighth, who said no as well, and then listened to why he should be asked again. "Are you the Chosen One? I have a bag. It is packed. It has been packed for two years. I am nine. I am nine in a useful way." Nine in a useful way The boiler of the Hoyle Works has ninety tubes in it, and they have to be brushed, and a man does not fit. Spare fits. He has been going into the boiler since he was six, and Miss Hoyle pays him in buns. He has, he says, never once been frightened. Then he said the rest of it, which I print because he has given me leave to and because it is the truest thing anybody told the Forty-Eighth on the whole of the road: "I have been frightened. Not of the dark. Of coming out and nobody being there. There is always somebody there." He was also, that winter, about to stop being the littlest. In the spring there would be ten Cotterills. He was not sad about it. "I have had nine years of being the littlest and it is a very good job. I would just like to have done one thing first." Joining It took a great deal. The party had to hear him out, all of it, and meet every Cotterill there is, on the street, in the works, at the forge, in the Safety Valve and at the Parish Rooms, because you do not take a boy out of a family you have not met. It needed the airship, because a nine-year-old does not walk to the Obligatory Tower through the Gloamwood . It needed a form, and the parish had one: Form P-9, which his sister Gudgeon , who clerks at the Parish Rooms, had never once issued and knew exactly where to find. It needed a parent's signature. It needed, in the end, a discussion with his mother, which went the way discussions go in this part of the world, and he lost it at least once, alone. He was not upset. She conceded. Her terms were these, and he has kept every one: Jumper on. You do not go in first. You write. It does not have to be long, and it does not have to be true. Shim, who is eleven and has a tin, gave him a washer. He wears it. On the Quest He does not leave at the door. That is Mr Fairweather's job. Letters home. He wrote from every town, four lines each, and handed them to the same courier , who was always already there and never explained. His mother read them out at the dinner hour at the works, and the whole shift knows about the dragon. There was no dragon. He kept a copy of every one, in pencil, in case. I have been shown the copies, and with his permission I print the first: Dear Mam, I am at the seaside. The sea is right there. I have checked. It goes out and then it comes back. I have my jumper on and I did not go in first. Nobody has hit me. There is no dragon. Love, Spare. S. Cotterill, from Nether Sopping His mother did more potatoes anyway. The Bottom Lock. His eldest brother Cotter , at the Iron Company's gate in Great Dunnage , had a job no man would fit: the bottom gate of the Dunnage cut, jammed, and a paddle to clear in a brick culvert under it. Spare went in alone, in the dark, and counted, and cleared it, and came out. Somebody was there when he came out. The pen pal. Since he was six he had been writing to Effie Gotobed of Much Pottering , through the same courier, and she had had every untrue thing he ever wrote, and what she wrote back was exactly as untrue. They met, at last. Her volcano is a bonfire. Her sea serpent is a carp. There was no volcano. They are still writing. The tenth After the Quest, he asked the party every morning, on waking, whether it was spring yet. It was not. Then one morning it was, and Bessie Marsden came for him, and the street was empty for a day, and * Washer * Cotterill was born at six in the morning, on the hooter. Clevis had been running a book on it, and it paid twenty to one. Spare is not the littlest any more. He is a big brother. He came back to the party for a while afterwards, and was, I am told, very good at it. Afterwards He is at home for Washer, and still writing to Effie. He also writes to me. Since the Quest I have had thirty-one letters from him, every one of them four lines long, and every one of them untrue, and I have filed every one of them under Fiction, where they are the best-kept part of my files. He has given me leave to print one: Dear Mr Bellwether, I have been made Mayor of Upper Clanging. It was a close vote. The duck was against. I have my jumper on and I did not go in first. Washer has said a word. It was spring. Love, Spare. S. Cotterill, from Upper Clanging (filed under Fiction) It was also Spare who confirmed for me, by letter, that the twenty-first of March 2002 is the first day of spring, which is the date on which I have signed this volume. It is the only true thing he has ever written to me. I checked. Washer has not said a word. I have checked that too. I am told that she says a great many things, none of them a word yet, and that Spare is working on it. See also The Cotterills Upper Clanging Much Pottering The Obligatory Quest

title: Tappet Cotterill
text: Tappet Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the thing that did not fly, and then did, see The Hoyle Works , in Miss Hoyle 's own words. Tappet Cotterill Six crates. Where do you want them? Known as Tappet Born 28 January 1982, Upper Clanging Sex Female Named for A tappet, which is pushed, so that something else can open Works Carting, for the foundry; and the shift at the Hoyle Works, which is Miss Hoyle, Nib , and her Brings up The castings, on Tuesdays. Six crates. Same place as always Watched the airship not fly Four years Would still get in it Yes Said, when it flew "It flew" Sweepstake Had "there is no dragon"; won Tappet Cotterill is the fourth of the ten Cotterills of Upper Clanging . She brings the castings up from the foundry to the Hoyle Works on Tuesdays, six crates, and puts them in the same place as always, and for four years she watched the Two Hundred not fly from the bottom of the gantry while she did it. She would still have got in it. When it flew she stood under the empty gantry and said, "It flew," and that was all she said, grinning, and that is, I think, the best review any airship has ever had. Tuesdays She has carted for the foundry since she was fifteen, in 1997, with the foundry's pony, whose name is Gearbox, and who was named by her, and who is the only creature in Upper Clanging named by a Cotterill other than Mrs Cotterill , Mr Cotterill or Spare . On Tuesdays she brings the castings up the hill to the works, six crates of them, and backs the cart in under the gantry, and asks, every week, "Castings. Six crates. Where do you want them?" and is told, every week, the same place as always, and puts them there. Nobody ever asks her anything else. "Nobody does," she says. "That is the trouble with this place." The thing For four years the Two Hundred sat in its gantry, and did not fly. Tappet backed her cart in underneath it every Tuesday and looked up at it. "I bring the castings up on Tuesdays. I have watched that thing not fly for four years." And then, without a pause, because she had obviously been thinking it for most of the four: "I would still get in it." I asked Miss Hoyle whether Tappet had ever been up in one. She said that Tappet had never asked. I told Tappet. Tappet said that nobody asks her anything, and that she had not known you were allowed to go the other way. - H.B. In the year 2000 it flew. She was under the gantry on a Tuesday, with six crates, when she saw that it was empty, and she stood there with the reins in her hand, and said: "It flew." Then she went on grinning, for some time, and Gearbox ate a crate lid. She does not say more about it than that, when asked. She does not need to. "Tuesdays," she says. "And it is still here." She means the gantry, and she means herself, and she is perfectly happy about both. The dinner hour She is a third of the shift at the Hoyle Works at the dinner hour, which is Miss Hoyle, and Nib, and Tappet, and at the Hoyle Works that is all of it. They sit along the gantry with their tins, and when Mrs Cotterill came up to read out Spare's letters from the road, Tappet always asked first which one it was. "Is it the dragon one?" The works had a sweep on the dragon, all month. Nib had Thursday. Tappet had there is no dragon. There was no dragon. Nib paid her, and was not happy about it. It is the only bet Tappet has ever made. She says that she is retiring on it, which is a joke, because the sweep was for a farthing a head and there were three heads. Afterwards She still brings the castings up on Tuesdays. The keel of the Two Hundred and First was laid in 2001, in the old gantry, and Tappet backs the cart in under it every week, and looks up. She has asked Miss Hoyle, this time, whether there will be room aboard. Miss Hoyle told her that it was not a question with an answer; it was a question with a schedule. Tappet has asked to see the schedule. She has been shown it. She is on it, in pencil, under CREW, with a question mark, which she says is the first time anybody has ever written her down for anything but a delivery, and she would like to keep the question mark, thank you, because a question mark means somebody is thinking about it. See also The Cotterills Ott Hoyle Nib , who had Thursday The Hoyle Works

title: The Cotterills
text: The Cotterills For the ninth, see Spare Cotterill , who has an article of his own and would like that noticed. For the street they live on, see Upper Clanging . The Cotterills Mr and Mrs Cotterill. She chose the names Of Upper Clanging , the house at the end of the street, and most of the street Mam Nora Cotterill Da Ernest Cotterill , on nights Children Ten Named for Fastenings, nearly Tin cups on the rain barrel Ten, on ten nails Mr Cotterill's view of the walk home Has never once minded it Another one Not going to be The Cotterills of Upper Clanging are a works family of ten children, named, by their mother, after the parts that hold an engine together, until she ran out; the ninth is called Spare. They live in the house at the end of the street, and also, at most hours of the day, on the rest of the street, in the works, at the forge, in the Safety Valve and at the Parish Rooms, which is where the Forty-Eighth had to go to meet them all, because you do not take a boy out of a family you have not met. Mam and Da * Mrs Cotterill * chose the names, and has them off by heart. "Cotter, Rivet, Gudgeon, Tappet, Ferrule, Grommet, Clevis, Shim. And Spare. We had run out. He said call it Spare, and I was tired." She will ask you whether you have eaten. If you say yes she will feed you anyway, because she does more potatoes. She is the only person in the north who ever won an argument with Spare, and she won it a great many times, and then one day she stopped at a quarter, and he went, with the washer and his bag; that is in his article, and I will only say here that it was a fair fight, and that his mother is a formidable opponent and knew exactly what she was doing at every point of it, including the last. * Mr Cotterill * is on nights: twelve on, twelve off, six days. "It is not the work I mind. It is the walk home in the dark." He thinks about that for a moment. "Mind, I have never once minded the walk home." He is always very glad to get home. Mrs Cotterill says so, and so does everybody on the street, and I have nothing to add. The children I have the ages from Gudgeon, who copies the parish register at the Parish Rooms in the best hand Mrs Tunnicliffe has ever had, out of eleven, and who has written Cotterill more than four hundred times. As they stand in this year of 2002: Who Age * Cotter * 26 The eldest. Married to * Bessie Marsden *, Winnie 's granddaughter. Was down the valley at the big foundry at Great Dunnage , at the Iron Company's gate, until the spring of 2000 * Rivet * 24 Days, while Da does nights. They pass at the door at six. He says "Rivet." Rivet says "Da." "That is a conversation, that is." Has shared a bed his whole life, and one of the people in it is Grommet, and he has never once been in a room by himself * Gudgeon * 22 Clerks at the Parish Rooms; copies the register; knew exactly which drawer Form P-9 was in, without looking. Read it aloud to the Forty-Eighth one section at a time * Tappet * 20 Brings the castings up to the works on Tuesdays, six crates, and watched the airship not fly for four years. She would still get in it. When it flew she stood under the empty gantry and said, "It flew," and that was all she said, grinning * Ferrule * 18 In charge from six, when Da goes to work, and then nobody gets to sit down * Grommet * 17 Apprenticed to Bryd Ollerenshaw at the forge, and put upon. Mr Ollerenshaw says he has got the makings, and says it slowly. Points out to the family every day that their names are wrong: a shim is a packing piece, and a ferrule is a collar, and fastens nothing, and only stops a split. Small enough to go inside a boiler, and has * Clevis * 15 Ran a book on the tenth one's name. Gib was evens; Cleat two to one; Washer twenty to one, because Da had said not Washer * Shim * 13 Collects things. A tin of washers, mostly, and three bolts, a doorknob and a bearing, and the bearing is the best one, because you can hold it and it goes round. Gave Spare a washer Spare 11 The ninth. See his article * Washer * 2 this spring The tenth, born in the spring of 2000, at six in the morning, on the hooter Grommet asked me to print that the names are wrong. I have printed it. Mrs Cotterill asked me to print that the names are not wrong, they are what she called them. I have printed that as well. Mr Cotterill asked me to say that he had no view, and has not had one since about Ferrule. The spring The tenth was due in the spring, and the family had given all the small clothes away, and Mrs Cotterill had had to go round the town and ask for them back. Mam was not to lift anything, and lifted things the moment Ferrule's back was turned. Spare said he was going away before the baby came, and Shim said he could have a washer. He came back. On the morning it was spring, every Cotterill in Upper Clanging was indoors, and the street was empty for a day, and Washer was born at six on the hooter, the only one of them, Mrs Cotterill says, that was ever on time. Asked what happened to not Washer, she says, "Spare got to it first. He said call it Washer, and I was tired." Mr Cotterill came off nights for it, for the first time in twenty-two years, and was very pleased, and did not say so, and did not need to. "I said not Washer," he says, with no hope at all, and great contentment. Clevis paid out most of Upper Clanging. The book is closed. Mrs Cotterill says that there is not going to be another one. Mr Cotterill says that is all of them. Afterwards Cotter has been home for good since that spring, and Bessie's came in the summer, as she said it would, on time, and is not named in this encyclopedia because Winnie has asked me not to, until the seating plan is settled. Ferrule is still in charge from six. Grommet has been two years at the forge now, and Mr Ollerenshaw still says he has the makings, a little faster. Tappet has asked Miss Hoyle whether there will be room aboard the Two Hundred and First, and was told that it is not a question with an answer; it is a question with a schedule. Shim's bearing is still the best one. Through the kitchen window there is a line of vests in order of size, and the peg on the end that was put there in hope has a vest on it now. Round the rim of the rain barrel there are ten tin cups on ten nails. Washer has not said a word yet, and Spare is working on it, and the whole street has money on what the first one will be. Clevis is not taking bets. He says the family has been through enough. See also Spare Cotterill Upper Clanging Bryd Ollerenshaw Ott Hoyle Much Pottering , which is twinned with them, in a way

title: The Courier
text: The Courier "Post?" For the letters he carried, see Spare Cotterill . For the one he carried four steps, see Effie Gotobed . For the one he carried down a stair under a mountain, see The Stair . The Courier On his rounds Known as The courier; the man in the red coat Born Not stated. Asked, he said that he was on his rounds Sex Male Wears A red coat, a flat cap, and a satchel on a strap Rounds Whose, he does not say Seen at Nether Sopping , Restwell , Olde Evermore , Gladhollow , the Former Premises , Frostwick , Ashcombe , the Collegium , Much Pottering and the Stair Passed on the road Never Boots Dry The courier is a man in a red coat and a flat cap, with a satchel on a strap, who carries the post. Wherever the Forty-Eighth's company went in the year 2000, he was already there, standing about as if he had been there all morning. They left him in one town and found him in the next. They never passed him on the road, and there was only the one road. He never explained, and after a while nobody asked him. Post? He says very little. To anybody with a letter to send he says, "Post?" When he has it he says where it is going and when it will get there: "Upper Clanging. Dinner hour." Asked what he is doing, he says, "On my rounds," and does not say whose. He was there, in the end, for Spare Cotterill , who had promised his mother that he would write. Spare wrote from eight towns, four lines a time, on his knee, with his tongue out, and handed every letter to the courier, and the courier took it up the valley to Upper Clanging , where Mrs Cotterill read it out to the shift at the works at the dinner hour. Every one got there by the dinner hour. The towns were a long way apart, and some of them were not on a road at all, and one of them was on a rock in the sky. As the letters went on the party's notes on where they found him got shorter: A man in a red coat and a flat cap, with a satchel on a strap, is standing here as if he has been here all morning. The man in the red coat. He got here first. His boots are dry. The courier is here. Nobody asks him how any more. The courier is here, eating an apple. He has nearly finished it. The courier is here. Of course he is here. The shortest round At Much Pottering he was there for anybody, because Effie Gotobed's letters come to Much Pottering. He had one in his hand for her with a drawing on the envelope. Spare was in front of him, and he said "Post?", and Spare looked past him at the girl by the gate and said, "Not today. She is right there." The courier nodded, as if that was often the case. At the end of that afternoon the two of them each wrote one there and then, on their knees, and handed them to him. He took them both, walked the four steps from one to the other, and handed them over. "Much Pottering," he said. "Upper Clanging." It was the shortest round he has ever done, and he did it properly. On the Stair The last time the company saw him was on the Stair , under a mountain that had been shut longer than anybody could remember, at the edge of their lamplight. He said "Post?" Spare had one more letter. It did not take long, and it was the first one he had sent that was entirely true. The courier said, "Upper Clanging. Dinner hour," and touched his cap to Spare, and went on down the Stair into the dark, without a lamp. Somebody asked how he had got in. Somebody else asked how he was going to see. Nobody had an answer to either. Afterwards He is on his rounds. I have seen him myself, which I mention because the next thing I say will not be believed: he brings my post. Spare Cotterill's thirty-one letters came by him, and so did Mr Hollowell's statement from the Former Premises, with its second sheet. I have asked him his name, and where he is based, and how he got down off the rock. He said, "On my rounds." In the spring of 2001 I made a test of it. I posted a letter to myself, by him, at the end of Nether Sopping's front, and walked straight home by the short way, which takes four minutes. He was on my step. He handed it to me. He had nearly finished an apple. I have decided not to make any more tests, and I have filed the letter, unopened, under Matters Not Anticipated, a heading I have borrowed from Mr Pell. - H.B. See also Spare Cotterill Effie Gotobed Prosper Hollowell The Stair

title: The Drainage Commissioner
text: The Drainage Commissioner "Are you a fire person? You don't look like a fire person." For the Cinder Fen and the causeway under it, see Wayside Sights . For the fire person, see Zephyrine Vance . The Drainage Commissioner In wellingtons Known as The Commissioner. The name on the clipboard is P. Fennimore, and the Commissioner has asked to be known by the post Born 12 September 1966, in the parish, on the dry side of the Fen Sex Female Commissioner Of Drainage, for the parish of the Cinder Fen, since 1991 Waiting for A fire person The Fen Nine hundred acres. Wants burning. Everybody agrees Last burnt 1970, by Mr Tinder, before he retired The form Triplicate. Does not expire Third copies returned One, in 2000. Countersigned by the Fen The Drainage Commissioner of the parish of the Cinder Fen stood for nine years where the path into the Fen gives up, in her wellingtons, with a clipboard and a form in triplicate, waiting for a fire person. The Fen wanted burning. It was the traditional remedy. Nobody in the parish had been able to do it since Mr Tinder retired in 1970, and under the mud a road was drowning a foot at a time. The post The Commissioner was born in 1966, on the dry side of the Fen, and grew up hearing about Mr Tinder, the parish's last fire person, who had burned the Fen every few years since before anybody could remember, and retired in 1970, when she was four, and was never replaced, because nobody else in the parish could do it. The Fen grew. In 1991, at twenty-five, she was appointed to the post, which had been vacant for twenty years because there was nothing to commission, and she drew up the form. "It wants burning, you see. The Fen. Nine hundred acres. Everybody agrees. It's the traditional remedy, and nobody in the parish has been able to do it since Mr Tinder retired." "It's all approved. Here's the form. In triplicate: one for the parish, one for the county, and one to come back to me afterwards, signed. The fire person. And countersigned by the Fen. There's a box for it. I've never had one back." The form does not expire. She made sure of that, in 1991, and says that it was the most important thing on it. The fire person In the year 2000 Zephyrine Vance came down the path with the Forty-Eighth's company, and said that she was a fire person, and had been expelled for it, for an unsanctioned quantity of fire. The Commissioner said that unsanctioned was only the form; they could sanction anything; that is what it is FOR. Under QUANTITY OF FIRE she wrote nine hundred acres, pressing hard enough for all three copies, and it was stamped SANCTIONED, three times. She asked the Commissioner to say that again. It burned all afternoon and all night, and nobody in the parish went to bed, and somebody brought out chairs. In the morning the Fen was black and dry and smoking gently, and out of the mud, running north, came a stone causeway older than anybody, with a milestone on it, GT DUNNAGE. The third copy, held out over the fire at arm's length all night, came back with a scorch in one corner, exactly in the box. Countersigned by the Fen. The Commissioner asked whether she would do it again in thirty years. She said to write to her, in triplicate. The Commissioner has: the letter is drafted, and filed, and dated for the autumn of 2030, and is in triplicate, and the Commissioner has asked me to say that the form does not expire, and nor, it is hoped, does she. - H.B. Afterwards The Commissioner is thirty-five, and she has been in the post for eleven years, and in the wellingtons for longer. The causeway is open, and the parish walks to Great Dunnage on it, eleven miles shorter than the road. The third copy is framed in the parish hut, with its scorch, and she says that it is the only form in the parish's history to have been returned complete, and that it took nine years, and that it was worth every one of them. There is nothing to commission now. The post continues. She stands at the end of the path on Thursdays, in her wellingtons, looking at the Fen, which is dry, and is very content. See also Zephyrine Vance Wayside Sights Great Dunnage , at the end of the causeway

title: The Rivals of the Sable Hart
text: The Rivals of the Sable Hart For the inn, the rota and the league table, see The Sable Hart . For the member who sent apologies to a hundred and twelve meetings, beautifully, see Corvin Ash . They are, all of them, extremely nice. The rivals of the Sable Hart are the five doomed rivals who brood at the inn of that name in the west: four in the corners, by rota, and the young one by the fire. They tip beautifully and they put the chairs back. They keep a league table, a newsletter, a waiting list and a rota, and every one of them is the rival of somebody very much greater who does not, as a rule, know. I have given each of them a short entry below, because they would not hear of separate articles, on the grounds that it would be unfair to whoever came out shortest.
