Hollin Crake Silas Veyle Thaddeus Rook Lucan Morrow Kit Blackwood Mrs Garrow Member Born Sex Corner Rival of Table, 2000 Hollin Crake 12 November 1931 Male The Secretary's, by the window Not stated, out of tact Third, 36 Silas Veyle 31 October 1966 Male The darkest, until Monday Not stated, out of drama First, 41 (the scar) Thaddeus Rook 6 April 1954 Male The darkest, from Monday A very great archer, east coast, ninety-three this year Fourth, 35, by himself Lucan Morrow 20 December 1968 Male The one by the coat hooks Mr Pennock, a very great wizard, who does not know Second, 37 (a vow, in the rain) Kit Blackwood 1 March 1979 Male None. The stool by the fire Nobody yet. There is a list Twelve (keen) Hollin Crake, Secretary "Good evening. Hollin Crake, Secretary. Are you anybody's rival at all?" He is the only man in the history of brooding who stands up when you come in. He has the Secretary's corner, by the window, because somebody has to be able to read the rota, and his tankard sits on a coaster he brought from home, so as not to mark the table. He was born in 1931 and has been a member since 1958, and Secretary since 1972, and he devised the rota in 1985, when a fifth member was elected and there were, as he says, four corners and five of us. You can see the difficulty. The darkest corner changes hands on a Monday. NOBODY broods in it out of turn, however rainy. He would not tell me whose rival he was. He said that it would be unkind to the other party, who was a very great man, and who had been dead since 1971, and had never known, and that a rivalry was a private matter between a man and his own shortcomings. He said that the other party's widow sends him a card at Christmas, and that he has never told her either. Silas Veyle "...Leave me. The shadows are mine. Until Monday. Sorry. That came out very possessive. They're mine until Monday, and then they're Rook's, and he's earned them." He has the darkest corner, in rotation, and the scar, and the most points on the table, forty-one, mostly for the scar. Don't ask about the scar. Nobody asks about the scar, and he looks, very briefly, disappointed. The curtain behind him is drawn, and there is no window behind it, and he says it makes a real difference. His pint is untouched; it is for atmosphere. He orders a fresh one at nine and leaves that too. I asked about the scar. He was so delighted to be asked that he could not, for some minutes, speak, and then he said, with great feeling, "Don't ask about the scar," and bought me a drink. Mrs Garrow told me afterwards that he got it in 1988, on a garden rake, in her mother's time, and that it is the best thing that ever happened to him, and that I was not to say she said so. - H.B. Thaddeus Rook "Thaddeus Rook. I keep the table. Points for a vow, a scar, a dramatic exit, and standing about in the rain." He keeps the league table, ruled in red, beside the rota. Standing in the rain is two points. Standing in the rain on purpose is one. They are quite strict. A dramatic exit through a door that turns out to be a cupboard is minus two. He was fourth in 2000, "because I never give myself the benefit of the doubt. That's the whole point of keeping the table." He is the rival of a very great archer on the east coast, who was ninety-one in 2000, and he is giving him every chance. When Corvin Ash was reviewed for points in 2000 and was found to have sat in one corner of the Slain Wyvern for eleven years, Mr Rook was asked whether there was a category. "There is now." He then moved himself down to fifth, by his own request, and was visibly happier there. Lucan Morrow "Lucan Morrow. I edit the newsletter. There's one on the table. It's free. It's always been free." The newsletter is Overshadowed, and it is free, and he has edited every issue since the first, in 1990. He is the rival of a Mr Pennock, who is a very great wizard, and who does not know. Morrow writes to him at Christmas. "Every year. A lovely card. He thinks I'm his cousin." Morrow has never corrected him, and says that it is the warmest correspondence of his life, and that if Mr Pennock ever finds out he will have to give up either the rivalry or the cousin, and that he does not know which, and would rather not be made to choose. Kit Blackwood "Could I have that category, one day? When I've got a corner?" He is new, and first on the waiting list for a corner, any corner, and has been since March of 2000. Until he gets one he broods on a stool by the fire, in the warmest and brightest seat in the inn, as hard as he possibly can. It is quite hard to brood by a fire. He is getting better. Mr Crake says he has a gift for a long silence. He is nobody's rival yet. There is a list for that, too. In the winter of 2001 he made his first dramatic exit, the door having been planed at last, and it was a cupboard, minus two, and he took it extremely well, plus one, a new category. Mrs Garrow Mrs Garrow keeps the house, and was born in 1962, and has kept it since 1985, and says they are no trouble, love: four in the corners and the young one by the fire, every night of the year, and the middle of the room empty as a church. She buys the bottles with the gloomy labels because her regulars prefer them, and what is inside is elderflower cordial. The tankards each have a small knitted hood over them, to keep the dust off. She knitted them. She says that she has never once in seventeen years been asked to, and that they are her regulars, and they ought to look the part. Afterwards Corvin Ash attends now. Not every week. He sends apologies when he does not. "We find it very reassuring." He is second on the table, behind the scar, with thirty-nine points in a category of his own, and his stool at the middle table is still kept, and still dusted. Kit Blackwood is still first on the waiting list, and has been offered the Secretary's corner, temporarily, by Mr Crake, on a Wednesday, and has declined it, on the grounds that it would not be fair to the rota, which Mr Crake says is the most promising thing he has heard from a young member in forty years. See also The Sable Hart Corvin Ash A Glossary of Cliches , for the doomed rival

title: Tibb
text: Tibb For the other child on the front, see Sops . For the Dark Lord who stays at home, and the one who now comes down the street, see Cobb Lorrimer . Tibb "Nobody's the Dark Lord." Known as Tibb; "the other child", by the front Born 30 July 1990, Nether Sopping , in the end house of Rope Walk Sex Male Plays Chosen One, on the front, in the afternoons Has never been The Dark Lord Mum says We're not to have stolen things. She says it twice Co-author of The list Last item on the list ONE DARK LORD (WHO LOSES) Tibb is a boy of Nether Sopping who plays Chosen One on the front with Sops in the afternoons, and who settled, with Sops, the question of who should have to be the Dark Lord, which the Prophecy had not settled in two thousand years, by deciding that nobody should, and that the Dark Lord had stayed at home. The settlement "We're both the Chosen One now. Nobody's the Dark Lord. He's at home." I asked Tibb whose idea that had been. He said it had been both of theirs, at once, on a Tuesday, after a long argument about whose turn it was, and that once you thought of it, it was obvious, and that it was strange nobody had thought of it before. I agreed that it was strange. I have since put the question to the Prophecy Committee , who minuted it as Noted. The difficulty with a game in which nobody is the Dark Lord is that nothing happens in it. He and Sops would walk north along the front together, to the end of the harbour wall, both Chosen, and there would be nobody there, and they would walk back. "Still no Dark Lord," Tibb told the Forty-Eighth. "Still working." It was said without complaint. It was said, I think, the way an engineer says that a thing is under review. The list When Nix and Cobb Lorrimer had their contest on the front in the year 2000, it was Sops and Tibb who wrote the list. Lorrimer came back with a helmet out of the outfitters' window and a sword off the knees of a man having a day off, who came up the street after it in his socks. "I STOLE them," said Lorrimer. "I'm a thief. It's the whole point of me." "Mum says we're not to have stolen things. She says it twice." Nix came back with a rope, a pot and an oar, each lent until sundown and signed for. Then Tibb said, "There's one more thing on it." It was ONE DARK LORD (WHO LOSES). Neither child would be it. Nobody in the town would be it. Lorrimer was it, in a teal hood, under protest, and lost, and has lost every afternoon since, and the game has had, for the first time, somebody at the end of the harbour wall. I called on his mother, Mrs Ada Tibbett, on Rope Walk, to ask whether the name was short for anything. She said that it was short for Tibbett, which is what we all are, and that I was not to put that in, and that she had said it twice. I have put it in once. - H.B. Afterwards Tibb is eleven, and he still plays on the front, and is still the Chosen One, and Sops still is as well, and they still do not take turns. Lorrimer comes down the street in the afternoons. Tibb says that Lorrimer loses better than he used to, and has started losing in a different place each day, to keep it interesting, and that yesterday he lost on the harbour steps, and fell in, on purpose, and that it was the best one yet. See also Sops Cobb Lorrimer Nix , and the list Nether Sopping

title: Tobias Frayne
text: Tobias Frayne This article is about the man and his cottage on the coast road, which are hard to take apart. For the Sister who would not make it twelve, see Merribell . Tobias Frayne Putting the kettle on Known as Mr Frayne Born 20 May 1946, the cottage on the coast road; the first time he was carried out of it Sex Male Of A green-roofed cottage on the coast road, between the road and the beach Revived Eleven times, in thirty years The ladder Four The well Two The bull Two The cliff One Others Two. He was in a hurry and it was silly Twelfth Declined, on his behalf The jar Paid out Tobias Frayne lives in a cottage on the coast road, and has been revived by passing adventurers eleven times in thirty years, on the grounds that they were going that way anyway. He was never in danger, and did not think he was. He had found a thing that always worked out, and a great many kind people, and he liked both. He has not died since 2000, on medical advice. The cottage It is one room, with a green roof, on a square of grass between the coast road and the beach. Visitors are welcome, and told to come in, and to mind the ladder. "Well - don't mind it. Stand wherever you like." The ladder goes up the wall to a hatch in the ceiling, and its third rung was, until recently, cracked clean through. "Goes like a biscuit. Thirty years I've meant to mend it, and it's never quite been the moment." A new rung leant against the wall beside it, planed and sound and still in its paper, and the paper had gone yellow. On the table there is a book, ruled in four columns, WHEN, WHAT, WHO, REMARKS, with eleven entries in it. I give seven, as he wrote them: Ladder. A paladin. Very kind. Well. Two elves. Sang to me. Bull. A cleric. Cried a bit. Ladder. Same paladin. Less kind. Cliff. Four of them. Carried me up. Ladder. A wizard. Did it from the gate. Bull. Same cleric. Laughed this time. and four more in the same hand. Every remark in the last column is some way of saying lovely. There is a shelf of tonics, liniments and smelling salts, hardly any of them in his hand: each label has a date on it, and a name, and in case, from the eleven, who came back afterwards with something for him. And there was a stoneware jar on the table, the lid tied down with string, heavy with crowns, labelled in the book's hand: FOR WHOEVER IS GOING THAT WAY. The eleven "Oh, nobody DIES on the coast road," he says. "Somebody always comes by. Adventurers. They're going that way anyway, they say. And they're ever so kind about it. Kneel down. Hold your hand. Ask your name. Ask it twice, sometimes. You don't get that from the parish." I set this down without comment, because it does not need one, and because Mr Frayne does not think there is anything to comment on, and I was brought up to take a man's word about his own house. The first was in 1970. The book had a twelfth line, ruled, and dated each day, with nothing in it, and the pen beside it, uncapped. The treatment In the year 2000 Merribell called, with the Forty-Eighth, and he offered to pop up the ladder while the kettle was on, and she said that he would not, and had his wrist before he reached it, and counted. Pulse, good. Colour, good. Collarbone, set four times. Wrist, set twice, by a paladin, beautifully. ("Didn't charge, either.") "There is nothing wrong with you, Mr Frayne. That's the trouble." She looked at the book, and at the shelf of tonics with other people's names on them, and at the twelfth line. "I am not going to raise you a twelfth time. Nobody is. That is the treatment." He asked who would come by, then. She said the parish. Ask them to tea. Through the door. On purpose. He asked whether you could do that. "People do it every day, and they don't fall off anything first." He thought about that for a long time. Then he cut the string on the jar with the bread knife and tipped it out on the table, a hundred crowns for every one of the eleven, put by for thirty years for whoever would not take it, and said that it was for whoever was going that way, and that she was going that way; she had said. She said thank you, Mr Frayne. Then she said that now they would leave, and that that was the other half of it, and on the way out she told the company not to look back, because it was part of it. Behind them the door shut, and the kettle went on, and nobody went up the ladder. Afterwards He has had the parish to tea. "Twice. Nobody fell off anything." That was in 2000; it has been a good many times since, and the parish comes through the door, like people, and he says it is lovely, and means it the same way the book does. He mended the ladder himself, not very well. It holds. The new rung is fitted by somebody who has never fitted a rung before, and the old paper is in the fire. The twelfth line in the book is still empty. The pen has been capped, and put away in the drawer. The jar is on the table, empty, with the string cut, and the label still says FOR WHOEVER IS GOING THAT WAY, and he has started, he tells me, putting crowns back into it, a few at a time, for no reason he can explain, except that somebody might be. See also Merribell The Order of Whatever Works

title: Toby Wendle
text: Toby Wendle Welcome to Gladhollow! For the town, the well and the pot beside the well, see Gladhollow . For his granny's barrels, read on, and put the potion back. Toby Wendle Welcome to Gladhollow! Known as Toby; the Welcomer (2000); the Farewell Boy (2001-) Born Tobias Wendle, 2 February 1990, Gladhollow , in the house behind the barrels Sex Male Post The Welcomer, west gate, 1997-2001. One sentence Ways of saying it Fifteen. The fifteenth was not finished Headgear A saucepan. It rings like a bell Falls over Never. He has had a great deal of practice Has told nobody About the bookcase, the well, or the pot. It is all in the duties Promoted Farewell Boy, spring 2001. Two sentences. The cap fits Toby Wendle was the Welcomer at the west gate of Gladhollow in the year 2000, aged ten, with a saucepan on his head. He was allowed one sentence, Welcome to Gladhollow! , and no other, and so he worked on it, and had fifteen ways of saying it, written out on his kitchen table under the heading FIFTEEN WAYS. He told the Forty-Eighth everything about the town without saying a single other word. It was all in the duties. The saucepan He was born in 1990 in the house behind his granny's barrels, the younger of two boys, and became the Welcomer at seven, in 1997, when the post fell vacant because the previous Welcomer, his brother Ned, was promoted to Farewell Boy. The post came with a saucepan. The saucepan is the Welcomer's, and has been since anybody can remember; it is the town's, and is kept on a nail by the gate, and is worn on the head, because heroes coming into a town do not look where they are going, and walk into the Welcomer, and it is better for everybody if it rings. It rings like a bell. He does not fall over. He straightens the saucepan, takes a deep breath, beams, and says Welcome to Gladhollow!, and there is no rest of it, and he is delighted. Fifteen ways He is not allowed a second sentence. He has worked on the first. The list on the kitchen table runs: the Standard; the Formal; the Whisper; the Song; the Salute; the Surprised; the Slow One; the Dramatic Pause; the Rainy Day; the Very Loud; the Sorry; the Tour; the Evening; the Classic; and the fifteenth, which in the year 2000 was not finished. The Forty-Eighth heard all fifteen, in order, over several visits, and at the fifteenth Toby tried it anyway, going up at the end: Welcome to Gladhollow? And then he looked anxiously to see whether a question counted as a second sentence. It was decided that it did not. He wrote something on the back of his hand. Once, overexcited, he got as far as "Welcome BACK to Glad-", and stopped dead, and said, very quietly, "...I'm not allowed that one," and then, with enormous restraint, "...Welcome to Gladhollow." The Slow One, one word at a time, is for anybody from abroad. The job description does not mention anybody from abroad. He checked. He did it anyway, and when I asked him why, he said Welcome to Gladhollow , very slowly, one word at a time, and looked at me until I understood that I was from abroad, which, from Nether Sopping , I suppose I am. - H.B. The duties Asked about the town, he says Welcome to Gladhollow, with his eyes on the mayor's house, and both hands flat beside him, pushing, like somebody sliding a very heavy bookcase aside. His eyes go to the well, and the pot beside the well, and the well, and the pot, and then, very innocently, to the sky. Then he points at his granny's barrels, and at his granny, and puts his hand on his heart. He has said nothing. It is all in the duties. What a hero does with this is the hero's business, and the Forty-Eighth found the bookcase, and the well, and the key under the pot, and gave Granny Wendle a potion back out of her barrels, which she said was Tuesday's knee sorted. Toby said Welcome to Gladhollow! about it, the Very Loud, which is for people on horses, and nobody was on a horse. Granny Wendle His granny's barrels stand outside her door, and every hero who comes through has the potions out of them. She does not mind. They are very good potions. She would like them back, though. They are for her knees. Each is rolled in a stocking in the straw with a label sewn in, PLEASE RETURN TO MRS WENDLE, GLADHOLLOW. Toby has, since he was seven, quietly gone round after every hero and asked for the stocking back, and has got, by his count, thirty-one stockings and four potions. He says the stockings are the important part. They are hers. Afterwards He is twelve. In the spring of 2001 Ned went to be apprenticed to the wheelwright, and Toby was made Farewell Boy, at the east gate, in the cap, which fits. He has two sentences now, Farewell from Gladhollow! Mind how you go!, and he uses both of them with enormous care, and I am told that Mind how you go is said fifteen different ways. The new Welcomer is a girl of eight, who has been given the saucepan, and has asked him how he managed. He has not told her, because it is not in his duties. He has given her the list. See also Gladhollow A Glossary of Cliches , for the welcomer who says one thing

title: Tolly
text: Tolly For the man on the log, see Godfrey Stopford , the Forty-Sixth, whose name I have off her envelopes. For the other half of the correspondence, see Nabb . Tolly "He's worth two stamps." Known as Tolly, of the Forty-Sixth; Miss Toller, on the post office's books Born Margaret Toller, 2 March 1960, Nether Sopping Sex Female Party The Forty-Sixth's, 1980; maps Writes Every month, in the narrow hand Stamps Bought in twos. It's a long way Sheet of stamps Bought, once, 1989. Gone off the counter. Came back, 2000. Forty Knows That the letters are unanswered; that Nabb thinks she doesn't; that reading them is the answer Tolly carried the maps for the Forty-Sixth's party in 1980, and was there when he sat down. She has written to him every month since, in the narrow hand, and she does the stamps, two to a letter, because it is a long way, and he is worth two stamps. She addresses the envelopes, and that is how I have his name. The maps She was the party's map-reader, at twenty, in 1980, having been for four years the junior clerk at the harbour office who kept the charts. She says that she had the whole of the road north drawn out in pencil, every turning to the Obligatory Tower , on a sheet she had copied herself, and that they used about an inch of it. She still has the sheet. The inch is worn through. The rest is as clean as the day she drew it, and she says that is how it should be, and that a map nobody uses is a map that has kept somebody safe. The letters She writes once a month, and Nabb writes once a month, and the letters go out on Thursdays. Nabb thinks that Tolly does not know they are never answered. "She asks about the letters, does she. Nabb thinks I don't know they're unanswered. Nabb has thought that for eleven years." She has known all along. She has known, too, what the Forty-Sixth told the Forty-Eighth: that reading them is the answer. She has not told Nabb. She says that Nabb is happier thinking she is protecting her friend from something, and that Tolly herself is happier letting Nabb think it, and that the Forty-Sixth is happiest of all, sitting down, and that it would be a poor sort of friend who spoiled a thing like that by explaining it. "Two stamps. It's a long way, and he's worth two stamps." The sheet of stamps In 1989 she bought a whole sheet of stamps, once, forty of them at the old rate, off the counter at the Wyvern , to save going in every month, and was very pleased with herself, and put it down on the counter while she paid for her half, and it was gone. She never found out where. She went back to buying them in twos the next month, and has bought them in twos since, and says that she found she did not mind, because going in to buy them had turned out to be part of it. In the year 2000 Nix came into the Wyvern with the eleven things on the first page of her ledger, which she had taken in 1989, at fifteen, and had never sold, and was taking back to their owners. "Stamps. A sheet of forty, off the Wyvern's counter. The old rate." "We don't buy them by the sheet. We buy them in twos." "You bought a sheet once," said Nix. "Eleven years ago. I've had it ever since." Tolly counted them. There were forty. "Twenty letters, then. He's worth two." She went back to her envelope, and it had two stamps on it before she had finished the sentence. The rate has gone up since 1989, and a stamp at the old rate is not, strictly, enough for the Gloamwood . Tolly knows this. She has made up the difference every month in coppers, taped to the envelope, and the man who collects the post has never once said anything, and the Forty-Sixth, she says, will have noticed, and will think it is very funny, and will not say so either. - H.B. Afterwards She is forty-two. She still writes in the narrow hand, and still lets Nabb think what Nabb thinks. She is working through the sheet, two at a time, and has used, as I write, twenty-two of the forty, and says that when it is done she will go back to buying them in twos, on Thursdays, and that she is looking forward to it. See also Godfrey Stopford Nabb Nix , who counted the sheet The Slain Wyvern

title: Walt Ashbury
text: Walt Ashbury "Going up? Say the word. I'll play you up." For the inn, see Restwell . For his wife, who cooks, see Hester Ashbury . For the doctor who watches him, see Dr Pike . Walt Ashbury Eight bars Known as Walt Born Walter Ashbury, 21 June 1950, the shortest night of the year, at Restwell , upstairs at the Eight Hours, in room six Sex Male Married Hester , 1973 Plays The fiddle, on the bottom step of the stairs at the Eight Hours Plays whom up Everybody Repertoire Eight bars. The same eight, every time Since 1974 Tried a different tune Once. They came down tired Guests a year About twelve hundred, every one of them better Walt Ashbury sits on the bottom step of the stairs at the Eight Hours in Restwell , with a fiddle, where he can see the whole room, and plays every guest up to bed: eight bars, the same eight bars, every time, since 1974. Every guest comes down in the morning better than they went up, whatever was wrong with them, and nobody can say why, least of all the retired doctor by the fire, who has a theory, and does not like it. The step He was born in 1950 upstairs at the Eight Hours, in room six, on the shortest night of the year, which his mother said was the only night she ever spent there that she did not sleep through. His father kept the inn, and played the fiddle in the evenings, badly, in the bar. Walt took it up at nine. By twenty he could play anything, and did, in the bar, and the guests went up to bed at all hours and came down as tired as anybody does at an inn. In 1974, at twenty-four, on an evening when the bar was full and he had played everything, he sat down on the bottom step of the stairs to rest, and began to play, without thinking, eight bars he had never played before, and the guest who was going up at that moment, a carter with a bad back, went up, and slept, and came down in the morning without a bad back, and said that he had not slept like that since he was a boy. Walt played the same eight bars for the next guest, and the next. He has played them for every guest since. He does not know where they came from. He says that he did not make them up, exactly; that they were there, on the step, and he played them. "Everybody. Twenty-six years. Same eight bars, every time." "It has to be that one. I tried a different one, once. They came down tired." The tune I have heard it, twice: once going up, and once from the bar, sitting where I could see. It is eight bars long, in what I believe Piper Quill would call a minor key that is not sad, and it goes up, and it does not come down again at the end, but stops, at the top, as if it had arrived somewhere. Miss Quill, who has stayed at the Eight Hours, has tried to write it down, and says that she can write down the notes and that the notes are not it, and that she has stopped trying, and that it is the only tune in the world she has ever stopped trying to write down. I went up to bed at the Eight Hours on my way back from the coast road, and he played me up, and I came down, and it was morning, and I agreed that it was. I looked at the clock and I would rather not say. I have written in the register: eight hours. Remarks: I am a historian, and I should like to have stayed longer. I have said that elsewhere in this volume. I find that I wanted to say it twice. - H.B. The tired The night he tried a different tune was in 1983, for a wedding party, who asked for something cheerful. He played them up with a jig. They came down in the morning tired, every one of them, and cross, and the bride said that she had not slept a wink and that she was to be married that afternoon and would look a fright, and she did, she says, in every picture, and she has never let him forget it, and she comes back every year, on the anniversary, with her husband, and asks for the eight bars, and sleeps like a top, and is delighted. Hester His wife Hester has listened to those eight bars twelve hundred times a year for twenty-eight years, from the kitchen, and has never once asked him to stop. "He is very good at it." That is all she says about it. It is all he needs. He says that he would play the eight bars for nobody but the guests, and that he plays something else for her, in the kitchen, when the house is asleep, and that it is not eight bars, and that it is none of my business, and I have not asked. Afterwards He is fifty-one. He is still on the step. The Eight Hours has had more guests since 2000 than ever, because the road to the Tower is busy with people going to see the chair, and every one of them goes up to the eight bars and comes down better, and many of them come back on the way home. Dr Pike still watches him. Walt says that the doctor is welcome to watch, and that he has watched himself, often, and has never found out anything either. See also Hester Ashbury Restwell Dr Pike , who has theories Piper Quill , who stopped trying

title: Washer Cotterill
text: Washer Cotterill For the family, see The Cotterills . For the book on the name, see Clevis Cotterill . For the brother who named the tenth, and was nine at the time, see Spare Cotterill . Washer Cotterill 21 March 2000, on the hooter Known as Washer; the tenth; "not Washer", formerly, by Da Born 21 March 2000, at six in the morning, on the hooter, at the house at the end of the street, Upper Clanging Sex Female Age Two, today, as this volume goes to press Named for A washer, which goes under a nut, so that it holds. Grommet has not ruled on it; it is the only one he says he would not dare to Named by Spare, who got to it first. Mam was tired Price Twenty to one On time Yes. The only Cotterill who ever was Register Entered at a quarter to seven, in ink, in a new column, ruled First word Not yet. The whole street has money on it Is owed One washer, by Shim , when bigger Washer Cotterill is the tenth and youngest of the Cotterills of Upper Clanging , born at six in the morning on the first day of spring in the year 2000, on the hooter, the only one of them, Mrs Cotterill says, who was ever on time. Mr Cotterill had said not Washer. Spare got to it first. Before The tenth was expected in the spring. Every Cotterill in the town knew it, and so did the Forty-Eighth, the moment he came up the street, because Mrs Cotterill told him at the door, "Nine. And one in the oven," and then, "Ten in the spring. Mr Cotterill is very pleased." The family had given all the small clothes away and Mrs Cotterill had to go round the town and ask for them back. Ferrule was in charge of her not lifting anything. Winnie Marsden had been to the seating plan of the Class of 'Nineteen and found that it had no column for it. Clevis had opened a book on the name, with Gib at evens and Washer at twenty to one, because Da had said not Washer. Shim had said that Spare could have a washer if he went away before the baby came, and Spare had gone away, with the washer, to the Obligatory Tower . So Washer was talked about, priced, provided for, argued over and twice named before being born, and she was, at the time, the most discussed person in the north who had not yet done anything. Spring The Forty-Eighth's company came down from the Tower, and after the ending Spare went down the Stair under Hithermost , and on the Stair, in the lamplight, a man in a red coat asked whether there was any post. Spare wrote his ninth letter home on his knee, and it said Dear Mam. Is it spring yet? Spare., and it was the first one he had ever sent that was entirely true. He asked every morning, on waking. Is it spring yet? He was told not yet, and took it extremely well, and was told soon, and asked how soon, and looked at the sky as if it were late with something, and said that he would ask tomorrow, and did. Then one morning the light was a different colour, and the air smelt green, and something was singing that had not been singing the day before, and he was told yes. "Then I have to go home. Mam said ten in the spring. It is the spring." He had the bag on before anybody had finished saying it. It was, as everybody who was with him has told me, the first deadline in the whole of the Quest that anybody could actually have missed, and he did not intend to. He was home by the evening. Every Cotterill in Upper Clanging was indoors, and the street was empty, which nobody in the town could remember happening before, and every window in the house was lit. Bessie was at the Cotterills' door, not her own, and saw him, and opened it, and held it. "I have to go in now," said Spare to the company. "Come back in the morning. Not before. Mam said." He went in with the bag, and the door shut. Mr Cotterill came off nights for it, for the first time in twenty-two years, and he and Rivet passed at the door at six the next morning, the both of them going in. At six o'clock exactly the works hooter went for the day shift, and Washer was born on it. Bessie told it at the door to anybody who came by: "Washer. Six o'clock this morning, on the hooter. Mrs Cotterill says it is the only one of them that was ever on time." Gudgeon entered it in the register at a quarter to seven, in ink, and had to rule a new column, because the old one was full. Clevis paid out most of Upper Clanging. Cotter came home on the Saturday, for good. And Spare came out onto the step, and told the company, as if they could not possibly have heard: "It is a baby. It is very small. It got hold of my finger and it would not give it back. I am not the youngest any more. I am a big brother." He said it, I am told, the way other people say they have been knighted. The name Mrs Cotterill had always had Washer in reserve. Mr Cotterill had said not Washer. She has given me the whole of what happened, and it is short: "Ten. Washer. Spare got to it first. He said call it Washer, and I was tired." Mr Cotterill's account is shorter. "I said not Washer." He says it now with no hope at all, and great contentment, and has added, since: "Washer. I have stopped saying not." Asked why Washer, Spare told me, in a letter that I have not filed under Fiction, that a washer is the thing that goes under the nut, so that the nut can hold, and that you do not notice it, and that without it the whole thing works loose. He was nine. The letter is four lines long, and three of them are about something else. The washer that Shim gave Spare, and that went to the top of the Tower on his bootlace, was taken out of her tin the winter before Washer was born and has never been back in it. There is a second one in the tin now, in a twist of paper, labelled WASHER'S, for when she is bigger. I do not think anybody in the family has noticed that the tenth Cotterill has been given a washer twice over, once by name and once by Shim, and I have not pointed it out, because in that house, if you point a thing out, somebody opens a book on it. - H.B. Now Washer is two today, the twenty-first of March 2002, the first day of spring, which Spare has confirmed by letter, and which is why I have dated this volume as I have. She is walking, and has not said a word yet, and looks, when Grommet starts on the names at breakfast, at Grommet, with what Grommet calls an expression. Spare is working on the first word. The whole street has money on it. Clevis is not taking bets. Clevis says the family has been through enough. She is a girl, which is the one thing about her that nobody in Upper Clanging had a book on, because Mrs Cotterill let it be known in the autumn of 1999 that it was none of the town's business, and in that town, when Mrs Cotterill says a thing is none of its business, the town goes and finds some other business. It makes five and five. Ferrule has noted it on the slate in the kitchen, under BALANCE, and nobody is allowed to rub it out. The peg at the end of the line of vests in the kitchen window, which was put up in hope, has a vest on it now, the smallest. Round the rim of the rain barrel are ten tin cups on ten nails, and the tenth is Washer's, and is the only one with a handle on both sides. See also The Cotterills Spare Cotterill , who named her Clevis Cotterill , who priced her Shim Cotterill , who is keeping a washer for her Ernest Cotterill , who said not

title: Wilhelmina Blagg
text: Wilhelmina Blagg "Chair, Festival committee." For the town and its Working Group on the Winter, see Frostwick . For her grandchild, who has read everything, see Clem Blagg . Wilhelmina Blagg "It's an asset." Known as Mrs Blagg; the Chair; Nan, to Clem Born Wilhelmina Thorley, 30 April 1941, Frostwick Sex Female Chairs The Working Group on the Winter, since 1979; the Festival committee, which is the same people on a different day Apologies for absence None, ever. Nobody in Frostwick has missed a meeting The curse An asset. Page one of the register Depreciating at Four per cent a year Towards Spring, eventually. Budgeted for Asset register, item 4 Mr Stagg . Struck through. NOT AN ASSET. A PERSON. - W.B. Ceiling Most interesting of all Wilhelmina Blagg chairs the Working Group on the Winter at Frostwick , which governs the town, and which has never once had apologies for absence. She will tell you that the curse is an asset. It is on page one of the register, depreciating at four per cent a year, towards spring, eventually, which has been budgeted for. The auditor called it forward-looking. He came in August. It was snowing. He was very impressed. The Working Group She was born in 1941 in Frostwick, under the old winter, the daughter of the town's accountant, and was keeping her father's books at sixteen. She was nineteen in the spring when Perce Stagg came down the hill and the snow began to drip, and she was at the extraordinary meeting on the twelfth day, as her father's clerk, and took the founding minutes, which are the ones I print in the article on the town, and which end, item five, The peas. Deferred. She has been chair since 1979, when her father retired from it, and in twenty-three years she has introduced the asset register, the depreciation, the budget for spring, and the auditor, and has moved and carried the renewal of Miss Pargeter 's contract, on time, three times. She says that a town that lives off its winter ought to know what its winter is worth, and that it is worth a great deal, and that she has it written down. "The curse? It's an asset. Page one of the register. Depreciating at four per cent a year. Spring, eventually. We've budgeted for it." The register's fourth item was, originally, Mr Stagg. It is struck through, and beside it, in her hand: NOT AN ASSET. A PERSON. - W.B. She has asked me to say that this was a clerical error by a junior member of the Working Group in 1981, and that she corrected it the same afternoon, and that Mr Stagg has never been told, and that I am not to tell him, because he would only go pink. The ceiling "The minutes are on the table. Do read them. Clem has. Clem has read everything." Clem has. In the year 2000, at seven, he told the Forty-Eighth, unprompted, that Nan says Mrs Stagg has never once been cold, not in forty winters, and that it must be Mr Stagg's lanterns. The committee, I am told, found the ceiling very interesting, and Mrs Blagg found it most interesting of all. I asked Mrs Blagg about it. She said that the remark had been made in a private conversation, in her own kitchen, about the fire Mr Stagg lays every morning, and that it had been entirely innocent, and that he had reported it entirely accurately, and that that was the trouble with Clem. She then moved that the subject be closed. It was carried. There were no apologies for absence. - H.B. Afterwards She is sixty, and still in the chair. The register has been audited again, in 2001, in August, in the snow, and the auditor was very impressed again, and the curse has depreciated by a further four per cent, and spring is, by her figures, about twenty-three years off, which she says is well within the budget. She has put Clem on the Festival committee, as a co-opted member, without a vote, to take the minutes. He takes them off by heart, and writes them up afterwards, and they are, she says, the most accurate minutes the Working Group has ever had, and she is sometimes sorry about that. See also Clem Blagg Frostwick Pargeter , under contract Perce Stagg , not an asset The Eleven Days

title: Winnie Marsden
text: Winnie Marsden For the town and the Safety Valve, see Upper Clanging . For her granddaughter, who has her face, see Bessie Cotterill . For the dinner, you cannot get in. You had to be born in it. Winnie Marsden Class of 'Nineteen Known as Winnie; Mrs Marsden; "Gran", by Bessie, and since the summer of 2000 by Cotter, who was told to Born Winifred Platt, 4 October 1919, Upper Clanging , in the Cold Winter 's autumn Sex Female Class Of 'Nineteen. Two hundred and forty, near enough all together Married Albert Marsden, pattern-maker, 1941; widowed 1979 Drinks A half of shandy, on a doily embroidered CLASS OF '19 Dinner Every year, second Saturday Seating plan Settled when they were four, in 1923 Column for the Cotterills None, until 2000. Drawn in, in pencil Not being unkind about it No Winnie Marsden sits by the fire at the Safety Valve in Upper Clanging with a half of shandy on a doily embroidered CLASS OF '19. She was born in the autumn after the Cold Winter, when the foundry was banked down for six weeks and there was no heat in the whole town but what was in the houses, along with two hundred and thirty-nine others, and they have had a dinner on the second Saturday every year since, with a seating plan settled when they were four. You cannot get in. She is not being unkind about it. The Cold Winter In January 1919 the foundry at Upper Clanging was banked down for six weeks, for the first and only time in its history, for want of coke. There was no work. There was no heat in the whole town but what was in the houses. In the autumn two hundred and forty children were born, near enough all together, and the town has called them the Class of 'Nineteen ever since. Mrs Tunnicliffe at the Parish Rooms, who keeps the census, says so, and so does the census, which, as she says, is only dates. Winifred Platt was born on the fourth of October, in the middle of them, at the house behind the Safety Valve, a fitter's daughter. She says that she does not remember a time before the Class, and that she supposes nobody does, it being the sort of thing you are born into, like a family, only larger and with a better dinner. The plan The Class went to school together in 1923, at four, in two rooms, and the teacher, Miss Agnes Thewlis, sat them in alphabetical order on the first morning, and wrote the order down on a sheet of foolscap, and that sheet, kept by Winnie since 1950 in a biscuit tin, is the seating plan of the Class of 'Nineteen's dinner, and has been used at every dinner since the first, in 1939. It has two hundred and forty places on it. It does not have a column for anything else. "Class of 'Nineteen. We have a dinner. I do not suppose you would know about the dinner." "There is a seating plan. There has been a seating plan since we were four. You cannot get in. I am not being unkind about it. You had to be born in it." She married Albert Marsden, a pattern-maker at the foundry, in 1941, and he was not Class of 'Nineteen, and in thirty-eight years of marriage he never once went to the dinner, and he said he did not mind, and she says that he did not, and that he waited up. The Class of 'Nineteen is eighty-two this year. Of the two hundred and forty, a little over sixty came to the dinner last October. Every place on the plan is laid all the same, and every place that is not filled has a card on the plate with the name on it, in Winnie's hand, and the dinner is served round them, and nobody in Upper Clanging thinks this is anything but the right way to do it, and nor, having been allowed to stand at the door for five minutes, do I. - H.B. The Cotterills In 1999 her granddaughter Bessie married Cotter Cotterill , the eldest of the foundry family, at the chapel, on a Saturday. Winnie spent the reception at a side table with the plan. "My granddaughter has married one of the foundry family. There are nine of them. Ten in the spring. They will all want seats. There is a plan. It was settled when we were four. It does not have a column for this." She went home early and sat up with it, and nobody has been told what she said to it. In the spring of 2000, when the tenth came: "Ten, then. I have been to the plan. There is a column for it now. I drew it in myself. In pencil." And then, in the summer, when Bessie's came: "Second Saturday. There will be a high chair." It is the first thing on that plan that has ever been in pencil. Bessie says it is the first time she has ever known her gran to leave anything open to revision, and Winnie says that it is not open to revision, it is in pencil, which is a different thing, and that pencil is for things that are going to change, and that a baby is going to change, and that is all. Afterwards She is eighty-two. She still sits by the fire at the Safety Valve, on the same chair, on the same doily, and Mr Kell still brings the half without being asked. The plan has a pencil column now, with eleven Cotterills in it and a high chair. Bessie's child, her great-grandchild, is not named in this volume, at her request, until the seating plan is settled, and she has told me that she does not expect it to be settled, and that that is rather the point of pencil. See also Bessie Cotterill Mrs Tunnicliffe , born in June The Cotterills Upper Clanging The Cold Winter

title: Wren Halloway
text: Wren Halloway For her work, see the Bestiary , which is hers, and which I have printed whole and not touched. For the goose, see The Goose , in the same. Wren Halloway Not to be jogged Known as W. Halloway; the Cataloguer Born 17 April 1972. She has not said where, and has corrected two people who guessed Sex Female Of A corner of the Slain Wyvern, and then outside it, and then a seat under the goose Trade Cataloguer of monsters, by what they are Carries A crossbow; seventeen specimen jars; the monograph Good at Several hits at range, poison, taking armour off things, getting two of whatever they drop Bad at Raw damage; tolerating the phrase "basically a dragon" Published The Fauna of the Valley , by What They Are , 2000 Reviewers Three, one a duck Named Bramus agricola On the wyvern A goose Wren Halloway is a cataloguer: she does not hunt monsters, she documents them, and the fighting is a step in the methodology that she resents. "You cannot measure a wing that is actively in use." She went north with the Forty-Eighth, came back with eleven type specimens and the only honest monograph on the creatures of this region, and is the author of the Bestiary in this volume, which I commissioned from her and have not altered by one word, because she would know. She met the Forty-Eighth in the Slain Wyvern, at a table of specimens, and the first thing she said to him was, "Don't jog the table. Nothing in here is dead enough to be casual about." Her terms for joining were first refusal on anything unusual, that she write the entries, and that nobody - "NOBODY" - say "it's basically a dragon". She has since drafted a clause about the phrase. The discipline Everybody else names monsters after how they died. She names them after what they are, which she calls the same job done properly. Taxonomy, for her, is a moral position. The difficulty is the previous authority. Doctor Amias Rowbotham FRS spent forty years naming some three hundred species after himself, his subscribers and his dogs, and the standard work is therefore a monument to a man rather than a description of a valley. Every correction she publishes reads to the field as an attack on a dead man they were all rather fond of. She published once, at twenty-three, and was reviewed by three of his students. She does not discuss the reviews. I have read them, and she is right not to. The goose She was thrown out of the Slain Wyvern for saying that the wyvern over its mantel is a goose. It is a goose. Halloran Vance , the Forty-First, brought it home from the marshes in 1940 and made it into a wyvern with wire, in two days, because a whole town was waiting on the quay for a monster and he had nothing to give them. Mrs Dorcas Thrupp keeps the Wyvern, and would not take the wyvern down, or have it corrected, because the Forty-First was a good man and brought back what he could, and that is where the conversation ends. Miss Halloway was right, and she was right at length, and she was asked to leave for it. Of everything that happened to anybody in the company, it is the nearest thing to unfair. What came of it is a second plaque. It is beside the first. It does not correct the first, and does not repeat it. It says what the bird is, and where it was got, and by whom, and why. Mrs Thrupp read it twice, said nothing, and put it up herself. Both plaques are on the wall now. On the Quest The monograph. Publication at the Collegium Arcanum required a type specimen, intact, for every entry: eleven fights she objected to and conducted anyway, with a very bad grace and very good results. It required a subscription list, which she got, and three Fellows to review it, which she got, one of whom is the Collegium's duck. The Fauna of the Valley, by What They Are, by W. Halloway, is on the Collegium's shelf, in a gap exactly an inch wide that had been waiting for it. It has eleven type specimens and three reviewers. Page four hundred says goose. The Gloamwood Society. The Society had existed for forty years to prove that the Thing In The Woods is not there, with a newsletter, nine members and an annual walk. She proved it comprehensively. The Society was delighted. Its newsletter had its best ever issue. One member was quietly devastated, and was looked after very carefully by everybody else, and was fine by the end of the walk. The Fenmarch Collection. At Fenmarch Hall there is a gallery of impossible animals in glass cases, and she was engaged to authenticate them. They were composed by Mr Ottershaw , taxidermist, who is ninety and unrepentant and an artist: he did not forge them, he composed them, and the joins are magnificent. She wrote it up honestly, which required her to say that the workmanship is the finest she has seen, which she meant. Seventy-nine of the animals are composed. The family has never been prouder. Case forty was not examined. Bramus agricola. She named a new species after the Forty-Eighth: a small brown thing that lives in turnip fields, is of no consequence whatever, and is remarkable for one attribute, which is that it survives things it has no business surviving, by luck, repeatedly, in a manner she describes in print as "statistically indefensible". He was deeply touched until she explained why, and then deeply touched anyway, because it was accurate. The Prophecy does not read journals. It has read this one. Afterwards She is welcome in the Slain Wyvern, which she affects not to care about. She sits under the goose, by choice, most evenings, writing. Volume two of the monograph is in hand. It will contain a corrigendum about one specimen, which she will not name. I asked her whether case forty at Fenmarch had been left unexamined by accident. She said that a cataloguer does not examine a specimen she has not been engaged to examine, and that I should mind my own entries. I have looked at case forty myself, through the glass. I do not know what it is. That is not my field. See also The Bestiary , by W. Halloway The Goose Bramus agricola The Slain Wyvern The Obligatory Quest

title: Ysolde Marrow
text: Ysolde Marrow For the man she kept alive, see Ambrose Fitch . For the table she chairs, see the Healers' Table . Ysolde Marrow With the kit open Known as Mrs Marrow; the Forty-Fourth's Born 19 January 1922, Nether Sopping Sex Female Trade Field medicine, forty years of it Of Nether Sopping , the table by the bar in the Slain Wyvern Age Eighty Kept alive The Forty-Fourth, nine years, on and off; a duke's son, nine weeks His hit points Four. She counted Chairs The Healers' Table Never been to Thistlewick Argued with it anyway Forty years Ysolde Marrow is a field medic of Nether Sopping , who kept Ambrose Fitch , the Forty-Fourth Chosen One, alive for nine years, on and off, and has had an argument with a village she has never been to for forty years since. She sits at the table by the bar in the Slain Wyvern with a canvas roll of field medicine open in front of her, out of habit. She is eighty, and will tell you so, usually as a reason why you are not to argue with her. The trade She will tell you, if you ask what the job was like, about the duke's son. The party was paid to walk him from the coast to the Tower , for the exposure, they said; for his character. He had four hit points. She counted them. He walked into every fight they had, not bravely, but the way you walk into a room, and she stood in front of him for nine weeks. He made it. He runs a shipping concern now, and sent her a card once, with a Y in the wrong place in her name. Everybody in the Wyvern has heard about the duke's son. Everybody nods anyway, because it is a very good one. What she says about the trade itself she has from Ambrose: you keep someone alive, and then they go and live, and you don't get to see much of it. "He was right about most things." In her kit, which every fold of is worn where somebody's hand went, there is one bottle labelled FOR AFTER. It is tea. The Forty-Fourth When they put Ambrose in the mound, with a curse on it, she had a good deal to say, and has said it at the bar for forty years to anybody from Thistlewick who would stand still. "Forty years they ignored him, and then they did THAT." In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth came back from the Barrow and found her looking up before he had said anything at all. "You've been out to the mound." He told her what Ambrose had asked for, and that it was there now, on the top, facing the sea. He told her, too, the message: that she was right about the four hit points. She was quiet for what felt like a long time. Nobody in the room looked over. Everybody in the room was listening. "Forty years I've had that argument with a village I've never been to. They wanted a hero in a mound. He wanted somewhere to put his legs up." Then she gave the Forty-Eighth her kit, forty years of field medicine in a canvas roll, and told him not to argue, because she was seventy-eight and had had a night. "You're going north. They all go north. Come back, and I'll want it back, and I'll be very rude about the state you've got it into. Do you hear me? Come back." The Table Once a year she chairs the Table, in the back room of the Wyvern behind the red curtain: every party medic within forty miles, around a long table, the worst thing each of them has ever had to improvise with, round the table, in turn. In 2000 the Table had a new member, Merribell of Thistlewick, who is the youngest by thirty-eight years, and who had nothing to tell them, because nobody had ever died on her. Mrs Marrow told her to write it down, all of it, every cup of water and every pair of socks, while she still thinks it is boring, because one day it won't be. "And the day it doesn't, you come down here, and you tell us. That's what the Table is for, love." The Table's kit went to the youngest. It always has. It had been a while. Afterwards The kit came back. I am not able to say what state it was in, having been told by Mrs Marrow that the state it was in is a matter between her and the Forty-Eighth, and having heard, from the other side of the bar, what she said to him about it, which took some time and was very rude, as promised. She has it open in front of her again, out of habit. The bottle labelled FOR AFTER has been refilled. When Bram told her he had been in Ambrose's cottage, she asked whether he had watered that thing in the pot. He had. "He watered it every morning for forty years. It was dead when he bought it. He said it was the principle." She has been out to the Barrow since, once, and sat on the bench, and come back, and has not said a word about it to anybody, which is the longest she has gone without saying a word about Thistlewick in forty years. The Table sat again in 2001, and Merribell spoke, for eleven minutes, and the minutes record it as the most useful address in the Table's history, and the subject was water. Mrs Marrow chaired. She has told me that she is not going to retire, and that if I print anything to the contrary she will want it back. See also Ambrose Fitch The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth Merribell The Slain Wyvern The Healers' Table

title: Zephyrine Vance
text: Zephyrine Vance For the institution, see The Collegium Arcanum . For the duck, see the same, under Fellows . Zephyrine Vance Fine Known as Formerly of the College Born 15 January 1968. She says she was very small and nothing caught fire, and her mother says otherwise Sex Female Of The Gilded Turnip , Thistlewick, "just passing through" since 1989 Trade Hedge mage; fire person Educated The Collegium Arcanum ; best in her year at Kindle Standing there Disputed by everybody, including her Good at Elemental damage, in quantity Bad at Being hit; budgeting Votes held One, by proxy, unused Fire, unsanctioned One quantity, 1989 Fire, sanctioned Nine hundred acres, 2000, in triplicate Zephyrine Vance is a hedge mage who has lived in Thistlewick since 1989, when she left the Collegium Arcanum after an incident involving the Dean, a duck, and what the enquiry called, twice, "an unsanctioned quantity of fire". The Dean is fine. The duck is fine. She would like it understood that everyone is fine. When Bram came to her table in the Gilded Turnip and began to speak, she said, "Don't. Whatever it is, don't." He said it was a quest. She asked what sort. He said a tower, with a Dark Lord in it. "That's the most fire-adjacent thing anyone has said to me in eleven years," she said. "Give me my hat." The incident The facts are these. In 1989, at a dinner at the Collegium, Miss Vance said aloud that a junior fellow's paper had gone out under somebody senior's name. She was told to let it go. She did not let it go. Some time later in the evening there was fire, in a quantity that had not been sanctioned, in the vicinity of the Dean and a duck. Nobody was hurt. The enquiry used the phrase twice. I have read the enquiry. I have also read the paper: On the Kindling of Damp Materials, by Dr Hapgood, which went out under the name of the Master, and the Master is a committee. The quantity of fire was unsanctioned. The point she was making was correct. Both of those have been true since 1989, and for eleven years only one of them was in the file. She was the best student of her year. Hedge magic is the discipline of doing the same work with worse equipment in somebody's garden, and she has been very good at it for a long time. It was not what she trained for, and she drank at the Gilded Turnip in the manner of somebody waiting for a letter. The letter It came. It bore the Collegium's crest, and it informed her that she was on study leave. "STUDY leave. I was EXPELLED. There was an ENQUIRY. It used the phrase TWICE." It turned out that the papers expelling her had been drafted and initialled and never filed, and she had therefore been on unpaid study leave for eleven years, in good standing, and owed eleven years of library fines. The fines were the largest sum of money anyone on the Quest ever saw written down. Sub-Librarian Prewitt was courteous, immovable and correct. How the matter ended depends on whom you ask, and I have asked her, and the answer I got was a look. The Collegium's register says she is a member of the Collegium in good standing, with her fines paid on the Library desk out of a purse. I have also seen a letter, in her hand, filing her own expulsion, eleven years after the event, at her own request. I have printed both, because one of them is true, and she has asked me to leave it that way. The duck The duck survived the incident, and the Collegium, not knowing what else to do with a bird that had given evidence at a formal enquiry, made it an Honorary Fellow. It has since sat in Congregation, held a chair, and acquired views on the endowment. In 2000 a vote was called and the quorum was short by one duck, which was on a pond four miles away. It had to be walked. It has four hit points and walks into everything. The party walked it. The Collegium has been quorate ever since. The duck's vote is held by proxy, permanently, by Zephyrine Vance. She has not yet used it. She is saving it. Other fires The Cinder Fen. Nine hundred acres of sodden fen had been drowning the road to Great Dunnage since the parish's last fire person retired in 1970. The remedy is fire, and in 2000 she was asked for it, in writing, with a form that asked her to state the quantity. "It's the first piece of paper about me and fire that I've liked." The fen was burnt, sanctioned, in triplicate; the road is dry; the form came back countersigned. * Dean Fenwold .* The Dean has made a second career of being the man who was fine, and does an after-dinner talk about it. He asked her to do the fire again, small, in a hall, with buckets. She refused, then agreed, on terms. It went wrong in exactly the way it had gone wrong the first time, for exactly the same reason, which is that the room was wrong. His talk now ends with the room being wrong, and Dr Hapgood's paper has Dr Hapgood's name on it. I take that to have been the terms. The lay-by. The hedge mages have an association. It meets in a lay-by on the west road, because none of them will host, and has been trying to agree a name for nine years. One of them taught himself out of a book with four pages missing, and is therefore better than the Collegium at exactly four things. It has four members now, and still no name. Item one is carried forward. Afterwards She is still in Thistlewick, now on purpose. She no longer drinks at the Gilded Turnip like somebody waiting for a letter, because the letter came. She still has the duck's vote, and still has not used it. I asked her what she was saving it for and she said she would know it when she saw it, and that it would not be soon, and that I was not to put that in. I have put it in. She is welcome to set fire to the page. Middle C on the Gilded Turnip's piano is a little warm. She tells me that is her, and has been since 1989. See also The Collegium Arcanum Dean Fenwold The Gilded Turnip The Obligatory Quest The Incident at the Collegium

title: Ashcombe
text: Ashcombe This article is about the village by the lake, and the one under it. For its best-known son, who took its name, see Corvin Ash . Ashcombe Known as Ashcombe; the village that is fine Where The east, on the shore of Ashcombe Lake Flooded 1989, on a Tuesday Lost Nobody. Not so much as a hen Dry by Teatime Rebuilt Only better Distance from the old village Eight miles, by the road. A stone's throw, as the crow flies Drains Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, a fall of one in two hundred Puddles since None Post Every letter answered. It's policy Ashcombe is a village on the shore of a lake in the east. Thirteen years ago the lake came up over the old village, on a Tuesday, and every soul in it walked up the hill with the kettles, and was dry by teatime, and by teatime had decided to build it again, only better. It did. The old village is under the lake. The new one has the best drains in the world, and is extremely cheerful about all of it. The village The plaque is polished stone, facing the lake, with the gilt still bright: HERE, ON THE DAY OF THE WATER, EVERY SOUL IN OLD ASHCOMBE CAME SAFE UP THE HILL, AND WAS DRY BY TEATIME. WE BUILT IT AGAIN, ONLY BETTER. And under that, smaller: MIND THE DRAINS. THEY ARE VERY GOOD. VISIT THE MUSEUM! (FREE.) Everything is new. The church is pale stone with a green roof and coloured glass in every window, and the bell is the old one, brought up the hill on a cart on the day of the water, because nobody saw why they shouldn't. It rings at six for dinner, and if you ring it at any other time a door flies open up the street and somebody shouts COMING! and then, rather put out, Oh. It isn't six. The church door's card says SERVICE AT SIX. KEY WITH THE BELL. The bell is at the top of the tower. The school has a brass plate, ASHCOMBE SCHOOL, polished, and under it, also polished, 'Very Good.' - H.M. Inspector of Schools. The blackboard has a history of Ashcombe on it: 1. IT WAS THERE. 2. IT WAS WET. 3. WE MOVED IT. On every desk there is a paper boat. Wilf, a small boy with another paper boat, is looking for somewhere to sail it, and there are no puddles, and Mr Weir says there will not ever be a puddle again, and says it like it's good. In one front room a line is painted on the wall at knee height, with a date beside it, and a smiley face. In another a family is at tea with every chair on little stilts. Old habits. The scarecrow wears waders and a life ring. The post office, kept by Mrs Dimmock, answers every letter that comes to Ashcombe. It's policy. ALL LETTERS ANSWERED, says the card in the window, and under it, WE MEAN IT. Years ago they had one addressed to THE RUINS OF ASHCOMBE, and so the Ruins wrote back, a lovely long letter, hoping he was keeping warm. The post box by the door is iron, painted red, with a slot like a polite smile, and is Hob Grumnir 's, and he asked for it back, a while, and Mrs Dimmock asked where the letters would go, and said that box had had a letter from the Ruins of Ashcombe in it, and you cannot take a box back after that. Hob said no, you can't. The Drainage Museum The Ashcombe Drainage Museum is free, and so is the enthusiasm. * Mr Hubert Weir *, Curator, in a coat with gold frogging, stands in the middle of the room with his hands behind his back, the way a man stands in a room he is proud of. Fourteen hundred yards of culvert, a fall of one in two hundred, and not one puddle in Ashcombe since the day they went in. The flood, he says, was a tremendous success: everybody out by dinner, everybody dry by tea, and not so much as a hen lost. They have the Roll. The new village is eight miles from the old one, by the ROAD, sir. The road goes all the way round the lake. As the crow flies you could skim a stone on to the old church roof. The exhibits are worth an afternoon. The plan of the drains, on a great sheet of parchment, every culvert named in copperplate; the longest is called Hubert. Grown men have stood in front of that plan and gone quite quiet. Exhibit one is the stone that was set in the old high street over the only drain old Ashcombe had, carved DRAIN, and the card beside it says, kindly, It was not up to it. An empty plinth, beautifully polished: THE FLOOD (ON LOAN TO THE LAKE). Exhibits fourteen and fifteen are a plant (dry) and another plant (also dry). The painting, The Lake, at Evening, painted for the Flood Dinner, has the old church spire painted in under the water, very small, and it is the best bit of the picture, and they know it. The Roll was taken on the hill on the day of the water, in the schoolmistress's hand: every name in the old village, a tick by each, and after every tick one word, DRY. Two hundred and six ticks. Beside one name, in place of a tick, in the same careful hand: Away. (Written to.) That is Corvin's. Two hundred and six people stood on a hill in the rain and counted, and when they got to him they wrote down where he was, and then they wrote to him. He was in a corner of the Slain Wyvern , being away, on purpose. They counted him anyway. The Flood Dinner Every year there is a Flood Dinner at the church hall, with soup, a fish, a pudding and speeches, and the toast is TO THE WATER, WHICH WAS VERY GOOD ABOUT IT. The menus are pinned up in the museum, one for every year, and at the foot of each is the speaker: the Curator; the Curator; Mrs Ash, on knitting; the Curator; the Curator. The notice for the year 2000 read: SPEAKER: TO BE CONFIRMED, and under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Again. It was confirmed: C. ASH. (CONFIRMED.) And under it, in pencil, Mr Weir has kindly offered. Next year. Two hundred and six people, and the old bell rung for six exactly. What Corvin Ash said is in his article, and I shall not shorten it here, except to say that he brought the name back, and that they may as well have it, because they were using it, and that the toast was to the water, which was very good about it. Mrs Ash cast off the last stitch in the front row, and stood, and held up a scarf that went most of the way down the aisle, bright yellow, the yellow of the new roofs, which is the wrong colour for everything Corvin owns. If she had done it in black, nobody would ever see him in it. He wears it everywhere. He was asked back to the Flood Dinner of 2001, and went, and was early. Mr Weir spoke that year, on culverts, for some time. Mrs Ash * Mrs Ash * has a kitchen so new the paint still smells of it, with a big window over the lake, and she knits something long and does not stop. Mind the step. It's new. It's all new. Isn't it lovely? The old kitchen was DARK; you couldn't see your potatoes. She can see every potato she owns. Her boy wrote to say that he had taken the name Ash, after the village, in its memory, and she thought, well, that's nice, and took it as well, to save the postman, and now they are all Ashes and the post comes lovely. He is very deep, her boy. She wrote to him at the Slain Wyvern, Wednesdays and Saturdays, for eleven years, and he wrote back once, to the Ruins of Ashcombe, and the Ruins wrote back. She thought he would like that. He did. His room upstairs is bigger now, and has the light, and is a study at the minute, where the papers of the Flood Dinner Committee are kept: Hon. Sec., Mrs Ash. Up the wall by the window are pencil marks with ages, C., 6; C., 9; C., 12; C., 16; C., 19. The old ones went under with the old wall. These were put back from memory, and every one of them is a little taller than a boy would have been, and the last is exactly the top of his head. She drew where he would be. Old Ashcombe Once a year, in the week of the Flood Dinner, they let the lake down for the sluices, and the old street comes up for air, at the bottom of a slope of wet mud below the shore. On a still day, they say, you can hear the old church bell ringing under the water. You cannot. It is up the road in the new Ashcombe, calling somebody in for their dinner. They took it with them. In sluice week the old street is mud and stones and lily pads. There is the sign of the Anchor, face up, where Corvin was not allowed in and sat outside and waited. There is a gatepost with a hinge on it that still turns. A rose has got through the gap where a gate was, and flowers on the lake side. A coot has built a nest on the old maypole stump and sits on it very seriously. Round a stump somebody has pressed a ring of shells into the mud; somebody who comes down here sometimes, and sits. At the edge of the old street there is a doorstep with nothing behind it, and cut into it are letters in the old script, the ones on the tang of Corvin's sword, and under them, in plain capitals, for visitors, MIND THE STEP. His grandfather cut that, and made the sword as well, and it stood there forty years holding the door open. That is its name. In the schoolroom next door a strongbox held a report for every child old Ashcombe ever had, dry, in oilcloth, in the schoolmistress's hand, and Corvin's was near the top, from the last year. It is a fair report. It is one fewer in the box now. At the end of the street the road goes on into the water, and just under the surface is a green roof: the old church, up to its eaves. You could skim a stone on to it. Corvin Ash showed me his report, which he carries in his coat, next to the scarf. I asked whether I might print it. He said no, and then he said that I might print the last line, and I do: Corvin could do anything he put his mind to, and has put it to waiting. He will go far, if he ever gets up. See also Corvin Ash The Slain Wyvern , and its corner The Sable Hart The Day of the Water

title: Carn Drey
text: Carn Drey For the guest star whose prophecy this was, see Roland Fairweather . Carn Drey Known as Carn Drey; the hill east of Great Dunnage On top A field, with sheep in it Underneath A stone, a sword, and the Worm The gate Iron. Not locked. Nobody ever tried it The plate THE WORM. NOT READY. (FELLOW BLUNT, QUARTERLY.) Under it, in pencil READY. DONE. (R.F.) Prophecy Roland Fairweather's. Discharged, 2000, with help The Worm Asleep again. In no hurry Carn Drey is a hill east of Great Dunnage with a field on top and a cave in its side, and under it, at the foot of a long stair, a stone with a sword in it, and at the bottom, coiled three times round the room, the Worm. It was Roland Fairweather 's prophecy, and had been since he was twelve. The gate Across the mouth of the cave is an iron gate with a plate: THE WORM. NOT READY. (FELLOW BLUNT, QUARTERLY.) The prophecy's keeper, Fellow Blunt , came out quarterly for twenty-two years and checked the stone from the gate, and never went down. The gate is not locked. Nobody ever tried it. Under NOT READY, in pencil, somebody has written READY. DONE. (R.F.) The stone At the foot of the stairs is a stone with a sword in it to the hilt, and twenty-two years of dust on the hilt, and none at all on the stone. Roland stood in front of it for a long time, in the year 2000, and asked whether it was ready. He was told that it looked ready. Nobody had ever said that to him. He put his hand on the hilt the way you might put a hand on a horse you were not sure of, and the sword came out of the stone as if it had only been waiting to be asked. He said, Oh. It's ready. Then he went on down, with it. The stone has a slot in it now, the shape of a sword. On the way down, a wall is cracked across, and at about shoulder height there is a smooth place where somebody once leaned to get their breath before going on. A tall rock further down has been passed so often by something very long, going down and coming back, that one side of it is polished like a banister. The Worm The Worm had been waiting since before Roland was born for a hero of nineteen. Roland was thirty-four, and said that he was sorry, and that he did mean to come sooner. The Worm, which is old and very large and had been looking forward to it, uncoiled. It was over in about the time it takes to say so. The Worm of Carn Drey was ended, as the prophecy said, and the land, which is a field with sheep in it, is presumably glad. Then Roland asked whether everybody would mind being surprised, only a little, and everybody was, not at the Worm but at Roland Fairweather, who had finished something, standing in the dark at the bottom of a hill with his mouth open. He laughed until he had to sit down on the floor and wipe his eyes, and then he thanked each of the company by name, which took a while, because he meant it. The Worm, which had waited twenty-two years, is in no hurry, and went back to sleep. Neither is Roland. He has been down again since, after tea. I am told that it is very good about it. I asked Roland what had become of the sword out of the stone. He said that he wears it. He kept it as far as the tower door, the first time, and at the door it was handed back, and after the ending he went up again and stood at the foot of the tower, out of habit, and waited to be called away, and nothing happened, and went on not happening. He says that the bit after is very quiet. See also Roland Fairweather Great Dunnage

title: Coldbarrow
text: Coldbarrow This article is about the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant. For the Order, see The Order of the Errant . For the knight with nine pins, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Coldbarrow Known as The Chapter House Where In the snow of the far north, west of Frostwick Of The Order of the Errant Clerk Mordaunt System One knight, one pin Pins in Sir Aldric Nine, until 2000. Now one, carried Committee Sits on Thursdays. Quorate Daybook PINS REVIEWED. PINS REVIEWED (WITH TEA) Ceremonial armour Do not go on a quest in Coldbarrow is the Chapter House of the Order of the Errant, a hall in the snow of the far north where the Order keeps a great map of the island with a pin in it for every knight in the field. It is kept by the Order's clerk, Mordaunt , who reads the map the way other people read a will. One knight, one pin. That is the system. The map The great map is the island in the Order's own survey, four sheets wide. Each knight in the field is a white-headed pin, spread thin, standing where they were put. Until the year 2000 there were also nine red ones, all over it, for one knight, three of them labelled in the same hand: SAME WEEK. SEE COMMITTEE. The knight was Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore the Third. Six of his pins were correct, on different dates. Three of them were the same week: Frostwick, and Fenmarch , and a lay-by in the west. The Order had not lost his file. People said it had. It had nine of them, on the bottom shelf, nine fat volumes each labelled PEMBERTON-GORE, and each one certain that it was the real one. Mordaunt's ledger lay open at P, and every entry on the page had been crossed out and written in again somewhere else. He asked anybody who saw Sir Aldric to note the place, the date and the time, in ink. Not pencil. Pencil is how they got there. The committee A committee was formed to review the map, the pins and the week. It sat on Thursdays, at a table with two chairs and two stools, all of them empty, because the committee was Mordaunt, appointed to it four times, and quorate. In the year 2000 Sir Aldric came in, and Mordaunt put his pins down on the desk very carefully, as if they might go off, and said that it was Thursday, and the committee would see him now, and sat in each chair and on each stool in turn and then stood behind all of them. Its findings were three. Nine pins. All nine correct. Three of them the same week. The committee had been unable to fault the pins, and had therefore had to fault the knight, and Sir Aldric said that that was entirely fair. It recommended that he be requested to remain in one place for the duration of the review, and offered him Knight Commander of the Chapter, with a desk, there, and a pin that did not move, contingent on his remaining in one place. It was the one thing he could not do, and the one thing he had always wanted to be asked. He said that it was the finest thing he had been offered in nine years, and thanked Mordaunt, and said no. A knight who stays put is a post. He should be at that desk by nine every morning, and he should never once find it twice. But Mordaunt had asked, and nobody asks a man to stay, and he would like that put in the minutes. In ink. Mordaunt wrote for some time, and crossed nothing out, which the ledger on his desk would tell you was a first. Then he said that the committee had a data problem: the knight could not stay with the pin. Resolved, that the pin go with the knight. He took the nine red pins out of the map one at a time, and put eight of them in a heap on his desk, and held out the ninth. KNIGHT ERRANT, AT LARGE, a rank of the Order, created that Thursday. Wherever the knight is, the map is correct. That is the system now. The card on the committee's table reads: REVIEW OF PINS (PEMBERTON-GORE): CONCLUDED. SIR A. INFORMED. OFFERED THE CHAPTER. DECLINED. And under it, smaller, in ink: Beautifully. (Minuted at his request.) On the great map there are no red pins now, and in the margin a small card in Mordaunt's hand: PEMBERTON-GORE. AT LARGE. PIN CARRIED. I wrote to Mordaunt to ask for the Order's records of Sir Aldric since the review. He replied that Sir Aldric is wherever he is, and that the map is correct.
