They did not speak for thirty years. "That's not a falling-out. We just stopped one day and neither of us started again. So we send each other things instead." In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth carried a jar south for her, warm on one side, which he was told not to shake or ask about, and carried a reply back north which was heavier, and deliberately worse, and had been under construction for some time. Prudence laughed. She has written since: four pages, two of them about the Forty-Eighth, and one of those complimentary. The sisters' locket, two portraits facing opposite ways, which had been in a drawer since they were girls, went north on the Quest. "That was HER idea, that was." The Regular, whose cousin was the Thirty-Ninth. Lovely tower, apparently. Since the ending, lovely coast, apparently. The Gloamwood Society, which meets at the table by the door on Thursdays: nine members, forty years, a walk once a year, and a quarterly, The Sighting, edited by Mr Dunmore. Mrs Lumb does the talking. Miss Pellow saw the Thing in the Woods in 1971, and counted nine, and was the only one who got it right. The Society's long work came to its conclusion in the year 2000, with the help of Miss Halloway, and is described under The Gloamwood . Zephyrine Vance drank at the table by the window for eleven years, being just passing through, like somebody waiting for a letter. The letter came, on thick cream paper with a purple seal, and Prudence propped it against the glass where she would see it: the Collegium Arcanum 's eleventh notice of outstanding fines. See her article. The table is still hers when she wants it. She does not sit at it like that any more. There is a scorch mark on the ceiling above it, which was a moth. Piper Quill was standing on a table when the Forty-Eighth first came in, describing him, out loud, in the third person, as he approached. The tavern had not fallen silent. The tavern was ignoring her. Through the window from the square you can still hear somebody in there singing a song about the Forty-Eighth which rhymes Bram with jam. It is hers. The jam was a placeholder. It has tested very well. I stayed a night at the Gilded Turnip on my visit, at twenty crowns, and the breakfast was turnip. Prudence asked after her sister, and I said that she was well, and Prudence said "I didn't ask," and then asked again, more particularly, about the shelf. See also Thistlewick The Slain Wyvern , the sister house Piper Quill , for the rhyme Zephyrine Vance , for the letter The Turnip , and the question of which came first

title: The Gloamwood
text: The Gloamwood For what lives in it, as opposed to what was said to, see Miss Halloway's Bestiary . For the man on the log, see Godfrey Stopford , the Forty-Sixth. The Gloamwood Known as The wood; the woods; "enough" Where Across the north road, between Thistlewick and the Obligatory Tower Ways through One. The gap is the road Contents Trees; mushrooms, named; beanstalks, dead; a chest The chest A mimic. Everybody knows Residents The Forty-Sixth , on a log Things in it Argued about for two hundred years. See below, and the Bestiary Society The Gloamwood Society (1960), nine members Searched Yes. The logs say so The Gloamwood is a dark wood across the north road out of Thistlewick , and the only way north. The road ends at a wall of trees. There is a gap. The gap is the road now. Every Chosen One has gone through it, and one of them, the Forty-Sixth, went no further, and is still there, sitting down. "You think about it," the Forty-Eighth told me, of the moment at the mouth of the wood. "It does not improve." The first path The near half of the wood is a long path between big trees, much walked, and dressed, over the years, by everybody who has walked it. The carved tree. Somebody has carved an arrow into the bark, pointing north. Underneath it, in a shakier hand, a second arrow points back the way you came. Further on, a boulder has an arrow chalked on it pointing north, and under it, by a different hand: ARE YOU SURE? A mossy log has its moss on the north side, as the books say it should, and somebody has nailed a small sign to the south side: OTHER WAY. The logs. Every hollow log on the path has a hand-lettered sign at one end: SEARCHED. Somebody has been along the whole path with these, and it saves everybody a great deal of time. The beanstalks. One goes straight up into the canopy and stops, as though it had thought better of it, with a card nailed to the bottom: GIANT NOT IN. PLEASE DO NOT CLIMB. THIS MEANS YOU, JACK. The others are dead. One has a little wooden marker in front of it like a gravestone: HERE LIES A MAGIC BEAN. IT WAS NOT. The mushrooms. Pale ones in a neat row, which are edible and, I am told by a naturalist, delicious, and which I am to tell nobody about or there will be a society. (There is a society. It is about something else.) Red ones with white spots, of the kind in every picture book with a gnome sitting on top: there is no gnome, but there is a very small dent in the top of the biggest one, as if one had just left. One has a tiny door painted on the stalk, very carefully, by somebody with a very fine brush and a great deal of hope. The boulder is hunched over in exactly the shape of a sleeping troll. It is a boulder. You may check from the other side, to be sure, and then a third time, and by the third time you will feel that it knows. The chest. A treasure chest, alone, in the middle of a wood, on a path, in perfect condition. It is a mimic. Everybody knows it is a mimic. Nearly everybody opens it. Not far from it are a helmet, a boot, and a note in a jar: IF FOUND, I WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE MIMIC. The mimic was carrying an Elixir about with it as bait, which is either clever or very sad. It is splinters now. The man on the log Half way along the first path is a log across the way, with a cushion on it, and a little card on the cushion: RESERVED - NUMBER FORTY-SIX. The Forty-Sixth is a man in very good armour, and he is sitting on the log. He set out in 1980, and got as far as the woods, and decided that the woods were enough. "Nobody writes songs about that. But I'm here, and I'm forty-six, and I'm sitting down." Beside the log is a sack of letters, a great many, in two hands, one round and one narrow, going back years. They are from Nabb and Tolly , of his old party, who write every month, both of them. He does not write back. "I read them. Reading them's the answer. They know that. Nabb doesn't, but Tolly does, and Tolly does the stamps." I know Nabb, and Tolly. They drink at the Slain Wyvern , and Nabb gave the Forty-Eighth one of the six accounts in my history, which is the whole story: he stopped, on the path, and said the woods were enough, "and we looked at each other, and we said: fair." Everyone wants there to be more. There isn't more. Post goes out on Thursdays. Tolly buys the stamps in twos, because it is a long way, and he is worth two stamps. Nabb says the man who collects the post says he reads them. The deep wood Beyond the log the path goes into the dark part of the wood, where the trees are a wall, and there is a clearing, and there is the Thing. The Thing in the Woods has been argued about in Thistlewick for two hundred years. Is it a bear? Is it several bears? Is it a bear-shaped hole in the idea of a wood? Nobody ever got close enough to settle it. The Forty-Eighth got close enough, and the Thing stopped being in the woods, and Thistlewick has never believed him, and he has never told them anyway. What it was, in the sense of what it was, is a matter for a naturalist, and the naturalist has dealt with it in the Bestiary. The clearing has a ring of mushrooms round it, very large, very even and very obviously magic, with a little rope round it and a sign: SITE OF SPECIAL INTEREST. DO NOT DANCE IN. Each mushroom has a label on a stick: MUSHROOM 14 OF 31. THE SOCIETY COUNTS THEM EVERY YEAR. There were thirty-one last year as well. Near by there is a log with a flask, a sandwich box and a notebook on it, all labelled G.S., which has been the Society's picnic spot for forty years. There are some bones, and a sign beside them in the Society's hand: THESE ARE A SHEEP'S. THE SOCIETY HAS CHECKED. IT WAS A VERY OLD SHEEP AND IT DIED HAPPY. PLEASE STOP REPORTING IT. The Society has given each of the pale mushrooms a name. One of them is called Norman. Miss Halloway has written to them to say that it is a Cyril. The Gloamwood Society The Gloamwood Society was founded in 1960 to prove that the Thing in the Woods is not there. It has nine members, meets at the Gilded Turnip on Thursdays, walks the wood once a year, and has published The Sighting four times a year for forty years, edited by Mr Dunmore. For forty years it took anything: a shape, a smell, a feeling. For forty years it found nothing, so far, that would stand up. In the year 2000 Miss Halloway read all forty years of The Sighting in an afternoon, and told them that she could prove it did not exist, and that it never had, and the whole Society leaned forward as one. The walk was that night. It is always that night, when there is news. I was not there, and I have the account from Mr Dunmore's issue one hundred and sixty, which they printed extra of, and from Miss Halloway, who corrected it. There is nothing in the Gloamwood. That is proved, in writing, by a professional. The Society cheered. The method, and what the sightings were sightings of, are in the Bestiary, where Miss Halloway has asked me to leave them. One member did not cheer. Miss Edith Pellow saw something in the clearing in 1971, and wrote it up in issue forty-four, and counted nine. Nobody had seen it since. Miss Halloway had read issue forty-four. She told Miss Pellow that of forty years of sightings, hers was the only accurate one. On the walk home the whole Society contrived, without anybody arranging it, to be on either side of her, and by the edge of the wood she was telling everybody about the nine, and nobody minded in the least. Miss Halloway was made an honorary member, the first, and given the badge. She wears it on the cloak. The Society's walk of 2001 was, as the tally promised, very well attended: three hundred and twelve walkers, in good boots, with lanterns. Nothing was found. It was minuted with satisfaction. Miss Pellow led it. I am told she stopped the walk in the clearing, at dusk, and pointed, and said "There," and that three hundred and twelve people looked, and that there was nothing there, and that it was the best walk the Society has ever had. Bassoons The Gloamwood is the only road between the south and the works town of Upper Clanging , and it is a hard road to walk at night with eight feet of folded tube in a case. Mr Enoch Bagshawe, first bassoon of the Works Band, sat on the milestone at the mouth of the wood for some time, many nights, because if anything so much as looked at him he would drop the case, and that would be the reed, and the reed took three weeks. The band had never had a bassoon. It is a brass band; he is aware. Nix took him through. She halves encounters; it is a knack. With mothballs as well, which the Band keeps the uniforms in, he crossed the whole wood by night without a single encounter, or half of one, and at the north end he opened the case in the road and played one long low note on the reed by moonlight, for no reason but that he could. The Works Band has a bassoon. See also Thistlewick , to the south The Obligatory Tower , to the north Godfrey Stopford , the Forty-Sixth The Chosen Ones Wren Halloway The Bestiary

title: The Lighthouse of Saint Bother
text: The Lighthouse of Saint Bother For the town it is seen from, which it is not for, see Nether Sopping . The Lighthouse of Saint Bother Known as The light at the point Where A headland east of Nether Sopping , at the end of a road that goes nowhere else Keeper Ferrety Bother , fourth generation Saint His great-grandmother. She'd have hated the fuss Last ship 1909 For The ones coming back down the north road at night Takes One gallon Out One spring, until the year 2000 Lit Yes Rule two There is no rule two The Lighthouse of Saint Bother stands on a headland on the south coast, east of Nether Sopping, at the end of a road that goes nowhere else. No ship has passed the point since 1909. It is kept lit anyway, by the fourth generation of Bothers, because it can be seen from the crossroads on the north road, and it is what the ones coming home walk home by. The keeper * Ferrety Bother * keeps the light. "It's a family name. The saint was my great-grandmother and she'd have hated the fuss." There are tapestries of her on the ground floor: with a lantern, glaring at a ship, which looks very sorry; telling off a storm, which is leaving; and in a deckchair with her feet up and the lamp lit, with, embroidered underneath by a great-grandson, SHE'D HAVE HATED THE FUSS. Her book is on the top floor, Lighthouses I Have Known, by S. Bother. It is a very short book. She only knew the one, and she did not think much of the others anyway. He has been up the stairs eleven thousand times, and would like somebody else to do it once. The light The Guild paid a stipend for the light until the shipping stopped, which was ninety-one years before the Quest. The keepers' ship-in-a-bottle shelf, one bottle for every ship that passed the point, ends in 1909. After that the bottles go on, one a year, each with a tiny lighthouse in it, lit. The ships book has, under the last ship, in the same hand, again and again down four hundred pages: no ship. light lit. Before that, in the older books: ship. light lit. ship waved. And before that, in a much older hand: got her in. "It isn't for the ships. Hasn't been for four generations. It's for the ones coming back down the north road at night. You can see this light from the crossroads. It's what you walk home by." Forty-seven times that light was lit for somebody. It was lit for nobody a great deal more often than that. In the spring before the Quest the oil ran out, and Mrs Barrow at Wick & Barrow had oil, and also a price, and there was no stipend. For the rest of that spring and the summer after it, there was no light at the point. The Chandler's in Nether Sopping, which keeps its hours by the light, was shut the whole time. In the year 2000 the Forty-Eighth's company bought a gallon of oil from Mrs Barrow, who charged them, and carried it out to the point, and up all the stairs, and lit the lamp. The brass went from cold to warm to something you have to look away from, and out through the glass the whole south coast got an edge on it. Ferrety Bother pressed a keeper's lamp on them at the bottom of the stairs without a word, which from him is a speech. The Prophecy's tally of the Quest records it: The Lighthouse of Saint Bother is lit again. You can see it from the crossroads, which is the whole of what it is for. The tower The lighthouse is six floors, with the lamp at the top. The rooms are kept the way the Bothers have always kept them. A selection: Plates for thirty, from when the light had a crew. Ferrety uses one plate, and washes it, and dusts the other twenty-nine on Sundays. Barrels marked LAMP OIL, OIL, OIL, OIL and OIL, every one hollow all the way down. A jar of old wicks, trimmed square, each tagged with its year. The wick in the lamp is trimmed square every week, regardless. Crates of spare lenses, packed in straw, for a lamp that has had the same lens since it was built and is not about to change now. Ship's biscuit, in a crate stencilled 1908. It is the same biscuit they sell in Nether Sopping, and very probably the same batch. A message in a bottle, legible through the glass: IF FOUND, PLEASE RETURN TO THE LIGHTHOUSE. It is in the lighthouse. Somebody has, technically, returned it. Ferrety's wardrobe, which contains a very large number of identical jumpers, all of them with a lighthouse on. The Keeper's Handbook. Rule one: keep the light lit. There is no rule two. There has never been any need for one. A Book of Coast Birds, kept by four generations of Bothers. Every entry says GULL. One says NOT A GULL (?). The next says GULL. A book of ghost stories for keepers on long nights, every one of which ends with the keeper lighting the lamp and the ghost going home, satisfied. A chart of the coast with every rock and wreck in red ink and every ship that ever got past in green. There is a great deal more green than red. Somebody was very good at this. Almanacs of the sky, one a year, for working out when it will be dark enough to bother with the light. This is the family joke, and they have made it every year for a hundred years. Ferrety Bother told the Forty-Eighth that he had walked out to the crossroads at midnight once, to check, and stood there, and looked back. I asked him, when I went out to see the light for this article, whether he had been again since it was relit. He said no. He said he did not need to. Then he said that he might, one night, if somebody was coming home. I said I did not think anybody was. He said that you never knew, and that that was the whole of the job. Since the Quest The lamp needed oil again in the spring of 2001, and somebody got it, now that somebody has. The light has not gone out since. The Chandler's is open. See also Nether Sopping The Chosen Ones , who walked home by it

title: The Long Field
text: The Long Field Contributed by O. Hoyle, of the Hoyle Works, Upper Clanging I asked Miss Hoyle whether she would read over what I had written about the Long Field. She sent it back with a line through all of it and this memorandum attached, which I print whole. The field is hers. For the town above it, see Upper Clanging . For the works, see The Hoyle Works . - H.B. The Long Field Known as The field Where Below the town, on the slope, off the spur road Keeper The Hoyle Works Fenced A hundred yards of wrought-iron railing, stopping abruptly at both ends Attempts One hundred and ninety-nine Here One hundred and ninety-seven Plaques Twelve readable. And one made Gaps None, now THE HOYLE WORKS. MEMORANDUM. TO: Mr H. Bellwether, Nether Sopping. FROM: O. Hoyle. RE: Your draft, "The Long Field". DATE: 14 March 2002. Your draft is returned. It is very kind, and it says "graveyard" four times. It is not a graveyard. It is a record. A record is a kindness to whoever stands here in a hundred years, and it has to be right, so I have written it again. The field. The Long Field is where the works keeps its attempts. Every airship this works has built since the first has come down, and when one comes down we bring her back here, or what there is of her, and give her a plot and a plate. The plates say where she was lost and why. That is all they say. A plate is not a place for feelings. People who want those may scratch them underneath, and some have. The gatepost. The gatepost reads THE HOYLE WORKS, and under it, on a smaller plate: ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-NINE ATTEMPTS. ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-SEVEN ARE HERE. The second number has been re-cut four times. I re-cut it. Somebody has to keep it right. The plates. There are twelve that may be read without moving ivy. Visitors are asked to read all of them, and in the order given, and nobody does. In the order given: ATTEMPT 3. LOST IN THIS FIELD. CAUSE: NEVER LEFT IT. 4.1. The oldest plate. The only one that gives a distance. The distance is eleven feet. 4.2. ATTEMPT 41. LOST OVER THE WEST ROAD. CAUSE: ENVELOPE, SEAM. Somebody has scratched underneath, in a better mood than the plate: the seam was fine. so was he. he walked home. I have checked the seam. The seam was not fine. He did walk home. 4.3. ATTEMPT 60. LOST OVER THE GLOAMWOOD. CAUSE: BALLAST, RELEASED IN ERROR. Under it, smaller: ALL HANDS RECOVERED. ONE ANNOYED. 4.4. ATTEMPT 84. LOST OVER THE LONG FIELD. CAUSE: blank. The only blank cause line in the field. See paragraph 6. 4.5. ATTEMPT 101. LOST OVER THE SEA. CAUSE: FIRE, WHICH WAS EXPECTED. The works wrote FIRE on her flight plan before she left the shed, in the box headed ANTICIPATED DIFFICULTIES. Nobody has ever said that we do not plan. 4.6. ATTEMPT 123. LOST OVER THE STANDING STONES. CAUSE: FIRE, WHICH WAS NOT. 4.7. ATTEMPT 137. LOST OVER THE GLOAMWOOD. CAUSE: FRACTURE, MAIN SPAR. 4.8. ATTEMPT 138. LOST OVER THE GLOAMWOOD. CAUSE: FRACTURE, MAIN SPAR (DIFFERENT SPAR). Eleven months apart. I do not wish to discuss the eleven months. 4.9. ATTEMPT 155. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: WIND. Somebody underlined WIND twice. Somebody else, later, put a small question mark beside it. The question mark is mine. 4.10. ATTEMPT 176. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: NO FAULT FOUND. Every system was recovered, stripped and tested. Every system passed. 4.11. ATTEMPT 184. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. The first plate in this field to say so. 4.12. ATTEMPT 199. LOST IN SIGHT OF THE TOWER. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Eleven years under review in 2000. Her plot is empty. See paragraph 7. Things in the grass. A propeller blade, half sunk, polished on the side that faces the sky; the other side is the field's. A strip of envelope cloth on a bush, faded to the colour of the grass, which lifts in the wind, the way it was made to. A twist of brass too small for a plate of its own, with a tag on it: ONE OF THEM. KEPT. A single rivet, with a ring of small white stones round it so that nobody treads on it. The stones are Mr Sowerby 's. He will not be told to move them and nobody has tried. * Attempt Eighty-Four .* Came down in 1860, in her own plot, and did not stay there. She made herself good out of the rows either side of her, a piece at a time, for a hundred and forty years, and went north up the field doing it, and left a furrow behind her three feet deep and as wide as her plot. Nobody taught her that. Nobody could have. At the top of the field she got a foot off the ground, and then did not, and then tried again, and was still trying in the year 2000. 6.1. She was stopped. It was the Forty-Eighth who stopped her, and I came down from the works afterwards. She got further than any of them. I have not tried very hard to work out how she was still doing it, and I am not going to. 6.2. Her governor came off with two turns of a spanner and was given to the Forty-Eighth, rather than taken. She never needed it. She did not once run away with herself in a hundred and forty years, and I have a field to prove it. 6.3. There is a bay in the shed with 84 over it. For a hundred and forty years there was nothing under it. There is now. It will take years. Nobody has costed it and nobody has asked to. 6.4. I had told a great many people that there would not be a two hundred and one. The keel of the Two Hundred and First was laid in 2001. I have told the same people. Attempt 199. She is not in the field. She is on a crag in the north-west, at the end of a track the works keeps cut, right way up, and every system aboard her still works. Pressure in her. Water in the glass. Lubricators full, bearings cool. The clock in the wheelhouse is a good clock and was serviced that spring; somebody walks out twice a year and winds it and sets it right, and it keeps perfect time, and it is at nine forty again when you go back. It has been set right eleven times. The log is open on the chart table: 0938. TOWER IN SIGHT. ALL WELL. 0939. ALL WELL. 0940. 0947. ON THE CRAG. ALL HANDS. NO INJURIES. NOTHING TO REPORT BETWEEN 0940 AND 0947. 7.1. The last line is in the other hand, the steadier one: WE ARE WALKING HOME. They did. All four. 7.2. ITEM 1 was aboard her, chocked and strapped down four ways. It is not aboard her now. ITEM 1 is not the subject of this memorandum. Attempt 112. One hundred years dead on a sea stack in the north-western approaches, which nobody could get out to, so there was no plate, so there was a gap in the row between 101 and 123. Whoever kept this field before me left the space, and put a post in it with two brass bolts four inches apart and nothing between them, and behind the bolts a card: ATTEMPT 112. LOST. CAUSE: LOST. 8.1. Every other plate names the part that failed. Nobody ever got to her to find out which part. Somebody wrote it out correctly in five words and would not put up a wrong one instead. 8.2. In 2000 the Two Hundred flew out to the stack, and her number-plate came off in one turn of a spanner, and it is on the bolts now. It fits. Of course it fits. That is the thirteenth plate. There are twelve readable plates in this field, and the thirteenth is one you make, and it does not count, because twelve is twelve. The Two Hundred. The two hundredth attempt reached the tower and landed adjacent. She is not in this field and is not going to be. The attempt log reads REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. CAUSE: UNDER REVIEW. Mr Bellwether has asked me what is under review. It is under review. For the record. Nobody reads the field. The field is for us. If you have read all of it, you may come up to the works and say so, and I will believe you. O. HOYLE. I have been to the field, and read all of it, and went up to the works and said so. Miss Hoyle believed me. She said that nobody reads the field, and then asked me which plate I had liked best, and I said Attempt 41, and she said that the seam was not fine, and that he did walk home, and that it was a long way. See also Upper Clanging The Hoyle Works Ott Hoyle The Obligatory Tower , where the Two Hundred landed adjacent The Flight of the Two Hundred

title: The Obligatory Tower
text: The Obligatory Tower This article is about the building. For its occupant, see Grimspite the Inevitable . For why anybody went there, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the names it nearly had, see Prophecy Hall . The Obligatory Tower Known as The Tower; the Dark Lord's tower Where At the top of the north road, two hundred leagues from Thistlewick by the fingerpost Established Approx. 4,800 years ago, by the contract; about two thousand, by the calendar Management The same throughout Floors Four, and the top Door At the bottom. Ground floor Key Under the mat Visitors 47, by the signpost; latterly about one a month Survivors [the number has been scratched off] Made of Not known. Nobody ever asked Please Wipe your feet The Obligatory Tower stands at the top of the north road, and is where the Dark Lord lives, and has lived, under the Prophecy of Thistlewick, for four thousand eight hundred years by the contract's count. Forty-eight Chosen Ones have climbed it. It is exactly as tall as everybody said, which is somehow the most unsettling thing about it. The engagement was held, before the Tower, at a castle on a cloud which no hero could ever reach, and its caretaker keeps the Committee's letter on the subject face down on his lectern, unfolded and folded again a great many times. It is headed NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE OF ADDRESS, and gives the new venue as The Obligatory Tower. Ground floor. Door at the bottom. Please amend your records. See The Former Premises . The plaque by the door says the Tower was established approximately four thousand eight hundred years ago. I wrote to its occupant to ask whether "approximately" was the plaque-maker's or his. He wrote back, in a very beautiful hand, that it was his; that the plaque had originally said exactly ; that he had thought it presumptuous; and that he had hoped I was keeping well. He did not say how approximately. I did not ask him how old he is, having asked once. The approach The north road comes out of the Gloamwood and climbs the valley. On the way is a wayshrine: a roof, a bench, and a box of supplies with a note, FOR CHOSEN ONES. PLEASE REPLACE WHAT YOU TAKE. NOBODY EVER REPLACES WHAT THEY TAKE. Inside is a visitors' book with forty-seven names in it. The last entry reads Feeling good about this one! It is the Forty-Seventh's. The Forty-Eighth added his name, and did not add a comment. The southern signpost, at the fork, says NORTH, the Obligatory Tower, and under that somebody has freshly carved HE IS NOT THAT BAD ACTUALLY, and somebody else has carved YES HE IS underneath it. Both were right, in their way, and I have been to some trouble to find out who carved the first one, and failed. The northern signpost, at the foot of the Tower: THE OBLIGATORY TOWER. VISITORS: 47. SURVIVORS: [the number has been scratched off]. PLEASE WIPE YOUR FEET. The number has been scratched off because it was forty-seven as well, and the Tower thought it looked like showing off. That is my guess, and it is marked as one. The door At the door the Tower's long habit of being visited has left a great many arrangements, and the one everybody remembers is upstairs. The way to the top is through a heavy door on the fourth floor, barred from the other side, and in front of it there is a mat. It says WELCOME, which for a Dark Lord's tower raises a number of questions. Under it is a key, labelled SPARE - DO NOT LOSE AGAIN. Four thousand years of this and the answer was the mat. Not every party needs the key. A party with Nix in it does not, because the bar is on the inside, which means there is a gap, and a gap is just a door that hasn't been asked properly. Beside the door is a plaque: THE OBLIGATORY TOWER. EST. APPROX. 4,800 YEARS AGO. UNDER THE SAME MANAGEMENT. Roland Fairweather left here. At the foot of the Tower, in the year 2000, he stopped walking, and looked like a man who had been checking the time all week, and said, "Ah. Yes. There it is." He had to be somewhere. He never knew where. He put everything he was carrying on the grass, including his sword, and shook hands with everybody, including, carefully, anyone who was not looking, and was forty paces off before he had finished saying that he would stay to watch. It was the eleventh door. See his article . Maud Penhallow waited here, by one account. Forty paces off, Roland stopped, and looked back once, at a girl standing beside the door with a practice sword. She raised it to him, the way you are taught to at nine. "He said somebody ought to see the end of one," she said. "I'm the understudy. I'll wait here. When you come out, I'll go and tell him how it ends." There is another account, in which she was not here at all, and heard the end over a pie; her article gives both, and is vague, at her request, about which. The Two Hundred landed here. Not at the door. Beside it. Miss Hoyle 's airship came down on the grass two squares from the door, ticking as she cooled, and the party walked the two squares, because clause seven requires a Chosen One to go on foot, and nothing that flies has ever been allowed to set down at the door. The attempt log at the Hoyle Works records it as REACHED THE TOWER. LANDED ADJACENT. Miss Hoyle's account of it is hers to give, and she has given it in her own article, in numbered paragraphs. Inside The Tower is four floors and the top, each floor its own maze of halls, and the stairs are in a different place on every one, so that a flight up comes out above itself on the floor above and you have to cross the whole floor to find the next. I have this from everybody who has climbed it, and they all say it with feeling. It is furnished in the manner the Prophecy expects of a dark tower, and it is plain, from every room, that the occupant has never once believed in it. I give a selection, from the accounts of the company and of the forty-seven, which agree on this if on nothing else. The ground floor. A notice in the stairwell, at eye level: MIND THE STEP. I MEAN IT. THE STEP HAS TAKEN MORE OF YOU THAN I HAVE. - G. A night porter's straw bed, with a card, NIGHT PORTER (OFF DUTY), and a cold cup of cocoa with a biscuit on the saucer. A card table, set for four, with the hands dealt and never played; one of them is a very good hand indeed, in front of the empty chair nearest the stairs. A skeleton slumped against the wall, with a cushion behind it and a blanket over its knees, because it is a draughty tower. A pot with nothing in it but a note: I WOULDN'T EITHER. - G. A barrel stencilled DUNGEON SUPPLIES - GLOOM, which is empty, because the gloom has got out and is everywhere. A crate of ROCKS (SPARE), for when a corridor has started to look too tidy. The skeleton of a dragon, curled round on itself like a dog asleep by a fire, with a sign on the tail, PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH, which may be meant for you or for the dragon. A banner with the Dark Lord's arms, a tower rampant on a field of slightly more tower; another with a laundry label, HAND WASH ONLY. DO NOT TUMBLE. DO NOT LET THE CHOSEN ONE SET FIRE TO IT (AGAIN). A cobweb, LISTED. DO NOT DUST. - G. The barracks. The minions' lockers, GRUB, SNAG and GRUB (THE OTHER ONE). Grub's has a packed lunch and a card: IF YOU ARE THE CHOSEN ONE, THE KEY IS NOT IN HERE. IT IS NEVER IN THE LOCKERS. Snag's has clean socks, folded, and a letter from home that begins DEAR SNAG, ARE YOU EATING. Grub (the Other One)'s is locked, with a card in the door: NICE TRY. A bunk with a teddy bear under the pillow in a horned helmet. Clipboards on the bunks: SICK LEAVE, SICK LEAVE, ANNUAL LEAVE, SICK LEAVE. The Tower has very good terms and conditions. The staff canteen: MONDAY, GRUEL; TUESDAY, GRUEL; WEDNESDAY, CHEF'S SPECIAL (GRUEL); one bottle of brown sauce, ONE SQUEEZE EACH. THAT MEANS YOU, SNAG. Three cells for Chosen Ones who have been captured, never used, because in four thousand eight hundred years nobody has ever been captured. It seemed rude. One has a little vase of dried flowers on a shelf, in case. A clock stopped at twenty past three, labelled: SOMETIMES IT IS TWENTY PAST THREE. THEN IT IS RIGHT, AND I FEEL BETTER. - G. The galleries. A statue of a knight in HEROIC POSE NO. 3, with a chart round the side of the plinth showing poses one to twelve; number seven is mostly pointing. A gargoyle with a little bell round its neck so that it cannot creep up on anybody. A wardrobe of black cloaks on numbered hangers, one of them very slightly less black than the others from being washed with something red. A row of coffins, every one marked RESERVED, because the management was told that a tower ought to have coffins, for the look of it: one has a fern in it, doing beautifully in the dark, one is the dry store and full of spare candles sorted by length, one smells of lavender, and the last is OUT OF ORDER. A banner, ABANDON HOPE, and under it in smaller and newer stitching, (BUT DO WIPE YOUR FEET). The basin. On the third floor, a basin of clear water, in a tower with no plumbing. Scratched into the rim: HE LEAVES IT OUT FOR US. NOBODY KNOWS WHY. The Obelisk. An obelisk covered in very small writing. It is a list: forty-seven entries, each a date and a name and the word RENEWED. There is room for a forty-eighth. There will not be one. The barred door, on the fourth floor, with the stairs to the top beyond it. See above, under mats. The Contingency Cache. A cupboard, six feet from the stairs, with ten hooks inside, each with a small brass label: CHOSEN ONE. HEALER. SMITH. MAGE. SPECIALIST. KNIGHT. MUSICIAN. Two more were added later, in a different hand and a cheaper brass: RIVAL. CATALOGUER. The tenth hook is labelled GUEST, and underneath it in pencil: HE WON'T BE HERE. HE NEVER IS. I LEAVE IT OUT ANYWAY. On every hook but that one, a legendary weapon for that kind of Chosen One. On the inside of the door: RESTOCKED EVERY CENTURY. NOBODY HAS EVER OPENED THIS CUPBOARD. IT IS SIX FEET FROM THE STAIRS. I DO NOT UNDERSTAND ANY OF YOU. The Forty-Eighth's company opened it, and it now has ten empty hooks and a very smug note. The library, under a great mural in an old script, whose translation card says STAFF NOTICES. PLEASE WASH YOUR CUP. (Another inscription, cut deep: THE PREVIOUS MANAGEMENT REGRETS ANY INCONVENIENCE.) On the shelves: Villainy for Beginners, read once, carefully, a very long time ago, with a bookmark in chapter one. The Monologue: A Handbook, of which chapter one is called "Don't", and there are no other chapters. The Prophecy of Thistlewick, Annotated, every margin full, clause twelve underlined so often that there is a hole in the page. A Thousand And One Things To Do With A Tower, all ticked, with a thousand and two written on the back: LEAVE IT. Reading a Renewal Clause, by a firm of lawyers in Great Dunnage , the most worn book on the shelf, which falls open at notice. Bungalows of the Coast, with photographs, one page turned down at the corner: a small white one with a view of the sea. Tea: A History, volumes one to nine. Knitting for the Dark Hours, with a scarf pattern in the back and a note in the margin, AUNT M - TOO LONG? A wine rack, full of cold tea, corked and labelled with the year, going back further than wine could possibly keep. A globe, with one pin in it, on a little spot by the sea, labelled ONE DAY. And on a stand, a book: What To Say When They Arrive. Every page is a different speech, crossed out. The last page has one word on it, and it has not been crossed out: Tea? The top The top of the Tower is the throne room, and its furniture and its occupant are described in his article : the tablet behind the throne, which is not a curse but a rota; the two statues of an aunt; the mirror that is late and the mirror that shows where you would rather be; the two seeing-orbs, which show only each other, except when somebody in another tower picks one of his own up by accident and apologises; and the four skeletons, which are plaster, for the look of the thing. Nobody has ever died up here. "Forty-seven of them, and they all won. Do you know how that looks, to the forty-eighth?" Carved into the wall behind the throne, forty-seven times: THE DARK LORD SHALL RISE AGAIN. It is not a threat. It is a renewal notice. The forty-eighth carving will not be needed. Since the Quest The Tower is not a Dark Lord's tower any more, contractually, and nobody has had the heart to tell the furniture. Its occupant is retired, and stays on, in his chair, with a kettle and the book at the bookmark. The door is not barred. The mat is still there, and the key is still under it, labelled. The Tower gets about one visitor a month, most of them people who would like to see the chair, and the Forty-Eighth once a year, on the day, and the kettle is on. Roland Fairweather came back to the Tower after the ending, with the party, and stopped at the foot of it, out of habit, and waited. Nothing happened. He waited a little longer, to be sure. Nothing went on happening. "So this is the bit after," he said. "It's very quiet." He went up. I have been invited to the top, more than once, by letter, and have said that I do not climb things. A historian is not obliged to visit every place he writes about; he would never finish. But I have counted the floors from the accounts and there are four, and the top, and I have begun to wonder, this winter, whether that is very many. See also Grimspite the Inevitable The Prophecy of Thistlewick The Obligatory Quest The Gloamwood Ott Hoyle , for landing adjacent

title: The Sable Hart
text: The Sable Hart This article is about the inn. For doomed rivals, and brooding in corners, see the Glossary of Cliches . For its seventeenth member, who is now its second, see Corvin Ash . The Sable Hart Known as The Hart Where The west, on its own, by the road Kept by Mrs Garrow Regulars Five, hooded Corners Four The difficulty See above Darkest corner North-east, by rota, changes on a Monday Newsletter Overshadowed , free, always has been Bottles Black labels. Elderflower cordial The middle of the room Empty as a church, until 2000 The Sable Hart is an inn in the west where doomed rivals go to brood, and has been for longer than anybody there can say. There are four corners and five of them. You can see the difficulty. They have solved it with a rota. The regulars See also The Rivals of the Sable Hart , with their dates. They are, all of them, extremely nice. They tip beautifully and they put the chairs back. Mrs Garrow, who keeps the house, says they are no trouble, love: four in the corners and the young one by the fire, every night of the year, and the middle of the room empty as a church. A tinker sat in the middle once, in the rain. They were ever so nice to him. He left before his pie came. She buys the bottles with the gloomy labels because her regulars prefer them, and what is inside is elderflower cordial. The tankards on the shelf each have a small knitted hood over them, to keep the dust off. Hollin Crake, Secretary, stands up when you come in, which nobody brooding in a corner has ever done, and asks whether you are anybody's rival at all. He has the Secretary's corner, by the window, because somebody has to be able to read the rota. His tankard sits on a coaster he brought from home, so as not to mark the table. Silas Veyle has the darkest corner, until Monday, with a scar and a pint. The shadows are his. He is sorry; that came out very possessive. They are his until Monday, and then they are Rook's, and Rook has earned them. Don't ask about the scar. Nobody asks about the scar, and he looks, very briefly, disappointed. The curtain behind him is drawn, and there is no window behind it, and he says it makes a real difference. His pint is untouched; it is for atmosphere, and he orders a fresh one at nine, and leaves that too. Thaddeus Rook keeps the table: points for a vow, a scar, a dramatic exit, and standing about in the rain. Standing in the rain is two points; standing in the rain on purpose is one; they are quite strict. A dramatic exit through a door that turns out to be a cupboard is minus two. He was fourth, in 2000, because he never gives himself the benefit of the doubt, which is the whole point of keeping the table. He is rival to a very great archer on the east coast who is ninety-three this year, and he is giving him every chance. Lucan Morrow edits the newsletter, Overshadowed, which is free and always has been. He is rival to a Mr Pennock, a very great wizard, who does not know. Morrow writes to him at Christmas, and every year gets a lovely card back. Mr Pennock thinks he is his cousin. Kit Blackwood is new, and first on the waiting list for a corner, any corner, and has been since March of 2000. Until he gets one he broods on a stool by the fire, in the warmest and brightest seat in the inn, as hard as he possibly can. It is quite hard to brood by a fire. He is getting better. Mr Crake says he has a gift for a long silence. He is nobody's rival yet. There is a list for that, too. The table The league table is ruled in red and pinned up beside the rota. When the Forty-Eighth called it read: 1. S. VEYLE, 41 (the scar). 2. L. MORROW, 37 (a vow, in the rain). 3. H. CRAKE, 36. 4. T. ROOK, 35 (under review, by himself). The rest was under the rota, which was pinned over the bottom half with four pins and a fifth, to be sure. Under it were Blackwood, 12 (keen); eleven members by post, in order of their last letter; and, seventeenth of seventeen, C. ASH, 0 (no meetings attended). Mr Ash had been a member for some years. He had sent apologies to a hundred and twelve meetings. Beautifully. His chair was kept. It always had been. It was a stool at the empty table in the middle of the room, in the light, where nobody broods, and somebody had dusted it, and it did not look as if it had been easy. In the year 2000 Corvin Ash took the fifth pin out and read down to the bottom, and sat down at the nearest table, which was the one in the middle. Crake rang the little bell, and the four corners and the fire came into the middle of the room, which none of them had stood in for years, and held a meeting, quorum two, and reviewed his points. A vow, paid for, two crowns to a fortune-teller: binding, two points. A scar: no. Standing in the rain: he had sat in one corner of the Slain Wyvern for eleven years. In ONE corner? Out of turn? There was not a rota. Nobody had ever sat in one corner for eleven years. Mr Rook was asked whether there was a category, and said there was now. He did the sum twice, in the margin, and ruled a new line in red: C. ASH, thirty-nine, one corner, eleven years. Second, behind the scar. Rook moved himself down to fifth, by his own request, and was visibly happier there. Veyle offered Corvin the dark corner, Monday being only four days off, and Crake said NOBODY out of turn, however rainy; besides, his chair was kept. Mrs Garrow brought him a pie, and he stayed for it. Mr Ash attends now. Not every week. He sends apologies when he does not. They find it very reassuring. The newsletter is free. I have issue one hundred and thirteen, which has a stop press: PRESENT: C. ASH. A NEW CATEGORY (ONE CORNER, ELEVEN YEARS). ONE STOOL DUSTED. Issue one hundred and twenty, which I had this winter, reports that Mr Blackwood made his first dramatic exit, the door having been planed at last, and that it was a cupboard, minus two, and that he took it extremely well, plus one, a new category. See also Corvin Ash The Slain Wyvern , and its corner

title: The Slain Wyvern
text: The Slain Wyvern This article is about the tavern at Nether Sopping. For the creature over the mantel, see The Goose , in Miss Halloway's Bestiary. For its sister house, see The Gilded Turnip . For the back room, see The Healers' Table . The Slain Wyvern Known as The Wyvern Of Nether Sopping , on the front Landlady Dorcas Thrupp Rooms 25, over 20, over 15, over a very faint 2 Breakfast Fish. Don't ask what fish Over the mantel One wyvern (slain). (Goose.) Plaques Two, one either side of the fire. Neither mentions the other Not permitted Swords on the bar; spells in the bar; dragons in the bar, even small ones, even if it is a goose Patrons Retired adventurers, mostly; at capacity, eleven parties Clock Ten to twelve. Right twice a day Also My table, by the fire The Slain Wyvern is the tavern on the front at Nether Sopping , kept by Dorcas Thrupp , and is where the heroes of the Obligatory Quest drink after they have been sent to the coast. Everybody in the room has been on one. It has a wyvern over the mantel, which is a goose, and a historian by the fire, who is me. I have done most of my life's work at that table, and most of the work in this volume, and when I say that the room would not tell a historian anything, I say it with great affection, and with the scars. Its sign is a painted tankard, dented, with a bite out of one side. The bite is about the size and shape of a goose. The board outside reads THE SLAIN WYVERN. ROOMS. HOT FOOD. ONE WYVERN (SLAIN), and very small, at the bottom, where the paint has been scratched off and done again, (GOOSE). The wyvern Mounted over the fireplace: a wyvern, wings out, jaws open, about the size of a large goose. It is, on any inspection at all, a goose. Under it is a brass plaque: SLAIN BY H. VANCE, CHOSEN ONE #41, IN THE MARSHES, AFTER A LONG STRUGGLE. Halloran Vance , the Forty-First, came back from the marshes in 1940 with nothing, and a whole village waiting on the quay for a monster. So he brought them a monster. It took him two days, with wire, and a goose, and he never once smiled about it. "He was a good man," Dorcas says, "and he needed it to be a wyvern, and it's been a wyvern in my house for sixty years. So." For sixty years everybody agreed. Nobody in the room looks at it while you are looking at it, which is its own kind of answer. In the year 2000 Miss Halloway looked at it, and said what it was, and named it, Anser anser, greylag, adult female, with two bats' wings wired on and the whole thing varnished, and was asked to leave. She was entirely right, and she was asked to leave, and both of those were true at once. She asked, later, for a retraction, and was told no. She asked instead for a second plaque, one that would not correct the first and would not repeat it, and Dorcas said brass, not paper, this is a house, and that she would read it first. She read it twice. Then she fetched a screwdriver from behind the bar, and a chair, and put it up herself, on the other side of the fire: A GREYLAG GOOSE, ANSER ANSER, OF A FARM ON THIS COAST. MADE INTO A WYVERN IN 1940, IN TWO DAYS, WITH WIRE, BY H. VANCE, CHOSEN ONE #41, BECAUSE THE VILLAGE WAS WAITING ON THE QUAY. Somebody polishes both of them. Under the crossed swords there is a notice, NO DRAGONS IN THE BAR, EVEN SMALL ONES, and added later, EVEN IF IT IS A GOOSE. - D. THRUPP. There is a bucket by the fire marked FOR THE GOOSE. The goose has been on the wall since 1940. The bucket is filled every morning anyway. Nobody remembers who started it. Miss Halloway sits under the goose now, by choice, when she is in. The house Dorcas Thrupp has kept the Wyvern for longer than she will say. Her sister Prudence keeps the Gilded Turnip at Thistlewick , and they did not speak for thirty years, and sent each other things instead. The jar the Forty-Eighth brought south is on the highest shelf, where it can be seen from every table in the room. She has had a letter from her sister since, the first in thirty years, four pages, and two of them are about him. Rooms are twenty-five. For him they are still twenty-five; don't start. "It's the bedding I mind. You lot heal in it and it never recovers." Behind the bar, bottles, each labelled in Dorcas's hand with what it is, how much it is, and who in this room it is not to be served to; every label has at least one name on it. Sopping biscuits, BAKED THIS MORNING, and very small, SOME MORNING. A jar of a thing that has been pickled for so long it has turned into a different thing, and is now quite happy. A ship in a bottle, with a tiny bottle on its deck, and in that a tinier ship. Somebody's tankard with a mat on top that says SAVED; by the dust, it has been saved since the spring. The tap, with a sign on it: HEROES WILL WAIT THEIR TURN LIKE EVERYBODY ELSE. The piano. Every key has a name pencilled on it, somebody who sat at this bar and swore they could play. Most keys have two. Middle C has eleven, and one of them, in a child's writing, is SOPS. If you play the one tune you know, twenty retired adventurers will turn round at once, the way people do who have heard a trap click. The board by the bar has the rooms down the left and names down the right. Room four has a line drawn through it. It has not been down since Tuesday. "Best guests I have ever had. No trouble. No noise to speak of. I leave the tray on the mat. Lovely to see newlyweds happy." The house register has a last column headed PURPOSE OF VISIT, and of forty entries on the page thirty-nine say business. The fortieth said something else, and has been crossed out, once, neatly, in Dorcas's hand, and business written above it. She has not made a fuss about it. I mention these only because they are on the board and the register, which are public documents, and I say nothing further about either. * Sops * is the potboy, and will tell you that you look like a Chosen One, because of the standing. "Like you're waiting for someone to tell you where to go. All of 'em do it. Mrs Thrupp says it's the prophecy posture and it ruins the chairs." He picks the flowers for the bedrooms upstairs. They are mostly dandelions, arranged with enormous care. Upstairs are the beds Dorcas sells. One has a card on the pillow: A CHOSEN ONE SLEPT HERE, and underneath, SO DID ALL THE OTHERS. IT IS THAT SORT OF INN. One has a dip in the middle exactly the shape of a man in full plate, which Dorcas has tried everything on; the bed remembers him. The clock on the landing chimes the quarters, except between three and four in the morning, which is when the adventurers get in. There are drawers of lost property (a monocle, a ring of keys to a castle in some other story, PLEASE RETURN) and a shelf of books left by guests. Among them, I am obliged to record, is Volume One of my history, which is a pamphlet. Volume Two is downstairs, and is the size of a door. The room The patrons of the Wyvern are, mostly, people who went north with somebody, and came back, and were sent here, and have been here since, telling each other how it ended. The long table in the middle of the room is laid with a different meal from a different country at every place, and nobody has eaten a thing; they are all too busy. I give some of the room as it was in the year 2000. * Ysolde Marrow *, seventy-eight at the time, who kept the Forty-Fourth alive for nine years, on and off, and once, for nine weeks, a duke's son with four hit points. She sits at the table by the bar, and keeps a canvas roll of field medicine open on the table in front of her out of habit. One bottle in it is labelled FOR AFTER. It is tea. She chairs the Table in the back room. * Hulda Bole *, the Fetcher, eleven years and four hundred and six jobs: "It wasn't FOR. It was a list. I was the legs." If anybody asks you to fetch twelve of anything, ask what the thirteenth is for. * Nabb and Tolly *, of the Forty-Sixth 's party, who write to him every month. See The Gloamwood . * Merrow Halgate *, a big man in old armour, drinking carefully, of the party of twenty that fought the Dark Lord at the bridge and lost, as clause fourteen required. He has made his peace with losing. He has not made his peace with the paperwork. "He apologised. Halfway through, he stopped, and he apologised, and then he carried on." Councillor Dree, an elderly gentleman who sits alone, deliberately, and was the kindly old advisor of his party, and was suspected, from week three, of not being, and was tied to a chair in week eleven and asked to reveal himself, and revealed that he needs spectacles. They bought him a hat. * Perpetua Small *, a young woman with excellent posture and a tiara she does not appear to have noticed, who woke on the beach six years before the Quest with no memory and has been told nothing, very kindly, by the whole room, which wants to see her get there on her own. She folds every napkin into a little crown and does not know why. A bottle of very good wine with a crest arrives every month from a palace somewhere, addressed TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN. It will come back to her. She expects it will be something dull. Dairy. Two very ordinary travellers, Jack Furrow and Jill Furrow , no relation, peasants, in peasant crowns, who have been in Nether Sopping four months, and are unacquainted, and met on the road yesterday, and are holding hands, and are beans people. Their table has two plates: one of beans, untouched; one of roast pheasant, eaten to the bone. Their luggage is a crate stencilled PEASANT LUGGAGE, with gold corners, and a little velvet cushion on top for sitting on. The town is starting to enjoy them. The Forty-Second and his wife, who come every year for the anniversary. Sops would like it known that they are sixty. Corvin Ash, who sat in the darkest corner of the room for eleven years, hood up, at the table where the light did not reach. He sits at a table in the middle of the room now. See his article . * Roland Fairweather *, at his table by the fire, between engagements, lit very slightly better than the rest of the room. When he begins, Dorcas says "here we go". Me, at the table by the fire, with a book so large it has its own table. The page I had open when the Forty-Eighth first read over my shoulder was Chapter Three Hundred and Twelve. The Forty-Eighth arrives, and stands about. He said it was the most accurate thing anybody had written about him. The chapter before is called "Lunch". Six accounts Volume Two of my history was compiled at that table, and finished, because the Forty-Eighth went round the room and was told: six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. I describe the arrangement in my own article , which I was made to write. Of all the Chosen Ones who have stood in the Wyvern, he is the only one who sat down. The alumni On one evening in the year 2000 the board carried a card, in a good square hand: THE FAIRWEATHER ALUMNI. DINNER, TONIGHT, THE SLAIN WYVERN. ALL PARTIES WELCOME. - F. ICKWORTH (DAME), WHO WAS FIRST. Dame Florence Ickworth's party had done the Wyrm of Ickworth in 1977, with an eleven-year-old page who could already disarm her, and who left at the wyrm's door. She thought there might be three of them. There were eleven parties, and the Wyvern was at capacity. Brother Anselm of the Seven Bells; Mags Turvey, who fed him a fortnight on the walls of Wenlow and called him our Roland; Pim Corrow, the Lost Heir, whom he found; Captain Odile Marchbank of the Ninth Lancers, who had his whetstone; Old Jory, who drew the last mile of the Last Survey from his say-so; Hettie Brack, who got the Goblin King's last riddle, and the answer was a door; Lord Tobin Fairley-Vane, Ned Scarrow, Saul Pennock and Major Royce. By the end of the evening the whole room had worked it out, one table at a time, and had not said so: eleven last doors, each one finished without him, and every one of them had thought, until about an hour before, that he was theirs. Dame Florence stood up. "We finished because you got us to the door, and taught us what to do on the other side of it." The room raised eleven glasses. To Roland Fairweather, who got us all to the door. Nobody said anything else at all. On the board there is still a dinner card signed eleven times, with a ring on it from somebody's glass. The back room Behind the red curtain by the fire there is a door that most patrons have never noticed, with a card on it: THE TABLE. MEDICS ONLY. Behind it is a cellar room, a long table, a medicine shelf, and once a year every party medic within forty miles. Its business, and what Sister Merribell said there, are under The Healers' Table . I am not on the list, and somebody inside says so. I have been asked, by visitors who have read Volume Two, which table is mine. It is the one by the fire with the book on it. I have been asked whether they may sit at it. They may. I have been asked whether I will tell them a story. I tell them that everybody in this room has been on one, and that they should go round and be told. Most of them get two, and go and look at a dungeon. See also Nether Sopping The Gilded Turnip The Goose The Healers' Table Roland Fairweather Hosea Bellwether

title: The Stair
text: The Stair This article is about the stair behind the Door into the Mountain at Hithermost . For the knight whose chalk is on it, see Sir Dunstable of the Vale ; whether he is alive is disputed , and is not settled here either. For what is at the bottom, see the Bestiary . The Stair Known as The mountain stair Way in The Door into the Mountain, Hithermost Admittance Not without a lamp. By order Lamps on hooks None. Borrowed. Back directly Light What you bring Hazards Scheduled, six Half way Not Chalk D. 1 to D. 212 Below D. 212 Nothing written. Then the bottom Misfortune Continued, through the chapel porch The Stair goes down into the mountain from the Door at the top of Hithermost , in the dark, for a great deal further than anyone in the village had been. It has a schedule of hazards nailed up inside the door, and chalk on its walls in a cheerful hand from one end nearly to the other. After the Quest the Forty-Eighth took a borrowed lamp and his companions and went down it, to the bottom, where nobody had been. The schedule Inside the Door, nailed up, is a board: PARISH OF HITHERMOST. THE MOUNTAIN STAIR. SCHEDULE OF HAZARDS. BY ORDER. 1. The dark. 2. The draught (puts lamps out). 3. The echo (do not answer it). 4. Somebody coming up. 5. The warden of the half-way landing. 6. Anything else: NOT ANTICIPATED. Chalked under it, in a cheerful hand: All present and correct. - D. Chalked beside item six, in a different hand, in the year 2000: Anticipated. Item one is the dark, and it is thorough. There is no light on the Stair but what you bring, and a little circle of it round you, and the rock, and the next flight. Item two puts lamps out, and the parish has hung hooks for spare lamps at intervals down the Stair, LAMP ON HOOK, and there is no lamp on any of them, and beside one of them is chalked Borrowed this one too. Back directly. - D. The chalk From the top step down, the rock is chalked in the same cheerful hand, a D. and a number, each a little deeper than the last. I copy a selection, in order, from the Forty-Eighth's notes: D. 1. Went in. Had a look round. Grand day. D. 2. Bit further. D. 3. Bit further. Nothing happened. D. 14. Signed the Book first. Just in case. D. 21. Somebody coming up. Charming fellow. Couldn't see him. Lovely manners. D. 40. Nothing happened. Rather a lot of it. D. 61. TEA. (Beside a cup on a saucer, set down on the floor of the ledge. It is still warm. Nobody is drinking it.) D. 88. Lamp went out. Lit it again. Fine. D. 96. Asked the draught to shut the door. It did not. D. 100. HALF WAY! Tea. D. 101. Not half way. D. 102. Told the warden. He took it badly. D. 131. The echo. Said good afternoon. It said it back. Lovely manners. D. 150. Wet. D. 177. Still wet. Nothing happened. D. 211. Bit further than yesterday. D. 212. Bit further than yesterday. Back directly. There are no marks below D. 212. The stair goes on down past it into the dark, and nobody has written on any of that. The boulders are chalked too: Good boulder. Sat on it; Second-best boulder; an arrow pointing down, That way, I expect; TEA, with an arrow, and under it, If there is any; STILL GOING, rather bigger than usual. On a boulder just above D. 212 is a little drawing of the sun, with rays, and under it, For later. Both sides of the question about Sir Dunstable have found evidence on this stair, and I have set it all out under Hithermost . I would only add here that the chalk is very cheerful the whole way down, and that it is the same hand at the bottom as at the top. Half way Over a landing some way down, cut into the rock in letters a foot high: HALF WAY. Under it, in chalk, much smaller: NOT. At the head of the flight below it stood the warden of the half-way landing, in black armour, as still as the rock, with a hook on its belt and nothing on the hook. It said HALT. HALF WAY. NONE PASS THE HALF-WAY LANDING UNINSPECTED. The Forty-Eighth mentioned D. 101. The warden looked round, down the flight behind it, into the dark, for a long time, and said that it had been told, and had been told before, and had not taken it well. Then it said INSPECTION, and inspected them, which is a long story and is in the account. Afterwards it sat down on the top step, heavily, and then got up and moved out of the way, because it was in it. It sits a little to one side of the landing now, and says Not half way to itself every so often, quietly, getting used to it. When anybody comes down it says HALT. HALF -, and then, Oh. You again. The post Somewhere above the warden, on a stair under a mountain that had been shut for longer than anybody could remember, at the edge of the lamplight, there was a man in a red coat and a flat cap , with a satchel. Nobody said anything. Nobody could think of anything that would help. He said Post?, and Spare Cotterill said that he had one for Upper Clanging , and wrote it on his knee, and it did not take long: Dear Mam. Is it spring yet? Spare. It was the first letter Spare had sent that was entirely true. The courier touched his cap to Spare and went on down the Stair, into the dark, without a lamp. Somebody asked how he had got in, and somebody else asked how he was going to see, and nobody had an answer to either. It was spring in Upper Clanging the next morning. See Spare Cotterill . Misfortune A fight lost on the Stair does not end where fights end. The party comes back in through the porch of the Chapel of Continuance, whole, with the lamp, and signs the Book again, and Brother Quillon does not remember them, because the Order forbids it. The Forty-Eighth's party came back in through the porch at least once. Sir Dunstable met them in the chapel and asked whether they had come in by the porch, same as him, and said that nothing had happened, he expected. The bottom Below D. 212 the stair goes on, for one more flight, and then it ends, and the dark stops all at once, like a door shutting behind you. The bottom of the Stair is a chamber with lamps on every ledge, dozens of them, and every one is lit. There is somebody at the bottom , and it was very pleased to see them. It is not on the schedule, except as item six, and it is not in the Prophecy , and it asked. Nobody is obliged to fight it, and so nobody ever had, and it asked whether they would, only if they had the afternoon. The Forty-Eighth's party had the afternoon. It said afterwards that it was the best afternoon it had ever had, because nobody made them. It had written a bounty card for itself, a long time before, because nobody would put it on anything: BOUNTY: SOMETHING UNSCHEDULED. Lives at the bottom of the Stair. Would love to meet you. Reward: on production of a witness. It was not official. It wanted a stamp, and it did not know where you would get one. You get one at the Adventurers' Guild in Nether Sopping , from Mr Pell, who had kept a Form Z, Matters Not Anticipated, in a drawer for forty years, in case, and had never once used it, because in forty years every matter had been anticipated, by somebody, on something. He filled it in. His hand was not quite steady. The bounty was discharged on Form Z, and there is a copy on the Guild's board, stamped DISCHARGED, and under it, Witnessed. Form Z. Then he took the Forty-Eighth's Guild Card, which said Provisional, and gave him one that does not. After the fight it saw them up the Stair, all of it. It took no time at all, and afterwards none of them could say how. They were standing under the Door, and from somewhere a very long way down, something waved, and then said, oh, oh no, was that too much, it was sorry, it did not get the practice. Miss Halloway's entry on it is in the Bestiary , and she has asked me not to call it a Thing, so I have not. The Forty-Eighth has the lamp still. Sir Dunstable has not asked for it back. I asked the Forty-Eighth whether he would go down again, and he said that he had been down three times since, on free afternoons, because it is a long way down for somebody to get no visitors, and that it always asks if they have the afternoon, and that it always says nobody made them. See also Hithermost , and the Chapel of Continuance Sir Dunstable of the Vale The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) , and Form Z Spare Cotterill

title: Thistlewick
text: Thistlewick This article is about the village. For its contract, see The Prophecy of Thistlewick . For the forty-eight people it sent north, see The Chosen Ones . For its committee, see The Prophecy Committee . Thistlewick Known as The village that sends the Chosen Ones Crest A turnip rampant, on a field of slightly different turnips Motto Non nobis, nisi forte : not us, unless it has to be Produce Turnips Other produce Chosen Ones, forty-eight Governed by The Prophecy Committee, in session Councillor A goat Fish in the pond None Wishing wells None. Stop it Distance to the Tower 200 leagues, by the fingerpost. Feels like more Distance to the coast Forty miles, which nobody in the village mentions Thistlewick is a turnip-farming village at the bottom of the north road, and the signatory of the Prophecy . Every hundred years, by the Committee's reckoning of a hundred years, it chooses one of its own and sends him north to the Obligatory Tower to put down the Dark Lord . It has done so forty-eight times, and it worked forty-seven times, and the forty-eighth time it worked rather better than anybody had arranged. Thistlewick believes that it is the middle of the world. It is not; it is about a third of the way up the left-hand side of it, and the world goes on in every direction for a great deal further than the village has ever been told. Until the year 2000 nobody in Thistlewick had ever mentioned that there is a town on the south coast. There is. It is forty miles away, and it is where Thistlewick's heroes go afterwards (see Nether Sopping , and the gradient described under Two Reckonings ). The village The north gate stands at the top of the square, and has stood open for as long as anybody can remember. The Gatekeeper has waved forty-seven Chosen Ones through it, and looks north for a while when he says so, and does not say how many came back. He will not let a Chosen One through alone, under section four, subsection b: a Chosen One travels with a party, minimum one other person. "It's about the optics." The gate turned out to have a key, which had been in its lock, and which Nix had had for eleven years. It hangs on a nail beside the gate now, where it will be very safe. Just outside it is a sign, POINT OF NO RETURN, to which somebody has added in smaller letters that you can come back whenever, they just like the sign. Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III spent six years looking for the north gate, which is forty paces north of where he stood and has never moved. He is the subject of a notice on the board. See his article, and the date of 9 June 2001. The square has a well, which a sign says is NOT A WISHING WELL, and a water butt beside it which a second sign says is also not a wishing barrel. There is a coin at the bottom of the water butt anyway. Thistlewick is a village of optimists, and of people who do not read notices. There is a market stall (FRESH! MOSTLY!), whose fish, on ice, are CAUGHT LOCALLY, although the only water in Thistlewick is the pond. There is a crate stencilled THIS WAY UP with the arrow pointing at the ground, which was stacked by somebody who trusted the arrow. The fingerpost reads: NORTH, the Obligatory Tower, 200 leagues; SOUTH, the turnip fields, 40 paces; EAST, the pond, there are no fish in it; WEST, also the turnip fields. Somebody has scratched out the 200 and written FEELS LIKE MORE. The notice board has had the same notices on it for as long as I have been asking about it: a goat lost, which answers to Councillor; a Chosen One wanted, position filled; the well; and Sir A. Pemberton-Gore, missing, six years, if found point him at the north gate, he will not go, point anyway. In the year 2000 it carried, for one week, a notice of a farewell tea for B. Thistle, the Forty-Eighth, Friday, bring a plate. "There is never anything new," says the board, and is wrong only that once. The pond has no fish in it. The Fisher has fished it for thirty-one years. "You know what keeps a man going, lad? Not catching anything, and coming back anyway." The Forty-Eighth has said since that it was the best advice anybody gave him that day. The Fisher has a keep net now, which Nix returned to him, and he put it into the water with enormous ceremony, and it is empty, and it is somehow less empty than the pond was. The turnip fields go round the village on three sides. One row has a tiny flag in it, very old, KEPT BACK FOR THE CHOSEN ONE'S SUPPER; they plant a fresh turnip under it every spring, just in case, and it has been very good for the turnips. Another row has a small tired sign asking the public not to pull the turnips up to see if one of them is a sword in a stone. NONE OF THEM IS. WE HAVE CHECKED. ALL OF THEM. The scarecrow wears Bram's old coat, and a note pinned to it: CHOSEN ONE (RESERVE). One of the Thistle rows has a neat hole in it with a label on a stick, and the creature that lives there is in the Bestiary under Bramus agricola . The people The village has two hundred or so souls, and the Quest met a great many of them on its first morning, which is the morning they all came out to look. I give the ones I have been able to speak to. The Old Man, whose boy was the Forty-Seventh. "Everyone tells you it's an honour. Nobody tells you it's a rota. Come back, lad. That's all. Come back." He waits at the edge of the square. Since Nix brought his kitchen chair back he waits sitting down, which is better for waiting. When the Forty-Eighth came back he took his hand and held on to it for a while. The Farmer, who asked who was doing the west field, and is still of the opinion that the weevils were the more pressing problem. There is a ploughshare at the end of the west field now, which Hob made, and the weevils have kept their distance from it for the first year in ten. The Gossip, who will tell you that the Forty-Eighth was chosen on the second vote, and that the first vote was the goat. The goat abstained. Very dignified about it. The Dog, and his Neighbour, who interprets him. The dog has not made a sound in my presence. The Neighbour says that he says to take a coat. A Child, who has heard that there is a DUNGEON, to the NORTH, and will tell you, and will tell you again. * Mrs Thistle *, Bram's mother, who is alive, and was making a pie (see Bram Thistle ). The goat is Councillor, and is the second of the name. The first is buried in the churchyard under a small stone: IN MEMORY OF COUNCILLOR (THE FIRST). A GOAT. SERVED THREE TERMS. NEVER ONCE SPOKE OUT OF TURN. The present Councillor is sometimes seen standing beside it, looking thoughtful, and eating the flowers. He wears a good iron bell, which Hob made, and declined a brass one. He abstained from it. The buildings * Prophecy Hall *, the gold one, up the road, where the Committee sits. It is always in session. It is how they know they exist. The Chapel of Whatever Works, with a teapot over the door on a bracket, because the Order never chose a symbol: it held a meeting about one, and somebody made tea, and that was the meeting. On cold mornings it steams. Inside there is a basin, FREE, DRINK IT, YOU ARE DEHYDRATED, YES YOU, and a pew RESERVED FOR THE TIRED, and Merribell . See The Order of Whatever Works . * The Gilded Turnip *, the inn, under a tin tankard that creaks in the rhythm of its favourite song. * Nix's Emporium *, EST. RECENTLY, which buys anything and asks nothing. Grumnir's Smithy, under a hammer on a bracket which is just a hammer, and is not Beatrice, because Beatrice would never be left out in the rain. It is Hob Grumnir 's, and his article is the place for it. The window is black with soot except for one clean circle about the size of a nose. In it now, framed, is a written apology from an apprentice bandit, in a very good hand, next to nothing Hob made. The Thistles' house, at the bottom of the lane, with geraniums on the sill and a turnip in a pot that is being grown as an experiment and has not done anything you would call an experiment. Over the fireplace is a clean rectangle of wall where a sword used to be. The churchyard The churchyard is behind the chapel, through a gate that used to stick. You had to lift it, and shove, and it scraped. It does not stick now. It was hung by Hob Grumnir in the year 2000, in good iron, true on its hangings, and the latch drops shut under its own weight. Somebody says the latch wants a spring. It has one now. The stones are worth an afternoon: BEATRICE GRUMNIR. SMITH. 1919 - 1989. The parish's own plain headstone. The grass round it is cut every week, and nobody says who. MABEL THISTLE, 1890 - 1979, the Forty-Eighth's great-grandmother. SHE GREW A TURNIP AS BIG AS A CHAIR, AND SAT ON IT, AND THEN IT WAS THE CHAIR. The chair is still in the family. Mrs Thistle uses it for the good visitors. I have sat on it. ELSPETH MOORE, 1902 - 1994, who won the turnip show forty-one years running. Underneath, in smaller and much angrier capitals: THE FORTY-SECOND WAS FIXED. Somebody leaves a rosette on her stone that says SECOND. OSWIN FARROW. HE SAID IT WAS PROBABLY FINE. There is a hard hat on the stone. WALTER PIKE. HE KNEW A SHORTCUT. There is a little arrow carved under it, pointing at the hedge. Nobody has ever been brave enough. Councillor (the First), as above. Since the Quest The village has not changed very much, which is what it would want me to say. The fields are the same fields, and the 2001 harvest was the best in the parish. The Committee asked whether it had been prophesied. It had not. The Prophecy is kept rolled in the Hall, with clauses twelve and nineteen struck, and is consulted at every meeting, out of habit, and the consultation is minuted. The north gate stands open. Nobody has gone through it on the Committee's business since the year 2000, and nobody needs to: clause twelve is struck, and in its place there is a note in the minute book reading SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. The Forty-Eighth lives where he always lived, two fields from the square. He walks north once a year, on the day, because there is a kettle on at the top, and he comes back. Clause nineteen is struck as well, and so the next person to come home to Thistlewick from anywhere will come home to Thistlewick, which is how most villages manage it. I asked the Gatekeeper, on my visit, whether the gate would be shut now that nobody need go through it. He looked north for a while. Then he said that it had been open for forty-seven of them and it could stay open for whoever was next, and that it was not a gate for keeping people in. I wrote that down. Then I asked him how many had come back. He said, "All of them, I'm told." And then, after a while, "One of them came back here." See also Prophecy Hall The Gilded Turnip Nix's Emporium The Prophecy Committee The Gloamwood , which is the next thing north Nether Sopping , which is the next thing south, and which Thistlewick does not mention

title: Upper Clanging
text: Upper Clanging This article is about the town. For the works, its airships and its two hundred years, see The Hoyle Works , which Miss Hoyle has written up herself. For the field below the town, see The Long Field . For its most travelled resident, see Spare Cotterill . Upper Clanging Known as Clanging Where Up the west road from the Gloamwood 's north mouth, on a hill, under its own chimneys Motto It will be quieter soon (a works hazard plate on a post) Industry The works Occupation At the works. See the parish register, eighty years of it Weather Rain, which comes down already a pale shade of grey Time Four minutes fast, since 1841 The hooter Six o'clock. Sundays as well. The parish has considered it Cotterills Ten Twinned with Much Pottering , which it has never visited Upper Clanging is a works town in the north-west, at the top of the west road, built on a hill round the sheds of the Hoyle Works , which have been trying to fly to the Obligatory Tower for two hundred years. It is loud, early, grey and extremely proud of all three. In the year 2000 the two hundredth attempt got there. The town read the Prophecy two hundred years ago, believed every word of it, and made an engineering programme out of "every hundred years". It does not count. It has never needed to. Everybody up here is too busy. The street The sign is a works hazard plate on a post, repainted: UPPER CLANGING. IT WILL BE QUIETER SOON. Further up, beside the parish rooms, there is a bench with a little plate, IN MEMORY OF THE QUIET, and somebody has scratched under it, IT WILL BE BACK SOON. Nobody in the town believes either of them, and both are kept painted. The clock has been four minutes fast since 1841. The town sets its watches by it, and is therefore four minutes early for everything, and has been for a hundred and sixty years, and gets a great deal done. There is a card under the copy in the Safety Valve: THIS CLOCK IS RIGHT. EVERYWHERE ELSE IS LATE. The hooter sounds at six, as usual, and at six on Sunday as well. The parish notices say that the parish has been asked about this, and that the parish has considered it. The minutes of the parish council have the hooter as item one, the hooter again as item two, and the hooter under any other business. It has its own book, on the shelf at the inn: The Hooter: Its History, Its Uses, Its Critics. The works is at the top of the street, and has no sign. It has never needed one: it is where the noise is. There is an enamel plate beside the door, DANGER. HOT. LOUD. EARLY, and all four are true.
