There is a tank marked COAL OIL with NO WIZARDS WITHIN TEN YARDS chalked under it, which Zephyrine Vance took personally, and says she was not wrong to. There is a skip with the boiler of Number 147 in it, and somebody has chalked on the boiler, very small: ALMOST. Smaller things worth stopping for. A pump marked DRINKING WATER, and under it, SORT OF. An oil drum leaking into a gutter somebody dug for it, which runs to a bucket, which is full, and has a gutter of its own, to the next bucket. A front room in which every ornament on every shelf has been turned round to face the works, out of loyalty. Geraniums in a window box, grey like everything else in Clanging, and trying. A pillar box, collections at nine, twelve and five, with a little step built in front of the slot, worn smooth, for somebody quite small who posts a great many letters. The Safety Valve The inn, kept by * Mr Kell *, is named for the one part of a boiler whose entire job is to give up before anything else does. They are very proud of it. A plate under the sign reads IN THE EVENT OF PRESSURE, GO TO BED, and a plate on the foot of each bed reads IN CASE OF EMERGENCY, LIE DOWN, which is the whole philosophy of the house on one plate. Beds are thirty crowns. You will be dry, and up here that is worth thirty. On the wall is a framed list in a very good hand, Things That Are Not To Happen Again, numbered to sixty-three. I give a selection: 7. THE GEESE. 19. NOT LIKE THAT. 31. HOT. 44. MR PADGETT'S HAT (AND MR PADGETT). 58. ANY OF IT. 61. OLLERENSHAW. Number sixty-three is one very long word, and nobody in the room will say it aloud. There is a commentary on the list, much longer, which is not allowed out of the inn. I have not seen it. On the dresser is the inn's best china, with a card on top, FOR WHEN SHE FLIES. It was dusted every week for as long as anybody can remember, and never used. I am told that it has now been used once, and dusted since, and put back. * Winnie Marsden * sits by the fire with a half of shandy on a doily embroidered CLASS OF '19. The Class of 'Nineteen is the town's Cold Winter year: the foundry was banked down for six weeks that January, there was no work, there was no heat in the whole town but what was in the houses, and two hundred and forty children were born the following autumn, near enough all together. They have had a dinner every year since, on the second Saturday, with a seating plan settled when they were four. You cannot get in. You had to be born in it. Mrs Tunnicliffe at the parish rooms keeps the census, and was born in June, and is not invited. I put down here only what the census says, which is dates. The forge * Ollerenshaw 's* is at the foot of the street, under a painted sword and three lines of lettering: BRYD - SMITH; THE BEST IN THE NORTH; and, in a different paint, SAYS WHO. The third line is Hob Grumnir 's, from the year 2000. He asked me not to tell Bryd. Bryd knows. Bryd Ollerenshaw has the forge from his father, who had it from his mother. If it is iron and it has to hold, it goes to him. Miss Hoyle sends him a drawing every spring, and every spring it is a spar. He and Hob were apprenticed together, and he has waited twenty years for Hob to admit that some jobs want two smiths. The meeting between them in the year 2000 consisted of each saying the other's surname and finding something wrong with the other's anvil, and was described to me by a child of the town as "what they do every time". They then made the Two Hundred 's main spar in an afternoon without a word, and went down the hill to the house that does a pale, already arguing about who was buying. Half the town has money on which of them will admit the other is the better smith. Nobody has collected. In the forge there is a certificate, BEST SMITH IN THE NORTH, awarded by B. Ollerenshaw to B. Ollerenshaw, in real gold leaf. There is a cabinet of three drawers: RIVETS; OTHER RIVETS; RIVETS (GRUMNIR'S - DO NOT USE). There is a quenching tub which hisses faintly whenever anybody in the room says Thistlewick. Merribell has told me that it is steam, and that I am not to encourage it. The parish rooms The Parish Rooms take births, deaths and whatever else nobody else will take on. * Mrs Tunnicliffe * keeps the register, the census, the counter, the tea, the urn and the hymn board; the rota says so, and under it, EVERYTHING ELSE - SEE ABOVE. There are three tea urns, for the three sizes of parish emergency: a funeral, a wedding and the fete. Every one of those is on a Saturday. The parish register lies open at OCCUPATION, and every line of it reads AT THE WORKS, page after page, in one hand, for eighty years. One entry, dated 1802, reads AT THE WORKS (THINKING). Somebody has pencilled HOYLE in the margin beside it and then rubbed it out, because the register does not take marginal notes. The parish lost-and-found book has the entry FOUND: ONE BOY, NINE, WITH A PACKED BAG, ON THE SOUTH ROAD. RETURNED, and then FOUND: THE SAME. RETURNED, and it goes on like that for two pages. The Cotterills The house at the end of the street is the Cotterills ', and the street is mostly theirs as well. * Mrs Cotterill * has the names off by heart, because she chose them: Cotter , Rivet , Gudgeon , Tappet , Ferrule , Grommet , Clevis , Shim , and Spare, because they had run out, and Mr Cotterill said call it Spare, and she was tired. Mr Cotterill is on nights, twelve on and twelve off, and is always very glad to get home. He says that he has never once minded the walk. The tenth, * Washer *, was born in the spring of 2000, at six in the morning, on the hooter. Mrs Cotterill says it is the only one of them that was ever on time. Mr Cotterill had said not Washer. Spare got to it first. Clevis was running a book on the name, and Washer came in at twenty to one, because half the works had a farthing on it once Mr Cotterill said not Washer, and Clevis had to pay out most of Upper Clanging. The book is closed. Mrs Cotterill says that there is not going to be another one. I have the family's ages from Gudgeon, who copies the register and has written Cotterill more than four hundred times in the best hand Mrs Tunnicliffe has had: in this year of 2002 Cotter is twenty-six, Rivet twenty-four, Gudgeon twenty-two, Tappet twenty, Ferrule eighteen, Grommet seventeen, Clevis fifteen, Shim thirteen, Spare eleven, and Washer is two today, which is the first day of spring. Through the kitchen window there is a line of vests in order of size, and the peg on the end that was put there in hope has a vest on it now. Round the rim of the rain barrel there are ten tin cups on ten nails. Cotter married Bessie Marsden, Winnie's granddaughter, and there was a cradle by their range in the year 2000 which nobody had mentioned and everybody had looked at. Hers came in the summer, as she said it would, on time. The Class of 'Nineteen's seating plan has a high chair in it now, which Winnie drew in herself, in pencil. Spare's own article tells what Spare did. Here I will say only that there is a parish form, P-9, Application by a Minor to Accompany a Chosen One, which nobody had ever asked for, and that Gudgeon knew exactly which drawer it was in without looking. Mrs Cotterill reads Spare's letters out to the works at the dinner hour, all four lines of each, slowly, with the punctuation in. I asked whether she had kept them. She has kept all of them. She said that there was no dragon, and that she did more potatoes anyway. See also The Hoyle Works The Long Field Spare Cotterill Ott Hoyle Bryd Ollerenshaw Much Pottering , its twin The Cold Winter

title: Wayside Sights
text: Wayside Sights This article collects the places by the road that are not towns, have no inn, and are worth stopping for anyway. For the larger places, see the Places index. The world has a great many things beside its roads, most of which are a field. These are the ones that are not, in no particular order, because the Forty-Eighth found them in no particular order, and so will you. The Sky Anvil In the snow beside a road in the far north there is a little stone shrine with a round grey stone set in the top of it like an egg in an egg cup. The pilgrims call it the Sky Anvil , and built the shrine round it in 1750, and come up every summer to look at it. It came down out of the sky in 1749, into the top field, on a Tuesday, and Elias Meech's great-great-grandfather set it up for a gatepost, because it was there. It was the best gatepost in the county, and outlasted eleven gates. Mr Meech did not mind the pilgrims. They kept the frost off. In the year 2000 Mr Meech was between gates, the last having gone at Michaelmas. He had never thrown a gate out; all eleven were in the hedge-bottom along the top field, where each was put when it went, rusting quietly in order. Hob Grumnir put his hand flat on the stone, the way you would put it on a horse, and said that it was star-iron, come down out of the sky. Mr Meech said, on a Tuesday. Hob had the eleven gates out one after another, and sorted them on the snow into what would do and what would not, and worked the afternoon through, cold, and made a gate out of eleven gates, true on its hangings, and fitted the latch with a spring he had been carrying in his pocket since a churchyard in Thistlewick . Mr Meech hung it on the shrine himself, and said that that was a very good gate, and told Hob to take the stone, and to mind his back. It was very heavy. Hob did not mention this. The shrine has a gate on it now and nothing in the top. The pilgrims come up and open it and shut it all afternoon. Nobody had ever given them anything to open before. What Hob made of the star-iron is in his article, and is one sword, and he has not said who it is for. The Lay-By At the end of a lay-by on the west road, on the grass, there is an igloo. It is not melting. There are voices inside it, disagreeing politely. It is the annual general meeting of the association of hedge mages, which is not its name, because it has not got a name; that is item one, and has been for nine years, now eleven. The igloo is neutral ground. None of them would host, so Mrs Quickset made it the first winter, and it is nobody's house, so nobody has to do the biscuits. It has not melted in all that time, and it is the one thing the association has ever agreed on. * Dunnock * says that they did not agree on it; she just did it. Miss Privet takes the minutes, and a member of the public who looks in will be asked to propose a name, strictly for the minutes, and the name will be carried forward under nine years of other things carried forward. Dunnock is self-taught, from a book with four pages missing, which he worked out for himself, and did better, as it turned out; he is better than the whole Collegium at exactly four things. Somebody inside says Collegium in the voice people use for weather. In the year 2000 Zephyrine Vance was admitted, over one objection, which was withdrawn after Dunnock showed her page twenty-three, Kindle, which you do not aim, but sort of mean, at everything, and it sorts itself out. She said that was not how fire works. A gorse bush, a milestone and the lay-by's litter bin caught fire all at once, neatly, and went out, with nobody anywhere near them. She said that it should not have worked. Dunnock said the page was missing. There is a chair at the folding table now with nobody's coat on it. She proposed a name. It was a good name. It was carried forward. The Cinder Fen In the far south a path goes out into the Cinder Fen and gives up. Under the cracked mud on top, nine hundred acres of water were drowning a road a foot at a time, and the Drainage Commissioner stood where the path gave up, in her wellingtons, with a clipboard, waiting for a fire person. The Fen wanted burning; it was the traditional remedy, and nobody in the parish had been able to do it since Mr Tinder retired, thirty years before. The form was in triplicate, one for the parish, one for the county, and one to come back to the Commissioner signed by the fire person and countersigned by the Fen. There was a box for it. She had never had one back. Zephyrine Vance said that she was a fire person, and had been expelled for it, for an unsanctioned quantity of fire, which was in her file. The Commissioner said that unsanctioned was only the form; they could sanction anything; that is what it is FOR. Under QUANTITY OF FIRE she wrote nine hundred acres, pressing hard enough for all three copies, in the hand of a person who had been told for eleven years that hers was the wrong amount. It was stamped SANCTIONED, three times. She asked the Commissioner to say that again. It burned all afternoon and all night, and nobody in the parish went to bed, and somebody brought out chairs. In the morning the Fen was black and dry and smoking gently, and out of the mud, running north, came a stone causeway older than anybody, with a milestone on it that says GT DUNNAGE, a foot under since Mr Tinder retired. The third copy, held out over the fire at arm's length all night, came back with a scorch in one corner, exactly in the box. Countersigned by the Fen. The Certificate of Burning that had been waiting thirty years for a name has hers on it, and she says it is the first piece of paper about her and fire that she has liked. The Commissioner asked whether she would do it again in thirty years. She said to write to her, in triplicate. The Wrong Dragon In the far south-east, in a cave in the rocks above the water, something very large breathes slowly, the way people breathe when they are reading. The map says it is a dragon. It is a dragon, it will tell you, in the sense that the map says so, and not in the sense anybody means. Its cave is dark and warm and full of books, in the order it read them, which is nobody else's, and it sits in an armchair at the back with a blanket over what may be its knees. People come about the dragon, and are relieved, and then a little disappointed, and then they stay for tea. Eight years before the Quest a young knight came, very correct, with a commission with dragon on it and a great deal of armour, and they talked about Horace until it got dark. It hoped he had found his dragon. He had not; his dragon was done in by somebody else, a year or two later, who drinks in the Slain Wyvern and is, I can confirm, insufferable about it. In the year 2000 Sir Aldric came back, and it emerged that Horace is a poet, Roman, the Odes, and that Sir Aldric had believed for four hours that they were talking about his horse, and that it had wondered why the Odes had so much in them about oats. It asked him to read to it. Its eyes are not what they were; that is why it talks so much. He lit a lamp, and read the Odes until dark, and they are not about oats. On the back of his commission, before he left, he wrote his first report in eight years: DRAGON: FOUND. NOT SLAIN. READ TO. P-G. He goes back. He usually cannot find the way, and it keeps the lamp lit, and when he can, he takes the book down off the shelf. Nobody describes the rest of the cave, which you see by lamplight, and I am not going to start. The Fair In the sand of the far south, a long way from anywhere, the way fairs always are, there is a big tent with a fair in it: swingboats, a coconut shy with no coconuts, and at the back a little striped booth, MOTHER SELVIDGE . NEVER WRONG. TWO CROWNS. She will tell you that you are going to go a long way and meet a great many people, and that at the end of it somebody is going to be very surprised to see you, and that you will eat a turnip, and that one is free. She has never once been wrong. Ask anybody she has read. She told Corvin Ash , at nineteen, that he was the rival of a great hero. In the year 2000, when he came back and asked her again, she told him: a long life, a useful trade, something with his hands, no destiny whatsoever. And then, when he asked again, she put the cards down and told him that she says the rival of a great hero to about four young men a year, lads at nineteen, sat in a heap, and that it is the reading that makes them stand up straight, and it has never once been wrong. They all went and did something. He said that he had sat in a corner for eleven years. She said, and then you got up. The Duck's Pond Four miles from the Collegium Arcanum there is a small pond with a duck on it, wearing round its neck, on a ribbon, the little silver medal the Collegium gives its Fellows. It is an Honorary Fellow. It sets off across the pond to get a better look at visitors, and walks into the bank, and then, with great dignity, into the bank again. If you bow, it inclines its head, as one Fellow to a member of the public. It was at the enquiry, in 1989, with Zephyrine Vance and the Dean and an unsanctioned quantity of fire, and in the year 2000 it was walked four miles to Congregation, because it was the quorum, and gave its proxy. It does not intend to be walked again. It is also one of the three reviewers of Miss Halloway's monograph, and read page four hundred, apparently, and sat down on it, which is acceptance, and it is the warmest review she has ever had. When it is away there is a stick at the edge of the pond with GONE TO CONGREGATION on it in pencil. Smaller sights The Standing Stones of Uncertain Purpose, beside the west road. Six theories are current: a calendar; a temple; a boundary; a tomb; an early form of the Prophecy ; and that they were put up by Wat Pardle of that parish to mark where his gate was, and that Wat Pardle is standing over there and will say so. Theory six is footnoted, Not favoured. The other five are more interesting and Mr Pardle has been asked to stop coming to the site. Beside the plaque is a second board, newer, smaller and screwed down much harder: THEORY SEVEN HAS BEEN REMOVED AT THE REQUEST OF THE PARISH AND THE FAMILY. I have nothing to add to the board. Ashcombe Lake, where on a still day you can hear the old church bell ringing under the water. You cannot. See Ashcombe . The Middle Distance, a hill with a bench on it, and * the Hermit *, who needed cheese. See the Barrow of the Forty-Fourth . Miss Halloway's type specimens, eleven of them, each where she found it, from the Common Hedge Egg near Thistlewick to the Pond Kappa by Ashcombe Lake. They are hers, and are in her Bestiary , and she would rather you did not touch them. See also Zephyrine Vance , for the Lay-By, the Fen and the duck Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III , for the Wrong Dragon Corvin Ash , for the Fair Hob Grumnir , for the Sky Anvil

title: Weeping Bottom
text: Weeping Bottom This article is about the valley and the Sisterhouse in it. For the Order, see The Order of Whatever Works . For the Sister who left it, and came back for an afternoon, see Merribell . For the vigil kept in its chapel, see Sir Aldric Pemberton-Gore III . Weeping Bottom Known as The Sisterhouse Where The bottom of a valley on the south coast, in a drizzle Founded 1702, by Mother Ursula Pym, for the air The air Comes in off the sea, settles, and stays. It is very loyal Orders Two, until 2000: Whatever Works (west), and What Ought To Work (east) Doctrine Four lines, one about socks Soup Leek. It's always leek. It works Symposia Ten held. The eleventh not Physic garden Ferns Knight in the field Sir Hamo Tench, in bed, on the line Weeping Bottom is a valley on the south coast with the Sisterhouse of the Order of Whatever Works in the bottom of it, founded in 1702 by Mother Ursula Pym for the sea air, which is the finest cure for the chest in the opinion of every physician consulted, none of whom had been. It is the mother house of the Order. It drizzles there. It has been drizzling since about 1702. The valley The founder's stone is beaded all over with damp, and the letters are cut deep, which is as well: THE SISTERHOUSE OF THE ORDER OF WHATEVER WORKS. FOUNDED 1702 BY MOTHER URSULA PYM, IN THIS VALLEY, FOR THE AIR. Under it, smaller: The sea air being the finest cure for the chest, in the opinion of every physician consulted. Under that, in a newer hand: None of whom had been. The air comes in off the sea, settles in the bottom of the valley, and stays. On the shore Sister Pim, in a white cap and apron, lines up three patients twice a day and has them breathe it, in through the nose; it is prescribed, Founder's orders, and nobody has ever countermanded them, because it seemed rude, with her on the stone. Mr Crouch finds it lovely and bracing, and coughs, bracingly. Mrs Liddy came for the damp on her chest, and it is doing wonderfully; she has never had so much of it. Mr Oakes was only visiting, because his brother came in with a cough, in the spring, and his brother has gone home now, and Mr Oakes has it instead. The Sisters planted a physic garden, with feverfew and sage and rosemary and comfrey. The valley grew ferns. Every plant in the garden is a fern, and they are doing splendidly. There are mushrooms on the path, the wall and a bench, and the Sisters stopped trying in about 1750; one of them has a very small bandage on it, because nobody goes untreated in Weeping Bottom. Through one window a Sister is hanging washing up indoors. It is the only way anything in Weeping Bottom ever gets dry, and it does not. In the chapel window Mother Ursula holds up a pair of socks like a holy relic. They are dry. They are the only dry thing in any window in the Order. The line The board at the gate reads WEEPING BOTTOM. THE SISTERHOUSE OF THE ORDER OF WHATEVER WORKS. VISITORS WELCOME. MIND THE STEP; IT IS WET. Painted in underneath, more recently and very neatly, in black: AND OF THE ORDER OF WHAT OUGHT TO WORK. (EAST DOOR.) There was one door. In the year 2000 the ward was split down the middle by a line. The west half was Whatever Works', under * Prioress Aveline Stope *, which had no doctrine; it had soup. The east half was What Ought To Work's, under * Sister Bewick *, in the same white habit with every trim dyed black, which had a doctrine, and had been examined on it, and had passed. Over the line hung a notice: PATIENTS WILL KINDLY REMAIN IN THE HALF OF THE WARD TO WHICH THEY WERE ADMITTED. They did not. They walked across in the night, because they said there was soup. Sister Bewick had lost eleven that month, to the other half of the ward. Sister Lamb ladled leek soup out of a pot the size of a bath on the west side. It is for everything: colds, falls, fevers. Mr Nuttall came in on the Tuesday with his arm, started on the east side, crossed on the Wednesday, and says it is much better on the west, where nobody asks you anything except whether you are warm. On the east side Mr Dace had a splinter, which Sister Bewick has in writing is how the ague starts, and was on the correct treatment, day four, and was looking wistfully across the line at the soup. Sister Bewick's Correct Treatment of the Weeping Bottom Ague is in eleven stages, each with its authority, and stage eleven reads The patient will now feel better, underlined twice. Her notes are in eleven volumes, one for each stage, and volume eleven is very thin. Toast was permitted at stage nine. The Prioress held symposia. An order that holds one symposium is thinking, she says; an order that holds eleven has stopped. She said it the way a physician names a symptom she has seen before, in other people. The minutes of ten are on the table by the line, and every one ends the same way: Resolved, that the matter be referred to the next symposium. The eleventh, Whether Anything Works, was set for three o'clock, in the chapel, with the Prioress in the chair. The chairs are still in the chapel in two rows, facing one another, like a wedding where the families have not been introduced. The queue The eleventh symposium was not held. Merribell, who had left the Sisterhouse at twenty-two because it had begun holding symposia, came back for an afternoon in the year 2000, and there was a queue at the gate, forty and more coming up the track, numbered, in the wet. Thirty-five, chest, it's the air. Thirty-six, not ill, Mum said to queue. Thirty-seven, knee, it's kept since Michaelmas. Thirty-eight, hoping for soup. Thirty-nine, doesn't know what it is, that's why there's a queue. Forty, last; somebody's always last; wet, an' all. Merribell's proposal, which the Prioress laughed at, once, and which Sister Bewick wanted in writing immediately, and had, in eleven clauses, was: don't hold the symposium; open the door; twenty patients to each half, and whoever is through first is right. * Sir Hamo Tench * kept the score from the bed on the line, which both orders treat, and is very fair. Whatever Works was through its twenty while What Ought To Work was on patient one, stage eleven. Patient one was a fisherman, Mr Grebe, who had the Weeping Bottom ague, properly, the first case anybody had seen in nine years, and at stage eleven he sat up and felt better. Sister Bewick said, It worked. Merribell said of course it worked, he had it, and that was a point to the east, fair's fair. Nineteen to one, on points. Sir Hamo said it was very fair. Sister Bewick asked to be examined on the Order's doctrine, since that is how a doctrine is settled. The Prioress took Mother Ursula's own pamphlet out of a drawer, where it had been since the first symposium: four pages, stitched, damp at the corners, with the Rule of Life on the first page. Sister Bewick read it twice, and was examined on it, and passed. She said that it was very short, and she could find nothing wrong with it, and that that was very annoying. There was soup on both sides of the line at three. She had some. She wrote in her notebook: Intervention. Supported. The eleventh minute reads, in the Prioress's hand: Not held. A queue instead. Whatever Works, on points. Soup. Sir Hamo Sir Hamo Tench, of the Order of the Errant , in the field, stands at the foot of the bed that is exactly on the line, in a nightshirt with a knight's surcoat over it. He came for the sea air sixteen years ago with a cough. Both lots treat him: soup at noon, correct treatment at four. The cough is exactly the same. Very fair. He writes to Coldbarrow every quarter, IN THE FIELD, and it is true, too; they have a pin in him. The Order's chapel for the west is across the yard. The Sisters lend it. For thirty years a shield hung over its door, inside, that nobody came for: a knight in a field, looking back over his shoulder, which the Sisters had always taken for a pun about vigilance. It was Sir Aldric's. He had been due to keep his vigil under it at sixteen, and kept it in the wrong chapel instead, eleven times, two of them Coldbarrow's Chapter House, which says CHAPTER HOUSE on the door and which he thought was being modest, and one of them a barn with a weathercock. In the year 2000 he kept it in the right one, dusk to dawn, with Sir Hamo standing sponsor and his friends keeping the watch, and something came in under the door at midnight. His article tells the rest. The shield is not over the door now. There is a paler patch on the wall, the shape of a shield. I asked Merribell whether she would go back to Weeping Bottom. She said that she had been back twice since, to see the Prioress, and that they talk, now, and that the Sisterhouse holds no symposia, and that the patients sit down. Then she told me to drink a glass of water, and I did, and she watched me do it.
